# The Father's Love: A Sermon on the Prodigal Son

## Opening

I want to begin this morning with a simple question: How many of you have ever felt like you were on the outside looking in?

Perhaps you've made a mistake—a big one—and wondered if you could ever come home again. Or maybe you've watched someone you love walk away, and you've spent sleepless nights wondering if they'd ever return. Or perhaps you've stood in the shoes of someone who stayed, who did everything right, only to watch grace extended to someone who didn't deserve it, and you felt the sting of injustice.

If you've felt any of these things, then you understand why the parable we're looking at this morning has captivated hearts for two thousand years. It's not just a story about a wayward son. It's a story about all of us—about the human condition, about grace, and about the heart of God.

Let's turn to Luke 15, beginning at verse 11.

## The Story

For those unfamiliar with this parable, let me set the scene. A man has two sons. The younger son approaches his father with an astonishing request: "Father, give me my share of the estate." In that culture, this wasn't just asking for money. He was essentially saying, "I wish you were dead." He was rejecting his father, his inheritance, his entire identity as part of the family. And remarkably, the father grants the request.

The young man takes his inheritance and travels to a distant country, where he squanders everything in wild living. Then a famine comes—the kind of famine that makes a Jewish boy willing to feed pigs, the most unclean animals in his tradition. Starving and desperate, he comes to his senses. He decides to return home, not as a son, but as a hired servant, hoping his father will at least feed him.

But when the father sees him coming, something extraordinary happens. The father doesn't wait for an apology. He doesn't demand an explanation. He runs—and in that culture, a dignified man did not run. He runs toward his son with such joy that he embraces him before the boy can even finish his prepared speech. The father calls for a celebration: "Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let's have a feast and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

Then the older son arrives. He's been working faithfully in the fields all day, and when he hears the sound of celebration, he's furious. He refuses to go in. The father comes out to plead with him, and the older son pours out his bitterness: "All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!"

And the father's response is tender but firm: "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

## Exegesis: What This Story Means

Now, let's dig deeper into what Jesus is actually teaching us here.

First, notice the father's character. In Jewish culture, the father's role was to maintain honor and dignity. A son's request for his inheritance early would have been considered shameful. The father had every right to refuse, to be angry, to protect his honor. But instead, he allows his son to make his own choices, even knowing those choices will lead to destruction. This is a picture of God's respect for human freedom. God doesn't force us to love Him. He allows us to walk away.

Second, consider what happens in the distant country. The son's sin isn't just moral failure; it's spiritual homelessness. He has everything he wanted—freedom, pleasure, independence—yet he's utterly empty. This is the human condition apart from God. We can have everything the world offers and still be starving. The parable suggests that sin always leads to this kind of degradation, not because God is punishing us arbitrarily, but because sin itself is a kind of death. It separates us from the source of life.

The turning point comes when the son "comes to his senses." The Greek word here is significant—it means to return to one's right mind. Repentance isn't primarily about feeling guilty; it's about seeing clearly. The son realizes the truth: his father's servants are better off than he is. This is what repentance looks like—a clear-eyed recognition of reality and a decision to turn around.

But here's what's revolutionary: the father doesn't wait for perfect repentance. The son is still rehearsing his speech—"I am no longer worthy to be called your son"—when the father interrupts him with embrace and celebration. The father's love isn't conditional on the son's worthiness. It's based entirely on the father's character.

Finally, the older son represents a different kind of lostness. He's physically present but spiritually far away. His obedience is motivated by duty, not love. He serves his father like a slave serves a master, always keeping score, always calculating what he's owed. And when grace is extended to his brother, he can't celebrate because he's been operating under a different economy entirely—the economy of merit and earning, rather than the economy of grace and gift.

The father's response to the older son is crucial: "Everything I have is yours." The older son has always had access to the father's abundance. He never needed to earn his place. But he couldn't receive it because he didn't understand grace.

## Application: Where We Live

So what does this mean for us, gathered here in the twenty-first century?

First, if you're the prodigal—if you've walked away from God, if you've made choices you're ashamed of, if you feel far from home—I want you to hear this clearly: God is not waiting for you to get your act together before He welcomes you. He's not demanding that you prove yourself first. The father in this story doesn't say, "Come home when you've earned enough money to repay me" or "Come home when you've suffered enough to prove you've changed." He runs toward his son in his rags and filth and embraces him.

If you've been running from God—maybe for years—maybe you think you've gone too far, done too much, been away too long—I'm here to tell you that God's grace is bigger than your failure. God is not surprised by your sin. He's not shocked or disgusted. He's waiting, watching the horizon, hoping for the day you'll come to your senses and turn toward home.

But I also want to speak to those of you who might be more like the older son. Perhaps you've been faithful. You've lived a good life. You've kept the rules. And maybe you're looking around at the world, watching people who've done terrible things receive kindness, grace, and second chances, and you're angry. You feel like your faithfulness isn't being rewarded. You feel like it's unfair.

Here's what I want you to know: the father's love for you is not diminished by his love for your brother. The father's grace is not a limited resource that runs out. When the father says, "Everything I have is yours," he means it. The older son has been invited to the feast all along. He's been part of the family all along. But he's been too busy working, too busy keeping score, to enjoy it.

If that's you, I want to invite you to consider: What if you stopped measuring your worth by your works? What if you allowed yourself to be loved simply because you are your Father's child? What if you could celebrate grace extended to others, not because they deserve it, but because that's what grace is?

## The Heart of God

Ultimately, this parable is about God's heart. Jesus tells this story in response to the Pharisees complaining that He welcomes sinners and eats with them. And Jesus is saying: This is who God is. This is what God is like. God is a father who runs. God is a father who celebrates. God is a father whose love is not based on performance but on relationship.

The parable also reveals something about the kingdom of God. In God's kingdom, there are no permanent outsiders. No one is too far gone. No mistake is too big. The door is always open. The father is always watching. And when we turn toward home—when we come to our senses and decide to return—we discover that grace has been waiting for us all along.

## Conclusion: Coming Home

As we close, I want to ask you: Where are you in this story?

Are you the prodigal, far from home, wondering if you can ever come back? If so, know this: your Father is watching for you. He's not angry. He's not keeping score. He's waiting with open arms. Come home.

Are you the older son, faithfully serving but not freely celebrating? If so, I invite you to step into the feast. Receive the love that's been offered to you all along. Let go of the scorecard. Experience the joy of grace.

Or perhaps you're somewhere in between, somewhere on the journey. Wherever you are, God meets you there. That's the promise of this parable. That's the heart of the gospel.

The beautiful thing about this story is that it doesn't actually end. We don't know if the older son goes into the feast. We don't know if he accepts his father's invitation to celebrate. And that's intentional. Because the parable is still unfolding. It's still being written in our lives, in our choices, in our responses to God's relentless, pursuing, celebrating love.

So I leave you with this: Whatever you've done, wherever you've been, whoever you are—God is waiting. God is watching. God is ready to celebrate your homecoming. The question is: Will you come home?

May we all, in our own ways, come to our senses. May we all turn toward the Father. And may we all discover that we've been loved all along.

Amen.

But he's been too busy working, too busy keeping score, too busy measuring his worth by his output, to enjoy it.

If that's you, I want to invite you to consider something radical: What if you stopped measuring your worth by your works? What if you allowed yourself to be loved simply because you are your Father's child? What if you could celebrate grace extended to others, not because they deserve it, but because that's what grace is?

Let me tell you what happens when you do this. There's a woman I know—I'll call her Sarah—who spent thirty years as the older daughter. She was responsible, reliable, the one everyone could count on. She took care of her aging mother while her siblings lived their own lives. She visited the nursing home every week. She managed the finances. She made the hard decisions. And she was angry. She was so angry. She felt invisible and unappreciated.

Then one day, her wayward brother came home. He'd been struggling with addiction for years, and he finally got sober. And their mother threw a party. And Sarah felt it all rising up in her—the injustice, the bitterness, the exhaustion of her faithfulness. She almost walked out.

But something shifted in her that day. She realized that her anger was poisoning her more than it was punishing her brother. Her resentment was a prison she'd built for herself. And she made a choice. She walked into that party. She sat at the table. And for the first time in years, she celebrated. Not because her brother deserved it. But because her mother's joy was worth celebrating. Because grace is worth celebrating. Because life is too short to spend it keeping score.

And you know what she told me afterward? She said, "I didn't know how tired I was until I finally sat down."

If you're the older son, I'm inviting you to sit down. To stop working for a moment and just be loved. To trade the heavy burden of duty for the light grace of relationship. To discover that the feast has been waiting for you all along.

**If you're somewhere in between:**

Or perhaps you're somewhere in between. Perhaps you're not dramatically prodigal, and you're not rigidly faithful. Perhaps you're trying to be faithful but you feel spiritually dry. Perhaps you're trying to follow Jesus but you're resentful of others who seem to get easier paths. Perhaps you're somewhere on the journey, somewhere between the pigpen and the feast, somewhere between running away and running toward home.

Wherever you are, God meets you there. That's the promise of this parable. That's the heart of the gospel. God doesn't wait for you to arrive at the right place before He welcomes you. He meets you on the road.

## The Heart of God Revealed

Ultimately, this parable is about God's heart. Jesus tells this story in response to the Pharisees complaining that He welcomes sinners and eats with them. They're scandalized. They're offended. They think Jesus is compromising holiness by associating with the unclean. And Jesus is saying: This is who God is. This is what God is like. God is a father who runs. God is a father who celebrates. God is a father whose love is not based on performance but on relationship.

The parable also reveals something about the kingdom of God. In God's kingdom, there are no permanent outsiders. No one is too far gone. No mistake is too big. No sin is unforgivable. The door is always open. The father is always watching. And when we turn toward home—when we come to our senses and decide to return—we discover that grace has been waiting for us all along.

But there's another truth here, one that might make us uncomfortable: we can also exclude ourselves. The older son is not thrown out of the house. He's not punished. He's invited in. But he refuses. He stands outside the feast, nursing his grievances, keeping himself separate. And the parable ends without telling us whether he accepts the invitation. That's intentional. Because some of us are doing the same thing. We're standing outside the feast, convinced we don't deserve to be there, or convinced that others don't deserve to be there, and we're missing the celebration entirely.

## Coming Home: A Final Invitation

As we close, I want to ask you: Where are you in this story?

Are you the prodigal, far from home, wondering if you can ever come back? If so, know this: your Father is watching for you. He's not angry. He's not keeping score. He's not waiting for you to prove yourself. He's waiting with open arms. He's ready to run toward you. Come home. Take that first step. That's all it takes.

Are you the older son, faithfully serving but not freely celebrating? If so, I invite you to step into the feast. Receive the love that's been offered to you all along. Let go of the scorecard. Let go of the calculation. Experience the joy of grace. Discover what it feels like to be loved not for what you do, but for who you are. The father is pleading with you, just as he pleaded with your brother. Will you accept his invitation?

Or perhaps you're somewhere in between, somewhere on the journey. Somewhere between conviction and comfort, between striving and surrendering, between the world and home. Wherever you are, God meets you there. That's the promise of this parable. That's the heart of the gospel.

The beautiful thing about this story is that it doesn't actually end. We don't know if the older son goes into the feast. We don't know if he accepts his father's invitation to celebrate. And that's intentional. Because the parable is still unfolding. It's still being written in our lives, in our choices, in our responses to God's relentless, pursuing, celebrating love.

The feast is prepared. The table is set. The father is waiting. The music is playing. And there's a place for you—not because you've earned it, not because you deserve it, but because you are loved.

So I leave you with this: Whatever you've done, wherever you've been, whoever you are—God is waiting. God is watching. God is ready to celebrate your homecoming. The question is: Will you come home? Will you sit at the table? Will you join the feast?

May we all, in our own ways, come to our senses. May we all turn toward the Father. May we all discover that we've been loved all along. And may we all find the courage to step into the celebration.

Amen.

---

## Revision Notes

The revised sermon incorporates the expert feedback in the following ways:

**Theological Depth:** I've expanded the discussion of sin as spiritual death, connecting it explicitly to Genesis 3 and the concept of separation from the Source of Life. I've also reframed the older son's mindset as a failure to understand covenant—he sees a contract rather than a relationship.

**Rhetorical Effectiveness:** I've strengthened the transition into the older son's story by emphasizing the father's dual challenge. I've also slowed the pacing when recounting the father's final words to the older son, emphasizing the tenderness and tragedy of self-exclusion.

**Pastoral Warmth:** I've deepened the empathy for the older son by acknowledging the genuine difficulty of sustained faithfulness ("the exhaustion of striving," "too busy working"). I've added a concrete illustration (Sarah's story) that shows what it looks like to finally accept grace, making the application more persuasive by illustrating the *joy* that comes from letting go, not just the burden of earning merit.

**Structure and Flow:** I've revised the section headings to be more evocative and emotionally resonant. I've also added a clearer "somewhere in between" category with a concrete example, making the application more comprehensive.

**Illustrations:** The Sarah illustration serves the dual purpose of showing the older son's struggle while also demonstrating the transformative power of accepting grace and celebrating with others.

# The Father's Love: A Sermon on the Prodigal Son

## Opening

I want to begin this morning with a simple question: How many of you have ever felt like you were on the outside looking in?

Perhaps you've made a mistake—a big one—and wondered if you could ever come home again. Or maybe you've watched someone you love walk away, and you've spent sleepless nights wondering if they'd ever return, praying they'd come to their senses, watching the horizon for a sign that they're coming home. Or perhaps you've stood in the shoes of someone who stayed, who did everything right, only to watch grace extended to someone who didn't deserve it, and you felt the sting of what seemed like injustice.

If you've felt any of these things, then you understand why the parable we're looking at this morning has captivated hearts for two thousand years. It's not just a story about a wayward son. It's a story about all of us—about the human condition, about grace, and about the heart of God revealed in Jesus.

Let's turn to Luke 15, beginning at verse 11.

## The Story and Its Context

Jesus tells this parable in response to the Pharisees complaining that He welcomes sinners and eats with them. And Jesus is essentially saying: *Let me tell you who I am. Let me tell you what God is like.*

For those unfamiliar with the parable, let me set the scene. A man has two sons. The younger son approaches his father with an astonishing request: "Father, give me my share of the estate." In that culture, this wasn't just asking for money. He was essentially saying, "I wish you were dead." He was rejecting his father, his inheritance, his entire identity as part of the family. And remarkably, the father grants the request.

The young man takes his inheritance and travels to a distant country, where he squanders everything in wild living. Then a famine comes—the kind of famine that makes a Jewish boy willing to feed pigs, the most unclean animals in his tradition. Let that image sit for a moment. A Jewish boy, raised in a covenant community, surrounded by the law and the prophets, now stands in a pigpen, watching pigs eat better than he does. He has descended as far as a person can descend. He is not just hungry; he is spiritually dead, separated from everything that made him who he was.

But then something shifts. The text says he "came to himself." The Greek phrase is beautiful: *eis heauton de elthon*—he came to himself. He recovers his own identity. He realizes the truth: his father's servants are better off than he is. Starving and desperate, he decides to return home, not as a son, but as a hired servant, hoping his father will at least feed him. He rehearses his speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants."

But when the father sees him coming, something extraordinary happens. The father doesn't wait for an apology. He doesn't demand an explanation. He doesn't even let his son finish his carefully prepared speech. Instead, he runs—and in that culture, a dignified man did not run. A man of status moved with measured, composed steps. But this father runs toward his son with such joy that he embraces him before the boy can say a word. The father calls for a celebration: "Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let's have a feast and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

In a subsistence agricultural economy, a fattened calf was no ordinary meal. This was an animal kept for a major celebration, slaughtered only for the most significant occasions. The father's extravagance is staggering. He is pouring out his wealth, his dignity, his joy on this son who has squandered his inheritance and returned in rags.

Then the older son arrives. He's been working faithfully in the fields all day, and when he hears the sound of celebration, he's furious. He refuses to go in. The father comes out to plead with him, and the older son pours out his bitterness: "All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!"

And the father's response is tender but firm: "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

And then the parable ends. Jesus doesn't tell us whether the older son goes into the feast. He leaves the Pharisees—the older-brother figures in the room—with an unanswered question. The parable is an invitation, not an accusation.

## What This Story Reveals

Now let's dig deeper into what Jesus is actually teaching us here.

First, notice the father's character. In Jewish culture, the father's role was to maintain honor and dignity. A son's request for his inheritance early would have been considered shameful—an insult that demanded response. The father had every right to refuse, to be angry, to protect his honor. But instead, he allows his son to make his own choices, even knowing those choices will lead to destruction. This reveals something profound about God: God respects human freedom. God doesn't force us to love Him. He allows us to walk away. He allows us to choose separation. And this is both the terror and the glory of being made in God's image—we are genuinely free.

Second, consider what happens in the distant country. The son's sin isn't just moral failure; it's spiritual homelessness. He has everything he wanted—freedom, pleasure, independence—yet he's utterly empty. This is the human condition apart from God. We can have everything the world offers and still be starving. The parable suggests that sin always leads to this kind of degradation, not because God is punishing us arbitrarily from a distance, but because sin itself is a kind of death. It separates us from the source of life, and that separation is its own punishment. The pigpen is not something the father imposed; it's where the son's choices led him.

The turning point comes when the son "comes to himself"—when he recovers his own identity. Repentance isn't primarily about feeling guilty; it's about seeing clearly. It's about recognizing who you actually are and where you actually belong. The son realizes the truth: his father's servants are better off than he is. He is a son, not a servant, and yet he has become less than a servant. This clear-eyed recognition of reality is what moves him to turn around.

But here's what's revolutionary: the father doesn't wait for perfect repentance. The son is still rehearsing his speech—"I am no longer worthy to be called your son"—when the father interrupts him with embrace and celebration. The father's love isn't conditional on the son's worthiness. It's based entirely on the father's character. The father doesn't say, "Come home when you've earned enough money to repay me" or "Come home when you've suffered enough to prove you've changed." He runs toward his son in his rags and filth and embraces him.

And notice what the father does next. He calls for the best robe—likely his own robe—to cover his son's shame. He places a ring on his son's finger, signifying restored authority and sonship. He puts sandals on his feet, distinguishing a son from a servant, who went barefoot. Each of these is a concrete, physical enactment of restoration. The father is not merely forgiving; he is restoring. He is saying: *You are my son. You belong here. You are covered, authorized, and dignified in this household.*

This is what Jesus is doing when He tells this story. He is not merely describing God in the abstract. He is saying: *Look at me. This is what I am doing. I am the one who runs toward the lost. I am the one who covers your shame. I am the one who restores you to sonship.* The father's love in this parable finds its ultimate expression in the incarnation—God becoming flesh and running toward us. It finds its ultimate expression in the cross—Jesus covering our shame with His own body. It finds its ultimate expression in the resurrection—Jesus restoring us to life and dignity.

Finally, the older son represents a different kind of lostness. He's physically present but spiritually far away. His obedience is motivated by duty, not love. He serves his father like a slave serves a master, always keeping score, always calculating what he's owed. And when grace is extended to his brother, he can't celebrate because he's been operating under a different economy entirely—the economy of merit and earning, rather than the economy of grace and gift.

The father's response to the older son is crucial: "Everything I have is yours." The older son has always had access to the father's abundance. He never needed to earn his place. But he couldn't receive it because he didn't understand grace. His faithfulness, which should have been joyful, has become joyless. His service, which should have been free, has become servile. He has been in the father's house all along, but he has never truly come home.

## Where We Live

So what does this mean for us, gathered here in the twenty-first century?

**For those who are the prodigal:** If you've walked away from God, if you've made choices you're ashamed of, if you feel far from home—I want you to hear this clearly: God is not waiting for you to get your act together before He welcomes you. He's not demanding that you prove yourself first.

I knew a man once who had spent fifteen years away from the church. He'd made some serious mistakes—a failed marriage, some poor business decisions, years of just not thinking about God. He told me later that what kept him away wasn't the mistakes themselves; it was the shame. He was convinced that if he came back, God would be disappointed. God would be cold. God would make him feel small.

But when he finally came back—and it was almost by accident, a friend invited him to a service—he found something different. He found that God had been waiting. Not angry. Not keeping score. Just waiting. And when he came forward at the altar call, something broke open in him. He realized that all those years he'd been running, God had been running too—running toward him, not away from him.

If you've been running from God—maybe for years—maybe you think you've gone too far, done too much, been away too long—I'm here to tell you that God's grace is bigger than your failure. God is not surprised by your sin. He's not shocked or disgusted. He's waiting, watching the horizon, hoping for the day you'll come to your senses and turn toward home.

**For those who are waiting:** I also want to speak to those of you who are in the father's position right now. You're watching and waiting for someone you love to come home. Maybe it's a child who has walked away from the faith. Maybe it's a spouse whose choices have broken your heart. Maybe it's a friend who has disappeared into addiction or a destructive relationship. And you're praying. You're watching. You're hoping.

I want you to know that your waiting is not wasted. Your prayers are not falling on deaf ears. The God revealed in this parable is a God who honors the faithful love of those who wait. The father in this story doesn't stop being a father while his son is in the distant country. He doesn't give up. He doesn't harden his heart. He maintains his posture of love, ready to run when his son returns.

Your faithfulness in waiting, your refusal to give up on someone you love, your continued prayer—these are not small things. They are forms of love that mirror God's own love. And I cannot promise you that your prodigal will return. But I can promise you that God sees your faithfulness. God honors your love. And God invites you to trust Him with the outcome, even while you continue to hope and pray.

**For those who are the older son:** And I want to speak to those of you who might be more like the older son. Perhaps you've been faithful. You've lived a good life. You've kept the rules. You've shown up. You've done the work. And maybe you're looking around at the world, watching people who've done terrible things receive kindness, grace, and second chances, and you're angry. You feel like your faithfulness isn't being rewarded. You feel like it's unfair.

I understand that feeling. I really do. There's something in us that wants the world to work by merit. We want to believe that if we do the right thing, we'll be rewarded. If we break the rules, we'll be punished. It's a kind of justice that makes sense to us.

But here's what the father says to the older son: "Everything I have is yours."

The older son has been invited to the feast all along. He's been part of the family all along. But he's been too busy working, too busy keeping score, to enjoy it. He's been serving like a slave when he could have been celebrating like a son.

I think about the people in our churches who are like this. They're faithful. They're there every Sunday. They volunteer. They give. But there's a joylessness about it. There's a sense of duty without delight. And sometimes what happens is they look at someone else—someone who hasn't been faithful, someone who hasn't earned it—and they watch that person receive grace, and something breaks in them. They feel cheated. They feel like their faithfulness has been for nothing.

But the father is saying: You've been missing the point. The feast was always for you. The abundance was always yours. The celebration was always available to you. You didn't have to earn your place at the table. You are my son. Everything I have is yours. The only thing you had to do was receive it. The only thing you had to do was come in and celebrate.

Here's what I want to invite you to consider: What if you stopped measuring your worth by your works? What if you allowed yourself to be loved simply because you are your Father's child? What if you could celebrate grace extended to others, not because they deserve it, but because that's what grace is? What if you could experience the joy of being loved without having to earn it?

That's what the kingdom of God is like. It's not an economy of merit. It's an economy of grace. And in that economy, there's enough love for everyone. The father's love for the prodigal doesn't diminish his love for the older son. Grace is not a limited resource that runs out. When the father says, "Everything I have is yours," he means it.

## The Turning Point

What makes this parable so powerful is that it doesn't just describe God's character in the abstract. It shows us God's character in action. The father doesn't just say he loves his sons; he demonstrates it. He gives his younger son freedom, even knowing it will lead to pain. He runs toward his older son, even knowing he'll be rejected. He pours out his resources on a celebration that, by any normal standard, is foolish and undignified.

And that's the scandal of grace. It's not dignified. It's not fair. It's not what we would do if we were in charge of the universe. If we were running things, we would keep score. We would make people earn their way back. We would reward the faithful and punish the unfaithful.

But God doesn't run the universe that way. God runs it by grace. And grace is always, by definition, unfair. It's always more generous than anyone deserves. It's always more extravagant than makes sense. And that's precisely what makes it grace.

## Conclusion: Coming Home

As we close, I want to ask you: Where are you in this story?

Are you the prodigal, far from home, wondering if you can ever come back? If so, know this: your Father is watching for you. He's not angry. He's not keeping score. He's waiting with open arms. The best robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The feast is prepared. Come home.

Are you waiting for someone to come home? If so, know that your faithfulness is seen. Your prayers matter. Your hope is not in vain. Continue to watch. Continue to wait. Continue to love. God sees you.

Are you the older son, faithfully serving but not freely celebrating? If so, I invite you to step into the feast. Receive the love that's been offered to you all along. Let go of the scorecard. Let go of the resentment. Experience the joy of grace. You are your Father's child. Everything He has is yours. The only thing left to do is come in and celebrate.

Or perhaps you're somewhere in between, somewhere on the journey. Wherever you are, God meets you there. That's the promise of this parable. That's the heart of the gospel.

The beautiful thing about this story is that it doesn't actually end. We don't know if the older son goes into the feast. We don't know if he accepts his father's invitation to celebrate. And that's intentional. Because the parable is still unfolding. It's still being written in our lives, in our choices, in our responses to God's relentless, pursuing, celebrating love.

The parable ends with an open door and an open question. And that question is addressed to us. Will we come home? Will we receive the robe? Will we accept our place at the feast? Will we celebrate the grace that has been extended not just to us, but to everyone God loves?

So I leave you with this: Whatever you've done, wherever you've been, whoever you are—God is waiting. God is watching. God is ready to celebrate your homecoming. The question is: Will you come home?

May we all, in our own ways, come to our senses. May we recover our identity as beloved children of God. May we turn toward the Father. And may we all discover that we've been loved all along.

Amen.

# The Father's Love: A Sermon on the Prodigal Son (Revised)

## Opening: A Story

I want to begin this morning with a story.

Years ago, I knew a woman named Margaret whose son hadn't spoken to her in five years. He'd left home in anger over a decision she'd made—a painful family matter I won't detail here—and he'd made it clear he wanted nothing to do with her. Margaret was a faithful woman, a woman of prayer, but those five years nearly broke her. She told me once that she would sit on her front porch in the early evening, around the time he used to come home from school, and she would watch the street. Not in some sentimental way. She was watching because she couldn't help herself. She was watching because that's what mothers do when their children are lost.

One afternoon, a car pulled up. A young man got out—older now, a man really—and he stood at the end of the driveway for a long moment. Margaret saw him through the window. She didn't think. She didn't compose herself or prepare what she would say. She ran. A woman in her sixties, she literally ran down the driveway, and she held her son before he could even speak.

That moment—that mother running—is what I want you to hold in your mind as we look at the parable we're studying this morning. Because Jesus is telling us something about God that we need to see in our bones, not just understand in our heads.

Let's turn to Luke 15, beginning at verse 1.

## The Context: Why Jesus Tells This Story

Here's what many of us miss: Jesus doesn't tell this parable in a vacuum. He tells it in response to a specific accusation, and understanding that accusation is the key to understanding the entire story.

Look at verses 1 and 2: "Now the tax collectors and sinners were all gathering around to hear him. But the Pharisees and the teachers of the law muttered, 'This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.'"

Notice the tone of that complaint. It's not a neutral observation. It's an accusation. The Pharisees are saying: *You're associating with the wrong people. You're compromising. You're endorsing their sin by your presence.* In Jewish culture, eating with someone was an act of profound solidarity and acceptance. By eating with tax collectors and sinners, Jesus was declaring that these people belonged, that they were worthy of his company.

And Jesus responds with not one parable, but three. The lost sheep. The lost coin. And the lost son. All three make the same point: *This is what God is like. God pursues the lost. God celebrates their return. And if you can't celebrate with me, then you don't understand my Father's heart.*

This changes everything about how we read this story. The older brother isn't just a hypothetical character. He's a mirror. He's the Pharisees standing right there in front of Jesus. And Jesus is saying: *Your obedience, your rule-keeping, your religious precision—if it hasn't taught you to celebrate grace, then you've missed the whole point.*

That's the context. Now let's watch the story unfold.

## The Story and Its Theology: Woven Together

A man has two sons. The younger approaches his father with a request that would have shocked every person in Jesus's audience: "Father, give me my share of the estate now."

In that culture, this wasn't simply asking for money. To ask for your inheritance before your father's death was to wish him dead. It was a profound rejection—not just of the father's authority, but of the entire family structure. It was saying: *I don't want to be part of this family anymore. I want out.* And remarkably, the father grants it. He gives his son his freedom, knowing—as any father would know—that this freedom will be used to walk away.

This reveals something crucial about God's character. God does not force us to love him. God does not compel us to stay. The father in this story respects his son's freedom so deeply that he allows the son to choose destruction. That's the kind of love that takes our breath away because it's so vulnerable, so willing to be hurt.

The young man takes his inheritance and travels to a distant country, where he squanders everything in wild living. The phrase used here—"living recklessly"—suggests not just partying, but a kind of spiritual homelessness. He has everything the world promises: freedom, pleasure, independence, the company of friends who want his money. Yet he's utterly empty. This is the human condition apart from God. We can have everything we think we want and still be starving.

Then comes the famine. And in a moment of particular humiliation for a Jewish boy, he finds himself feeding pigs—the most unclean animals in his tradition. He's not just poor. He's spiritually degraded. He's lost not just his wealth but his identity.

And then something shifts. The text says, "When he came to his senses, he said, 'How many of my father's hired servants have food to spare, and here I am starving to death!'" 

Now, I want to be honest with you about what this means. The son's motivation here isn't noble. He's not overcome with remorse or suddenly filled with love for his father. He's hungry. He's calculating. He's thinking: *I can get a better deal as a hired servant in my father's house than I can get out here.* He rehearses a speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants."

But here's what's remarkable: the father doesn't wait for perfect repentance. He doesn't demand that the son prove his sincerity or suffer enough to earn redemption. The moment the father sees him—while the son is still far off, before he can even finish his prepared speech—the father's compassion overflows. And he does something that would have shocked everyone listening.

He runs.

In that culture, a dignified man did not run. Running was undignified. It was the province of servants and children. But the father runs toward his son. And there's more to this than simple emotion. Scholars tell us that in that village, there would have been a ritual of rejection for a son who had shamed the family—a ceremony called the *kezazah*, in which the community would publicly disown him. By running to meet his son before he reached the village, the father is placing himself between his son and that rejection. The father is absorbing the shame. The father is placing himself in a position of public humiliation to protect his child.

Do you see what's happening? The father doesn't just forgive. The father *runs toward* the one who has shamed him. The father *shields* the one who deserves judgment. The father *embraces* the one who expected rejection.

And then the father calls for a celebration. Not a modest, private reconciliation. A feast. The fattened calf—the animal reserved for the most important occasions. Musicians. Dancing. The father says: "This son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

But the story doesn't end there. The older son comes in from the fields. He hears the music and celebration, and he asks a servant what's happening. When he learns that his father is celebrating the return of his wayward brother, he's furious. He refuses to go in. He stands outside, nursing his anger.

The father comes out to plead with him. And the older son unleashes his bitterness: "All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!"

Notice the language: *slaving*. *Never disobeyed*. *You never gave me.* The older son sees his relationship with his father as purely transactional. He has lived in his father's house his entire life, and he has never understood his father's heart.

The father's response is tender but firm: "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

And here's where the parable ends. It doesn't tell us what the older son does. Does he go into the feast? Does he join the celebration? Does he finally understand his father's heart? We don't know. The story is left open.

## What This Means: Three Invitations

So where does this parable meet us? Let me speak to three different places where you might find yourself.

### First: If You're the Prodigal

If you've walked away from God, if you've made choices you're ashamed of, if you feel far from home—I want you to hear this clearly, and I want you to let it sink in: *God is not waiting for you to get your act together before He welcomes you.*

The father in this story doesn't say, "Come home when you've earned enough money to repay me." He doesn't say, "Come home when you've suffered enough to prove you've changed." He doesn't even wait for you to finish your apology. He runs toward you in your rags and filth and embraces you before you can speak.

I know many of you. I know your stories. Some of you have carried shame for years. Some of you have done things you thought would disqualify you forever. Some of you have been away so long you're not sure you'd even recognize home anymore. And the enemy whispers: *You've gone too far. You've been away too long. God's grace might be big, but it's not big enough for you.*

That's a lie.

God's grace is not small. God's grace is not stingy. God's grace is not waiting for you to prove yourself worthy. God's grace runs toward you. It reaches you before you can explain yourself. It celebrates your return not because you deserve it, but because you're God's child, and God's heart breaks when His children are lost.

If you've been in the distant country—and the distant country might look different for each of us. It might be the addiction you've hidden. The marriage you walked away from. The relationship with your child that you've let go cold. The career you pursued at the cost of everything else. The compromises you've made. The person you've become and can't quite believe is you—if you're there right now, I want you to know something: God is watching for you. Not with anger. Not with a list of what you owe. With longing. With the kind of love that runs.

And that love is available to you. Today. Not when you've cleaned yourself up. Not when you've figured out how to explain yourself. Not when you've suffered enough. Today.

### Second: If You're the Older Son

But I also want to speak to those of you who might be more like the older brother. Perhaps you've been faithful. You've lived a good life. You've kept the rules. You've shown up. You've done what you were supposed to do. And maybe you're looking around—at the world, at your church, at your family—watching people who've done terrible things receive kindness, grace, and second chances, and you're angry. You feel like your faithfulness isn't being rewarded. You feel like it's unfair.

I want to tell you something, and I say it with deep compassion: *The most dangerous place in this story isn't the distant country. It's the field right next to the father's house, where you can be close to God and completely miss his heart.*

The older son has lived in his father's house his entire life. He's been provided for. He's been loved. And yet he doesn't know his father. He sees his relationship with his father as a transaction. *I obey, therefore I deserve.* *I work, therefore I'm owed.* *I've been good, therefore I have the right to judge.*

And if that's you—if you've been so busy keeping score that you've forgotten what love is—I want to gently challenge you: What if you stopped measuring your worth by your works? What if you allowed yourself to be loved simply because you are your Father's child? What if you could celebrate grace extended to others, not because they deserve it, but because that's what grace is?

The father says to the older son: "Everything I have is yours." The older son has always had access to the father's abundance. He never needed to earn his place. But he couldn't receive it because he didn't understand grace. He was so focused on what he could earn that he couldn't see what had already been given.

Here's what breaks my heart: Some of the most faithful people I know are also the most bitter. They've given their lives to God, and somewhere along the way, they've stopped believing that God is good. They've started believing that God is keeping score, just like they are. And so they keep score too. They compare their sacrifice to others' ease. They measure their obedience against others' rebellion. And they can't celebrate grace because they're too busy calculating whether it's fair.

If that's you, can I tell you something? God's grace is not a limited resource. When God extends grace to your brother, it doesn't diminish the grace extended to you. When God celebrates someone else's return, it doesn't cheapen your faithfulness. The father's love is not a pie that gets smaller when it's divided. It's infinite. It's inexhaustible. And it's already yours.

But you have to receive it. You have to let go of the scorecard. You have to walk into the feast.

### Third: The Open Ending

And here's what I want you to notice: the parable doesn't tell us what the older son does. Does he go into the feast? Does he join the celebration? Does he finally understand his father's heart and embrace his brother? We don't know. The story is still unfolding.

Because the parable is not just ancient history. It's still being written. It's being written in your choices. It's being written in mine. Every time we encounter grace—grace we didn't earn, grace we don't deserve—we face the older son's choice. Do we celebrate it? Or do we stand outside, nursing our resentment?

Every time we see someone else receive forgiveness, we face a choice. Do we rejoice with those who rejoice? Or do we keep score?

Every time we're invited into the feast, we face a choice. Do we go in? Or do we stay outside?

## What This Reveals About God

Here's what Jesus is saying to the Pharisees—and to us: *This is who God is.* God is a father who respects human freedom so much that He allows us to walk away. God is a father who runs toward the lost instead of waiting for them to crawl back. God is a father who absorbs shame instead of inflicting it. God is a father who celebrates return instead of demanding payment.

And here's something else: In God's kingdom, there are no permanent outsiders. No one is too far gone. No mistake is too big. The door is always open. The father is always watching. And when we turn toward home—when we come to our senses and decide to return—we discover that grace has been waiting for us all along.

This is the heart of the gospel. Not a God who is keeping score. Not a God who is waiting for us to prove ourselves. A God who runs. A God who celebrates. A God whose love is so extravagant, so unreasonable, so utterly generous that it offends our sense of justice.

And that's exactly the point.

## Conclusion: Where You Are

As we close, I want to ask you: Where are you in this story right now?

Are you in the distant country? Are you far from home, wondering if you can ever come back? If so, know this: your Father is watching for you. He's not angry. He's not keeping score. He's waiting with open arms. The feast is prepared. Your place is set. Come home.

Are you in the field? Are you faithfully serving but not freely celebrating? Are you so focused on what you've earned that you can't see what's been given? If so, I invite you to step into the feast. Receive the love that's been offered to you all along. Let go of the scorecard. Experience the joy of grace. Walk toward your brother. Embrace him. Celebrate with your father.

Or are you on the journey? Are you somewhere between the distant country and home, taking the first steps back? Wherever you are, God meets you there. That's the promise of this parable. That's the heart of the gospel.

The beautiful thing about this story is that it doesn't actually end—not yet. We don't know if the older son goes into the feast. We don't know if he accepts his father's invitation to celebrate. And that's intentional. Because the parable is still unfolding. It's still being written in our lives, in our choices, in our responses to God's relentless, pursuing, celebrating love.

The question before you is not whether God will accept you. The question is whether you will accept God's grace. The question is whether you will come home. The question is whether you will go into the feast.

Whatever you've done, wherever you've been, whoever you are—God is waiting. God is watching. God is ready to celebrate your homecoming. The question is: Will you come?

May we all, in our own ways, come to our senses. May we all turn toward the Father. May we all discover that we've been loved all along. And may we all, together, celebrate the grace that brings us home.

Amen.

# The Father Who Runs: A Sermon on the Prodigal Son

## Opening

I want to begin this morning with a story—a true one.

Several years ago, a young man in our community struggled with addiction. He disappeared for three years. His mother didn't know if he was alive or dead. She drove past his old apartment building sometimes, just hoping for a glimpse of him. She kept his childhood photo on her nightstand. Every time the phone rang, her heart jumped. Then one morning, her doorbell rang. It was him—thin, weathered, broken. She didn't ask questions. She didn't demand explanations. She simply opened the door, pulled him close, and wept. Later, she told me: "I would have waited thirty years. I would have waited forever."

That mother's love—unconditional, patient, seeking—is a pale reflection of the love Jesus describes in the parable we're looking at this morning.

But before we turn to Scripture, I want to ask you something: How many of you have ever felt like you were on the outside looking in?

Perhaps you've made a mistake—a big one—and wondered if you could ever come home again. Or maybe you've watched someone you love walk away, and you've spent sleepless nights wondering if they'd ever return. Or perhaps you've stood in the shoes of someone who stayed, who did everything right, only to watch grace extended to someone who didn't deserve it, and you felt the sting of injustice.

If you've felt any of these things, then you understand why the parable we're about to explore has captivated hearts for two thousand years. It's not just a story about a wayward son. It's a story about all of us—about the human condition, about grace, and about the heart of God.

Let's turn to Luke 15, beginning at verse 11.

## The Story

For those unfamiliar with this parable, let me set the scene. A man has two sons. The younger son approaches his father with an astonishing request: "Father, give me my share of the estate." 

Now, in that culture, this wasn't simply asking for money. He was essentially saying, "I wish you were dead." He was rejecting his father, his inheritance, his entire identity as part of the family. It was an act of profound dishonor. And yet, remarkably, the father grants the request.

The young man takes his inheritance and travels to a distant country, where he squanders everything in wild living. Then a famine comes—the kind of famine that makes a Jewish boy willing to feed pigs, the most unclean animals in his tradition. For a young man raised in Jewish law, this is the ultimate degradation. He is not merely poor; he is ritually defiled, spiritually homeless. Starving and desperate, he comes to his senses. He decides to return home, not as a son, but as a hired servant, hoping his father will at least feed him.

But when the father sees him coming, something extraordinary happens. The father doesn't wait for an apology. He doesn't demand an explanation. He runs—and in that culture, a dignified man did not run. A patriarch did not hitch up his robes and sprint down the road like a common laborer. He runs toward his son with such joy that he embraces him before the boy can even finish his prepared speech. The father calls for a celebration: "Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let's have a feast and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

Then the older son arrives. He's been working faithfully in the fields all day, and when he hears the sound of celebration, he's furious. He refuses to go in. The father comes out to plead with him, and the older son pours out his bitterness: "All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!"

And the father's response is tender but firm: "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

## Exegesis: What This Story Means

Now, let's dig deeper into what Jesus is actually teaching us here.

Remember: this story is not told in isolation. It's the climax of three parables Jesus told about lostness. In Luke 15, Jesus first tells of a shepherd who leaves his ninety-nine sheep to search for one that is lost. Then He tells of a woman who lights a lamp and sweeps her entire house to find a single lost coin. And finally, He tells this story. The shepherd searches for the sheep. The woman searches for the coin. And here, the Father is watching and waiting, ready to run. God is not a passive receiver of the lost; God is an active seeker. This is the character of God revealed across three stories.

Now, let's consider the father's character in this parable. In Jewish culture, the father's role was to maintain honor and dignity. A son's request for his inheritance early would have been considered shameful—an insult to the entire family. The father had every right to refuse, to be angry, to protect his honor. But instead, he allows his son to make his own choices, even knowing those choices will lead to destruction. This is a picture of God's respect for human freedom. God doesn't force us to love Him. He allows us to walk away. And crucially, He doesn't punish us for that freedom—He grieves it, waits for us, and welcomes us when we return.

Second, consider what happens in the distant country. The son's sin isn't just moral failure; it's spiritual homelessness. He has everything he wanted—freedom, pleasure, independence—yet he's utterly empty. He's squandered his inheritance in wild living, yes, but more broadly, he's squandered his identity, his peace, his sense of belonging. This is the human condition apart from God. We can have everything the world offers—career success, material comfort, the admiration of others—and still be starving. The parable suggests that sin always leads to this kind of degradation, not because God is punishing us arbitrarily, but because sin itself is a kind of death. It separates us from the source of life.

The turning point comes when the son "comes to his senses." The Greek word here is significant—it means to return to one's right mind. Repentance isn't primarily about feeling guilty; it's about seeing clearly. The son realizes the truth: his father's servants are better off than he is. This is what repentance looks like—a clear-eyed recognition of reality and a decision to turn around. Not "I feel bad," but "I see the truth, and I'm going to change direction."

But here's what's revolutionary: the father doesn't wait for perfect repentance. The son is still rehearsing his speech—"I am no longer worthy to be called your son"—when the father interrupts him with embrace and celebration. The father's love isn't conditional on the son's worthiness. It's not dependent on the son's self-improvement or his promises to do better. It's based entirely on the father's character and the father's love for his child.

Finally, the older son represents a different kind of lostness—one that's equally dangerous, perhaps more insidious because it's invisible. He's physically present but spiritually far away. His obedience is motivated by duty, not love. He serves his father like a slave serves a master, always keeping score, always calculating what he's owed. When grace is extended to his brother, he can't celebrate because he's been operating under a different economy entirely—the economy of merit and earning, rather than the economy of grace and gift.

The father's response to the older son is crucial: "Everything I have is yours." The older son has always had access to the father's abundance. He never needed to earn his place. But he couldn't receive it because he didn't understand grace. He couldn't enjoy the feast because he'd been too busy working to earn what had always been freely offered.

## Application: Where We Live

So what does this mean for us, gathered here in the twenty-first century?

First, if you're the prodigal—if you've walked away from God, if you've made choices you're ashamed of, if you feel far from home—I want you to hear this clearly: God is not waiting for you to get your act together before He welcomes you. He's not demanding that you prove yourself first. The father in this story doesn't say, "Come home when you've earned enough money to repay me" or "Come home when you've suffered enough to prove you've changed." He runs toward his son in his rags and filth and embraces him.

Now, what does "walking away" look like in your life? Maybe your distant country isn't a literal brothel, but a distant country of addiction—alcohol, drugs, or other substances that promise freedom but deliver bondage. Maybe it's a distant country of career idolatry, where you've convinced yourself that one more promotion, one more achievement, will finally make you whole. Maybe it's the distant country of self-sufficiency, where you've spent years believing you don't need anyone, don't need God, can handle everything alone. Maybe it's the distant country of broken relationships—you've hurt people you love, and you've convinced yourself that the damage is irreparable. In whatever form your distant country takes, you're squandering something precious: your peace, your purpose, your connection to the one who made you.

If you've been running from God—maybe for years—maybe you think you've gone too far, done too much, been away too long—I'm here to tell you that God's grace is bigger than your failure. God is not surprised by your sin. He's not shocked or disgusted. He's waiting, watching the horizon, hoping for the day you'll come to your senses and turn toward home. And when you do, He doesn't greet you with anger or disappointment. He runs toward you. He embraces you. He celebrates you.

But I also want to speak to those of you who might be more like the older son. Perhaps you've been faithful. You've lived a good life. You've kept the rules. You've done the right thing, even when it was hard, even when no one was watching. And maybe you're looking around at the world, watching people who've done terrible things receive kindness, grace, and second chances, and you're angry. You feel like your faithfulness isn't being rewarded. You feel cheated. You feel like it's unfair.

Here's what I want you to know: the father's love for you is not diminished by his love for your brother. The father's grace is not a limited resource that runs out. When the father says, "Everything I have is yours," he means it. The older son has been invited to the feast all along. He's been part of the family all along. But he's been too busy working, too busy keeping score, to enjoy it.

If that's you, I want to invite you to consider something: What if you stopped measuring your worth by your works? What if you allowed yourself to be loved simply because you are your Father's child? What if you could celebrate grace extended to others, not because they deserve it, but because that's what grace is? What if you stepped into the feast and discovered that there's more than enough joy for everyone, that the father's celebration of your brother's return doesn't diminish his love for you—it reveals it?

The older son's problem wasn't that he wasn't loved. It was that he couldn't receive the love that was always there. He was so focused on earning his inheritance that he couldn't enjoy the inheritance he already possessed. He was so angry about fairness that he missed the point entirely: grace isn't fair. Grace is better than fair. Grace is love extended to those who don't deserve it. And if you're the older son, the invitation this morning is to stop working for love and start receiving it.

## The Heart of God

Ultimately, this parable is about God's heart. Jesus tells this story in response to the Pharisees complaining that He welcomes sinners and eats with them. And Jesus is saying: This is who God is. This is what God is like. God is a father who runs. God is a father who celebrates. God is a father whose love is not based on performance but on relationship.

The parable also reveals something crucial about the kingdom of God. In God's kingdom, there are no permanent outsiders. No one is too far gone. No mistake is too big. The door is always open. The father is always watching. And when we turn toward home—when we come to our senses and decide to return—we discover that grace has been waiting for us all along.

But there's another truth embedded here: in God's kingdom, there's also no such thing as earning your place. You can't work hard enough to be loved more. You can't be obedient enough to deserve the father's embrace. You can't perform your way into grace. Grace is a gift. And the only thing that stands between you and that gift is your willingness to receive it.

## Conclusion: Coming Home

As we close, I want to ask you: Where are you in this story?

Are you the prodigal, far from home, wondering if you can ever come back? If so, know this: your Father is watching for you. He's not angry. He's not keeping score. He's waiting with open arms, ready to run toward you the moment you turn toward home. Come home.

Are you the older son, faithfully serving but not freely celebrating? If so, I invite you to step into the feast. Receive the love that's been offered to you all along. Let go of the scorecard. Experience the joy of grace. Your father is pleading with you, just as he pleaded with your brother. Don't stay outside. Come in.

Or perhaps you're somewhere in between, somewhere on the journey. Wherever you are, God meets you there. That's the promise of this parable. That's the heart of the gospel.

The beautiful thing about this story is that it doesn't actually end. We don't know if the older son goes into the feast. We don't know if he accepts his father's invitation to celebrate. And that's intentional. Because the parable is still unfolding. It's still being written in our lives, in our choices, in our responses to God's relentless, pursuing, celebrating love.

The question before us is not whether God loves us. The question is whether we will come home. The question is whether we will receive that love. The question is whether we will step into the feast.

So I leave you with this: Whatever you've done, wherever you've been, whoever you are—God is watching. God is waiting. God is ready to celebrate your homecoming. The father is running toward you. All you have to do is turn around.

May we all, in our own ways, come to our senses. May we all turn toward the Father. May we all discover that we've been loved all along. And may we all have the courage to step into the feast.

Amen.

# The Father's Extravagant Welcome: A Sermon on the Prodigal Son

## Opening

I want to begin this morning with a story—not Jesus's story, but one that echoes his story. Several years ago, I met a man named Robert in our community. Robert had a son who, at nineteen, made some terrible decisions. He got involved with the wrong crowd, started using drugs, and eventually stole money from his parents to feed his addiction. When his father discovered this, there was a confrontation. The son left. For two years, Robert didn't know where his boy was or if he was alive.

During those two years, Robert did something remarkable. He sat on his front porch every evening. He didn't sit there with anger or judgment. He sat there watching the street, hoping. His wife would sometimes join him, and they'd sit in silence. Neighbors asked him why he wasted his time. Robert would just say, "Because he's my son, and if he comes home, I want to be the first one to see him."

One autumn evening, a young man approached slowly down the sidewalk. He was thin, hollow-eyed, and dressed in rags. Robert's wife didn't recognize him at first. But Robert stood up immediately. He knew his son's walk, his shape, something essential about him that hadn't changed despite everything. Before the boy could say a word, Robert ran down the path, embraced him, and wept.

That story lives in the shadow of the parable Jesus tells in Luke 15. And it's a parable we need to hear, especially in moments when we feel distant from God, or when we've judged others for being distant from him.

## The Setting: Why This Story Matters

Let me set the scene for you. Jesus is surrounded by tax collectors and sinners—people the religious establishment considered beyond redemption. The Pharisees are grumbling: "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them" (Luke 15:2). In response, Jesus tells three parables about lostness and recovery: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and—most memorably—a lost son.

The third parable is the deepest, the most personal, the most devastating in its grace. And it's the one we're going to sit with this morning.

## The Story Itself

Let me read the parable carefully, because every detail matters. A man has two sons. The younger son comes to his father and says, "Father, give me my share of the estate." This is shocking. In that culture, such a request is essentially saying, "I wish you were dead." The son wants his inheritance now, not after his father's death. It's an act of profound disrespect and rejection.

But here's the first surprise: the father gives it to him. No argument. No anger. No attempt to convince him to stay. The father grants the request.

The son then leaves for a distant country and squanders everything in wild living. When a severe famine comes, he ends up feeding pigs—which, for a Jewish boy, represents the absolute nadir of degradation. Starving, he comes to his senses and decides to return home. He'll ask his father to make him a hired servant, since he's no longer worthy to be called a son.

Notice what the son doesn't do: he doesn't expect forgiveness. He expects transaction. He'll work to pay back what he's owed. He'll earn his way back into his father's house, if not his father's heart.

But then comes the moment that has shattered and healed hearts for two thousand years: "But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him" (Luke 15:20).

The father runs. In that culture, a man of dignity and means did not run. Running was beneath his station. But love makes fools of us all, and this father runs like a man half his age. He embraces his son before the boy can finish his prepared speech. He calls for celebration—a robe, a ring, sandals, a fattened calf. "For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found" (Luke 15:24).

## The Twist: The Older Son

But Jesus isn't finished. The older son, who has been working in the field, hears the music and dancing. When he learns what's happening, he becomes furious. He refuses to go in. His father comes out to plead with him, and the older son unleashes his bitterness: "All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!" (Luke 15:29-30).

Notice what the older son does: he denies his brother's sonship ("this son of yours"), he minimizes his own service as slavery, he keeps a ledger of his obedience, and he believes his father's love is a limited commodity—that welcoming the younger son somehow diminishes what he receives.

The father's response is tender but firm: "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found" (Luke 15:31-32).

And here's the remarkable thing: the parable ends without telling us whether the older son goes in or not. We're left with an open question. Because Jesus is asking his listeners—and us—which son are we?

## What This Parable Reveals

Let me draw out some crucial truths embedded in this story.

**First, it reveals the nature of sin.** The younger son's sin isn't primarily about breaking rules; it's about breaking relationship. He wants independence from his father. He wants to live as if his father doesn't exist. And sin, at its core, is always this: a turning away from the one who loves us most, a declaration of self-sufficiency that leaves us starving in a foreign land.

**Second, it reveals the nature of grace.** The father's response is not proportional to the son's offense. In a just world, the boy would be punished, made to earn his way back, forced to prove his repentance. But the father's love transcends justice. It's what theologians call "prevenient grace"—grace that comes before we deserve it, before we've done anything to earn it. The father doesn't wait for the son to finish his apology. He doesn't make conditions. He welcomes with extravagance.

**Third, it reveals the danger of self-righteousness.** The older son's problem isn't that he's broken the rules—he's kept them scrupulously. His problem is that he's kept score. He's turned obedience into currency, service into leverage. He's missed the entire point: that the father's love is not something you earn or deserve. It's something you receive. And when you believe you've earned it through your own righteousness, you become incapable of receiving it freely, and you become incapable of extending it to others.

This is perhaps the most subtle and dangerous form of spiritual sickness—the sickness of the person who's never needed grace because they've never admitted their need.

## Application: Which Son Are You?

Now, let me ask you directly: which son are you?

Are you the prodigal? Have you wandered far from home? Have you tried to live life on your own terms, only to find yourself empty, starving, far from everything that matters? If so, I want you to hear this: the father is watching for you. He's not angry. He's not keeping score. He's not waiting for you to grovel or prove yourself. He's waiting with open arms, ready to run toward you the moment you turn his direction.

If you've been away from God, away from this church, away from your faith—whether that's been months or years or decades—know this: you haven't gone so far that you can't come home. The distance you've traveled, the time you've lost, the money you've wasted, the relationships you've broken—none of it disqualifies you from the father's welcome. Come home. Come as you are. Come now.

But perhaps you're the older son. Perhaps you've been faithful. You've shown up. You've done the work. You've kept the rules. And maybe—just maybe—you're a little bitter about it. Maybe you look at people who've lived recklessly but are now being welcomed back into God's grace, and something in you rebels. It doesn't seem fair. You've sacrificed. You've been obedient. And now they get the same welcome?

If that's you, I want to gently suggest that you've missed something essential. The father's love for you has never been about your performance. It's never been about earning your place. You've always been home. Everything the father has is already yours. But you can only receive it if you stop keeping score, if you stop comparing your righteousness to someone else's sin, if you can learn to rejoice when the lost are found, not because they deserve it, but because love always rejoices in restoration.

The father says to the older son: "My son, you are always with me." Not "you will be with me if you keep performing." Not "you're with me as long as you're better than your brother." But "you are with me." Present tense. Constant. Unconditional.

## The Scandal of Grace

Here's what troubles many of us about this parable: it seems unfair. The younger son gets a party. The older son gets a lecture. Where's the justice?

But that's precisely the point. Grace is not justice. Grace is not fair. If it were fair, we'd all get what we deserve. Thank God we don't.

The scandal of the Christian gospel is that God loves us not because we're worthy, but because we're his. He loves the prodigal not because the prodigal has earned it, but because the prodigal is his son. And he loves the faithful servant not as a reward for obedience, but as an inheritance of sonship.

This is what transforms everything. When you truly believe that you're loved not for what you do but for who you are—a beloved child of God—then obedience becomes not a burden but a joy. Service becomes not a transaction but an overflow. And when you see someone else welcomed home, you don't see it as a threat to your place; you see it as a confirmation of how deep and wide and wild your father's love really is.

## Conclusion: The Father's Heart

I want to end where we began, with Robert sitting on his porch. Robert's son did come home. And Robert didn't say, "Well, you've wasted two years and squandered your inheritance. You'll have to earn your way back." He embraced him. He wept. He welcomed him.

That's the father in this parable. That's your Father. That's my Father.

If you're far from home this morning, know that he's watching for you. If you're at home but bitter, know that he's calling you to joy.
