To ask for your inheritance while your father still lived was essentially to say, "I wish you were dead. You are worth more to me as a dead man than as a living father. Give me what's mine, and let me go."

And the father — notice this — the father gives it to him. He divides his property between his two sons. He does not argue. He does not withhold. He lets his son go. This is not indifference. This is the terrible respect that love has for freedom. God does not compel us to stay. He will not chain us to the table. Love that forces is not love at all.

The younger son gathers everything and travels to a far country. The text says he squandered his property in "reckless living." The Greek word is *asōtōs* — riotous, wasteful, self-destructive. He is living as though there is no tomorrow, no consequence, no story larger than his own appetites. We know what this looks like. It looks like the person who burns through every relationship chasing the next thrill. It looks like the slow erosion of a life that has lost its center.

And then the famine comes. It always does. Not always as dramatically, but it comes. The far country always runs out of what it promised. The son ends up feeding pigs — for a Jewish audience, this is the absolute bottom. He is ritually unclean, socially degraded, starving, and alone. He has arrived at the place where every false self finally arrives: emptiness.

And then Luke gives us this remarkable phrase: "He came to himself."

I love that. He came to *himself.* Not to a stranger. To himself. As if the person who left home was not truly him. As if sin is not our identity but our exile from our identity. The real self is the one that remembers the father's house.

He rehearses a speech. "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants." It's a reasonable speech. It's a contractual speech. He is trying to negotiate his way back in, to earn a place he thinks he's forfeited. He will work for his food. He will not presume upon relationship.

He does not yet understand what kind of father he has.

---

**The Father**

Now we come to the center of the story. We've seen the son's rebellion and ruin. What does the Father do with all of it?

Here is the verse that should stop us in our tracks.

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."

While he was still a long way off. Which means the father was watching. The father was at the window. The father was on the road, scanning the horizon, day after day, looking for a silhouette he recognized.

And when he sees him — the father *runs.*

In the ancient Near East, a dignified older man did not run. To run, he would have to hitch up his robes, exposing his legs, which was considered shameful. A patriarch waited for others to come to him. He did not sprint down a dirt road like a child.

But this father doesn't care about his dignity. His son is coming home, and dignity can wait. Honor can wait. Protocol can wait. Nothing — nothing — will slow him down.

This is more than a portrait of love's urgency. This is a complete reversal of the honor-shame culture that governed every relationship in that world. The father publicly humiliates himself to restore the son. He absorbs the shame so the boy doesn't have to. Does that sound familiar? It should. Paul would later write, "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them" (2 Corinthians 5:19). And in Romans: "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). *While we were still sinners.* While we were still a long way off. The pattern is the same. God moves first. God always moves first.

He falls on the boy's neck. He kisses him. The Greek suggests he kissed him repeatedly, fervently — this dust-covered, pig-smelling, broken young man.

The son begins his rehearsed speech. "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son —"

But the father cuts him off. The son never gets to the part about being a hired servant. The father will not hear it. Instead, he turns to his servants and says: "Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate."

Every one of these gifts carries weight. The best robe is the restoration of honor — not privately, but before the whole village. It is the father saying to every neighbor and onlooker, *This one belongs to me; treat him accordingly.* The ring is a signet ring, the family seal — restoration of authority and trust, like being handed back the keys and told, "I believe in you again." The shoes mark him as a free person, because only slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes. And the fattened calf — reserved for the most significant occasions — signals that this is not a quiet, private reconciliation. This is a public feast. The whole community is invited to witness and celebrate the son's return.

The father is not accepting a servant. He is reinstating a son. Fully. Immediately. Without probation, without a waiting period, without a lecture.

And then that line — that glorious, thundering line: "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found."

Not "this foolish boy." Not "this disgraceful child." *This my son.* He never stopped being a son. Even in the pig pen, even in the far country, even at his lowest — the relationship was never revoked in the father's heart.

This is the gospel, friends. He runs. He restores. He invites. Before you clean yourself up. Before you get your speech right. Before you finish your apology. While you are still a long way off — God runs.

---

**The Older Son**

If grace does this for the prodigal, how does it challenge the one who stayed? This is where the story turns, and this is where it gets uncomfortable — because Jesus is telling this parable to the Pharisees and scribes, remember? And the older brother is for them.

The older son hears music and dancing. He asks a servant what's going on. When he learns his brother has returned and his father has thrown a party, he is angry. He refuses to go in.

And notice — the father comes out to him, too. The father pursues both sons. He goes out to the one who wandered far, and he goes out to the one who stayed home but whose heart wandered just as far.

The older son's speech is revealing: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came back, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"

Listen to the language. "I have *served* you." He uses the word for slave labor. He has been in his father's house all along, but he has been living like a hired servant — exactly what the younger brother was afraid he'd become. He has stayed home, but he has not known the father's love. He has obeyed, but out of duty, not delight. He has been close in proximity but far in his heart.

And notice: "this son of *yours.*" He won't even say "my brother." He has disowned him.

We know this posture, don't we? It's the person who keeps a mental ledger of every sacrifice they've made for God and quietly resents anyone who seems to get grace without paying the same price. It's the church member who has served faithfully for decades and feels invisible when a newcomer with a dramatic testimony receives attention and celebration. It's any of us, in our honest moments, when we look at mercy given to someone we think doesn't deserve it and feel something tighten in our chest.

The father's response is gentle but devastating: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours."

Everything was already available to him. The fatted calf, the robe, the ring, the celebration — he could have had it all, at any time, if he had only understood that he was a beloved son and not a hired servant. His poverty was not material; it was relational. He had a father's love and didn't know it.

"It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."

*This your brother.* The father gently corrects him. You are connected to this man. His homecoming is your homecoming. His restoration is your joy.

And the story ends — and this is crucial — the story ends without resolution. We never learn whether the older brother goes in to the party. Jesus leaves it open. He leaves it open because the Pharisees and scribes are standing right there, and the question is for them: *Will you come in? Will you join the celebration? Or will you stand outside in your resentment, clutching your record of good behavior, while the music plays without you?*

---

**Coming Home**

So where are you in this story this morning?

Some of you are the younger son. You have wandered. You have squandered. You carry shame like a stone in your chest, and you have rehearsed your speech a thousand times. You think that if you could just get the words right, if you could just prove you've changed, maybe — maybe — God would take you back on some kind of probationary basis. Maybe you've been away from faith for years, or maybe the distance is more subtle — a slow drift into numbness, a quiet estrangement from the God you once knew.

Hear me: He is already running toward you. You don't need a better speech. You need to start walking home. And the walking home can be slow and uncertain. It doesn't have to be dramatic. It just has to be toward him.

Some of you are the older brother. You have done everything right — or at least you've tried to. You've served on committees. You've tithed. You've shown up every Sunday. And somewhere along the way, your faith became a ledger, and your obedience became a transaction, and you lost the joy of simply being a child of God. You look at others who receive grace and you think, *That's not fair.* And you're right — it's not fair. It's grace. Grace is not fair. Grace is better than fair.

Come inside. The party is for you, too.

And some of you — perhaps most of you — are both sons at different times, in different areas of your life. Running away in one area, keeping score in another. That's the human condition. We are all, in various ways, trying to find our way home.

But here is the good news — the news that is almost too good, the news that we must hear again and again because we keep forgetting: The Father is not waiting for you to arrive. The Father is running down the road to meet you.

He is not checking your record. He is not demanding your résumé. He is not interested in your rehearsed speech.

He wants *you.* Not your performance. Not your penance. You.

This my son. This my daughter. Dead, and alive again. Lost, and found.

God runs. We turn. We feast on grace.

So this week, I want to leave you with two things to carry with you. First, a question to sit with — alone, or with someone you trust: *Where in my life am I still living like a hired servant instead of a beloved child?* And second, an invitation: if there is someone you need to reach out to — someone you've distanced yourself from, someone you've quietly disowned like the older brother — take one step toward them. One call. One conversation. Grace moves first, and sometimes we get to be the ones who run.

Let us pray.

*Father, you run to us. Teach us to turn toward you. And give us the courage to go inside — to the feast, to the joy, to the life you have always intended for us. In the name of the One who came to seek and save the lost. Amen.*

# Coming Home: The Father Who Runs

**A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32**

---

There's a moment that stays with me from years ago. I was sitting in an airport terminal, waiting for a delayed flight, watching the usual parade of travelers shuffling past with their rolling bags and their tired eyes. And then I saw something that made me stop.

A woman — maybe sixty years old — was standing near the arrivals gate. She was holding a handmade sign, the kind you might make for a child coming home from college. But the sign didn't say "Welcome Home, Graduate" or anything like that. It just said a name. And she was trembling.

When a young man finally came through the gate — thin, cautious, eyes cast down — she dropped the sign and ran. She ran to him the way you run when you've forgotten about your dignity, when something deeper than propriety takes over. She grabbed him, and she held on, and she wept. And he wept. And I wept, sitting there in my plastic chair with my lukewarm coffee, watching two strangers fall apart in each other's arms.

I don't know their story. I don't know what had separated them or for how long. But I know what I saw. I saw what Jesus was talking about in the fifteenth chapter of Luke. I saw the gospel with skin on.

---

## The Story We Think We Know

The parable of the Prodigal Son is perhaps the most beloved story Jesus ever told. It is so familiar to us that we are in danger of no longer hearing it. We have domesticated it. We have turned it into a greeting card. And so I want to ask you, this morning, to hear it again — as if for the first time. Because if this story doesn't shock you, you haven't understood it yet.

Let's set the scene. Jesus is under fire. Luke tells us in the opening verses of chapter 15 that the tax collectors and sinners are drawing near to listen to him, and the Pharisees and scribes are grumbling: *"This man receives sinners and eats with them."* That complaint is the occasion for not one, not two, but three parables — the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. Jesus is defending his ministry to the margins. He is explaining why he keeps such scandalous company. And the explanation he gives is nothing less than a portrait of the heart of God.

## The Younger Son: The One Who Left

"Father, give me the share of the property that will belong to me."

We read that line too quickly. In the culture of first-century Palestine, this request was breathtaking in its cruelty. To ask for your inheritance while your father is still alive was essentially to say, "I wish you were dead. You are worth more to me as a corpse than as a father. Give me what I'm owed, and let me go."

And here is the first shock of the parable: the father gives it to him. No lecture. No ultimatum. No disowning. He divides his property between his two sons and lets the younger one walk away. The God Jesus describes is not a God who forces anyone to stay. Love that coerces is not love. The father's grief must have been immense, but he opens his hand and lets his son go.

The son goes to a far country and squanders everything in what Luke delicately calls "dissolute living." The word in Greek is *asōtōs* — it means reckless, wasteful, without hope of saving. He burns through his inheritance and ends up in the most degrading situation a Jewish audience could imagine: feeding pigs. Unclean animals. He has lost not only his money but his identity, his dignity, his place in the community of God's people. He is as far from home as it is possible to be.

And then comes the turning point. Luke says, "He came to himself." Some translations say he came to his senses. There is a moment of clarity in the pigsty — a moment when the fog lifts and he sees where he is and what he has become. He remembers his father's house. He remembers that even the hired servants have bread enough to spare.

Now, let me be honest with you about something. The son's repentance is complicated. He rehearses a speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants." Is this genuine contrition, or is it a survival strategy? Is he truly sorry, or is he just hungry?

I think Jesus leaves that ambiguous on purpose. Because here is the truth about coming home to God: our motives are almost never pure. We come back to God because we are broken, because we are desperate, because the pigsty has finally become unbearable. We come with mixed motives and half-formed prayers and hearts that are still tangled up in selfishness. And the stunning message of this parable is that *it doesn't matter*. The father doesn't wait for a perfect repentance. The father doesn't administer a theological exam at the door.

## The Father: The One Who Runs

"But while he was still far off, his father saw him."

This is the hinge of the entire parable, and I want you to feel the weight of it. The father saw him while he was *still far off*. Which means the father was watching. Which means the father had been watching — perhaps every day, perhaps for months or years, scanning the horizon, hoping against hope that today might be the day.

And then: "He was filled with compassion." The Greek word is *esplanchnisthē* — it refers to a visceral, gut-level emotion. It is the same word used to describe Jesus' own compassion when he saw the crowds, when he encountered the leper, when he met the widow burying her only son. This is not a mild sentiment. This is love that aches.

"He ran."

In the ancient Near East, a distinguished older man did not run. To run, he would have to hitch up his robes, exposing his legs — an act of profound indignity. A patriarch maintained his composure. He waited for others to come to him. He preserved his honor.

This father throws his honor away. He runs down the road like a child, like a fool, like someone who has forgotten everything except that his son is coming home. He reaches the boy before the boy reaches him. He falls on his neck. He kisses him — the verb in Greek suggests repeated kissing, again and again, covering his filthy face with kisses.

The son begins his rehearsed speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son —"

But the father cuts him off. He never lets him finish. He never lets him get to the part about being a hired servant. Instead, he turns to his servants — his actual servants — and says: "Quickly, bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet. And get the fatted calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate."

The robe is the father's own robe — a sign of honor and restored status. The ring is a signet ring — a sign of authority and family identity. The sandals distinguish a son from a slave, because slaves went barefoot. Every detail is a declaration: *This is not a hired hand. This is my son. He was always my son. He will always be my son.*

Do you see what Jesus is saying? He is saying that God does not reluctantly accept us back. God does not stand at the door with arms folded, waiting for us to grovel sufficiently. God runs. God runs to us in our disgrace, in our failure, in our pigsty, and God's first instinct is not punishment but embrace.

## The Older Son: The One Who Stayed

And now we come to the part of the parable that most of us would rather skip, because it is the part that is most likely about us.

The older son has been in the field — faithful, dutiful, obedient. He hears music and dancing. He learns that his brother has returned and that his father has thrown a party. And he is furious.

"Listen! For all these years I have been working like a slave for you, and I have never disobeyed your command; yet you have never given me even a young goat so that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came back, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fatted calf for him!"

Notice: he says "this son of yours," not "my brother." He has disowned his sibling even as he accuses his father of favoritism. And notice the self-portrait he paints: "I have been working like a slave for you." The older son, who has lived in his father's house his entire life, who has had access to everything the father owns, has experienced his life at home as slavery. He has been physically present but emotionally far away. He has obeyed out of duty, not love. He has been keeping score.

And here is the piercing truth: the older son is just as lost as the younger one. He is lost in his own righteousness. He is lost in his resentment. He is standing right next to the father's house and he cannot bring himself to go inside.

Jesus is looking straight at the Pharisees when he tells this part of the story. He is saying: You who have kept all the rules, you who have never left home, you who have tithed your mint and dill and cumin — do you know the father's heart? Or have you been so busy earning your place that you've never realized it was a gift?

The father comes out to the older son, too. Notice that. He doesn't stay inside at the party. He leaves the celebration to pursue his angry, self-righteous child with the same love he showed the wayward one. "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours."

The parable ends without resolution. We never learn whether the older son goes inside. Jesus leaves the door open — because the Pharisees are still deciding, and because, if we are honest, so are we.

## Coming Home

So where are you in this story this morning?

Some of you are the younger son. You have wandered far. You have made choices that have cost you dearly. You are sitting in a pigsty of your own making — maybe it's addiction, maybe it's a broken relationship, maybe it's a quiet despair that no one else can see — and you are wondering if it's too late to come home. Hear me: it is not too late. The Father is watching the road. The Father is ready to run.

Some of you are the older son. You have done everything right — or at least you've tried to. You have been faithful. You have showed up. And you are exhausted, and you are bitter, and somewhere along the way your faith became a transaction instead of a relationship. You are keeping score with God, and the math never works out in your favor. Hear me: you don't have to earn what has already been given. All that the Father has is yours. It always was.

And some of you — perhaps most of you — are both sons at different times, in different seasons, sometimes in the same day. We wander and we resent. We run away and we keep score. We are, all of us, in constant need of the same grace.

But here is what I want you to carry with you out of this place today. This parable is not finally about either son. It is about the Father. It has been misnamed for centuries. It should not be called the Parable of the Prodigal Son. It should be called the Parable of the Prodigal Father — because *prodigal* means recklessly extravagant, and that is exactly what this father is. Recklessly extravagant in his love. Lavish beyond reason. Running when he should walk. Throwing a party when he should be delivering a lecture. Giving a robe when a rebuke would be justified.

This is your God. This is the God who, in Jesus Christ, hitched up his robes and ran toward us — all the way to a cross — because he could not bear for us to be far away one moment longer.

Whatever far country you have been living in, the road home is shorter than you think. The Father is already running.

Let us come home.

*Amen.*

Let us come home.

# Coming Home: The Father Who Runs

**A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32**

---

There's a moment that stays with me from years ago. I was sitting in an airport terminal, waiting for a delayed flight, watching the usual parade of travelers shuffling past with their rolling bags and their tired eyes. And then I saw something that made me stop.

A woman — maybe sixty years old — was standing near the arrivals gate. She was holding a handmade sign, the kind you might make for a child coming home from college. But the sign didn't say "Welcome Home, Graduate" or anything like that. It just said a name. And she was trembling.

When a young man finally came through the gate — thin, cautious, eyes cast down — she dropped the sign and ran. She ran to him the way you run when you've forgotten about your dignity, when something deeper than propriety takes over. She grabbed him, and she held on, and she wept. And he wept. And I wept, sitting there in my plastic chair with my lukewarm coffee, watching two strangers fall apart in each other's arms.

I don't know their story. I don't know what had separated them or for how long. But I know what I saw. I saw what Jesus was talking about in the fifteenth chapter of Luke. I saw the gospel with skin on.

---

## The Story We Think We Know

The parable of the Prodigal Son is perhaps the most beloved story Jesus ever told. It is so familiar to us that we are in danger of no longer hearing it. We have domesticated it. We have turned it into a greeting card. And so I want to ask you, this morning, to hear it again — as if for the first time. Because if this story doesn't shock you, you haven't understood it yet.

Let's set the scene. Jesus is under fire. Luke tells us in the opening verses of chapter 15 that the tax collectors and sinners are drawing near to listen to him, and the Pharisees and scribes are grumbling: *"This man receives sinners and eats with them."* That complaint is the occasion for not one, not two, but three parables — the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. Jesus is defending his ministry to the margins. He is explaining why he keeps such scandalous company. And the explanation he gives is nothing less than a portrait of the heart of God.

## The Younger Son: The One Who Left

"Father, give me the share of the property that will belong to me."

We read that line too quickly. In the culture of first-century Palestine, this request was breathtaking in its cruelty. To ask for your inheritance while your father is still alive was essentially to say, "I wish you were dead. You are worth more to me as a corpse than as a father. Give me what I'm owed, and let me go."

And here is the first shock of the parable: the father gives it to him. No lecture. No ultimatum. No disowning. He divides his property between his two sons and lets the younger one walk away. The God Jesus describes is not a God who forces anyone to stay. Love that coerces is not love. The father's grief must have been immense, but he opens his hand and lets his son go.

The son goes to a far country and squanders everything in what Luke delicately calls "dissolute living." The word in Greek is *asōtōs* — it means reckless, wasteful, without hope of saving. He burns through his inheritance and ends up in the most degrading situation a Jewish audience could imagine: feeding pigs. Unclean animals. He has lost not only his money but his identity, his dignity, his place in the community of God's people. He is as far from home as it is possible to be.

And then comes the turning point. Luke says, "He came to himself." Some translations say he came to his senses. There is a moment of clarity in the pigsty — a moment when the fog lifts and he sees where he is and what he has become. He remembers his father's house. He remembers that even the hired servants have bread enough to spare.

Now, let me be honest with you about something. The son's repentance is complicated. He rehearses a speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants." Is this genuine contrition, or is it a survival strategy? Is he truly sorry, or is he just hungry?

I think Jesus leaves that ambiguous on purpose. Because here is the truth about coming home to God: our motives are almost never pure. We come back to God because we are broken, because we are desperate, because the pigsty has finally become unbearable. We come with mixed motives and half-formed prayers and hearts that are still tangled up in selfishness. And the stunning message of this parable is that *it doesn't matter*. The father doesn't wait for a perfect repentance. The father doesn't administer a theological exam at the door.

## The Father: The One Who Runs

"But while he was still far off, his father saw him."

This is the hinge of the entire parable, and I want you to feel the weight of it. The father saw him while he was *still far off*. Which means the father was watching. Which means the father had been watching — perhaps every day, perhaps for months or years, scanning the horizon, hoping against hope that today might be the day.

And then: "He was filled with compassion." The Greek word is *esplanchnisthē* — it refers to a visceral, gut-level emotion. It is the same word used to describe Jesus' own compassion when he saw the crowds, when he encountered the leper, when he met the widow burying her only son. This is not a mild sentiment. This is love that aches.

"He ran."

In the ancient Near East, a distinguished older man did not run. To run, he would have to hitch up his robes, exposing his legs — an act of profound indignity. A patriarch maintained his composure. He waited for others to come to him. He preserved his honor.

This father throws his honor away. He runs down the road like a child, like a fool, like someone who has forgotten everything except that his son is coming home. He reaches the boy before the boy reaches him. He falls on his neck. He kisses him — the verb in Greek suggests repeated kissing, again and again, covering his filthy face with kisses.

The son begins his rehearsed speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son —"

But the father cuts him off. He never lets him finish. He never lets him get to the part about being a hired servant. Instead, he turns to his servants — his actual servants — and says: "Quickly, bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet. And get the fatted calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate."

The smell of the pigsty was still on the boy's skin when the father draped his own robe over those bony shoulders. Grace covers us before we are clean.

The ring is a signet ring — a sign of authority and family identity. The sandals distinguish a son from a slave, because slaves went barefoot. Every detail is a declaration: *This is not a hired hand. This is my son. He was always my son. He will always be my son.*

Do you see what Jesus is saying? He is saying that God does not reluctantly accept us back. God does not stand at the door with arms folded, waiting for us to grovel sufficiently. God runs. God runs to us in our disgrace, in our failure, in our pigsty, and God's first instinct is not punishment but embrace.

## The Older Son: The One Who Stayed

If the story ended here, it would be a beautiful story of forgiveness. But Jesus doesn't stop. Because there is someone else outside the house. And this is the part of the parable that most of us would rather skip — because it is the part most likely about us.

The older son has been in the field — faithful, dutiful, obedient. He hears music and dancing. He learns that his brother has returned and that his father has thrown a party. And he is furious. He will not go in.

"Listen! For all these years I have been working like a slave for you, and I have never disobeyed your command; yet you have never given me even a young goat so that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came back, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fatted calf for him!"

Notice: he says "this son of yours," not "my brother." He has disowned his sibling even as he accuses his father of favoritism. And notice the self-portrait he paints: "I have been working like a slave for you." The older son, who has lived in his father's house his entire life, who has had access to everything the father owns, has experienced his life at home as slavery. He has been physically present but emotionally far away. He has obeyed out of duty, not love. He has been keeping score.

And here is the piercing truth: the older son is just as lost as the younger one. He is lost in his own righteousness. He is lost in his resentment. He is standing right next to the father's house and he cannot bring himself to go inside.

Jesus is looking straight at the Pharisees when he tells this part of the story. He is saying: You who have kept all the rules, you who have never left home, you who have tithed your mint and dill and cumin — do you know the father's heart? Or have you been so busy earning your place that you've never realized it was a gift?

The father comes out to the older son, too. Notice that. He doesn't stay inside at the party. He leaves the celebration to pursue his angry, self-righteous child with the same love he showed the wayward one. "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours."

The parable ends without resolution. We never learn whether the older son goes inside. Jesus leaves the door open — because the Pharisees are still deciding, and because, if we are honest, so are we.

## Coming Home

So where are you in this story this morning?

Some of you are the younger son. You have wandered far. You have made choices that have cost you dearly. You are sitting in a pigsty of your own making — maybe it's addiction, maybe it's a broken relationship, maybe it's a quiet despair that no one else can see — and you are wondering if it's too late to come home. Hear me: it is not too late. The Father is watching the road. The Father is ready to run.

Some of you are the older son. You have done everything right — or at least you've tried to. You have been faithful. You have showed up. Maybe you're the one who unlocks the doors every Sunday morning, who teaches the class, who serves on the committee, and you're quietly wondering why God seems to bless the person who just showed up last week with a messy life while you feel dry and empty. You look at your service record, your tithing, your clean moral sheet, and you wonder why the music isn't playing for you. Hear me: you don't have to earn what has already been given. You are working for a wage, but God wants you to enjoy an inheritance. All that the Father has is yours. It always was.

And some of you — perhaps most of you — are both sons at different times, in different seasons, sometimes in the same day. We wander and we resent. We run away and we keep score. We are, all of us, in constant need of the same grace.

But here is what I want you to carry with you out of this place today. This parable is not finally about either son. It is about the Father. It has been misnamed for centuries. It should be called the Parable of the Prodigal Father. We think of *prodigal* as meaning wasteful — and it does. But it also means to spend until you have nothing left. And that is exactly what this father is. He is reckless with his dignity. He is wasteful with his grace. Lavish beyond reason. Running when he should walk. Throwing a party when he should be delivering a lecture. Giving a robe when a rebuke would be justified.

This is your God.

And Jesus told this story to show us the Father's heart, but Jesus himself is also part of the story in a way the parable only hints at. The older brother in the parable stayed outside and refused to pay the cost of his brother's return — that fatted calf came from the estate he considered his. But our True Elder Brother did what the older son in the story would not. Jesus left the Father's house, came into the far country, and paid the debt himself. He was stripped of his robe on the cross so that we could be clothed in his righteousness. He bore the cost of the party so that we could come inside.

Whatever far country you have been living in, the road home is shorter than you think. The Father is already running. And I want you to picture his face — not stern, not disappointed, not keeping a record of wrongs — but the face of that woman in the airport, the face of someone who has been watching the road for a long, long time, and who, at the first glimpse of you on the horizon, forgets every dignified thing and simply runs.

Let us come home.

*Amen.*

Jesus is defending his ministry to the margins. He is explaining why he keeps such scandalous company. And the explanation he gives is nothing less than a portrait of the heart of God.

## The Younger Son: The One Who Left

"Father, give me the share of the property that will belong to me."

We read that line too quickly. In the culture of first-century Palestine, this request was breathtaking in its cruelty. To ask for your inheritance while your father is still alive was essentially to say, "I wish you were dead. You are worth more to me as a corpse than as a father. Give me what I'm owed, and let me go."

And here is the first shock of the parable: the father gives it to him. No lecture. No ultimatum. No disowning. He divides his property between his two sons and lets the younger one walk away. The God Jesus describes is not a God who forces anyone to stay. Love that coerces is not love. The father's grief must have been immense, but he opens his hand — and we could spend a lifetime trying to understand why God permits what God grieves — and he lets his son go.

The son goes to a far country and squanders everything in what Luke delicately calls "dissolute living." The word in Greek is *asōtōs* — reckless, wasteful, without hope of saving. He burns through his inheritance and ends up feeding pigs. For a Jewish audience, this was the bottom. Unclean animals. He has lost not only his money but his place among God's people. He is in the far country in every sense of the word.

And then comes the turning point. Luke says, "He came to himself." There is a moment of clarity in the pigsty — a moment when the fog lifts and he sees what he has become. He remembers his father's house. He rehearses a speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants."

Now, let me be honest with you. Is this genuine contrition, or is it a survival strategy? Is he truly sorry, or is he just hungry?

I think Jesus leaves that ambiguous on purpose. Because here is the truth about coming home to God: our motives are almost never pure. We come back because we are broken, because we are desperate, because the pigsty has finally become unbearable. We come with mixed motives and half-formed prayers and hearts still tangled up in selfishness. And the stunning message of this parable is that *it doesn't matter*. The father doesn't wait for a perfect repentance. The father doesn't administer a theological exam at the door.

## The Father: The One Who Runs

"But while he was still far off, his father saw him."

This is the hinge of the entire parable, and I want you to feel the weight of it. The father saw him while he was *still far off*. Which means the father was watching. Which means the father had been watching — perhaps every day, perhaps for months or years, scanning the horizon, hoping against hope that today might be the day.

And then: "He was filled with compassion." The Greek word is *esplanchnisthē* — it refers to a visceral, gut-level emotion. It is the same word used to describe Jesus' own compassion when he saw the crowds, when he encountered the leper, when he met the widow burying her only son. That is not a coincidence. The Father's compassion and Jesus' compassion are the same compassion. When you see Jesus weeping at a graveside, you are seeing the heart of the Father. When you see Jesus reaching out to touch an untouchable, you are seeing the Father's hand.

"He ran."

In the ancient Near East, a distinguished older man did not run. To run, he would have to hitch up his robes, exposing his legs — an act of profound indignity. A patriarch maintained his composure. He waited for others to come to him. He preserved his honor.

This father throws his honor away. He runs down the road like someone who has forgotten everything except that his son is coming home. He reaches the boy before the boy reaches him. He falls on his neck. He kisses him — the verb in Greek suggests repeated kissing, again and again, covering his filthy face with kisses.

And I want you to hold that image — a father humiliating himself, absorbing shame, running toward the one who wronged him — because it is a preview. It is a preview of what God will do in Christ, when he takes on flesh and enters our far country, when he absorbs not just social shame but the full weight of human sin, all the way to a cross. The father running down the road and the Son of God running toward Golgotha are the same movement of the same love. This is who God is. This is what God does. God closes the distance.

The son begins his rehearsed speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son —"

But the father cuts him off. He never lets him finish. He never lets him get to the part about being a hired servant. Instead, he turns to his servants and says: "Quickly, bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet. And get the fatted calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate."

The robe is the father's own — a sign of honor and restored status. The ring is a signet ring — a sign of authority and family identity. The sandals distinguish a son from a slave, because slaves went barefoot. Every detail is a declaration: *This is not a hired hand. This is my son.*

God does not reluctantly accept us back. God does not stand at the door with arms folded, waiting for us to grovel sufficiently. God runs. God's first instinct is not punishment but embrace.

## The Older Son: The One Who Stayed

And now we come to the part of the parable that most of us would rather skip, because it is the part that is most likely about us.

The older son has been in the field — faithful, dutiful, obedient. He hears music and dancing. He learns that his brother has returned and that his father has thrown a party. And he is furious.

"Listen! For all these years I have been working like a slave for you, and I have never disobeyed your command; yet you have never given me even a young goat so that I might celebrate with my friends."

Now here is a detail worth noticing. When the father divided his property at the beginning of the story, he divided it between *both* sons. The older son has already received his share. Everything the father has is already his. His complaint — "you never gave me even a young goat" — is not just bitter. It is factually wrong. He is standing in the middle of his inheritance and cannot see it. He has been so busy keeping score that he has lost count of what he's been given.

And notice how he refers to his brother: "this son of yours — who has devoured your property with prostitutes." Not "my brother." He has disowned his sibling even as he accuses his father of favoritism.

You want to know what older-son syndrome looks like? It looks like the longtime church member who quietly seethes when a newcomer with a messy past receives public attention and prayer. It looks like the volunteer who keeps a mental ledger of every unreciprocated act of service. It looks like the parent who did everything "right" and cannot forgive a child who didn't. It looks like someone who has lived in the father's house for decades and experienced the whole thing as slavery.

The older son is just as lost as the younger one. He is lost in his own righteousness. He is lost in his resentment. He is standing right next to the father's house and cannot bring himself to go inside.

Jesus is looking straight at the Pharisees when he tells this part of the story. He is saying: You who have kept all the rules, you who have never left home — do you know the father's heart? Or have you been so busy earning your place that you've never realized it was a gift?

And the father comes out to the older son, too. Notice that. He doesn't stay inside at the party. He leaves the celebration to pursue his angry, self-righteous child with the same love he showed the wayward one. "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours."

The parable ends without resolution. We never learn whether the older son goes inside. Jesus leaves the ending open — and that is not just a storytelling technique. It is an invitation. The parable itself enacts the father coming outside. Jesus, in the very telling of this story, is stepping out of the banquet hall and extending his hand to the Pharisees, to the rule-keepers, to anyone who has been standing outside in the cold of their own resentment. He is saying: *Will you come in?*

## Coming Home

So where are you in this story this morning?

Some of you are the younger son. You have wandered far. You have made choices that have cost you dearly — maybe it's addiction, maybe it's a broken relationship, maybe it's a quiet despair that no one else can see — and you are wondering if it's too late to come home. Hear me: it is not too late. The Father is watching the road. The Father is ready to run.

And some of you are in a far country you never chose. Not because you wandered there, but because life dragged you there — through illness, through loss, through someone else's cruelty, through circumstances no one would have chosen. I want you to know: the Father runs toward that far country too. The pigsty is not always a destination we walk to. Sometimes it is a place we wake up in. And the Father's compassion does not depend on how you got there.

Some of you are the older son. You have been faithful. You have showed up. And you are exhausted, and you are bitter, and somewhere along the way your faith became a transaction instead of a relationship. You are keeping score with God, and the math never works out in your favor. Hear me: you don't have to earn what has already been given. All that the Father has is yours. It always was.

And some of you — perhaps most of you — are both sons at different times, sometimes in the same day. We wander and we resent. We run away and we keep score. We are, all of us, in constant need of the same grace.

But here is what I want you to carry with you out of this place today. This parable is not finally about either son. It is about the Father. It has been misnamed for centuries. It should not be called the Parable of the Prodigal Son. It should be called the Parable of the Prodigal Father — because *prodigal* means recklessly extravagant, and that is exactly what this father is. Recklessly extravagant in his love. Lavish beyond reason. Running when he should walk. Throwing a party when he should be delivering a lecture. Giving a robe when a rebuke would be justified.

This is your God. This is the God who, in Jesus Christ, hitched up his robes and ran toward us — all the way to a cross — because he could not bear for us to be far away one moment longer.

Whatever far country you have been living in — whether you walked there or were carried — the road home is shorter than you think. The Father is already running.

Let us come home.

*Amen.*

When a young man finally came through the gate — thin, cautious, eyes cast down — she dropped the sign and ran. She ran to him the way you run when you've forgotten about your dignity, when something deeper than propriety takes over. She grabbed him, and she held on, and she wept. And he wept. # Coming Home: The God Who Runs

## A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

---

There's a moment that every parent knows. Maybe you know it too.

A few years ago, a friend of mine told me about the worst night of his life. His teenage daughter had left home after a terrible argument. She said things she meant and things she didn't. She packed a bag and walked out the front door, and he let her go because he was angry, and because he told himself she needed to learn. That night, he sat in the living room with every light on in the house. He kept the porch light burning. He checked his phone every three minutes. He walked to the window so many times that the dog stopped getting up to follow him. He told me, "I rehearsed two speeches. One was everything I wanted to say to correct her. The other was everything I wanted to say to welcome her back. By midnight, I'd forgotten the first speech entirely."

She came home at two in the morning. And he told me — a grown man, a serious man, not someone given to drama — he told me, "I saw her headlights turn into the driveway, and I ran out of the house in my bare feet."

I think about that story every time I read the parable of the Prodigal Son. Because I think Jesus told this parable to show us a God who runs out of the house in His bare feet.

---

Let's set the scene. Luke tells us in the opening verses of chapter 15 that tax collectors and sinners were gathering around Jesus. The Pharisees and scribes were muttering: "This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them." That muttering matters. It's the reason Jesus tells not one but three parables in a row — the lost sheep, the lost coin, and finally this one, the longest and most devastating parable He ever told. Jesus is not teaching in a vacuum. He is answering a specific accusation: *Why do you welcome the wrong people?*

Keep that context in your heart as we walk through this story, because it will change the way you hear every word.

**The Younger Son**

"Father, give me my share of the estate." We've heard this line so many times that we may have lost the shock of it. In first-century Jewish culture, this request was more than rude. It was a kind of death wish spoken in reverse. The inheritance came when the father died. This son is essentially saying, "I wish you were dead. Give me what I'm owed, and let me go."

And notice — the father gives it to him. He divides his property between his two sons. He does not argue. He does not lock the door. Love that is coerced is not love. God has always granted human beings the terrible dignity of walking away.

The younger son turns everything into cash and heads for a distant country. Luke uses a wonderful Greek word here — *asōtōs* — which means he lived "dissolutely," wastefully, without any thought of saving himself. He scattered his life the way you scatter seed on bad ground. And when the money ran out, so did the friends. A famine came. He found himself feeding pigs — an unthinkable degradation for a Jewish young man. Pigs were unclean animals. He has gone about as far from home, as far from identity, as far from the covenant community as it is possible to go. And Luke gives us this devastating line: "No one gave him anything."

That is the economy of the far country. It takes everything and gives nothing.

But then, verse 17: "He came to himself." Some translations say "he came to his senses." I love that phrase. It implies that sin is a kind of insanity, a departure from our true selves. This is not yet repentance in the fullest sense — the son rehearses a speech designed to secure a position as a hired servant. He's negotiating. He's managing. He still thinks in transactional terms. "I'll say the right words, and maybe I can earn my way back to a meal." But something has shifted. He has remembered that there is a home, and that even the servants in that home eat well.

Sometimes coming to yourself is enough. Sometimes all grace needs is for you to turn around.

**The Father**

Now we reach the heart of the parable, and I want you to lean in here, because this is where Jesus says something that would have stunned His original audience.

"While he was still a long way off, his father saw him."

How do you see someone who is a long way off? You see them only if you are looking. You see them only if you have been watching the road, day after day, scanning the horizon. This father has not moved on. This father has not written his son out of the story. He has been waiting.

"And he was filled with compassion."

The Greek word is *esplanchnisthē* — he was moved in his bowels, in his guts. This is not a sentimental feeling. This is visceral, physical, the kind of compassion that seizes your body before your mind can catch up.

"He ran to his son."

In the ancient Near East, a dignified older man did not run. To run, he would have to hitch up his robes, exposing his legs — a shameful act for a patriarch. Scholars like Kenneth Bailey have pointed out that the father's running may have served another purpose as well: by reaching his son before the son reached the village, the father shielded him from the mockery and judgment of the community. The father absorbs the shame so the son doesn't have to.

Does that sound like anyone else you know?

The son begins his rehearsed speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son —" But the father cuts him off. The son never gets to the part about being made a hired servant. The father will not hear it. Instead, he calls for the best robe — likely his own robe, a sign of honor and restored identity. He calls for a ring — a signet ring, a sign of authority and belonging. He calls for sandals — because servants went barefoot, but sons wore shoes. And he calls for the fattened calf, the one reserved for the most significant celebrations.

Do you see what is happening? The son came home hoping to negotiate a position as a hired worker. The father restores him as a *son*. The son's repentance, imperfect as it was, meets a grace that is out of all proportion to what was expected or deserved. This is not a transaction. This is a resurrection. "This son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

This is the gospel. Not that we make ourselves presentable and then approach God with a good enough speech. But that while we are still a long way off — still smelling of pig, still rehearsing our inadequate words — God sees us, God is moved, and God runs.

**The Older Son**

But the parable doesn't end there, and if we stop with the younger son's homecoming, we miss half of what Jesus is saying — and perhaps the more important half, given His audience.

The older son comes in from the fields. He hears music and dancing. He asks a servant what's happening, and when he learns that his brother has returned and that his father is throwing a party, he becomes angry and refuses to go in.

Notice: the older son is now the one who is outside. The younger son is inside at the feast. The positions have reversed.

The father comes out to him — just as he went out to the younger son. This father is always going out, always pursuing, always leaving his own comfort to meet his children where they are.

And the older son's complaint is revealing: "Look! All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!"

Listen to the language. "Slaving." "Orders." "Never disobeyed." The older son has been in the father's house the whole time, but he has been living like a servant, not a son. He has been keeping the rules, but he has not been experiencing the relationship. He has been *near* the father without being *close* to the father. And notice — he doesn't say "my brother." He says "this son of yours." He has already disowned his sibling in his heart.

The father's response is gentle and devastating: "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours." Everything. It was already his. The feast, the joy, the intimacy — it was always available. The older son's poverty was not material. It was relational. He had access to everything and experienced nothing, because he had reduced the relationship to a ledger of obedience and reward.

Now — remember who Jesus is talking to. The Pharisees. The rule-keepers. The ones who muttered about Jesus eating with sinners. Jesus is saying: *You are the older brother. And you are just as lost as the younger one. You are standing outside the party, and the door is open, and the Father is calling you in.*

Some of you are the younger son. You have wandered. You have wasted. You are in a far country — maybe not geographically, but spiritually, emotionally, relationally. You've been feeding pigs, and you're starving. You've been thinking about home, but you're afraid. You're rehearsing a speech, trying to figure out the right words to say to God, to your family, to yourself. Hear me: you don't need the right words. You just need to turn around. The Father is already watching the road.

Some of you are the older brother. You have been faithful. You have shown up. You have served. And you are angry — angry that grace seems unfair, angry that people who have done far less seem to receive far more, angry that your obedience has not been rewarded the way you expected. You are in the Father's house, but you are not at the Father's table. You have made your faith a transaction, and the joy has gone out of it. Hear the Father's voice: "Child, you are always with me. Everything I have is yours." Stop slaving. Start living as a son, as a daughter.

And some of you — maybe all of you, at one time or another — need to hear the deepest truth of this parable, which is not finally about either son. It is about the Father. It is about a God whose compassion is visceral, whose grace is reckless, whose dignity means nothing compared to His love for His children. It is about a God who divides His property and lets you go, and then watches the road every single day until you come home. It is about a God who will not let your worst decision be your last chapter. It is about a God who runs.

---

The porch light is on, beloved. It has always been on.

Whatever far country you have wandered into — whatever pigpen you are sitting in — whatever field of dutiful, joyless labor you have been working — the Father is not waiting for you to get yourself together. He is not waiting for the right speech. He is not standing at the door with His arms crossed.

He is running down the road to meet you.

Come home.

*Amen.*

# Coming Home: The God Who Runs

## A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

---

There's a moment that almost every parent knows. You're standing in a grocery store, or a park, or a crowded shopping mall, and you look down — and your child is gone. Your heart seizes. The world narrows to a single, desperate question: *Where is my child?* You scan the crowd. You call their name. And then — there they are. Maybe one aisle over. Maybe twenty feet away, completely oblivious to your panic. And what do you do? You don't walk. You don't stroll. You *run*. You close the distance as fast as your legs will carry you, and you gather that child into your arms, and for a moment nothing else in the world matters.

Hold that image in your mind this morning. Because Jesus is about to tell us something about the heart of God that should change the way we understand everything — our sin, our shame, our worth, and the nature of the love that will not let us go.

---

Turn with me to Luke chapter 15, beginning at verse 11.

Now, before we read a single word of this parable, we need to understand *why* Jesus tells it. Look at the opening verses of the chapter. The tax collectors and sinners are gathering around Jesus to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes are grumbling: "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them." That complaint is the occasion for not one, not two, but *three* parables — the lost sheep, the lost coin, and this, the longest and most detailed of them all. Jesus is answering a question that religious people have asked in every generation: *Why would God welcome people like that?*

So Jesus says: "There was a man who had two sons."

And with those words, he opens a story that has echoed across two thousand years of human history, because every one of us — every single person in this room — will find ourselves somewhere inside it.

---

**The Younger Son: The Far Country of the Heart**

The younger son comes to his father and says, "Father, give me my share of the estate." Now, we can read past this too quickly if we're not careful. In the culture of first-century Palestine, this request was breathtaking in its cruelty. To ask for your inheritance while your father was still alive was essentially to say, "I wish you were dead. You are worth more to me as a dead man than as a living father. Give me what I'm owed, and let me go."

And the father — notice this — the father gives it to him. He does not argue. He does not lock the door. He divides his property between his two sons, and he lets the younger one walk away.

There is a sermon in that detail alone. God does not hold us captive. The love of God is not coercive. You are free — terrifyingly, beautifully free — to take everything God has given you and walk into the far country. God will let you go. Not because he doesn't care, but because love that forces itself on the beloved is not love at all.

And so the son goes. He squanders everything in what Luke delicately calls "wild living." He spends it all. And then a famine comes — because famines always come — and he finds himself in the worst position imaginable for a Jewish young man: feeding pigs. Unclean animals. He has sunk as low as a person can sink. He is so hungry he longs to eat the pods he's throwing to the swine, and no one gives him anything.

This is what the far country looks like, friends. It doesn't always look like a pigsty. Sometimes it looks like a corner office. Sometimes it looks like a perfectly curated life on social media. Sometimes it looks like a pew in a church where you've been going through the motions for years. The far country is anywhere you have taken the gifts of God and used them to build a life without God at the center of it.

But then — verse 17 — "he came to himself." What a phrase. He came to *himself*. As if he had been someone else all along. As if sin had made him a stranger to his own soul. And in that moment of clarity, he remembers his father's house. He remembers that even the hired servants have food to spare. And he rehearses a speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants."

It's a reasonable speech. It's a humble speech. But notice — it's also a *transactional* speech. He's trying to negotiate his way back. He's thinking in terms of earning, deserving, working off his debt. He doesn't yet understand what's waiting for him at home.

---

**The Father: The Scandal of Grace**

And here we come to the absolute heart of this parable — the moment that would have made Jesus' original audience gasp.

"While he was still a long way off, his father saw him."

Stop there. The father *saw him*. Which means the father was *looking*. Day after day, scanning the horizon, waiting. This was not a father who had written his son off. This was a father who had never stopped watching the road.

"And he was filled with compassion for him."

The Greek word here is *esplanchnisthē* — he was moved in his bowels, in his gut. This is not polite sympathy. This is the deep, visceral ache of a parent's love. It is the word the Gospels use most often to describe the emotions of Jesus himself when he encounters human suffering.

"He ran to his son."

Now listen to me carefully. In the ancient Near East, a dignified patriarch did not run. To run, a man would have to hitch up his robes, exposing his legs — an act considered shameful and undignified. Older men walked with gravity and deliberation. They did not sprint down the road like children.

But this father runs. He throws dignity to the wind. He doesn't care what the neighbors think. He doesn't care about propriety or protocol. His son is home, and he *runs*.

He reaches the boy, and he falls on his neck and kisses him. The verb tense in the Greek suggests he kissed him *repeatedly*, lavishly, covering that pig-stinking face with kisses. And the son starts his rehearsed speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son—"

But the father cuts him off. The boy never gets to the part about being made a hired servant. The father will not hear it. Instead, he turns to his servants and says: "Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let's have a feast and celebrate."

The robe — that's restoration of honor. The ring — that's restoration of authority. The sandals — servants went barefoot; sons wore shoes. That's restoration of identity. And the feast — that's restoration of joy and community. The father is not merely forgiving the son. He is *reinstating* him. Fully. Completely. Without probation. Without a waiting period. Without a single condition.

"For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

This, brothers and sisters, is the gospel. This is what God is like. Not a reluctant judge who must be persuaded to show mercy. Not a distant deity keeping score. But a Father who runs — who absorbs the shame, who closes the distance, who restores what was lost before the apology is even finished.

---

**The Older Son: The Far Country Next Door**

But the story isn't over. And if we stop with the younger son, we miss half of what Jesus is saying.

The older son comes in from the field. He hears music and dancing. He asks a servant what's going on, and when he finds out, he is furious. He refuses to go in.

And now the father comes out again. Notice — the father goes out to *both* sons. He pursues the obedient one just as he pursued the rebellious one.

The older son's complaint is revealing: "Look! All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when *this son of yours* — " not "my brother," but "*this son of yours*" — "who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!"

Do you hear it? The older son has been in the father's house all along, but his heart has been in the far country too. He doesn't say "I've been *living* with you." He says "I've been *slaving* for you." He sees himself as a servant, not a son. He has reduced the relationship to a transaction — obedience in exchange for reward. And when the father's grace doesn't fit his ledger, he is outraged.

The older son is the Pharisee. The older son is the religious person who has done everything right and quietly resents the people who haven't. The older son is anyone who believes that their moral record is what makes them worthy of the Father's love.

And Jesus leaves this part of the story *unfinished*. The father pleads: "Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

We never learn whether the older son goes in to the party. The story is left open. And it's left open because Jesus is looking directly at the Pharisees and asking: *What will you do? Will you come in?*

---

**Coming Home**

So where are you this morning?

Maybe you're the younger son. Maybe you've wandered far. Maybe you've made choices you're ashamed of, and you've rehearsed your speech a hundred times. You've told yourself you're not worthy. You've told yourself you've gone too far. You've told yourself that God might take you back as a servant, but never again as a child.

Hear the gospel: the Father is already running toward you. Before you finish your confession, before you clean yourself up, before you get your life together — he is running. The robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The feast is being prepared. You don't have to earn your way back. You just have to come home.

Or maybe you're the older son. Maybe you've been faithful. Maybe you've served in this church for decades. Maybe you've never missed a Sunday, never missed a tithe, never missed a prayer meeting. And somewhere along the way, your faithfulness became a scoreboard, and your obedience became a currency, and you started to resent the people who receive the same grace you do without having paid the same price.

Hear the gospel: everything the Father has is already yours. You are not a slave. You are a son, a daughter. And the Father's grace toward others does not diminish his grace toward you. It reveals it. Come into the party. Your brother is home.

Or maybe — and I suspect this is true for many of us — you are both sons at different times, in different areas of your life. Rebellious in one season, resentful in another. Running away from God on Monday, keeping score with God on Sunday.

The beautiful, relentless truth of this parable is that the Father comes out to meet us in both conditions. He does not wait for us to get it right. He does not wait for us to figure it out. He hitches up his robes, and he runs.

The far country is real. But so is the road home. And on that road, there is a Father who has never stopped watching, never stopped waiting, never stopped loving.

Come home. The door is open. The table is set. And the Father is running to meet you.

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.
