# The Father Who Runs

### A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

---

Imagine you are sitting at your kitchen table one morning, drinking your coffee, when your phone rings. It's your child — the one you haven't heard from in two years. The one who left in anger, who said things that still echo in the quiet rooms of your house at night. Your hand trembles a little as you answer.

"I'm coming home," they say.

What do you do?

Do you sit very still and wait, composing yourself, preparing a measured response? Do you rehearse, perhaps, a list of conditions — a conversation you've needed to have for a long time? Or do you knock over the chair getting up from the table, fumble for your keys, and drive to wherever they are — just to close the distance?

Most of us, I suspect, know something about that second impulse. That wild, undignified rush toward the person we love. And if you know that feeling — if you have ever loved anyone that fiercely — then you are already standing at the edge of one of the most beautiful stories ever told.

---

## The Story Jesus Tells

In Luke 15, Jesus is in trouble — at least in the eyes of the religious establishment. The Pharisees and scribes are grumbling because he keeps eating with sinners. Tax collectors, prostitutes, the morally disreputable. "This man welcomes sinners," they mutter, "and eats with them." It is meant as an accusation. Jesus receives it as a description.

In response, he tells not one but three stories — a lost sheep, a lost coin, and finally this: the story of a lost son. Or rather, as we will see, the story of a father with two lost sons.

"There was a man who had two sons," Jesus begins. Already we are leaning in.

The younger son approaches his father with a request that, in the ancient Near Eastern world, would have landed like a slap across the face. "Father, give me the share of property that will come to me." In other words: *I want what I'll get when you die. Give it to me now.* 

To ask for your inheritance while your father is still living was, in that culture, tantamount to wishing him dead. It was a public humiliation, a severing of relationship, a declaration that you valued his money more than his life. Any self-respecting patriarch in first-century Palestine would have been within his rights — within his *cultural* rights — to disown the boy on the spot.

Instead, the father divides the property between his sons. He gives the younger one what he asked for.

Why? Jesus doesn't explain. He doesn't need to. We already sense it: because love does not coerce. Because the father knows that a son kept home by force is not really home at all.

---

## The Far Country

The younger son gathers everything, heads to a distant country, and — in one of the most compressed sentences in all of Scripture — "squanders his wealth in wild living." The Greek word translated "wild" is *asotos*, which suggests not just excess but a kind of reckless, unsaved, wasteful existence. He is not merely having fun. He is disappearing.

And then the famine comes. And the money runs out. And the friends evaporate. And the boy who once had servants finds himself feeding pigs — which, for a Jewish audience hearing this story, is about as low as a human being can sink. He is so hungry that the pods he's throwing to the pigs look appetizing.

Then Jesus gives us one of the most important phrases in the whole parable: *"He came to himself."*

He came to himself. There is a beautiful theological weight in those four words. They suggest that in his sin, in his self-destruction, the boy had somehow left himself behind — had become, in his waywardness, a stranger to his own soul. And now, in the mud and the stench, something like clarity breaks through.

He rehearses a speech. He'll go home, he decides, and say: *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants."* Notice what he's doing. He is preparing a transaction. He will trade his sonship for a job. He has so thoroughly absorbed the logic of the world — the logic that says love must be earned, that grace is a myth, that you only get what you pay for — that he cannot imagine any other kind of homecoming than a negotiated one.

He heads home, rehearsing his lines.

---

## The Father Who Runs

Now comes the hinge of the entire story. The moment everything turns.

*"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him."*

Still a long way off. Which means the father had been looking. Which means that every morning, perhaps, the old man had walked to the edge of his property and shaded his eyes against the sun and looked down that road. Which means hope had not died in him, even when there was no reasonable basis for hope.

And when he sees the boy — this distant, ragged, half-starved figure — he doesn't wait. He doesn't compose himself. He doesn't arrange his face into an expression of dignified expectation. He *runs*.

In the ancient world, a man of standing did not run. Running required you to gather up your robes, to expose your legs, to abandon the posture of authority. It was undignified. Embarrassing. Beneath a patriarch.

The father runs anyway.

He falls on his son's neck. He kisses him — the Greek suggests he kissed him repeatedly, urgently, the way you hold onto something you thought you'd lost forever. And the boy begins his rehearsed speech: *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son—"*

The father interrupts him.

He doesn't let him finish. He doesn't hear the part about becoming a hired servant, because he's already calling to the servants himself: *"Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let's have a feast and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."*

Dead and alive. Lost and found. These are resurrection words. This is not merely a story about family reconciliation. Jesus is telling us something about the nature of God.

---

## The God We Meet Here

Here is the theology embedded in this parable, and it is staggering: God is the father who runs.

Not the God who sits on a distant throne, waiting to see whether your repentance is sufficiently sincere before he considers your case. Not the God who meets you halfway, who says *I'll come to you when you've come far enough toward me*. Not the God who requires you to clean yourself up before you're allowed into the house.

This is the God who, while you are still a long way off — while you are still covered in the mud of your worst decisions, while the smell of the pigsty is still on you, while your rehearsed speech of self-justification is still on your lips — this God sees you. And runs.

The robe the father calls for is the *best* robe. The ring is a signet ring — a symbol of authority and belonging. The sandals are what distinguished family members from servants, who went barefoot. Before the boy can negotiate his way into the servant quarters, the father has already restored him to full sonship. The transaction the boy had prepared is simply irrelevant. The father is not interested in transactions.

He is interested in his son.

This, Jesus is saying to the Pharisees, is why I eat with sinners. Because this is what God is like. And if you find that offensive — if the sight of the reckless and the broken being welcomed to the table makes you grumble — then you need to hear the second half of this story.

---

## The Elder Son

The older brother has been out in the field, working. He hears the music and the dancing and asks a servant what's happening. When he's told — *your brother has come home and your father has killed the fattened calf* — he refuses to go in. He is angry.

And the father, remarkably, comes out to him too. He doesn't send a servant. He goes himself, to the son who is sulking at the edge of the celebration.

The elder son's complaint is revealing: *"All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours — this son of yours, not my brother — comes home after wasting your property with prostitutes, you kill the fattened calf for him."*

The elder son has been home all along, but he has been living with the heart of a servant, not a son. He has reduced his relationship with his father to a ledger of performance and reward. He has been in the house, but he has not known the father's heart. And now, confronted with grace, he is furious — because grace is deeply threatening to anyone who has organized their life around merit.

The father's response is tender: *"Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours."* He doesn't argue. He doesn't defend himself. He simply reminds the elder son of what has always been true. *You have had me. You have had the inheritance. You have had access to everything.* The tragedy of the elder son is not that he was cheated. It is that he was so busy keeping score that he never enjoyed what was already his.

---

## Where Are You in This Story?

Jesus leaves the parable open-ended. We never learn whether the older brother goes into the party. That open ending is deliberate. Because Jesus is looking at the Pharisees — and he is looking at us — and asking: *Which son are you today?*

Some of us are the younger son. We have taken what God gave us and run from him. We have spent ourselves in far countries of our own making — chasing things we thought would satisfy, ending up empty. And perhaps we have been rehearsing a speech, trying to figure out how to make our way back to God, assuming that the distance between us is something we have to close by our own effort.

Hear this: the father has already seen you. He is already running.

Others of us are the elder son. We have been in the church for years. We know the right answers. We serve, we give, we show up. But somewhere along the way, our faith became a transaction — a record of what we've done and what we're owed. And when we see grace extended to people we think haven't earned it, something in us tightens. Something in us resents the party.

The father comes out to us too. He comes not to condemn but to invite. *Come inside. Everything I have is yours. Can you not rejoice that your brother, who was dead, is alive?*

---

## Come to the Table

The story ends at the threshold of a party. The fattened calf is roasting. The music is playing. The father has run to one son and walked out to another. Both invitations are open.

The gospel is not primarily a set of demands. It is an announcement — the announcement that God, in Jesus Christ, has crossed every distance we have ever put between ourselves and him. He has come to us while we were still a long way off. He has put the best robe on our shoulders and a ring on our finger. He has prepared a feast.

The only question left is whether we will go in.

The door is open. The father is waiting.

Come home.

---

*Amen.*

But I want to be precise here, because this is not merely a picture of what God is *like*. It is a picture of what God has *done*. In Jesus Christ, the Father did not send a message or a policy or a set of requirements. He ran to us — not metaphorically, but in flesh and blood. He took on our humanity, entered our far country, and went all the way to a cross to close the distance we had put between ourselves and him. The father in the parable runs down a road. God, in Christ, ran all the way to Calvary. The robe, the ring, the sandals — these are not merely symbols of restored relationship. They are previews of what the resurrection would accomplish: the full restoration of our dignity as children of God, purchased at the cost of everything.

This, Jesus is saying to the Pharisees, is why I eat with sinners. Because this is what God is like. And if you find that offensive — if the sight of the reckless and the broken being welcomed to the table makes you grumble — then you need to hear the second half of this story.

---

The older brother has been out in the field, working. He hears the music and the dancing and asks a servant what's happening. When he's told — *your brother has come home and your father has killed the fattened calf* — he refuses to go in.

And perhaps we have been rehearsing a speech, trying to figure out how to make our way back to God, assuming the distance between us is something we have to close by our own effort.

Hear this: the father has already seen you. He is already running.

Some of us are the elder son. We have been in the church for years. We know the right answers. We serve, we give, we show up. But somewhere along the way, our faith became a transaction — a record of what we've done and what we're owed. And when we see grace extended to people we think haven't earned it, something in us tightens. Something in us resents the party.

He does not conclude, after a reasonable interval, that hope is no longer rational. He keeps looking. And when the figure appears on the horizon, he runs. Let that be your permission — to keep hoping, to keep watching, to refuse to let love calcify into resignation.

---

The story ends at the threshold of a party. The fattened calf is roasting. The music is playing. The father has run to one son and walked out to another. Both invitations are open. The door has not closed.

The gospel is not primarily a set of demands. It is an announcement — the announcement that God, in Jesus Christ, has crossed every distance we have ever put between ourselves and him. He has come to us while we were still a long way off. He has put the best robe on our shoulders and a ring on our finger. He has prepared a feast.

We don't know if the elder brother went in. Jesus leaves us standing at that threshold, with the father's voice still in the air, still warm, still asking. But that is where we live, isn't it — at the threshold, making our choice, hearing the music from inside.

The door is open. The father is waiting.

Come home.

---

*Amen.*

The younger son approaches his father with a request that, in the ancient Near Eastern world, would have landed like a slap across the face. "Father, give me the share of property that will come to me." In other words: *I want what I'll get when you die. Give it to me now.*

To ask for your inheritance while your father is still living was, in that culture, tantamount to wishing him dead. It was a public humiliation, a severing of relationship, a declaration that you valued his money more than his life. Any self-respecting patriarch in first-century Palestine would have been within his rights — within his *cultural* rights — to disown the boy on the spot.

Instead, the father divides the property between his sons. He gives the younger one what he asked for.

He could have refused. He could have closed his fist around that inheritance and said, *Not while I'm breathing*. No one would have blamed him. But he doesn't. The younger son gathers everything, heads to a distant country, and — in one of the most compressed sentences in all of Scripture — "squanders his wealth in wild living." He is so hungry that the pods he's throwing to the pigs look appetizing.

He came to himself. There is a beautiful theological weight in those four words. Come home.

# The Father Who Runs

### A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

---

Imagine you are sitting at your kitchen table one morning, drinking your coffee, when your phone rings. It's your child — the one you haven't heard from in two years. The one who left in anger, who said things that still echo in the quiet rooms of your house at night. Your hand trembles a little as you answer.

"I'm coming home," they say.

What do you do?

Do you sit very still and wait, composing yourself, preparing a measured response? Do you rehearse, perhaps, a list of conditions — a conversation you've needed to have for a long time? Or do you knock over the chair getting up from the table, fumble for your keys, and drive to wherever they are — just to close the distance?

Most of us, I suspect, know something about that second impulse. That wild, undignified rush toward the person we love. And if you know that feeling — if you have ever loved anyone that fiercely — then you are already standing at the edge of one of the most beautiful stories ever told.

---

## The Story Jesus Tells

In Luke 15, Jesus is in trouble — at least in the eyes of the religious establishment. The Pharisees and scribes are grumbling because he keeps eating with sinners. Tax collectors, prostitutes, the morally disreputable. "This man welcomes sinners," they mutter, "and eats with them." It is meant as an accusation. Jesus receives it as a description.

In response, he tells not one but three stories — a lost sheep, a lost coin, and finally this: the story of a lost son. Or rather, as we will see, the story of a father with two lost sons.

"There was a man who had two sons," Jesus begins. Already we are leaning in.

The younger son approaches his father with a request that, in the ancient Near Eastern world, would have landed like a slap across the face. "Father, give me the share of property that will come to me." In other words: *I want what I'll get when you die. Give it to me now.*

To ask for your inheritance while your father is still living was, in that culture, tantamount to wishing him dead. It was a public humiliation, a severing of relationship, a declaration that you valued his money more than his life. Any self-respecting patriarch in first-century Palestine would have been within his rights — within his *cultural* rights — to disown the boy on the spot.

Instead, the father divides the property between his sons. He gives the younger one what he asked for.

Why? Jesus doesn't explain. He doesn't need to. We already sense it: because love does not coerce. Because the father knows that a son kept home by force is not really home at all.

---

## The Far Country

The younger son gathers everything, heads to a distant country, and — in one of the most compressed sentences in all of Scripture — "squanders his wealth in wild living." The Greek word translated "wild" is *asotos*, which suggests not just excess but a kind of reckless, unsaved, wasteful existence. He is not merely having fun. He is disappearing.

We tend to imagine the far country as a place of obvious, dramatic sin. And sometimes it is. But the far country has many addresses. For some, it is a bottle or a needle. For others, it is a career pursued with such ferocity that family and faith become background noise. It is the endless chase for romance that will finally make you feel whole, or the hunger for approval that has you performing for an audience that doesn't even know your name. The far country is any place we go when we take what God has given us and run from him — convinced that we know better, that we can build a life that satisfies on our own terms.

And it never satisfies. It never does.

Then the famine comes. And the money runs out. And the friends evaporate. And the boy who once had servants finds himself feeding pigs — which, for a Jewish audience hearing this story, is about as low as a human being can sink. He is so hungry that the pods he's throwing to the pigs look appetizing.

Then Jesus gives us one of the most important phrases in the whole parable: *"He came to himself."*

He came to himself. There is a beautiful, complicated weight in those four words. They suggest that in his sin, in his self-destruction, the boy had somehow left himself behind — had become, in his waywardness, a stranger to his own soul. But we should be careful not to romanticize this moment too quickly. Is this genuine repentance? Or is it desperation? Look at what he's actually thinking: *My father's servants have food. I'm starving. I'll go back and offer to work for him.* There is still a transactional logic operating here. He is not yet running toward his father's love — he is calculating his way toward his father's pantry. The speech he rehearses on the road home is not yet the cry of a broken heart. It is a negotiation.

The real repentance, we will find, comes later — when the father's embrace makes the prepared speech collapse in his throat.

---

## The Father Who Runs

Now comes the hinge of the entire story. The moment everything turns.

*"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him."*

Still a long way off. Which means the father had been looking. Which means that every morning, perhaps, the old man had walked to the edge of his property and shaded his eyes against the sun and looked down that road. Which means hope had not died in him, even when there was no reasonable basis for hope.

And when he sees the boy — this distant, ragged, half-starved figure — he doesn't wait. He doesn't compose himself. He doesn't arrange his face into an expression of dignified expectation. He *runs*.

In the ancient world, a man of standing did not run. Running required you to gather up your robes, to expose your legs, to abandon the posture of authority. It was undignified. Embarrassing. Beneath a patriarch.

But there is something else happening here that we must not miss. In a village culture, the whole community would have known what this boy had done. The shame of it would have belonged to the whole town. When a son like this shuffled back down the road, the village would have been waiting — and not with a welcome. There was an ancient practice called the *kezazah*, in which the community would publicly cut off a Jewish boy who had squandered his inheritance among Gentiles, breaking a pot in front of him to symbolize that he was broken off from his people. The boy walking home that day was walking into a gauntlet of shame.

But the father runs.

By running to his son before the boy reaches the village, the father places himself between his son and the community's judgment. He takes the humiliation upon himself — the gathered robes, the exposed legs, the spectacle of an old man sprinting down a road — so that his son does not have to face the village alone. He absorbs the shame. He takes it on himself.

He falls on his son's neck and kisses him — the Greek suggests he kissed him repeatedly, urgently, the way you hold onto something you thought you'd lost forever. And the boy begins his rehearsed speech: *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son—"*

The father interrupts him.

He doesn't let him finish the transaction. He's already calling to the servants: *"Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let's have a feast and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."*

Dead and alive. Lost and found. These are resurrection words. And the robe, the ring, the sandals — these are not sentimental gifts. The best robe signals honor. The signet ring restores authority and belonging. The sandals distinguish a son from a servant, who went barefoot. Before the boy can negotiate his way into the servant quarters, the father has already restored him to full sonship. The transaction is simply irrelevant. The father is not interested in transactions.

He is interested in his son.

This is the theology embedded in this parable, and it is staggering: God is the father who runs. Not the God who sits on a distant throne, tallying your sins before deciding if your repentance is sincere enough. Not the God who meets you halfway. Not the God who requires you to clean yourself up before you're allowed through the door.

This is the God who, while you are still a long way off — still covered in the mud of your worst decisions, the smell of the pigsty still on you, your rehearsed speech of self-justification still on your lips — this God sees you. And runs. And absorbs every shame that should have been yours. And throws a party.

I know that for some of you, the word "Father" does not conjure up warmth. It conjures up distance, or silence, or anger. If that is your experience, I want you to hear this gently but clearly: Jesus is showing you the Father you always longed for, even if you never had him. The father in this story is not like any earthly father any of us has known perfectly. He is the Father we were made for. And he is running toward you.

---

## The Elder Son

The older brother has been out in the field, working. He hears the music and the dancing and asks a servant what's happening. When he's told — *your brother has come home and your father has killed the fattened calf* — he refuses to go in. He is angry.

And the father, remarkably, comes out to him too. He doesn't send a servant. He goes himself — again — to the son who is sulking at the edge of the celebration.

The elder son's complaint is revealing: *"All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours — this son of yours, not my brother — comes home after wasting your property with prostitutes, you kill the fattened calf for him."*

Do you hear the exhaustion in that speech? *All these years I've been slaving.* This man has been in his father's house, but he has been living with the heart of a servant. He has reduced his relationship with his father to a ledger — inputs and outputs, performance and reward. He has been in the house, but he has never known the father's heart. And now, confronted with grace, he is furious — because grace is deeply threatening to anyone who has organized their entire life around merit.

Have you ever felt that heat? The injustice of watching someone receive what they clearly haven't earned? Maybe it shows up as gossip dressed in the language of concern — *I'm just worried about her choices.* Maybe it's the quiet satisfaction when someone who left the faith struggles, and the quiet irritation when they come back and are celebrated. Maybe it's the subtle keeping of score — the tithing, the serving, the showing up — and the unspoken expectation that God owes you something for it. The elder brother is not a villain. He is tired. And he is lost — not in a far country, but in his own father's house, imprisoned by a merit system of his own construction.

The father's response is tender: *"Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours."* He doesn't argue. He doesn't defend himself. He simply reminds the elder son of what has always been true. *You have had me. You have had access to everything. You were never a servant. You were always a son.* The tragedy of the elder brother is not that he was cheated. It is that he was so busy keeping score that he never enjoyed what was already his.

---

## Where Are You in This Story?

Jesus leaves the parable open-ended. We never learn whether the older brother goes into the party. That open ending is deliberate. Because Jesus is looking at the Pharisees — and he is looking at us — and asking: *Which son are you today?*

Here is the honest truth: most of us oscillate. We are the younger son on Saturday night and the elder brother on Sunday morning. We carry both hungers — the hunger to run, and the hunger to be recognized for not running. And both of those hungers leave us standing outside the party, for different reasons.

Some of us are the younger son. We have taken what God gave us and run. We have spent ourselves in far countries of our own making, and we have ended up empty. And perhaps we have been rehearsing a speech, trying to figure out how to negotiate our way back to God, assuming the distance between us is something we have to close by sheer effort.

Hear this: the father has already seen you. He is already running.

Others of us are the elder son. We have been faithful, or at least we have been present. But somewhere along the way, faith became a transaction — a record of what we've done and what we're owed. And when we see grace extended to people we don't think have earned it, something in us tightens.

The father comes out to us too. Not to condemn, but to invite. *Come inside. Everything I have is yours. Can you not rejoice that your brother, who was dead, is alive?*

---

## Come to the Table

The story ends at the threshold of a party. The fattened calf is roasting. The music is playing. The father has run to one son and walked out to the other. Both invitations are open.

And here is the breathtaking thing: the father paid for that feast. The cost of the reconciliation — the property, the dignity, the shame absorbed on the road — all of it came from him. Grace is free to us precisely because it was not free to him. In the Christian story, we see this most fully in Jesus himself, the one who tells this parable and then lives it — who runs toward us in the flesh, who takes on our shame at the cross, who prepares a table for us not because we have earned our place at it, but because he loves us.

There are two ways to be lost. You can lose yourself in the far country, or you can lose yourself in the near country of religion and resentment. The same Father saves both. The same table has room for the rebel and the religious, for the one who ran and the one who stayed and resented it.

The door is open. The father is waiting.

Come home.

---

*Amen.*

Then the famine comes. The money runs out. The friends evaporate. And the boy who once had servants finds himself feeding pigs — which, for a Jewish audience hearing this story, is about as low as a human being can sink. He is so hungry that the pods he's throwing to the pigs look appetizing.

Then Jesus gives us one of the most important phrases in the whole parable: *"He came to himself."*

He came to himself. There is a beautiful theological weight in those four words. They suggest that in his sin, in his self-destruction, the boy had somehow left himself behind — had become, in his waywardness, a stranger to his own soul. The idols he chased did not expand him. They diminished him. And now, in the mud and the stench, something like clarity breaks through.

He rehearses a speech. He'll go home, he decides, and say: *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants."* Notice what he's doing. He is preparing a transaction. He will trade his sonship for a job. He has so thoroughly absorbed the logic of the world — the logic that says love must be earned, that grace is a myth, that you only get what you pay for — that he cannot imagine any other kind of homecoming than a negotiated one.

He heads home, rehearsing his lines.

---

## The Father Who Runs

Now comes the hinge of the entire story. The moment everything turns.

*"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him."*

Still a long way off. Which means the father had been looking. Which means that every morning, perhaps, the old man had walked to the edge of his property and shaded his eyes against the sun and looked down that road. Which means hope had not died in him, even when there was no reasonable basis for hope.

And when he sees the boy — this distant, ragged, half-starved figure — he doesn't wait. He doesn't compose himself. He doesn't arrange his face into an expression of dignified expectation. He *runs*.

In the ancient world, a man of standing did not run. Running required you to gather up your robes, to expose your legs, to abandon the posture of authority. It was undignified. Embarrassing. Beneath a patriarch.

The father runs anyway.

He falls on his son's neck. He kisses him — the Greek suggests he kissed him repeatedly, urgently, the way you hold onto something you thought you'd lost forever. And the boy begins his rehearsed speech: *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son—"*

The father interrupts him.

He doesn't let him finish. He doesn't hear the part about becoming a hired servant, because he's already calling to the servants himself: *"Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let's have a feast and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."*

Dead and alive. Lost and found. These are resurrection words. This is not merely a story about family reconciliation. Jesus is telling us something about the nature of God.

Here is the theology embedded in this parable, and it is staggering: God is the father who runs.

Not the God who sits on a distant throne, waiting to see whether your repentance is sufficiently sincere before he considers your case. Not the God who meets you halfway. Not the God who requires you to clean yourself up before you're allowed into the house. This is the God who, while you are still a long way off — while you are still covered in the mud of your worst decisions, while the smell of the pigsty is still on you, while your rehearsed speech of self-justification is still on your lips — this God sees you. And runs.

And here is what I want you to hear, especially if you feel too far gone, if the shame is too heavy to stand up straight under: God does not wait for you to straighten your posture. He runs to meet you in your mess. The robe he calls for is the *best* robe. The ring is a signet ring — a symbol of authority and belonging. The sandals are what distinguished family members from servants, who went barefoot. Before the boy can negotiate his way into the servant quarters, the father has already restored him to full sonship. The transaction the boy prepared is simply irrelevant. The father is not interested in transactions.

He is interested in his son.

This, Jesus is saying to the Pharisees, is why I eat with sinners. Because this is what God is like. And if you find that offensive — if the sight of the reckless and the broken being welcomed to the table makes you grumble — then you need to hear the second half of this story.

---

## The Elder Son

But the story doesn't end with the embrace. Because for many of us, the hardest distance to cross isn't the one we ran away from — it's the one we never left.

The older brother has been out in the field, working. He hears the music and the dancing and asks a servant what's happening. When he's told — *your brother has come home and your father has killed the fattened calf* — he refuses to go in. He is angry.

And the father, remarkably, comes out to him too. He doesn't send a servant. He goes himself, to the son who is sulking at the edge of the celebration.

The elder son's complaint is revealing: *"All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours — this son of yours, not my brother — comes home after wasting your property with prostitutes, you kill the fattened calf for him."*

The elder son has been home all along, but he has been living with the heart of a servant, not a son. He has reduced his relationship with his father to a ledger of performance and reward. He has been in the house, but he has not known the father's heart. His far country isn't a distant land — it's the isolation born of self-righteousness. He has stood in the same rooms as his father for years and remained, in the most important sense, a stranger to him.

And now, confronted with grace, he is furious — because grace is deeply threatening to anyone who has organized their life around merit. When the scoreboard is all you have, it is terrifying to discover that the game has been called off.

The father's response is tender: *"Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours."* He doesn't argue. He doesn't defend himself. He simply reminds the elder son of what has always been true. *You have had me. You have had the inheritance. You have had access to everything.* The tragedy of the elder son is not that he was cheated. It is that he was so busy keeping score that he never enjoyed what was already his.

---

## Where Are You in This Story?

Jesus leaves the parable open-ended. We never learn whether the older brother goes into the party. That open ending is deliberate. Because Jesus is looking at the Pharisees — and he is looking at us — and asking: *Which son are you today?*

Some of us are the younger son. We have taken what God gave us and run from him. We have spent ourselves in far countries of our own making — chasing things we thought would satisfy, ending up empty. And perhaps we have been rehearsing a speech, trying to figure out how to make our way back to God, assuming that the distance between us is something we have to close by our own effort, that we need to arrive cleaned up, composed, with the right words ready.

Stop rehearsing the speech that earns you a job. You don't need to negotiate your way back into the house. Today, just start walking. Take one step toward the horizon — because he is already looking for you. He has been looking every morning. And the moment you appear on that road, he will run.

Others of us are the elder son. We have been in the church for years. We know the right answers. We serve, we give, we show up. But somewhere along the way, our faith became a transaction — a record of what we've done and what we're owed. And when we see grace extended to people we think haven't earned it, something in us tightens. Something in us resents the party.

The father comes out to us too. He comes not to condemn but to invite. And coming inside, for the elder brother, means something very specific and very difficult: it means choosing to celebrate the grace shown to someone else, even when you feel you haven't received it yet. It means setting down the ledger. It means choosing joy over scorekeeping — not because the other person deserves it, but because that is what the father's house is like, and you have always had access to it.

*Come inside. Everything I have is yours. Can you not rejoice that your brother, who was dead, is alive?*

---

## Come to the Table

Do you remember the phone call at the beginning? The trembling hand, the voice on the other end of the line, the question of what you do next?

Here is what this parable tells us: God already answered that question. Before you dialed. Before you found the words. Before you worked up the courage to start walking home. He was already at the edge of the property, scanning the horizon. And the moment he saw you — ragged, rehearsed speech in hand, smelling of everything you're ashamed of — he ran.

The gospel is not primarily a set of demands. It is an announcement: that God, in Jesus Christ, has crossed every distance we have ever put between ourselves and him. He has come to us while we were still a long way off. He has put the best robe on our shoulders and a ring on our finger. He has prepared a feast, and the music is already playing.

The only question left is whether we will go in.

Not whether we are worthy of the feast — that question has already been answered by the One who set the table. The only question is whether we will accept the invitation of the Father who runs.

The door is open.

Come home.

---

*Amen.*

# The Father Who Runs

### A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

---

Imagine you are sitting at your kitchen table one morning, drinking your coffee, when your phone rings. It's your child — the one you haven't heard from in two years. The one who left in anger, who said things that still echo in the quiet rooms of your house at night. Your hand trembles a little as you answer.

"I'm coming home," they say.

What do you do?

Do you sit very still and wait, composing yourself, preparing a measured response? Do you rehearse, perhaps, a list of conditions — a conversation you've needed to have for a long time? Or do you knock over the chair getting up from the table, fumble for your keys, and drive to wherever they are — just to close the distance?

Most of us, I suspect, know something about that second impulse. That wild, undignified rush toward the person we love. And if you know that feeling — if you have ever loved anyone that fiercely — then you are already standing at the edge of one of the most beautiful stories ever told.

---

## The Story Jesus Tells

In Luke 15, Jesus is in trouble — at least in the eyes of the religious establishment. The Pharisees and scribes are grumbling because he keeps eating with sinners. Tax collectors, prostitutes, the morally disreputable. "This man welcomes sinners," they mutter, "and eats with them." It is meant as an accusation. Jesus receives it as a description.

In response, he tells not one but three stories — a lost sheep, a lost coin, and finally this: the story of a lost son. Or rather, as we will see, the story of a father with two lost sons.

"There was a man who had two sons," Jesus begins. Already we are leaning in.

The younger son approaches his father with a request that, in the ancient Near Eastern world, would have landed like a slap across the face. "Father, give me the share of property that will come to me." In other words: *I want what I'll get when you die. Give it to me now.*

To ask for your inheritance while your father is still living was, in that culture, tantamount to wishing him dead. It was a public humiliation, a severing of relationship, a declaration that you valued his money more than his life. Any self-respecting patriarch in first-century Palestine would have been within his rights — within his *cultural* rights — to disown the boy on the spot.

Instead, the father divides the property between his sons. He gives the younger one what he asked for.

Why? Jesus doesn't explain. He doesn't need to. We already sense it: because love does not coerce. Because the father knows that a son kept home by force is not really home at all.

---

## The Far Country

The younger son gathers everything, heads to a distant country, and — in one of the most compressed sentences in all of Scripture — "squanders his wealth in wild living." The Greek word translated "wild" is *asotos*, which suggests not just excess but a kind of reckless, unsaved, wasteful existence. He is not merely having fun. He is disappearing.

And then the famine comes. And the money runs out. And the friends evaporate. And the boy who once had servants finds himself feeding pigs — which, for a Jewish audience hearing this story, is about as low as a human being can sink. Picture it for a moment: the smell of the pen, the cold mud beneath his feet, the grunting of animals indifferent to his misery. He is utterly alone. He is so hungry that the pods he's throwing to the pigs look appetizing. There is no one to call, no one who remembers his name with any warmth, no one coming down the road for him. He has traveled as far from home as it is possible to travel, and the distance is not only geographical. He has become a stranger to himself.

Then Jesus gives us one of the most important phrases in the whole parable: *"He came to himself."*

He came to himself. There is a beautiful theological weight in those four words. They suggest that in his sin, in his self-destruction, the boy had somehow left himself behind — had become, in his waywardness, a stranger to his own soul. And now, in the mud and the stench, something like clarity breaks through.

He rehearses a speech. He'll go home, he decides, and say: *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants."* Notice what he's doing. He is preparing a transaction. He will trade his sonship for a job. He has so thoroughly absorbed the logic of the world — the logic that says love must be earned, that grace is a myth, that you only get what you pay for — that he cannot imagine any other kind of homecoming than a negotiated one.

He heads home, rehearsing his lines.

---

## The Father Who Runs

Now comes the hinge of the entire story. The moment everything turns.

*"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him."*

Still a long way off. Which means the father had been looking. Which means that every morning, perhaps, the old man had walked to the edge of his property and shaded his eyes against the sun and looked down that road. Which means hope had not died in him, even when there was no reasonable basis for hope.

And when he sees the boy — this distant, ragged, half-starved figure — he doesn't wait. He doesn't compose himself. He doesn't arrange his face into an expression of dignified expectation. He *runs*.

The father runs anyway.

He falls on his son's neck. He kisses him — the Greek suggests he kissed him repeatedly, urgently, the way you hold onto something you thought you'd lost forever. And the boy begins his rehearsed speech: *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son—"*

The father interrupts him.

He doesn't let him finish. He doesn't hear the part about becoming a hired servant, because he's already calling to the servants himself: *"Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let's have a feast and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."*

Dead and alive. Lost and found. These are resurrection words. This is not merely a story about family reconciliation. Jesus is telling us something about the nature of God.

---

## The God We Meet Here

Here is the theology embedded in this parable, and it is staggering: God is the father who runs.

Not the God who sits on a distant throne, waiting to see whether your repentance is sufficiently sincere before he considers your case. Not the God who meets you halfway, who says *I'll come to you when you've come far enough toward me*. Not the God who requires you to clean yourself up before you're allowed into the house.

This is the God who, while you are still a long way off — while you are still covered in the mud of your worst decisions, while the smell of the pigsty is still on you, while your rehearsed speech of self-justification is still on your lips — this God sees you. And runs.

And here is the breathtaking thing: this parable is not only a picture of what God is *like*. It is a picture of what God *did*. The father who runs to close the distance is the same God who, in Jesus Christ, did not wait for us to find our way home, but crossed every boundary himself — heaven to earth, glory to flesh, life to death — to meet us in our far country. The Incarnation is the father gathering up his robes. The cross is the father falling on his son's neck. When Jesus eats with sinners, he is not merely being kind. He is enacting the very parable he is telling. He *is* the father who runs.

The robe the father calls for is the *best* robe. The ring is a signet ring — a symbol of authority and belonging. The sandals are what distinguished family members from servants, who went barefoot. Before the boy can negotiate his way into the servant quarters, the father has already restored him to full sonship. The transaction the boy had prepared is simply irrelevant. The father is not interested in transactions.

He is interested in his son.

This, Jesus is saying to the Pharisees, is why I eat with sinners. Because this is what God is like. And if you find that offensive — if the sight of the reckless and the broken being welcomed to the table makes you grumble — then you need to hear the second half of this story.

---

## The Elder Son

The party was in full swing. The music was playing, the fattened calf was roasting, and the house was full of laughter. But the story is not yet complete. For outside, standing in the dark, was the other son — the one who had never left.

The older brother had been out in the field, working. He hears the music and the dancing and asks a servant what's happening. When he's told — *your brother has come home and your father has killed the fattened calf* — he refuses to go in. He is angry.

And the father, remarkably, comes out to him too. He doesn't send a servant. He goes himself, to the son who is sulking at the edge of the celebration.

The elder son's complaint is revealing: *"All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours — this son of yours, not my brother — comes home after wasting your property with prostitutes, you kill the fattened calf for him."*

Notice the language he uses: *slaving*. Not serving. Not living. *Slaving.* The elder son has been home all along, but he has been living with the heart of a hired hand, not a son. He has reduced his relationship with his father to a ledger of performance and reward — every obedience an entry on one side, every blessing owed on the other. He has been in the house, but he has not known the father's heart.

You may recognize this person. He's the one who has volunteered a hundred hours at the church but secretly simmers when a newcomer gets a warm welcome he feels he never received. She's the one who has done everything right — the quiet faithfulness, the years of showing up — and who finds, to her own shame, that grace extended to someone else feels like an injustice. We don't like to admit we know this feeling. But many of us do.

The elder son is not a villain. He is a warning. He shows us that it is entirely possible to live inside the father's house and still be a stranger to the father's heart. And now, confronted with grace, he is furious — because grace is deeply threatening to anyone who has organized their life around merit.

The father's response is tender: *"Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours."* He doesn't argue. He doesn't defend himself. He simply reminds the elder son of what has always been true. *You have had me. You have had the inheritance. You have had access to everything.* The tragedy of the elder son is not that he was cheated. It is that he was so busy keeping score that he never enjoyed what was already his.

---

## Where Are You in This Story?

Jesus leaves the parable open-ended. We never learn whether the older brother goes into the party. That unresolved ending is deliberate. Because Jesus is looking at the Pharisees — and he is looking at us — and asking: *Which son are you today?*

Some of us are the younger son. We have taken what God gave us and run from him. We have spent ourselves in far countries of our own making — chasing things we thought would satisfy, ending up empty. And perhaps we have been rehearsing a speech, trying to figure out how to make our way back to God, assuming that the distance between us is something we have to close by our own effort. We are calculating what we owe, wondering whether the debt is too large to repay, not sure we even deserve to ask.

Hear this: the father has already seen you. He is already running.

Others of us are the elder son. We have been in the church for years. We know the right answers. We serve, we give, we show up. But somewhere along the way, our faith became a transaction — a record of what we've done and what we're owed. And when we see grace extended to people we think haven't earned it, something in us tightens. Something in us resents the party.

The father comes out to us too. He comes not to condemn but to invite. *Come inside. Everything I have is yours. Can you not rejoice that your brother, who was dead, is alive?*

---

## Come to the Table

The story ends at the threshold of a party. The fattened calf is roasting. The music is playing. The father has run to one son and walked out to another. Both invitations are open.

The gospel is not primarily a set of demands. It is an announcement — the announcement that God, in Jesus Christ, has crossed every distance we have ever put between ourselves and him. He did not send a message. He did not post a notice on the door. He came himself, in flesh and blood, gathering up his robes and running. He has put the best robe on our shoulders and a ring on our finger. He has prepared a feast.

The only question left is whether we will go in.

The door is open. The father is waiting.

Come home.

---

*Amen.*

# The Father Who Runs

## A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

---

There is a painting that hangs in the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, Russia. Rembrandt van Rijn spent the last years of his life working on it, and many art historians believe it was the final major work he completed before his death. It depicts a single moment from the story we read this morning — the moment the younger son returns home. In the painting, the father is bent over his son, both enormous hands resting on the boy's back. One hand is broad and strong, a father's hand. The other is slender and gentle, almost a mother's hand. The son's head is pressed against the father's chest. His shoes are worn through. His head is shaved like a slave's. And the father's face — Rembrandt painted it in a wash of gold light — holds no anger, no recrimination, no trace of *I told you so*. Only unbearable tenderness.

Henri Nouwen, the great spiritual writer, sat in front of that painting for hours. Days, eventually. He said it changed his life. He said he finally understood, looking at those two figures — one broken, one bending — what the gospel actually is.

This morning, I want to sit with this story together. Not rush through it. Not reduce it to a moral lesson or a self-help principle. I want us to feel the weight of it, because Jesus told it for a reason, and that reason is as urgent today as it was two thousand years ago.

---

## The Context: Why Jesus Told This Story

Before we enter the parable itself, we need to understand why Jesus told it. Luke 15 opens with a scene that would have been scandalous to the religious leaders of the day: *"The Pharisees and the scribes were grumbling and saying, 'This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them.'"*

In the ancient world, sharing a meal was not a casual act. It was a statement of solidarity, of acceptance, of belonging. When Jesus sat down at the table with tax collectors and prostitutes and social outcasts, the religious establishment was outraged. And so Jesus tells three parables in a row — the lost sheep, the lost coin, and this one, the longest and richest of the three — to explain what he is doing. More than that: to explain what God is like.

This is not merely a story about family dysfunction. This is a story about the heart of God.

---

## The Younger Son: The Far Country

The younger son's request is, by the standards of his culture, almost unspeakably offensive. To demand your inheritance while your father is still living is essentially to say: *I wish you were dead. Give me what I'm owed and let me be done with you.* 

Rabbinical law at the time allowed a father to distribute his estate before death, but it was almost never done this way — demanded by the child, with such naked contempt. The father would have been publicly humiliated. In that honor-shame culture, the community would have expected the father to respond with fury, perhaps with disinheritance, perhaps with the kind of formal rejection that would have been legally and socially final.

Instead, the father divides the property. He gives the boy what he asks for.

This alone tells us something profound about the God Jesus is describing. God does not force love. He does not chain us to himself. He allows us to walk away, even when it breaks his heart.

The younger son goes to "a far country" — and that phrase is doing more work than it might appear. In Luke's world, a Jewish boy feeding pigs in a foreign land has hit the absolute bottom. Pigs were unclean animals. To tend them was to be rendered ritually impure, cut off from the covenant community, from the temple, from God himself. The "far country" is not just geographical. It is spiritual. It is the place of maximum distance from home.

And then comes the turning point, rendered in one of the most beautiful phrases in all of Scripture: *"He came to himself."*

He came to himself. There is a whole theology of repentance in those four words. The boy had been living outside of himself, outside of reality, outside of who he was created to be. Sin does that. It is a kind of madness — a departure from the self God made. And in the pigpen, hungry and humiliated, something breaks open in him. He remembers. He remembers his father's house, where even the hired servants have enough bread. He remembers who he is.

He rehearses a speech on the way home. *Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.* It is a speech of genuine contrition, but notice — it is also still a transaction. He is still trying to earn his way back. He is still calculating. He will trade his sonship for employment. He will work off the debt.

He does not yet understand his father.

---

## The Father Who Runs

*"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him."*

Still a long way off. Which means the father was watching. Which means the father had been watching every day, scanning the horizon, waiting. There is no casual glance here. This is a man who has been looking for his son.

And then — and this is the moment Rembrandt painted, the moment that stopped Henri Nouwen in his tracks — the father runs.

In the ancient Near East, a dignified older man did not run. Running required gathering up your robes, exposing your legs, abandoning the gravity and composure that social standing demanded. It was considered undignified. Embarrassing. The kind of thing you simply did not do if you had any regard for your reputation.

The father runs anyway.

He reaches his son before his son can reach him. He falls on his neck. He kisses him — the Greek word suggests he kissed him repeatedly, urgently, the way you kiss someone you thought you had lost forever. The son begins his rehearsed speech, and the father barely lets him finish it. He cuts him off. He turns to the servants: *Bring the best robe. Put a ring on his finger. Sandals on his feet. Kill the fattened calf. Let us eat and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.*

The robe is the father's own robe — a sign of honor and covering. The ring is a signet ring, a symbol of authority and belonging. The sandals mark him as a son, not a servant. And the fattened calf — that is a feast. That is a party for the whole village.

Notice what the father does not do. He does not make the boy prove himself first. He does not put him on probation. He does not say, *Let's see how you behave for a few months and then we'll talk about the ring.* The restoration is immediate, total, and extravagant. Before the boy has done a single thing to earn it.

This is grace. This is what grace looks like when it has a face.

---

## The Elder Son: The Other Far Country

We might be tempted to end the sermon here, wrapped in the warmth of that reunion. But Jesus doesn't end there. He introduces the elder son, and in doing so, he turns the story toward the people who most need to hear it — the Pharisees outside, grumbling, and perhaps some of us inside, doing the same.

The elder son comes in from the field. He hears music and dancing. He asks a servant what's happening, and when he's told, he refuses to go in. He is furious.

The father comes out to him — again, the father moves toward the son, not the other way around. And the elder son's speech is devastating in its bitterness: *"Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came — this son of yours, he can't even bring himself to say 'my brother' — who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him."*

The elder son has been home all along. And he has been in a far country of his own.

His far country is the country of religion without relationship. Of duty without delight. Of service without love. He has been working for his father for years, but he has been working *for* him the way an employee works for a boss, not the way a son lives with a father. He says, *I have served you.* He has never understood that everything the father has is already his — *"Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours."* He has been living like a hired servant in his father's own house.

This is the danger Jesus is pointing to for the religious leaders, and for all of us who have been in church our whole lives. It is possible to be technically present and spiritually absent. It is possible to keep all the rules and miss the relationship entirely. It is possible to be so focused on your own faithfulness that you lose the capacity for joy when someone else is found.

The elder son's anger reveals that he has never really known his father's heart. If he had, he would have been on the road with his father, running.

---

## A Word to Both Sons — and to Us

Here is what I want you to hear this morning, wherever you find yourself in this story.

If you are the younger son — if you have walked away, if you are in a far country, if you have made choices you are ashamed of and you wonder whether the door is still open — the father is on the porch. He has been watching. And the moment he sees you, he will not walk toward you with folded arms and a list of grievances. He will run. The robe is ready. The ring is ready. The table is set. *Come home.*

If you are the elder son — if you have been faithful for years but you have grown tired and resentful, if you have started keeping score, if the joy has drained out of your obedience and left only duty — the father comes out to you too. He does not abandon you for your bitterness. He comes to where you are and he says, *You are always with me. Everything I have is yours.* The question is whether you will come in. Whether you will let yourself be loved, not for your performance, but simply because you are his.

And if you are not sure which son you are — perhaps you are both, at different seasons of your life, sometimes running away and sometimes standing outside in the cold, arms crossed — know this: the father in this story never stops being the father. His love is not contingent on your behavior or your location. It is the fixed point around which the whole story turns.

---

## Conclusion

Jesus told this parable to people who had forgotten what God was like. He tells it to us for the same reason.

God is not a distant judge tallying our failures. God is not a disappointed employer waiting to see if we'll finally get it right. God is a father who scans the horizon. Who gathers up his robes and runs. Who throws a party before the apologies are even finished. Who comes out to the angry son standing in the dark and says, *Come in. Please. Come in.*

The gospel is not primarily a set of demands. It is an invitation.

The music has already started. The table is already set. The question this morning — the only question that matters — is whether you will come in.

---

*"For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."*

And they began to celebrate.

---

*Let us pray.*

# The Father Who Runs

### A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

---

Imagine for a moment that you are standing at the edge of your front porch, looking down the long road that stretches away from your house. It has been months — maybe years — since someone you love walked away from you down that road. You didn't know if they were alive or dead. You didn't know if they were eating. You didn't know if they had anyone to hold them when the nights got cold and the world got hard. But every morning, you got up. And every morning, you looked down that road.

That image — a parent standing at the edge of their world, watching, waiting, hoping — is the beating heart of one of the most beloved stories Jesus ever told. We call it the Parable of the Prodigal Son, though as we'll see this morning, it might just as easily be called the Parable of the Waiting Father, or even the Parable of Two Lost Sons. Because this story, when we sit with it long enough, has something to say to all of us — whether we have wandered far from home, or whether we have never left the yard but have somehow managed to lose ourselves anyway.

Let us open our Bibles to Luke chapter 15, beginning at verse 11.

---

## The Setting: Why Jesus Told This Story

Before we enter the story itself, we need to understand why Jesus told it. Luke 15 opens with a scene that would have been scandalous to the religious establishment of Jesus' day. Tax collectors and sinners — the people society had written off, the morally compromised, the ritually unclean — were drawing near to hear Jesus. And the Pharisees and scribes were grumbling. *"This man receives sinners and eats with them."*

That complaint is the fuse that lights this entire chapter. Jesus responds not with an argument, but with three stories: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son. Each story escalates in intimacy and intensity. A sheep is valuable. A coin is precious. But a son? A son is irreplaceable.

Jesus was not simply telling a heartwarming family story. He was holding up a mirror to everyone in the crowd — the wanderers and the self-righteous alike — and asking them to find themselves in the frame.

---

## The Younger Son: The Far Country of Our Choosing

*"Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me."*

To a first-century Jewish audience, these words would have landed like a slap. In that culture, requesting your inheritance while your father was still alive was tantamount to saying, *"I wish you were dead."* It was not merely rude — it was a profound rupture of relationship, a declaration that the son valued what the father *had* more than he valued the father *himself*.

And yet — and here is the first stunning grace in this story — the father gives it to him. He doesn't argue. He doesn't threaten. He divides his property and lets the boy go. This is not a picture of a passive or weak father. This is a picture of a father who loves his son enough to let him make catastrophic choices. There is no love without the freedom to refuse it.

The younger son gathers everything and leaves for "a far country." The Greek word here, *makran*, means a great distance — not just geographically, but existentially. He goes as far from home as a person can go. And there he squanders everything in what Luke calls "reckless living." The word in Greek is *asotos* — wastefully, without any thought of saving. He burns through his inheritance like a man on fire.

Then the famine comes. And here is where the story turns quietly devastating. The son who had everything now has nothing. He hires himself out to a citizen of that far country and is sent to feed pigs — an occupation that, for a Jewish boy, represented the absolute bottom. He was so hungry that the slop he was slopping into the pig troughs started to look like a meal.

And then Luke gives us one of the most beautiful phrases in all of Scripture: *"He came to himself."*

He came to himself. As if the real boy had been somewhere else all along — asleep inside the reckless, spending, running young man — and suddenly woke up. He remembered who he was. He remembered whose he was. He rehearsed a speech: *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants."*

Notice that even his repentance is a bit calculating. He's not coming home because he's sorry for breaking his father's heart. He's coming home because he's hungry. His motives are mixed, as our motives so often are. And yet — and here is the grace again — the father doesn't wait for a perfect repentance. He doesn't require a clean heart before he opens the door.

He just runs.

---

## The Father Who Runs

*"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."*

This is the center of the entire parable. Everything else orbits around this moment.

The father *saw* him while he was still a long way off. Which means the father had been looking. Day after day, the father had been scanning that road. The theologian Henri Nouwen once wrote that the father must have gone to the edge of his property every morning and evening, watching, because there is no other way to explain how he spotted his son at such a distance. The watching was not passive. It was an act of love sustained over time.

And when he saw him, he *ran*. In the ancient Near East, a man of dignity and status did not run. Running required you to hitch up your robes, to expose your legs, to abandon the gravity and composure expected of a patriarch. It was undignified. It was embarrassing. It was exactly what this father did, without a moment's hesitation.

He ran. He embraced. He kissed. The Greek word for kissed here is *katephilesen* — he kissed him repeatedly, fervently, the way you kiss someone you were afraid you might never see again.

The son begins his rehearsed speech. *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy—"* And the father interrupts him. He doesn't let him finish. He's already calling to the servants: *"Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found."*

The robe. The ring. The shoes. These are not incidental details. The robe covers the rags of the far country. The ring restores his status as a son, not a servant. The shoes on his feet — in a world where servants went barefoot — declare that he belongs to this household. The father is not reinstating the boy on probation. He is fully, extravagantly, publicly restoring him.

*"My son was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found."*

This is the Gospel in a sentence. This is the whole story of Scripture compressed into fourteen words. God does not receive us back as hired hands. He receives us back as sons and daughters — robed, ringed, shod, and celebrated.

---

## The Elder Son: Lost in the Yard

But the story doesn't end there. And this is where Jesus turns his gaze from the tax collectors and sinners to the Pharisees and scribes who had been grumbling at the edge of the crowd.

The elder son comes in from the field and hears music and dancing. He asks a servant what's happening. And when he learns that his brother has come home and his father has thrown a party, he is furious. He refuses to go in.

His father comes out to him — notice this: the father goes out to *both* sons. He is not a father who plays favorites, even when one son is clearly behaving better.

The elder son's speech is a masterpiece of wounded self-righteousness: *"Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came — who has devoured your property with prostitutes — you killed the fattened calf for him!"*

He calls him "this son of yours." He cannot bring himself to say "my brother." He has been in the house all along, but in his heart, he is just as far away as his brother ever was. He has been serving his father like an employee, keeping score, nursing grievances, measuring out his obedience in exchange for rewards he never received. He has been in the far country of his own resentment without ever leaving home.

And the father — still tender, still patient — says: *"Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."*

*Your brother.* The father gently corrects the elder son's language. He is your brother. And the story ends without telling us whether the elder son ever went in. Jesus leaves it open. Because the question is not really about a fictional older brother. The question is for the Pharisees. The question is for us.

---

## Application: Which Son Are You?

Here is the pastoral question this parable asks every one of us this morning: *Which son are you today?*

Some of you are the younger son. You have wandered — maybe not across geographic distance, but across the distance of the heart. You have taken the gifts of your life and spent them in ways that left you empty. You have ended up in a far country of your own making, feeding pigs, wondering how you got here. And you have rehearsed the speech. You know you don't deserve to be called a son or a daughter anymore.

I want you to hear this with everything I have: the father is already running. Before you get the words out. Before your repentance is perfect. Before you've cleaned yourself up. He saw you a long way off, and he is already running down the road, and when he reaches you, he is going to hold you so tightly you will feel the years of his waiting in his arms.

Come home. You are more welcome than you know.

And some of you are the elder son. You have been faithful. You have shown up. You have done the right things. And somewhere along the way, the faithfulness curdled into resentment. You've started keeping score. You look at people who seem to receive grace they haven't earned, and something in you tightens. You're standing outside the party, arms crossed, refusing to go in.

The father is coming out to you, too. And he is asking you the same thing he asked that elder son: *Will you come in? Will you let your brother be your brother again? Will you let grace be grace, even when it seems extravagant — especially when it seems extravagant?*

---

## Conclusion: The Party That Never Ends

The music and dancing in this parable are not incidental details. They are a picture of heaven itself. Jesus told this story to make clear that when one lost person finds their way home, all of heaven celebrates. There is joy in the presence of the angels over one sinner who repents.

The father in this story is not a careful, measured dispenser of second chances. He is a God who runs — who hitches up his robes and sprints down the road to meet us, who throws the best robe around our filthy shoulders, who puts the ring back on our fingers, who calls for the music to start.

This is who God is. This is what grace looks like when it has legs.

The party is already happening. The question is whether you will let yourself come in.

Come in.

*Amen.*
