# The Father Who Runs

### A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

---

There is a moment that every parent knows — or perhaps every person who has ever loved someone deeply enough to be afraid of losing them. It is the moment when you are watching the road. Maybe it is a teenager who missed curfew. Maybe it is a phone that keeps ringing and ringing without answer. Maybe it is a chair at the dinner table that sits empty when it should be full. You are watching the road, and every pair of headlights that sweeps across the curtains makes your heart leap, and then fall, and then wait again.

That image — a figure watching the road — is at the heart of one of the most famous stories Jesus ever told. We call it the Parable of the Prodigal Son. But I want to suggest to you this morning that we have been giving the wrong character top billing. This story is not primarily about a lost son. It is about a waiting father. And everything depends on understanding the difference.

---

## The Wound of the Request

Let us begin at the beginning, because the beginning is more shocking than we usually let ourselves feel.

*"Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me."*

In the ancient Near Eastern world, this request was not simply rude. It was, in the words of one scholar, the social equivalent of saying, "Father, I wish you were dead." Inheritance was distributed after a father's death. To demand it while the father still lived was to declare that, as far as the son was concerned, the father was already gone — that the relationship between them had no value beyond what could be extracted from it.

The father divides his property. He gives the younger son his share. And the son leaves.

Notice what Jesus does not give us here: he does not give us a scene of the father weeping, or raging, or pleading. He simply says the father divided his property and the son went away. The wound is inflicted quietly, the way real wounds often are, and then the story moves on. But we should not move on too quickly. We should sit for a moment with what it cost this father to open his hand and let his child go.

---

## The Far Country

The younger son travels to a far country and squanders everything. The Greek word Luke uses — *diaskorpizo* — means to scatter, to throw in every direction, the way you might throw seed, except that what he is throwing is his life. He spends everything on what the older brother will later call "prostitutes," though the text itself does not confirm this — it is the accusation of a bitter sibling, and we would do well to notice that. What the text tells us simply is that he wasted it. He scattered it. And then the money was gone.

A famine comes. He hires himself out to a citizen of that country who sends him to feed pigs. For a Jewish audience, Jesus could not have chosen a more degrading image. Pigs were unclean animals. To tend them was to be at the very bottom of the social and religious order. And then comes the line that should break our hearts open: *"He was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything."*

No one gave him anything.

He has spent his whole life learning to take. He demanded his inheritance. He scattered his resources. He consumed everything around him. And now, at the bottom of the far country, he has discovered the terrible logic of a life lived only for itself: when you have taken everything, there is nothing left to receive.

---

## The Turn

Then something happens. The text says, *"He came to himself."* 

That is a remarkable phrase. It implies that the boy had been away from himself — that the far country was not just a geographical location but a spiritual one, a place of self-exile, a place where he had become a stranger to his own soul. And now, sitting in the mud among the pigs, something in him wakes up.

He rehearses a speech. *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants."* This is not yet repentance in the fullest sense — not yet. He is calculating. He is working out the math of survival. He knows that his father's servants eat better than he does. He is coming home not because he loves his father but because he is hungry. And yet — and this is important — God uses even that. He uses even the hunger. He uses even the calculation. Because the direction of travel matters, even when the motivation is impure. He gets up. He turns toward home.

---

## The Father Who Runs

Now we arrive at the center of the story. The center of the story is not the son's return. The center of the story is what the father does before the son even reaches the door.

*"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him."*

The father saw him. Which means the father was looking. Which means that every day since the boy left, the father had been watching the road. This is not a man who had written off his son, who had hardened his heart, who had decided that the wound was too deep to risk again. This is a man who had been watching the road.

And when he sees the boy — still a long way off, still a silhouette on the horizon — the father does something that, in his culture, was as scandalous as the son's original request. He runs. Men of dignity and status did not run in the ancient world. Running required gathering up your robes, exposing your legs, abandoning the composed and measured pace that marked a man of honor. To run was to make yourself undignified. To run was to make yourself vulnerable.

The father runs anyway.

He falls on his son's neck. He kisses him. The boy begins his rehearsed speech — *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you"* — and the father interrupts him. There is no lecture. There is no probationary period. There is no "we'll see how you do." There is a robe and a ring and sandals and a fatted calf and a party, because *"this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found."*

The theologians have a word for what the father does. The word is *grace*. Grace is not the reward for getting your life together. Grace is not the prize at the end of the obstacle course. Grace is the father running down the road before you have finished your apology. Grace is the robe placed on your shoulders while you are still smelling of the pigsty.

---

## The Elder Brother

But Jesus is not finished. He gives us a second son, and this son is the one we often overlook because he is the one we are most likely to be.

The elder brother comes in from the field and hears music. He asks a servant what is happening. He learns that his brother has returned and his father has thrown a party. And he is furious. He will not go in.

The father comes out to him — notice that the father goes out to both sons, that the grace moves in both directions — and the elder brother's bitterness pours out: *"Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends."*

There it is. The elder brother has been in the house all along, but he has been in the far country too — a far country of resentment and scorekeeping and joyless duty. He has been obedient, but his obedience has been transactional. He has kept the rules, but he has not known the father's heart. He has been present in the home without ever being at home.

And so the father says to him, with extraordinary tenderness: *"Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."*

The parable ends there. We never find out if the elder brother goes in. Jesus leaves it open, and I believe he leaves it open on purpose — because the Pharisees and scribes who were listening, the ones who had been grumbling that Jesus ate with sinners, were the elder brothers in the story. And Jesus was giving them the same invitation the father gave: *Come in. The party is for you too. But you have to let go of the scorecard.*

---

## What This Means for Us

So what do we do with this story? Let me offer you three things to carry with you.

**First: You are more welcomed than you feel.** If you are sitting here this morning carrying the weight of something you have done — a relationship you have broken, a choice you cannot undo, a version of yourself you are ashamed of — I want you to hear this. The father in this story is not a metaphor. He is a portrait. Jesus is telling us what God is actually like. He is the one who has been watching the road. He is the one who runs. He does not need you to have your speech perfected before he embraces you. He meets you while you are still a long way off.

**Second: The direction of travel matters more than the purity of your motives.** The younger son came home partly because he was hungry. His repentance was mixed up with self-interest. God was not put off by that. He used the hunger to bring the boy home. If you are finding your way back to God — even haltingly, even imperfectly, even because life has hit you hard enough that you have no other options — that turning matters. Come home. God will meet you on the road.

**Third: Examine your own elder-brother tendencies.** This is perhaps the harder word for those of us who have been in the church a long time. It is possible to be faithful in attendance and barren in joy. It is possible to know all the right answers and miss the heart of the Father entirely. When someone whose life has been messier than ours finds grace, does it feel like good news? Or does it feel, if we are honest, a little like an injustice? The elder brother's tragedy is not that he stayed home. It is that he never truly believed the home was a place of abundance. He lived like a servant in his own father's house. The father's invitation to him — and to us — is to come inside, to discover that the party is not a threat to us but a gift, and to find that there is more than enough joy to go around.

---

## A Closing Word

There is a father watching the road.

He is watching for the one who left in anger, who wasted everything, who is still a long way off. He is watching for the one who never left physically but whose heart has grown cold and distant. He is watching for the skeptic, the burned-out, the grieving, the ashamed. He is watching for you.

And the moment he sees you — the moment you turn toward home — he will not wait for you to arrive. He will not stand at the door with folded arms, waiting to hear your explanation. He will gather up his robes and he will run, and he will fall on your neck, and he will call for the robe and the ring.

Because that is who God is.

That is the whole gospel, wrapped in a single story.

Come home.

The party has already started.

---

*"For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found."*
— Luke 15:24

# The Father Who Runs

## A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

---

There is a painting that has haunted me for years.

It hangs in the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, Russia — Rembrandt's *The Return of the Prodigal Son*, completed just before the great artist's death in 1669. In it, a ragged young man kneels before an elderly father. The boy's head is shaved — a sign of slavery or utter destitution. His sandals are worn through. His coat is barely a coat. And the old man bends over him, hands pressed gently against his son's shoulders, one hand broad and strong, one hand soft and tender. Rembrandt reportedly painted those two hands deliberately different — one masculine, one feminine — as though the father contains within himself every kind of love a person could need.

What strikes most people who stand before that painting is not the son. It is the father's face. He is not looking down with judgment. He is not looking away in disgust. He is looking at his son with an expression so full, so complete, so utterly without reservation, that theologian Henri Nouwen — who spent days sitting before that painting — said it changed his life. He wrote: "The Father is the one who, from the beginning, has been waiting for the return of his children."

That is the painting. Now let us open the text that inspired it.

---

### The Story Jesus Told

In Luke 15, Jesus is surrounded by tax collectors and sinners — the wrong kind of people, by the reckoning of the religious establishment. The Pharisees and scribes are muttering. *This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.* It is meant as an accusation. Jesus receives it as a compliment, and then he tells three stories about lost things: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son. The third story is the longest. It is the one we call the Parable of the Prodigal Son, though as we will see, the title might be missing the point.

The younger of two sons comes to his father and asks for his share of the inheritance. We should feel the weight of what he is doing. In the ancient Near East, to ask for your inheritance while your father is still living is tantamount to saying, *I wish you were dead.* It is not simply rude. It is a public declaration of contempt. It severs the relationship. It dishonors the family before the entire community.

And yet the father divides his property between them.

He gives the boy what he asked for. He does not chase him down the road. He does not send servants after him. He lets him go.

This is the first extraordinary thing in the story, and we often rush past it. The father could have refused. He could have punished. Instead, he opens his hands — and lets go.

---

### The Far Country

The younger son gathers everything and travels to a distant country. The Greek word Luke uses — *makran*, "far away" — is doing theological work. This is not merely geographical distance. This is the distance between who we were made to be and who we have become. It is the distance between home and the wasteland we sometimes choose.

He squanders everything in what the text calls "reckless living." Then famine strikes the land — as famines have a way of striking precisely when we have nothing left — and he finds himself feeding pigs for a Gentile farmer, longing to eat the pods the pigs are eating. For a Jewish audience, there is no lower image. He has become unclean in every sense the word could carry. He is starving, humiliated, and utterly alone.

And then — and this is one of the most beautiful phrases in all of Scripture — *he came to himself.*

He came to himself. As if the person he truly was had been waiting somewhere inside him, patient and quiet, while the other version of himself burned through every good thing. He remembers his father's house. He remembers that even the hired servants have bread enough to spare. He rehearses a speech: *Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.*

Notice what he is not doing here. He is not expecting restoration. He is not expecting forgiveness. He is hoping, at best, for employment. He has done the math on his own worthiness, and the numbers don't lie. He knows what he has done. He is not asking to be a son again. He is asking to be a servant.

He gets up. He begins the long walk home.

---

### The Father Who Runs

Now comes the moment that would have made Jesus's audience gasp.

*But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him.*

The father was watching. He had been watching. Every day, perhaps, standing at the edge of the road, scanning the horizon. He sees his son while the boy is still *a long way off* — which means the father was looking. Which means the father never stopped looking.

And then the text says something utterly undignified: *he ran.*

In the ancient world, a man of means and honor did not run. Running required you to hitch up your robes, to expose your legs, to abandon all the gravity and composure that social standing demanded. It was considered beneath a patriarch's dignity. And yet this father, seeing his son still far away, *hitches up his robes and runs.* He does not wait for the boy to complete his journey. He does not make him walk the last painful mile alone. He runs to him.

He falls on his neck. He kisses him. He is weeping before the boy can get a single word of his rehearsed speech out.

The son begins his confession. *Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son—*

He never finishes. He doesn't get to the part about being a hired servant. The father is already shouting instructions to the servants: *Bring the best robe. Put a ring on his finger. Sandals on his feet. Kill the fattened calf. We are going to have a party.*

The robe is the best robe — an honor robe, the kind draped over a guest of distinction. The ring is a signet ring — a symbol of authority and family identity. The sandals are significant because servants went barefoot; sons wore sandals. With each gift, the father is saying, *You are not a servant. You are not a hired hand. You are my son. You have always been my son.*

*For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.*

And they began to celebrate.

---

### The Elder Brother

We might be tempted to end the story there, wrapped in warmth. But Jesus is not finished, because Jesus never forgets the Pharisees standing at the edge of the crowd.

The elder brother comes in from the field and hears the music. He asks a servant what is happening. When he learns that his younger brother has returned — and that his father has thrown a party — he is furious. He refuses to go in. And the father, remarkably, comes out to him too.

The elder brother's speech is a masterpiece of resentment: *Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came — he doesn't even say "my brother" — who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.*

Every word is technically true. And every word is utterly loveless.

The elder brother has been home all along, and yet he too has been living in a far country — the far country of obligation, of scorekeeping, of a relationship with his father built entirely on performance. He has never run away, but he has never truly come home either. He calls his service "slavery." He has never understood that everything the father has is his, not because he earned it, but because he is loved.

The father does not rebuke him. He says, *Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.*

Jesus ends the story there. We never find out if the elder brother goes in. The ending is open — deliberately so — because the Pharisees are still standing at the edge of the crowd, and Jesus is asking them: *Will you come in? Will you celebrate? Or will you stand outside in your righteousness, refusing to rejoice over what God rejoices over?*

---

### What This Means for Us

This parable is not really about a prodigal son. It is about a prodigal father — a father extravagantly, recklessly, almost scandalously generous with his love.

And here is the question it asks each of us: Which son are you?

Some of us know exactly what it is to be the younger son. We have taken what was given to us — our health, our relationships, our years, our faith — and we have spent it badly. We have ended up somewhere we never intended to be, feeding pigs in a far country, ashamed to look up. And we have told ourselves the same lie the younger son told himself: *I am no longer worthy. I cannot go back. The best I can hope for is to be tolerated.*

If that is you, I want you to hear the text again. *While he was still a long way off, his father saw him.* The father is watching the road. He has been watching the road. And the moment you turn toward home — not when you arrive, not when you have cleaned yourself up, not when you have composed the perfect apology — the moment you turn, he runs. He runs to you. He is not waiting to hear your speech. He is already calling for the robe, the ring, the sandals, the feast.

You do not have to earn your way back. You cannot earn your way back. That is the whole point.

But some of us are the elder brother. We have never left. We have shown up, done the work, followed the rules, and quietly seethed at those who didn't — and then seemed to get away with it. We have confused faithfulness with earning, and we have built a prison out of our own virtue. We stand outside the party, arms crossed, and we call it righteousness.

The father comes out to us too. *Everything I have is yours.* But we have to choose to come in. We have to choose to celebrate what God celebrates. We have to learn that grace is not a reward distributed to the deserving — it is the very nature of the One who made us.

---

### Come Home

There is a seat at the table with your name on it. There has always been a seat at the table with your name on it. The Father did not set it reluctantly. He set it with joy, with hope, with the kind of love that gets up early and watches the road and runs — runs — at the first sight of you coming home.

You are not a servant in this house.

You are a son. You are a daughter. You have always been.

Come in.

The feast has already begun.

---

*Let us pray.*

*Father, you are the one who runs. Forgive us for the ways we have wandered into far countries, and forgive us for the ways we have stood outside the party, refusing to rejoice. Meet us where we are. Bring us home. Teach us to love what you love, to celebrate what you celebrate, and to live as sons and daughters rather than servants. In the name of Jesus, who told this story because he is this story. Amen.*

# The Father Who Runs

### A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

---

Imagine you are standing at your kitchen window on an ordinary Tuesday afternoon. The dishes are drying in the rack. A pot of something warm is on the stove. And then, far down the road — farther than you should even be able to see — you recognize a silhouette. Something in the way those shoulders move, something in the particular rhythm of that walk. Your heart does something involuntary. Before your mind has finished the thought, your feet are already moving. You are out the door. You are running.

You haven't run like this in years. You don't care. The neighbors can watch. The dinner can burn. Nothing in this moment matters except closing the distance between you and the one you thought you might never see again.

That image — the running father — is the beating heart of the story Jesus tells in Luke 15. And if we can find our way into that image, I believe it will change the way we understand not just this parable, but the entire character of God.

---

## The World Jesus Was Talking Into

Before we enter the story itself, we need to understand *why* Jesus told it. Luke 15 opens with a scene that would have been genuinely scandalous to its first audience: "Now the tax collectors and sinners were all gathering around to hear Jesus. But the Pharisees and the teachers of the law muttered, 'This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.'"

That's the provocation. The religious establishment is offended — not by what Jesus is teaching, but by *who he is eating with*. In the ancient world, to share a meal with someone was to declare solidarity with them, to say: *your honor is my honor, your shame is my shame.* The Pharisees had built their entire identity around careful separation from the contaminating influence of sinners. And here is this rabbi, this supposed man of God, pulling up a chair and breaking bread with the very people they had written off.

Jesus responds not with an argument but with three stories: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. Each one is an answer to the muttering. Each one is saying: *You think I shouldn't be running toward these people? Let me tell you about a father who ran.*

---

## The Younger Son: The Far Country

"There was a man who had two sons," Jesus begins. Simple. Domestic. But what happens next would have made every Jewish listener in the crowd catch their breath.

The younger son approaches his father and asks for his share of the estate. Now. Today. While the father is still living.

To ask for your inheritance before your father's death was not merely rude in that culture. It was, in essence, saying: *I wish you were dead.* The father's wealth was tied up in land — land that represented family identity, ancestral legacy, the covenant of belonging. To liquidate it was to sever yourself from all of that. Scholars tell us that in the ancient Near East, a son who made such a demand could be publicly beaten. The community might disown him entirely.

But the father does something astonishing. He divides his property between his sons. He absorbs the insult. He lets him go.

The younger son gathers everything and heads off to "a distant country" — and that phrase matters. The Greek word is *makran*, far away, far off. He is not just geographically distant. He is spiritually, morally, relationally far. He is in exile. He squanders everything in what the text calls "wild living" — reckless, wasteful, the kind of spending that feels like freedom until the money runs out.

Then comes the famine. Then comes the humiliation. He ends up feeding pigs — and for a Jewish audience, there is no lower image available. He is feeding *unclean* animals and longing to eat their food. He has arrived at the absolute bottom.

And it is there, in the pigpen, that something happens. The text says, "he came to himself." What a phrase. He came to himself. As if the person he truly was had been somewhere else — had been lost — and only now, in the worst moment of his life, does he return to his own senses, his own identity, his own story.

He rehearses a speech. *Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.* He is not expecting restoration. He is hoping for employment. He is aiming for survival, not sonship. He has so thoroughly internalized his own unworthiness that the best he can imagine is a wage and a cot.

So he sets off toward home.

---

## The Father Who Runs

Here is where the story breaks open.

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him."

The father sees him while he is still far off. Which means the father has been looking. Which means that every morning, perhaps, this man has walked to the edge of the road and scanned the horizon. He has not moved on. He has not filled the silence with anger or wounded pride. He has been *watching*.

And when he sees his son, he does not compose himself. He does not wait for the boy to arrive and make his speech. He does not prepare a measured response that balances grace with appropriate consequence. He runs.

In the ancient world, a man of dignity — a landowner, a patriarch — did not run. Running meant lifting your robes, exposing your legs, abandoning the posture of authority. It was undignified. It was the kind of thing servants did, not masters.

The father runs anyway.

He reaches his son and falls on his neck and kisses him. The son begins his rehearsed speech — *Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you, I am no longer worthy to be called your son* — and the father is already calling to the servants. *Bring the best robe. Put a ring on his finger. Sandals on his feet.* These are not small gestures. The robe signals honor. The ring signals authority. The sandals signal that this person is not a servant — servants went barefoot. The father is not restoring the boy to hired-hand status. He is restoring him completely. *Kill the fattened calf. Let us eat and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.*

This is the gospel in miniature. This is what grace actually looks like when it puts on skin and runs down a road.

---

## The Elder Son: The Near Country

But Jesus is not finished. Because there are two sons in this story, and the second son is equally lost — just in a different way.

The elder son is in the field when the party starts. He hears music and dancing and asks a servant what's going on. When he's told his brother has come home and the father has thrown a feast, he refuses to go in. He is furious.

His father comes out to him — notice that the father goes out to *both* sons — and pleads with him. And the elder son unloads decades of resentment: "Look! All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!"

The elder son has been home the whole time, and yet he is just as far from his father as his brother was in the distant country. He has been serving, but not out of love — out of a ledger-keeping, merit-accumulating, score-settling sense of obligation. He calls his brother "this son of yours" — he cannot even say *my brother*. He has written him off completely.

And notice what else he reveals: he never believed the father's love was freely given. He thought it was *earned*. He has been in the father's house, eating the father's food, working the father's land — and he has never understood that it was all already his. "Son," the father says gently, "you are always with me, and everything I have is yours."

The elder son's lostness is harder to see because it is dressed in respectability. He has never run away. He has never embarrassed anyone. But his heart is as far from his father as his brother's ever was. He cannot celebrate grace because he has never believed he needed it.

Jesus leaves the story open-ended. We do not know if the elder son goes in to the party. That open ending is deliberate. Because Jesus is looking at the Pharisees when he tells this story, and he is asking them — he is asking *us* — which son are you? And will you come in?

---

## The God This Story Reveals

This parable is sometimes called the Parable of the Prodigal Son, but many theologians have suggested it should be called the Parable of the Prodigal Father — because *prodigal* means lavishly, recklessly generous, and it is the father whose extravagance is most on display here.

The God Jesus is revealing in this story is not a God who waits behind a closed door, arms folded, making you prove your sincerity before he'll consider letting you back in. He is not a God who says, *Well, let's see how things go for a few months and then we'll talk about your status.* He is a God who has been scanning the horizon. He is a God who sees you while you are still a long way off. He is a God who lifts his robes and runs.

That is the answer to the Pharisees' muttering. That is why Jesus eats with sinners. Because the God he knows — the God he *is* — cannot wait for the lost to find their way back. He goes to meet them.

---

## Where Do You Find Yourself?

So let me ask you gently, this morning: where do you find yourself in this story?

Some of you are in the far country right now. You have made choices that have taken you far from where you thought you'd be, far from who you thought you'd be. You have rehearsed your speech — the one where you ask for the minimum, where you settle for hired-hand status because you've decided you've forfeited the right to be called a child. I want you to hear this: the father is already running. You don't have to have the speech perfect. You don't have to have yourself cleaned up. You just have to turn toward home.

Some of you are the elder son. You've been in the church for years. You've served on committees and sung in the choir and shown up faithfully. But somewhere along the way, faith became a transaction, and you've been keeping score — of your own goodness, of other people's failures, of who deserves grace and who doesn't. And when you see grace given to someone you've decided doesn't deserve it, something in you tightens rather than rejoices. The father is coming out to you, too. He is pleading with you to come inside. There is room at this table for the self-righteous as well as the reckless — but you have to be willing to sit down next to each other.

And some of you simply need to be reminded, today, that you are loved. Not because of what you've done or what you've avoided. Not because of how well you've managed your spiritual life this week. You are loved because the father has been watching for you, and when he sees you, he runs.

---

## Conclusion

There is a feast being prepared. There is music already playing. The best robe is being brought out. The ring is ready.

The father is standing at the edge of the road, looking out, and he sees you coming. He has always seen you coming.

And he is running.

Come home.

---

*Amen.*

# The Father Who Runs

### A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

---

Imagine for a moment that you are standing at the window of your house. You have been standing there a long time — days, maybe weeks, maybe longer than you can honestly remember. You are watching the road. The road that leads away from your property and disappears over the hill. The road your child walked down without looking back.

Every morning you pull back the curtain. Every evening you watch the light fade over that empty stretch of dirt. Your neighbors have stopped asking about your son. Your older child has stopped mentioning his name. But you — you cannot stop watching. Because somewhere in you, beneath the grief and the humiliation and the unanswered questions, there is something that refuses to give up. Something that says: *he could still come home.*

And then one morning, you see a figure in the distance. Ragged. Slow-moving. Barely recognizable. But something in the way he walks — something in the slope of those shoulders — makes your heart lurch in your chest.

And you run.

This is the story Jesus tells in Luke 15. And if we let it, it will undo us completely — in the best possible way.

---

## The World Into Which Jesus Speaks

Before we enter the story itself, we need to understand *why* Jesus tells it. Luke 15 opens with a scene that would have made the religious establishment deeply uncomfortable. Tax collectors and sinners were gathering around Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes were grumbling: *"This man receives sinners and eats with them."*

That word — *receives* — is worth pausing on. It doesn't just mean Jesus tolerated their presence. It means he welcomed them. He sat with them. He shared meals with them, which in the ancient world was an act of profound social and spiritual intimacy. You didn't eat with just anyone.

And so Jesus responds to the grumbling not with an argument, but with three stories. A lost sheep. A lost coin. And then this — the longest, most layered, most devastating of the three. A story about a lost son. Or rather, if we read carefully, about *two* lost sons. And about a father who is the real protagonist of the whole thing.

---

## The Younger Son: The Audacity of Departure

*"There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, 'Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.'"* (Luke 15:11-12)

In the first-century Jewish world, what this son is doing is almost unthinkable. To demand your inheritance while your father is still living is, in effect, to say: *I wish you were dead. You are only useful to me as a source of wealth. I want what you can give me, not you yourself.*

The father, shockingly, gives it to him. This is the first glimpse of something unusual about this father — he does not coerce. He does not chain his son to the property. He lets him go.

The son takes everything and travels to a "far country," and there, Luke tells us with almost brutal economy, he "squandered his property in reckless living." The Greek word is *diaskorpizō* — to scatter, to throw to the winds. Everything his father worked for, everything that represented years of labor and love and legacy — scattered.

Then a famine comes. And the son finds himself feeding pigs for a Gentile farmer, hungry enough to eat the pods he's throwing to the animals. For a Jewish listener, this is the absolute bottom. Pigs were unclean animals. This young man has ended up as far from home, as far from his people, as far from his God as it is possible to be.

And then — and this is the hinge of the whole story — *"he came to himself."* 

I love that phrase. *He came to himself.* As if he had been somewhere else entirely. As if the real him had been buried under layers of fantasy and foolishness and had finally clawed its way back to the surface. He remembers his father's house. He remembers that even the hired servants have bread enough to spare. And he makes a decision.

He rehearses a speech on the way home. *"Father, I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants."* It's a good speech. Humble. Realistic. He has done the math on his own dignity and found it wanting.

But the father has been watching the road.

---

## The Father Who Runs

*"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."* (Luke 15:20)

Here is where the story does something so unexpected that its original hearers would have gasped.

In the ancient Near East, a man of standing did not run. Running required hitching up your robes, exposing your legs — it was considered undignified, even shameful, for a patriarch. And yet this father sees his son "still a long way off" — which means he was looking, which means he had been watching — and he runs. He abandons his dignity. He sprints down the road toward the wreck of his child.

He doesn't wait for the speech. He doesn't make the son grovel on the doorstep. He falls on his neck and kisses him — the word in Greek suggests repeated, fervent kissing, the kind of greeting you give someone you thought you would never see again.

The son begins his rehearsed speech. The father barely lets him finish before he's calling for the robe, the ring, the sandals. The robe — the best one, a mark of honor. The ring — a signet ring, a symbol of restored authority and belonging. The sandals — because servants went barefoot; this son is not going to be a servant. And then the feast. The fatted calf. The music. The dancing.

*"For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found."*

Notice what the father does *not* say. He does not say: "Well, let's see how he does for a few months before we celebrate." He does not say: "He'll need to earn back my trust." He does not say: "We should probably talk about what you did before we can move forward." The welcome is total. Immediate. Overwhelming. It is not based on the son's performance or promise of future good behavior. It is based entirely on the father's love.

This, Jesus is saying to the grumbling Pharisees, is what God is like. This is what it looks like when a sinner comes home. Heaven does not wait cautiously to see if the repentance is genuine. Heaven throws a party.

---

## The Elder Son: The Danger of Being Right

But the story doesn't end there, and this is what makes Luke 15 so remarkable. Because Jesus knows his audience. He knows there are people listening who have never run off to a far country. Who have stayed home. Who have been faithful. Who have done everything right.

*"Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing."* (Luke 15:25)

The older son refuses to go in. And when the father comes out to him — and notice that the father comes out to *him* too, just as he ran to the younger — the older son's anger pours out:

*"Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"*

There is real pain here. Real grievance. And Jesus doesn't dismiss it. The older son has worked hard. He has been loyal. His complaint is not entirely without merit.

But listen to what he says: *"I have served you."* Served. Like a slave, not a son. And: *"you never gave me."* As if the relationship were a transaction, a ledger of debits and credits. And then the chilling distance in his language: *"this son of yours"* — not "my brother." He has already disowned him.

The elder son has been in the house all along, but he has never understood what the house is. He has been working for wages in his father's home when he could have been living as a beloved son. His obedience has been real, but somewhere along the way it curdled into resentment. He kept all the rules, and the rules kept him — but they could not give him what he most needed, which was the simple joy of knowing he was loved.

The father's response is tender: *"Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours."* Everything. It was always already yours. You never had to earn it.

The story ends without resolution. We don't know if the older son goes in. We don't know if he joins the party. Luke leaves it open — because Jesus is looking at the Pharisees as he tells this story, and the question hangs in the air between them: *Will you come in? Or will you stand outside, arms folded, certain you are right, while the music plays without you?*

---

## What This Means for Us

Here is the uncomfortable and beautiful truth: most of us are both sons at different times in our lives.

There are seasons when we are the younger son — when we have taken the gifts of God and wandered off with them, when we have spent ourselves on things that left us empty, when we have ended up somewhere we never intended to be. If that is you today — if you are somewhere in that far country, or just beginning to "come to yourself" — then hear this: *the Father has been watching the road.* He is not waiting with a list of conditions. He is not going to make you prove yourself before he welcomes you back. He will run to you before you finish your apology.

And there are seasons when we are the older son — when we have been faithful and diligent and quietly, secretly, resentful. When someone else's grace feels like an injustice to us. When we have been so busy being right that we have forgotten how to celebrate. If that is you — if you find yourself outside the party, arms crossed, watching others receive what you feel you deserve — then hear this too: *the Father comes out to you as well.* He has not forgotten you. All that is his is yours. But you have to come in.

---

## The Father Who Still Runs

The parable of the Prodigal Son is, in the end, not primarily a story about sons at all. It is a story about a father. A father whose love is so extravagant, so undignified, so relentlessly pursuing that it breaks every expectation we have about how love should work.

The theologian Henri Nouwen spent years meditating on Rembrandt's painting of this scene — the old father with his hands on the kneeling son's shoulders, one hand strong and masculine, one hand soft and gentle, both of them holding. Nouwen came to believe that the deepest call of the Christian life is not just to *receive* that embrace, but eventually to *become* that father. To become people of such extravagant, undignified, pursuing love that we too run down roads and throw parties and come out to the ones who are standing in the dark.

But we cannot give what we have not received.

So let us receive it first. Let us stand still for a moment and let the Father run to us. Let us stop rehearsing our speeches about how we'll do better, and let him put the robe on our shoulders. Let us hear the music that has been playing all along.

And then — then — let us go and throw open the door for someone else.

*Thanks be to God.*

---

*Amen.*

## The Unseen Welcome: A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

**Opening Illustration: The Two Empty Chairs**

Good morning. If you look around this sanctuary, you’ll likely see a few empty seats. We might assume they’re just for the regulars who are out of town or under the weather. But I’d like you to imagine, for a moment, two particular empty chairs. The first belongs to someone who feels they have wandered too far. They’ve made choices they deeply regret, burned bridges, and squandered precious things. They believe the door to this place, to this community, to God’s family, is locked tight against them. They sit at home, convinced their story is one of irreversible loss.

The second empty chair belongs to someone who is, by all accounts, here. They haven’t missed a service in years. They serve on committees, they give faithfully, they know the right answers. But in their heart, there’s a chilling emptiness. Their faith feels like a long, joyless duty, a contract they are fulfilling without ever feeling the embrace of the one who made it. Resentment simmers beneath a polished surface. They, too, in their own way, are far from home.

Both of these chairs, you see, represent the same profound human problem: a fractured relationship with a loving Father. And into this aching space, Jesus tells perhaps his most beloved and misunderstood story. It’s a story not just about a wayward son, but about two lost sons and one unfathomably gracious Father. It’s a story for the one who has run, and for the one who has never left the property but has never truly come home. It’s the parable of the Prodigal Son.

**I. The Younger Son: The Lostness of Rebellion (Luke 15:11-19)**

Jesus begins: “There was a man who had two sons.” The younger one makes a shocking, heart-rending request: “Father, give me the share of the property that will belong to me.” In that culture, this was more than a financial transaction. It was a symbolic death wish. He was saying, “I wish you were dead. Your money means more to me than your presence. I want my inheritance, but I don’t want you.” It is the essence of sin: not just breaking rules, but demanding autonomy from God, treating Him as a means to our ends, a dispenser of blessings we can take and use as we please.

The Father, in a stunning act of heartbreaking love, grants the request. He lets him go. And the son goes to a distant country, a place of moral and relational distance from everything he knew. There, he “squandered his property in dissolute living.” The Greek word here is *diaskorpizō*—to scatter, to waste, to dissipate. It’s a picture of the human soul fragmented by the pursuit of pleasure, significance, and freedom apart from the Father’s design. And it always ends in famine. The world’s promises run out.

Hitting rock bottom, he attaches himself to a citizen of that country who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For Jesus’ Jewish audience, this was the ultimate degradation: a son of Israel, caring for unclean animals, longing to eat their food. In his desperation, he “came to himself.” This is not yet repentance, but a moment of brutal clarity. He sees his situation for what it is: utter ruin. He rehearses a speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired hands.”

Notice the transactional nature of his planned return. It’s a business proposal: “I am no longer worthy of sonship, so let me earn my keep.” This is the logical end of rebellion: the belief that we must now work our way back into favor. He understands his sin, but he has not yet grasped the nature of his Father’s love.

**II. The Father: The Unseen Welcome (Luke 15:20-24)**

“But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion.” This is the pivot of the parable, the hinge on which everything turns. The Father wasn’t passively waiting; he was actively watching, scanning the horizon for a silhouette he would recognize anywhere. His love was not dormant; it was expectant.

And then he runs. In ancient Middle Eastern culture, patriarchs did not run. They walked with dignity. But this Father, throwing dignity to the wind, hikes up his robes and runs—a shocking, undignified, public display of eager love. He runs to close the gap that the son could never bridge on his own.

Before the son can finish his rehearsed speech of unworthiness and transaction, the Father interrupts him. He doesn’t let him finish the part about being a hired hand. Instead, he showers him with symbols of restoration: the best robe (a sign of honor and authority), a ring (a sign of family identity and authority), sandals (for a son, not a barefoot slave), and the fatted calf (a celebratory feast for the whole community).

“For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.” The Father’s declaration is absolute. The son’s identity is not “former wastrel” or “probationary worker.” He is “my son.” His return is not a negotiation; it is a resurrection. The welcome is not earned; it is given. It is grace.

**III. The Older Son: The Lostness of Resentment (Luke 15:25-30)**

Now we meet the second empty chair. The older son, coming in from the field, hears the music and dancing. He learns the reason and becomes angry. He refuses to go in. His Father, once again showing incredible grace, comes out and pleads with him. And the older son’s heart spills out: “Listen! For all these years I have been working like a slave for you, and I have never disobeyed your command; yet you have never given me even a young goat so that I might celebrate with my friends.”

His speech is a masterpiece of resentment. Notice the pronouns: “I,” “me,” “my.” Notice the language: “working like a slave.” He has been home all along, but he has never understood sonship. He sees his relationship with his Father as a contract of works: obedience in exchange for rewards. He has kept the rules but lost the relationship. He is obedient but joyless, faithful but furious.

And then the devastating accusation: “But when this son of yours came back…” He cannot even say “my brother.” He distances himself. “This son of yours,” this wastrel, this sinner. And he levels the charge: “who has devoured your property with prostitutes.” Was that true? The text doesn’t say that. It’s the older brother’s interpretation, layered with self-righteous judgment. His heart, so long confined by duty, has become a prison of comparison and bitterness. He is just as lost as his brother, but his lostness is more insidious because it wears the clothes of fidelity. He is outside the house, outside the feast, by his own choice.

**IV. The Father’s Plea: An Invitation to Both Sons (Luke 15:31-32)**

The Father’s response to this older son is just as tender, just as revealing. “Son,” he says—*teknon*, a term of endearment. “You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” The Father affirms his constant presence and his full inheritance. The older son never had to work for a young goat; the entire estate was already his! He had been living like a hired hand in his mind, while enjoying the privileges of a son all along.

“But we had to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.” The Father reframes everything. He calls the younger son “this brother of yours,” re-establishing the familial bond the older son denied. And he explains the feast not as a reward for bad behavior, but as the necessary, joyful response to a resurrection. The verb is *euphrainō*—to make merry, to rejoice with heartfelt gladness. It is what grace does. It throws a party.

And here, Jesus ends the parable. He leaves it open-ended. Does the older son soften, drop his resentment, and go in to the feast? Or does he choose to remain outside, arms crossed, in the darkness of his own correctness? We are not told. Because the question is now addressed to us, the listeners.

**Application: Coming Home to the Feast**

So, which empty chair do you occupy this morning?

Perhaps you identify with the younger son. You know the distant country. You know the shame of squandered gifts, broken trust, and selfish choices. You’ve rehearsed the speech: “God, if I just work harder, serve more, pray longer, maybe then I’ll be worthy of a place at the edge of your table.” Hear the Father interrupt you today. He sees you, even while you are far off. His compassion is already moving toward you. He is not waiting to be persuaded by your penance. He is waiting to restore you by his grace. Your confession is not a business proposal; it is simply telling the truth: “Father, I have sinned.” And then receiving the stunning truth he speaks over you: “You are my beloved child. Welcome home.”

Or perhaps, and this is often harder to see, you identify with the older son. Your faith has been marked by dutiful service, but it has grown cold, mechanical. You look at those who seem to have “gotten away with it” and feel a quiet resentment. You measure your worth by your moral resume and find others lacking. You may be in the house of God, but you have never truly celebrated, never felt the joyful freedom of a loved child. You are working *for* God, but not resting *in* Him. # The Unseen Welcome: A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

**Opening Illustration: The Two Empty Chairs**

Good morning. Look around this sanctuary. You’ll see familiar faces, the comforting rhythm of our gathered family. But you’ll also likely see a few empty seats. We might assume they’re just for the regulars who are traveling or feeling unwell. But I’d like you to imagine, for a moment, two particular empty chairs.

The first chair belongs to someone who feels they have wandered too far to ever find their way back. They’re not just physically absent; they are convinced they are permanently disqualified. Their story is written in the ink of regret: choices that burned bridges, words that can’t be taken back, trust that was squandered. They believe the door to this place, to this community, to God’s own family, is locked tight against them. They sit in the silence of their own homes, nursing the deep conviction that their chapter in God’s story is one of irreversible loss.

The second empty chair is more subtle. It belongs to someone who is, by all external accounts, *here*. Their body is in the pew. They haven’t missed a service in years. They serve faithfully on committees, their giving is regular, their doctrine is sound. But if you could see into their heart, you’d find a chilling emptiness. Their faith feels like a long, joyless duty—a contract they are fulfilling out of obligation, without ever feeling the warm, secure embrace of the one who made the covenant. A low-grade resentment simmers beneath a polished surface of correctness. They, too, in a profound and dangerous way, are far from home.

Both of these chairs represent the same core, human problem: a fractured relationship with a loving Father. And into this aching space—a space we all know, whether we’ve run to the far country or just to the far edge of the property—Jesus tells perhaps his most beloved and most misunderstood story. It’s a story not just about a wayward son, but about two lost sons and one unfathomably gracious Father. It’s for the one who has run, and for the one who has never left but has never truly come home. Let’s listen together to the parable of the Prodigal Son.

**I. The Younger Son: The Lostness of Rebellion (Luke 15:11-19)**

Jesus begins with a simple, devastating line: “There was a man who had two sons.” The younger one approaches his father with a request that would have sucked the air out of the room: “Father, give me the share of the property that will belong to me.” In that honor-shame culture, this was more than a financial transaction. It was a symbolic death wish. By asking for his inheritance now, he was saying, “Your continued presence in my life is an inconvenience. I value what you can give me more than I value you. I wish you were dead so I could get on with my life.” This is the ugly heart of sin, isn’t it? It’s not merely breaking rules. It is demanding autonomy from God, treating Him as a means to our ends—a divine vending machine for the blessings we want to take and use as we please.

And the Father, in a stunning act of heartbreaking love, grants the request. He liquidates assets, he divides the property, and he lets him go. Love that controls is not love at all. So the son goes, cash in hand, to a “distant country.” This is more than geography; it’s a place of moral and relational distance from everything that defined him—his name, his family, his identity.

There, Jesus says, he “squandered his property in dissolute living.” The Greek word is *diaskorpizō*—it means to scatter, to waste, to dissipate. It’s the perfect picture of the human soul fragmented by the pursuit of pleasure, significance, and freedom apart from the Father’s design. We can imagine the scene: the flashy new friends, the rounds of parties, the thrill of being his own man, the slow numbing of conscience. But it always ends in famine. The world’s promises are finite. They run out.

And they do. A severe famine hits, and he is destitute. So he does the unthinkable: he attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For Jesus’ Jewish audience, this was the ultimate degradation. A son of Israel, caring for unclean animals, longing to fill his stomach with the carob pods the pigs were eating. He is not just broke; he is ritually unclean, socially exiled, and utterly alone.

It is here, in the rock-bottom silence of the pigsty, that he “came to himself.” This is not yet full repentance, but it is a moment of brutal, clarifying sanity. The fog of rebellion lifts, and he sees his situation for what it truly is: utter ruin. He rehearses a speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired hands.”

Do you hear the calculus in his plan? It’s a business proposal. “I am no longer worthy of sonship, so let me earn my keep. I’ll work my way back into your good graces.” This is the logical end of rebellion: the belief that after we’ve taken our inheritance and wrecked it, we must now become the architects of our own rehabilitation. He understands his sin, but he has not yet grasped the nature of his Father’s heart.

**II. The Father: The Unseen Welcome (Luke 15:20-24)**

“But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion.” This is the pivot of the parable, the hinge on which everything turns. The Father wasn’t passively waiting indoors; he was actively watching. Day after day, he likely took his place where he could scan the horizon, hoping for a silhouette he would recognize anywhere. His love was not dormant; it was expectant, aching, and watchful.

And then, he runs. We must not miss the scandal of this. In the ancient Middle East, patriarchs did not run. Running meant hiking up your tunic, exposing your legs—it was undignified, shameful behavior for a man of his station. But this Father, throwing dignity to the wind, runs. He runs to close the gap that the son could never bridge on his own. In a profound sense, he takes upon himself the shame and the scorn the son deserved from the watching village. He intercepts the shame before it can reach his child.

He reaches his son, embraces him, and kisses him. The Greek implies repeated kissing—not a stiff, formal greeting, but an outpouring of affection. And before the son can finish his rehearsed speech of unworthiness and transaction, the Father interrupts him. He doesn’t let him get to the part about becoming a hired hand. The speech of penance is cut off by the poetry of restoration.

He calls to his servants: “Quickly! Bring out the best robe—the one reserved for honored guests—and put it on him.” This covers his filth. “Put a ring on his finger”—a sign of family authority and identity. “Sandals on his feet”—for sons wore sandals, slaves went barefoot. “And kill the fatted calf!” This is not a quiet family meal; this is a celebratory feast for the whole community, a public declaration that the son is restored.

“For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.” The Father’s declaration is absolute. The son’s identity is not “former wastrel” or “probationary worker.” He is “my son.” His return is not a negotiation; it is a resurrection. The welcome is not earned; it is given. It is sheer, scandalous, prodigal grace.

**III. The Older Son: The Lostness of Resentment (Luke 15:25-30)**

Now, the scene shifts, and we meet the occupant of the second empty chair. The older son is coming in from the field—dutiful, responsible, where he should be. He hears the music and dancing. He calls a servant and learns the reason: your brother has returned, and your father has killed the fatted calf. His response is not joy, but anger. A deep, burning fury. He refuses to go in.

Once again, the Father shows incredible grace. He doesn’t command him to enter; he goes out and pleads with him. And the older son’s heart spills out in a torrent of resentment: “Listen! For all these years I have been working like a slave for you, and I have never disobeyed your command; yet you have never given me even a young goat so that I might celebrate with my friends.”

Let’s be pastoral here for a moment. Can we feel the weight of his complaint? In a purely transactional sense, he’s right. It *is* unfair. He *has* been obedient. He *has* stayed. Many of you know this feeling. You’re the one who showed up. You did the hard, faithful, unseen work. And it hurts when the party seems thrown for the one who didn’t help. Jesus is not dismissing the older brother’s pain; he is exposing the source of it.

Notice the pronouns in his outburst: “I,” “me,” “my.” Notice the language: “working like a slave.” He has been home all along, but he has never understood sonship. He sees his relationship with his Father as a contract of works: obedience in exchange for rewards. He has kept the rules but lost the relationship. He is obedient but joyless, faithful but furious. His heart has become a prison of comparison and meritocracy.

And then the devastating, distancing accusation: “But when this son of yours came back…” He cannot even say “my brother.” He disowns him. “This son of yours,” this wastrel. And he levels a specific charge: “who has devoured your property with prostitutes.” Was that true? The text doesn’t say that. It’s the older brother’s interpretation, layered with self-righteous judgment and likely gossip. He is just as lost as his brother, but his lostness is more insidious because it wears the clothes of fidelity. He is outside the house, outside the feast, by his own bitter choice.

**IV. The Father’s Plea: An Invitation to Both Sons (Luke 15:31-32)**

The Father’s response to this older son is just as tender, just as revealing. “Son,” he says—*teknon*, a term of endearment. “You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” Do you hear the breathtaking generosity in this? The Father affirms his constant presence and his full inheritance. The older son never had to work for a young goat; the entire estate was already his! He had been living like a hired hand in his mind, slaving for wages, while enjoying the privileges of a beloved son all along. He was so focused on the reward he felt he was owed that he missed the riches he already possessed.

“But we had to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.” The Father reframes everything. He re-establishes the familial bond the older son denied: “this brother of yours.” And he explains the feast not as a reward for bad behavior, but as the necessary, joyful response to a resurrection. The verb is *euphrainō*—it means to make merry, to rejoice with a joy that vibrates through the whole community. It is the sound of a family becoming whole again. It is what grace does: it throws a party.

Does he drop his resentment, let his father embrace him, and go in to the feast? Or does he choose to remain outside, arms crossed, vindicated in his anger but alone in the darkness? We are not told.

Jesus leaves it unfinished because he is telling this story to a group of religious leaders—older brothers—who are grumbling about his welcome of sinners. The question hangs in the air for them: “Will you come in?” And now, it hangs in the air for us.

Maybe your far country wasn’t a literal place of wild living, but a far country of the heart—chasing career success until your family became strangers, pursuing a political ideology with religious fervor, or simply building a life where God was an afterthought. You know the shame of squandered time, broken trust, selfish choices. And now, even in your longing to return, you’ve rehearsed the speech: “God, if I just work harder, serve more, pray longer, maybe then I’ll be worthy of a place at the edge of your table.” Hear the Father interrupt you today. He sees you, even while you are far off. His compassion is already moving toward you. He is not waiting to be persuaded by your penance. He is waiting to restore you by his grace. Your confession is not a business proposal; it is simply telling the truth: “Father, I have sinned.” And then receiving the stunning truth he speaks over you: “You are my beloved child. **Application: Coming Home to the Feast**

So, which empty chair do you occupy this morning?

Hear the Father’s tender word to you today: “My child, you have always been with me. Everything I have is already yours.” What does coming in to the feast look like for you? It means allowing yourself to celebrate God’s scandalous grace for others, and finally, for yourself.

**Conclusion: The True Older Brother**

But this parable, while complete in itself, points us to an even greater reality. We have a Father whose love is prodigal—a word that means “recklessly extravagant.” But we also have a True Older Brother, one who did not stay resentfully in the field.

The Gospel of Luke shows us Jesus, the eternal Son, who left the riches of his Father’s house not in rebellion, but in obedient love. He journeyed to the ultimate distant country—into our brokenness, our sin, our death. He entered the pigsty of our human condition. And on the cross, he absorbed the full cost of our rebellion and our resentment. He paid the debt we could never pay, so that the Father could run to us without compromising his justice. The fatted calf of heaven’ celebration was prepared at the cost of the Son’s own life.

So this morning, the invitation is for both sons—for the rebel and the resentful, for the one who has run and the one who has labored without love. The Father’s arms are open. The music is playing.

So this morning, the invitation is for both sons—for every mix of runaway and rule-keeper in this room. The Father’s arms are open. The fatted calf has been prepared at the cost of the Son’s own life. The music is playing.

Will you, from whatever far country or nearby field you find yourself in, turn and receive the welcome that has been waiting for you all along? Will you come in to the feast?

Let’s pray.

Father, we see ourselves in this story. Some of us are far off, convinced we could never be welcomed. Some of us are nearby, yet far in our hearts, serving out of duty instead of delight. Meet us where we are. Interrupt our speeches. Help us to hear you call us “son,” call us “daughter.” Overwhelm our transaction with your grace. Give us the courage to drop our resentment and our regret, and to simply walk into the joyful feast you have prepared. Through Jesus Christ, our true and gracious brother. Amen.

# The Unseen Welcome: A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

**Opening Illustration: The Two Empty Chairs**

Good morning. If you look around this sanctuary, you’ll likely see a few empty seats. We might assume they’re just for the regulars who are out of town or under the weather. But I’d like you to imagine, for a moment, two particular empty chairs. The first belongs to someone who feels they have wandered too far. They’ve made choices they deeply regret, burned bridges, and squandered precious things. They believe the door to this place, to this community, to God’s family, is locked tight against them. They sit at home, convinced their story is one of irreversible loss.

The second empty chair belongs to someone who is, by all accounts, here. They haven’t missed a service in years. They serve on committees, they give faithfully, they know the right answers. But in their heart, there’s a chilling emptiness. Their faith feels like a long, joyless duty, a contract they are fulfilling without ever feeling the embrace of the one who made it. Resentment simmers beneath a polished surface. They, too, in their own way, are far from home.

Both of these chairs, you see, represent the same profound human problem: a fractured relationship with a loving Father. And into this aching space, Jesus tells perhaps his most beloved and misunderstood story. It’s a story not just about a wayward son, but about two lost sons and one unfathomably gracious Father. It’s a story for the one who has run, and for the one who has never left the property but has never truly come home. It’s the parable of the Prodigal Son.

**I. The Younger Son: The Lostness of Rebellion (Luke 15:11-19)**

Jesus begins: “There was a man who had two sons.” The younger one makes a shocking, heart-rending request: “Father, give me the share of the property that will belong to me.” In that culture, this was more than a financial transaction. It was a symbolic death wish. He was saying, “I wish you were dead. Your money means more to me than your presence. I want my inheritance, but I don’t want you.” It is the essence of sin: not just breaking rules, but demanding autonomy from God, treating Him as a means to our ends, a dispenser of blessings we can take and use as we please.

The Father, in a stunning act of heartbreaking love, grants the request. He lets him go. This love was not passive; it was costly. The Father absorbed a profound financial and emotional wound, liquidating assets and accepting loss, all to allow the son the terrible freedom to learn the hard lesson of life apart from grace. And the son goes to a distant country, a place of moral and relational distance from everything he knew. There, he “squandered his property in dissolute living.” The Greek word here is *diaskorpizō*—to scatter, to waste, to dissipate. It’s a picture of the human soul fragmented by the pursuit of pleasure, significance, and freedom apart from the Father’s design. And it always ends in famine. The world’s promises run out.

Hitting rock bottom, he attaches himself to a citizen of that country who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For Jesus’ Jewish audience, this was the ultimate degradation: a son of Israel, caring for unclean animals, longing to eat their food. In his desperation, he “came to himself.” This is not yet repentance, but a moment of brutal clarity. He sees his situation for what it is: utter ruin. He rehearses a speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired hands.”

Notice the transactional nature of his planned return. It’s a business proposal: “I am no longer worthy of sonship, so let me earn my keep.” This is the logical end of rebellion: the belief that we must now work our way back into favor. He understands his sin, but he has not yet grasped the nature of his Father’s love.

**II. The Father: The Unseen Welcome (Luke 15:20-24)**

“But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion.” This is the pivot of the parable, the hinge on which everything turns. The Father wasn’t passively waiting; he was actively watching, scanning the horizon for a silhouette he would recognize anywhere. His love was not dormant; it was expectant.

And then he runs. In ancient Middle Eastern culture, patriarchs did not run. They walked with dignity. But this Father, throwing dignity to the wind, hikes up his robes and runs—a shocking, undignified, public display of eager love. He runs to close the gap that the son could never bridge on his own.

Before the son can finish his rehearsed speech of unworthiness and transaction, the Father interrupts him. He doesn’t let him finish the part about being a hired hand. Instead, he showers him with symbols of restoration: the best robe (a sign of honor and authority), a ring (a sign of family identity and authority), sandals (for a son, not a barefoot slave), and the fatted calf (a celebratory feast for the whole community).

“For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.” The Father’s declaration is absolute. The son’s identity is not “former wastrel” or “probationary worker.” He is “my son.” His return is not a negotiation; it is a resurrection. The welcome is not earned; it is given. It is grace.

**III. The Older Son: The Lostness of Resentment (Luke 15:25-30)**

But the Father’s joy was not universal. While the younger son was being restored, a different kind of lostness was brewing just outside the door. The older son, coming in from the field, hears the music and dancing. He learns the reason and becomes angry. He refuses to go in. His Father, once again showing incredible grace, comes out and pleads with him. And the older son’s heart spills out: “Listen! For all these years I have been working like a slave for you, and I have never disobeyed your command; yet you have never given me even a young goat so that I might celebrate with my friends.”

His speech is a masterpiece of resentment. Notice the pronouns: “I,” “me,” “my.” Notice the language: “working like a slave.” He has been home all along, but he has never understood sonship. He sees his relationship with his Father as a contract of works: obedience in exchange for rewards. He has kept the rules but lost the relationship. He is obedient but joyless, faithful but furious.

And then the devastating accusation: “But when this son of yours came back…” He cannot even say “my brother.” He distances himself. “This son of yours,” this wastrel, this sinner. And he levels the charge: “who has devoured your property with prostitutes.” Was that true? The text doesn’t say that. It’s the older brother’s interpretation, layered with self-righteous judgment. His heart, so long confined by duty, has become a prison of comparison and bitterness. He is just as lost as his brother, but his lostness is more insidious because it wears the clothes of fidelity. He is outside the house, outside the feast, by his own choice.

**IV. The Father’s Plea: An Invitation to Both Sons (Luke 15:31-32)**

The Father’s response to this older son is just as tender, just as revealing. “Son,” he says—*teknon*, a term of endearment. “You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” The Father affirms his constant presence and his full inheritance. The older son never had to work for a young goat; the entire estate was already his! He had been living like a hired hand in his mind, while enjoying the privileges of a son all along.

“But we had to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.” The Father reframes everything. He calls the younger son “this brother of yours,” re-establishing the familial bond the older son denied. And he explains the feast not as a reward for bad behavior, but as the necessary, joyful response to a resurrection. The verb is *euphrainō*—to make merry, to rejoice with heartfelt gladness. It is what grace does. It throws a party.

And here, Jesus ends the parable. He leaves it open-ended. Does the older son soften, drop his resentment, and go in to the feast? Or does he choose to remain outside, arms crossed, in the darkness of his own correctness? We are not told. Because the question is now addressed to us, the listeners.

**Application: Coming Home to the Feast**

So, which empty chair do you occupy this morning?

Perhaps you identify with the younger son. You know the distant country. You know the shame of squandered gifts, broken trust, and selfish choices. You’ve rehearsed the speech: “God, if I just work harder, serve more, pray longer, maybe then I’ll be worthy of a place at the edge of your table.” Hear the Father interrupt you today. He sees you, even while you are far off. His compassion is already moving toward you. He is not waiting to be persuaded by your penance. He is waiting to restore you by his grace. Your confession is not a business proposal; it is simply telling the truth: “Father, I have sinned.” And then receiving the stunning truth he speaks over you: “You are my beloved child. Welcome home.”

Or perhaps, and this is often harder to see, you identify with the older son. Your faith has been marked by dutiful service, but it has grown cold, mechanical. You look at those who seem to have “gotten away with it” and feel a quiet resentment. You see this same impulse in daily life: the colleague who cuts corners yet gets promoted, the family member who disappears only to return to a hero’s welcome, the neighbor who lives recklessly yet seems blessed. You measure your worth by your moral resume and find others lacking. You may be in the house of God, but you have never truly celebrated, never felt the joyful freedom of a loved child. You are working *for* God, but not resting *in* Him. Hear the Father’s tender word to you today: “My child, you have always been with me. Everything I have is already yours. Stop laboring like a slave. Come in and enjoy the feast I have prepared. Let my joy be your joy.”

**Conclusion: The True Older Brother**

But this parable, while complete in itself, points us to an even greater reality. We have a Father whose love is prodigal—a word that means “recklessly extravagant.” But we also have a True Older Brother, one who did not stay resentfully in the field.

The Gospel of Luke shows us Jesus, the eternal Son, who left the riches of his Father’s house not in rebellion, but in obedient love. He journeyed to the ultimate distant country—into our brokenness, our sin, our death. He entered the pigsty of our human condition. And on the cross, he absorbed the full cost of our rebellion and our resentment—the very cost the earthly father foreshadowed when he liquidated the estate. Jesus paid the debt we could never pay, so that the Father could run to us without compromising his justice. He is the True Older Brother who searches for us in our lostness, who paid the price to bring us home, and who now stands at the door of the Father’s house saying, “Come, everything is ready. The feast is for you.”

So this morning, the invitation is for both sons—for the rebel and the resentful, for the one who has run and the one who has labored without love. The Father’s arms are open. The fatted calf has been prepared at the cost of the Son’s own life. The music is playing.

Will you, from whatever far country or nearby field you find yourself in, turn and receive the welcome that has been waiting for you all along? Will you come in to the feast?

Let us pray.
