## The Unseen Love: A Journey Home

Good morning. I want you to think for a moment about the most important thing you’ve ever lost.

Maybe it was a set of car keys, and you tore the house apart in a frantic, sweating panic. Maybe it was a precious family heirloom—a wedding ring, a watch—and you retraced your steps, your heart sinking with every fruitless search. Perhaps, and this is the deepest kind of loss, it was a relationship. A friendship fractured by harsh words, a child who has drifted into a life you don’t recognize, a sense of your own faith that has grown cold and distant.

What did you do when you realized it was gone? You likely didn’t shrug and say, “Oh well.” If it mattered, you searched. You turned over couch cushions, you made awkward phone calls, you prayed desperate prayers. The intensity of the search is always a measure of the value of what was lost.

This is the backdrop against which Jesus tells three stories in Luke 15: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son. The religious leaders are grumbling, “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.” Their complaint reveals a heart that sees people as problems to be avoided, not treasures to be recovered. So Jesus tells a story—a story so rich, so layered, it has been called the crown jewel of all the parables. It’s often called the Parable of the Prodigal Son, but that title is too small. It’s really a story about a lost son, a watching father, and an angry brother. It’s a story about grace that offends our sense of fairness, and a love so vast it’s almost impossible to believe.

Let’s enter the story together. “There was a man who had two sons.” From the outset, we know this is a family story. It’s about inheritance, identity, and the complex bonds that tie us together. The younger son, in an act of breathtaking cruelty, says to his father, “Father, give me the share of the property that will belong to me.” In that culture, this was tantamount to saying, “I wish you were dead. Your money matters more to me than you do. I want my life, but I don’t want you in it.” It is the primal sin of humanity: the rejection of the Father’s goodness in pursuit of our own autonomous kingdom.

And here comes the first shocking detail: the father agrees. He divides his property. He lets him go. God’s grace is such that it allows us the freedom to leave. He does not chain us to the hearth. Love that is not freely given is not love at all. So the son takes his inheritance, his identity as a son bundled into cash, and he goes to a distant country. Distance in the parable isn’t just geographical; it’s relational, spiritual, moral. He is putting as much space as possible between himself and the father’s gaze, the father’s rules, the father’s love.

We know what happens next. He squanders it. The word “prodigal” means recklessly extravagant. He is extravagant in his wastefulness. And when the money runs out, a famine hits. He is now doubly bankrupt: financially and socially. He attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For Jesus’ Jewish listeners, this was the lowest conceivable point: a son of Israel, reduced to caring for unclean animals, longing to eat their food. This is the end of the road of self-invention. He went out to find himself, and he lost everything, including his self-respect. He is not just hungry; he is “no longer worthy to be called a son.” He rehearses a speech: “Father, I have sinned… treat me like one of your hired hands.”

Now, pause here. This is often called “coming to his senses,” and it is. But let’s be clear: his motivation is mixed at best. He is not overcome with sorrow for wounding his father; he is overcome with hunger. He remembers that his father’s hired hands have bread to spare. This is not pure repentance; it is calculated desperation. And friends, this is such good news for us. Because God accepts not only the perfectly penitent. He receives the broken, the desperate, the ones who are crawling home not out of flawless love, but because they have run out of options. The door is open even to those whose motives are a tangled mess of need and faint regret.

Now, we come to the heart of the story, the image that changes everything. “But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion; he ran and put his arms around him and kissed him.”

Do you see it? The father wasn’t inside the house, nursing his bitterness. He was watching. Daily, he must have gone to that point on the property where he could see the road, scanning the horizon for a silhouette he longed to see. And when he sees him—while he is still far off, still smelling of pig sty, still rehearsing his hired-hand speech—the father does something undignified, shocking for an ancient patriarch: he hikes up his robes and he runs. He runs to close the distance his son created. He doesn’t wait for a full apology; he interrupts the rehearsed speech with an embrace. The kiss is not a perfunctory peck; it is the kiss of reconciliation, of welcome, of belonging restored.

He doesn’t even let the son finish. The son gets out, “I am no longer worthy to be called your son,” but the father turns to the servants and says, “Quickly! Bring the best robe—that’s my robe, the sign of my authority. Put a ring on his hand—the sign of the family seal and authority. Sandals on his feet—for slaves go barefoot, but sons wear shoes.” And then, “Kill the fattened calf!” The entire village would be invited. This is more than a quiet reunion; this is a public, lavish, joyous declaration: “My son was dead, and is alive again! He was lost, and is found!”

This is the gospel in a single picture. This is God. This is the heart of the Father, revealed in Christ, who came running to a lost world while we were still far off. We don’t earn our way back into the family; we are swept up into the arms of a love that has been waiting, watching, longing for our return.

But the story doesn’t end there. If it did, we could leave feeling warm, perhaps identifying with the prodigal. But Jesus has a second act, and it is for the religious, the obedient, the ones who have never outwardly left home. The elder brother is in the field. He hears the music and dancing. When he finds out why, he becomes angry and refuses to go in. His father, again showing incomprehensible grace, comes out and pleads with him.

Listen to the elder brother’s speech: “Look! All these years I’ve been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has devoured your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!”

Do you hear the difference? The younger son said, “Father, I have sinned.” The elder brother says, “Look what I have done.” His language is not of sonship, but of slavery: “slaving for you.” He doesn’t say “my brother”; he says “this son of yours.” He sees his relationship with the father as a transaction: obedience in exchange for rewards. And because the father’s grace doesn’t operate on a system of merit, he feels cheated. His anger reveals that he, too, is lost. He is lost at home. He inhabits the father’s house but has never understood the father’s heart. He is obedient but resentful; present but distant; moral but joyless.

And the father’s words to him are just as tender: “Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours.” The father doesn’t dismiss his service. He reframes it: “You are not a slave; you are a son. The inheritance was already yours! The party was always available! But we had to celebrate, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again.” The invitation is the same: come in from the cold field of your resentment. Join the party of grace. See yourself not as a worker, but as a beloved child.

So, what does this mean for us here today?

**For those who feel like the younger brother:** You may be in a distant country right now. Maybe you walked away from faith, from family, from what you knew was good. Maybe your pursuit of freedom led to a cage of your own making. You feel ashamed, unworthy. Hear this: the Father’s love is not a reward for the cleaned-up. It is the cause of your cleaning up. Your first step home isn’t to perfect your speech; it’s to turn around. And you will find He has already closed most of the distance. You are welcomed, not as a hired hand, but as a son, as a daughter. The robe of Christ’s righteousness is waiting.

**For those who feel like the elder brother:** You’ve been faithful. You show up. You serve. But perhaps a slow bitterness has grown. You look at the world, at the church, and think, “I’ve followed the rules, and where’s my celebration?” You feel God owes you for your service. Friends, the Father’s word to you is, “Everything I have is already yours.” Don’t let your service become a joyless slavery. Don’t let your obedience become a currency to earn what is already a gift. Come in from the field. The feast of grace is for you, too. Rejoice that the Father’s heart is big enough for the reckless and the rigid, for the wanderer and the worker.

And for all of us, this story redefines God. He is not a distant scorekeeper, a cold patriarch, or an indulgent grandfather. He is the Running Father. His love is proactive, seeing us from afar. His grace is extravagant, adorning us with dignity we don’t deserve. His joy is immense, throwing a party at the slightest hint of a return.

This is why Jesus came. He is the true and perfect Son who, though He was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped. He went into the far country of our sin and lostness, experiencing the famine and the shame we deserved, so that He could bring us home. On the cross, He wore our rags so we could wear the robe. He was treated as a slave so we could be called sons and daughters. He endured the ultimate famine—separation from the Father—so we could be welcomed to the eternal feast.

So today, wherever you find yourself—in the pig sty of your own making, or in the weary field of your own righteousness—look up. See the Father, waiting, watching, ready to run. The journey home begins with a single step of turning. And it ends not with a scolding, but with an embrace; not with a probation, but with a party; not with a question of worth, but with a declaration of worthiness bestowed by love itself.

“My son was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.” That is the Father’s heart. That is our hope. That is the gospel.

Let us pray.

## The Unseen Welcome: A Sermon on the Prodigal Son

**(Begin with a moment of silence, a warm, open posture)**

Good morning. I’d like you to picture, for a moment, a home. Not just any home, but *your* home. The one you grew up in, or the one you’ve made for your own family. Think of its particular smell—maybe of coffee brewing, or bread baking, or the unique scent of books and old wood. Think of the sounds that belong there—the hum of the refrigerator, the creak of a specific floorboard, the way laughter echoes in the hallway. Now, imagine leaving that home. Not for a vacation or a brief trip, but in a way that severs the bond. You pack your bags with a heart full of resentment or restless ambition. You walk out, and you don’t just leave the building; you leave the belonging. You exile yourself from the love that was woven into the very walls.

And then, imagine, years later, standing at the end of the road that leads back. The home is still there, but you are not the same. You are worn, ashamed, carrying the dust of a thousand wrong turns. You have rehearsed your speech a thousand times: “I am no longer worthy.” You wonder: Will the door be locked? Will the windows be dark? Will the love that once lived there have grown cold in your absence?

It is to this profound, universal ache of exile and the terrifying, glorious hope of return that Jesus speaks in one of his most beloved stories. We find it in Luke’s Gospel, chapter 15. This whole chapter is Jesus’ answer to the grumbling of the religious leaders who said, “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.” So he tells three stories: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and then, to drive the point home with devastating intimacy, a lost son. Let’s listen together to the story, not as a familiar fable, but as if hearing it for the first time, as an announcement about the very heart of God.

**(Read Luke 15:11-32)**

This is a story of two lost sons and one breathtaking father. It is a story in three acts: Rebellion, Ruin, and Return; followed by a painful epilogue: Resentment.

**Act One: The Rebellion of “Give Me.”**
Jesus begins: “There was a man who had two sons. The younger one said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of the estate.’” In that culture, this request was unthinkable. It wasn’t just a financial transaction; it was a symbolic death wish. A son asking for his inheritance while his father still lived was essentially saying, “I wish you were dead. Your stuff means more to me than you do. I want what is rightfully mine, but I want it without you, without the relationship, without the burden of being your son.”

And here is the first astonishing detail: the father complies. He divides his property. He lets him go. God, in his terrifying and gracious freedom, allows us our rebellion. He does not chain us to his hearth. Love that is not freely given is not love at all, so the father, with a heart surely breaking, watches his son walk away, cash in hand, into the far country of his own choices.

The younger son’s journey is the journey of every soul that seeks life on its own terms. He is the portrait of the “sinner” the Pharisees despised: he squanders his substance in wild living. He is living the dream, until the dream runs out. His money, his friends, his self-sufficiency—all evaporate. And then a famine hits. Not just an external famine, but the famine that has been growing within him all along—a famine of the soul.

**Act Two: The Ruin and the Turning.**
He hits rock bottom. He attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For Jesus’ Jewish listeners, this was the ultimate degradation. Pigs were unclean. This boy, a son of Israel, is now so desperate he longs to fill his stomach with the pods the pigs were eating. He is starving, alone, and profoundly unclean. The text delivers its devastating summary: “No one gave him anything.”

This is the end of the road for the philosophy of “give me.” It always leads to a place where “no one gives.” The far country is not just a geographic location; it is the spiritual state of alienation, where we are cut off from the source of all good gifts. It is the hollow ache after the party ends. It is the silence after we’ve gotten everything we thought we wanted.

But then comes the pivotal moment: “He came to his senses.” The Greek word here means “to return to oneself,” to come home to the truth of who you are. It’s not merely a moral calculation; it’s a waking up. He remembers. He remembers his father’s house. Notice his speech: “How many of my father’s hired servants have food to spare, and here I am starving to death!” His plan is one of calculated unworthiness. He will return, not as a son, but as a hired hand. He will earn his keep. He will say, “I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me as one of your hired servants.” This is repentance born of hunger, but it is still a transactional repentance. It’s a deal he hopes to make: my labor for your bread.

He turns and begins the long walk home.

**Act Three: The Father’s Run.**
Now, we arrive at the center of the universe, the truth upon which all Christian hope rests. “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him.”

Do not rush past this. In the ancient Near East, patriarchs did not run. Running was undignified, especially for an elder with flowing robes. But this father runs. He has been watching. Every day, perhaps, he has gone to that point on the road, scanning the horizon for a familiar silhouette. His love is not passive; it is expectant, watchful, aching.

He sees his son “a long way off.” He sees him in his ragged, pig-stained shame. And he is “filled with compassion.” The Greek word for compassion, *splanchnizomai*, is a gut-level word. It means to be moved in the deepest, most visceral parts of your being. God’s love is not a cool, distant approval. It is a passionate, heart-wrenching movement toward the broken.

Then, he runs. He embraces him and kisses him repeatedly. The son begins his rehearsed speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.” But he doesn’t even get to the part about becoming a hired servant. The father interrupts him. He is not interested in his son’s deal. He is restoring his son’s identity.

He calls to his servants: “Quick! Bring the best robe” — the robe of honor, likely his own. “Put a ring on his finger” — the ring of authority, reinstating him to the family. “Sandals on his feet” — slaves went barefoot; sons wore sandals. “Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let’s have a feast and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.”

The father doesn’t say, “Let’s have a feast because my son has made a good deal.” He says, “Let’s have a feast because my heart cannot contain this joy.” The restoration is immediate, total, and lavish. It is based not on the son’s worthiness, but on the father’s character. The son was prepared to negotiate for a servant’s cot; the father showers him with a son’s inheritance all over again. This is grace: not a wage we earn, but a gift we receive with empty, open hands.

**The Epilogue: The Resentment of “I Never.”**
But the story isn’t over. Jesus now turns the spotlight on the elder brother, who has been in the field, working dutifully. He hears the music and dancing, and when he learns why, he is angry and refuses to go in. His father, just as he went out to meet the younger, now comes out and pleads with him.

Listen to the elder brother’s speech. It is the mirror image of the younger’s “give me.” It is the cry of “I never.” “Look! All these years I’ve been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends.” Do you hear it? “Slaving.” Not “serving with joy,” but slaving. “I never disobeyed.” His relationship with his father is also transactional. It’s a contract: my obedience for your rewards. He sees himself not as a beloved son, but as an under-appreciated employee. And he is furious that his brother’s rebellion seems to be rewarded, while his dutiful service goes unrewarded.

This is the portrait of the “righteous”—the Pharisee in all of us. The one who believes their place in the father’s house is secured by their own good behavior. The one who, deep down, feels they deserve more because they have done more. His heart is also in a far country—a cold, resentful country of merit and comparison. He is just as lost as his brother, but he is lost at home. He is outside the party, alienated by his own sense of superiority.

And the father’s words to him are achingly tender: “My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours.” The father’s plea is, “Don’t you see? The feast was always yours for the asking. The story ends abruptly. We don’t know if the elder brother goes in. This parable is not just a story about a wayward young man. It is the definitive revelation of God’s posture toward a lost world.

Or you may be there because of quiet desperation—a sense of emptiness, a secret shame, a feeling that you’ve failed so deeply you could never come home. Hear the father’s heart: He is watching the road. His compassion is already moving toward you. Your repentance doesn’t need to be perfect; it just needs to be a turning. Stop trying to cut a deal. Stop saying, “I’ll work my way back.” Just come home. He will run to meet you. He will interrupt your confession of unworthiness with a celebration of welcome.

**To those in the elder brother’s field:** You may be the one who has tried so hard. You’ve been faithful, you’ve served, you’ve followed the rules. But your heart has grown cold. You feel entitled. You resent God’s grace toward “those people”—the ones who made a mess of their lives. You’ve forgotten that your relationship with God is not a contract, but a covenant of love. The Father’s word to you today is, “Everything I have is yours. Don’t slave; come and feast. The music is playing for you, too. Let go of your ledger of merits, and step into the party of grace.”

Our calling as a church is to be a community that lives out this parable. We are to be the ones who scan the horizon for the returning, ready to run. We are to be the ones who throw the party for the found, not grudgingly, but with the Father’s own joy. And we are to be constantly checking our own hearts, lest we find ourselves outside the feast, mumbling, “I never…”

**Conclusion**

So, let us return to that image of the home at the end of the road. The door is not locked. The lights are on. More than that—the Father is standing on the porch, his hand shading his eyes, peering down the road. He will run.

He will run with a compassion that shatters dignity.
He will embrace you with the smell of the far country still on your clothes.
He will interrupt your carefully prepared speech.
He will clothe you in honor.
He will seal you with his authority.
He will call for a feast, and the music will start to play.

Will you come in?

## The Unfolding Embrace: Finding Ourselves in the Prodigal Son

Brothers and sisters, imagine this: You’re standing in an airport, the air thick with the anticipation of reunions. You see a young man, early twenties maybe, shuffling through the terminal. He’s wearing clothes that are clearly too big, his face is gaunt, and his eyes dart around nervously. He looks lost, utterly and completely lost. You see him approach an older man, standing patiently by the gate. As the young man gets closer, the older man’s face softens. He drops his bag, throws his arms wide, and embraces this disheveled figure with a ferocity that seems to defy the years etched on his face. He holds him tight, whispering something in his ear. The young man, initially stiff, slowly melts into the embrace, his shoulders shaking with silent sobs.

What is happening in this moment? What story lies behind this reunion? Is it a tale of reckless abandon, of forgiveness, of unconditional love? This scene, played out in countless variations across the world, echoes a story that has resonated through the ages, a story we find in the Gospel of Luke, chapter 15: the parable of the Prodigal Son.

Let's turn to Luke 15, beginning at verse 20. We'll read through verse 32. As we do, let us open our hearts and minds to the timeless truths contained within this narrative, truths that speak directly to our own journeys of faith, failure, and ultimately, homecoming.

(Read Luke 15:11-32)

This parable, nestled within a chapter dedicated to lost things – a lost sheep, a lost coin – is arguably the most famous and beloved of all Jesus’ parables. It’s a story we think we know, a story we’ve heard countless times. But familiarity can sometimes obscure the depths of its meaning. So, let's delve into the details, unpacking the layers of truth that Jesus so skillfully wove into this seemingly simple narrative.

First, we meet the younger son. He is impatient, entitled, and frankly, foolish. He demands his inheritance – a request that, in that cultural context, was akin to wishing his father dead. He wants his freedom, his independence, his chance to make his own way in the world, unburdened by the constraints of his family and his father's authority. He doesn't just *want* his inheritance; he *demands* it. This reveals a deep-seated selfishness and a profound lack of understanding of the true value of family and belonging.

And what does the father do? He grants his son’s request. He doesn’t argue, he doesn’t plead, he doesn’t try to force him to stay. He allows him to go. This is the first glimpse of the father’s profound love – a love that respects the son’s freedom, even when it leads him down a path of self-destruction. God gives us free will, knowing we might misuse it, but respecting our agency nonetheless.

The younger son, flush with newfound wealth, journeys to a “distant country” – a metaphor for the spiritual distance he puts between himself and his father. There, he squanders his inheritance on “dissolute living.” He indulges in the fleeting pleasures of the world, chasing after happiness in all the wrong places. He believes that freedom lies in unrestrained indulgence, but he soon discovers that true freedom is not the absence of boundaries, but the responsible and wise use of our gifts and resources.

As quickly as the money came, it vanishes. A severe famine strikes the land, and the younger son finds himself in desperate straits. He is forced to take a job feeding pigs – a task considered unclean and degrading for a Jew. He is so hungry that he longs to eat the pig’s food, but even that is denied to him. He has hit rock bottom. He is utterly alone, destitute, and consumed by regret.

And it is in this moment of utter despair that something remarkable happens. “He came to himself.” He realizes the folly of his ways, the emptiness of his pursuits, and the stark contrast between his current misery and the abundance he had known in his father’s house. He remembers the servants in his father’s household, even they are better off than he is now. This realization is a moment of profound clarity, a turning point in his journey. He recognizes his sin, his rebellion, and his desperate need for redemption.

He formulates a plan: he will return to his father, not as a son, but as a servant. He will confess his sin and beg for mercy. He doesn’t expect to be welcomed back as a son; he only hopes to be given a place among the hired hands. This humility, born out of suffering, is a sign of genuine repentance.

Now, let’s focus on the father. As the son makes his long and arduous journey home, the father is watching. He is constantly scanning the horizon, hoping to catch a glimpse of his lost boy. And when he finally sees him, still a “long way off,” he doesn’t wait for the son to reach him. He is filled with compassion, and he runs to meet him.

This is a pivotal moment. The father, a man of dignity and standing in his community, abandons all decorum and sprints towards his son. He doesn’t care about what others might think; he only cares about reaching his child and bringing him home.

He embraces him, showering him with kisses. He doesn’t allow the son to finish his rehearsed speech of repentance. He cuts him off, silencing his self-condemnation and replacing it with an outpouring of love and acceptance. He doesn't dwell on the past; he focuses on the present – the joy of his son’s return.

He then orders his servants to bring the best robe, a ring for his finger, and sandals for his feet – symbols of honor, authority, and belonging. He commands them to prepare a feast, a celebration of his son’s homecoming. “For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.”

This is the heart of the parable: the extravagant, unconditional love of the father. It is a love that transcends all boundaries, a love that forgives all sins, a love that rejoices in the restoration of what was lost. It is a love that mirrors the love of God for each and every one of us.

But the story doesn’t end there. We are then introduced to the older brother, who represents a different kind of lostness. He has remained at home, diligently working in the fields, obedient to his father’s commands. He is the epitome of righteousness, at least on the surface. But when he hears the music and dancing, when he learns that his brother has returned and is being celebrated, he becomes angry.

He refuses to go inside, to join the celebration. He feels resentful, overlooked, and unappreciated. He complains to his father, listing all the ways he has been faithful and all the ways his brother has been unworthy. “All these years I have slaved for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!”

The older brother’s anger reveals a deep-seated pride and a lack of understanding of his father’s love. He sees his relationship with his father as a transaction, a system of rewards and punishments. He believes that he deserves special treatment because of his obedience. He doesn’t understand that his father’s love is not earned, but freely given. He doesn’t rejoice in his brother’s return; he is consumed by envy and self-pity.

The father, once again, responds with compassion. He goes out to the older brother and pleads with him to come inside. “My son,” he says, “you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.”

The parable ends without telling us whether the older brother ever relents and joins the celebration. This open ending challenges us to examine our own hearts and to ask ourselves: Are we more like the prodigal son, who strayed from the path and needed to be welcomed back? Or are we more like the older brother, who remained faithful but struggled with resentment and a lack of compassion?

So, what does this parable mean for us, here and now? How does it speak to our lives, our struggles, and our hopes?

Firstly, it reminds us that we are all prodigals in some way. We have all, at some point in our lives, strayed from the path, made mistakes, and fallen short of God’s expectations. We have all experienced moments of rebellion, doubt, and despair. We have all chased after false idols, seeking happiness in things that ultimately leave us empty.

But the good news is that God, like the father in the parable, is always waiting for us to return. He is always watching, always hoping, always ready to embrace us with open arms. No matter how far we have strayed, no matter how deep our sins, His love is boundless and His forgiveness is complete.

Secondly, the parable challenges us to examine our own attitudes towards others. Are we quick to judge and condemn those who have made mistakes? Or are we willing to extend grace and compassion, to offer a helping hand to those who are struggling? Are we able to rejoice in the restoration of others, even when we feel that we have been overlooked or unappreciated?

The older brother’s resentment reminds us that righteousness without love is empty and meaningless. True faith is not just about following the rules; it is about cultivating a heart of compassion and a willingness to forgive.

Finally, the parable calls us to embrace the joy of homecoming. It invites us to celebrate the restoration of broken relationships, the healing of wounded hearts, and the triumph of love over despair. It reminds us that we are all part of God’s family, and that there is always a place for us at His table.

Brothers and sisters, the parable of the Prodigal Son is not just a story about a wayward son and a forgiving father. It is a story about each and every one of us. It is a story about our own journeys of faith, our own struggles with sin and temptation, and our own longing for God’s love and acceptance.

Let us, therefore, embrace the message of this parable. Let us confess our sins, seek God’s forgiveness, and return to His loving embrace. And let us also strive to be more like the father in the story, extending grace and compassion to others, rejoicing in their restoration, and celebrating the joy of homecoming. For in the unfolding embrace of God's love, we find our true selves, our true belonging, and our eternal home. Amen.

The young man, initially stiff, slowly melts into the embrace, his shoulders shaking with silent sobs.

What is happening in this moment? What story lies behind this reunion? Is it a tale of reckless abandon, of forgiveness, of unconditional love? This scene, played out in countless variations across the world, echoes a story that has resonated through the ages, a story we find in the Gospel of Luke, chapter 15: the parable of the Prodigal Son.

It is a story about our own journeys of faith, our own struggles with sin and temptation, and our own longing for God’s love and acceptance.

This is his pigsty moment. Maybe your pigsty isn't literal poverty. Maybe it's a corner office where you're successful but empty. Maybe it's scrolling Instagram at 2:00 AM, feeling entirely alone, comparing yourself to everyone else's highlight reel.

In this moment of utter despair, "he came to himself." He remembers the abundance of his father's house. Even the servants are better off than he is. He realizes the depth of his sin and the folly of his choices. He decides to return, not as a son, but as a servant, hoping for a scrap of mercy.

Now, the father. Every day, he scans the horizon, longing for his son’s return. And when he sees him, still a "long way off," he doesn't wait. He *runs*.

Think about that for a moment. In that time, in that culture, for a man of his age and status to hike up his robes and run was an act of utter humiliation. It was shameful. Many scholars believe he ran to get to his son before the villagers did. They would have mocked him, ostracized him. The father took the shame upon himself, so his son wouldn't have to face it alone. He embraces him, kisses him, and silences his rehearsed confession. The father is not interested in dwelling on the past. He is only interested in celebrating the present – his son is home.

He orders the best robe, a ring, and sandals – symbols of restored honor, authority, and belonging. He throws a lavish party. “For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.” This is the scandalous, overwhelming love of God. A love that doesn’t keep score, a love that doesn’t hold grudges, a love that simply rejoices in the return of the lost.

But the story doesn't end there. The older brother enters the scene. He represents a different kind of lostness – the lostness of self-righteousness. He's been dutiful, obedient, a "good son." But when he hears the music and dancing, he's furious.

He refuses to join the celebration. “All these years I have slaved for you," he complains, "and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!”

The older brother sees his relationship with his father as a transaction: obedience equals reward. He's trying to put God in his debt. He doesn't understand that his father's love isn't earned; it's freely given. He's so focused on his own righteousness that he can't rejoice in his brother's return. He's trapped in a prison of his own making.

And here’s where Jesus really challenges the Pharisees – and us. The father goes out to the older brother, pleading with him. “My son,” he says, “you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.”

The parable ends without resolution. Does the older brother come to the party? We don't know. Jesus leaves us hanging, forcing us to confront ourselves.

As we look at these two brothers, we have to look in the mirror. Which one stares back at you? Are you the younger brother, who ran away and messed up? Or are you the older brother, who stayed and resented?

Let's be honest: many of us in the church today are more like the older brother. We've been faithful, we've followed the rules, and it's *hard* to see those who break the rules get blessed. It's easy to feel resentful, overlooked, and unappreciated. Maybe you volunteer every week, give faithfully, and haven't missed a Sunday in years. And then someone who's been living a completely different lifestyle suddenly shows up, gets a warm welcome, and maybe even gets more attention than you do. It feels unfair.

But the father's love isn't about fairness; it's about grace. It's not about what we deserve; it's about what we need. The older brother had always been with the father, had access to everything the father had. His problem wasn't a lack of resources; it was a lack of understanding. He didn't understand the depth of his father's love, a love that extends to *both* sons, regardless of their choices.

We, too, can fall into the trap of thinking we can earn God's love through our good deeds. We can become so focused on following the rules that we forget the heart of the matter: love, compassion, and forgiveness. We can become so busy "being good" that we miss the opportunity to celebrate the goodness in others.

The invitation to the party is for *both* brothers. It’s an invitation to lay down our pride, our resentment, and our self-righteousness, and to embrace the joy of homecoming. It's an invitation to recognize that we are all broken, we are all in need of grace, and we are all loved beyond measure.

Brothers and sisters, the parable of the Prodigal Son isn't just a story; it's an invitation. The Father is at the gate. He has been scanning the arrivals board for years. He sees you. He isn't checking your baggage; he isn't looking at your wrinkled clothes. He is running. The only question left is: will you drop your bags and let Him hold you? Amen.

## The Unfolding Embrace: Finding Ourselves in the Prodigal Son

Brothers and sisters, imagine this: You’re standing in an airport, the air thick with the anticipation of reunions. You see a young man, early twenties maybe, shuffling through the terminal. His clothes are clearly too big, his face gaunt, and his eyes dart around nervously. He looks lost, utterly and completely lost. You see him approach an older man, standing patiently by the gate. As the young man gets closer, the older man’s face softens. He drops his bag, throws his arms wide, and embraces this disheveled figure with a ferocity that seems to defy the years etched on his face. He holds him tight, whispering something in his ear. The young man, initially stiff, slowly melts into the embrace, his shoulders shaking with silent sobs.

What is happening in this moment? What story lies behind this reunion? Is it a tale of reckless abandon, of forgiveness, of unconditional love? This scene, played out in countless variations across the world, echoes a story that has resonated through the ages, a story we find in the Gospel of Luke, chapter 15: the parable of the Prodigal Son. This morning, let's explore the transformative power of God's grace, a grace that meets us in our brokenness and calls us home.

Let's turn to Luke 15, beginning at verse 20. We'll read through verse 32. As we do, let us open our hearts and minds to the timeless truths contained within this narrative, truths that speak directly to our own journeys of faith, failure, and ultimately, homecoming.

(Read Luke 15:11-32)

This parable, nestled within a chapter dedicated to lost things – a lost sheep, a lost coin – is arguably the most famous and beloved of all Jesus’ parables. It’s a story we think we know, a story we’ve heard countless times. But familiarity can sometimes obscure the depths of its meaning. So, let's delve into the details, unpacking the layers of truth that Jesus so skillfully wove into this seemingly simple narrative.

First, we meet the younger son. He is impatient, entitled, and frankly, foolish. He demands his inheritance – a request that, in that cultural context, was akin to wishing his father dead. He wants his freedom, his independence, his chance to make his own way in the world, unburdened by the constraints of his family and his father's authority. He doesn't just *want* his inheritance; he *demands* it. This reveals a deep-seated selfishness and a profound lack of understanding of the true value of family and belonging. It’s a stark picture of a young man who believes happiness can be bought and sold.

And what does the father do? He grants his son’s request. He doesn’t argue, he doesn’t plead, he doesn’t try to force him to stay. He allows him to go. This is the first glimpse of the father’s profound love – a love that respects the son’s freedom, even when it leads him down a path of self-destruction. God gives us free will, knowing we might misuse it, but respecting our agency nonetheless. It reminds me of a parent letting go of a child’s hand as they learn to ride a bike, knowing a fall is possible, but trusting they will learn to balance.

The younger son, flush with newfound wealth, journeys to a “distant country” – a metaphor for the spiritual distance he puts between himself and his father. There, he squanders his inheritance on “dissolute living.” He indulges in the fleeting pleasures of the world, chasing after happiness in all the wrong places. He believes that freedom lies in unrestrained indulgence, but he soon discovers that true freedom is not the absence of boundaries, but the responsible and wise use of our gifts and resources. The bright lights and empty promises of the world lure him in, only to leave him hollow.

As quickly as the money came, it vanishes. A severe famine strikes the land, and the younger son finds himself in desperate straits. He is forced to take a job feeding pigs – a task considered unclean and degrading for a Jew. He is so hungry that he longs to eat the pig’s food, but even that is denied to him. He has hit rock bottom. He is utterly alone, destitute, and consumed by regret. The laughter has faded, the friends have disappeared, and all that remains is the gnawing emptiness of his choices.

And it is in this moment of utter despair that something remarkable happens. “He came to himself.” This wasn’t just a moment of regret, but a moment of *metanoia* – a turning of his heart and mind, a complete reorientation of his life. True repentance isn't just saying "I'm sorry"; it's turning away from the pigsty and setting your face towards home. He realizes the folly of his ways, the emptiness of his pursuits, and the stark contrast between his current misery and the abundance he had known in his father’s house. He remembers the servants in his father’s household, even they are better off than he is now. This realization is a moment of profound clarity, a turning point in his journey. He recognizes his sin, his rebellion, and his desperate need for redemption. It is the Holy Spirit, working within him, convicting him of his sin and drawing him back to the Father.

He formulates a plan: he will return to his father, not as a son, but as a servant. He will confess his sin and beg for mercy. He doesn’t expect to be welcomed back as a son; he only hopes to be given a place among the hired hands. This humility, born out of suffering, is a sign of genuine repentance. He understands that he has forfeited his right to be called a son.

Now, let’s focus on the father. As the son makes his long and arduous journey home, the father is watching. He is constantly scanning the horizon, hoping to catch a glimpse of his lost boy. And when he finally sees him, still a “long way off,” he doesn’t wait for the son to reach him. He is filled with compassion, and he runs to meet him.

This is a pivotal moment. The father, a man of dignity and standing in his community, abandons all decorum and sprints towards his son. He doesn’t care about what others might think; he only cares about reaching his child and bringing him home. Imagine the whispers rippling through the village as the elder, robes flying, races towards the disheveled figure approaching.

He embraces him, showering him with kisses. He doesn’t allow the son to finish his rehearsed speech of repentance. He cuts him off, silencing his self-condemnation and replacing it with an outpouring of love and acceptance. He doesn't dwell on the past; he focuses on the present – the joy of his son’s return. The father's actions mirror the very heart of God, who, in Jesus Christ, ran to meet us, broken and lost, offering forgiveness and reconciliation through the cross. Jesus *is* the embodiment of this father's love, the ultimate expression of God's desire to bring us home.

He then orders his servants to bring the best robe, a ring for his finger, and sandals for his feet – symbols of honor, authority, and belonging. He commands them to prepare a feast, a celebration of his son’s homecoming. “For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.”

This is the heart of the parable: the extravagant, unconditional love of the father. God's love, like the father's, is offered freely, unconditionally. But that doesn't mean it leaves us unchanged. It's a love that calls us to become more like Christ, to live lives of love, service, and obedience. It's a love that invites us into a new way of being. It is a love that transcends all boundaries, a love that forgives all sins, a love that rejoices in the restoration of what was lost. It is a love that mirrors the love of God for each and every one of us.

But the story doesn’t end there. We are then introduced to the older brother, who represents a different kind of lostness. He has remained at home, diligently working in the fields, obedient to his father’s commands. He is the epitome of righteousness, at least on the surface. But when he hears the music and dancing, when he learns that his brother has returned and is being celebrated, he becomes angry. The younger son wallowed in the mud; the elder brother simmers in resentment.

He refuses to go inside, to join the celebration. He feels resentful, overlooked, and unappreciated. He complains to his father, listing all the ways he has been faithful and all the ways his brother has been unworthy. “All these years I have slaved for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!” We can easily judge the older brother, but haven't we all felt a twinge of resentment when someone else receives praise or recognition? Haven't we all felt like our hard work goes unnoticed?

The older brother’s anger reveals a deep-seated pride and a lack of understanding of his father’s love. He sees his relationship with his father as a transaction, a system of rewards and punishments. He believes that he deserves special treatment because of his obedience. He doesn’t understand that his father’s love is not earned, but freely given. He doesn’t rejoice in his brother’s return; he is consumed by envy and self-pity. The father's love isn't a reward system; it's a relationship. It is the difference between dutiful obligation and joyful belonging.

The father, once again, responds with compassion. He goes out to the older brother and pleads with him to come inside. “My son,” he says, “you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.”

The parable ends without telling us whether the older brother ever relents and joins the celebration. This open ending challenges us to examine our own hearts and to ask ourselves: Are we more like the prodigal son, who strayed from the path and needed to be welcomed back? Or are we more like the older brother, who remained faithful but struggled with resentment and a lack of compassion? Which brother do we see reflected in the mirror of our own souls?

So, what does this parable mean for us, here and now? How does it speak to our lives, our struggles, and our hopes?

Firstly, it reminds us that we are all prodigals in some way. We have all, at some point in our lives, strayed from the path, made mistakes, and fallen short of God’s expectations. We have all experienced moments of rebellion, doubt, and despair. We have all chased after false idols, seeking happiness in things that ultimately leave us empty. Perhaps you've poured your energy into a career that promised fulfillment but delivered only stress. Or maybe you've chased after relationships that left you feeling more alone than ever.

But the good news is that God, like the father in the parable, is always waiting for us to return. He is always watching, always hoping, always ready to embrace us with open arms. No matter how far we have strayed, no matter how deep our sins, His love is boundless and His forgiveness is complete. As the hymn says, "There's a wideness in God's mercy, like the wideness of the sea."

Secondly, the parable challenges us to examine our own attitudes towards others. Are we quick to judge and condemn those who have made mistakes? Or are we willing to extend grace and compassion, to offer a helping hand to those who are struggling? Are we able to rejoice in the restoration of others, even when we feel that we have been overlooked or unappreciated? Perhaps a colleague at work makes a serious error – do we offer support, or do we secretly revel in their misfortune?

The older brother’s resentment reminds us that righteousness without love is empty and meaningless. True faith is not just about following the rules; it is about cultivating a heart of compassion and a willingness to forgive. It’s about recognizing that we are all flawed, all in need of grace.

Finally, the parable calls us to embrace the joy of homecoming. It invites us to celebrate the restoration of broken relationships, the healing of wounded hearts, and the triumph of love over despair. It reminds us that we are all part of God’s family, and that there is always a place for us at His table.

Brothers and sisters, the parable of the Prodigal Son is not just a story about a wayward son and a forgiving father. It is a story about each and every one of us. It is a story about our own journeys of faith, our own struggles with sin and temptation, and our own longing for God’s love and acceptance.

Therefore, I urge you this week to take concrete steps towards embracing the message of this parable. First, identify one relationship in your life where you need to extend forgiveness. Perhaps it's a family member, a friend, or a colleague. Offer them the grace that God has so freely offered you. Second, pray for someone you struggle to show compassion to. Ask God to soften your heart and to help you see them as He sees them. Finally, reflect on your own sense of entitlement and ask God to reveal any hidden pride that may be hindering your relationship with Him and with others.

Let us confess our sins, seek God’s forgiveness, and return to His loving embrace. And let us also strive to be more like the father in the story, extending grace and compassion to others, rejoicing in their restoration, and celebrating the joy of homecoming. For in the unfolding embrace of God's love, we find our true selves, our true belonging, and our eternal home. Amen.

(Congregation takes seats after worship, quiet murmurs, then silence as the preacher approaches the pulpit.)

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

There’s a story, a true story, that has always stuck with me. It’s about a man named Frank. Frank had a temper, a quick fuse that often left scorched earth in its wake. One particularly bad argument with his teenage son, Mark, escalated beyond anything they’d experienced. Harsh words were exchanged, doors were slammed, and Mark, in a fit of righteous anger and youthful rebellion, packed a bag and left. He left a note: "I’m gone. Don’t look for me."

Frank was devastated. Days turned into weeks, weeks into months. He called everyone he knew, posted flyers, even hired a private investigator, but Mark had vanished. The silence in the house was deafening, filled only with Frank’s regret and the hollow ache of a father’s broken heart. He replayed the argument endlessly, wishing he could unsay his words, wishing he could just see his son again.

One day, nearly a year later, Frank was reading the newspaper, a desperate, daily ritual in case Mark’s name appeared. He saw an article about a local homeless shelter needing volunteers. Something in his heart stirred. Maybe, just maybe, Mark might be there, or someone who knew him. He went. He started volunteering, serving meals, listening to stories. He never found Mark, but something profound began to happen to Frank. His anger started to melt, replaced by a quiet compassion. He learned patience, humility, and discovered a capacity for love he didn't know he possessed. He was, in a way, being remade.

Then, one cold evening, as he was serving soup, a young man with a worn backpack and haunted eyes shuffled into the line. Frank’s heart stopped. It was Mark. Thinner, older, but unmistakably his son. Mark didn’t see him at first, his gaze fixed on the steaming bowl. Frank couldn’t speak, a lump in his throat. But as Mark reached the front, their eyes met. For a long moment, the world stood still. Then, Mark’s eyes welled up. Frank simply put down the ladle, walked around the counter, and without a word, enveloped his son in a bear hug. No questions, no accusations, just an embrace that spoke volumes of love, forgiveness, and an unbearable longing finally satisfied.

This story, or one like it, plays out in countless variations in human experience. It speaks to our deep-seated need for belonging, for forgiveness, for a place to call home, and for a love that doesn't count the cost. And it is this very human longing, and God's divine answer to it, that Jesus addresses in one of his most profound and beloved parables, found in Luke chapter 15.

You see, Jesus told this parable in a very specific context. Just before it, we read that "all the tax collectors and sinners were coming near to listen to him. And the Pharisees and the scribes were grumbling, 'This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them.'" (Luke 15:1-2). So, Jesus tells three parables in response: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and then, the most detailed and poignant of all, the lost son – often called the Prodigal Son. He is speaking to two audiences simultaneously: the "lost" who are drawn to him, and the "religious" who are critical of him. Let’s open our Bibles to Luke 15, starting at verse 11, and listen to this timeless story as if for the first time.

**(Read Luke 15:11-32)**

This parable is a masterpiece, a theological gem that reveals the very heart of God. It's often called the "Parable of the Prodigal Son," but perhaps a more fitting title would be the "Parable of the Prodigal Father" or the "Parable of Two Lost Sons." Let's unpack it, character by character.

**I. The Younger Son: The Journey of Rebellion and Repentance**

The story begins with a young man who makes an astonishing and deeply offensive request: "Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me." In that culture, this was akin to wishing your father dead. It was a profound insult, a rejection of family, tradition, and honor. He wanted his inheritance *now*, so he could live life on his own terms, free from parental oversight. He wasn't interested in relationship; he was interested in what he could *get* from the relationship.

And the father, remarkably, grants his wish. He divides his property. This act of grace, or perhaps painful acquiescence, sets the younger son on his journey. He packs up, leaves home, and heads to a "distant country," a place where he can truly be "free." And what does he do with this freedom? He "squandered his property in dissolute living." The Greek word here, *asōtōs*, means "wastefully, recklessly, extravagantly." He was a true prodigal – one who wastes resources, especially money, in a reckless and extravagant way.

But his reckless freedom soon turns to ruin. A severe famine strikes, and he finds himself utterly destitute. He takes the most degrading job imaginable for a Jew: feeding pigs. Not only is he starving, but he's surrounded by unclean animals, so hungry he longs to eat their slop. This is rock bottom. This is the pit of despair, the ultimate consequence of his choices.

And then, a pivotal moment: "he came to himself." This isn't just regret over his circumstances; it's a profound self-awareness, a moment of clarity. He realizes the vast difference between his current state and even the lowliest servants in his father's house. He devises a plan: "I will get up and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired hands.'" This is genuine repentance – a change of mind that leads to a change of direction, a willingness to humble himself and return, even if it means sacrificing his sonship for servanthood. He’s not expecting a party; he's hoping for survival.

This younger son represents all of us who have, at some point, tried to live life our own way, apart from God. We pursue our own desires, thinking we know best, seeking freedom in things that ultimately enslave us. We run from God, chase fleeting pleasures, and often find ourselves in a spiritual famine, starving for true meaning and connection. But no matter how far we stray, no matter how deep the pit, there is always a "coming to our senses" moment available, a moment of repentance where we realize the Father's house is always better than the distant country.

**II. The Father: The Image of God's Extravagant Love**

Now, let's turn our gaze to the father, the true hero of this story. While the son was in the distant country, squandering his inheritance, what was the father doing? The text tells us: "But while he was still far off, his father saw him." This implies constant watching, daily longing, scanning the horizon for any sign of his lost boy. He hadn't given up hope. He hadn't closed his heart.

And when he sees him, what does he do? He doesn't wait for his son to arrive, groveling at the doorstep. He doesn't send a servant. "His father was filled with compassion; he ran and put his arms around him and kissed him." In that culture, for an older, dignified man to hitch up his robes and *run* was undignified, even scandalous. But love transcends cultural norms. This father, our Heavenly Father, is willing to sacrifice his dignity for the sake of his child.

He runs *to* his son, embraces him, and kisses him – a sign of acceptance and reconciliation *before* a single word of apology is uttered. The son begins his prepared confession: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son." But the father doesn't let him finish the part about becoming a hired hand. His love is so overwhelming that he interrupts the confession with an outpouring of grace.

"Quickly, bring out a robe—the best one—and put it on him; put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. And get the fatted calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate; for this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!"

Each of these actions is laden with significance:
*   **The best robe:** A symbol of honor and restoration to full sonship.
*   **A ring:** A sign of authority and belonging, perhaps even a family signet ring.
*   **Sandals:** Servants went barefoot. Sandals signified freedom and the status of a son.
*   **The fatted calf:** Reserved for special celebrations, indicating a feast of immense joy and importance.

This is not just forgiveness; it is radical, extravagant restoration. The father doesn't just tolerate his son's return; he celebrates it with unbridled joy. He doesn't care about the money, the wasted inheritance, or the public shame. He only cares that his son, who was as good as dead, is now alive, and who was lost, is now found.

This father is the perfect picture of our God. He is a God who waits, who watches, who runs to us, who embraces us before we can even fully articulate our repentance. He doesn't just forgive our sins; He restores us to full sonship and daughtership, clothing us in His righteousness, giving us His authority, and celebrating our return with unimaginable joy. His love is not earned; it is freely given. His grace is not limited by our past failures; it is boundless.

**III. The Older Son: The Challenge of Self-Righteousness**

But the story isn't over. Jesus, remember, is also speaking to the Pharisees and scribes – the "older brothers" of his day.

The older son, who has been faithfully working in the fields, hears the sounds of celebration. When he learns the reason – his prodigal brother has returned, and a feast is being held – he becomes "angry and refused to go in."

His response reveals a heart far from his father's. He confronts his father with bitter resentment: "Listen! For all these years I have been slaving for you, and I have never disobeyed your command; yet you have never given me even a young goat so that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came back, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fatted calf for him!"

Notice his language: "all these years I have been slaving for you." He views his relationship with his father as one of servitude, of earning his keep, of transactional obedience. He sees his brother not as "my brother" but as "this son of yours." He can't celebrate because he feels he's been wronged. He's focused on fairness, on what he *deserves*, and on the perceived injustice of his brother's undeserved grace. He was in the father's house, but his heart was far from the father's heart. He was "lost" in a different way – lost to joy, lost to compassion, lost to grace.

And again, the father's patience and love shine through. He goes out to *him* too, pleading, "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But we had to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found."

The parable ends there. We don't know if the older son ever joins the celebration. Jesus leaves it open, a challenge to his audience, and to us. Will we, the "older brothers and sisters" who have perhaps always tried to do the right thing, who have diligently served, embrace the radical grace of God and celebrate with Him when the lost are found? Or will we stand outside, grumbling, resentful that others receive what we feel they don't deserve?

**IV. Application for Us Today**

So, what does this timeless parable mean for us, here and now?

**1. For the "Younger Sons and Daughters" among us:**
Perhaps you feel you've strayed far from God, or from the path you know is right. Maybe you've made choices you deeply regret, squandered opportunities, or lived a life that feels empty and distant from faith. The good news is this: **Your Father is waiting.** He sees you "while you are still a long way off." He is filled with compassion. He is ready to run to you, embrace you, forgive you completely, and restore you fully. Your past mistakes do not define your future with God. Your worth is not determined by your performance, but by His unconditional love. All it takes is to "come to yourself," turn around, and start the journey home. He will meet you more than halfway.

**2. For the "Older Sons and Daughters" among us:**
Perhaps you've been faithful, diligent, and committed to your faith for a long time. You've worked hard, served faithfully, and tried to live a good life. Be careful not to let self-righteousness creep into your heart. Are you grateful for the grace you've received, or do you subtly judge those who seem to receive it "too easily"? Do you begrudge God's radical mercy to others, feeling that your own faithfulness should earn you more?
The Father tells the older son: "All that is mine is yours." You are already in the house, with full access to His blessings, His presence, and His love. Don't miss the joy of being with the Father by focusing on what others have or don't deserve. God's grace is not a limited resource; it's an overflowing fountain. Join the celebration! Embrace the joy of another soul found, another life restored.

**3. For all of us, as the Church:**
This parable calls us to be like the Father. We are called to be a community that actively looks for the lost, that runs to embrace those who return, and that celebrates with extravagant joy when a life is reconciled to God. We are to be a place of radical welcome, where no one is too broken, too sinful, or too far gone to find forgiveness and full restoration. We must guard against the spirit of the older brother, ensuring our doors and our hearts are always open to those who are returning, and that we do not put up barriers of judgment or resentment.

**Conclusion**

The Parable of the Prodigal Son is, at its heart, the Gospel in miniature. It is the story of God's relentless, extravagant, and unconditional love for every single one of us. It reminds us that no matter our past, no matter our present struggles, God's arms are always open, His heart is always longing for our return, and His grace is always sufficient.

Are you a younger son or daughter, longing for home? Hear the Father calling, see Him running, and know that you are loved beyond measure. Come home.

Are you an older son or daughter, perhaps weary or resentful? See the Father’s enduring love for you, and for all His children. Open your heart to His joy, and join the celebration.

Let us never forget that God is a God of second chances, of endless grace, of profound forgiveness. He is the Father who waits, who runs, who embraces, who restores, and who celebrates. May we, His children, reflect that same boundless love to a world desperately in need of it.

Let us pray.

This parable is a masterpiece, a theological gem that reveals the very heart of God. It's often called the "Parable of the Prodigal Son," but perhaps a more fitting title would be the "Parable of the Prodigal Father" or the "Parable of Two Lost Sons." The beauty of this story is that it holds a mirror up to every single one of us, because we all have the potential to be one of these three figures. Let's unpack it, character by character.

### I. The Reckless Pursuit of Freedom (The Younger Son)

The story begins with a young man who makes an astonishing and deeply offensive request: "Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me." In that culture, this was akin to wishing your father dead. It was a profound insult, a rejection of family, tradition, and honor. He wanted his inheritance *now*, so he could live life on his own terms, free from parental oversight. He wasn't interested in relationship; he was interested in what he could *get* from the relationship.

And the father, remarkably, grants his wish. He divides his property. This act of grace, or perhaps painful acquiescence, sets the younger son on his journey. He packs up, leaves home, and heads to a "distant country," a place where he can truly be "free." And what does he do with this freedom? He "squandered his property in dissolute living." The Greek word here, *asōtōs*, means "wastefully, recklessly, extravagantly." He was a true prodigal – one who wastes resources, especially money, in a reckless and extravagant way.

But his reckless freedom soon turns to ruin. A severe famine strikes, and he finds himself utterly destitute. He takes the most degrading job imaginable for a Jew: feeding pigs. Not only is he starving, but he's surrounded by unclean animals, so hungry he longs to eat their slop. This is rock bottom. This is the pit of despair, the ultimate consequence of his choices.

And then, a pivotal moment: "he came to himself." This isn't just regret over his circumstances; it's a profound self-awareness, a moment of clarity. He realizes the vast difference between his current state and even the lowliest servants in his father's house. He devises a plan: "I will get up and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired hands.'" This is genuine repentance – a change of mind that leads to a change of direction, a willingness to humble himself and return, even if it means sacrificing his sonship for servanthood. He’s not expecting a party; he's hoping for survival.

This younger son represents all of us who have, at some point, tried to live life our own way, apart from God. We pursue our own desires, thinking we know best, seeking freedom in things that ultimately enslave us. We run from God, chase fleeting pleasures, and often find ourselves in a spiritual famine, starving for true meaning and connection. But no matter how far we stray, no matter how deep the pit, there is always a "coming to our senses" moment available, a moment of repentance where we realize the Father's house is always better than the distant country.

Now, let's turn our gaze to the father, the true hero of this story. While the son was in the distant country, squandering his inheritance, what was the father doing? The text tells us: "But while he was still far off, his father saw him." This implies constant watching, daily longing, scanning the horizon for any sign of his lost boy. He hadn't given up hope. He hadn't closed his heart.

And when he sees him, what does he do? He doesn't wait for his son to arrive, groveling at the doorstep. He doesn't send a servant. "His father was filled with compassion; he ran and put his arms around him and kissed him." In that culture, for an older, dignified man to hitch up his robes and *run* was not just undignified, it was scandalous. It was an act of public self-abasement. For a father to run to a son who had brought such shame upon the family was to take on that shame himself, to absorb the public scorn, to become vulnerable for the sake of his child. This isn't just about dignity; it’s about the father *taking on the shame* of the son before the son can even confess it. It is a profound foreshadowing of Christ's own humiliation, who "though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men. The Father, our Heavenly Father, is willing to sacrifice everything for the sake of His child.

He runs *to* his son, embraces him, and kisses him – a sign of acceptance and reconciliation *before* a single word of apology is uttered. The son begins his prepared confession: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son." But the story isn't over. Jesus, remember, is also speaking to the Pharisees and scribes – the "older brothers" of his day. And just as the father's radical grace has sunk into our hearts, Jesus introduces a new layer to the family dynamic.

Or will we stand outside, grumbling, resentful that others receive what we feel they don't deserve?

So, what does this timeless parable mean for us, here and now?

**1. For the "Younger Sons and Daughters" among us:**
Perhaps you feel you've strayed far from God, or from the path you know is right. Maybe you've made choices you deeply regret, squandered opportunities, or lived a life that feels empty and distant from faith. He is ready to run to you, embrace you, forgive you completely, and restore you fully. Your past mistakes do not define your future with God. Your worth is not determined by your performance, but by His unconditional love. All it takes is to "come to yourself," turn around, and start the journey home. He will meet you more than halfway, take on your shame, and welcome you with open arms.

**2. For the "Older Sons and Daughters" among us:**
Perhaps you've been faithful, diligent, and committed to your faith for a long time. You've worked hard, served faithfully, and tried to live a good life. Be careful not to let self-righteousness creep into your heart. Are you grateful for the grace you've received, or do you subtly judge those who seem to receive it "too easily"? Do you begrudge God's radical mercy to others, feeling that your own faithfulness should earn you more?
The Father tells the older son: "All that is mine is yours." You are already in the house, with full access to His blessings, His presence, and His love. Don't miss the joy of being with the Father by focusing on what others have or don't deserve. God's grace is not a limited resource; it's an overflowing fountain. Join the celebration! Embrace the joy of another soul found, another life restored. True life in the Father’s house means finding your deepest joy not in your own ledger of good deeds, but in the sheer, unearned joy of seeing someone else saved and restored.

**3. For all of us, as the Church:**
This parable calls us to be like the Father. We are called to be a community that actively looks for the lost, that runs to embrace those who return, and that celebrates with extravagant joy when a life is reconciled to God. We are to be a place of radical welcome, where no one is too broken, too sinful, or too far gone to find forgiveness and full restoration. We must guard against the spirit of the older brother, ensuring our doors and our hearts are always open to those who are returning, and that we do not put up barriers of judgment or resentment. When someone new walks through our doors who looks broken or distant, do we offer them the Father’s robe of welcome and restoration, or do we eye them suspiciously like the older brother, demanding they earn their place? Our call is to reflect the Father's heart, always ready to celebrate.

**Conclusion**

The Parable of the Prodigal Son is, at its heart, the Gospel in miniature. It is the story of God's relentless, extravagant, and unconditional love for every single one of us. It reminds us that no matter our past, no matter our present struggles, God's arms are always open, His heart is always longing for our return, and His grace is always sufficient.

Are you a younger son or daughter, longing for home? Hear the Father calling, see Him running, and know that you are loved beyond measure. Come home.

Are you an older son or daughter, perhaps weary or resentful? See the Father’s enduring love for you, and for all His children. Open your heart to His joy, and join the celebration.

Let us never forget that God is a God of second chances, of endless grace, of profound forgiveness. He is the Father who waits, who runs, who embraces, who restores, and who celebrates. May we, His children, reflect that same boundless love to a world desperately in need of it.

Let us pray.

Heavenly Father, we thank You for the profound truth revealed in this parable. Thank You for being a God who waits, who runs to us, who embraces us in our brokenness, and who celebrates our return. Forgive us for the times we have strayed like the younger son, and for the times we have judged like the older son. Soften our hearts, Lord, that we may always run to You in repentance, and that we may always welcome others with Your extravagant love and grace. Help us to live as Your beloved children, always in Your presence, always celebrating Your goodness. We ask this in the name of Your Son, Jesus Christ, our Savior. Amen.
