You rehearse the speech. *“I’ll say this, and then if they say that, I’ll admit to this part, but I’ll explain why I did it...”* We negotiate the terms of our surrender. We try to find a way to manage the shame, to craft a sentence that might just salvage a scrap of our dignity. We think that if we can just find the right words, we can mitigate the damage.

In the famous parable we read today—often called the Parable of the Prodigal Son—we find a young man doing exactly this. He is starving, he is broken, and he is rehearsing his speech. *“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”*

It is a good speech. It is humble. It is theological. And, as we will see, it is completely unnecessary.

We often treat this story as a simple tale for those who have wandered far from church—a story about a “bad boy” who comes home. But if we look closer, we find that Jesus is doing something far more subversive. He is telling a story about two sons, not just one. And more importantly, He is telling us a story about a Father whose love is so extravagant, so undignified, and so persistent, that it shatters our categories of fairness and rewrites the definition of God.

**Part 1: The Scandal of the Departure**

The story begins with a shock that reverberates through the first-century Middle Eastern context. “A man had two sons. The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’”

To our modern ears, this sounds like a trust fund baby asking for an early withdrawal. But in the culture of Jesus’ day, this is a slap in the face. Inheritance was given when the father died. By asking for his share now, the younger son is effectively saying, “Dad, you are taking too long to die. I want your things, but I don’t want you. I would prefer you were dead so I can get on with my life.”

The community would have expected the father to explode in rage. He should have slapped the boy. He should have cut him off immediately. But the text says something breathtakingly simple: “And he divided his property between them.”

The father grants the request. He allows his heart to be broken to preserve the boy’s freedom. He liquidates his assets—likely selling off land that had been in the family for generations—diminishing his own standing in the community to give the boy what he wants.

So the son gathers all he has and journeys to a “far country.” We don’t know where this is geographically, but we know where it is spiritually. The far country is anywhere we go to be our own boss. It is that place where we believe the lie that freedom is found in the absence of restraint.

And for a while, it works. He has money. He has friends—or at least, people who like his money. But then, the inevitable happens. The money runs out. A famine strikes. The friends vanish.

The text tells us he “began to be in need.” He attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him to feed pigs. For a Jewish boy, raised in the covenant, this is the absolute bottom. Pigs were unclean. He is feeding animals he isn't even supposed to touch, and he is so hungry he envies their food.

Here is the tragedy of sin: it promises liberty, but it always leads to slavery. He wanted to be free from his father’s authority, and he ended up a slave to a stranger, starving in a pigsty.

Then comes the pivot point of the parable. Verse 17 says, “But when he came to himself.” The madness of sin lifted. He remembered who he was. He remembered his father’s house.

But notice his theology is still a bit warped. He constructs his plan: *“I will go back. I will apologize. And I will ask to be a hired servant.”*

He thinks the relationship is transactional. He thinks, *“I have blown my credit as a son. I cannot be a son anymore. But maybe, if I work hard enough, if I pay him back over twenty years, I can earn a place in the bunkhouse.”* He is hoping for a job interview. He is hoping to pay off his debt.

In that culture, a Jewish boy who lost his inheritance to Gentiles could face a ceremony called the *kezazah*—the cutting off. The village would break a pot at his feet and banish him forever. He expects rejection. He expects to be yelled at.

But he doesn’t meet the village.

This is the most startling image in the New Testament. In that culture, distinguished, elderly patriarchs did not run. To run, a man had to hike up his long robes, exposing his legs. It was considered shameful, undignified. A Middle Eastern father of that stature moves slow and demands respect.

It wasn't just to get to the boy before the village did, to intercept the shame and take the indignity upon himself—though that is certainly true. He ran because of who He is. The Greek word for "compassion" here is visceral; it speaks of a churning in the gut. But behind that emotion lies a deep theological reality: the Hebrew concept of *Hesed*.

*Hesed* is God’s covenantal love. It is a stubborn, loyal, refusing-to-let-go love. It is love that does not depend on the loveliness of the object, but on the character of the lover. The Father runs because His love is stronger than His dignity.

The father throws his arms around the boy. The boy starts his speech: “Father, I have sinned... I am no longer worthy...” But notice what happens. The father interrupts him! He doesn’t let him get to the part about being a “hired servant.”

But the father refuses to accept the son’s *payment plan*. The son wanted to offer his labor to earn his way back. The father says, "No."

The Father shouts to the servants, “Bring quickly the best robe.” That’s the father’s robe—restoring his honor. “Put a ring on his hand.” That is the family signet—restoring his authority and access to the wealth. “Put sandals on his feet.” Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes.

The son wanted a job; the Father gave him a feast. The son wanted to earn his way back; the Father covered him in grace.

This is the Gospel. You cannot earn your way back to God. You cannot clean yourself up in the pigsty before you come home. If the story ended there, it would be a beautiful testimony of God’s love for the rebellious. But Jesus doesn’t stop. To understand why, we have to look at who Jesus is talking to.

Luke 15:1-2 sets the stage: "Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, 'This man receives sinners and eats with them.'"

Second, he says, “I never disobeyed.” He is resting his righteousness on his moral performance.

Third, he says, “This son of yours.” He refuses to say, “my brother.”

Here is the shocking revelation: **Both sons are lost.**

The younger son was lost in the far country of rebellion. The older son is lost in the field of religious duty. The younger son wanted the father’s things, so he ran away. The older son wanted the father’s things, so he stayed and obeyed. But neither of them truly loved the father. They were both using him.

One tried to control the father by being bad; the other tried to control the father by being good.

This is a warning to us—the churchgoers, the rule-keepers, the responsible ones. We can be sitting in the pew every Sunday, tithing, serving, and avoiding the “big sins,” and yet be completely alienated from the heart of God. We can be lost right here in the Father’s house.

We see this attitude in our own hearts, don't we? Imagine the faithful church volunteer. You arrive early every Sunday to set up the chairs. You brew the coffee. You attend the committee meetings. You tithe gross, not net. And then, a guy shows up who hasn't been to church in ten years. His life is a mess. He smells like smoke and trouble. And suddenly, the leadership is pouring resources into him, celebrating him, and giving him attention.

And a little voice inside you whispers: *“Wait a minute. I’ve been here the whole time. Where is my party? This isn’t fair.”*

If it were fair, the younger brother would be in the pigsty, and the older brother would be judged for his pride. Grace is not fair; grace is a gift. Perhaps you are the **Younger Son**. You feel like you’ve blown it. You’ve made choices that have led you into a far country of addiction, or debt, or broken relationships, or secret sin. You feel the mud of the pigsty on your soul. You are sitting here thinking, *“I need to fix this. I need to clean myself up. I need to work hard for a few years, and then maybe I can approach God.”*

The Father says to you: **Stop.** Stop rehearsing the speech. Stop trying to negotiate a servant’s wage. Just come home. The Father is not waiting to scold you; He is waiting to drape His robe around your shoulders. He wants to restore you, not employ you. You don’t have to earn what He has already decided to give you freely.

Or, perhaps you are the **Older Son**. You have done everything right. You are the responsible one. You’ve kept the rules. But if you are honest, you are tired. You are bitter. You feel like life—and God—owes you something. You look at people who live wild lives and then convert on their deathbeds, and a part of you thinks, *“What a waste of my obedience.”*

The Father comes out to you today, too. Notice the tenderness in verse 31. “Son,” he says. He appeals to relationship. “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.”

The Father challenges the older brother’s transactional mindset. He says, *“Why do you want a goat? You have Me! You have been in my house. You have had access to my presence, my love, my ear, every single day. Is that not the reward?”*

If we only obey God to get things from Him, we will always be angry when He gives things to others. But if we obey God to get *God*, to be near Him, then we can rejoice when others come home, because our reward is not a fattened calf—our reward is the Father’s presence.

The cure for the younger brother is to repent of his sins. The cure for the older brother is to repent of his self-righteousness. Both must surrender their agenda and accept the Father’s love.

There is something frustrating about this parable. It ends on a cliffhanger.

The father says to the older son, “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

And... that’s it. The story ends. The credits roll.

We don’t know what the older brother did. Did he drop his rock of resentment and go into the party? Did he embrace his brother? Or did he turn his back, cross his arms, and stay out in the dark, nursing his grudge while the music played inside?

Jesus leaves the ending open for a reason. He leaves it open because the older brother was standing right in front of Him. The Pharisees were the older brothers. Jesus was pleading with them: *“Come in. The party is for you, too. Don't let your pride keep you from the feast of grace.”*

And He leaves it open because the question is for us. The pen is in our hands. How will we finish the story today?

But while the story of the *sons* is unfinished, the story of the *Father* is complete.

The music is playing. The Father has run the race. The price has been paid—not by a fattened calf, but by the Lamb of God, Jesus Christ.

You see, Jesus is the True Elder Brother. In the parable, the older brother stayed home and sulked. But our True Elder Brother, Jesus, did not stay in the Father's house. He left his glory. He came to the far country. He entered the pigsty of our world to carry us back. He was stripped naked on the cross so we could be given the best robe. He took the silence of the Father so we could hear the music of the feast. He paid the debt we tried to work off, and He absorbed the unfairness we complain about.

Because of Him, the doors are open. The Father is waiting. Whether you are coming from the pigsty of rebellion or coming from the field of pride, the invitation is the same.

Come inside. Come home.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we thank You that You are the Running God. Thank You for Your 'Hesed' love—that stubborn, covenantal love that chases us down. For those of us who feel far away, give us the courage to turn for home. For those of us who feel self-righteous and bitter, soften our hearts to see that we, too, are in need of grace. Help us to see that having You is the greatest reward of all. Bring us all into the feast. In Jesus’ name, Amen.*

The father grants the request. He tears his estate apart—which likely involved selling land, diminishing the family’s standing in the community—to give the boy what he wants. He allows his heart to be broken to preserve the boy’s freedom.

So the son gathers all he has and journeys to a “far country.” We don’t know where this is geographically, but we know where it is spiritually. The far country is not just a place of debauchery; it is the place where we go to be our own boss.

What does the "far country" look like today? For some, it is the pursuit of career success at the cost of your soul—where your net worth becomes your self-worth. For others, it is romantic obsession, believing that if you just find the right partner, you will finally be whole. For others, it is intellectual cynicism, where you decide you are too smart for God and too sophisticated for faith. The far country is simply anywhere we believe the lie that freedom is found in the absence of the Father’s authority.

And for a while, it works. The son has money. He has friends—or at least, people who like his money. But then, the inevitable happens. The money runs out. A famine strikes. The friends vanish into the woodwork.

The text tells us he “began to be in need.” He attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him to feed pigs.

We must pause here to feel the weight of this. For a Jewish boy, raised in the covenant, this is the absolute bottom. Pigs were unclean animals. He isn't just poor; he is ritually defiled. He is doing work that makes him repulsive to his own people.

Imagine the scene. The mud. The stench. The noise of the swine. He is so hungry that his stomach cramps with violence. He looks at the carob pods the pigs are chewing—hard, fibrous, tasteless pods meant only for beasts—and he thinks, *“I wish I could eat that.”* He has lost his money, his friends, his religion, and now, he is losing his humanity.

Here is the tragedy of sin: it promises liberty, but it always leads to slavery. He wanted to be free from his father’s rules, and he ended up a slave to a stranger, starving in a pigsty.

Then comes the pivot point of the parable. Verse 17 says, “But when he came to himself.” The madness of sin lifted. The illusion of the far country shattered. He remembered who he was. He remembered his father’s house.

He thinks the relationship is transactional. He thinks, *“I have blown my credit as a son. I cannot be a son anymore. But maybe, if I work hard enough, if I pay him back over twenty years, I can earn a place in the bunkhouse.”* He is hoping for a job interview. He is hoping to pay off his debt.

He starts the long walk home. He is likely barefoot, smelling of the pigsty, gaunt, and humiliated. As he approaches the village, he is terrified. Scholars of the era, such as Kenneth Bailey, tell us of a custom called the *kezazah*—the "cutting off." If a Jewish boy lost his inheritance to Gentiles, the village could break a pot at his feet and banish him forever. He is walking toward a gauntlet of shame.

But he doesn’t meet the village.

“But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.”

He ran to get to the boy before the village did. He ran to intercept the shame. He took the indignity upon himself so the son wouldn’t have to face the scorn of the community. The Father sprints through the dust, hiking up his robes, abandoning his dignity to save his son.

The father throws his arms around the boy. The boy starts his rehearsed speech: “Father, I have sinned... I am no longer worthy...”

But notice what happens. The father interrupts him! He doesn’t let him get to the part about being a “hired servant.” The Father doesn't want a servant.

He shouts to the servants, “Bring quickly the best robe.” That’s the father’s own robe—restoring his honor. “Put a ring on his hand.” That is the family signet—restoring his authority and access to the wealth. “Put sandals on his feet.” Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes.

The son wanted a job; the Father gave him a feast. The son wanted to earn his way back; the Father covered him in grace.

This is the Gospel. You cannot earn your way back to God. You cannot clean yourself up in the pigsty before you come home. You come home because He is watching for you. You come home because He runs to meet you.

**Part 3: The Other Lost Son**

If the story ended there, it would be a beautiful testimony of God’s love for the rebellious. The credits would roll, the music would swell, and we would all go home happy.

But Jesus keeps the camera rolling. He pans away from the feast, away from the music and the dancing, out the window to the dark fields outside.

“Now his older son was in the field.”

The older son comes near the house and hears music. He asks a servant what is happening. When he hears that his wastrel brother has returned and his father has killed the fattened calf—the prize of the herd—he becomes angry and refuses to go in.

The father, in his infinite patience, comes out to him, just as he went out to the younger brother.

Listen to the older son’s complaint. It is a speech just as rehearsed as the younger brother's, but it comes from a very different place:

“Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat... But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!”

Do you hear his heart?

First, he says, “I have served you.” The Greek word used there is actually closer to “I have slaved for you.” He doesn’t view the father as a father; he views him as a boss. He views his obedience as a wage.

Second, he says, “I never disobeyed.” He is resting his righteousness on his moral performance. He believes the father owes him because he has been good.

Third, he says, “This son of yours.” He refuses to say, “my brother.”

Here is the shocking revelation: **Both sons are lost.**

The younger son was lost in the far country of rebellion. The older son is lost in the field of religious duty. The younger son wanted the father’s things, so he ran away. The older son wanted the father’s things, so he stayed and obeyed. But neither of them truly loved the father. They were both using him.

One tried to control the father by being bad; the other tried to control the father by being good.

This is a warning to us—the churchgoers, the rule-keepers, the responsible ones. We can be sitting in the pew every Sunday, tithing, serving in the nursery, and avoiding the “big sins,” and yet be completely alienated from the heart of God. We can be lost right here in the Father’s house.

If we believe that God owes us a good life because we have been good people, we have the heart of the older brother. If we look at the “sinners” of the world—the addicts, the broken, the messy people—and feel resentful that God offers them the same grace He offers us, we are standing outside the feast.

We must have some empathy for the older brother. His anger makes sense. It *isn't* fair. He *did* stay. He *did* work. And now the party is for the one who wasted everything?

The older brother is angry because grace isn't fair. And he is right. Grace is not fair. If it were fair, the younger brother would be in the pigsty, and the older brother would be judged for his pride. Grace is not fair; grace is a gift.

**Application: Coming Home**

So, where do you find yourself in this story today?

Perhaps you are the **Younger Son**. You feel like you’ve blown it. You’ve made choices that have led you into a far country of addiction, or debt, or broken relationships, or secret sin. You feel the mud of the pigsty on your soul. You are sitting here thinking, *“I need to fix this. I need to clean myself up. I need to work hard for a few years, and then maybe I can approach God.”*

The Father says to you: **Stop.** Stop rehearsing the speech. Stop trying to negotiate a servant’s wage. Just come home. The Father is not waiting to scold you; He is waiting to drape His robe around your shoulders. He wants to restore you, not employ you. You don’t have to earn what He has already decided to give you freely.

Or, perhaps you are the **Older Son**. This is often harder to admit. You have done everything right. You are the responsible one. You’ve kept the rules. But if you are honest, you are tired. You are bitter. You feel like life—and God—owes you something.

What does "Older Brother" lostness look like in our lives?
It looks like a judgmental spirit, looking down your nose at people who don't vote like you or live like you.
It looks like an inability to forgive, holding onto grudges because "they need to pay for what they did."
It looks like a joyless service, where you volunteer at church not out of love, but because you think you have to keep God happy.

If that is you, the Father comes out to you today, too. Notice the tenderness in verse 31. “Son,” he says. He appeals to relationship. “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.”

The Father challenges the older brother’s transactional mindset. He says, *“Why do you want a goat? You have Me! You have been in my house. You have had access to my presence, my love, my ear, every single day. Is that not the reward?”*

The cure for the younger brother is to repent of his sins. The cure for the older brother is to repent of his self-righteousness. Both must surrender their agenda and accept the Father’s love.

**Conclusion: The True Elder Brother**

There is something frustrating about this parable. It ends on a cliffhanger.

The father says to the older son, “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

And... that’s it. The story ends.

We don’t know what the older brother did. Did he drop his rock of resentment and go into the party? Did he embrace his brother? Or did he turn his back, cross his arms, and stay out in the dark, nursing his grudge while the music played inside?

Jesus leaves the ending open for a reason. He leaves it open because the older brother was standing right in front of Him. The Pharisees were the older brothers. Jesus was pleading with them: *“Come in. The party is for you, too. Don't let your pride keep you from the feast of grace.”*

But there is another reason the story feels incomplete. It’s because there is a character missing.

In a functional family, when the younger brother ran away, who should have gone after him? It was the job of the firstborn son—the older brother—to keep the family together. The older brother should have said, "Father, I will go to the far country. I will find him. I will bring him home at my own expense."

But in the parable, the older brother stays home. He doesn't care.

This is where the good news breaks through. We have a better Older Brother. We have a True Elder Brother.

Jesus Christ is the brother who did not stay in the Father’s house. He left the glory of heaven. He came into the far country of this broken world. He entered the pigsty of our sin. And unlike the brother in the story, Jesus didn't just complain about the cost; He paid it.

He was stripped naked on a cross so we could be clothed in the best robe. He took the shame of the *kezazah*—the cutting off—so we could be brought in. He took the silence of the Father on Calvary so we could hear the music of the feast.

Because of Jesus, the True Elder Brother, the doors are open. The Father has run the race. The price has been paid.

Whether you are coming from the pigsty of rebellion or coming from the field of pride, the invitation is the same.

Come inside. Come home.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we thank You that You are the Running God. Thank You that You do not treat us as our sins deserve, nor do You repay us according to our iniquities. For those of us who feel far away, give us the courage to turn for home. For those of us who feel self-righteous and bitter, soften our hearts to see the beauty of Your grace. Help us to see that having You is the greatest reward of all. Bring us all into the feast. In Jesus’ name, Amen.*

If the story ended there, it would be a beautiful testimony of God’s love for the rebellious. But Jesus doesn’t stop. Remember, Jesus is telling this parable to a specific audience. Luke 15:1-2 tells us the Pharisees were grumbling because Jesus ate with sinners.

The first half of the story is for the sinners. The second half is for the religious people. And this, arguably, is the more tragic half of the story.

“Now his older son was in the field.”

The older son comes near the house and hears music and dancing. He asks a servant what is happening. When he hears that his wastrel brother has returned and his father has killed the fattened calf, he becomes angry and refuses to go in.

The father, in his infinite patience, comes out to him, just as he went out to the younger brother.

Listen to the older son’s complaint: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat... But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!”

Do you hear his heart?

First, look at the verb he uses. “I have served you.” The Greek word is *douleuō*, which literally means “to slave.” “I have slaved for you!” This reveals the darkness in the older brother’s heart. He has been living in the father’s house, eating the father’s food, but in his mind, he is not a son. He is a slave. He views his obedience as a wage. He believes he is putting the father in his debt.

Second, he says, “I never disobeyed.” He is resting his righteousness on his moral performance. He is proud of his resume.

Third, he says, “This son of yours.” He refuses to say, “my brother.”

Here is the shocking revelation: **Both sons are lost.**

The younger son was lost in the far country of rebellion. The older son is lost in the field of religious duty. The younger son wanted the father’s things, so he ran away. The older son wanted the father’s things, so he stayed and obeyed. But neither of them truly loved the father. They were both using him.

One tried to control the father by being bad; the other tried to control the father by being good.

This is a warning to us—the churchgoers, the rule-keepers, the responsible ones. We can be sitting in the pew every Sunday, tithing, serving, and avoiding the “big sins,” and yet be completely alienated from the heart of God. We can be lost right here in the Father’s house.

We see this dynamic today. It is the volunteer who runs the church nursery every week, never missing a Sunday, but who secretly resents the parents who drop off their kids and go to brunch. It is the person who has lived a moral life and feels a spike of anger when they see a notorious sinner convert and receive the same grace, the same welcome, the same joy.

The older brother is angry because grace isn't fair. And he is right. Grace is not fair. If it were fair, the younger brother would be in the pigsty, and the older brother would be judged for his pride. Grace is not fair; grace is a gift.

**Application: Coming Home**

So, where do you find yourself in this story today?

For some of you, you are the **Younger Son**. You feel like you’ve blown it. You’ve made choices that have led you into a far country of addiction, or debt, or broken relationships, or secret sin. You feel the mud of the pigsty on your soul. You are sitting here thinking, *“I need to fix this. I need to clean myself up. I need to work hard for a few years, and then maybe I can approach God.”*

The Father says to you: **Stop.** Stop rehearsing the speech. Yes, you must repent—you must turn around and come home. But do not confuse repentance with payment. You cannot pay for what you have done. The Father is not waiting to employ you; He is waiting to restore you.

For others—and perhaps for many of us who have been in church a long time—you are the **Older Son**. You have done everything right. You are the responsible one. You’ve kept the rules. But if you are honest, you are tired. You are bitter. You feel like life—and God—owes you something. You are slaving for a Father who wants you to be a Son.

The Father comes out to you today, too. Notice the tenderness in verse 31. “Son,” he says. He appeals to relationship. “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.”

The Father challenges the older brother’s transactional mindset. He says, *“Why do you want a goat? You have Me! You have been in my house. You have had access to my presence, my love, my ear, every single day. Is that not the reward?”*

So what does it look like to come home?

It doesn't mean you have to walk down an aisle or make a grand gesture. It means dropping the performance. It means praying a terrifyingly honest prayer: *“God, I am tired of trying to earn your love. I am tired of my self-righteousness. I am coming in from the field.”*

The cure for the younger brother is to repent of his sins. The cure for the older brother is to repent of his righteousness. Both must surrender their agenda and accept the Father’s love.

As we close, we have to deal with the ending. There is something frustrating about this parable. It ends on a cliffhanger.

The father says to the older son, “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

But in the parable, the older brother stays home. He doesn’t care.

We need a better Elder Brother.

And the good news of the Gospel is that we have one. Jesus told this story to show us what the Pharisees failed to be, and what He came to be.

Jesus Christ is the True Elder Brother. He did not stay in the Father’s house. He left the glory of heaven. He came into the far country of our world. He came into the pigsty of our sin.

But He didn't just come to find us. He came to pay the debt we couldn't pay.

In the parable, the younger son gets the robe, and the older son gets nothing. He took the shame of the *kezazah*—the cutting off—so that we could receive the ring of belonging. He drank the cup of the Father’s silence so that we could hear the music of the feast.

The doors are open. The Father is waiting. The price has been paid by the Brother who came for you.

Whether you are coming from the pigsty of rebellion or the field of pride, the invitation is the same.

Come inside. Come home.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we thank You that You are the Running God. Thank You that You do not treat us as our sins deserve, nor do You repay us according to our iniquities. For those of us who feel far away, give us the courage to turn for home. For those of us who feel self-righteous and bitter, soften our hearts to see the beauty of Your grace. Help us to see Jesus as the Brother who came to find us. Bring us all into the feast. In Jesus’ name, Amen.*

**Title:** The Two Lost Sons and the Running Father
**Text:** Luke 15:11-32

**Introduction: The Rehearsed Speech**

We have all been there. It is that moment in the middle of the night, staring at the ceiling, or perhaps on a long drive with the radio off. The moment when the weight of our own mistakes presses down so hard it becomes difficult to breathe. You know you have to apologize. You know you have to go back and face the person you hurt. And so, you begin to write the script in your head.

You rehearse the speech. *“I’ll say this, and then if they say that, I’ll admit to this part, but I’ll explain why I did it...”* We negotiate the terms of our surrender. We try to find a way to manage the shame, to craft a sentence that might just salvage a scrap of our dignity.

In the famous parable we read today—often called the Parable of the Prodigal Son—we find a young man doing exactly this. He is starving, he is broken, and he is rehearsing his speech. *“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”*

It is a good speech. It is humble. It is theological. And, as we will see, it is completely unnecessary.

We often treat this story as a simple tale for those who have wandered far from church—a story about a bad boy who comes home. But if we zoom out, we see that Jesus is doing something far more subversive. This story is actually the third in a trilogy. In Luke 15, the Pharisees are grumbling because Jesus is eating with sinners. So, Jesus tells three stories: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and finally, two lost sons.

He is building a case. And in this final story, He tells us about a Father whose love is so extravagant, so undignified, and so persistent, that it shatters our categories of fairness and rewrites the definition of God.

**Part 1: The Scandal of the Departure**

The story begins with a shock. “A man had two sons. The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’”

In the first-century Middle Eastern context, this is not merely a request for a loan. This is a slap in the face. Inheritance was given when the father died. By asking for his share now, the younger son is effectively saying, “Dad, you are taking too long to die. I want your things, but I don’t want *you*. I would prefer you were dead so I can get on with my life.”

The community would have expected the father to explode in rage. He should have slapped the boy. He should have cut him off. But the text says something breathtakingly simple: “And he divided his property between them.”

The father grants the request. He allows his heart to be broken to preserve the boy’s freedom.

So the son gathers all he has and journeys to a “far country.” We don’t know where this is geographically, but we know where it is spiritually. The far country is anywhere we go to be our own boss. It is that place where we believe the lie that freedom is found in the absence of restraint.

And for a while, it works. He has money. He has friends—or at least, people who like his money. But then, the inevitable happens. The money runs out. A famine strikes. The friends vanish.

The text tells us he “began to be in need.” He attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him to feed pigs. For a Jewish boy, raised in the covenant, this is the bottom. Pigs were unclean. He is feeding animals he isn't even supposed to touch, and he is so hungry he envies their food.

Here is the tragedy of sin: it promises liberty, but it always leads to slavery. He wanted to be free from his father’s authority, and he ended up a slave to a stranger, starving in a pigsty.

**Part 2: The Return and the Race**

Then comes the pivot point of the parable. Verse 17 says, “But when he came to himself.”

This is a fascinating phrase. Does it mean he repented? Not exactly. If we look closely, his motivation is mixed. He isn't thinking about his father’s broken heart; he is thinking about his own empty stomach. He realizes that even the servants back home have bread.

This is important for us. We often think we need to have perfect, pure motives to turn back to God. We think we need to be fully sanctified before we can pray. But the Father meets us in the mess. He accepts even our imperfect, hunger-driven turns toward home.

So, the son constructs his plan: *“I will go back. I will apologize. And I will ask to be a hired servant.”*

He thinks the relationship is transactional. He thinks, *“I have blown my credit as a son. I cannot be a son anymore. But maybe, if I work hard enough, if I pay him back over twenty years, I can earn a place in the bunkhouse.”* He is hoping for a job interview. He is hoping to pay off his debt.

He starts the long walk home. He is likely barefoot, smelling of the pigsty, gaunt, and humiliated. As he approaches the village, he is terrified. Some scholars of Middle Eastern culture, such as Kenneth Bailey, suggest that a Jewish boy who lost his inheritance to Gentiles could face a ceremony of community rejection—a public "cutting off." The village would break a pot at his feet and banish him forever. The son likely expects to run a gauntlet of shame before he even reaches his front door.

But he doesn’t meet the village.

“But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.”

This is the most startling image in the New Testament. In that culture, distinguished, elderly patriarchs did not run. To run, a man had to hike up his long robes, exposing his legs. It was considered shameful, undignified. Aristotle once said, "Great men never run in public."

Why did the Father run?

He ran to get to the boy before the village did. He ran to intercept the shame. He took the indignity upon himself so the son wouldn’t have to face the scorn of the community.

The father throws his arms around the boy. The boy starts his speech: “Father, I have sinned... I am no longer worthy...” But notice what happens. The father interrupts him! He doesn’t let him get to the part about being a “hired servant.”

The Father shouts to the servants, “Bring quickly the best robe.” That’s the father’s robe—restoring his honor. “Put a ring on his hand.” That is the family signet—restoring his authority and access to the wealth. “Put sandals on his feet.” Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes.

The son wanted a job; the Father gave him a feast. The son wanted to earn his way back; the Father covered him in grace.

This is the Gospel.

You cannot earn your way back to God. You cannot clean yourself up in the pigsty before you come home. You come home because He is watching for you. You come home because He runs to meet you.

**Part 3: The Other Lost Son**

If the story ended there, it would be a beautiful testimony of God’s love for the rebellious. We would all leave here feeling warm and comforted.

But Jesus doesn’t stop. And if you are feeling comfortable right now, brace yourself. Because Jesus is about to turn the story on the people who think they don't need it.

“Now his older son was in the field.”

The older son comes near the house and hears music and dancing. He asks a servant what is happening. When he hears that his wastrel brother has returned and his father has killed the fattened calf, he becomes angry and refuses to go in.

The father, in his infinite patience, comes out to him, just as he went out to the younger brother.

Listen to the older son’s complaint: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat... But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!”

First, he says, “I have served you.” The Greek word used there (*douleuō*) is actually closer to “I have slaved for you.” He doesn’t view the father as a father; he views him as a boss. He views his obedience as a way to put the father in his debt.

Second, he says, “I never disobeyed.” He is resting his righteousness on his moral performance.

Third, he says, “This son of yours.” He refuses to say, “my brother.”

Let me give you a picture of what this looks like today. Imagine a woman named Sarah. Sarah has been a member of the church for thirty years. She teaches Sunday School. She brings casseroles to every funeral. She never swears, never drinks too much, and tithes down to the penny. But Sarah is exhausted. She is tired of being the responsible one. And deep down, she is bitter.

When she sees someone new come into the church—someone with a messy past, maybe a history of addiction or a broken marriage—and she sees them getting attention, getting help, getting celebrated for simply showing up, something in her tightens. She thinks, *“I’ve been here for thirty years. No one throws a party for me. Why does God make it so easy for them?”*

Sarah looks like a saint on the outside, but inside, she is just as lost as the boy in the pigsty.

Here is the shocking revelation of the parable: **Both sons are lost.**

The younger son was lost in the far country of rebellion. The older son is lost in the field of religious duty. The younger son wanted the father’s things, so he ran away. The older son wanted the father’s things, so he stayed and obeyed. But neither of them truly loved the father. They were both using him.

One tried to control the father by being bad; the other tried to control the father by being good.

This is a warning to us—the churchgoers, the rule-keepers, the responsible ones. We can be sitting in the pew every Sunday, avoiding the “big sins,” and yet be completely alienated from the heart of God. We can be lost right here in the Father’s house.

If we believe that God owes us a good life because we have been good people, we have the heart of the older brother. If we look at the “sinners” of the world and feel resentful that God offers them the same grace He offers us, we are standing outside the feast.

The older brother is angry because grace isn't fair. And he is right. Grace is not fair. If it were fair, the younger brother would be in the pigsty, and the older brother would be judged for his pride. Grace is not fair; grace is a gift.

**Application: Coming Home**

So, where do you find yourself in this story today?

Perhaps you are the **Younger Son**. You feel like you’ve blown it. You’ve made choices that have led you into a far country. Maybe it’s addiction or debt. Or maybe it’s not that dramatic—maybe it’s just the slow drift of a heart that stopped praying months ago and didn't notice until now. You feel the mud of the pigsty on your soul. You are sitting here thinking, *“I need to fix this. I need to clean myself up. I need to work hard for a few years, and then maybe I can approach God.”*

The Father says to you: **Stop.** Stop rehearsing the speech. Stop trying to negotiate a servant’s wage. Just come home. The Father is not waiting to scold you; He is waiting to drape His robe around your shoulders. He wants to restore you, not employ you. You don’t have to earn what He has already decided to give you freely.

Or, perhaps you are the **Older Son**. You have done everything right. You are the responsible one. But if you are honest, you are tired. You feel like life—and God—owes you something.

I want to ask you a hard question: When was the last time you were genuinely happy that someone else got a blessing you felt you deserved more?

The Father challenges the older brother’s transactional mindset. He says, *“Why do you want a goat? You have Me! You have been in my house. You have had access to my presence, my love, my ear, every single day. Is that not the reward?”*

Or perhaps—and this is the hardest possibility—you are **Both**. Perhaps you are the younger son on Saturday night and the older son on Sunday morning. Perhaps you swing between guilt for your sins and pride in your performance.

The invitation is the same. The cure for the younger brother is to repent of his sins. The cure for the older brother is to repent of his self-righteousness. Both must surrender their agenda and accept the Father’s love.

**Conclusion: The Missing Ending**

There is something frustrating about this parable. It ends on a cliffhanger.

The father says to the older son, “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

And... that’s it. The story ends. The credits roll.

We don’t know what the older brother did. Did he drop his rock of resentment and go into the party? Did he embrace his brother? Or did he turn his back, cross his arms, and stay out in the dark, nursing his grudge while the music played inside?

Jesus leaves the ending open for a reason. He leaves it open because the older brother was standing right in front of Him. The Pharisees were the older brothers. Jesus was pleading with them: *“Come in. The party is for you, too. Don't let your pride keep you from the feast of grace.”*

But there is a deeper reason the story feels incomplete. It’s because the story is missing a True Elder Brother.

In the parable, the younger son has no one to come looking for him. And the older son refuses to welcome him home. But in reality, we have a better Brother.

Jesus is the True Elder Brother. He didn’t stay in the house; He left the Father’s side and came into the far country to find us. He didn’t strip us of our dignity; He was stripped naked on the cross so that we could be clothed in the best robe of His righteousness.

In the parable, a fattened calf is killed to celebrate the son’s return. In the Gospel, the Lamb of God is slain to *make possible* the son’s return. Jesus took the silence of the Father on the cross so that we could hear the music of the feast. He took the exile we deserved so that we could have the welcome we don't.

The doors are open. The Father has run the race. The True Brother has paid the price.

Whether you are coming from the pigsty or coming from the field of pride, the invitation is the same.

Come inside. Come home.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we thank You that You are the Running God. Thank You that You do not treat us as our sins deserve, nor do You repay us according to our iniquities. For those of us who feel far away, give us the courage to turn for home. For those of us who feel self-righteous and bitter, soften our hearts to see the beauty of Your grace. Help us to see that having You is the greatest reward of all. Bring us all into the feast. In Jesus’ name, Amen.*

**Title:** The Two Lost Sons and the Running Father
**Text:** Luke 15:11-32

**Introduction: The Rehearsed Speech**

We have all been there. It is that moment in the middle of the night, staring at the ceiling, or perhaps on a long, silent drive where the radio has been turned off for miles. It is the moment when the weight of our own mistakes presses down so hard it becomes difficult to breathe. You know you have to apologize. You know you have to go back and face the person you hurt. And so, you begin to write the script in your head.

You rehearse the speech. *“I’ll say this, and then if they say that, I’ll admit to this part, but I’ll explain why I did it...”* We negotiate the terms of our surrender. We try to find a way to manage the shame, to craft a sentence that might just salvage a scrap of our dignity. We think, *If I can just find the right words, maybe I can minimize the damage.*

In the famous parable we read today—often called the Parable of the Prodigal Son—we find a young man doing exactly this. He is starving, he is broken, and he is rehearsing his speech. *“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”*

It is a good speech. It is humble. It is theological. It is deeply repentant. And, as we will see, it is completely unnecessary.

We often treat this story as a simple evangelistic tract for those who have wandered far from church—a story about a "bad boy" who comes home. But if we look closer, we find that Jesus is doing something far more subversive. He is telling a story about two sons, not just one. And more importantly, He is telling us a story about a Father whose love is so extravagant, so undignified, and so persistent, that it shatters our categories of fairness and rewrites the definition of God.

**Part 1: The Scandal of the Departure**

The story begins with a shock that would have made the original first-century listeners gasp. “A man had two sons. The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’”

In our modern context, this sounds like a trust fund baby asking for an early withdrawal. But in the first-century Middle Eastern context, this is not merely a financial transaction. This is a slap in the face. Inheritance was given when the father died. By asking for his share now, the younger son is effectively saying, “Dad, you are taking too long to die. I want your things, but I don’t want you. I would prefer you were dead so I can get on with my life.”

The community would have expected the father to explode in rage. He should have struck the boy. He should have cut him off. But the text says something breathtakingly simple: “And he divided his property between them.”

The father grants the request. He allows his heart to be broken to preserve the boy’s freedom.

So the son gathers all he has and journeys to a “far country.” We don’t know where this is geographically, but we know where it is spiritually. The far country is anywhere we go to be our own boss. It is that place where we believe the lie that freedom is found in the absence of restraint.

And for a while, it works. He has money. He has friends—or at least, people who like his money. But then, the inevitable happens. The money runs out. A famine strikes. The friends vanish.

The text tells us he “began to be in need.” He attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him to feed pigs. For a Jewish boy, raised in the covenant, this is the absolute bottom. Pigs were unclean animals. He is feeding beasts he isn't even supposed to touch, and he is so hungry he begins to envy their food.

Here is the tragedy of sin: it promises liberty, but it always leads to slavery. He wanted to be free from his father’s authority, and he ended up a slave to a stranger, starving in a pigsty.

**Part 2: The Return and the Race**

Then comes the pivot point of the parable. Verse 17 says, “But when he came to himself.” The madness of sin lifted. He remembered who he was. He remembered his father’s house.

But notice his theology is still a bit warped. He constructs his plan: *“I will go back. I will apologize. And I will ask to be a hired servant.”*

He thinks the relationship is transactional. He thinks, *“I have blown my credit as a son. I cannot be a son anymore. But maybe, if I work hard enough, if I pay him back over twenty years, I can earn a place in the bunkhouse.”* He is hoping for a job interview. He is hoping to pay off his debt.

He starts the long walk home. He is likely barefoot, smelling of the pigsty, gaunt, and humiliated. As he approaches the village, he is terrified. In that culture, a Jewish boy who lost his inheritance to Gentiles could face a ceremony called the *kezazah*—the cutting off. The village elders would break a pot at his feet and banish him forever. He expects rejection. He expects shame.

But he doesn’t meet the village.

“But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.”

We must pause here, because the English translation "felt compassion" is too polite. The Greek word used is *splagchnizomai*. It comes from the word for "bowels" or "guts." It means the father was moved in his deepest parts. He wasn't just intellectually sympathetic; he was physically, viscerally devastated by the sight of his broken boy.

And because of that gut-wrenching love, the Father does the unthinkable. He runs.

In that culture, distinguished, elderly patriarchs did not run. To run, a man had to hike up his long robes, exposing his legs. It was considered shameful, undignified. Aristotle once said, "Great men never run in public." But this Father hikes up his robes and sprints.

Why? Many scholars suggest he ran to get to the boy before the village did. He ran to intercept the shame. He took the indignity upon himself so the son wouldn’t have to face the scorn of the community.

The father throws his arms around the boy. The boy starts his rehearsed speech: “Father, I have sinned... I am no longer worthy...” But notice what happens. The father interrupts him! He doesn't let him get to the part about being a “hired servant.”

God doesn't grade your apology on a curve. He doesn't wait for you to negotiate the terms of your return.

The Father shouts to the servants, “Bring quickly the best robe.” That’s the father’s own robe—restoring his honor. “Put a ring on his hand.” That is the family signet—restoring his authority and access to the wealth. “Put sandals on his feet.” Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes.

We call this the Parable of the Prodigal Son. The word "prodigal" means "recklessly extravagant" or "wasteful." We usually apply it to the son because he wasted his money. But surely, the true Prodigal in this story is the Father. He is prodigal with his grace. He is wasteful with his love. He lavishes honor on a boy who deserves shame.

The son wanted a job; the Father gave him a feast. The son wanted to earn his way back; the Father covered him in grace. This is the Gospel. You cannot clean yourself up in the pigsty before you come home. You come home because He is watching for you. You come home because He runs to meet you.

**Part 3: The Other Lost Son**

If the story ended there, it would be a beautiful testimony of God’s love for the rebellious. But Jesus doesn’t stop. He can’t stop, because of who is listening to Him. Luke 15:1-2 tells us the Pharisees were grumbling because Jesus ate with sinners.

The first half of the story is for the rebels. The second half is for the religious.

“Now his older son was in the field.”

The older son comes near the house and hears music and dancing. He asks a servant what is happening. When he hears that his wastrel brother has returned and his father has killed the fattened calf, he becomes angry and refuses to go in.

The father, in his infinite, prodigal patience, comes out to him, just as he went out to the younger brother.

Listen to the older son’s complaint: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat... But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!”

Do you hear his heart? It is not just the heart of anger; it is the heart of a slave.

First, he says, “I have served you.” The Greek word used there is actually closer to “I have slaved for you.” He doesn’t view the father as a father; he views him as a boss. He views his obedience as a wage.

Second, he says, “I never disobeyed.” He is resting his righteousness on his moral performance.

Third, he says, “This son of yours.” He refuses to say, “my brother.”

Here is the shocking revelation: **Both sons are lost.**

The younger son was lost in the far country of rebellion. The older son is lost in the field of religious duty. The younger son wanted the father’s things, so he ran away. The older son wanted the father’s things, so he stayed and obeyed. But neither of them truly loved the father. They were both using him.

One tried to control the father by being bad; the other tried to control the father by being good.

This is a warning to us—the churchgoers, the rule-keepers, the responsible ones. We can be sitting in the pew every Sunday, tithing, serving in the nursery, leading the committees, and avoiding the “big sins,” and yet be completely alienated from the heart of God. We can be lost right here in the Father’s house.

The older brother is angry because grace isn't fair. And he is right. Grace is not fair. If it were fair, the younger brother would be in the pigsty, and the older brother would be judged for his pride. Grace is not fair; grace is a gift.

**Application: Coming Home**

So, where do you find yourself in this story today?

Perhaps you are the **Younger Son**. You feel like you’ve blown it. You’ve made choices that have led you into a far country. Maybe it’s not a geographical distance, but a distance of the heart. Maybe your pigsty is a mountain of debt you’re hiding from your spouse. Maybe it’s a secret addiction that has its claws in you. Maybe it’s a relationship you know is wrong but you can’t seem to leave. You feel the mud of the pigsty on your soul.

You are sitting here thinking, *“I need to fix this. I need to clean myself up. I need to work hard for a few years, prove I'm reliable, and then maybe I can approach God.”*

The Father says to you: **Stop.** Stop rehearsing the speech. Stop trying to negotiate a servant’s wage. Just come home. The Father is not waiting to scold you; He is waiting to drape His robe around your shoulders. He wants to restore you, not employ you. You don’t have to earn what He has already decided to give you freely.

Or, perhaps you are the **Older Son**. You have done everything right. You are the responsible one. You’ve kept the rules. But if you are honest, you are tired. You are so tired.

You look at your life and think, "I have worked so hard for God. I have sacrificed. I have stayed when others left." And deep down, there is a root of bitterness. You feel like life—and God—owes you something. You look at people who live wild lives and then convert on their deathbeds, or the messy people who seem to get all the attention and grace, and a part of you thinks, *“What a waste of my obedience. Why doesn't anyone kill a fattened calf for me?”*

The Father comes out to you today, too. He leaves the party to find you in the field of your resentment. Notice the tenderness in verse 31. “Son,” he says. He appeals to relationship. “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.”

The Father challenges the older brother’s transactional mindset. He says, *“Why do you want a goat? You have Me! You have been in my house. You have had access to my presence, my love, my ear, every single day. Is that not the reward?”*

The cure for the younger brother is to repent of his sins. The cure for the older brother is to repent of his self-righteousness. Both must surrender their agenda and accept the Father’s love.

**Conclusion: The Missing Brother**

There is something deeply frustrating about this parable. It ends on a cliffhanger.

The father says to the older son, “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

And... that’s it. The story ends.

We don’t know what the older brother did. Did he drop his rock of resentment and go into the party? Did he finally hug his brother? Or did he turn his back, cross his arms, and stay out in the dark, nursing his grudge while the music played inside?

Jesus leaves the ending open for a reason. He leaves it open because the older brother was standing right in front of Him. The Pharisees were the older brothers. Jesus was pleading with them: *“Come in. The party is for you, too. Don't let your pride keep you from the feast of grace.”*

But there is another reason the story feels incomplete. In a true family, if a younger brother goes missing, who is supposed to go look for him? The older brother. The older brother is supposed to leave the safety of the home, go into the far country, and bring the lost one back.

But in this story, the older brother stays home. He doesn't care.

We need a better Elder Brother.

And the good news of the Gospel is that we have one. Jesus didn't tell us about a true elder brother in the story because *He is* the True Elder Brother telling the story.

Jesus is the Brother who didn't stay in the comfort of the Father's house. He came into the far country. He came into the pigsty of our world to carry us back.
The younger son came home in shame, but Jesus bore the shame of the cross so we could be forgiven.
The younger son was given the best robe, but Jesus was stripped naked on Calvary so we could be clothed in righteousness.
The younger son was given the shoes of a son, but Jesus allowed nails to be driven through his feet so we could walk with God.
The younger son feasted, but Jesus took the cup of wrath so we could drink the cup of salvation.

Because of our True Elder Brother, the road home is open. The Father has run the race. The price has been paid.

The doors are open. The music is playing. The Father is waiting. Whether you are coming from the pigsty of rebellion or coming from the field of pride, the invitation is the same.

Come inside. Come home.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we thank You that You are the Running God. Thank You that Your compassion is not just a feeling, but a force that drove You to send Your Son to find us. For those of us who feel far away in the pigsty, give us the courage to turn for home. For those of us who are tired, bitter, and standing in the field, soften our hearts to see that having You is the greatest reward of all. We praise You for Jesus, our True Elder Brother, who brought us home. Bring us all into the feast. In His name, Amen.*

**Introduction: The Script in the Car**

Imagine the scene. You have just left a meeting where you made a catastrophic error that cost your company a major client. Or perhaps you have just walked out of a house where harsh words were spoken—words that shattered a relationship you swore you’d protect.

Now you are in your car. The radio is off. The silence is deafening. And in that silence, you begin to write a script.

You rehearse the apology. You play out the chess moves of reconciliation in your mind. *“If I walk in and admit to X, maybe they won’t ask about Y. If I offer to work late for the next three months, maybe I can keep my job. If I take full blame for the argument, maybe I can salvage some dignity.”*

We negotiate the terms of our surrender. We try to find a way to manage the shame, to craft a sentence that allows us to pay for our mistakes rather than simply being forgiven for them. Because, if we are honest, we prefer payment to grace. Payment allows us to keep a shred of control; grace requires us to be helpless.

In the famous parable we read today—often called the Parable of the Prodigal Son—we find a young man doing exactly this. He is starving, he is broken, and he is rehearsing his speech. *“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”*

It is a sensible speech. It is humble. It is theologically accurate. But as we will see, it is based on a fundamental misunderstanding of who his Father is.

We often treat this story as a simple evangelistic tract for those who have wandered far from the church—a story about a "bad boy" who comes home. But if we look closer, we find that Jesus is doing something far more subversive. He is telling a story about two sons, not just one. And He is revealing a Father whose love is so extravagant, so undignified, and so persistent, that it shatters our categories of fairness and rewrites the definition of God.

**Part 1: The Scandal of the Departure**

The story begins with a shock that would have made Jesus’s original listeners gasp. “A man had two sons. The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’”

In the first-century Middle Eastern context, this is not merely a request for a loan or a startup capital. Inheritance was given when the father died. By asking for his share now, the younger son is effectively saying, “Dad, you are taking too long to die. I want your things, but I don’t want you. I would prefer you were dead so I can get on with my life.”

The community would have expected the father to explode in rage. He should have slapped the boy. He should have cut him off. But the text says something breathtakingly simple: “And he divided his property between them.”

The father grants the request. He allows his heart to be broken to preserve the boy’s freedom.

So the son gathers all he has and journeys to a “far country.” We don’t know where this is geographically, but we know where it is spiritually. The far country is anywhere we go to be our own boss. It is that place where we believe the lie that freedom is found in the absence of restraint.

For the original hearers, this meant a Gentile city with loose morals. But for us? The far country isn't always a place of "wild living" in the traditional sense.

The far country can be the corner office where we sacrifice our families on the altar of achievement. It can be the endless scroll of social media where we hunt for the dopamine hit of approval. It can be the quiet resentment we nurse in private. It is anywhere we go to find our value apart from the Father’s love.

And for a while, it works. But then, the inevitable happens. The money runs out. A famine strikes. The friends who loved his wallet vanish when it’s empty.

The text tells us he “began to be in need.” He attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him to feed pigs. For a Jewish boy, raised in the covenant, this is the absolute bottom. Pigs were unclean. He is feeding animals he isn't even supposed to touch, and he is so hungry he envies their food.

Here is the tragedy of sin: it promises liberty, but it always leads to slavery. He wanted to be free from his father’s authority, and he ended up a slave to a stranger, starving in a pigsty.

**Part 2: The Return and the Race**

Then comes the pivot point of the parable. Verse 17 says, “But when he came to himself.” The madness of sin lifted. He remembered who he was. He remembered his father’s house.

But notice his theology is still a bit warped. He constructs his plan: *“I will go back. I will apologize. And I will ask to be a hired servant.”*

Why a hired servant? Because a hired servant is a contractor. A servant has a wage. A servant can pay off a debt. The son realizes he has broken the *covenant* of the family, so he tries to negotiate a *contract* of employment. He thinks, *“I have blown my credit as a son. I cannot be a son anymore. But maybe, if I work hard enough, if I pay him back over twenty years, I can earn a place in the bunkhouse.”*

He starts the long walk home. He is likely barefoot, smelling of the pigsty, gaunt, and humiliated. As he approaches the village, he is terrified. In that culture, a Jewish boy who lost his inheritance to Gentiles could face a ceremony called the *kezazah*—the cutting off. The village would break a pot at his feet and banish him forever. He expects scorn. He expects to be yelled at.

But he doesn’t meet the village.

“But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.”

This is the most startling image in the New Testament. In that culture, distinguished, elderly patriarchs did not run. To run, a man had to hike up his long robes, exposing his legs. It was considered shameful, undignified. Aristotle once said, "Great men never run in public."

Why did the Father run?

Many scholars suggest he ran to get to the boy before the village did. He ran to intercept the shame. He took the indignity upon himself so the son wouldn’t have to face the scorn of the community.

The father throws his arms around the boy. The boy starts his rehearsed speech: “Father, I have sinned... I am no longer worthy...”

He gets the confession out. That part is good; that part is true. But then, something wonderful happens. Before the son can get to the part about being a “hired servant”—before he can offer his contract—the Father interrupts him.

The Father shouts to the servants, “Bring quickly the best robe.” That’s the father’s robe—restoring his honor. “Put a ring on his hand.” That is the family signet—restoring his authority and access to the wealth. “Put sandals on his feet.” Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes.

The son wanted a job; the Father gave him a feast. The son wanted to earn his way back; the Father covered him in grace.

This is the Gospel. You cannot earn your way back to God. You cannot clean yourself up in the pigsty before you come home. You come home because He is watching for you. You come home because He runs to meet you.

**Part 3: The Other Lost Son**

If the story ended there, it would be a beautiful testimony of God’s love for the rebellious. But Jesus doesn’t stop. And He doesn’t stop because He is telling this parable to a specific audience. Luke 15:1-2 tells us the Pharisees were grumbling because Jesus ate with sinners. These were the Bible scholars, the moral pillars of the community.

The first half of the story is for the "sinners." The second half is for the religious people.

“Now his older son was in the field.”

The older son comes near the house and hears music and dancing. When he discovers that his wastrel brother has returned and his father has killed the fattened calf, he becomes angry and refuses to go in.

Once again, the father comes out. Just as he went out to the pigsty for the younger son, he comes out to the courtyard for the older son.

Listen to the older son’s complaint: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat... But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!”

Do you hear his heart?

First, he says, “I have served you.” The Greek word used there is actually closer to “I have slaved for you.” He doesn’t view the father as a father; he views him as a boss. He views his obedience as a way to put the father in his debt.

Second, he says, “I never disobeyed.” He is resting his righteousness on his moral resume.

Third, there is a glaring theological error in his complaint. He says, "You never gave me a young goat." But remember verse 12? The father "divided his property between them." The older brother already owned the goats! The farm was his. He could have thrown a party with his friends any time he wanted. But he didn't, because he was too busy trying to earn what he already possessed.

Here is the shocking revelation: **Both sons are lost.**

The younger son was lost in the far country of rebellion. The older son is lost in the field of religious duty. The younger son wanted the father’s things, so he ran away. The older son wanted the father’s things, so he stayed and obeyed. But neither of them truly loved the father. They were both using him to get what they wanted.

One tried to control the father by being bad; the other tried to control the father by being good.

This is a warning to us—the churchgoers, the rule-keepers, the responsible ones. We can be sitting in the pew every Sunday, tithing, serving on committees, and avoiding the “big sins,” and yet be completely alienated from the heart of God. We can be lost right here in the Father’s house.

What is your "field"? Maybe it's not a literal farm. Maybe your field is your reputation for being the dependable one. Maybe it's your political correctness or your theological precision. Maybe it's the volunteer role that has become your identity.

If we believe that God owes us a good life because we have been good people, we have the heart of the older brother. If we look at the “sinners” of the world—the addicts, the broken, the messy people—and feel resentful that God offers them the same grace He offers us, we are standing outside the feast.

Jesus leaves us to draw the inference: if the Father runs to the one who was dead, how must He feel about the one who refuses to celebrate life?

**Application: Coming Home**

So, where do you find yourself in this story today?

The truth is, most of us oscillate between the two. One day we are the younger brother, chasing comfort and distraction. The next day we are the older brother, judging those who aren't as disciplined as we are.

Perhaps today you identify as the **Younger Son**. You feel the weight of your mistakes. You feel the mud of the pigsty on your soul—whether that comes from a secret addiction, a broken marriage, or just the realization that you have wasted years living for yourself. You are sitting here thinking, *“I need to fix this. I need to clean myself up. I need to work hard for a few years, and then maybe I can approach God.”*

The Father says to you: **Stop.** Stop rehearsing the speech. Stop trying to negotiate a servant’s wage. Just come home. The Father is not waiting to scold you; He is waiting to drape His robe around your shoulders. He wants to restore you, not employ you. You don’t have to earn what He has already decided to give you freely.

Or, perhaps today you are the **Older Son**. You have done everything right. You are the responsible one. You’ve kept the rules. But if you are honest, you are tired. You are bitter. You feel like life—and God—owes you something. You look at the "wild" people who convert on their deathbeds, and a part of you thinks, *“What a waste of my obedience.”* You have kept the ledger balanced, but your hands are cramped from clutching it so tightly.

The Father comes out to you today, too. Notice the tenderness in verse 31. “Son,” he says. He appeals to relationship. “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.”

The Father challenges the older brother’s transactional mindset. He says, *“Why do you want a goat? You have Me! You have been in my house. You have had access to my presence, my love, my ear, every single day. Is that not the reward?”*

The cure for the younger brother is to repent of his sins. The cure for the older brother is to repent of his self-righteousness. Both must surrender their agenda and accept the Father’s love.

**Conclusion: The True Elder Brother**

There is something frustrating about this parable. It ends on a cliffhanger.

The father says to the older son, “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

And... that’s it. The story ends. The credits roll.

We don’t know what the older brother did. Did he drop his rock of resentment and go into the party? Did he embrace his brother? Or did he turn his back, cross his arms, and stay out in the dark, nursing his grudge while the music played inside?

Jesus leaves the ending open because the older brother was standing right in front of Him. The Pharisees were the older brothers. Jesus was pleading with them: *“Come in. The party is for you, too. Don't let your pride keep you from the feast of grace.”*

But there is another reason the story feels incomplete. It’s because the older brother in the story is not the brother we need. The older brother in the story stayed in the field. He didn't go looking for the younger son. He didn't offer to pay the debt.

But we have a **True Elder Brother**.

We have a Brother who did not stay in the Father’s house. We have a Brother who came out to the far country—not to judge us, but to find us. Jesus Christ left the glory of heaven to enter the pigsty of our world. He didn't just run to meet us; He walked the road to Calvary for us.

In the parable, the younger son returns at the cost of the father’s property. In our reality, we return at the cost of the Son’s life. Jesus was stripped naked on the cross so we could be given the best robe. He took the silence of the Father so we could hear the music of the feast. He was cut off outside the gate so we could be brought inside.

And now, He has prepared a table for us. In a few moments, we will come to the Communion table. This is the feast of the fattened calf. This is the celebration of the lost being found.

The doors are open. The Father is waiting. The True Elder Brother has paid your way home.

Whether you are coming from the pigsty of shame or the field of pride, the invitation is the same. Drop your script. Drop your scorecard.

Come inside. Come home.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we thank You that You are the Running God. Thank You that You do not treat us as our sins deserve, nor do You repay us according to our iniquities. For those of us who feel far away, give us the courage to turn for home. For those of us who feel self-righteous and bitter, soften our hearts to see the beauty of Your grace. We thank You for Jesus, our True Elder Brother, who came to find us when we could not find You. Bring us all into the feast. In Jesus’ name, Amen.*
