**Title:** The Running Father and the Two Lost Sons
**Text:** Luke 15:11-32

**Introduction: The Longing for Home**

There is a word in the Welsh language that has no direct English translation: *hiraeth*. It describes a deep, visceral longing for a home you can no longer return to, or perhaps a home that never was. It is a blend of homesickness, nostalgia, and grief. It is the feeling that, somehow, we are all displaced persons, wandering in a world that doesn’t quite fit, looking for a place where we are fully known and fully loved.

We spend our lives trying to cure this *hiraeth*. Some of us try to cure it by chasing adventure, pleasure, and autonomy, convinced that "home" is a cage we must escape. Others try to cure it by building fences, following rules, and accumulating a resume of good behavior, convinced that we can build a perfect home with our own hands.

In Luke chapter 15, Jesus tells a story that addresses this universal longing. We call it "The Parable of the Prodigal Son," but that title is somewhat misleading because it focuses on only one character. A better title might be "The Parable of the Running Father and His Two Lost Sons."

As we open this text, we must remember who was standing there listening to Jesus. Luke tells us in the first verses of the chapter that two groups were present: the "tax collectors and sinners" (the outcasts, the rebels) and the "Pharisees and scribes" (the religious elite, the rule-keepers). The Pharisees were grumbling because Jesus was eating with sinners.

So, Jesus tells a story about a father with two sons. And in this story, he holds up a mirror to both groups—and to us.

**I. The Younger Son: Lost in the Far Country**

The story begins with a shock. The younger son approaches his father and says, "Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me."

In the cultural context of the first-century Middle East, this was not just a request; it was a slap in the face. Inheritance was given when the father died. By asking for it now, the son is effectively saying, "Dad, you are taking too long to die. I want your things, but I don’t want you. I want my independence more than I want our relationship."

Amazingly, the father does not explode in anger. He doesn't lecture. He divides his property. He allows his son the freedom to leave.

The younger son gathers everything and travels to "a far country." This isn't just a geographical distance; it is a spiritual distance. It represents life lived entirely on one’s own terms. And for a while, it probably felt like freedom. He squanders his wealth in "reckless living." The Greek word used here is *asōtōs*, meaning "unsaved" or "wasteful." He burns through his resources trying to buy happiness.

But then, the inevitable happens. A severe famine arises. The money runs out. The friends disappear. The illusion of autonomy shatters.

He finds himself attached to a citizen of that country, who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For a Jewish audience, this is the absolute bottom. Pigs were unclean animals. To feed them was humiliating; to envy their food, as the son did, was a dehumanizing desperation. He has lost his money, his religion, his family, and his dignity.

Then comes the pivot point of the first half of the story: "But when he came to himself..." (v. 17).

The madness of sin lifts. He remembers home. But notice carefully his internal monologue. He prepares a speech: "I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'"

This is a speech of repentance, yes, but it is also a speech of *strategy*. He knows he has lost the right to be a son. So, he drafts a plan to become an employee. He thinks, "If I can just work for him, I can pay him back. I can earn my way into the bunkhouse, get three square meals, and regain some self-respect."

He turns toward home, expecting a negotiation. He expects a boss. He is about to meet a Father.

**II. The Father: The God Who Runs**

Verse 20 contains perhaps the most beautiful imagery of God in the entire Bible: "But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."

The father was looking. He hadn't written the boy off. And when he sees that ragged, limping figure on the horizon, the father does something unprecedented for a Middle Eastern patriarch: he runs.

In that culture, for an older, wealthy man to run was considered undignified. To run, he would have to hike up his robes, exposing his legs, subjecting himself to shame and ridicule. Why does he run?

Some scholars suggest he ran to get to the son before the village did. A boy who wasted the family inheritance among Gentiles would face the *kezazah* ceremony—the community would break a pot at his feet and banish him. The father runs to intercept the shame. He takes the indignity upon himself so the son doesn't have to bear it.

The father throws his arms around the boy—who smells of pigs and sweat—and kisses him.

The son starts his rehearsed speech: "Father, I have sinned... I am no longer worthy..." But before he can get to the part about being a "hired servant," the father interrupts him.

"Bring quickly the best robe," the father commands. The robe stands for status and restoration of honor.
"Put a ring on his hand." The ring represents authority and the family seal.
"Shoes on his feet." Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes.
"Bring the fattened calf and kill it." This is a feast for the whole village.

The father refuses the son's offer to be an employee. You cannot earn your way back into this family. You can only be received. The younger son wanted to negotiate a contract; the father gave him a coronation.

This is the Gospel for the "younger brothers" among us. You may have run far. You may have made a mess of your life. You may feel utterly unworthy. You may think you need to clean yourself up, pay your dues, and work your way back to God. But God isn't interested in your payment. He is interested in *you*. He runs to meet you in your shame and covers you with His grace.

**III. The Older Son: Lost in the House**

If the parable ended here, it would be a beautiful story of forgiveness. But it doesn't end here. There is another son.

"Now his older son was in the field..." (v. 25).

The older son hears the music and dancing. When he finds out his wasteful, rebellious brother has returned and—insult of insults—the father has killed the fattened calf for him, he becomes angry. He refuses to go in.

The father, displaying the same extravagant love he showed the younger son, comes out to entreat him. He leaves the party to plead with the older brother.

Listen to the older son's complaint in verse 29: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear the heart of the older brother?
"I have *served* you." The Greek word is *douleuō*—"I have slaved for you."
"I never disobeyed."

Here is the tragedy of the older son. He stayed home, but he was just as distant from the father’s heart as the younger son was in the far country. The younger son wanted the father's things; the older son wanted the father's reward. Neither wanted the father.

The younger son was lost in badness; the older son was lost in goodness.

The older son believed that his obedience placed the father in his debt. He thought, "Because I have followed the rules, you owe me." This is the mindset of the Pharisee. It is the mindset of religious moralism. It says, "I am not like those sinners. I work hard. I pray. I give. Therefore, God must bless me."

When the father shows grace to the "undeserving" younger brother, the older brother's mask slips. His anger reveals that he never did these things out of love. He did them to gain leverage. He is not a son; he is a bitter employee.

He won't even call his brother "brother." He says to the father, "But when *this son of yours* came..."
The father gently corrects him: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for *this your brother* was dead, and is alive."

The father challenges the older son's entire worldview. He says, in effect, "You think the reward for being in my house is a goat? You think the reward is payment? The reward is *me*. You have had me the whole time, but you never enjoyed me. You were slaving when you could have been son-ing."

**IV. Application: Which Son Are You?**

As we sit here today, this parable reads us. It divides the human race not into "good people" and "bad people," but into two types of lostness.

Some of you relate to the **Younger Son**. You know what it is to run. You know the emptiness of the "far country." You carry the weight of regret. You feel like you've disqualified yourself from God's love.
The message of this text for you is that the Father is scanning the horizon. He is not waiting with a stick; He is waiting with a robe. Repentance isn't about groveling until you are hired; it's about accepting the embrace of the Father who restores you to sonship. Come home. The feast is ready.

But others of you—perhaps many of you who have been in church your whole lives—might relate to the **Older Son**. You are dutiful. You are moral. You serve on committees. You follow the rules. But if you are honest, there is a coldness in your heart. You are judgmental toward those who don't have it together. You resent it when "sinners" get off easy. You feel like God owes you a quiet life because you’ve been good.
The message of this text for you is a warning, but also a tender invitation. The Father comes out to you, too. He loves you too much to let you stay outside in the cold darkness of your own self-righteousness. He invites you to drop the burden of "slaving" for God and start enjoying the relationship with God. He invites you to the party.

You see, both sons were alienated from the father. One was alienated by his sins; the other was alienated by his morality. Both needed the father’s grace.

**Conclusion: The True Elder Brother**

There is a fascinating detail about how the story ends. Or rather, how it *doesn't* end.

The parable cuts off. We are left standing outside with the father and the older son. Did the older son go in? Did he drop his pride and hug his brother? Or did he stay outside, nursing his grudge?

Jesus doesn't tell us. Why? Because the older brothers were standing right in front of Him. The Pharisees were the older brothers. Jesus left the story open-ended because *they* had to write the ending.

And so do we.

But there is one final difference between the story and reality. In the story, the younger son had no one to go get him. He had to come to his senses on his own. In the story, the older brother refused to pay the cost of finding his brother.

But in reality, we have a True Elder Brother.
We have a Brother who didn't stay in the comfort of the Father's house.
We have a Brother who came to the "far country" of this broken world to find us in the pigsty.
We have a Brother who didn't just risk ridicule; He endured the ultimate shame of the Cross.
We have a Brother who didn't just give up a fattened calf; He gave up His life.

Jesus Christ is the True Elder Brother who paid the debt for the younger siblings and melted the pride of the older siblings. Because of Him, the Father’s house is open. The table is spread. The music is playing.

Whether you have been running away or slaving away, the invitation is the same: Come in. The Father is waiting.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, thank You for Your extravagant, undignified love. Thank You that You run to meet us when we are far off, and You come out to find us when we are hard-hearted. Forgive us for our rebellion, and forgive us for our self-righteousness. Help us to see the beauty of Your grace, displayed in our True Brother, Jesus, so that we might enter the feast with joy. Amen.*

Then, the owner’s rebellious son, who has never worked a day in his life and has publicly embarrassed the family, walks in and is given the corner office. The employee is furious. Why? Because the relationship was transactional. It was about earning, not loving.

The older son believed that his obedience placed the father in his debt. He thought, "Because I have followed the rules, you owe me." This is the mindset of the Pharisee. It is the mindset of religious moralism. It says, "I am not like those sinners. I work hard. I pray. I give. Therefore, God must bless me."

When the father shows grace to the "undeserving" younger brother, the older brother's mask slips. His anger reveals that he never did these things out of love. He did them to gain leverage. He is not a son; he is a bitter employee.

He won't even call his brother "brother." He says to the father, "But when *this son of yours* came..."
The father gently corrects him: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for *this your brother* was dead, and is alive."

The father challenges the older son's entire worldview. He says, in effect, "You think the reward for being in my house is a goat? You think the reward is payment? The reward is *me*. You have had me the whole time, but you never enjoyed me. You were slaving when you could have been son-ing."

**IV. Application: Which Son Are You?**

As we sit here today, this parable reads us. It divides the human race not into "good people" and "bad people," but into two types of lostness, two ways of trying to cure our *hiraeth* without God.

Some of you relate to the **Younger Son**. You know what it is to run. You know the emptiness of the "far country." You carry the weight of regret. You feel like you've disqualified yourself from God's love.
The message of this text for you is that the Father is scanning the horizon. He is not waiting with a stick; He is waiting with a robe. Repentance isn't about groveling until you are hired; it's about accepting the embrace of the Father who restores you to sonship. Come home. The feast is ready.

But others of you—perhaps many of you who have been in church your whole lives—might relate to the **Older Son**. You are dutiful. You are moral. You serve on committees. You follow the rules. But if you are honest, there is a coldness in your heart.

Ask yourself: Do you resent it when God shows mercy to people who haven't "put in the work" like you have? Do you serve God out of delight, or do you serve Him to put Him in your debt? Are you tired of "slaving" for a God you don't actually enjoy?

The message of this text for you is a warning, but also a tender invitation. The Father comes out to you, too. He loves you too much to let you stay outside in the cold darkness of your own self-righteousness. He invites you to drop the burden of earning your keep.

You see, both sons were alienated from the father. One was alienated by his sins; the other was alienated by his morality. Both needed the father’s grace.

But here is the question that haunts us: How can the Father just forgive? How can He simply run to the younger son and ignore the wasted inheritance? How can He invite the older son in despite his insolence?

Forgiveness is never free. If someone breaks your lamp, and you forgive them, you pay for the lamp. The cost has to go somewhere. In this story, the Father absorbs the cost. He absorbs the shame of the run. He absorbs the cost of the feast. He absorbs the insult of the older brother.

**Conclusion: The True Elder Brother**

There is a fascinating detail about how the story ends. Or rather, how it *doesn't* end.

The parable cuts off abruptly. We are left standing outside with the father and the older son. Did the older son go in? Did he drop his pride and hug his brother? Or did he stay outside, nursing his grudge?

Jesus doesn't tell us. Why? Because the older brothers were standing right in front of Him. The Pharisees were the older brothers. Jesus left the story open-ended because *they* had to write the ending.

And so do we.

But there is one final difference between the story and reality. In the story, the younger son had no one to go get him. He had to come to his senses on his own. In the story, the older brother refused to pay the cost of finding his brother.

But in reality, we have a True Elder Brother.
We have a Brother who didn't stay in the comfort of the Father's house.
We have a Brother who came to the "far country" of this broken world to find us in the pigsty.
We have a Brother who didn't just risk ridicule; He endured the ultimate shame of the Cross.
We have a Brother who didn't just give up a fattened calf; He gave up His life.

Jesus Christ is the True Elder Brother. He paid the debt for the younger siblings so they could come home without money. And He melts the pride of the older siblings by showing us that our works can never buy what He offers freely.

Because of Him, the Father’s house is open. The table is spread. The music is playing.

Whether you have been running away or slaving away, the invitation is the same: Come in. The Father is waiting.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, thank You for Your extravagant, undignified love. Thank You that You run to meet us when we are far off, and You come out to find us when we are hard-hearted. Forgive us for our rebellion, and forgive us for our self-righteousness. Help us to see the beauty of Your grace, displayed in our True Brother, Jesus, so that we might enter the feast with joy. Amen.*

**Introduction: The Longing for Home**

There is a word in the Welsh language that has no direct English translation: *hiraeth*. It describes a deep, visceral longing for a home you can no longer return to, or perhaps a home that never was. It is a blend of homesickness, nostalgia, and grief. It is the feeling that, somehow, we are all displaced persons, wandering in a world that doesn’t quite fit, looking for a place where we are fully known and fully loved.

We spend our lives trying to cure this *hiraeth*. We try to fill the void with career success, with relationships, with pleasure, or with moral performance. But the ache remains.

In Luke chapter 15, Jesus tells a story that addresses this universal longing. We usually call it "The Parable of the Prodigal Son," but that title is somewhat misleading because it focuses on only one character. A better title might be "The Parable of the Running Father and His Two Lost Sons."

As we open this text, we must remember the scene. Luke tells us in the first verses of the chapter that two groups were present: the "tax collectors and sinners" (the outcasts, the moral failures) and the "Pharisees and scribes" (the religious elite, the rule-keepers). The Pharisees were grumbling because Jesus was receiving sinners and eating with them.

So, Jesus turns to them and tells a story about a father with two sons. And in this story, he holds up a mirror to both groups—and to us.

**I. The Younger Son: Lost in the Far Country**

The story begins with a shock. The younger son approaches his father and says, "Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me."

In the cultural context of the first-century Middle East, this was not just a request; it was a slap in the face. Inheritance was strictly processed upon a father's death. By asking for it now, the son is effectively saying, "Dad, you are taking too long to die. I want your things, but I don’t want you. I want my independence more than I want our relationship."

Amazingly, the father does not explode in anger. He divides his property. He allows his son the freedom to leave.

The younger son gathers everything and travels to "a far country." This isn't just a geographical distance; it is a spiritual distance. It represents life lived entirely on one’s own terms. And for a while, it probably felt like freedom. He squanders his wealth in "reckless living." The Greek word used here is *asōtōs*. It implies a life of dissipation, a life that is utterly wasted. He burns through his resources attempting to buy happiness, trying to cure his *hiraeth* with adrenaline and autonomy.

But then, the inevitable happens. A severe famine arises. The money runs out. The friends disappear. The illusion of autonomy shatters.

He finds himself attached to a citizen of that country, who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For a Jewish audience, this is the absolute bottom. Pigs were unclean animals. To feed them was humiliating; to envy their food, as the son did, was dehumanizing. He has lost his money, his religion, his family, and his dignity.

Then comes the pivot point of the first half of the story: "But when he came to himself..." (v. 17).

This is a profound moment. The madness of sin lifts. We might say this is the first quiet work of the Holy Spirit—the restoration of sanity. He remembers home. But notice carefully his internal monologue. He prepares a speech: "I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'"

This is a speech of repentance, yes, but it is also a speech of *strategy*. He knows he has lost the right to be a son. So, he drafts a plan to become an employee. He thinks, "If I can just work for him, I can pay him back. I can earn my way into the bunkhouse, get three square meals, and regain some self-respect."

He turns toward home, expecting a negotiation. He expects a boss. He is about to meet a Father.

**II. The Father: The God Who Runs**

So he gets up. He starts walking. The road is long, and his doubts must have been heavy. But then, verse 20 gives us perhaps the most beautiful imagery of God in the entire Bible: "But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."

The father was looking. He hadn't written the boy off.

I recall a story of a father whose son had run away into a life of addiction. For years, the father kept the porch light on, every single night. He refused to change the locks. He sat by the front window every evening, not to catch the boy trying to break in, but hoping to catch him trying to come home. That is the posture of God in this text.

And when he sees that ragged, limping figure on the horizon, the father does something unprecedented for a Middle Eastern patriarch: he runs.

In that culture, for an older, wealthy man to run was considered undignified. To run, he would have to hike up his robes, exposing his legs, subjecting himself to shame and ridicule. Aristotle once said, "Great men never run in public." But this Father runs. Why?

Some scholars suggest he ran to get to the son before the village did. A Jewish boy who wasted the family inheritance among Gentiles would face the *kezazah* ceremony—the community would break a pot at his feet and banish him, cutting him off forever. The father runs to intercept the shame. He takes the indignity upon himself so the son doesn't have to bear it.

The father throws his arms around the boy—who smells of pigs and sweat—and kisses him.

The son starts his rehearsed speech: "Father, I have sinned... I am no longer worthy..." But before he can get to the part about being a "hired servant," the father interrupts him. He refuses to hear the job application.

"Bring quickly the best robe," the father commands. The robe stands for status and restoration of honor.
"Put a ring on his hand." The ring represents authority and the family seal.
"Shoes on his feet." Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes.
"Bring the fattened calf and kill it."

The father refuses the son's offer to be an employee. You cannot earn your way back into this family. You can only be received. The younger son wanted to negotiate a contract; the father gave him a coronation.

This is the Gospel for the "younger brothers" among us. You may have run far. You may have made a mess of your life. You may feel utterly unworthy. You may think you need to clean yourself up, pay your dues, and work your way back to God. But God isn't interested in your payment. He is interested in *you*. He runs to meet you in your shame and covers you with His grace.

**III. The Older Son: Lost in the House**

If the parable ended here, it would be a beautiful story of forgiveness. But it doesn't end here. There is another son.

"Now his older son was in the field..." (v. 25).

The older son hears the music and dancing. When he finds out his wasteful, rebellious brother has returned and—insult of insults—the father has killed the fattened calf for him, he becomes angry. He refuses to go in.

The father, displaying the same extravagant love he showed the younger son, comes out to entreat him. He leaves the party to plead with the older brother.

Do you hear the heart of the older brother?
"I have *served* you." The Greek word is *douleuō*—"I have slaved for you."
"I never disobeyed."

Some of you relate to the **Younger Son**. You know what it is to run. You know the emptiness of the "far country." You carry the weight of regret. You feel like you've disqualified yourself from God's love.

I’ve been here for twenty years paying the bills.* It looks like feeling that God owes you a quiet, comfortable life because you’ve been "good."

He invites you to the party.

Because of Him, the Father’s house is open. The table is spread. The music is playing.

Whether you have been running away to the far country or slaving away in the fields of your own pride, the invitation is the same: Come in. The Father is waiting.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, thank You for Your extravagant, undignified love. Thank You that You run to meet us when we are far off, and You come out to find us when we are hard-hearted. Forgive us for our rebellion, and forgive us for our self-righteousness. Help us to see the beauty of Your grace, displayed in our True Brother, Jesus, so that we might enter the feast with joy. Amen.*

**Title:** The Running Father and the Two Lost Sons
**Text:** Luke 15:1-3, 11-32

**Introduction: The Universal Longing**

There is a hauntingly beautiful word in the Welsh language that has no direct English translation: *hiraeth*. It describes a deep, visceral longing for a home you can no longer return to, or perhaps a home that never was. It is a blend of homesickness, nostalgia, and grief. It is the feeling that, somehow, we are all displaced persons, wandering in a world that doesn’t quite fit, looking for a place where we are fully known and fully loved.

We spend our lives trying to cure this *hiraeth*. Some of us try to cure it by chasing adventure, pleasure, and autonomy, convinced that "home" is a cage we must escape. Others try to cure it by building fences, following rules, and accumulating a resume of good behavior, convinced that we can build a perfect home with our own hands.

In Luke chapter 15, Jesus tells a story that addresses this universal longing. We traditionally call it "The Parable of the Prodigal Son," but that title is somewhat misleading because it focuses on only one character. A better title might be "The Parable of the Running Father and His Two Lost Sons."

To truly understand the weight of this story, we must look at the context in which it was told. Luke 15 opens with a scandal. The "tax collectors and sinners"—the moral outcasts—were drawing near to hear Jesus. Meanwhile, the "Pharisees and scribes"—the religious elite—were grumbling, saying, "This man receives sinners and eats with them."

In response, Jesus tells three parables. First, he tells of a shepherd searching for a lost sheep. Then, a woman sweeping her house for a lost coin. In both, the owner actively searches for what is lost. But in the third story, the climax of the trilogy, Jesus shifts the focus. He tells a story not about livestock or currency, but about a father and his children. And in this story, he holds up a mirror to both groups standing before Him—the rebels and the religious—and to us.

**I. The Younger Son: The Illusion of Freedom**

The story begins with a shock that would have made the original listeners gasp. The younger son approaches his father and says, "Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me."

In the cultural context of the first-century Middle East, this was not just a request; it was a slap in the face. Inheritance was given when the father died. By asking for it now, the son is effectively saying, "Dad, you are taking too long to die. I want your things, but I don’t want you. I want my independence more than I want our relationship."

He wants the gifts, but he rejects the Giver.

Amazingly, the father does not explode in anger. He doesn't lecture. He divides his property—his life—between them. He allows his son the terrifying freedom to leave.

The younger son gathers everything and travels to "a far country." This isn't just a geographical distance; it is a spiritual distance. It represents life lived entirely on one’s own terms. And for a while, it probably felt like freedom. He squanders his wealth in "reckless living." The Greek word used here is *asōtōs*, meaning "wasteful" or "unsaved." He burns through his resources trying to buy the cure for his *hiraeth*.

But then, the inevitable happens. A severe famine arises. The money runs out. The fair-weather friends disappear. The illusion of autonomy shatters.

He finds himself attached to a citizen of that country, who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For a Jewish audience, this is the absolute bottom. Pigs were unclean animals (Leviticus 11:7). To feed them was humiliating; to envy their food, as the son did, was a dehumanizing desperation. He has lost his money, his religion, his family, and his dignity. He is empty.

Then comes the pivot point of the first half of the story: "But when he came to himself..." (v. 17).

The madness of sin lifts. He remembers home. But notice carefully his internal monologue. He prepares a speech: "I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'"

This is a speech of repentance, yes, but it is also a speech of *strategy*. He knows he has lost the right to be a son. So, he drafts a plan to become an employee. He thinks, "If I can just work for him, I can pay him back. I can earn my way into the bunkhouse, get three square meals, and regain some self-respect."

He turns toward home expecting a negotiation. He expects a boss. He is about to collide with a Father.

**II. The Father: The Scandal of Grace**

Verse 20 contains perhaps the most beautiful imagery of God in the entire Bible: "But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."

Consider the implication: The father was looking. He hadn't written the boy off. In the previous parables, the shepherd went out, and the woman swept. Here, the Father scans the horizon, day after day, waiting for the return.

And when he sees that ragged, limping figure, the father does something unprecedented for a Middle Eastern patriarch: he runs.

In that culture, for an older, wealthy man to run was considered undignified. To run, he would have to hike up his robes, exposing his legs, subjecting himself to shame and ridicule. Aristotle once wrote, "Great men never run in public." It implies a lack of control; it implies desperation.

Why does he run?

Some scholars suggest a profound cultural reason. If a Jewish boy wasted the family inheritance among Gentiles, upon his return he would face the *kezazah* ceremony. The village would surround him, break a clay pot at his feet, and shout, "You are cut off from your people!"

The father runs to get to the son before the village does. He runs to intercept the shame. He takes the indignity upon himself so the son doesn't have to bear it.

The father throws his arms around the boy—who smells of pigs and sweat—and kisses him. The son starts his rehearsed speech: "Father, I have sinned... I am no longer worthy..." But before he can get to the part about being a "hired servant," the father interrupts him.

You see, the son wanted a contract. He wanted to say, "I will work, and you will pay." But the Father is not interested in a contract; He is interested in a covenant.

"Bring quickly the best robe," the father commands. The robe stands for the restoration of honor and righteousness.
"Put a ring on his hand." The ring represents authority and the family seal—access to the family wealth.
"Shoes on his feet." Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes.
"Bring the fattened calf and kill it." This is a feast for the whole village.

The father refuses the son's offer to be an employee. You cannot earn your way back into this family. You can only be received. The younger son wanted to negotiate his way out of debt; the father gave him a coronation.

This is the Gospel for the "younger brothers" among us. You may have run far. You may have made a mess of your life. You may feel utterly unworthy. You may think you need to clean yourself up, pay your dues, and work your way back to God. But God isn't interested in your payment. He is interested in *you*. He runs to meet you in your shame and covers you with His grace.

**III. The Older Son: Lost in the House**

If the parable ended here, it would be a beautiful story of forgiveness. But it doesn't end here. There is another son. And in many ways, his condition is more tragic because it is harder to see.

"Now his older son was in the field..." (v. 25).

The older son hears the music and dancing. When he finds out his wasteful, rebellious brother has returned and—insult of insults—the father has killed the fattened calf for him, he becomes angry. He refuses to go in.

This refusal is a public insult to the father. The father must leave his own party, humiliating himself a second time, to come out and plead with his son.

Listen to the older son's complaint in verse 29. It reveals the true condition of his heart: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear the bitterness?
"I have *served* you." The Greek word is *douleuō*—"I have slaved for you."
"I never disobeyed."

Here is the tragedy of the older son. He stayed home, but he was just as distant from the father’s heart as the younger son was in the far country. The younger son wanted the father's things; the older son wanted the father's reward. Neither wanted the father.

The younger son was lost in badness; the older son was lost in goodness.

We must have empathy for this older brother. Many of us know exactly how he feels. He is the responsible one. He is the one who stayed when things got hard. He is the one who kept the farm running while his brother was out partying. He feels the exhaustion of being "good." He feels the burden of maintaining the family reputation. And now, he sees the rules being broken. He thinks, "It’s not fair. I paid the price. He didn't. Why does he get the party?"

The older son believed that his obedience placed the father in his debt. He thought, "Because I have followed the rules, you owe me." This is the mindset of the Pharisee. It is the mindset of religious moralism. It says, "I am not like those sinners. I work hard. I pray. I give. Therefore, God must bless me."

When the father shows grace to the "undeserving" younger brother, the older brother's mask slips. His anger reveals that he never did these things out of love. He did them to gain leverage. He is not a son; he is a bitter employee.

He won't even call his brother "brother." He says to the father, "But when *this son of yours* came..."
The father gently corrects him: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for *this your brother* was dead, and is alive."

The father challenges the older son's entire worldview. He says, in effect, "You think the reward for being in my house is a goat? You think the reward is payment? The reward is *me*. You have had me the whole time, but you never enjoyed me. You were slaving when you could have been son-ing."

**IV. Application: Which Son Are You?**

As we sit here today, this parable acts as a mirror. It divides the human race not into "good people" and "bad people," but into two types of lostness, two ways of running from God.

Some of you relate to the **Younger Son**. You know what it is to run. You know the emptiness of the "far country"—whether that’s a life of addiction, sexual wandering, or simply a life lived for career and money, ignoring God. You carry the weight of regret. You feel like you've disqualified yourself from God's love.
The message of this text for you is that the Father is scanning the horizon. He is not waiting with a stick; He is waiting with a robe. Repentance isn't about groveling until you are hired; it's about accepting the embrace of the Father who restores you to sonship. Come home. The feast is ready.

But others of you—perhaps many of you who have been in church your whole lives—might relate to the **Older Son**. You are dutiful. You are moral. You serve on committees. You follow the rules. But if you are honest, there is a coldness in your heart. You are judgmental toward those who don't have it together. You resent it when "sinners" get off easy. You feel like God owes you a quiet life because you’ve been good.
The message of this text for you is a warning, but also a tender invitation. The Father comes out to you, too. He loves you too much to let you stay outside in the cold darkness of your own self-righteousness. He invites you to drop the burden of "slaving" for God and start enjoying the relationship with God. He invites you to the party.

You see, both sons were alienated from the father. One was alienated by his sins; the other was alienated by his morality. Both needed the father’s grace.

**Conclusion: The True Elder Brother**

There is a fascinating detail about how the story ends. Or rather, how it *doesn't* end.

The parable cuts off abruptly. We are left standing outside with the father and the older son. Did the older son go in? Did he drop his pride and hug his brother? Or did he stay outside, nursing his grudge?

Jesus doesn't tell us. Why? Because the older brothers were standing right in front of Him. The Pharisees were the older brothers. Jesus left the story open-ended because *they* had to write the ending. And so do we.

But there is one final difference between the story and reality. In the story, the younger son had no one to go get him. He had to come to his senses on his own. In the story, the older brother refused to pay the cost of finding his brother. He didn't want his inheritance diminished by the return of the prodigal.

But in reality, we have a True Elder Brother.
We have a Brother who didn't stay in the comfort of the Father's house.
We have a Brother who came to the "far country" of this broken world to find us in the pigsty.
We have a Brother who didn't just risk ridicule; He endured the ultimate shame of the Cross. He was stripped naked so we could be clothed in the best robe. He drank the cup of sorrow so we could drink the wine of the feast.
We have a Brother who didn't just give up a fattened calf; He gave up His life.

Jesus Christ is the True Elder Brother who paid the debt for the younger siblings and melted the pride of the older siblings. Because of Him, the Father’s house is open. The table is spread. The music is playing.

Whether you have been running away or slaving away, the invitation is the same: Come in. The Father is waiting.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, thank You for Your extravagant, undignified love. Thank You that You run to meet us when we are far off, and You come out to find us when we are hard-hearted. Forgive us for our rebellion, and forgive us for our self-righteousness. Help us to see the beauty of Your grace, displayed in our True Brother, Jesus, so that we might enter the feast with joy. Amen.*

Bz1tJL3LoXNvAel0vvVy6.text:
**Title:** The God Who Runs
**Text:** Luke 15:11-32

**Introduction: The Longing for Home**

There is a specific kind of ache that most of us have felt at one time or another. It isn’t just a physical pain; it is a spiritual displacement. It is the feeling of being unmoored, of waking up in a life that feels foreign, even if you are sleeping in your own bed. The Germans have a word for it: *fernweh*—a longing for a place you’ve never been. But the Bible has a simpler word for the cure to this ache. The word is "Home."

We spend our lives trying to construct a home. We build it out of career success, or romantic relationships, or moral uprightness, or political affiliation. We build walls to keep us safe and roofs to keep us dry, but eventually, the wind blows through the cracks. We realize that we are, in the words of the old hymn, "pilgrims and strangers."

Today, we are turning to perhaps the most famous short story ever told. It is a story about home, about leaving it, and about the struggle to find the door to get back in. We call it "The Parable of the Prodigal Son." But if we look closely, we might find that the title is too small. This isn’t just a story about a son who was bad; it’s a story about a father who was too good to be true.

**The Context: Two Audiences**

Before we walk down the dusty road of this narrative, we have to look at who is standing in the crowd listening to Jesus. Luke 15:1-2 sets the stage: *"Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them.’"*

Do you see the two groups?
On one side, you have the younger brothers: the tax collectors, the rule-breakers, the people who have made a wreck of their lives. They are drawn to Jesus.
On the other side, you have the older brothers: the Pharisees, the Bible scholars, the moral gatekeepers. They are offended by Jesus.

Jesus tells this parable not just to comfort the rule-breakers, but to dismantle the self-righteousness of the rule-keepers. He is holding up a mirror to both groups.

**Act I: The Scandal of Departure**

The story begins with a shock. *"A man had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’"*

In the first-century Middle Eastern context, this is not a simple financial request. Inheritance was given at death. To ask for it while the father was still in good health was to say, effectively, "Father, I wish you were dead. You are in my way. I want your stuff, but I don’t want you."

It is a breath-taking insult. The community would expected the father to explode in rage, to beat the boy, to drive him out. But the text says simply, *"he divided his property between them."* The father tears his life apart to give the son the freedom to leave him.

The boy gathers everything and journeys into a "far country." We’ve all been to the far country, haven’t we? The far country is anywhere we go to find happiness apart from the Father. It is the place where we say, "I am the master of my fate; I am the captain of my soul."

And for a while, it works. He has money. He has friends—or at least, people who like his money. But then, three things happen simultaneously: he spends everything, a famine arises, and he begins to be in need.

The descent is rapid. He attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him to feed pigs. For a Jewish boy, raised in the covenant, this is the ultimate degradation. Pigs were unclean. He has gone from the son of a wealthy landowner to a pig-feeder who envies the pigs their food. He has been dehumanized. Sin always dehumanizes us. It promises freedom but delivers slavery.

**Act II: The Walk of Shame**

Then comes the pivot point. The text says, *"He came to himself."* The insanity of sin lifted for a moment. He remembers home. But notice his theology. He prepares a speech: *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants."*

He has a plan. He will go back, but not as a son. He will go back as an employee. He thinks, "I have blown my credit. I have a massive moral debt. I will work it off. I will pay the Father back."

This is how many of us view repentance. We think we need to clean ourselves up, get our act together, and approach God with a payment plan. "God, if you take me back, I’ll go to church every week. I’ll stop swearing. I’ll be a hired servant."

So, he starts the long walk home. He is rehearsing the speech. He is hungry, he smells like the pigsty, and his head is down.

**Act III: The God Who Runs**

*"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."*

This is the theological center of the gospel.

In that culture, patriarchs did not run. Ancient robes were heavy and long; to run, a man had to hike up his garment, exposing his legs. It was considered undignified, shameful even. A Middle Eastern nobleman moved slowly. But this Father gathers up his robes and sprints.

Why does he run? Perhaps because he knows what the village will do. If a Jewish boy lost his inheritance among Gentiles, the village could perform a ceremony called the *kezazah*. They would break a pot in front of him and banish him forever. The Father runs to get to the boy before the village does. He takes the shame upon himself.

The son starts his speech: *"Father, I have sinned..."* But the Father interrupts him. He doesn't let him get to the "hired servant" part. You cannot be a hired servant in your Father's house.

The Father calls for three things:
1.  **The Best Robe:** This likely belonged to the Father himself. It covers the boy's filth and restores his status.
2.  **The Ring:** This is the signet ring, the credit card of the ancient world. It restores authority and trust.
3.  **The Sandals:** Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes. It signifies freedom.

There is no probation period. There is no "I told you so." There is only a feast. The Father says, *"This my son was dead, and is alive again."*

If the story ended here, it would be a beautiful picture of God’s grace for the rebellious. But remember, Jesus is talking to the Pharisees, too. There is another brother.

**Act IV: The Lostness of the Good Son**

The older son is in the field. He hears music and dancing. When he finds out why—that his wasteful, immoral brother has returned and a calf has been killed—he becomes angry and refuses to go in.

Once again, the Father leaves the house. Just as he went out to the younger son, he comes out to the older son. The Father is always coming out to us.

Listen to the older son’s complaint: *"Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat..."*

Do you hear his heart?
"I have *served* you." The Greek word is *douleuo*—"I have slaved for you."
"I never disobeyed."

Here is the tragedy of the older brother: He is just as lost as the younger brother, but he is lost in the house. The younger brother was lost in badness; the older brother is lost in goodness.

The younger brother wanted the Father’s things, so he left home to get them. The older brother wanted the Father’s things, so he stayed home to earn them. Neither of them wanted the Father. They both used the Father to get what they really loved: control, autonomy, stuff.

The older brother reveals that his relationship with the Father is based on wage-earning, not love. He thinks, "I’ve been good, so you owe me." This is the spirit of religion. Religion says, "I obey, therefore I am accepted." The Gospel says, "I am accepted, therefore I obey."

The older brother is so angry he won't even claim his family. He says, *"This son of yours..."* He won't say "my brother."

**The Father’s Plea**

The Father responds with incredible tenderness. He doesn't scold the older son for his arrogance. He says, *"Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours."*

He is saying, "Why did you want a goat to party with your friends? You had me. You had access to everything, but you didn't enjoy it because you were trying to earn it."

The parable ends on a cliffhanger. The music is playing. The younger son is inside, eating the calf. The Father is standing outside on the patio, pleading with the older brother to drop his self-righteousness and come join the party.

We never find out if the older brother goes in. And that is intentional. Jesus leaves the story open because he is looking at the Pharisees. He is asking them, "Will you come in? Will you rejoice that sinners are finding grace, or will you stay outside in the cold of your own moral superiority?"

**Application: Which Son Are You?**

Friends, as we sit here today, we have to ask ourselves: Which son are we?

Some of us are the **Younger Brother**.
You have run away. Maybe not physically, but in your heart. You’ve sought satisfaction in the "far country"—in ambition, in pleasure, in the approval of others. And maybe today you are sitting in a pigsty of your own making. You feel dirty. You feel unworthy. You think you’ve disqualified yourself from God’s love.

The message of this text is that the Father is scanning the horizon for you. He is not waiting with a stick; He is waiting with a robe. You don't have to clean yourself up before you come home. You don't have to negotiate a contract. You just have to turn toward Him. The walk of shame ends in the embrace of grace.

But some of us, perhaps many of us who have been in church a long time, are the **Older Brother**.
We have kept the rules. We serve in the ministries. We tithe. But deep down, we are angry. We look at the world, at the "sinners," and we feel superior. Or we look at how hard we work and feel that God owes us a better life than we have. We are joyless, critical, and insecure.

The danger of the older brother is that his sin is harder to see. You can spot the younger brother’s sin a mile away—it smells like pigs. But the older brother’s sin looks like righteousness. It looks like church attendance. But it is just as deadly, because it keeps you from the Father’s heart.

The Father is pleading with you, too. He is saying, "Let go of your resume. Let go of your pride. Stop trying to earn what I have already given you freely. Come into the feast."

**Conclusion: The True Elder Brother**

There is one final thing to notice. In a traditional Middle Eastern family, if the younger brother insulted the father and lost the inheritance, it was the job of the older brother to go get him. The older brother should have gone to the far country. He should have paid the debt and brought his brother home at his own expense.

But in Jesus’ story, the older brother stays home. He doesn't care.

But we know something the listeners then didn't know. We have a True Elder Brother.
Jesus Christ is the true Son who did not stay home. He left the comfort of the Father’s house. He came into the "far country" of this broken world. He didn't just run to us; He climbed onto the cross for us.

On the cross, Jesus was stripped naked so we could be given the best robe.
On the cross, Jesus was cut off from the Father, crying "My God, why have you forsaken me?" so that we could be brought in and hear, "You are always with me."
Jesus paid the debt of the younger brother and bore the penalty of the older brother.

The word "Prodigal" actually means "recklessly extravagant; spending until you have nothing left." We usually apply it to the son’s wastefulness. But truly, the hero of this story is the **Prodigal God**. The God who was recklessly extravagant with His grace. The God who spent everything—even His own Son—to bring us home.

The door is open. The music is playing. The Father is waiting. Whether you are coming from the pigsty or the pew, the invitation is the same: Come home.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we thank You for Your extravagant love. Thank You that You run to meet us when we are far off, and You come out to find us when we are hard-hearted. Forgive us for our rebellion and our self-righteousness. Clothe us in the robe of Christ’s righteousness and bring us to Your table. In Jesus’ name, Amen.*

_iT7F8bU-PsGn-Dk3bLrU.text:
**Title:** The God Who Runs
**Text:** Luke 15:11-32

**Introduction: The Distance of the Heart**

There is a specific kind of silence that falls over a house when a relationship has been broken. It isn’t a quiet peace; it is a heavy, suffocating silence. It is the silence of words unsaid, of apologies swallowed, of a chair at the dinner table that is conspicuously empty.

We have all felt, at one time or another, the urge to leave. To pack a bag, to find a horizon that doesn't have our current problems on it, to escape the weight of expectations. We think that freedom is a geography—that if we can just get to a "far country," we will finally be ourselves.

But we also know the other side of that coin. We know the feeling of staying put, doing our duty, following the rules, and yet feeling completely alone in a crowded room. We know what it is to be physically present but emotionally entirely absent.

Today, we are looking at perhaps the most famous story Jesus ever told. We call it "The Parable of the Prodigal Son." But if we look closely, we will see it isn’t really a story about one son. It is a story about two sons, both of whom are lost in different ways. And, more importantly, it is a story about a Father whose love breaks every cultural convention and theological boundary we try to set.

This is a story about the distance of the human heart, and the God who runs to close the gap.

**Part 1: The Scandal of the Younger Son**

The story begins with a shock. "A man had two sons. The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of the estate that falls to me.’"

To our modern Western ears, this sounds like a bratty teenager asking for an early inheritance so he can go backpack through Europe. But to the Middle Eastern listeners sitting around Jesus—the tax collectors, the sinners, and the Pharisees—this opening sentence was a gasp-inducing scandal.

In that culture, you inherited your father’s estate when your father died. To ask for it while he was still healthy and breathing was to say, effectively, "Dad, you are taking too long to die. I want your things, but I don’t want you. I want my autonomy, and you are in the way."

It was a request of supreme disrespect. By all rights, the father should have exploded in anger. He should have driven the boy out with nothing. But instead, Jesus tells us, the father "divided his wealth between them." He grants the request. He allows his heart to be broken so that his son can be free.

So, the younger son gathers everything and leaves for the "far country."

We know this country. It isn’t necessarily a place on a map. The far country is any place where we try to find fulfillment apart from God. It is the country of "I want what I want, when I want it." And for a while, it works. The money flows, the friends are plentiful, and the party never stops.

But then, the inevitable happens. The money runs out. A famine strikes. The fair-weather friends vanish into the mist.

Jesus paints a picture of utter degradation. The young Jewish boy ends up feeding pigs—animals that were ceremonially unclean to his people. He is so hungry he envies the pigs their carob pods. He has lost his religion, his family, his dignity, and his humanity. He has hit the absolute bottom.

In the mud of the pigsty, clarity finally comes. He comes to his senses. But notice his logic. He doesn't say, "I miss my father’s love." He says, "My father’s hired servants have bread enough to spare." He does the math. He formulates a plan. He prepares a speech: *“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”*

He is trying to negotiate a contract. He thinks, "I blew it as a son. Maybe I can apply for a job as a slave. I will earn my way back. I will pay off my debt."

So, he turns toward home. He is broken, he is smelly, and he is rehearsing his speech. He expects a lecture. He expects rejection. At best, he expects a bunkhouse in the servant’s quarters.

**Part 2: The Scandal of the Father**

What happens next is the emotional core of the gospel.

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion..."

Don’t miss this. How did the father see him from a long way off? Because the father was looking. Every day, perhaps for months or years, that father had been scanning the horizon. He had not washed his hands of the boy. He was waiting.

And then, the text says, the father "ran and embraced him and kissed him."

Again, we miss the cultural impact. In the first century, distinguished, elderly patriarchs did not run. To run, a man had to hike up his long robes, exposing his legs. It was considered undignified, shameful even. Aristotle once said, "Great men never run in public."

But this Father does not care about his dignity. He cares about his son. He exposes his legs to shame so he can cover his son’s shame. He sprints toward the boy.

The son starts his speech. "Father, I have sinned... I am no longer worthy..." But before he can get to the part about being a hired servant, the father interrupts him. The father isn't interested in the business proposition. He isn't interested in repayment.

He shouts to the servants, "Bring quickly the best robe... put a ring on his hand... and shoes on his feet."

These aren't random gifts.
*   **The Robe:** The best robe in the house belonged to the father. He covers the son's filth with his own honor.
*   **The Ring:** This was the signet ring, the family credit card. It represents authority and full reinstatement into the family business.
*   **The Sandals:** Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes.

The father is saying, "You are not my employee. You are my son. You cannot earn this. You can only receive it."

And they begin to feast. The lost is found. The dead is alive.

If the story ended here, it would be a beautiful tale of grace for the rebellious. But Jesus isn’t finished. Because standing in the shadows, just outside the party, is the other brother.

**Part 3: The Scandal of the Older Son**

"Now his older son was in the field."

He hears the music. He smells the roasted meat. He asks a servant what is happening, and when he finds out, he becomes furious. He refuses to go in.

The father, in his infinite patience, comes out to him, too. Just as he ran to the younger son in the pigsty, he leaves the party to plead with the older son in the courtyard.

Listen to the older son’s complaint. It reveals everything about his heart: *"Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat..."*

Do you hear it?
"I have *served* you." The Greek word used there is *douleuo*—it means "I have slaved for you."

Here is the tragedy of the older brother. He stayed home, but he was just as far away from the father as the younger brother was. The younger brother wanted the father’s things; the older brother wanted the father’s things. The younger brother tried to get control by being bad; the older brother tried to get control by being good.

The older brother believed that because of his moral performance, the father *owed* him. He viewed his father not as a loving parent, but as a boss to be pleased, a master to be obeyed so that he could get his paycheck. He didn't love the father; he used the father to get what he wanted.

And now, his self-righteousness is exposed. He is angry because grace is unfair. He cannot stand the fact that his brother got the ring without paying the price. He refers to him as "this son of yours," refusing to call him "my brother."

This part of the parable was aimed directly at the Pharisees—the religious leaders who kept all the rules, tithed their mint and cumin, and looked down on the "sinners" Jesus was eating with. Jesus is showing them that it is possible to be totally obedient and totally lost.

You can be lost in a brothel, and you can be lost in a church pew. You can be alienated from God by your sins, and you can be alienated from God by your morality.

**Part 4: The Application to Our Lives**

So, who are we in this story?

Some of us here today are the **Younger Brother**.
You know you’ve messed up. You feel dirty. You feel like you’ve wasted years of your life on things that didn't satisfy. You are sitting here thinking, "If God knew what I did last weekend, or last year, He wouldn't want me." You are rehearsing your speech. You are thinking, "I need to clean myself up, start attending church for six months, stop cussing, and then maybe God will accept me."

To you, the Father says: Stop the speech. You cannot earn your way back. The moment you turn toward Him, you will find He is already running toward you. He doesn't want to make you a servant; He wants to make you a son or a daughter. The robe is ready. The table is set. Come home.

But many of us... perhaps most of us in the church... struggle with the **Older Brother** spirit.
We have been good. We pay our taxes. We serve in the nursery. We give to the poor. And deep down, we feel that God owes us a smooth life. When things go wrong—when we get sick, when we lose a job—we get angry. We say, "God, I slaved for you! I never disobeyed! Why is this happening to me?"

Or, we look at "those people"—the ones with messy lives, the addicts, the people with different politics or lifestyles—and we resent them. We don't want them in our church unless they look like us and act like us. We stand outside the party, arms crossed, judging the wideness of God's mercy.

To the Older Brothers, the Father says the same thing he said in the parable: *"Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours."*

He is saying: "Why are you trying to earn what I have already given you? You are slaving for wages, but I want you to enjoy the inheritance. Come into the feast. Drop your pride. Drop your self-righteousness. It is keeping you from joy just as much as your brother's sin kept him from joy."

**Conclusion: The Missing Ending**

The genius of Jesus’ storytelling is how the parable ends.

We know what happened to the younger son. He went in to the feast. He was restored.
But the story ends on a cliffhanger regarding the older son. The father has invited him in. The music is playing. The door is open. But we don't know if the older brother went in.

Did he swallow his pride and hug his brother? Or did he stay out in the dark, nursing his resentment, convinced that he was right and his father was a fool?

Jesus leaves the ending open because *we* are the older brother. The Pharisees were the older brother. The ending of the story is written by how we respond today.

God is throwing a party. It is a party of grace. It is a feast for the broken, the failures, the burnouts, and the recovering hypocrites.

The Father is standing at the door. He has run to the younger son, and now He is pleading with the older son. He is pleading with all of us.

He says, "I don't care where you've been—whether you've been in the pigsty of immorality or the cold fortress of self-righteousness. You are both lost, and I love you both. I have paid the price for the robe. I have killed the fatted calf. The joy is real, and it is free."

The only way to miss the banquet is to think you don't need grace, or to think you're too bad to receive it.

The Father is waiting. The music has started.

Will you come in?

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we thank You that You are the God who runs. Thank You that You do not treat us as our sins deserve, nor do You treat us as our self-righteousness demands. We confess that we have been both the younger son and the older son. We have wandered far, and we have judged others. Forgive us. Clothe us in the robe of Jesus’ righteousness. Bring us to Your table, and give us the grace to welcome our brothers and sisters with the same love You have shown us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.*

**Title:** The Prodigal God and His Two Lost Sons
**Text:** Luke 15:11-32

**Introduction: The Definition of a Word**

If I were to ask you to play a word association game and I said the word "Prodigal," what would you say? Almost instinctively, most of us would say, "Son." The phrase "The Prodigal Son" has become so deeply embedded in our cultural lexicon that we rarely stop to think about what the adjective actually means.

In our modern usage, we tend to use "prodigal" to mean "wayward," "wandering," or perhaps "someone who returns home." But that is not what the word means. The word *prodigal* actually means "recklessly extravagant." It means to spend until you have nothing left. It implies a spending that is loose, immoderate, and without calculation.

When we look at Luke 15, we usually focus on the younger son who was prodigal with his money. But if we look closer, we find that the true prodigality in this story—the true reckless extravagance—belongs to the Father. He is prodigal with his grace. He spends his dignity to buy back his children.

Today, we are going to look at this familiar story, perhaps the greatest short story ever told. But we must remember the context. In the beginning of Luke 15, we are told that the tax collectors and sinners were gathering around Jesus, and the Pharisees were grumbling, saying, "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them."

Jesus tells this parable to two groups of people: the rule-breakers and the rule-keepers. And in doing so, he holds up a mirror to every single one of us.

**I. The Younger Son: The Lostness of Rebellion**

The story begins with a request that hits the listener like a slap in the face. The younger son goes to his father and says, "Father, give me the share of the estate that falls to me."

In the First Century Middle Eastern context, inheritance was something you received only after the patriarch died. By asking for it now, the son is effectively saying, "Dad, you are taking too long to die. I want your things, but I don’t want you. I want my independence, and you are in the way."

It is a breathtaking insult. It tears the fabric of the family and the community. By all rights, in a patriarchal society, the father should have struck him, disowned him, or driven him out. But the text says simply, "So he divided his property between them." The father absorbs the blow. He grants the freedom that will break his own heart.

The son gathers everything and travels to a "distant country." This isn't just geography; it is a spiritual condition. It is the place where we go when we decide that we know better than God what will make us happy. And for a while, it works. The money flows, the friends are plenty, and life is a party.

But then, the inevitable happens. The money runs out. A famine strikes. And the young man who wanted to be free finds himself enslaved. He attaches himself to a citizen of that country who sends him to feed pigs. For a Jewish boy, this is the bottom of the barrel. Pigs were unclean. He has lost his religion, his community, his family, and his dignity. He is so hungry he envies the pigs their carob pods.

Sin always follows this trajectory. It promises liberty—"No rules! Do what you want!"—but it always ends in slavery. It promises life, but it smells like a pigsty.

Then, we see the turning point. Verse 17 says, "When he came to his senses..." He remembers that even the hired hands in his father's house have bread. So he prepares a speech. Listen to his plan: "I will say, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.'"

We need to look carefully at this speech. Is it repentance? Yes, in part. But it is also a negotiation. He realizes he has lost his status as a son, so he formulates a plan to pay his father back. A hired servant was different from a slave; a hired servant was a wage earner. He thinks, *I will go back, I will get a job, I will pay off the debt, and I will earn my way back into the household.*

He is still trying to control the outcome. He is hungry, he is desperate, but he still thinks he can fix it.

**II. The Father: The Prodigality of Grace**

So, he starts the long walk home. He rehearses the speech. *Make me a servant. Make me a servant.*

But then, we read one of the most beautiful verses in all of Scripture: "But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him."

We must understand the cultural dynamics here to feel the weight of this. In that culture, a distinguished, elderly patriarch did not run. To run, he would have to hike up his robes, exposing his ankles and legs. It was considered shameful, undignified. Aristotle once said, "Great men never run in public."

Why does the father run?

Scholars tell us about a custom called the *kezazah*. If a Jewish boy lost his inheritance among Gentiles, when he returned to the village, the community would break a clay pot at his feet and yell, "You are cut off!" He would be shunned.

The father runs to get to the son before the village does. He takes the shame upon himself. He exposes his legs to cover his son’s exposure. He acts undignified to restore his son’s dignity.

The son starts his speech: "Father, I have sinned... I am no longer worthy..." But notice what happens. The father interrupts him! He doesn't let him get to the part about "make me a hired servant."

The father ignores the job application and starts barking orders to the servants. "Quick! Bring the best robe." That’s the father’s robe—restoring his status. "Put a ring on his finger." That’s the family signet ring—restoring his authority and credit. "Put sandals on his feet." Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes.

The father is saying, "You are not my servant. You are my son. You cannot earn this. You can only receive it."

This is the Gospel. The world says, "Change your life, and then you will be accepted." The Gospel says, "You are accepted in Christ; now your life will change." The younger son wanted to be an employee; the Father wanted a son.

**III. The Older Son: The Lostness of Religion**

If the story ended here, it would be a beautiful tale of forgiveness. But it doesn't end here. There is a second act. There is a second lost son.

"Meanwhile, the older son was in the field." He hears music and dancing. He asks a servant what is happening, and when he hears that his waste of a brother has returned and—worse—that his father has killed the fattened calf for him, he becomes angry and refuses to go in.

The father, once again, displays his humility. Just as he went out to the younger son on the road, he leaves the party to come out to the older son in the courtyard. He pleads with him.

And here, the older brother’s heart is revealed. Listen to his words: "Look! All these years I have been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear the tragedy in those words?
"I have been *slaving* for you."
The younger brother wanted to be a servant; the older brother actually *was* one in his heart. He didn't see the father as a father; he saw him as a boss.

"I never disobeyed your orders."
He is saying, "I have been good. I kept the rules. Therefore, you owe me."

This brings us to the shocking realization of this parable. Both sons are lost.
The younger son was lost in the "far country" of badness.
The older son was lost right there in the house, in the "near country" of goodness.

The younger son wanted the father's things, not the father.
The older son *also* wanted the father's things, not the father. He wanted the young goat. He wanted the reward. He was using his morality as a way to control the father, just as the younger son used his rebellion.

This is the warning for us, the "church people." It is possible to obey God, to read your Bible, to tithe, to serve in the nursery, and to be just as lost as the atheist or the hedonist. If you are doing these things to put God in your debt, to make him owe you a good life, then you are an Older Brother. You are not serving God; you are using God.

The older brother is furious because grace is unfair. And he is right. Grace *is* unfair. If it were fair, it would be justice. The older brother thinks, "I earned my place." The father says, "No one earns their place here. It is all by grace."

**IV. The True Elder Brother**

The parable ends on a cliffhanger. The father says, "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

And the curtain falls. We don't know if the older brother went into the party. Jesus leaves it open because he was looking at the Pharisees, and he is looking at us. The ending depends on you. Will you go in?

But there is one final question we must ask. Why couldn't the older brother go in? Why was he so angry?

He knew that for the younger brother to be restored, it cost something. The "fattened calf" wasn't just dinner; it was the prime asset of the estate. The robe, the ring, the inheritance—the younger brother had wasted his third. Now, he was being welcomed back, which meant he was eating into the *older brother's* share. Every dollar spent on the prodigal was a dollar taken from the older brother.

The older brother is saying, "I pay for this! He sinned, and I pay the bill." And his selfishness keeps him outside.

But we have a better Elder Brother.

Centuries later, we can look back at this story and see who is telling it. Jesus is the True Elder Brother. He is the one who truly never disobeyed the Father. He is the one who truly had the right to all the Father’s wealth.

But unlike the brother in the story, Jesus did not stay outside. He came into the far country. He came into the pigsty of our world. And he didn't just pay for the party; he became the meal. On the cross, Jesus was stripped naked so we could be clothed in the best robe. He was treated as an outcast so we could be given the ring of sonship. He drank the cup of justice so we could drink the cup of celebration.

The Pharisee in the story wouldn't pay the cost for his brother. But Jesus paid the ultimate cost for us—both for the younger brothers who have wrecked their lives, and for the older brothers who have wrecked their hearts with pride.

**Conclusion: The Invitation to the Feast**

So, where are you this morning?

Maybe you are the Younger Son. You’ve made a mess of things. You feel dirty, ashamed, and unworthy. You are sitting in the pigsty, wondering if God could ever want you back. You are rehearsing your speech, trying to figure out how to clean yourself up before you come to church.

Hear the good news: The Father is not waiting for you to clean yourself up. He is scanning the horizon, waiting for you to turn toward home. He is ready to run. He doesn't want your payment; he wants you. Come home.

Or maybe you are the Older Son. You’ve been in the church your whole life. You work hard. You have strong opinions about how people should behave. But deep down, you are tired. You are bitter. You feel like God owes you, and you are angry that life hasn't turned out the way you planned. You look at "those sinners" who get saved and seem so happy, and you resent them.

Hear the good news: The Father comes out to you, too. He loves you too much to leave you standing in the courtyard of your own self-righteousness. He says, "My child, everything I have is yours." You don't have to slave for him; you can simply enjoy him. Lay down your pride. Lay down your resume. Come in to the party.

The music is playing. The table is set. The Father is waiting. The only thing that can keep you out of the Kingdom of God is your refusal to accept that it is a gift.

Whether you have been running away or running on a treadmill of good works, the invitation is the same: Come home. The Prodigal God has spent everything to bring you in.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we thank You that Your love is reckless and extravagant. Thank You that You run to meet us when we are far off, and You come out to find us when we are standing stubbornly outside. Forgive us for our rebellion, and forgive us for our pride. Melt our hearts with Your grace, and bring us all—younger sons and older sons alike—to the table of Your joy. In the name of our True Elder Brother, Jesus Christ, we pray. Amen.*
