**Title:** The Scandal of Grace: Two Sons and a Running Father
**Text:** Luke 15:11-32

**Introduction: The Name in the Newspaper**

There is a famous short story, often attributed to Ernest Hemingway, about a Spanish father and his estranged son. The relationship had been shattered by rebellion and harsh words, and the boy, whose name was Paco, ran away from home to the bustling streets of Madrid. The father, heartbroken and desperate to reconcile, eventually went to the city to find him.

After weeks of fruitless searching, the father placed a small ad in the local newspaper, *El Liberal*. The ad read simply:

*“Paco, meet me at the Hotel Montana at noon on Tuesday. All is forgiven. I love you. Papa.”*

On Tuesday at noon, the father arrived at the hotel plaza. He did not find one Paco. According to the story, he found eight hundred young men named Paco, all waiting for their father, all hungering to hear the words: *All is forgiven.*

We are all, in some way, waiting in that plaza. Whether we have run far away into the chaos of the world or have stayed close to home but with hearts that feel distant and cold, there is a universal human longing to be known, to be fully seen, and yet to be fully loved.

Today, we turn to perhaps the most famous short story ever told: The Parable of the Prodigal Son. It is a story so familiar that we risk missing its shock value. We treat it like a cozy bedtime story, but in reality, it is a theological earthquake. It is a story about two lost sons, and the scandalous, undignified, overwhelming love of a Father who runs to find them both.

**I. The Younger Son: The Lostness of Rebellion**

To understand the weight of this story, we must look at who Jesus is talking to. Luke 15 begins by telling us that the tax collectors and sinners were gathering around Jesus, and the Pharisees—the religious elite—were grumbling. They said, “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.”

Jesus tells this parable to answer their grumbling. He begins with a younger son who approaches his father with a shocking request: *“Father, give me my share of the estate.”*

In the culture of the first-century Middle East, this was not merely a financial transaction. Inheritance was given only upon death. By asking for his share now, the younger son is effectively looking his father in the eye and saying, “I wish you were dead. You are in my way. I want your stuff, but I don’t want you.”

It is a breathtaking insult. It is a total rejection of the relationship. By all rights, the father should have exploded in anger. He should have driven the boy out with nothing. But instead, the text says the father *“divided his property between them.”* He gives the boy what he wants. He allows the son the freedom to leave.

And leave he does. The son gathers everything and travels to a “distant country.” This is the archetype of rebellion. The distant country isn't just a geographical location; it is a spiritual state. It is the place where we go when we decide that we know better than God. It is the place where we say, “I will be the captain of my own soul. I will define right and wrong.”

For a while, it works. The money flows, the parties are loud, and the friends are many. But the text tells us a severe famine hits the land. The money runs out, and so do the friends. The young man falls so low that he hires himself out to feed pigs—animals that were detestable and unclean to a Jewish boy. He is so hungry he longs to eat the carob pods the pigs are chewing.

This is the reality of sin. It always over-promises and under-delivers. It promises freedom, but it leads to slavery. It promises life, but it leads to the pigsty.

Finally, the scripture says, *“he came to his senses.”* He realizes that even his father’s hired servants have food to spare. So, he prepares a speech. Listen to his plan: *“I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.”*

Note carefully: He is not expecting to be a son again. He is looking for a job. He has a plan to pay his father back. He thinks, *If I work hard enough, if I slave long enough, maybe I can earn my way back into the household.* He is returning, but he is returning with a wage-earner’s mentality.

**II. The Father: The Scandal of Grace**

Now we come to the turning point of the parable. The son is walking home, rehearsing his speech. *“Make me a servant… make me a servant…”*

But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him.

This implies the father had been watching. Every day, perhaps, scanning the horizon. And when he sees the boy—ragged, smelling of the pigsty, walking with the shuffle of defeat—the father is filled with compassion.

And then, the father does the unthinkable. He runs.

In that culture, an older, distinguished patriarch did not run. To run, he would have to hike up his robes, exposing his legs. It was considered undignified, shameful even. Aristotle once said, "Great men never run in public." But this Father cares nothing for his dignity; he cares only for his son.

Why does he run? Some scholars suggest that if a Jewish boy lost his inheritance among Gentiles, the community would perform a *kezazah* ceremony—breaking a pot at his feet and cutting him off from the village forever. The Father runs, perhaps, to get to the boy before the village does. He takes the shame upon himself so the boy doesn't have to face it.

The Father throws his arms around him and kisses him. The son starts his speech: *“Father, I have sinned… I am no longer worthy…”*

But the Father interrupts him! He doesn't let him finish the part about being a hired servant. There will be no job application today. There will be no "pay-back plan."

Instead, the Father barks orders to the servants:
*   **"Bring the best robe."** This was likely the Father’s own robe. It signifies honor. The shame of the pigsty is covered by the honor of the Father.
*   **"Put a ring on his finger."** This was the signet ring, the credit card of the ancient world. It signifies authority and trust.
*   **"Put sandals on his feet."** Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes.
*   **"Kill the fattened calf."** This is a celebration for the whole village.

Do you see the Gospel here? The son thought he had to earn his way back. He thought repentance was a transaction: *I did bad, now I will do good to balance the scales.*

But the Father shows us that grace is not a transaction. Grace is a resurrection. The son was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found. The Father doesn't want a servant; He wants a son.

**III. The Older Son: The Lostness of Religion**

If the story ended here, it would be a beautiful tale of forgiveness. But it doesn't end here. There is another brother.

As the party begins, the older son comes in from the fields. He hears the music and dancing, and when he finds out why, he becomes furious. He refuses to go in.

Once again, the Father leaves the house. Just as he went out to the younger son, he now comes out to the older son, pleading with him.

And here, the older son’s heart is revealed. Listen to his words: *“Look! All these years I’ve been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!”*

Do you hear the bitterness?
First, he says, *“I’ve been slaving for you.”* He doesn't see himself as a son either! He sees himself as a superior employee. He views the father not as a loving parent, but as a boss who owes him a paycheck.

Second, he says, *“I never disobeyed.”* He is resting his righteousness on his moral performance.

Third, he says, *“This son of yours.”* He refuses to call him "my brother."

This reveals a terrifying truth. You can be lost in the "far country" of rebellion, but you can also be lost right here in the Father's house. The younger son was lost in badness; the older son was lost in goodness.

The younger son wanted the father’s things, so he ran away. The older son wanted the father’s things, so he stayed and obeyed. But neither of them truly wanted the Father. They were both using him. One used rebellion to get what he wanted; the other used religion.

The older brother represents the Pharisees. He represents the religious person who says, "God, I go to church, I pay my tithes, I follow the rules. Therefore, you owe me. You owe me a good life. And you certainly shouldn't be letting *those* people—the messy, the broken, the sinful—off the hook so easily."

The older brother is angry because grace is unfair. And he is right. Grace *is* unfair. If grace were fair, we would all be in the pigsty.

**IV. The True Elder Brother**

The parable ends on a cliffhanger. The Father speaks with incredible tenderness to the older son: *“My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again.”*

We don't know what happened next. Did the older brother go into the party? Did he drop his rock of self-righteousness and hug his brother? Or did he stay outside in the dark, nursing his grudge? Luke doesn't tell us. Why?

Because the older brother is the Pharisees. And the older brother is... us. Jesus leaves the story open because *we* have to write the ending for our own lives.

But there is a deeper layer here. In the end, we realize that we need a better Elder Brother.

In the parable, the older brother should have gone to the far country to find his little brother. He should have brought him home at his own expense. But he didn't. He stayed home and hoarded his inheritance.

But we have a True Elder Brother. We have a Brother who did not stay in the comfort of heaven. Jesus Christ, the Son of God, left the Father’s house. He came into the "far country" of this broken world. He didn't just run to us; He walked to the cross for us.

On the cross, Jesus was stripped naked so we could be clothed in the best robe.
On the cross, Jesus was forsaken so we could be given the ring of belonging.
On the cross, Jesus drank the cup of bitter suffering so we could drink the wine of the feast.

Jesus is the True Elder Brother who paid the price of our re-entry into the family. He took the younger brother’s punishment and the older brother’s self-righteousness, and He nailed them both to the tree.

**Conclusion: Come to the Feast**

So, where are you this morning?

Maybe you are the younger son. You’ve made a mess of things. You feel dirty, used, and ashamed. You feel like you’ve gone too far, sinned too much, and that God could never want you back.

Look at the Father. He is not standing with crossed arms, tapping his foot, waiting for you to grovel. He is hiking up his robes. He is running. He is weeping with joy. He doesn't want to make you a servant; He wants to carry you to the table. You don't have to clean yourself up before you come home. You come home to get cleaned up.

Or maybe you are the older son. You’ve been in the church your whole life. You work hard. You follow the rules. But if you are honest, your heart is dry. You are judgmental of people who aren't as "holy" as you. You are angry that God hasn't given you the life you think you deserve. You are slaving, not loving.

The Father comes out to you, too. He stands in the field of your duty and invites you into the party of His grace. He says, “You don't have to earn my love. You already have it. Everything I have is yours. Stop working for me, and start enjoying me.”

The banquet is ready. The table is set. The fattened calf has been killed—the Lamb of God has been slain. The music of heaven is playing.

Whether you are coming from the pigsty or the pew, the invitation is the same: Come in. Come home. The Father is waiting.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we are astounded by a love that runs. Thank you that You do not treat us as our sins deserve. For those of us running away, bring us to our senses. For those of us working to earn what You freely give, soften our hearts. Thank you for our True Elder Brother, Jesus, who came to find us in the far country. Bring us all into the feast of Your grace. In Jesus’ name, Amen.*

**Title:** The Running Father and the Two Lost Sons
**Text:** Luke 15:11-32

**Introduction: The Longing for Home**

There is a specific, hollow ache that most of us have felt at one time or another. It is the feeling of being far away when you desperately want to be close. It is the feeling of displacement. We have a word for it in English: homesickness. But the German language has a word that perhaps captures the spiritual weight of it better: *Fernweh*. It describes a longing for a place you have never been, or perhaps a place you left so long ago that you aren’t sure it still exists.

We spend our lives trying to cure this ache. We try to cure it with success, hoping that if we build a big enough castle, we will finally feel safe. We try to cure it with pleasure, hoping to numb the sensation of being out of place. We try to cure it with morality and rule-keeping, hoping that if we are "good enough," we will earn the right to belong.

Yet, the ache remains.

In Luke 15, Jesus tells a story—perhaps his most famous story—about this ache. We usually call it "The Parable of the Prodigal Son." But if we look closely, we see it isn’t really a story about one son. It is a story about two sons, both of whom are lost, and a Father who is desperate to bring them both home.

Jesus tells this story in a very specific context. Luke 15:1-2 tells us that "tax collectors and sinners were all gathering around to hear Jesus," and the Pharisees—the religious elite—were muttering, "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them."

The audience is split. On one side, the rule-breakers. On the other, the rule-keepers. And Jesus tells a story that dismantles the worldview of both groups, revealing a God who defies our categories and shatters our expectations with his grace.

**Part I: The Younger Son – The Lostness of Rebellion**

The story begins with a shock. "A man had two sons. The younger one said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of the estate.’"

To our modern ears, this sounds like a bratty demand. But in the Middle Eastern culture of the first century, this was a breathtaking insult. In that time, you only received your inheritance when your father died. By asking for it now, the younger son is effectively saying, "Dad, I wish you were dead. You are in my way. I want your stuff, but I don’t want you."

It is a rejection of relationship in favor of resources.

Remarkably, the father does not explode in anger. He does not strike the son. The text simply says, "So he divided his property between them." He grants the son his terrifying freedom.

The boy gathers everything and leaves for "a distant country." This is the dream of the rebel: total autonomy. No rules, no father looking over his shoulder, just cash and freedom. And for a while, it probably felt great. He spends everything on "wild living."

But then, the inevitable happens. The money runs out. A famine strikes. The friends who loved him for his wallet disappear. The boy who wanted to be free finds himself enslaved to hunger.

He ends up hiring himself out to a citizen of that country, who sends him to the fields to feed pigs. For a Jewish audience listening to Jesus, this is the rock bottom of rock bottoms. Pigs were unclean animals. This boy has lost his religion, his community, his family, and his dignity. He is so hungry he envies the pigs their pods.

This is the picture of sin. Sin always promises freedom ("You will be like God!"), but it always delivers slavery. It promises life, but it delivers the pigsty.

But then, we see the turning point. Verse 17 says, "When he came to his senses..."

He remembers his father. But notice his theology. He thinks, *My father has hired servants who have food. I will go back, admit I sinned, and ask for a job.* He prepares a speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants."

He is looking for a transaction. He thinks, *I blew it as a son. I can’t be a son anymore. But maybe I can be an employee. I will work off my debt. I will earn my keep.*

He turns toward home, expecting a frown, a lecture, and an application for employment.

**Part II: The Father – The Scandal of Grace**

Now we come to the heart of the story. The camera shifts to the Father.

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him."

Every detail here is explosive.

First, the father saw him "while he was still a long way off." What does that imply? It implies the father was looking. Day after day, scanning the horizon. The son had forgotten the father, but the father had never forgotten the son.

Second, the father *ran*. In that culture, distinguished patriarchs did not run. To run, you had to hike up your robes, exposing your legs. It was considered undignified, shameful even. Aristotle once said, "Great men never run in public." But this Father cares more about his son than his dignity. He takes the shame upon himself to get to his boy.

Third, he interrupts the speech. The son starts his rehearsed apology: "Father, I have sinned... I am no longer worthy..." But before he can get to the part about being a hired servant, the Father buries him in a hug.

The Father ignores the job application. instead, he barks orders to the servants—not to arrest the boy, but to restore him.

*   "Bring the best robe": This was likely the father’s own robe. It signifies status.
*   "Put a ring on his finger": This is the signet ring, the credit card of the ancient world. It signifies authority and trust.
*   "Sandals on his feet": Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes. This signifies freedom.
*   "Kill the fattened calf": Meat was a luxury, and the fattened calf was saved for a wedding or a massive celebration. This signifies joy.

The message is clear: You are not an employee. You are a son. You cannot earn your way back, because you never earned your way in. You are loved not because of what you have done, but because of who you are.

This is the Gospel. We come to God with our rehearsed speeches, promising to do better, to pray more, to be good servants. And God runs to us, silences our bargaining, and clothes us in the righteousness of Christ. He doesn't want employees; He wants children.

**Part III: The Older Son – The Lostness of Religion**

If the story ended here, it would be a beautiful tale of forgiveness. But Jesus keeps talking. There is another brother.

"Meanwhile, the older son was in the field."

He hears the music and dancing. He asks a servant what is happening. When he hears that his waste of a brother has returned and—worse—that his father has thrown a party, he becomes furious. He refuses to go in.

The father, in his incredible gentleness, comes out to this son, too. Just as he went out to the prodigal, he leaves the party to plead with the older brother.

And here, the older brother’s heart is revealed. Listen to his complaint: "Look! All these years I’ve been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!"

Do you hear the bitterness?

First, he says, "I’ve been slaving for you." He doesn't see himself as a son either! He sees himself as a superior employee. He views his relationship with his father as a business arrangement: I put in the obedience; you put in the blessings.

Second, he says, "I never disobeyed." He is proud of his moral record. He is basing his standing on his performance.

Third, he refers to his brother as "this son of yours." He refuses to claim him as a brother.

Here is the twist that must have stunned the Pharisees listening to Jesus: **The older son is just as lost as the younger son.**

The younger son was lost in the "far country" of badness. The older son is lost in the "home country" of goodness.

The younger son tried to escape the father by breaking the rules. The older son is trying to escape the father by keeping the rules. He doesn't want the father; he wants the father's things—the "young goat," the status, the inheritance. He is using his morality to put God in his debt. He thinks God *owes* him.

This is the danger of religion. It is possible to be in the church every Sunday, to read your Bible, to give your tithe, to never touch a drop of alcohol, and yet be completely alienated from the heart of God. You can be lost in the pigsty, and you can be lost in the pew.

The younger brother’s sin is easy to see. But the older brother’s sin is colder, harder, and more dangerous because it looks like righteousness. It is the sin of pride, of judgment, of a heart that says, "I thank you, God, that I am not like other men."

**Part IV: The True Elder Brother**

The parable ends on a cliffhanger. The father pleads with the older son: "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

The story stops there. We don't know if the older brother went in. Jesus leaves it open because he was looking at the Pharisees. He was asking them: *Will you come in to the party? Will you rejoice that sinners are coming home? Or will you stay outside in the cold darkness of your own self-righteousness?*

But for us today, there is one more layer to this story.

We all tend to be one of these two brothers. Some of us are the younger brother—we’ve made a mess of our lives, we feel dirty, we feel unworthy. Some of us are the older brother—we work hard, we are judgmental, we feel God owes us, we are bitter when "bad people" get blessed.

But we all need the same thing. We need a Father who runs.

However, there is something missing in the story. In a typical Jewish family, if the younger brother insulted the father and lost the inheritance, whose job was it to go after him? It was the job of the older brother. The older brother should have gone to the far country. He should have paid the debt. He should have brought his brother home.

But in the parable, the older brother stays home and sulks.

But we—we have a True Elder Brother.

We have a Brother who did not stay in the comfort of the Father’s house. Jesus Christ, the Son of God, looked at us in our "far country"—lost in our rebellion and our sins—and He came for us.

He didn't just run to meet us; He walked the long road to Calvary.
He didn't just give us a robe; He was stripped naked on the cross so we could be clothed in dignity.
He didn't just give us a cup of wine at a feast; He drank the cup of God’s wrath so we could drink the cup of salvation.

Jesus is the True Elder Brother who came to the pigsty to carry us home. And He did it at the cost of His own life.

**Conclusion: The Invitation**

So, where are you this morning?

Maybe you are the younger son. You feel like you’ve gone too far. You feel the mud of the pigsty on your soul. You think you’ve sinned away your right to be a child of God.

Hear the good news: The Father is scanning the horizon. He is not waiting for you to clean yourself up. He is not waiting for you to repay the debt. He is waiting for you to turn toward Him. If you take one step, He will run the rest of the way. Come home. The robe and the ring are ready.

Or maybe you are the older son. You are tired. You are striving. You are bitter because life hasn't gone the way you planned, despite all your hard work. You look around at others and think, "Why them and not me?" You are standing outside the party, arms crossed, convinced you are right.

Hear the good news: The Father comes out for you, too. He loves you too much to leave you in your bitterness. He says, "Everything I have is yours." You don't have to slave for it. You don't have to earn it. You just have to drop your pride, admit that you need grace just as much as the "sinner" next to you, and come inside.

The banquet is ready. The music has started. The Father is at the door.

Whether you are coming from the far country or the field, the invitation is the same: Come in. Come home.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we thank You that You are the God who runs. Thank You that You do not treat us as our sins deserve, nor do You treat us as our self-righteousness demands. Thank You for Jesus, our True Brother, who paid the price for our homecoming. Melt our pride, wash away our shame, and bring us all—younger and older brothers alike—into the joy of Your house. In Jesus’ name, Amen.*

ClWpUwDtrKodbky2je8pY.text:
**Title:** The Running Father and the Two Lost Sons
**Text:** Luke 15:11-32

**Introduction: The Face at the Window**

There is a universal, haunting image that appears in literature, in film, and perhaps in the memories of some sitting here today. It is the image of a face at the window. It is the parent who cannot sleep. It is the father or the mother pacing the floorboards in the quiet hours of the night, pulling back the curtain to look down the empty driveway, waiting for headlights that do not appear.

We have all known what it is to wait for something. But there is a specific kind of agony in waiting for *someone*. It is the agony of a love that has been rejected, a relationship that has been fractured, leaving behind nothing but silence and a vacant chair at the table.

Today, we turn our hearts to perhaps the most famous short story ever told. We often call it "The Parable of the Prodigal Son." It is a story so familiar that we risk losing its power. We treat it like a warm, fuzzy blanket—a nice story about forgiveness. But if we listen closely, with first-century ears, we will find that this story is not merely nice. It is shocking. It is offensive. And it is arguably the most beautiful picture of God ever painted in human language.

To understand it, we must remember who was listening. Luke 15 begins by telling us that "tax collectors and sinners" were gathering around Jesus. These were the outcasts, the moral failures, the people who had made a mess of their lives. Standing in the back, arms crossed, were the Pharisees and teachers of the law. They were the moral elite, the church-goers, the Bible-readers. And they were muttering, "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them."

Jesus tells this parable to answer that mutter. He tells a story about a father with two sons, and in doing so, he holds up a mirror to everyone in that crowd—and everyone in this room.

**I. The Younger Son: The Scandal of Rebellion**

The story begins with a request that drops like a bomb. The younger son goes to his father and says, "Father, give me my share of the estate."

In our modern context, this sounds like a bratty teenager asking for an early allowance. But in the ancient Near East, this was a devastating insult. Inheritance was only distributed upon death. By asking for his share now, the younger son is effectively saying, "Dad, you are taking too long to die. I want your things, but I don't want you. I want my independence, and you are in my way."

It is a request of breathtaking cruelty. The community would have expected the father to explode in rage, to beat the boy, to drive him out. But the father does the unthinkable. He divides the property. He grants the wish. He lets him go.

The son gathers his wealth and leaves for a "distant country." This isn't just a geographical move; it is a spiritual relocation. He wants to get as far away from the father's authority as possible. And there, the text says, he "squandered his wealth in wild living."

We know this part of the story well, don't we? It is the illusion of absolute freedom. It is the belief that if we can just cast off the rules, cast off the expectations of God and family, we will finally be happy.

But the famine always comes.

The money runs out. The friends vanish. The party ends. The young man finds himself in a desperate state, hiring himself out to a citizen of that country to feed pigs. For a Jewish audience, this is the rock bottom of rock bottoms. Pigs were unclean animals. He is not just poor; he is ritually defiled, socially dead, and starving. He creates a tragic equation in his mind: "Even the pigs are eating better than I am."

Then comes the pivot point: "When he came to his senses."

He prepares a speech. It is a good speech. A pragmatic speech. "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants."

Notice his plan. He is not going back to be a son; he assumes that bridge is burned. He is going back to be an employee. He thinks, "I will work it off. I will pay him back. I will earn my keep." He has a plan to save himself through works. He enters the road home, head down, rehearsing his lines, smelling of the pigsty, expecting rejection but hoping for mere survival.

**II. The Father: The Scandal of Grace**

Now, the camera shifts. We return to the house.

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion."

This implies the father had been looking. He had been the face at the window. He had been scanning the horizon day after day. And when he sees that familiar, broken gait in the distance, the father does something that would have shocked Jesus’s listeners: "He ran to his son."

In that culture, distinguished older men did not run. To run, a man had to hike up his long robes, exposing his legs. It was considered undignified, shameful. A patriarch walked with a slow, measured pace. But this father does not care about his dignity; he cares about his son. He takes the shame upon himself. He sprints toward the boy.

Imagine the scene. The son flinches, expecting a blow. Instead, he is engulfed in a crushing hug. The father throws his arms around him and kisses him.

The son tries to get his speech out. "Father, I have sinned... I am no longer worthy..." But the father interrupts him! He doesn't even let him get to the part about being a hired servant. The father ignores the job application and starts barking orders to the servants—not for punishment, but for a coronation.

"Quick! Bring the best robe." (This was likely the father's own robe—a symbol of status).
"Put a ring on his finger." (The signet ring—the credit card of the ancient world, restoring authority).
"Put sandals on his feet." (Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes).
"Kill the fatted calf." (We are having a feast that the whole village will hear).

Do you see what is happening here? The son thought his restoration depended on his repentance being perfect and his willingness to work. The father shows him that his restoration depends entirely on the father’s love.

This is the Gospel. We come to God with our bargained speeches: "Lord, I’ll go to church more, I’ll be a better person, just let me in the door." And God runs to us, silences our bargaining, and says, "You are not my employee. You are my child." Grace is not a wage we earn; it is a robe we are given.

**III. The Older Son: The Scandal of Self-Righteousness**

If the story ended here, it would be a beautiful tale for the "sinners" in the crowd. But remember, the Pharisees are standing there, too. Jesus adds a second act, specifically for them.

The party starts. The music is loud. The older son comes in from the fields. He hears the dancing, asks a servant what is happening, and finds out his scoundrel brother is home and the dad has killed the prize calf.

And he becomes angry. He refuses to go in.

The father, in his infinite patience, leaves the party. Just as he went out to the younger son, he now comes out to the older son. He pleads with him.

And here, the older son’s heart is revealed. Listen to his words: "Look! All these years I have been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear the bitterness?
"I have been *slaving* for you." He doesn't talk like a son; he talks like an employee.
"I never disobeyed." He is basing his standing on his moral record.

And then the real truth comes out. He says, "But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home..." He won't even call him "my brother." He calls him "this son of yours."

Here is the twist that cuts to the heart. Both sons were lost.

The younger son was lost in the "far country" of badness. He tried to escape the father by breaking the rules.
The older son was lost right there in the house, in the "near country" of goodness. He tried to escape the father by *keeping* the rules.

The older brother didn't want the father; he wanted the father's things. He wanted the reward. He wanted the status. He thought that by being good, he could put God in his debt. He is saying, "God, I did everything right. You *owe* me."

This is the terrifying warning of the parable. You can be alienated from God while sitting in the pew. You can be lost while reading your Bible. You can be just as far from the Father’s heart while obeying the law as the person in the pigsty is while breaking it, if your heart is full of pride, judgment, and self-righteousness.

The younger brother’s sin was obvious. The older brother’s sin was subtle, respectable, and religious. But both were separated from the father.

**IV. The True Elder Brother**

The story ends on a cliffhanger. The father speaks with incredible tenderness to the older son: "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

We don't know what happened next. Did the older brother drop his rock? Did he swallow his pride and go into the party? Or did he stay outside in the dark, nursing his grudge?

Jesus leaves it open because he is looking at the Pharisees. He is asking them: "What will you do? Will you come in to the feast of grace, or will you stay outside because you cannot bear to sit at the same table as sinners?"

But there is one final layer to this story.

When we look at this parable, we realize that we need an older brother. We need someone who, unlike the brother in the story, does not stay home when we run away. We need an older brother who says, "Father, my younger sibling has run off. I will go find him. I will go to the far country. I will enter the pigsty. I will take his shame upon myself."

And friends, we have that Brother.

Jesus Christ is the True Elder Brother.
The brother in the story wouldn't even share a goat with his friends. Jesus, the True Brother, gave his very lifeblood for his enemies.
The brother in the story stayed outside the party in resentful pride. Jesus left the glory of heaven, came down to our "far country," and took the shame of the cross—the ultimate pigsty of human sin—so that we could be brought home.

On the cross, Jesus was stripped of his robe so we could be clothed in the best robe of righteousness.
He was treated as an outcast so we could be given the ring of sonship.
He drank the cup of sorrow so we could drink the wine of the feast.

**Conclusion: The Invitation to the Feast**

So, where do you find yourself this morning?

Maybe you are the Younger Son. You have made a mess of things. You feel dirty, used, and unworthy. You think you’ve gone too far. You think God is angry and waiting to punish you.

Look at the Father! He is not tapping his foot; he is running toward you. He is not waiting for you to pay him back; he is waiting to embrace you. You don't have to clean yourself up before you come home. You come home, and *He* cleans you up. The door is open.

Or, maybe you are the Older Son. You’ve been in church your whole life. You are a good person. But if you are honest, you are tired. You are judgmental of those "sinners" out there. You feel like God owes you a better life because you’ve been so obedient. You are working for God, but you don't really love Him; you just want his stuff.

The Father comes out to you, too. He stands in the aisle of this church today and says, "My child, you are always with me. Stop trying to earn what I have already given you freely. Lay down your pride. Lay down your resume. Come in to the party. Learn to love what I love."

The banquet is ready. The table is spread. The Father is laughing with joy. The music has started.

Whether you are coming from the pigsty or the pew, the invitation is the same: Come home.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we are astounded by a love that runs. We confess that we have played the part of both sons. We have run from you in rebellion, and we have hidden from you in our pride. Thank you for the True Elder Brother, Jesus, who came to find us. Bring us home today. Clothe us in your grace, and let the celebration begin in our hearts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.*

jy6uR1qUX8zkxy1O8K0Ff.text:
**Title:** The God Who Runs
**Text:** Luke 15:11-32

**Introduction: The Longing for Home**

There is a specific kind of silence that falls over a house when a child leaves. It is a silence that echoes. Whether they leave for college, for a new job in a new city, or whether they leave in anger, slamming the door behind them—the silence they leave behind is heavy.

We all have a complicated relationship with the concept of "home." For some of us, home is a sanctuary, a place of warmth and safety. For others, home is a place of old wounds, a place we escaped. But regardless of our history, the human heart possesses a relentless, magnetic pull toward belonging. We spend our lives looking for a place where we are fully known and yet fully loved.

Today, we turn our attention to perhaps the most famous short story ever told. It is a story about home. It is a story about leaving, and a story about returning. We usually call it "The Parable of the Prodigal Son." But if we look closely at the text, we might find that is a misnomer. A "prodigal" is someone who spends money recklessly. And while the younger son certainly does that, he is not the only main character.

In Luke 15, Jesus is surrounded by two distinct groups of people. On one side, you have the "tax collectors and sinners"—the outcasts, the moral failures, the people who have made a mess of their lives. On the other side, you have the Pharisees and scribes—the religious elite, the moral successes, the people who follow all the rules.

The Pharisees are grumbling. They are offended that Jesus is eating with sinners. And in response to their grumbling, Jesus tells a story about a father with two sons. Not one lost son, but two. Both are lost, but in very different ways. And the Father loves them both.

Let us look at the Younger Son, the Older Son, and the Father who runs to meet them.

**I. The Younger Son: The Lostness of Rebellion**

The story begins with a shock. "A man had two sons. The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of the estate that falls to me.’"

To our modern ears, this sounds like a bratty demand. In the Middle Eastern culture of the first century, it was a request of unspeakable cruelty. A son received his inheritance only when the father died. By asking for it now, the younger son is essentially saying, "Father, you are taking too long to die. I want your things, but I don't want you. I want my independence, and you are in the way."

It is a breathtaking rejection. He breaks the community’s heart; he shames his family. But the Father does the unthinkable: he grants the request. He divides his *bios*—the Greek word for "life" or "livelihood"—between them. He tears his life apart to give the boy his freedom.

The son gathers everything and journeys to a "far country." This isn't just a geographical location; the "far country" is anywhere we go to be our own boss. It is the place where we decide we know better than God what will make us happy.

We know what happens next. He squanders everything in "loose living." He buys friends, he buys pleasure, he buys distraction. And it works—until the money runs out. A famine hits. The young man who demanded to be treated like a prince is now forced to hire himself out to a gentile citizen, feeding pigs.

For a Jewish audience, this is the narrative floor. Pigs were unclean animals. To feed them was humiliating; to envy their food, as this young man did, was to be dehumanized entirely. He has lost his religion, his family, his money, and his dignity.

Then, the text says, "He came to himself."

He realizes that even the servants back home have bread. So he creates a speech. He prepares a plan. He says, "I will get up and go to my father, and will say to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight; I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired men.’"

Notice carefully: this is not a plan to be a son again. He knows he forfeited that right. This is a business plan. He is trying to negotiate a way to pay back his debt. He thinks, *If I can just work hard enough, I can earn my way back into the household. I won't be a son, but at least I won't be starving.*

This is the first type of lostness: the lostness of the rebel. Many of you know this path. You tried to find life outside of God’s will. You thought freedom meant casting off restraint. But eventually, the party ended, the friends left, and you found yourself empty. You felt you had sinned too much to ever be a "son" or "daughter" again. You thought, *Maybe if I go back to church, maybe if I clean up my act, God will tolerate me.*

But the parable doesn't end there.

**II. The Father: The Scandal of Grace**

Verse 20 contains perhaps the most beautiful imagery in all of Scripture: "So he got up and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."

*While he was still a long way off.* This implies the Father had been watching. Every day, scanning the horizon. Waiting.

And then, the Father *ran*.

We must understand the cultural context to feel the weight of this. In that time, a patriarch, an older, wealthy nobleman, did not run. To run, he would have to hike up his long robes, exposing his legs. It was considered undignified. It was shameful. Men of honor walked slowly; everyone else waited for them.

But this Father does not care about his dignity. He cares about his son. He exposes his legs to shame so that he can cover his son’s shame.

Why did he run? Perhaps because he knew what the village would do. If a Jewish boy lost his inheritance among Gentiles, the community would perform a ceremony called the *kezazah*. They would break a pot in front of him and banish him forever. The Father runs to get to the boy before the village does. He interposes himself between his son and the judgment he deserves.

The son starts his rehearsed speech: "Father, I have sinned..." But the Father interrupts him! He doesn't even let him finish the part about "make me a hired servant." The Father ignores the job application and calls for a robe, a ring, and sandals.

*   **The Robe:** The best robe in the house (likely the Father’s own) signifies restored honor.
*   **The Ring:** Signet rings were used for business; this signifies restored authority and trust.
*   **The Sandals:** Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes. This signifies freedom.

The Father says, "Kill the fattened calf." In that culture, meat was a luxury, and the fattened calf was saved for a wedding or a massive celebration. The Father is saying, "My son was dead and has begun to live, and was lost and has been found."

This is the Gospel. The Younger Son thought he had to earn his way back. He thought repentance was a transaction: *I do this, and you give me that.* But grace is not a business transaction. Grace is a resurrection. The Father doesn't want an employee; he wants a son.

**III. The Older Son: The Lostness of Self-Righteousness**

If the story ended here, it would be a beautiful tale of forgiveness. But Jesus keeps talking. Remember, the Pharisees are listening. They identify with the big brother.

"Now his older son was in the field..."

He hears music and dancing. He asks a servant what is happening. When he hears that his wasteful, rebellious brother has returned and that his father has killed the fattened calf, he becomes angry. He refuses to go in.

The Father, in his incredible gentleness, leaves the party. He comes out to the older brother, just as he ran out to the younger one. He pleads with him.

And look at the older son’s response in verse 29: "Look! For so many years I have been serving you and I have never neglected a command of yours; and yet you have never given me a young goat, so that I might celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear his heart?
"I have been *serving* you." The Greek word implies slavery. "I have slaved for you."
"I never disobeyed a command."

Here is the shocking revelation: The Older Son is just as lost as the Younger Son.

The Younger Son was lost in the "far country" of badness. The Older Son is lost in the house of goodness.
The Younger Son wanted the Father's things, so he left home to get them.
The Older Son wanted the Father's things, so he stayed home to earn them.

Both sons are using the Father. Neither son actually loves the Father for who he is. The younger one used his rebellion to get control; the older one is using his morality to get control. He thinks, *Because I have been good, God owes me.*

This is the spirit of the Pharisee. It is the spirit of religion without relationship. It is the belief that if we check all the boxes, attend all the services, and avoid the "big sins," then God is obligated to bless us. And when God shows grace to people who haven't "worked" as hard as we have, we get angry.

The Older Brother's anger reveals that he doesn't really know his father. He says, "You never gave me a goat." The Father replies with infinite tenderness, "Son, you have always been with me, and all that is mine is yours."

The Older Son could have had a feast any time he wanted. He was living in the father's house, but he was living with a slave's heart. He was so focused on his duty that he missed the delight.

**IV. The True Elder Brother**

The parable ends on a cliffhanger. The Father invites the older son to come into the party. But Jesus doesn't tell us if he went in. The music is playing, the door is open, and the older brother is standing outside in the dark, arms crossed, nursing his resentment.

Why does it end there? Because Jesus is looking at the Pharisees. He is looking at *us*. The end of the story is ours to write.

Are you the Younger Son?
Have you run far from God? Have you made a mess of things? Do you feel like you’ve sinned your way out of God’s love? Do you think you need to clean yourself up before you come home?
The message of this text is: Stop walking. Stop negotiating. Just turn toward home. The Father is already running to meet you. He doesn't want to punish you; he wants to clothe you in his righteousness. He wants to throw a party because you are alive.

Are you the Older Son?
Have you been in the church your whole life? Do you pride yourself on your morality? Do you secretly look down on people who are "messy"? Do you feel like God owes you a better life because you’ve been good?
Your lostness is harder to see, and harder to heal. It is easy to repent of sins; it is very hard to repent of our self-righteousness. But the Father loves you, too. He is coming out to you today, in the darkness of your pride, and saying, "Everything I have is yours. Come in. Stop slaving. Start celebrating. Learn to love what I love."

There is one final thing to notice. In the beginning of the chapter, Jesus tells the parable of the Good Shepherd. When the sheep gets lost, the shepherd goes out to find it.
But in this story, who goes looking for the younger brother? No one.
In a normal Jewish family, it was the older brother’s job to go to the far country, to pay the debt, and to bring his brother home at his own expense.
But this older brother stays home. He doesn't care.

We need a better Elder Brother.

And we have one. Jesus Christ is the True Elder Brother. He didn't stay in the comfort of heaven. He came to the "far country" of this broken earth. He didn't just pay a sum of money; he paid with his life. He was stripped naked on a cross so we could be clothed in the best robe. He drank the cup of bitter judgment so we could drink the cup of the new covenant feast. He was treated as an outcast so we could be welcomed as sons and daughters.

**Conclusion**

Friends, the banquet has begun. The Father is at the head of the table. The music of the Gospel is playing.

It doesn't matter if you are coming from the pigsty or if you are coming from the pew. We are all saved by the same grace. We are all invited to the same table.

The Father is standing at the door. He has run to meet the rebel, and he has pleaded with the religious. Now, he simply opens his arms.

Come home.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, thank You that You are the God who runs. Thank You that You do not treat us as our sins deserve, nor do You treat us as our self-righteousness demands. You treat us as beloved children. For those of us who feel far away, give us the courage to turn to You. For those of us who feel superior, break our hearts with Your grace. Bring us all into the feast of Your love. In the name of our True Elder Brother, Jesus Christ. Amen.*

**Title:** The Scandal of the Running Father
**Text:** Luke 15:11-32
**Tone:** Pastoral, Warm, Theologically Grounded

### Introduction: The Rehearsed Speech

We have all done it. We have all stood in the shower, or sat in our cars in a parking lot, or stared at the ceiling at 3:00 AM, rehearsing a speech. It is usually a speech of defense or apology. We play out the scenario in our minds. We calculate the angles. *If I say this, maybe they will forgive me. If I phrase it just right, maybe I can minimize the damage. If I lower my expectations enough, maybe I won’t be disappointed.*

We try to write the script of our own redemption.

In the fifteenth chapter of Luke’s Gospel, Jesus tells us a story about a young man who is doing exactly that. He is rehearsing a speech. He is starving, he is broken, and he is covered in the filth of a pigsty. And as he prepares to walk the long road home, he mutters to himself: *“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”*

It is a sensible speech. It is a logical speech. It is a speech born of bargaining. He thinks that if he lowers the bar—if he offers to be a slave rather than a son—he might just survive.

But this parable, perhaps the most famous story Jesus ever told, is not about a speech. It is about the interruption of a speech. It is about a Father who refuses to stick to the script we write for Him.

Today, we are looking at the Parable of the Prodigal Son. But I would suggest to you that the title is a bit of a misnomer. A "prodigal" is someone who spends money recklessly and extravagantly. The son is certainly prodigal with his money. But as we shall see, the Father is the true prodigal of the story—reckless and extravagant with his grace.

### Part 1: The Scandal of the Departure

To understand the weight of this story, we must first understand the audience. Luke tells us at the start of the chapter that tax collectors and sinners were gathering around Jesus, and the Pharisees—the religious elite—were grumbling. They were saying, "This man receives sinners and eats with them."

They are offended by Jesus’s company. So, Jesus tells them a story about a father with two sons.

The story begins with a shock. The younger son comes to the father and says, "Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me."

In our modern ears, this sounds like a bratty teenager asking for an early allowance. But in the first-century Middle Eastern context, this was a breathtaking insult. In a culture deeply rooted in community and family honor, inheritance was something you received only after your father died.

By asking for it now, the younger son is effectively saying, "Dad, you are taking too long to die. I want your things, but I don’t want you. I want my life to begin, and you are in the way."

It is a request that warrants a slap in the face. It warrants exile. The community would have expected the father to explode in wrath. But the text says something simple and devastating: *"And he divided his property between them."*

The father grants the request. He endures the heartbreak. He allows the son to tear the family apart.

The son gathers everything and journeys to a "far country." We don’t know where this is geographically, but spiritually, we all know where the far country is. The far country is any place where we try to find life apart from the Father. It is the place where we believe the lie that freedom means the absence of restraint.

And for a while, it works. The money flows. The party rages. But the text tells us that a severe famine arose. The money runs out, the friends disappear, and the boy finds himself attached to a citizen of that country, who sends him into the fields to feed pigs.

For a Jewish boy, this is the absolute bottom. Pigs were unclean animals. To feed them was to be ritually defiled. He is so hungry he wants to eat the carob pods the pigs are eating. He has lost his money, his friends, his religion, his family, and his dignity. He is hollowed out.

This is the reality of sin. It promises liberty, but it delivers slavery. It promises a garden, but it leaves us in a pigsty.

### Part 2: The Scandal of the Return

Then, we read a beautiful phrase: *"But when he came to himself..."*

Sanity returns. He remembers his father’s house. He remembers that even the servants there have bread to spare. And so, he writes his script. He prepares his bargain. *I will go home. I will confess. But I won't ask to be a son. I’ll just ask for a job. I’ll work off my debt.*

He begins the long walk home. He is smelly, ragged, and likely terrified. He knows how the village works. If a Jewish boy lost his inheritance among Gentiles, the community would often perform a ceremony called the *kezazah*—the cutting off. They would break a pot at his feet and banish him. He expects shame. He expects rejection.

But then, we see the Father.

Verse 20: *"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."*

This is the theological center of the universe.

The father was looking. He had been scanning the horizon, perhaps for months, waiting for this silhouette to appear. And when he sees him, the father does something undignified. He runs.

In that culture, elderly, distinguished men did not run. To run, you had to hike up your robes, exposing your legs. It was considered shameful. But this father does not care about his dignity; he cares about his son. He sprints to the boy—perhaps to get to him before the village elders do, to protect him from their judgment.

The son begins his rehearsed speech: *"Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son..."*

But notice what happens. The father ignores the speech! He doesn't let the boy finish. The boy never gets to the part about being a hired servant. The father interrupts the confession with a coronation.

He barks orders to the servants:
*"Bring quickly the best robe."* That is the father’s robe. It signifies honor and restoration.
*"Put a ring on his hand."* That is the signet ring, the family credit card, the symbol of authority.
*"Put shoes on his feet."* Slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes.

The father is saying, "You are not my employee. You are not my servant. You are my son."

The boy came home looking for a wage; the father gave him a feast. This is the Gospel. We come to God hoping for a little mercy, hoping we can work off our bad karma, hoping to just scrape by into heaven. And God runs to us, hugs us in our filth, and says, "Welcome home, son. Welcome home, daughter."

Grace is not God reluctantly opening the door because we groveled enough. Grace is God hiking up His robes and running to meet us while we are still a long way off.

### Part 3: The Scandal of the Older Brother

If the story ended here, it would be a beautiful tale of forgiveness. But it doesn't end here. There is a third act. There is another lost son in the story.

As the music starts and the fatted calf is roasted, the older son comes in from the field. He hears the celebration and asks a servant what is happening. When he finds out that his wasteful, rebellious brother has returned and is being celebrated, he becomes angry and refuses to go in.

Now, pause for a moment. Who is Jesus talking to? He is talking to the Pharisees. The younger son represents the tax collectors and sinners—the immoral people. The older son represents the religious leaders—the moral people.

The older son’s reaction reveals that he is just as lost as his brother, even though he never left home.

Listen to what he says to the father: *"Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat..."*

Do you hear the language? *"I served you."* The Greek word used there is the word for *slaving*. He says, "I have been slaving for you."

Here is the tragedy of the older brother: He was in the father’s house, but he didn't share the father’s heart. He viewed his relationship with his father as a business transaction. *I keep the rules; you give me the stuff.* He didn't want the father; he wanted the father's assets, just like the younger brother. The younger brother wanted the assets by leaving; the older brother wanted the assets by staying and being "good."

Both sons were using the father. Both sons were alienated. One was lost in the far country of badness; the other was lost in the far country of goodness.

This is a warning to us, the churchgoers. We can sit in the pews every Sunday, tithe, and serve on committees, and yet be completely lost. If we believe that our morality puts God in our debt—if we look at sinners with contempt rather than compassion—we are standing outside the feast.

The older brother is angry because he believes grace is unfair. And he is right! Grace *is* unfair. If grace were fair, the younger son would be in the pigsty. But God is not interested in fairness; He is interested in redemption.

### Application: Which Son Are You?

The father’s response to the older son is just as tender as his response to the younger one. He leaves the party—again, a breach of protocol—and comes out into the darkness to plead with his angry son.

*"Son,"* he says, *"you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours."*

The father loves the legalist just as much as he loves the libertine. He wants both of his boys at the table.

So, as we sit here today, the question presses upon us: Which son are you?

**Maybe you are the Younger Son.**
Maybe you feel like you’ve blown it. You’ve made a mess of your life. You’ve wandered into a far country of addiction, or greed, or anger, or sexual brokenness. You feel the shame clinging to you like the smell of the pigsty. You are sitting here thinking, *I need to clean myself up before I can really approach God. I need to write a speech. I need to earn my way back.*

Hear the good news: The Father is not waiting for your speech. He is waiting for *you*. You do not have to clean yourself up to come home; you come home to get cleaned up. The moment you turn your heart toward Him, you will find He is already running toward you.

**Or, maybe you are the Older Son.**
You’ve been in the church your whole life. You’ve followed the rules. You are a decent, hard-working citizen. But if you are honest, you are tired. You feel like you’ve been "slaving" for God. And perhaps you harbor a secret resentment toward those people who live wild lives and then just "get saved" at the last minute. *It’s not fair,* you think.

Hear the warning, and the invitation: Your morality cannot save you any more than the younger son’s immorality could save him. You need the Father’s grace just as much. The Father is inviting you to lay down your pride, lay down your resume of righteousness, and come into the feast. He wants you to enjoy Him, not just work for Him.

### Conclusion: The True Elder Brother

The parable ends on a cliffhanger. The father says, *"It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."*

And that’s it. The story stops. We don’t know if the older brother went in. Did he drop his anger and join the dance? Or did he stay out in the dark, nursing his grudge?

Jesus leaves the ending open because the older brothers were standing right in front of Him. He was asking the Pharisees—and He is asking us—*How will you end the story? Will you come in?*

But there is one final thing to notice. To have a feast like this, it costs something. The father had to kill the fatted calf. There was a sacrifice involved in the reconciliation.

We have something the disciples and Pharisees didn't have yet. We know the end of the bigger story. We know that we have a True Elder Brother.

In the parable, the older brother refused to go out and look for the younger brother. He stayed home. But in reality, the Son of God, our True Elder Brother, did not stay home. He left the comfort of heaven. He came into the "far country" of this broken world. He didn't come to condemn us; He came to find us.

And on the cross, Jesus was stripped of his robe so we could be clothed in honor. He was treated as an outcast so we could be welcomed as family. He took the shame of the pigsty upon himself so we could attend the banquet of the Father.

Jesus paid the price of the feast.

So, whether you are running away from God in rebellion, or hiding from God in religion, the invitation is the same. The Father is running toward you. The door is open. The table is set.

Come home.

Let us pray.

*Heavenly Father, we are astounded by a love that runs. We confess that we have often wandered to far countries, and we have often stood outside the party in judgment and pride. Thank you that You do not treat us as our sins deserve. Thank you for the robe, the ring, and the sandals. Thank you for Jesus, who made the journey to bring us home. Help us to accept Your grace, and help us to extend that same extravagant grace to others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.*

**Title:** The Porch Light is On
**Scripture:** Luke 15:11-32

There is a short story by Ernest Hemingway titled *The Capital of the World*. In it, Hemingway briefly mentions a Spanish father who is desperately trying to reconcile with his runaway teenage son. The son’s name is Paco. After months of searching, the father is at his wits' end, so he places a short advertisement in the local Madrid newspaper. The ad reads: 

*“Paco, meet me at Hotel Montana. Noon Tuesday. All is forgiven. Papa.”* 

Paco is a very common name in Spain. Hemingway writes that on Tuesday at noon, the local police had to be dispatched to the Hotel Montana to manage the crowd. Eight hundred young men named Paco had shown up, all of them looking for forgiveness. All of them desperately hoping it was their father who had placed the ad. All of them longing to come home.

There is a universal ache inside the human heart. It is the ache of the exile. Whether we have run away from our families, run away from our true selves, or run away from our Creator, we all know what it feels like to be lost. And we all wonder, deep down in the quietest parts of our souls, if we can ever truly go back.

If you have your Bibles, I invite you to open them to the Gospel of Luke, chapter 15. Here, Jesus tells what is arguably the greatest short story ever told. We traditionally call it the Parable of the Prodigal Son. But as we look closely at the text today, we will see that this title is a bit misleading. The word "prodigal" doesn't mean "lost" or "wayward." It means recklessly extravagant. It means spending until you have nothing left. 

As we will see, there is a reckless son in this story, yes. But more importantly, there is a reckless, extravagant, prodigal Father. 

To understand this parable, we first have to look at the audience. Luke 15 opens by telling us exactly who is listening to Jesus. There are two groups. On one side of the room, you have the tax collectors and the "sinners"—the outcasts, the rebels, the rule-breakers. On the other side of the room, you have the Pharisees and the teachers of the law—the religious elite, the rule-keepers, the folks who never missed a Sabbath service. The religious folks are grumbling because Jesus is eating with the sinners. 

In response to this divided room, Jesus tells three parables. A story about a lost sheep (one out of a hundred). A story about a lost coin (one out of ten). And finally, a story about two lost sons (two out of two).

Jesus begins: *"There was a man who had two sons. The younger one said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of the estate.’"*

To our modern ears, this sounds a bit presumptuous, but in the ancient Middle East, it was an unthinkable insult. In a culture built entirely on honor and family loyalty, an inheritance was only distributed after the father’s death. By asking for his share now, the younger son is essentially saying, "Dad, I’m tired of waiting for you to die. I want your things, but I don't want you. As far as I'm concerned, you are dead to me."

It is a breathtaking rejection. Yet, the father does the unimaginable. He doesn't strike the boy. He doesn't banish him. He quietly divides his property between them. 

The younger son liquidates the assets, packs his bags, and journeys to a "distant country." 

Isn't that where sin always takes us? The distant country isn't necessarily a geographical location; it is a spiritual zip code. It is the place we go when we believe the lie that God is holding out on us, that His rules are meant to stifle our joy rather than protect our flourishing. We think freedom is found in autonomy—in casting off all restraint.

But the illusion of the distant country never lasts. The money runs out. A severe famine strikes. And the boy who thought he was a king finds himself working as a hired hand, feeding pigs. For a first-century Jewish audience, Jesus could not have painted a more repulsive picture of degradation. Pigs were ceremonially unclean. The boy has hit rock bottom. He is starving, looking at the carob pods the pigs are eating, and his stomach is rumbling. 

Then comes one of the most beautiful phrases in all of Scripture. Verse 17: *"When he came to his senses..."* 

He remembers his father's house. He remembers that even the hired servants at home have food to spare. So, he drafts a speech. "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants."

Notice his theology. He believes what many of us believe: *I broke the rules. I lost my status. I have to earn my way back.* He plans to ask for a job, not a restoration. He thinks he can pay off his debt through hard work. 

So he begins the long walk home. 

I want you to imagine the scene in the village. If a Jewish son lost his family inheritance among Gentiles, the community had a ceremony called the *kezazah*. If that boy ever returned, the villagers would break a large clay pot in front of him and yell, "You are cut off from your people!" He would be permanently exiled. 

The boy is walking back, rehearsing his apology, terrified of the *kezazah*, terrified of the villagers, terrified of his father's righteous anger. 

But look at verse 20. *"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him."*

Do not miss the scandal of this verse. The father saw him while he was *still a long way off*. Why? Because the father had been looking. Every day, he had been standing on the porch, scanning the horizon. The porch light was on. 

And when he sees his boy, the father does something a dignified Middle Eastern patriarch would never do. He runs. 

To run, a patriarch would have to gather up his long robes, exposing his bare legs. In that culture, it was deeply humiliating. It was shameful. But why does the father run? He runs to get to his son before the village does. He runs to take the shame upon himself so his son won't have to face the broken clay pot. He absorbs the humiliation to save his boy. 

Church, this is the Gospel! This is what God does for us in Jesus Christ. On the cross, Jesus took our shame, our humiliation, and our exile upon Himself. He bore the *kezazah*—He was cut off—so that we could be brought in.

The boy tries to give his rehearsed speech. "Father, I have sinned..." But the father doesn't even let him finish. He completely ignores the part about becoming a hired servant. Instead, he starts barking orders to the servants. 

"Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him." (The robe represents the father’s own honor).
"Put a ring on his finger." (The signet ring, representing the family authority).
"And sandals on his feet." (Slaves went barefoot; only sons wore shoes).

The father is saying, "You are not my employee. You are not on probation. You are my son." And he throws a massive feast.

If Jesus had stopped the story right there, it would be a beautiful tale of redemption. The tax collectors and sinners would be weeping with joy. But remember, there is another group in the room. The Pharisees. The rule-keepers. Jesus has a message for them, too.

Verse 25: *"Meanwhile, the older son was in the field."*

The older son hears the music and the dancing. He asks a servant what is happening, and when he finds out that his deadbeat, rebellious, money-squandering little brother is back, and that their father has thrown him a party, the older brother is furious. Verse 28 says, *"The older brother became angry and refused to go in."*

So, what does the father do? The exact same thing he did for the younger son. He goes out to him. The father leaves the joy of the feast, steps into the dark, and pleads with his angry boy.

Listen to the older brother's response in verse 29: *"Look! All these years I’ve been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!"*

Do you hear the bitterness? Do you hear the resentment? The older brother says, "I have been *slaving* for you." He doesn't see himself as a son either; he sees himself as an employee. He believes his obedience is a currency with which he can purchase his father's blessings. 

Furthermore, he distances himself. He doesn't say, "When my brother came home." He says, "When *this son of yours* came home."

The brilliant theologian Tim Keller, in his book *The Prodigal God*, points out something profound about this parable. Both sons wanted the exact same thing. They both wanted the father's things, not the father. The younger brother wanted the wealth, so he broke all the rules to get it. The older brother wanted the wealth (the goats, the parties, the control), so he *kept* all the rules to get it. 

The younger brother was lost in the distant country. But the older brother was just as lost—he was simply lost at home. 

The younger brother's sin was easy to see; it smelled like a pigpen. But the older brother's sin was hidden beneath a veneer of morality and religious duty. It smelled like self-righteousness, pride, and a cold, unforgiving heart. 

Jesus is looking directly at the Pharisees—and directly at us, the church folks, the people who show up every Sunday, who tithe, who volunteer in the nursery—and He is giving us a loving, pastoral warning. You can do all the right things, keep all the rules, and still be entirely alienated from the Father's heart. If your obedience makes you look down on others, if your religion makes you bitter, angry, and resentful of God's grace toward messy people, then you are standing outside the party in the dark. 

But look at the Father's response to the older brother. He doesn't yell at him. He doesn't say, "You ungrateful brat!" He speaks to him with profound tenderness. 

Verse 31: *"‘My son,’ the father said, ‘you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’"*

Notice the gentle correction. The older brother said, "This son of yours." The father replies, "This *brother* of yours." He is reminding him of their bond. He is inviting him into the joy of grace.

And then... the story ends. Jesus just stops talking. 

It is a cliffhanger. We never find out what the older brother does. Does he drop his pride, cross the threshold, and join the feast? Or does he cross his arms, turn his back on his father, and walk away into the night?

Jesus leaves the story open-ended because it wasn't just a story for the Pharisees; it is a question for you and me. 

Some of you here today identify with the younger brother. You have been in the distant country. You have made a mess of things. You have chased after money, or pleasure, or relationships, or addictions, and you have found that the distant country always over-promises and under-delivers. You feel dirty. You feel unworthy. You are terrified that if God really knew what you’ve done, He would reject you. 

Hear the Word of the Lord today: The Father is scanning the horizon for you. He is ready to run to you. He doesn't want your rehearsed apologies or your promises to work harder. He wants you. He has a robe, a ring, and a pair of sandals waiting for you. All is forgiven. Come home.

And some of you here today identify with the older brother. You have been in the church your whole life. You serve, you give, you try so hard to be good. But underneath it all, you are tired. You feel like you are slaving away for God, wondering when it’s going to be your turn to get a blessing. You find yourself judging the people out there in the world, or even the people sitting in the pew across from you. You have the Father's house, but you have lost the Father's heart.

Hear the Word of the Lord today: The Father has left the party to come out and find you, too. He is pleading with you. "Everything I have is yours. Lay down your heavy burden of self-righteousness. Let go of your pride. Come inside and join the feast."

Two brothers. Both lost. One Father, whose relentless, scandalous, extravagant grace is big enough to save them both. 

Whatever road you are standing on today—whether it is the dusty road from the distant country or the manicured path from the fields of your own self-righteousness—the porch light is on. The door is open. The Father is waiting. 

Let us pray. 

*Gracious God, we confess that we so often wander. Some of us wander by running away from Your rules, and some of us wander by using Your rules to keep our distance from Your heart.
