## The Scandal of the Father’s Embrace

(Luke 15:11-32)

May the words of my mouth and the meditations of all our hearts be acceptable in your sight, O Lord, our Rock and our Redeemer. Amen.

---

### Introduction: The Weight of Regret

We all carry a secret ledger of bridges we’ve burned.

If you are human, you know the crushing weight of regret—that moment when you realize you have made a choice so profoundly wrong, so destructive, that the path back seems not just difficult, but impossible. We look at the wreckage of our own making—a relationship carelessly destroyed, a season of moral drift, a reckless pursuit of independence—and a paralyzing fear sets in: *I have gone too far. I am unforgivable. I am unreturnable.*

It is precisely to those who feel unreturnable, and to those who secretly judge them, that Jesus tells a set of stories so rich we often fail to grasp their radical nature.

We must understand the context. Jesus is dining with known sinners and tax collectors—the outcasts—and the religious elite, the Pharisees and scribes, are grumbling. They are offended that a holy man would associate with the unholy.

In response to their judgment, Jesus tells three parables about lost things: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and finally, a lost son. The first two parables end with the owner seeking the lost item and finding it, followed by a communal call to "rejoice" (Luke 15:6, 9). The third parable, about the son, is the culmination of this theme, proving that God’s response to lostness is not a tribunal, but a party.

This story is not primarily about a bad son; it is about an extravagantly good Father. It is the story of divine love so radical it is scandalous.

---

### I. The Lostness of Rebellion: The Younger Son

Our story begins with the younger son, who makes a demand that, in the first-century context, was the ultimate insult: “Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.”

In essence, this son is saying, “Father, I wish you were dead. I want my inheritance now so I can be free of your authority, your rules, and your presence.” This was a profound rejection of the family structure and the father’s personhood.

The Father, in an equally shocking act of deference, acquiesces. He divides the property, and the younger son takes his wealth and travels to a “distant country.” The distant country is not merely a place on a map; it is a spiritual condition—a state of being where the Father’s love and influence have no jurisdiction.

There, he burns through his inheritance with reckless abandon, engaging in what the text calls “prodigal living”—wasteful, extravagant, and excessive.

The ultimate low point arrives. A famine strikes, and the son, a Jewish man, finds himself working for a Gentile, feeding pigs—the most unclean of all creatures. He has not only lost his money and his friends; he has lost his identity, his dignity, and his faith. He is so desperate he longs to eat the pigs’ food. This is the stench of the pigpen—the physical manifestation of utter spiritual degradation.

The turning point is found in verse 17: **“But when he came to himself…”**

Repentance is not merely a cognitive decision, though it starts there. The Greek word *metanoia* means a change of mind, a reorientation of the heart. The son stops living in the illusion of his false freedom and recognizes the crushing reality of his situation. He realizes that even his father’s hired servants live better than he does.

He devises a plan. It is a good, rational, human plan: *I will return, confess my sin, and ask to be treated not as a son, but as a hired servant.*

Notice the premise of his plan: he intends to **earn** his way back into the household by offering labor instead of love. This is the natural human approach to God: *I messed up, so I must offer penance, perform duty, and prove my worth before I can be accepted.* He is ready to enter into a business deal where his status is determined by his performance.

He begins the long walk home, carrying the weight of his failure and the fragile hope of conditional acceptance.

---

### II. The Scandal of Grace: The Father

The human drama of the younger son’s planned return is immediately overshadowed by the divine drama of the Father’s love.

As the son is still a long way off, the Father sees him. This detail implies the Father was not simply waiting, but **watching**. Every day, he must have scanned the horizon, grieving the loss but holding onto hope.

And when he sees his son—dirty, ragged, smelling of the pigpen—the Father does something culturally astounding: **he runs.**

In that culture, for an elderly, respected patriarch to lift his robes and run was undignified, even shameful. He casts aside his dignity for the sake of his son. The Father runs not just to greet him, but to intercept him. He is rushing to cover the son’s shame before the neighbors can see him, judge him, and enact the ancient communal shaming ritual reserved for those who squandered their inheritance. The Father's run is an act of proactive love and protection.

Here is the Christological connection we must grasp: **The Father who runs is the God who seeks us out.**

We do not have to climb out of our pigpen and scale the heavens to reach him. God did not wait for humanity to clean itself up. In Jesus Christ, God became flesh, taking on a form that was undignified and shameful (Philippians 2:7), descending into the far country of our sin to meet us where we were lost. The running Father is the clearest portrait of the Incarnation—God’s willingness to sacrifice dignity for the sake of relationship.

The son begins his carefully rehearsed speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son…”

But he never finishes the second half. The Father interrupts him before he can utter the words, “...make me like one of your hired servants.”

The Father rejects the earning system the son offers. He rejects the idea that forgiveness must be purchased through servitude. He replaces human merit with divine, immediate restoration.

He calls for four things, each symbolizing the complete reversal of the son’s status:

1.  **The best robe:** A symbol of honor and restoration of status. It is the garment of a guest, not a slave.
2.  **A ring:** A symbol of authority. The son is not just back in the house; he has legal power to transact business again.
3.  **Sandals:** Slaves went barefoot; sons wore sandals. This confirms his identity: he is free; he is a son.
4.  **The fatted calf:** This is a public feast, a community celebration. The Father is publicly declaring, “My son is restored, and I am not ashamed of him.”

The Father’s message is clear: **My love is not conditional upon your obedience, nor is my forgiveness partial.** You are a son, and you are welcomed home completely, regardless of the stench of the pigpen you carry. This is the scandal of grace—it is unearned, undeserved, and utterly extravagant.

---

### III. The Lostness of Religion: The Older Son

If the story ended there, it would be a beautiful tale of redemption. But Jesus adds a final, crucial character, one who was meant to speak directly to the grumbling Pharisees: the Older Son.

The text says, “Now his older son was in the field.” While the party was happening, the older son was absent, diligently working. He represents the person who has never left the house, who has obeyed all the rules, and who believes his obedience entitles him to favor. He is the **self-righteous.**

When he hears the music and dancing, he is furious. He refuses to enter the party. He stays outside, symbolically cut off from the joy and community, even though he is physically close to home.

The Father, who ran out to meet the rebellious son, now goes out again—this time to plead with the resentful son. This shows us that the Father’s love is equally directed toward the rule-breaker and the rule-keeper. Both are loved, but both, in their own ways, are lost.

The older son’s complaint reveals his heart: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends.”

His language is the language of a slave who demands wages, not a son who receives inheritance. He says, **“I have served you.”** He has performed duty, but he has not experienced intimacy. He views his relationship with his father as a transactional business arrangement. He is trapped in the anxiety of performance.

He is jealous, not because his brother is restored, but because he feels his own merit has been ignored. He believes grace given to his brother diminishes the value of his own obedience.

He had everything—security, status, wealth—but he was too busy keeping score to enjoy it. He was physically present but spiritually distant. He was in the house, but he was not home.

The older son’s problem was not that he was bad, but that he was **lost in his goodness.** He was so focused on his own performance that he missed the profound reality of his status as a son. He didn't need a goat; he already owned the entire flock.

The Father’s final words to the older son are heartbreakingly tender: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

Jesus tells this part of the story to remind the Pharisees (and us) that self-righteousness is just as separating as rebellion. The older son needed to repent of his pride and his judgmental heart just as much as the younger son needed to repent of his recklessness.

---

### IV. Application: Where Do You Stand?

This parable is a mirror, and it asks us today: Which son are you? And more importantly, are you accepting the Father’s love?

We must not compare our service to others’ shortcomings. The Father asks us to share his heart: a heart that rejoices, not resents, when the lost are found.

#### 1. To the Younger Son (The Wanderer):

Perhaps you are here today feeling the stench of the pigpen. You walked away, and now you are consumed by guilt and the fear that you have ruined everything. You are planning your servant speech; you are ready to promise to work twice as hard to make up for your failures.

I think of the woman who told me last week she couldn't take communion because her past actions made her "damaged goods." She had her servant speech ready. She didn’t realize the Father had already killed the fatted calf for her.

The message of the Father is this: **Stop planning your servitude, and accept your sonship.**

Your repentance is simply the decision to turn and walk toward him. Do not delay your return because you feel you must clean yourself up first. The Father does not wait for you to be worthy; he rushes out to meet you in your unworthiness. His grace is the speed of his feet running toward you.

If you are carrying the weight of unconfessed sin, if you feel you have burned too many bridges, hear the Father’s voice today: *“My child, you were dead, and you are alive. Come home. The celebration has already begun.”*

Furthermore, are you living like someone who has been restored? You have been given the **robe** of honor (Christ’s righteousness). You have been given the **ring** of authority. Are you still acting like a slave, afraid to use the spiritual authority Christ has granted you? Put on your sandals and walk in freedom.

#### 2. To the Older Son (The Judger):

Perhaps you have been faithful. You are here every Sunday. You serve, you give, you obey. And yet, when you look at the grace given to others—the easy forgiveness offered to those who seem to have tried less hard—a resentment wells up. You feel you deserve more credit, or perhaps that others deserve less grace.

If you find yourself thinking, “I’m glad God loves me because I’ve earned it,” you are not experiencing grace—you are experiencing the anxiety of a worker afraid of being fired. That exhaustion you feel? It’s the burden of trying to be your own savior.

The message to the older son is this: **You are missing the party because you are stuck on the balance sheet.**

Your spiritual pride is just as destructive as your brother's recklessness. You are still operating on a system of merit, forgetting that grace is the air we breathe. You are a son, not a slave. All the Father has is yours. You do not need to demand a goat; you simply need to realize you own the pasture.

We must stop comparing our faithfulness to others’ failures. We are called to share the Father's joy, not manage his justice. If we cannot rejoice when a brother or sister is found, we are outside the kingdom, regardless of how many rules we have kept.

---

### Conclusion: The Invitation to the Feast

Ultimately, this parable is a profound statement about the nature of God. God is not a distant judge waiting for us to meet an arbitrary standard of cleanliness. God is the Father who watches the road, who runs in undignified haste, who interrupts our confession of servitude with a declaration of sonship.

The Father never forces the sons to come in. The younger son had to choose to return, and the older son had to choose to enter the party.

The door to the feast is open right now.

If you are the younger son, turn your feet homeward. Do not fear the consequences; fear only the continued separation from the one who loves you most. Your repentance today might mean walking forward to receive prayer, confessing your sin to a trusted pastor, or finally making that call to the person you hurt. Turn, and the Father will run to meet you.

If you are the older son, step over the threshold of resentment and join the celebration. Lay down your ledger of good deeds and your spiritual pride. Your repentance might mean letting go of the need to judge, forgiving a person you thought undeserving, or simply sitting down and resting in the fact that your salvation is a gift, not a wage.

The party is already happening. Can you hear the music? The question is not whether the Father will welcome you, but whether you will join the dance.

Let us stand today in the light of the Father’s extravagant grace, knowing that in Christ, we are robed in honor, given the ring of authority, and welcomed to the eternal feast—the Marriage Supper of the Lamb.

Come home. The Father is waiting. Amen.

# The Scandalous Embrace: Finding Our Way Home

## Introduction: The Weight of Unfinished Business

Good morning, beloved. Please turn with me in your Bibles to the Gospel of Luke, chapter 15, verses 11 through 32. This passage, often called the Parable of the Prodigal Son, is perhaps the most famous short story ever told.

Before we dive into those familiar verses, let me start with a question: Have you ever had a relationship where you burned the bridge so thoroughly, you were sure it could never be rebuilt?

Maybe it was a harsh word spoken in anger that you can never take back. Maybe it was a betrayal of trust—a secret revealed, a promise broken. Or perhaps it was a slow, deliberate drift, where distance hardened into indifference, and indifference calcified into alienation.

We all carry the weight of unfinished business—the ghosts of relationships that ended badly, the silent shame of choices that separated us from those we love. We often believe that certain doors are slammed shut forever, bolted from the inside by our own pride or the legitimate hurt of the other person.

For many of us, this is precisely how we view our relationship with God. We know the things we’ve done. We know the distance we’ve created. We look at the wreckage of our lives and think, “I have gone too far. I have wasted too much. I am too broken to return.”

It is into this very human space of alienation and despair that Jesus speaks the Parable of the Prodigal Son. But I want to suggest this morning that this story is not primarily about a wayward son; it is about a radically welcoming Father. It is a story designed to shatter our expectations of what God is like and invite us into the scandalous embrace of unconditional love.

Let us listen to the Word of the Lord.

*(Read Luke 15:11-32)*

## I. The Anatomy of Alienation (Verses 11-16)

The story begins with a truly shocking demand.

> “There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’”

In the ancient Near East, asking for your inheritance while your father was still alive was tantamount to wishing him dead. It was an act of profound disrespect, a public rejection of the family unit, the community, and the father’s authority.

The younger son wasn't just asking for money; he was demanding freedom from relationship. He was saying, "I want the benefits of being your son, but I don't want you. I want your stuff, but not your presence."

And what does the father do? He grants the request. He divides his living among them. This act shows us the Father’s immense love, even in the face of rebellion. He honors the son’s freedom, even the freedom to destroy himself.

The son takes his wealth, travels to a distant country, and, as the text says, “squandered his property in reckless living.”

This “distant country” is more than a geographical location; it is a spiritual state. It is the place where we go when we seek to live life entirely on our own terms, severed from the source of life and love. It is the place where the illusion of self-sufficiency reigns supreme.

But the party always ends. The resources run out. A severe famine strikes, and the son, once wealthy, finds himself in the most humiliating position possible for a Jew: feeding pigs. He is so hungry that he longs to eat the very food the pigs were eating. He has reached rock bottom. He is utterly alone, utterly destitute.

This is the state of the soul alienated from God. When we chase after the things of this world—the fleeting pleasures, the false securities, the empty promises—we inevitably find ourselves in a spiritual famine, starving in the pigpen, longing for something real.

The son's journey is a mirror for our own wanderings. We leave the Father’s house when we choose self-gratification over obedience, when we prioritize our desires over God’s design. We leave when we confuse true freedom (which is found in relationship) with mere license (which leads to slavery).

## II. The Journey Home: Repentance and Rehearsal (Verses 17-20a)

It is in the pigpen that the crucial turning point occurs.

> “But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father…’”

He "comes to himself." This is the moment of clarity, the birth of genuine repentance. Repentance isn't just feeling bad about your actions; it is a fundamental change of mind that leads to a change of direction. It is the realization that the life you were living was a lie, and the Father’s house is the only place of true life.

The son meticulously plans his return speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”

Notice the humility. He is not demanding restoration to sonship; he is begging for a job, a place in the periphery. He knows he has forfeited his rights. He is prepared to accept the consequences of his actions. This is the humility required of all who would return to God: acknowledging the sin, accepting the unworthiness, and trusting in the Father’s mercy rather than our own merit.

The son sets off on the long, dusty road home.

## III. The Scandalous Embrace (Verses 20b-24)

Now we arrive at the heart of the parable—the Father’s reaction. This is the moment that defines the character of God.

> “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.”

The father was not waiting in the house, arms crossed, tapping his foot, demanding an explanation. He was watching. Every day, he was scanning the horizon, hoping for the slightest sign of his lost boy.

When he sees him—dirty, ragged, smelling of the pigpen—the father does two things that are culturally shocking.

**First, he runs.** In that culture, older, respectable men did not run. They maintained dignity. Running required hiking up the robes, exposing the legs—it was undignified. But this father throws dignity aside. Love compels him. He runs to meet his son, closing the gap the son had created, before the son can even reach the property line.

**Second, he embraces and kisses him.** He doesn't wait for the speech. He doesn't demand the rehearsal. He doesn't ask for an apology. Before the son can finish the line, “I am no longer worthy to be called your son,” the father interrupts him with an act of complete, unconditional acceptance.

This embrace is the Gospel in a single gesture. It tells us that God does not wait for us to clean ourselves up. He doesn't wait for us to earn our way back. He sees us in our mess, and his love compels him to run toward us. Our repentance is the journey home; the Father’s grace is the sprint to meet us.

But the Father is not finished. He initiates a full restoration. He orders:

1. **The best robe:** This is a garment of honor, symbolizing the restoration of his status as a son, not a servant.
2. **A ring on his finger:** This is the signet ring, symbolizing authority and trust. The son is given back his place in the business and the family.
3. **Sandals on his feet:** Servants went barefoot; sons wore sandals. This confirms his position as a full member of the family.
4. **The fattened calf:** The largest, most expensive feast possible.

The Father declares, **“For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”**

This is the scandalous nature of God’s grace. It is not proportional to our performance; it is overflowing, undeserved, and immediate. If you are here this morning, carrying the shame of a life lived far away, hear this truth: The Father is watching for you. He is ready to run. Your past does not disqualify you from his present embrace.

## IV. The Problem of the Elder Brother (Verses 25-32)

The parable could have ended there, a perfect story of redemption. But Jesus adds the second half, which is often more challenging for us to hear. This is the story of the elder brother.

The elder brother represents those who stay in the Father’s house but are alienated in their hearts. He is the one who tries to earn his way through perfect obedience, the one who views relationship as a transaction, not a gift.

When he returns from the field and hears the celebration, he becomes angry and refuses to go in. He tells his father, “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a command of yours, yet you never gave me even a young goat that I might celebrate with my friends.”

The elder brother’s anger reveals his true motivation: **He was not serving out of love, but out of a desire for reward.** He viewed his obedience as a currency to purchase the Father’s favor. He was physically present in the house, but spiritually just as far away as his younger brother in the pigpen. He was a servant trapped in a son’s body.

His ultimate rejection is directed at his brother: “But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!”

Notice he refuses to call the prodigal his brother. He calls him “this son of yours,” distancing himself from the very family he claimed to be loyal to.

The Father’s response to the elder brother is just as tender, just as compelling, as his response to the younger:

> “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

The Father gently exposes the elder brother’s blindness. He says, “Everything I have is already yours. You didn't need a goat; you could have taken one anytime. You have been focused on getting something *from* me, when what I want is for you to enjoy being *with* me.”

The elder brother suffers from the 'Scarcity Mindset.' He believes that the Father’s love is a finite resource, and if the younger brother gets a share, there is less for him. But the Father’s love is infinite. The celebration of the lost being found does not diminish the love shown to the faithful; it expands the joy of the whole family.

## V. Application: Where Do We Stand?

This parable is a mirror held up to every single person in this room. We are all represented by one of these three characters: the younger son, the elder son, or the Father.

### 1. For the Younger Sons and Daughters (The Prodigals)

If you are currently in a “distant country,” feeling the spiritual famine, believing you have sinned too greatly, wasted too much time, or broken too many promises, the message is for you: **Come home.**

Your return is not predicated on your worthiness, but on the Father’s grace. Stop rehearsing your apology and start walking. The Father is not waiting for you to clean up your life; he is waiting to run to you in your mess. Repentance is simply turning around and accepting the embrace. Jesus told this story to show that salvation is an immediate, full restoration, not a probationary period.

### 2. For the Elder Sons and Daughters (The Obedient but Alienated)

If you are here, outwardly faithful, serving diligently, but inwardly resentful, judgmental, or feeling that God owes you something for your good behavior, the message is for you: **Enter the joy.**

The elder brother’s sin is subtle but deadly: self-righteousness. He was unwilling to extend grace because he never truly accepted grace himself. If you find yourself looking down on others who struggle, or if you view your Christian life as a checklist for earning God’s love, you are standing outside the feast.

The Father invites you to recognize that everything is already yours through Christ. True joy is found not in earning status, but in celebrating the sheer, unmerited gift of belonging—for yourself and for others. Lay down your ledger of good deeds and step into the party!

### 3. For All of Us: Embodying the Father

Ultimately, Jesus calls us, his followers, to embody the character of the Father. We are called to be people who throw out the rule book of deservedness and run toward the broken.

The church is not a museum for saints; it is a hospital for sinners. We must be a community where the running embrace of the Father is visible to the world. Are we quick to run toward the hurting, or do we stand back, waiting for them to clean up their act? Do we welcome the newly repentant with a feast, or do we judge them with the cold resentment of the elder brother?

Our mission is to extend the Father’s scandalous embrace—an embrace that says, "We don't care where you've been or what you've done. You are loved, you are family, and we are celebrating your return."

## Conclusion: The Feast of Reconciliation

The Parable of the Prodigal Son does not give us a neat ending. We never find out if the elder brother enters the feast. Jesus leaves the door open, inviting us to choose: Will we join the party, or will we stand outside in the cold, clutching our self-righteousness?

God’s love is not logical; it is lavish. It is not earned; it is given.

The younger son found out that the Father’s love was greater than his rebellion.
The elder son was invited to realize that the Father’s love was greater than his resentment.

And we are invited to understand that the Father's love, demonstrated fully and finally on the cross of Jesus Christ, is greater than all our sin, all our shame, and all our striving. Jesus, the perfect Son, did not squander his inheritance, but he left the comfort of His Father's house, went to a distant country (earth), and allowed himself to be slaughtered (the fattened calf) so that we—the prodigals and the self-righteous alike—could be clothed in the best robe of His righteousness and welcomed home.

If you are lost, turn around. The Father is already running.
If you are resentful, lay down your pride. The feast is ready.

There is always room at the table. There is always a robe waiting. There is always a Father whose heart is bursting with joy simply because you are home.

Let us stand and receive the blessing of the God who runs. Amen.

They grumbled that God should only associate with the clean and the righteous.

In response, Jesus tells three stories about things that were lost and found: a sheep, a coin, and a son. These parables are not just moral lessons; they are Jesus’s defense of his ministry and a revelation of God’s character. They demonstrate that God is not a rigid accountant obsessed with merit, but a joyful seeker who actively pursues the lost.

I want to suggest this morning that this story is not primarily about a wayward son, but about a radically welcoming Father. It is a story designed to shatter our expectations of what God is like and invite us into the *scandalous embrace* of unconditional love.

Let us listen to the Word of the Lord.

*(Read Luke 15:11-32)*

This parable shows us that God’s grace breaks every boundary—so that prodigals, elder brothers, and all of us alike may be welcomed home, not because we deserve it, but because the Father’s love cannot be exhausted.

## I. The Anatomy of Alienation (Verses 11-16)

The story begins with a truly shocking demand.

> “There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’”

In the ancient Near East, asking for your inheritance while your father was still alive was an act of profound disrespect. It was a public rejection of the family unit, the community, and the father’s authority. The son wasn't asking for a loan; he was demanding his portion of the family wealth now, effectively saying, "I wish you were dead so I could have my money and my freedom."

The younger son was demanding freedom *from* relationship. He wanted the benefits of being in the family without the responsibilities, presence, or love of the Father.

And the Father does the unthinkable: He grants the request. He divides his living among them. This act shows us the Father’s immense, costly love, even in the face of rebellion. He honors the son’s freedom, even the freedom to destroy himself.

The son takes his wealth, travels to a distant country, and, as the text says, “squandered his property in reckless living.”

This “distant country” is more than a geographical location; it is a spiritual state. It is the place where we go when we seek to live life entirely on our own terms, severed from the source of life and love. It is the place where the illusion of self-sufficiency reigns supreme.

But the party always ends. The resources run out. A severe famine strikes, and the son, once wealthy, finds himself in the most humiliating position possible for a Jew: feeding pigs. He is so hungry that he longs to eat the very food the pigs were eating. He has reached rock bottom. He is utterly alone, utterly destitute.

This is the state of the soul alienated from God. When we chase after the world’s fleeting pleasures or false securities, we inevitably find ourselves in a spiritual famine, starving in the pigpen, longing for something real. The distance we create from God is not geographical; it is a distance of the heart, a distance that leads to emptiness and spiritual starvation.

From the pigpen, we glimpse the true distance we have created; now we must discover the road home.

## II. The Journey Home: Repentance and Rehearsal (Verses 17-20a)

It is in the pigpen that the crucial turning point occurs.

> “But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father…’”

He "comes to himself." This is the moment of clarity, the birth of genuine repentance. Repentance isn't just feeling bad about your actions; it is a fundamental change of mind that leads to a change of direction. It is the realization that the life you were living was a lie, and the Father’s house is the only place of true life.

The son meticulously plans his return speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”

Notice the humility. He is not demanding restoration to sonship; he is begging for a job, a place in the periphery. He knows he has forfeited his rights. He is prepared to accept the consequences of his actions. He is willing to trade his pride for survival.

This is the humility required of all who would return to God: acknowledging the sin, accepting the unworthiness, and trusting in the Father’s mercy rather than our own merit. The son sets off on the long, dusty road home, prepared to grovel for a job, unaware that the Father is not interested in hiring a servant, but in embracing a son.

## III. The Scandalous Embrace (Verses 20b-24)

Now we arrive at the heart of the parable—the Father’s reaction. This is the moment that defines the character of God.

> “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.”

The father was not waiting in the house, arms crossed, tapping his foot, demanding an explanation. He was watching. Every day, he was scanning the horizon, hoping for the slightest sign of his lost boy.

When he sees him—dirty, ragged, smelling of the pigpen—the father does two things that are culturally shocking.

**First, he runs.** In that culture, older, respectable men did not run. They maintained dignity. Running required hiking up the robes, exposing the legs—it was undignified. But this father throws dignity aside. Love compels him. He runs to meet his son, closing the gap the son had created, before the son can even reach the property line.

**Second, he embraces and kisses him.** He doesn't wait for the speech. He doesn't demand the rehearsal. He doesn't ask for an apology. Before the son can finish the line, “I am no longer worthy to be called your son,” the father interrupts him with an act of complete, unconditional acceptance.

This embrace is the Gospel in a single gesture. It tells us that God does not wait for us to clean ourselves up. He sees us in our mess, and his love compels him to sprint toward us. Our repentance is the journey home; the Father’s grace is the sprint to meet us. We are invited to approach the throne of grace with confidence (Hebrews 4:16).

But the Father is not finished. He initiates a full restoration, ordering the servants to bring:

1. **The best robe:** This is a garment of honor, symbolizing the restoration of his status as a son, not a servant.
2. **A ring on his finger:** This is the signet ring, symbolizing authority and trust. The son is given back his place in the business and the family.
3. **Sandals on his feet:** Servants went barefoot; sons wore sandals. This confirms his position as a full member of the family.

This full restoration mirrors the promise given to us through Christ. As Paul writes in Galatians 4:5-7, we receive "adoption as sons," and because we are sons, we are also heirs. The Father doesn't just forgive; he restores our identity.

Finally, the Father orders the celebration: **“Bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”**

This is the scandalous nature of God’s grace. It is not proportional to our performance; it is overflowing, undeserved, and immediate. If you are here this morning, carrying the shame of a life lived far away, hear this truth: The Father is watching for you. He is ready to run. Your past does not disqualify you from his present embrace.

If grace meets us running, what happens when that grace meets us inside the gates of the house? We must reckon with the elder brother’s heart as well as the prodigal’s return.

## IV. The Problem of the Elder Brother (Verses 25-32)

The parable could have ended there, a perfect story of redemption. But Jesus adds the second half, which is often more challenging for us to hear. This is the story of the elder brother.

The elder brother represents those who stay in the Father’s house but are alienated in their hearts. He is the one who tries to earn his way through perfect obedience, the one who views relationship as a transaction, not a gift. He is the one the Pharisees and scribes listening to Jesus would have recognized.

When he returns from the field and hears the celebration, he becomes angry and refuses to go in. He tells his father, “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a command of yours, yet you never gave me even a young goat that I might celebrate with my friends.”

The elder brother’s anger reveals his true motivation: **He was not serving out of love, but out of a desire for reward.** He viewed his obedience as a currency to purchase the Father’s favor. He was physically present in the house, but spiritually just as far away as his younger brother in the pigpen. He was a servant trapped in a son’s body.

His ultimate rejection is directed at his brother: “But when *this son of yours* came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!”

He refuses to acknowledge the prodigal as family. His self-righteousness is subtle but deadly, leading him to stand outside the joy of the family. He suffers from the 'Scarcity Mindset.' He believes that the Father’s love is a finite resource, and if the younger brother gets a share, there is less for him.

This is the danger of a works-based faith. If we believe we must earn God’s love, we will inevitably resent anyone who receives it freely. This is why the Apostle Paul insists that grace is a gift: "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9). The elder brother wanted to boast.

The Father’s response to the elder brother is just as tender, just as compelling, as his response to the younger:

> “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

The Father gently exposes the elder brother’s blindness. He says, “Everything I have is already yours. You didn't need a goat; you could have taken one anytime. You have been focused on getting something *from* me, when what I want is for you to enjoy being *with* me.”

The Father invites the elder brother to lay down his ledger of good deeds and step into the party! The celebration of the lost being found does not diminish the love shown to the faithful; it expands the joy of the whole family.

## V. Application: Where Do We Stand?

This parable is a mirror held up to every single person in this room. We are all represented by one of these three characters: the younger son, the elder son, or the Father.

### 1. For the Younger Sons and Daughters (The Prodigals)

If you are currently in a “distant country,” feeling the spiritual famine, believing you have sinned too greatly, wasted too much time, or broken too many promises, the message is for you: **Come home.**

Your return is not predicated on your worthiness, but on the Father’s grace. Stop rehearsing your apology and start walking. The Father is not waiting for you to clean up your life; he is waiting to run to you in your mess. Repentance is simply turning around and accepting the embrace.

**Actionable Response for the Prodigal:**

*   **Walk:** Take one concrete step this week to turn toward the Father (e.g., confess a hidden sin to a trusted pastor or friend; return to consistent prayer; participate in communion).
*   **Trust:** Accept the Father’s full restoration. Do not try to live as a hired servant; live as an adopted child.

### 2. For the Elder Sons and Daughters (The Obedient but Alienated)

If you are here, outwardly faithful, serving diligently, but inwardly resentful, judgmental, or feeling that God owes you something for your good behavior, the message is for you: **Enter the joy.**

You are standing outside the feast, clutching your merit badge, while everything the Father has is already yours.

**Actionable Response for the Elder Brother:**

*   **Lay Down the Ledger:** Confess your self-righteousness. Ask God to replace your resentment with wonder at His grace.
*   **Practice Rejoicing:** Actively celebrate someone else’s breakthrough or return. If you find yourself judging someone who has stumbled, pray for them until you feel the Father’s compassion for them.

### 3. For All of Us: Embodying the Father

Ultimately, Jesus calls us, his followers, to embody the character of the Father. We are called to be people who throw out the rule book of deservedness and run toward the broken.

The church is not a museum for saints; it is a hospital for sinners. We must be a community where the running embrace of the Father is visible to the world.

Are we quick to run toward the hurting, or do we stand back, waiting for them to clean up their act? Do we welcome the newly repentant with a feast, or do we judge them with the cold resentment of the elder brother?

Our mission is to extend the Father’s scandalous embrace—an embrace that says, "We don't care where you've been or what you've done. You are loved, you are family, and we are celebrating your return."

**Actionable Response for the Church:**

*   **Run:** Seek out the marginalized and the returning. Don’t wait for them to prove themselves worthy.
*   **Feast:** Practice radical hospitality. This week, invite someone to your table who might feel alienated or far from God, showing them the joy of belonging.

***

## Conclusion: The Feast of Reconciliation

The Parable of the Prodigal Son does not give us a neat ending. We never find out if the elder brother enters the feast. Jesus leaves the door open, inviting us to choose: Will we join the party, or will we stand outside in the cold, clutching our self-righteousness?

God’s love is not logical; it is lavish. It is not earned; it is given.

The younger son found out that the Father’s love was greater than his rebellion.
The elder son was invited to realize that the Father’s love was greater than his resentment.

How can the Father be so generous? Because the ultimate feast of reconciliation was paid for by the ultimate sacrifice. Jesus, the perfect Son, did not squander his inheritance, but he left the comfort of His Father's house, went to a distant country (earth), and allowed himself to be slaughtered. **He is the ultimate "fattened calf"**—the one whose life was sacrificed so that we—the prodigals and the self-righteous alike—could be clothed in the best robe of His righteousness and welcomed home.

The Father’s running love is fulfilled, tangibly, in Christ’s cross and empty tomb—that is the grounds of our invitation to come home and stay at the feast.

If you are lost, turn around. The Father is already running.
If you are resentful, lay down your pride. The feast is ready.

There is always room at the table. There is always a robe waiting. There is always a Father whose heart is bursting with joy simply because you are home.

Let us stand and receive the blessing of the God who runs.

Amen.

It is a story designed to shatter our expectations of what God is like and invite us into the **scandalous embrace** of unconditional love.

Let us listen to the Word of the Lord.

*(Read Luke 15:11-32)*

## I. The Anatomy of Alienation (Verses 11-16)

The story begins with a truly shocking demand.

> “There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’”

In the ancient Near East, asking for your inheritance while your father was still alive was tantamount to wishing him dead. It was an act of profound disrespect, a public rejection of the family unit, the community, and the father’s authority.

The younger son wasn't just asking for money; he was demanding freedom *from* relationship. He was saying, "I want the benefits of being your son, but I don't want you. I want your stuff, but not your presence."

And what does the father do? He grants the request. He divides his living among them. This act shows us the Father’s immense love, even in the face of rebellion. He honors the son’s freedom, even the freedom to destroy himself.

The son takes his wealth, travels to a distant country, and, as the text says, “squandered his property in reckless living.”

This “distant country” is more than a geographical location; it is a spiritual state. It is the place where we go when we seek to live life entirely on our own terms, severed from the source of life and love. It is the place where the illusion of self-sufficiency reigns supreme.

But the party always ends. The resources run out. A severe famine strikes, and the son, once wealthy, finds himself in the most humiliating position possible for a Jew: feeding pigs. He is so hungry that he longs to eat the very food the pigs were eating. He has reached rock bottom. He is utterly alone, utterly destitute.

This is the state of the soul alienated from God. When we chase after the things of this world—the fleeting pleasures, the false securities, the empty promises—we inevitably find ourselves in a spiritual famine, starving in the pigpen, longing for something real.

The son's journey is a mirror for our own wanderings. We leave the Father’s house when we choose self-gratification over obedience, when we prioritize our desires over God’s design. We leave when we confuse true freedom (which is found in relationship) with mere license (which leads inexorably to slavery).

## II. The Journey Home: Repentance and Rehearsal (Verses 17-20a)

It is in the pigpen that the crucial turning point occurs.

> “But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father…’”

He "comes to himself." This is the moment of clarity, the birth of genuine repentance. Repentance isn't just feeling regret or shame; it is a fundamental change of mind that leads to a change of direction. It is the realization that the life you were living was a lie, and the Father’s house is the only place of true life.

The son meticulously plans his return speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”

He knows he has forfeited his rights. He is prepared to accept the consequences of his actions. He is not demanding restoration; he is begging for a job, a place in the periphery. This is the humility required of all who would return to God: acknowledging the sin, accepting the unworthiness, and trusting in the Father’s mercy rather than our own merit.

The son sets off on the long, dusty road home.

## III. The Scandalous Embrace (Verses 20b-24)

Now we arrive at the heart of the parable—the Father’s reaction. This is the moment that defines the character of God.

> “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.”

The father was not waiting in the house, arms crossed, tapping his foot, demanding an explanation. He was watching. Every day, he was scanning the horizon, hoping for the slightest sign of his lost boy.

When he sees him—dirty, ragged, smelling of the pigpen—the father does two things that are culturally shocking and profoundly revealing about the nature of grace.

**First, he runs.** In that culture, older, respectable men did not run. They maintained dignity. Running required hiking up the robes, exposing the legs—it was undignified. But this father throws dignity aside. Love compels him. He runs to meet his son, closing the gap the son had created, before the son can even reach the property line. He takes on the public shame of reconciliation so his son doesn't have to face the community's scorn alone.

**Second, he embraces and kisses him.** He doesn't wait for the speech. He doesn't demand the rehearsal. He doesn't ask for an apology. Before the son can finish the line, “I am no longer worthy to be called your son,” the father interrupts him with an act of complete, unconditional acceptance.

Imagine the scene. The son is reeking of sweat and pig slop. He is filthy. But the father doesn't hold him at arm’s length. He pulls him close, likely ruining his own clean robes with the grime. He allows the dirt and the stench of the son’s life to transfer to himself. This is the Gospel in a single, visceral gesture: God does not wait for us to clean ourselves up; He comes to us in our mess and absorbs our uncleanness.

The Father initiates a full restoration, demonstrating that reconciliation is not a partial pardon but complete reinstatement:

1. **The best robe:** This is a garment of honor, symbolizing the restoration of his status as a son, not a servant.
2. **A ring on his finger:** This is the signet ring, symbolizing authority and trust. The son is given back his place in the business and the family.
3. **Sandals on his feet:** Servants went barefoot; sons wore sandals. This confirms his position as a full member of the family.
4. **The fattened calf:** The largest, most expensive feast possible.

The Father declares, **“For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”**

This is the scandalous nature of God’s grace. It is not proportional to our performance; it is overflowing, undeserved, and immediate. If you are here this morning, carrying the shame of a life lived far away, hear this truth: The Father is watching for you. He is ready to run. Your past does not disqualify you from his present embrace.

## IV. The Problem of the Elder Brother (Verses 25-32)

Just when we think the story has ended happily ever after, Jesus turns the camera away from the feast and focuses on the front porch.

We must remember the original audience for this parable. Luke 15 opens with the Pharisees and scribes grumbling, “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” The younger son represents the public sinners Jesus was embracing (tax collectors, prostitutes). The elder brother is Jesus’ primary target: the religious leaders who prided themselves on their meticulous obedience.

The elder brother represents those who stay in the Father’s house but are alienated in their hearts. He is the one who tries to earn his way through perfect obedience, the one who views relationship as a transaction, not a gift.

When he returns from the field and hears the celebration, he becomes angry and refuses to go in. He confronts his father: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a command of yours, yet you never gave me even a young goat that I might celebrate with my friends.”

The elder brother’s anger reveals his true motivation: **He was not serving out of love, but out of a desire for reward.** He viewed his obedience as a currency to purchase the Father’s favor. He was physically present in the house, but spiritually just as far away as his younger brother in the pigpen. He was a servant trapped in a son’s body.

His ultimate rejection is directed at his sibling: “But when **this son of yours** came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!”

He refuses to call the prodigal his brother. He distances himself from the very family he claimed to be loyal to. His sin is the subtle but deadly sin of self-righteousness.

The Father’s response to the elder brother is just as tender, just as compelling, as his response to the younger. He leaves the party, steps out into the darkness, and pleads:

> “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

The Father gently exposes the elder brother’s blindness. He says, “Everything I have is already yours. You didn't need a goat; you could have taken one anytime. You have been focused on getting something *from* me, when what I want is for you to enjoy being *with* me.”

The elder brother suffers from the 'Scarcity Mindset.' He believes that the Father’s love is a finite resource, and if the younger brother gets a share, there is less for him. This mindset is rooted in legalism: if grace is free, then my hard work was worthless. But the Father’s love is infinite. The celebration of the lost being found does not diminish the love shown to the faithful; it expands the joy of the whole family.

## V. Application: Choosing Our Place at the Table

This parable is a mirror held up to every single person in this room. We are all represented by one of these three characters, and we are constantly cycling through these roles in our relationship with God.

### 1. For the Younger Sons and Daughters (The Prodigals)

If you are currently in a “distant country,” feeling the spiritual famine, believing you have sinned too greatly, wasted too much time, or broken too many promises, the message is for you: **Come home.**

Your return is not predicated on your worthiness, but on the Father’s grace. Stop rehearsing your apology and start walking. The Father is not waiting for you to clean up your life; he is waiting to run to you in your mess and absorb your shame. Repentance is simply turning around and accepting the embrace. Jesus told this story to show that salvation is an immediate, full restoration, not a probationary period.

### 2. For the Elder Sons and Daughters (The Dutiful but Joyless)

If you are here, outwardly faithful, serving diligently, but inwardly resentful, judgmental, or feeling that God owes you something for your good behavior, the message is for you: **Enter the joy.**

Some of you are tired. You’ve tried so hard to be good. You’ve checked all the boxes, and yet, you feel no joy. You look at the grace given to the "sinners" and it feels unfair. The Father steps out to meet you too, saying: "You don’t have to earn my love. You can stop working *for* me and just start being *with* me."

The Father invites you to recognize that everything is already yours through Christ. True joy is found not in earning status, but in celebrating the sheer, unmerited gift of belonging—for yourself and for others. Lay down your ledger of good deeds and step into the party!

### 3. Embodying the Father: The Church’s Call

Ultimately, Jesus calls us, his followers, to embody the character of the Father. We are called to be people who throw out the rule book of deservedness and run toward the broken.

The church must be a community with no "do not disturb" signs on the door. When the world looks at us, they shouldn't see a pristine museum where perfect people are on display; they should see a triage unit where the broken are being mended by the Great Physician.

Our mission is to extend the Father’s scandalous embrace—an embrace that says, "We don't care where you've been or what you've done. You are loved, you are family, and we are celebrating your return." Are we quick to run toward the hurting, or do we stand back, waiting for them to clean up their act? Do we welcome the newly repentant with a feast, or do we judge them with the cold resentment of the elder brother?

## Conclusion: The Feast of Reconciliation

The Parable of the Prodigal Son does not give us a neat ending. We never find out if the elder brother enters the feast. Jesus leaves the door open, inviting us to choose: Will we join the party, or will we stand outside in the cold, clutching our self-righteousness?

God’s love is not logical; it is lavish. It is not earned; it is given.

The younger son found out that the Father’s love was greater than his rebellion.
The elder son was invited to realize that the Father’s love was greater than his resentment.

But let us pause one final time on the cost of this celebration. The Father declared, "We must celebrate... for this my son was dead." And to celebrate, the Father killed the fattened calf.

The Father’s embrace is free for us, but it was not cheap. It required the ultimate sacrifice. This points us beyond the earthly father to the Heavenly Father, who did not spare His own Son. Jesus Christ is the perfect Son who did not squander His inheritance, yet He willingly left the comfort of His Father’s house, journeyed to our distant country (earth), and became the ultimate sacrifice—the true Fattened Calf—slaughtered so that the feast of reconciliation could be eternally prepared.

He took the filth of our pigpen life onto His own clean robes on the cross, so that we could be clothed in the best robe of His righteousness.

The music is starting. The candles are lit. The Father is standing at the door. The only question remaining is not about your past, but about your present. Will you stand in the dark arguing about fairness, or will you come into the light and dance?

There is always room at the table. There is always a robe waiting. There is always a Father whose heart is bursting with joy simply because you are home.

Let us stand and receive the blessing of the God who runs. Amen.

> “But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father…’”

He "comes to himself." This is the moment of clarity, the birth of genuine repentance. Repentance isn't just feeling bad about your actions; it is a fundamental change of mind that leads to a change of direction. It is the realization that the life you were living was a lie, and the Father’s house is the only place of true life.

The son meticulously plans his return speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”

Notice the humility. He is prepared to accept the consequences of his actions. He knows he has forfeited his rights. He is begging for a job, a place in the periphery. This is the humility required of all who would return to God: acknowledging the sin, accepting the unworthiness, and trusting in the Father’s mercy rather than our own merit.

The son sets off on the long, dusty road home.

## III. The Scandalous Embrace (Verses 20b-24)

But the son's journey home is only half the story. What happens next reveals everything about the Father's heart.

> “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.”

The father was not waiting in the house, arms crossed, tapping his foot, demanding an explanation. He was watching. Every day, he was scanning the horizon, hoping for the slightest sign of his lost boy.

When he sees him—dirty, ragged, smelling of the pigpen—the father does two things that are culturally shocking.

**First, he runs.** In that culture, older, respectable men did not run. They maintained dignity. Running required hiking up the robes, exposing the legs—it was undignified. But this father throws dignity aside. Love compels him. He runs to meet his son, closing the gap the son had created, before the son can even reach the property line.

**Second, he embraces and kisses him.** He doesn't wait for the speech. He doesn't demand the rehearsal. He doesn't ask for an apology. Before the son can finish the line, “I am no longer worthy to be called your son,” the father interrupts him with an act of complete, unconditional acceptance.

If the son was prodigal in his wastefulness, the father is infinitely more **prodigal** in his grace.

This embrace is the Gospel in a single gesture. It tells us that God does not wait for us to clean ourselves up. He doesn't wait for us to earn our way back. He sees us in our mess, and his love compels him to run toward us. Our repentance is the journey home; the Father’s grace is the sprint to meet us.

But the Father is not finished. He initiates a full restoration. He orders:

1. **The best robe:** This is a garment of honor, symbolizing the immediate restoration of his status as a son, not a servant. This act foreshadows the imputation of Christ’s righteousness—we are clothed in a new status we did not earn.
2. **A ring on his finger:** This is the signet ring, symbolizing authority and trust. The son is given back his place in the business and the family.
3. **Sandals on his feet:** Servants went barefoot; sons wore sandals. This confirms his position as a full member of the family.
4. **The fattened calf:** The largest, most expensive feast possible.

The Father declares, **“For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”**

This is the scandalous nature of God’s grace. It is not proportional to our performance; it is overflowing, undeserved, and immediate. If you are here this morning, carrying the shame of a life lived far away, hear this truth: The Father is watching for you. He is ready to run. Your past does not disqualify you from his present embrace.

## IV. The Problem of the Elder Brother (Verses 25-32)

The parable could have ended there, a perfect story of redemption. But Jesus adds the second half, which is often more challenging for us to hear. This is the story of the elder brother.

The elder brother represents those who stay in the Father’s house but are alienated in their hearts. He is the one who tries to earn his way through perfect obedience, the one who views relationship as a transaction, not a gift.

When he returns from the field and hears the celebration, he becomes angry and refuses to go in. He tells his father, “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a command of yours, yet you never gave me even a young goat that I might celebrate with my friends.”

The elder brother’s anger reveals his true motivation: **He was not serving out of love, but out of a desire for reward.** He viewed his obedience as a currency to purchase the Father’s favor. He was physically present in the house, but spiritually just as far away as his younger brother in the pigpen. He was a servant trapped in a son’s body.

His ultimate rejection is directed at his brother: “But when *this son of yours* came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!”

Notice he refuses to call the prodigal his brother. He calls him “this son of yours,” distancing himself from the very family he claimed to be loyal to.

The elder brother suffers from the **Scarcity Mindset**. He believes that the Father’s love is a finite resource, and if the younger brother gets a share, there is less for him. He doesn't understand that the Father's resources and love are infinite.

The Father’s response to the elder brother is just as tender, just as compelling, as his response to the younger:

> “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

The Father gently exposes the elder brother’s blindness. He says, “Everything I have is already yours. You have been focused on getting something *from* me, when what I want is for you to enjoy being *with* me. The only thing you lacked was joy in your brother’s return.”

## V. Application: Where Do We Stand?

This parable is a mirror held up to every single person in this room. We are all represented by one of these three characters: the younger son, the elder son, or the Father.

If you are currently in a “distant country,” feeling the spiritual famine, believing you have sinned too greatly, wasted too much time, or broken too many promises, the message is for you: **Come home.**

Stop rehearsing your apology and start walking. The Father is not waiting for you to clean up your life; he is waiting to run to you in your mess. Your return is not predicated on your worthiness, but on the Father’s grace. Repentance is simply turning around and accepting the embrace. Jesus told this story to show that salvation is an immediate, full restoration, not a probationary period.

### 2. For the Elder Sons and Daughters (The Obedient but Alienated)

If you are here, outwardly faithful, serving diligently, but inwardly resentful, judgmental, or feeling that God owes you something for your good behavior, the message is for you: **Enter the joy.**

The elder brother’s sin is self-righteousness. If you find yourself looking down on others who struggle, or if you view your Christian life as a checklist for earning God’s love, you are standing outside the feast.

The Father invites you to recognize that everything is already yours through Christ. True joy is found not in earning status, but in celebrating the sheer, unmerited gift of belonging—for yourself and for others. Lay down your ledger of good deeds and step into the party!

### 3. For All of Us: Embodying the Father

Ultimately, Jesus calls us, his followers, to embody the character of the Father. We are called to be people who throw out the rule book of deservedness and run toward the broken.

The church is not a museum for saints; it is a hospital for sinners. We must be a community where the running embrace of the Father is visible to the world.

Think about the way we react to those who are returning, whether they are returning to faith, returning from addiction, or returning from a painful time away. Are we quick to run toward the hurting, or do we stand back, waiting for them to clean up their act?

When someone in our community admits their struggle—their "pigpen"—do we offer them a meal and a welcome, or a lecture and a list of demands? Do we greet the newly repentant with a feast, or do we judge them with the cold resentment of the elder brother?

Our mission is to extend the Father’s scandalous embrace—an embrace that says, "We don't care where you've been or what you've done. You are loved, you are family, and we are celebrating your return."

## Conclusion: The Feast of Reconciliation

These three invitations lead us to one final truth: The Parable of the Prodigal Son does not give us a neat ending. We never find out if the elder brother enters the feast. Jesus leaves the door open, inviting us to choose: Will we join the party, or will we stand outside in the cold, clutching our self-righteousness?

God’s love is not logical; it is lavish. It is not earned; it is given.

The younger son found out that the Father’s love was greater than his rebellion.
The elder son was invited to realize that the Father’s love was greater than his resentment.

And how could this Father—who gave away his inheritance once—afford to be so prodigal in his grace?

Because there was a **third** Son, the perfect Son, Jesus Christ, who did not squander his inheritance. He left the comfort of His Father's house, went to a distant country (earth), and allowed himself to be slaughtered (the fattened calf) on the cross. He took the shame of the pigpen and the self-righteousness of the elder brother upon himself. He died so that we—the prodigals and the self-righteous alike—could be clothed in the best robe of His righteousness and welcomed home.

The Father's feast is prepared. There is always room at the table. There is always a robe waiting. There is always a Father whose heart is bursting with joy simply because you are home.

If you are lost, turn around. The Father is already running.
If you are resentful, lay down your pride. The feast is ready.

Let us stand and receive the blessing of the God who runs. Amen.

Jesus adds the second half of the story, which is often more challenging for us, especially those of us who have stayed in the church our whole lives.

The elder brother represents those who stay in the Father’s house but are alienated in their hearts. He is the one who tries to earn his way through perfect obedience, the one who views relationship as a transaction, not a gift.

When he returns from the field and hears the celebration, he becomes angry and refuses to go in. He tells his father, “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a command of yours, yet you never gave me even a young goat that I might celebrate with my friends.”

The elder brother’s anger reveals his true motivation: **He was not serving out of love, but out of a desire for reward.** He viewed his obedience as a currency to purchase the Father’s favor. He was physically present in the house, but spiritually just as far away as his younger brother in the pigpen. He, too, was prodigal—he wasted his father’s presence through resentment.

His ultimate rejection is directed at his brother: “But when *this son of yours* came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!”

He refuses to call the prodigal his brother. He is judging the Father’s love by his own ledger.

If you are an elder son or daughter—outwardly faithful, serving diligently, but inwardly resentful, judgmental, or feeling that God owes you something for your good behavior—this message is for you: **You are standing outside the feast.**

The elder brother suffered from the ancient lie that love is limited, that grace is a zero-sum game. He believed in a God of ledgers, not a Father of infinite joy.

And before we point fingers, let me confess—I’ve been the elder brother. We all have. We calculate who deserves what. We struggle with the idea that God's grace is equally available to the teenager who just rolled her eyes at her parents, the retiree who feels his best years were wasted, or the ex-convict who just found Christ.

The Father’s response to the elder brother is just as tender, just as compelling:

> “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

The Father gently exposes the elder brother’s blindness. He says, “Everything I have is already yours. You didn't need a goat; you could have taken one anytime. You have been focused on getting something *from* me, when what I want is for you to enjoy being *with* me.”

True joy is found not in earning status, but in celebrating the sheer, unmerited gift of belonging—for yourself and for others.

## V. Embodying the Father: The Invitation to the Feast

Jesus leaves the parable open. We never find out if the elder brother enters the feast. Jesus leaves the door open, inviting *us* to choose: Will we join the party, or will we stand outside in the cold, clutching our self-righteousness?

This parable is not just about personal salvation; it is about community. Jesus calls us, his followers, to embody the character of the Father. The church is not a museum for saints; it is a hospital for sinners. We must be a community where the running embrace of the Father is visible to the world.

What does it look like to embody this scandalous embrace?

It means throwing out the rule book of deservedness. It means running toward the broken.

Last month, a young man walked into our recovery ministry—a man who had spent the last decade in and out of trouble, sure that the church would judge him. He was hesitant, smelling not of pigpen, but of the street. He was rehearsing his speech, ready to beg for a place in the periphery.

But before he could finish, three members of the team—people who know what it means to be rescued—didn't stand back and wait for him to clean up his act. They ran to him. They welcomed him not with a lecture, but with a coffee and a hug. They didn't care where he had been or what he had done. They said, "You are loved, you are family, and we are celebrating your first step home."

That is the Father’s embrace made real.

It means our welcome ministries are as prominent as our worship services. It means we celebrate the baptism of a newly converted ex-convict with the same, overwhelming joy as we celebrate the baptism of a child raised in the church.

We must resist the temptation of the elder brother to view grace as finite. When someone else receives mercy, our own standing with God is not diminished; our joy is magnified. Our mission is to extend the Father’s scandalous embrace—an embrace that says, "We don't care where you've been or what you've done. You are home."

## Conclusion: The Ultimate Reconciliation

The Parable of the Prodigal Son reveals the heart of God, a heart bursting with relentless, undignified love.

The younger son found out that the Father’s love was greater than his rebellion.
The elder son was invited to realize that the Father’s love was greater than his resentment.

And we are invited to understand that the Father's love, demonstrated fully and finally on the cross of Jesus Christ, is the only way home.

Jesus, the perfect Son, did not squander his inheritance, but He did leave the comfort of His Father's house, closing the infinite gap between God and humanity. He came to the distant country (earth) and laid down his life so that we—the prodigals and the self-righteous alike—could be clothed in the best robe of His righteousness and welcomed home.

The Father is not just waiting; He is running. He has provided the robe, the ring, the sandals, and the feast.

If you are lost, turn around. The Father is already running.
If you are resentful, lay down your pride and step inside. The feast is ready.

There is always room at the table. There is always a robe waiting. There is always a Father whose heart is bursting with joy simply because you are home.

Let us stand and receive the blessing of the God who runs. Amen.
