**Title:** The Runaway’s Return and the Elder’s Resentment: Finding Home in the Father’s Heart

**Scripture:** Luke 15:11-32

Let me begin with a picture that I suspect might resonate with many of us. Imagine a young man, eighteen years old, standing at the end of a driveway. The trunk of his car is packed with clothes, books, and a few sentimental keepsakes. He has the money he saved from a summer job, a full tank of gas, and a map that leads to a city where no one knows his name. As he slams the car door, the sound echoes like a period at the end of a sentence. He isn’t just leaving for college or a job; he is leaving because he feels suffocated. He believes that to truly become himself, he must get away from the rules, the expectations, and the history of his family. He is chasing a vision of freedom that he defines as the absence of accountability.

We all know this story. We have either lived it, or we have watched it play out in the lives of those we love. It is the story of the Great Escape. But what we often fail to see is that the driveway he is leaving, and the destination he is running toward, are both illusions. He thinks he is running toward freedom, but he is actually running toward a famine of the soul.

This is the raw material of the parable we call the Prodigal Son. It is the third and climactic story in a trilogy of lost things told by Jesus in Luke chapter 15—a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son. It is a story that has been painted by the masters, preached in cathedrals, and whispered in hospital rooms. But today, I want us to look not just at the boy who left, but at the Father who stayed, and the brother who stayed away.

**Part I: The Younger Son and the Illusion of Autonomy**

Jesus begins by setting the stage: "There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, 'Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.'"

We need to pause here to feel the weight of this request. In the ancient Near East, asking for your inheritance while your father is still alive was not merely a request for an early cash advance; it was a cultural equivalent of saying, "I wish you were dead." The father, in this culture, held the rights to the land and the authority over the household. To ask for the portion was to strip the father of his dignity and his standing in the village. It was a public rejection of the father’s continued presence in his life.

And yet, the text says, the father divided it to them. He didn’t argue. He didn’t negotiate. He allowed the son the dignity of his own disastrous choice.

The son takes his wealth and goes into a "far country." Notice the distance. He isn’t just moving to the next town; he is going where the reputation of his father cannot reach him. He wants to be anonymous. And there, he squanders his property in "reckless living." The Greek word here is *asōtōs*—literally, "without saving." He spends it all. He pours his life into a sieve, hoping satisfaction will pool at the bottom, but it never does.

Then comes the famine. It is often the way of the world. The party music stops, the friends drift away, and the pantry is bare. So, the boy attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For a Jewish listener, this is the rock bottom. Pigs were unclean animals. A son of Abraham, feeding the pigs, longing to eat their food. He is now lower than the livestock he tends.

But it is in the pigsty that the spell breaks. Verse 17 says, "He came to himself." This is a brilliant phrase. He didn’t just remember where he came from; he came to his right mind. He realized that the famine in his belly was nothing compared to the famine in his heart. He rehearses a speech: "I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'"

Notice his theology. He still believes in the transaction. He believes he has blown his capital as a son, so he hopes to negotiate a position as a servant. He thinks he can come back, but only on the margins. He hopes for a paycheck, not a relationship.

**Part II: The Father’s Scandalous Welcome**

What happens next subverts every expectation of the ancient world, and it subverts our understanding of God.

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."

In 1st Century Palestine, patriarchs did not run. To run was to expose one's legs, which was considered undignified, even shameful. Furthermore, to embrace the son would mean touching someone who was covered in the filth of the pigs, someone who had brought shame upon the family name. But the Father does not care about dignity. He sees the silhouette of his boy against the horizon, and he is undone. He hikes up his robes, ignoring the gasps of the villagers, and runs.

Before the son can even finish his rehearsed speech—the speech about being a hired servant—the Father interrupts. He doesn't let the boy finish. He issues rapid-fire commands to the servants: "Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate."

The best robe is likely the Father’s own robe. The ring signifies authority. The shoes signify freedom, for slaves went barefoot. And the fattened calf? That was reserved for the biggest celebrations. This is not a quiet "welcome home"; this is a festival.

This is the scandal of grace. The son was looking for justice (to be punished) or at best, transactional mercy (to be made a servant). Instead, he receives explosive, reckless, unconditional love. The Father restores him not just to the family, but to the status of a son. The Father covers his shame with a robe and his poverty with a ring.

Why? Because the Father does not want servants. He has plenty of servants. He wants sons. He wants daughters.

**Part III: The Elder Son and the Resentment of the Righteous**

Now, the story shifts. You would think the story ends here with a happy reunion. But Jesus isn’t done. He has one more character to introduce, and this one is perhaps the most difficult for us to deal with.

"His older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, 'Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.' But he was angry and refused to go in."

The older brother represents the religious establishment, the "good" people who have always stayed in the field, who have done everything right. He is angry. He feels cheated. He sees himself as the victim of his father’s generosity.

Notice where he stands: outside. He refuses to enter. He creates his own exile.

The Father, again, takes the initiative. He goes out to him. Just as he ran to the younger son, he now goes out to the older son. He pleads with him to come in. But the older son’s response is biting: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command. Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear the pathology in his voice? He calls his father "you," not "Father." He claims he has "slaved" for him. He views his relationship with the father not as a son, but as a hired hand who feels underpaid. He reduces his life to a ledger of moral credits and debits. He sees his brother’s return as a loss for himself. "This son of yours," he says, distancing himself from the family, "who devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"

The older brother is angry because grace threatens his hierarchy. If the younger son gets a party, then the older brother’s years of faithful service feel cheapened. He believes that acceptance is something to be earned, and he has earned it. The problem is, he doesn't love his father; he uses his father. He doesn't love his brother; he resents him.

And the Father’s response to the older son is heartbreakingly tender: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."

The Father reminds the older son of what he has lost sight of: You already have the inheritance. You have access to everything. You are home. You have never lacked for my presence.

**Application: Which Son Are We Today?**

So, what do we do with this story? What does it mean for us this morning?

First, to the "younger sons" and daughters in this room. Perhaps you identify with the boy in the pigsty. Maybe you are here today and you feel the weight of your own "far country." Maybe you have chased freedom in career, in addiction, in relationships, or in rebellion, and you have found only famine. You feel the mud on your skin, and you are convinced that the door to this church—and the door to God’s heart—is locked to you. You think you need to clean up your act before you can come home. You think you need to rehearse a speech about how you will do better.

Please hear me: The Father is already running. He is not waiting for you to get clean. He is not waiting for you to explain yourself. He sees you "a long way off." He knows the mess you are in, and He is coming to get you. You do not need to negotiate a position as a servant. You are a child. Come home. The robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The table is set.

Second, we must speak to the "older brothers." This is perhaps the more dangerous category because it often hides behind a mask of piety. Are you here today, checking your spiritual resume? Do you look around at the messy people in this congregation—the ones who are struggling, the ones who keep falling off the wagon—and feel a sense of superiority? Do you resent God’s grace given to those who haven't "earned" it?

The tragedy of the older brother is that he was physically in the house, but spiritually in the far country. He was close to the Father, but he didn't know the Father's heart. He served God out of duty, not delight. He thought God owed him a paycheck for his good behavior. If this is you, hear the whisper of the Spirit: "You are always with me." You don't have to earn the Father's love. You already have it. Stop slaving and start celebrating. The joy of the Gospel is not that we are good enough to get in; the joy is that the Father invites us to the party, not because we earned it, but because He loves to give it.

**Conclusion**

Friends, this parable is often called the story of the Prodigal Son, but it is really the story of the Extravagant Father.

Every single one of us is represented in this text. We are all the younger son, born with a heart that wanders, seeking satisfaction in things that cannot sustain us. And we are all the older son, born with a heart that wants to control God, demanding that life operate according to our sense of fairness.

And into this chaotic mix of rebellion and resentment steps Jesus.

You see, Jesus is telling this story to a group of sinners and Pharisees. But He isn't just telling them a story; He is living it. He is the true Son who leaves the Father’s side, not to squander an inheritance, but to seek the lost. He enters the far country of our brokenness. He descends into the mud and the mire. He takes upon Himself the shame and the poverty that we earned.

He is the one who says to the Father, "I will pay the debt." And on the Cross, He experiences the famine of being cut off from the Father so that we never have to.

And now, He stands with the Father, arms open wide, inviting us to the feast.

The question this morning is not about your past. It is not about how far you have run or how hard you have worked. The question is: Will you come in?

There is a party going on. The music is playing. The fatted calf is roasting. The table is broad enough for the reckless wanderer and the rule-keeper alike. The Father is at the door, not to scold, but to embrace.

Let us pray.

*Father, we confess that we are often like the younger son, seeking our own way, squandering your gifts, and ending up in the pigsties of our own making. Forgive us our wanderings.*

*Lord, we also confess that we are like the older son, holding onto our resentment, believing that our service makes us worthy, and despising your grace for others. Forgive us our pride.*

*Thank You that You are the Good Father who runs to us. Thank You that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Help us this day to lay down our burdens, to drop our defenses, and to come home. May we know the joy of Your presence, not as slaves, but as sons and daughters, in the name of Your Son, Jesus. Amen.*

We need to pause here to feel the weight of this request. In the ancient Near East, asking for your inheritance while your father is still alive was not merely a request for an early cash advance; it was a cultural equivalent of saying, "I wish you were dead." The father, in this culture, held the rights to the land and the authority over the household. To ask for the portion was to strip the father of his dignity and his standing in the village. It was a public rejection of the father’s continued presence in his life.

And yet, the text says, the father divided it to them. He didn’t argue. He didn’t negotiate. He allowed the son the dignity of his own disastrous choice.

The son takes his wealth and goes into a "far country." Notice the distance. He isn’t just moving to the next town; he is going where the reputation of his father cannot reach him. He wants to be anonymous. And there, he squanders his property in "reckless living." The Greek word here is *asōtōs*—literally, "wasteful" or "riotous" living. It signals a life poured down the drain, chasing hollow pleasures that leave the soul barren. He spends it all. He pours his life into a sieve, hoping satisfaction will pool at the bottom, but it never does.

Then comes the famine. It is often the way of the world. The party music stops, the friends drift away, and the pantry is bare. So, the boy attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For a Jewish listener, this is the rock bottom. Pigs were unclean animals. A son of Abraham, feeding the pigs, longing to eat their food. He is now lower than the livestock he tends.

But it is in the pigsty that the spell breaks. Verse 17 says, "He came to himself." This is a brilliant phrase. He didn’t just remember where he came from; he came to his right mind. He realized that the famine in his belly was nothing compared to the famine in his heart. He rehearses a speech: "I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'"

Notice his theology. He still believes in the transaction. He believes he has blown his capital as a son, so he hopes to negotiate a position as a servant. He thinks he can come back, but only on the margins. He hopes for a paycheck, not a relationship. He thinks he must perform his way back into the family.

**Part II: The Father’s Scandalous Welcome**

What happens next subverts every expectation of the ancient world, and it subverts our understanding of God.

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."

In 1st Century Palestine, patriarchs did not run. To run was to expose one's legs, which was considered undignified, even shameful. Furthermore, to embrace the son would mean touching someone who was covered in the filth of the pigs, someone who had brought shame upon the family name. But the Father does not care about dignity. He sees the silhouette of his boy against the horizon, and he is undone. He hikes up his robes, ignoring the gasps of the villagers, and runs.

Just as Jesus tells us that there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10), there is joy here that disrupts the grave dignity of the estate. Before the son can even finish his rehearsed speech—the speech about being a hired servant—the Father interrupts. He doesn't let the boy finish. He issues rapid-fire commands to the servants: "Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate."

The best robe is likely the Father’s own robe. The ring signifies authority. The shoes signify freedom, for slaves went barefoot. And the fattened calf? That was reserved for the biggest celebrations. This is not a quiet "welcome home"; this is a festival.

This is the scandal of grace. The son was looking for justice (to be punished) or at best, transactional mercy (to be made a servant). Instead, he receives explosive, reckless, unconditional love. The Father restores him not just to the family, but to the status of a son. The Father covers his shame with a robe and his poverty with a ring. This welcome is costly. It costs the father his reputation, and it costs the fatted calf—his livelihood.

Why? Because the Father does not want servants. He has plenty of servants. He wants sons. He wants daughters.

**Part III: The Elder Son and the Resentment of the Righteous**

Now, the story shifts. You would think the story ends here with a happy reunion. But Jesus isn’t done. He has one more character to introduce, and this one is perhaps the most difficult for us to deal with because he represents the dutiful, the religious, the "good" people.

"His older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, 'Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.' But he was angry and refused to go in."

The older brother represents those who have always stayed in the field, who have done everything right. He is angry. He feels cheated. He sees himself as the victim of his father’s generosity.

Notice where he stands: outside. He refuses to enter. He creates his own exile. He is physically near the house, but spiritually in a far country of his own making.

The Father, again, takes the initiative. He goes out to him. Just as he ran to the younger son, he now goes out to the older son. He pleads with him to come in. But the older son’s response is biting: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command. Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear the pathology in his voice? He calls his father "you," not "Father." He claims he has "slaved" for him. He views his relationship with the father not as a son, but as a hired hand who feels underpaid. He reduces his life to a ledger of moral credits and debits. He sees his brother’s return as a loss for himself. "This son of yours," he says, distancing himself from the family, "who devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"

The older brother is angry because grace threatens his hierarchy. If the younger son gets a party, then the older brother’s years of faithful service feel cheapened. He believes that acceptance is something to be earned, and he has earned it. The problem is, he doesn't love his father; he uses his father. He doesn't love his brother; he resents him. He wants the father's goods, but not the father's heart.

And the Father’s response to the older son is heartbreakingly tender: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."

The Father reminds the older son of what he has lost sight of: You already have the inheritance. You have access to everything. You are home. You have never lacked for my presence. The tragedy of the elder brother is that he works for a reward he already possesses.

**Application: Which Son Are We Today?**

So, what do we do with this story? What does it mean for us this morning?

First, to the "younger sons" and daughters in this room. Perhaps you identify with the boy in the pigsty. Maybe you are here today and you feel the weight of your own "far country." Maybe you have chased freedom in career, in addiction, in relationships, or in rebellion, and you have found only famine. You feel the mud on your skin, and you are convinced that the door to this church—and the door to God’s heart—is locked to you. You think you need to clean up your act before you can come home. You think you need to rehearse a speech about how you will do better.

Please hear me: The Father is already running. He is not waiting for you to get clean. He is not waiting for you to explain yourself. He sees you "a long way off." He knows the mess you are in, and He is coming to get you. You do not need to negotiate a position as a servant. You are a child. Come home. The robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The table is set.

If this is you, I want to invite you to take one concrete step this week. Stop trying to negotiate. Simply drop the act. Maybe that looks like making a phone call to confess to someone you’ve hurt, or falling to your knees in prayer and saying, "Father, I'm home." You don't need to fix your life to be accepted; you just need to be found.

Second, we must speak to the "older brothers." This is perhaps the more dangerous category because it often hides behind a mask of piety. Are you here today, checking your spiritual resume? Do you look around at the messy people in this congregation—the ones who are struggling, the ones who keep falling off the wagon—and feel a sense of superiority? Do you resent God’s grace given to those who haven't "earned" it?

The tragedy of the older brother is that he was physically in the house, but spiritually in the far country. He was close to the Father, but he didn't know the Father's heart. He served God out of duty, not delight. He thought God owed him a paycheck for his good behavior. If this is you, hear the whisper of the Spirit: "You are always with me." You don't have to earn the Father's love. You already have it.

For the older brother, the application is a call to celebration. This week, I challenge you to practice "unearned" grace. Is there someone in your life—a difficult neighbor, a contrary coworker, or a family member who has disappointed you—whom you view with a ledger of debts? Try to offer them a gift of kindness that they did nothing to deserve. A meal, a kind word, a moment of patience. As you do, you might find that you are stepping into the party you refused to enter.

**Conclusion**

Friends, this parable is often called the story of the Prodigal Son, but it is really the story of the Extravagant Father.

Every single one of us is represented in this text. We are all the younger son, born with a heart that wanders, seeking satisfaction in things that cannot sustain us. And we are all the older son, born with a heart that wants to control God, demanding that life operate according to our sense of fairness.

And into this chaotic mix of rebellion and resentment steps Jesus.

You see, Jesus is telling this story to a group of sinners and Pharisees. But He isn’t just telling them a story; He is living it. He is the true Son who leaves the Father’s side, not to squander an inheritance, but to seek the lost. He enters the far country of our brokenness. He descends into the mud and the mire. He takes upon Himself the shame and the poverty that we earned.

He is the one who says to the Father, "I will pay the debt." And on the Cross, He experiences the famine of being cut off from the Father so that we never have to.

And now, He stands with the Father, arms open wide, inviting us to the feast.

The question this morning is not about your past. It is not about how far you have run or how hard you have worked. The question is: Will you come in?

There is a party going on. The music is playing. The fatted calf is roasting. The table is broad enough for the reckless wanderer and the rule-keeper alike. The Father is at the door, not to scold, but to embrace.

If you are here today and you have been far from God, or perhaps close to God but far from His joy, we want to help you take that step. There are pastors and prayer partners at the back who would love to pray with you, to listen to your story, and to help you find your way home.

Let us pray.

*Father, we confess that we are often like the younger son, seeking our own way, squandering your gifts, and ending up in the pigsties of our own making. Forgive us our wanderings.*

*Lord, we also confess that we are like the older son, holding onto our resentment, believing that our service makes us worthy, and despising your grace for others. Forgive us our pride.*

*Thank You that You are the Good Father who runs to us. Thank You that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Help us this day to lay down our burdens, to drop our defenses, and to come home. May we know the joy of Your presence, not as slaves, but as sons and daughters, in the name of Your Son, Jesus. Amen.*

The older brother represents the religious establishment, the "good" people who have always stayed in the field, who have done everything right. He is angry. He feels cheated. He sees himself as the victim of his father’s generosity.

I want us to pause here and feel the weight of the older brother’s fatigue. We often judge him for his pride, but let’s be honest: he is tired. He is the one who stayed. He is the one who kept the farm running while his brother was out partying. He is the one who paid the bills, who tended the flocks, who held the family together. But the older son’s response is biting: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command. Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear the pathology in his voice? He calls his father "you," not "Father." He claims he has "slaved" for him. He views his relationship with the father not as a son, but as a hired hand who feels underpaid. He reduces his life to a ledger of moral credits and debits. Maybe you have chased freedom in career, in addiction, in relationships, or in rebellion, and you have found only famine. You feel the mud on your skin, and you are convinced that the door to this church—and the door to God’s heart—is locked to you. You think you need to clean up your act before you can come home. You think you need to rehearse a speech about how you will do better.

Please hear me: The Father is already running. He is not waiting for you to get clean. He is not waiting for you to explain yourself. He sees you "a long way off." He knows the mess you are in, and He is coming to get you. You do not need to negotiate a position as a servant. You are a child. Come home. The robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The table is set.

Second, we must speak to the "older brothers." This is perhaps the more dangerous category because it often hides behind a mask of piety. Are you here today, checking your spiritual resume? Do you look around at the messy people in this congregation—the ones who are struggling, the ones who keep falling off the wagon—and feel a sense of superiority? Do you resent God’s grace given to those who haven't "earned" it?

And we are all the older son, born with a heart that wants to control God, demanding that life operate according to our sense of fairness. We have all played the part of the runaway, and we have all played the part of the judge.

And into this chaotic mix of rebellion and resentment steps Jesus.

The younger son left the father and shamed the family, but Jesus, the True Son, leaves the glory of the Father to enter the far country of our brokenness. He doesn't leave to squander an inheritance; He leaves to seek what was lost.

He descends into the mud and the mire of this world. He takes upon Himself the shame and the poverty that we earned. He allows himself to be covered in the filth of our sin so that we might be covered in the robe of His righteousness.

While we were in the pigsty, looking at the pods and longing for life, He was the one standing in our place. He is the one who says to the Father, "I will pay the debt." And on the Cross, He experiences the ultimate famine. He is cut off from the Father so that we never have to be. He becomes the sacrifice—the Fattened Calf—slain so that the party could start.

The story ends with the Father pleading with the older brother. "Come in." The invitation is there. The door is open. The question is, will you stand outside in the dark resenting the grace given to others, or will you come inside and join the feast?

The question this morning is not about your past. It is not about how far you have run or how hard you have worked. The question is: Will you come in?

There is a party going on. The music is playing. The fatted calf has been slain. The table is broad enough for the reckless wanderer and the rule-keeper alike. The Father is at the door, not to scold, but to embrace.

Let us pray.

Thank You that Jesus is the True Son who went into the far country to bring us home. Help us this day to lay down our burdens, to drop our defenses, and to come home. May we know the joy of Your presence, not as slaves, but as sons and daughters, in the name of Your Son, Jesus. Amen.*

He is the Father who runs toward the mess. He is the one who initiates the rescue.

**The Elder Brother and the Resentment of the Righteous**

But the story doesn't end at the party. While the music is playing inside the house, a shadow falls across the doorway.

"His older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, 'Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.' But he was angry and refused to go in."

The older brother represents the religious establishment, the "good" people who have always stayed in the field, who have done everything right. He is angry. He feels cheated. He sees himself as the victim of his father’s generosity.

And honestly, if we stop and listen, we might feel a pang of sympathy for him. We can understand his frustration. He is the one who stayed. He is the one who slaved in the heat of the sun. He is the one who kept the rules. And suddenly, his brother—who took the money and ran—gets the parade? It feels unfair. It feels like his faithfulness has been devalued.

The Father, again, takes the initiative. He goes out to him. Just as he ran to the younger son, he now goes out to the older son. He pleads with him to come in. But the older son’s response is biting: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command. Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear the pathology in his voice? He calls his father "you," distancing himself emotionally. He claims he has "slaved" for him. He views his relationship with the father not as a son, but as a hired hand who feels underpaid. He reduces his life to a ledger of moral credits and debits. He sees his brother’s return as a loss for himself. "This son of yours," he says, disowning his sibling, "who devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"

Here is the tragedy: The older brother is doing the very thing he resents the younger son for. The younger son left home to find freedom in a far country; the older son is in the far country of his own heart, standing right in the driveway. The younger son treated the father like a bank; the older son treats him like a boss. Both sons want the father’s stuff, but neither wants the father’s heart.

The older brother is angry because grace threatens his hierarchy. If the younger son gets a party for nothing, then the older brother’s years of faithful service feel cheapened. He believes that acceptance is something to be earned, and he has earned it.

And the Father’s response to the older son is heartbreakingly tender: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."

The Father reminds the older son of what he has lost sight of: You already have the inheritance. You have access to everything. You are home. You have never lacked for my presence. The party isn't a reward for the younger brother's bad behavior; it's a celebration of life itself. And the older brother, by refusing to enter, is choosing the misery of the field over the joy of the feast.

**The True Son Who Brings Us Home**

So, what do we do with this story? What does it mean for us this morning?

We must see that this parable is actually about *two* sons who are both lost, though in different ways. One lost his life by squandering the inheritance; the other lost his joy by hoarding his resentment. Both are trying to manipulate the father to get what they want—one through rebellion, one through rule-keeping.

And into this chaotic mix of rebellion and resentment steps Jesus.

You see, Jesus is telling this story to a group of sinners and Pharisees, but He isn't just telling them a story; He is living it. He is the True Son who did not treat the Father as a bank to be robbed or a boss to be appeased. He is the Son who loves the Father.

The younger son left home to find freedom, but found slavery. Jesus, the Eternal Son, left the glory of the Father’s side to enter the far country of our brokenness. He didn't go there to squander an inheritance; He went to seek us. He descended into the mud and the mire of this world. He took upon Himself the shame and the poverty that we earned with our sin. He allowed himself to be treated like the prodigal so that we could be treated like the older brother—given the robe, the ring, and the feast.

On the Cross, Jesus experienced the famine of being cut off from the Father so that we never have to. He drank the cup of wrath so that the cup of celebration could be passed to us.

**Application: Will You Come In?**

This brings us to the threshold. This morning, the sermon is not just a story to be analyzed; it is an invitation to be received.

First, to the "younger sons" and daughters in this room. Perhaps you identify with the boy in the pigsty. Maybe you are here today and you feel the weight of your own "far country." Maybe you have chased freedom in career, in addiction, in relationships, or in rebellion, and you have found only famine. You feel the mud on your skin, and you are convinced that the door to this church—and the door to God’s heart—is locked to you. You think you need to clean up your act before you can come home. You think you need to rehearse a speech about how you will do better.

Please hear me: The Father is already running. He is not waiting for you to get clean. He is not waiting for you to explain yourself. He sees you "a long way off." He knows the mess you are in, and He is coming to get you. You do not need to negotiate a position as a servant. You are a child. Come home. The robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The table is set.

Second, we must speak to the "older brothers." This is perhaps the more dangerous category because it often hides behind a mask of piety. Are you here today, checking your spiritual resume? Do you look around at the messy people in this congregation—the ones who are struggling, the ones who keep falling off the wagon—and feel a sense of superiority? Do you resent God’s grace given to those who haven't "earned" it?

Perhaps you feel like the faithful church volunteer who has served for decades, never getting the credit you feel you deserve, while the new person with the messy past gets the applause. It is easy to slip into the mindset of a hired hand, serving God out of duty rather than delight, believing that God owes you something for your goodness.

If this is you, hear the whisper of the Spirit: "You are always with me." You don't have to earn the Father's love. You already have it. Stop slaving and start celebrating. The joy of the Gospel is not that we are good enough to get in; the joy is that the Father invites us to the party, not because we earned it, but because He loves to give it. He doesn't love you because you are faithful; He loves you because He is your Father.

**Conclusion**

Friends, the question this morning is not about your past. It is not about how far you have run or how hard you have worked. The question is: Will you come in?

There is a party going on. The music is playing. The fatted calf is roasting. The table is broad enough for the reckless wanderer and the rule-keeper alike. The Father is at the door, not to scold, but to embrace.

But the story ends with a question mark hanging in the air. We don't know if the older brother ever went in. He is left standing in the darkness of his own resentment, with the light of the party spilling out onto the lawn, listening to the sound of joy that he refuses to join.

Don't let that be you. Whether your hands are dirty with the pigsty or your hands are calloused from the field, the invitation is the same. Drop your defenses. Lay down your resume. Stop rehearsing your speech.

The True Son, Jesus Christ, has paid the price. The Feast is ready. Come, and taste and see that the Lord is good.

Let us pray.

*Father, we confess that we are often like the younger son, seeking our own way, squandering your gifts, and ending up in the pigsties of our own making. Forgive us our wanderings.*

*Lord, we also confess that we are like the older son, holding onto our resentment, believing that our service makes us worthy, and despising your grace for others. Forgive us our pride.*

*Thank You that You are the Good Father who runs to us. Thank You that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Help us this day to lay down our burdens, to drop our defenses, and to come home. May we know the joy of Your presence, not as slaves, but as sons and daughters, in the name of Your Son, Jesus. Amen.*

**Title:** The Runaway’s Return and the Elder’s Resentment: Finding Home in the Father’s Heart

**Scripture:** Luke 15:11-32

Let me begin with a picture that I suspect might resonate with many of us. Imagine a young man, eighteen years old, standing at the end of a driveway. The trunk of his car is packed with clothes, books, and a few sentimental keepsakes. He has the money he saved from a summer job, a full tank of gas, and a map that leads to a city where no one knows his name. As he slams the car door, the sound echoes like a period at the end of a sentence. He isn’t just leaving for college or a job; he is leaving because he feels suffocated. He believes that to truly become himself, he must get away from the rules, the expectations, and the history of his family. He is chasing a vision of freedom that he defines as the absence of accountability.

We all know this story. We have either lived it, or we have watched it play out in the lives of those we love. It is the story of the Great Escape. But what we often fail to see is that the driveway he is leaving, and the destination he is running toward, are both illusions. He thinks he is running toward freedom, but he is actually running toward a famine of the soul.

This is the raw material of the parable we call the Prodigal Son. But before we dive into the story itself, we have to understand why Jesus told it. This parable is the third and climactic story in a trilogy of lost things told by Jesus in Luke chapter 15—a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son.

Jesus is speaking to a very specific audience. On one side, you have the tax collectors and sinners—the "messy" people, the ones who have walked away from the driveway of God’s law. On the other side, you have the Pharisees and the scribes—the religious insiders, the ones who stayed home. The text tells us in verse 2 that the Pharisees were grumbling, saying, "This man receives sinners and eats with them." They were offended by the scandal of Jesus’ grace.

So, Jesus tells this story to answer their grumbling. He is painting a picture of the heart of God, and in doing so, he offends the religious while comforting the rebel. It is a story that has been painted by the masters, preached in cathedrals, and whispered in hospital rooms. But today, I want us to look not just at the boy who left, but at the Father who stayed, and the brother who stayed away.

**Part I: The Younger Son and the Illusion of Autonomy**

Jesus begins by setting the stage: "There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, 'Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.'"

We need to pause here to feel the weight of this request. In the ancient Near East, asking for your inheritance while your father is still alive was not merely a request for an early cash advance; it was a cultural equivalent of saying, "I wish you were dead." The father, in this culture, held the rights to the land and the authority over the household. To ask for the portion was to strip the father of his dignity and his standing in the village. It was a public rejection of the father’s continued presence in his life.

And yet, the text says, the father divided it to them. He didn’t argue. He didn’t negotiate. He allowed the son the dignity of his own disastrous choice.

The son takes his wealth and goes into a "far country." Notice the distance. He isn’t just moving to the next town; he is going where the reputation of his father cannot reach him. He wants to be anonymous. And there, he squanders his property in "reckless living." The Greek word here is *asōtōs*—literally, "without saving." He spends it all. He pours his life into a sieve, hoping satisfaction will pool at the bottom, but it never does.

Then comes the famine. It is often the way of the world. The party music stops, the friends drift away, and the pantry is bare. So, the boy attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For a Jewish listener, this is the rock bottom. Pigs were unclean animals. A son of Abraham, feeding the pigs, longing to eat their food. He is now lower than the livestock he tends.

But it is in the pigsty that the spell breaks. Verse 17 says, "He came to himself." This is a brilliant phrase. He didn’t just remember where he came from; he came to his right mind. He realized that the famine in his belly was nothing compared to the famine in his heart. He rehearses a speech: "I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'"

Notice his theology. He still believes in the transaction. He believes he has blown his capital as a son, so he hopes to negotiate a position as a servant. He thinks he can come back, but only on the margins. He hopes for a paycheck, not a relationship.

**Part II: The Father’s Scandalous Welcome**

What happens next subverts every expectation of the ancient world, and it subverts our understanding of God.

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."

In 1st Century Palestine, patriarchs did not run. To run was to expose one's legs, which was considered undignified, even shameful. A man of the father’s age would move slowly and deliberately to maintain his honor. To run through the village would be the talk of the town for weeks. Furthermore, to embrace the son would mean touching someone who was covered in the filth of the pigs, someone who had brought shame upon the family name.

But the Father does not care about dignity. He sees the silhouette of his boy against the horizon, and he is undone. He hikes up his robes, ignoring the gasps of the villagers, and runs. He is willing to sacrifice his reputation, his dignity, and his standing in the community, just to meet his son halfway. This is how desperate God is for your return. He is willing to look foolish so that he can be Father to you.

Before the son can even finish his rehearsed speech—the speech about being a hired servant—the Father interrupts. He doesn't let the boy finish. He issues rapid-fire commands to the servants: "Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate."

The best robe is likely the Father’s own robe. The ring signifies authority. The shoes signify freedom, for slaves went barefoot. And the fattened calf? That was reserved for the biggest celebrations. This is not a quiet "welcome home"; this is a festival.

This is the scandal of grace. The son was looking for justice (to be punished) or at best, transactional mercy (to be made a servant). Instead, he receives explosive, reckless, unconditional love. The Father restores him not just to the family, but to the status of a son. The Father covers his shame with a robe and his poverty with a ring.

Why? Because the Father does not want servants. He has plenty of servants. He wants sons. He wants daughters.

**Part III: The Elder Son and the Resentment of the Righteous**

Now, the story shifts. You would think the story ends here with a happy reunion. But Jesus isn’t done. He has one more character to introduce, and this one is perhaps the most difficult for us to deal with because he represents the "good" people.

"His older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, 'Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.' But he was angry and refused to go in."

The older brother represents the Pharisees, the religious establishment, the people who have always stayed in the field, who have done everything right. He is angry. He feels cheated. He sees himself as the victim of his father’s generosity.

Notice where he stands: outside. He refuses to enter. He creates his own exile.

The Father, again, takes the initiative. He goes out to him. Just as he ran to the younger son, he now goes out to the older son. He pleads with him to come in. But the older son’s response is biting: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command. Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear the pathology in his voice? He calls his father "you," not "Father." He claims he has "slaved" for him. The older brother’s tragedy is that he confused obedience with ownership. His sin is not rebellion; it is **self-righteous legalism**. He views his relationship with the father not as a son, but as a hired hand who feels underpaid. He reduces his life to a ledger of moral credits and debits. He sees his brother’s return as a loss for himself. "This son of yours," he says, distancing himself from the family, "who devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"

The older brother is angry because grace threatens his hierarchy. If the younger son gets a party, then the older brother’s years of faithful service feel cheapened. He believes that acceptance is something to be earned, and he has earned it. The problem is, he doesn't love his father; he uses his father. He doesn't love his brother; he resents him.

And the Father’s response to the older son is heartbreakingly tender: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."

The Father reminds the older son of what he has lost sight of: You already have the inheritance. You have access to everything. You are home. You have never lacked for my presence.

**The True and Better Son**

As we consider these two sons—the reckless rebel and the rule-keeping resenter—we might feel stuck. We see the rebellion in our own hearts, but we also see the pride. We know we are not worthy to be sons, but we also hate the idea that someone else might get what we don't deserve.

If the story ended here, it would be a tragedy. The younger son is home, but the older brother is outside, and the family is fractured. But Jesus is telling this story to reveal something about Himself.

You see, Jesus is the answer to the dilemma. He is the True Son of the Father. He is the one who never left the Father's side, never demanded the inheritance, and never disobeyed a command. Yet, He enters the far country. He leaves the glory of heaven to enter the mud and the mire of this broken world. He takes upon Himself the shame and the poverty that *we* earned—the shame of the younger son and the isolation of the older brother.

On the Cross, Jesus experiences the ultimate famine of being cut off from the Father so that we never have to. He pays the debt. He buys the robe. He secures the ring.

Jesus is telling the Pharisees, and He is telling us: "I am the one who will go out to the lost so that the Father can run to them. I am the one who will bear the shame so that the celebration can begin."

**Application: Which Son Are We Today?**

So, what do we do with this story? What does it mean for us this morning?

First, to the "younger sons" and daughters in this room. Perhaps you identify with the boy in the pigsty. Maybe you are here today and you feel the weight of your own "far country." Maybe you have chased freedom in career, in addiction, in relationships, or in rebellion, and you have found only famine. You feel the mud on your skin, and you are convinced that the door to this church—and the door to God’s heart—is locked to you. You think you need to clean up your act before you can come home. You think you need to rehearse a speech about how you will do better.

Please hear me: The Father is already running. He is not waiting for you to get clean. He is not waiting for you to explain yourself. He sees you "a long way off." He knows the mess you are in, and He is coming to get you. You do not need to negotiate a position as a servant. You are a child. Come home. The robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The table is set.

Second, we must speak to the "older brothers." This is perhaps the more dangerous category because it often hides behind a mask of piety. Are you here today, checking your spiritual resume? Do you look around at the messy people in this congregation—the ones who are struggling, the ones who keep falling off the wagon—and feel a sense of superiority? Do you resent God’s grace given to those who haven't "earned" it?

If this is you, the first step toward celebration is a difficult one: confession. You must confess that your obedience has often been driven by pride, not love. You must admit that you, too, are utterly dependent on grace, just like your brother. The tragedy of the older brother is that he was physically in the house, but spiritually in the far country. He was close to the Father, but he didn't know the Father's heart. He served God out of duty, not delight. He thought God owed him a paycheck for his good behavior.

If this is you, hear the whisper of the Spirit: "You are always with me." You don't have to earn the Father's love. You already have it. Stop slaving and start celebrating. The joy of the Gospel is not that we are good enough to get in; the joy is that the Father invites us to the party, not because we earned it, but because He loves to give it.

**Conclusion**

Friends, this parable is often called the story of the Prodigal Son, but it is really the story of the Extravagant Father.

Every single one of us is represented in this text. We are all the younger son, born with a heart that wanders, seeking satisfaction in things that cannot sustain us. And we are all the older son, born with a heart that wants to control God, demanding that life operate according to our sense of fairness.

And into this chaotic mix of rebellion and resentment steps Jesus.

He is the one who says to the Father, "I will pay the debt." And on the Cross, He experiences the famine of being cut off from the Father so that we never have to.

And now, He stands with the Father, arms open wide, inviting us to the feast.

The question this morning is not about your past. It is not about how far you have run or how hard you have worked. The question is: Will you come in?

There is a party going on. The music is playing. The fatted calf is roasting. The table is broad enough for the reckless wanderer and the rule-keeper alike.

The Father is not standing at the door with a ledger, demanding an account. He is standing there with the best robe draped over his arm, waiting to interrupt your confession of failure with a declaration of love. He is waiting for you to step out of the mud, or step out of your resentment, and into His embrace.

Let us pray.

*Father, we confess that we are often like the younger son, seeking our own way, squandering your gifts, and ending up in the pigsties of our own making. Forgive us our wanderings.*

*Lord, we also confess that we are like the older son, holding onto our resentment, believing that our service makes us worthy, and despising your grace for others. Forgive us our pride.*

*Thank You that You are the Good Father who runs to us. Thank You that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Help us this day to lay down our burdens, to drop our defenses, and to come home. May we know the joy of Your presence, not as slaves, but as sons and daughters, in the name of Your Son, Jesus. Amen.*

Do you hear the pathology in his voice? He calls his father "you," not "Father." He claims he has "slaved" for him. He views his relationship with the father not as a son, but as a hired hand who feels underpaid. He reduces his life to a ledger of moral credits and debits. He sees his brother’s return as a loss for himself. "This son of yours," he says, distancing himself from the family, "who devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"

The older brother is angry because grace threatens his hierarchy. If the younger son gets a party, then the older brother’s years of faithful service feel cheapened. He believes that acceptance is something to be earned, and he has earned it. The problem is, he doesn't love his father; he uses his father. He doesn't love his brother; he resents him.

And the Father’s response to the older son is heartbreakingly tender: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."

The Father reminds the older son of what he has lost sight of: You already have the inheritance. You have access to everything. You are home. You have never lacked for my presence. The tragedy of the older brother is that he was physically in the house, but spiritually in the far country. He was close to the Father, but he didn't know the Father's heart. He served God out of duty, not delight.

**The Father’s Invitation**

So, what do we do with this story? What does it mean for us this morning?

If you are the "younger son" or daughter in this room, perhaps you identify with the boy in the pigsty. Maybe you are here today and you feel the weight of your own "far country." Maybe you have chased freedom in career, in addiction, in relationships, or in rebellion, and you have found only famine. You feel the stench of your own wreckage, and you are convinced that the door to this church—and the door to God’s heart—is locked to you. You think you need to clean up your act before you can come home. You think you need to rehearse a speech about how you will do better.

Please hear me: The Father is already running. He is not waiting for you to get clean. He is not waiting for you to explain yourself. He sees you "a long way off." He knows the mess you are in, and He is coming to get you. You do not need to negotiate a position as a servant. You are a child. Come home. The robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The table is set.

Coming home this week might look like sending that text you’ve been avoiding to make amends. It might mean walking through these doors even when you feel like a hypocrite. It might mean confessing to your spouse or a trusted friend. The Father meets you in specific acts of return.

But we must also speak to the "older brothers." This is perhaps the more dangerous category because it often hides behind a mask of piety. We are the older brother when we resent the newcomer, the messy, the forgiven. We are the older brother when we look around at the messy people in this congregation—the ones who are struggling, the ones who keep falling off the wagon—and feel a sense of superiority. We are the older brother when we resent God’s grace given to those who haven't "earned" it.

If this is you, hear the whisper of the Spirit: "You are always with me." You don't have to earn the Father's love. You already have it. Stop slaving and start celebrating. The joy of the Gospel is not that we are good enough to get in; the joy is that the Father invites us to the party, not because we earned it, but because He loves to give it. The cure for your resentment is not to try harder, but to join the party. Dance with the younger brother. Share the fattened calf. Discover that the Father's joy is your joy.

**Conclusion**

Friends, this parable is often called the story of the Prodigal Son, but it is really the story of the Extravagant Father.

Every single one of us is represented in this text. We are all the younger son, born with a heart that wanders, seeking satisfaction in things that cannot sustain us. And we are all the older son, born with a heart that wants to control God, demanding that life operate according to our sense of fairness.

And into this chaotic mix of rebellion and resentment steps Jesus.

You see, Jesus is telling this story to a group of sinners and Pharisees. But He isn't just telling them a story; He is living it. He is the true Son who leaves the Father’s side, not to squander an inheritance, but to seek the lost. He enters the far country of our brokenness. He descends into the mud and the mire. He takes upon Himself the shame and the poverty that we earned.

He is the one who says to the Father, "I will pay the debt." And on the Cross, He experiences the famine of being cut off from the Father so that we never have to.

And now, He stands with the Father, arms open wide, inviting us to the feast.

Remember that young man at the end of the driveway? The one who slammed the car door and drove away into the night? The Father is running down that driveway right now. He has the robe in His arms. He has the ring in His pocket. He is not asking for an explanation. He is not demanding an apology. He is just running.

The question this morning is not about your past. It is not about how far you have run or how hard you have worked. The question is: Will you come in?

There is a party going on. The music is playing. The fatted calf is roasting. The table is broad enough for the reckless wanderer and the rule-keeper alike. The Father is at the door, not to scold, but to embrace.

Let us pray.

*Father, we confess that we are often like the younger son, seeking our own way, squandering your gifts, and ending up in the wreckage of our own making. Forgive us our wanderings.*

*Lord, we also confess that we are often like the older son. We admit that we know the voice of resentment, the feeling that we deserve more because we have worked harder. Forgive us our pride, and forgive us for thinking that Your love is something to be earned rather than a gift to be received.*

*Thank You that You are the Good Father who runs to us. Thank You that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Help us this day to lay down our burdens, to drop our defenses, and to come home. May we know the joy of Your presence, not as slaves, but as sons and daughters, in the name of Your Son, Jesus. Amen.*

**Title:** The Open Door and the Closed Heart: Finding Home in the Father’s Embrace

**Scripture:** Luke 15:11-32

Let me begin with a picture that might feel familiar. Imagine a young man, eighteen years old, standing at the end of a driveway. The trunk of his car is packed with clothes, books, and a few sentimental keepsakes. He has the money he saved from a summer job, a full tank of gas, and a map that leads to a city where no one knows his name. As he slams the car door, the sound echoes like a period at the end of a sentence. He isn’t just leaving for college or a job; he is leaving because he feels suffocated. He believes that to truly become himself, he must get away from the rules, the expectations, and the history of his family.

But we need to look closer at this scene. In the ancient world where our parable is set, this departure is not just a quest for independence; it is an act of violence. When the boy in our text asks for his inheritance, he is essentially saying to his father, "I wish you were dead." He wants the capital, but he does not want the relationship. He is trading his father’s presence for a payout.

We all know this story, or we know its echo. We have either lived it, or we have watched it play out in the lives of those we love. It is the story of the Great Escape. But what we often fail to see is that the driveway he is leaving, and the destination he is running toward, are both illusions. He thinks he is running toward freedom, but he is actually running toward a famine of the soul.

This parable is the third and climactic story in a trilogy told by Jesus in Luke chapter 15. First, He tells of a lost sheep—a piece of property that wanders away by accident. Next, a lost coin—something inanimate that is lost through carelessness. But now, the temperature rises. Jesus tells of a lost son—a human being with a moral will, who chooses to walk away. With each story, the stakes get higher, and the cost of recovery gets greater, forcing us to ask: What kind of God goes after the lost?

**Part I: The Younger Son and the Economics of Grace**

Jesus begins: "There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, 'Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.'" The father agrees. But we must pay close attention to the text here. It says, "he divided his property between *them*."

In that moment, the younger son got his share, but so did the older brother. The estate was split. The liquidity of the family was reduced. This is a crucial detail that we often miss, but it explains the anger that bubbles up later. The younger son takes his liquid assets and goes into a "far country." He isn’t just moving to the next town; he is going where the reputation of his father cannot reach him. He wants to be anonymous. And there, he squanders his property in "reckless living." The Greek word here is *asōtōs*—literally, "without saving." He spends it all. He pours his life into a sieve, hoping satisfaction will pool at the bottom, but it never does.

Then comes the famine. It is often the way of the world. The party music stops, the friends drift away, and the pantry is bare. So, the boy attaches himself to a citizen of that country, who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For a Jewish listener, this is the rock bottom. Pigs were unclean animals. A son of Abraham, feeding pigs, longing to eat their food. He is now lower than the livestock he tends.

But it is in the pigsty that the spell breaks. Verse 17 says, "He came to himself." This is a brilliant phrase. He didn’t just remember where he came from; he came to his right mind. He realized that the famine in his belly was nothing compared to the famine in his heart. He rehearses a speech: "I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.'"

Notice the phrase "against heaven." In Jewish idiom, "heaven" was a reverential way of saying "God." The son has had a theological awakening. He realizes his sin isn't just against his dad; it is against the Creator of the universe. He realizes he has sinned against the very source of his existence.

He continues his rehearsal: "I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants." Notice his theology. He still believes in the transaction. He believes he has blown his capital as a son, so he hopes to negotiate a position as a servant. He thinks he can come back, but only on the margins. He hopes for a paycheck, not a relationship.

**Part II: The Father’s Scandalous Welcome**

What happens next subverts every expectation of the ancient world, and it subverts our understanding of God.

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."

In 1st Century Palestine, patriarchs did not run. To run was to expose one's legs, which was considered undignified, even shameful. Furthermore, to embrace the son would mean touching someone who was covered in the filth of the pigs, someone who had brought shame upon the family name. But the Father does not care about dignity. He sees the silhouette of his boy against the horizon, and he is undone. He hikes up his robes, ignoring the gasps of the villagers, and runs.

Before the son can even finish his rehearsed speech—the speech about being a hired servant—the Father interrupts. He doesn't let the boy finish. He issues rapid-fire commands to the servants: "Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate."

The best robe is likely the Father’s own robe. The ring signifies authority. The shoes signify freedom, for slaves went barefoot. And the fattened calf? That was reserved for the biggest celebrations. This is not a quiet "welcome home"; this is a festival.

This is the scandal of grace. The son was looking for justice (to be punished) or at best, transactional mercy (to be made a servant). Instead, he receives explosive, reckless, unconditional love. The Father restores him not just to the family, but to the status of a son. The Father covers his shame with a robe and his poverty with a ring.

Why? Because the Father does not want servants. He has plenty of servants. He wants sons. He wants daughters.

**Part III: The Elder Son and the Resentment of the Righteous**

Now, the story shifts. You would think the story ends here with a happy reunion. But Jesus isn’t done. He has one more character to introduce, and this one is perhaps the most difficult for us to deal with because he represents the "good" people.

"His older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, 'Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.' But he was angry and refused to go in."

The older brother represents the religious establishment, the rule-keepers, the ones who have always stayed in the field. He is angry. He feels cheated. He sees himself as the victim of his father’s generosity.

Notice where he stands: outside. He refuses to enter. He creates his own exile.

The Father, again, takes the initiative. He goes out to him. Just as he ran to the younger son, he now goes out to the older son. He pleads with him to come in. But the older son’s response is biting: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command. Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear the pathology in his voice? He calls his father "you," not "Father." He claims he has "slaved" for him. He views his relationship with the father not as a son, but as a hired hand who feels underpaid.

But we must understand the depth of this resentment. Remember verse 12? The father divided the property between *them*. The older brother already received his share of the inheritance. Now, the father is killing the fattened calf—which came from the older brother’s portion of the estate—to celebrate the brother who squandered his half. The older brother is doing the math. He is watching his net worth diminish to pay for his brother’s party.

He reduces his life to a ledger of moral credits and debits. He sees his brother’s return as a loss for himself. "This son of yours," he says, distancing himself from the family, "who devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"

We see this spirit today. This is the church treasurer who has served faithfully for thirty years but can't rejoice when the former drug addict gets baptized, thinking, "He hasn't paid his dues." It is the parent who keeps a meticulous record of every slight and every sacrifice, harboring a cold bitterness against the child who messed up, while the "good" child feels invisible. The older brother is angry because grace threatens his hierarchy. If the younger son gets a party, then the older brother’s years of faithful service feel cheapened. He believes that acceptance is something to be earned, and he has earned it. The problem is, he doesn't love his father; he uses his father. He doesn't love his brother; he resents him.

And the Father’s response to the older son is heartbreakingly tender: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."

The Father reminds the older son of what he has lost sight of: You already have the inheritance. You have access to everything. You are home. You have never lacked for my presence. The tragedy of the older brother is that he was physically in the house, but spiritually in the far country. He was close to the Father, but he didn't know the Father's heart.

**Application: The Portrait of the Human Heart**

So, what do we do with this story? What does it mean for us this morning?

We often approach this parable asking, "Which son am I?" We might look at the younger son and say, "I’ve messed up." Or we look at the older son and say, "I’ve tried hard." But the truth is, the human heart is complex enough to be both.

Perhaps you identify with the boy in the pigsty. Maybe you are here today and you feel the weight of your own "far country." We often think the far country is a geographic location, but it is usually a state of mind. It is the far country of career ambition that has cost you your family. It is the far country of addiction, where you swore you could stop anytime. It is the far country of pornography, hiding behind a screen in the dark. It is the far country of bitterness, where you have nurtured a grudge until it has consumed you. You feel the mud on your skin, and you are convinced that the door to this church—and the door to God’s heart—is locked to you. You think you need to clean up your act before you can come home. You think you need to rehearse a speech about how you will do better.

Please hear me: The Father is already running. He is not waiting for you to get clean. He is not waiting for you to explain yourself. He sees you "a long way off." He knows the mess you are in, and He is coming to get you. You do not need to negotiate a position as a servant. You are a child. Come home. The robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The table is set.

But perhaps today you identify more with the older brother. This is the more dangerous category because it often hides behind a mask of piety. Are you here today, checking your spiritual resume? Do you look around at the messy people in this congregation—the ones who are struggling, the ones who keep falling off the wagon—and feel a sense of superiority? Do you resent God’s grace given to those who haven't "earned" it?

The tragedy of the older brother is that he was physically in the house, but spiritually in the far country. He was close to the Father, but he didn't know the Father's heart. He served God out of duty, not delight. He thought God owed him a paycheck for his good behavior. If this is you, hear the whisper of the Spirit: "You are always with me." You don't have to earn the Father's love. You already have it. Stop slaving and start celebrating. The joy of the Gospel is not that we are good enough to get in; the joy is that the Father invites us to the party, not because we earned it, but because He loves to give it.

Most of us fluctuate between these two identities. We are the younger son when we are caught in the grip of a sin we can't shake. We are the older brother when we look down on the politician we despise or the neighbor who offends us. We want grace for ourselves, but we want justice for them.

**Conclusion: The Unfinished Story**

Friends, this parable is often called the story of the Prodigal Son, but it is really the story of the Extravagant Father.

Every single one of us is represented in this text. We are all the younger son, born with a heart that wanders, seeking satisfaction in things that cannot sustain us. And we are all the older son, born with a heart that wants to control God, demanding that life operate according to our sense of fairness.

And into this chaotic mix of rebellion and resentment steps Jesus.

You see, Jesus is telling this story to a group of sinners and Pharisees. But He isn't just telling them a story; He is living it. He is the true Son who leaves the Father’s side, not to squander an inheritance, but to seek the lost. He enters the far country of our brokenness. He descends into the mud and the mire. He takes upon Himself the shame and the poverty that we earned.

He is the one who goes to the Cross—the ultimate pigsty—to pay the debt we could not pay. He experiences the famine of being cut off from the Father so that we never have to.

And now, He stands with the Father, arms open wide, inviting us to the feast.

But notice how the parable ends. It doesn't end with a neat moral. It ends with a cliffhanger. The father is outside, pleading with the older son to come in. The text does not tell us if the older brother relents. It does not tell us if he drops his resentment and joins the party.

Jesus ends the story there, leaving the door open, leaving the question hanging in the air. Why? Because He is speaking to the Pharisees, and He is speaking to us. He is asking us: What will you do?

The question this morning is not about your past. It is not about how far you have run or how hard you have worked. The question is: Will you come in?

There is a party going on. The music is playing. The fatted calf is roasting. The table is broad enough for the reckless wanderer and the rule-keeper alike. The Father is at the door, not to scold, but to embrace.

To the younger sons: The bath is ready. You are loved.
To the older brothers: The ledger is burned. You are loved.

Don't stay out in the dark. Come in.

Let us pray.

*Father, we confess that we are often like the younger son, seeking our own way, squandering your gifts, and ending up in the pigsties of our own making. Forgive us our wanderings.*

*Lord, we also confess that we are like the older son, holding onto our resentment, believing that our service makes us worthy, and despising your grace for others. Forgive us our pride.*

*Thank You that You are the Good Father who runs to us. Thank You that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Help us this day to lay down our burdens, to drop our defenses, and to come home. May we know the joy of Your presence, not as slaves, but as sons and daughters, in the name of Your Son, Jesus. Amen.*
