Opening hook

A few years ago I met a man who told me about his prodigal son in a way that stuck with me. The son grew up in a church-going family, learned the language of faith, and then wandered into a distant country of his own making. He burned through money, friendships, and his own sense of self-respect—until a famine came, and he found himself feeding hogs in a field too low to imagine mercy. Then a line from his childhood life surfaced: the memory of a door that had always stood open. Not a door to judgment, but a door to belonging. So he began rehearsing a plan: “I will rise and go to my father,” he told himself, “and I will say to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.” He returned not as a son, but as a servant. And the father—no longer the stern figure of discipline, but a living emblem of grace—saw him while he was still a long way off, ran to him, and welcomed him home with a robe, a ring, sandals, and a feast.

That father’s welcome is the heartbeat of today’s parable. Not because it makes light of sin, but because it declares the true nature of our God: a Father who takes the initiative to seek the lost, who will stop at nothing to bring a wayward child back into the circle of grace, and who invites all who will come to a feast of mercy. The prodigal son’s journey is our invitation to see how God’s hospitality breaks down every barrier that shame and pride attempt to erect between us and home.

An engaging reading of the text

Luke 15:11-32 is the third in a trio of parables about what is lost and found. The parable of the sheep who is found, the coin that is recovered, and finally, the son who returns. In this sequence, Jesus is addressing both the tax collectors and sinners who are drawn to him and the Pharisees and scribes who grumble that “this man receives sinners and eats with them.” The rhythms here are not merely anecdotal; they are theological. God’s heart is not content with what is merely clean or orderly. God is the One who seeks what is lost, who celebrates the return of the prodigal, and who unsettles the self-righteous by including the marginalized as heirs of grace.

The younger son asks for his inheritance as if the father were already dead—an audacious, even shocking request in first-century life. To speak of dividing the property while the father is alive is to declare the father’s life as a thing to be exploited rather than a belonging to be cherished. Yet the father does not insist on being spared disruption or control. He grants the request and allows the son to depart with his portion of the wealth. The departure is a moral and spiritual exile: from community, from identity, from the father’s house.

In the distant country, the younger son wastes his wealth on “riotous living” (the language of some translations). A famine strikes, and he ends up feeding pigs, longing to eat what the pigs eat. This is not merely poverty; it is humiliation—the social shame of a son who has forfeited his status and dignity. His turning point is not a dramatic conversion in a church service but an abrupt awakening to reality: he must acknowledge his sin, not merely his consequences. And so he rehearses a speech—an admission of sin before heaven and before his father, and a conditional offer to become one of the hired servants.

Meanwhile, the father keeps watch. He does not post a notice that calls the son back; he runs to him. In that culture, a father does not run. Heer would have been a public sign of shame. But in Luke’s story, the father’s action breaks every expectation. He embraces the son, kisses him, and gives him the signs of restoration—a robe to cover his filth, a ring to seal his authority, sandals to mark his rightful standing, and a feast to celebrate his return. The old agreement about the son’s place in the house is overturned by grace. The text notes that “this son of yours” was once lost and is found. The party that follows is not a private reconciliation; it is a public festival of reconciliation, a reversal of the earlier separation.

The elder brother enters the scene with a different cry. He has remained at home, but his heart has wandered into a kind of moral self-sufficiency. When told of the feast, he protests that he has served faithfully for years and never received so much as a goat for a celebration. His complaint is not about fairness but about the character of love: if grace is given to the prodigal, why not to him? The father’s response to the elder brother is instructive rather than punitive: “We had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive; he was lost and is found.” The elder brother’s posture, in being angry and outside the house, reveals a different sort of lostness—the hollowness of earning one’s place rather than receiving one’s place as a gift.

Exegesis: paying attention to the world of the story

To read this parable well, we must notice the social and familial grammar. The son’s demand for the inheritance is effectively a declaration that the father’s life is a resource to be spent and not a relationship to be cherished. The father's decision to grant the request is not a sign of weakness but a dramatic act of permissive love. He does not coerce trust; he creates space for a wrong choice to occur—and then he remains present, ready to welcome the lost back. The younger son does not negotiate his way into mercy; he admits his failure and returns, saying, “I have sinned.” It is crucial to hear that confession as the path to restoration, not as a plan to secure a “better deal” or to earn forgiveness.

The elder brother’s portion of the story is equally important. He stands with the father at the door of the feast yet remains apart from the life of the house. His complaint—“All these years I have served you, and you never gave me a young goat”—is a mirror held up to those who measure love by what is earned rather than what is freely given. The father’s insistence that “everything I have is yours” demonstrates that grace cannot be quantified by counting favors. The feast is not an amnesty for the prodigal’s misdeeds alone; it is a declaration that home, in the deepest sense, is a place of mercy that makes room for both the return and the reconciled heart.

In Luke’s gospel, the broader arc is clear: God’s kingdom is a place where the lost are found, where the morally humble are welcomed, and where the physicians of righteousness discover their own need for mercy. The parable does not erase or gloss over sin; it exposes sin’s consequences and then counters them with lavish mercy. This is not cheap grace. It is costly grace, because it costs the father something profound—the social cost of scandal and the risk of a broken heart in the face of a wayward child—and yet grace triumphs.

Theological anchors for the sermon

- Grace is the primary motif. The prodigal’s return is not earned by his confession or plan but is received because the father chooses to receive him. grace precedes effort; mercy precedes merit.

- The initiative of God. God’s love seeks the lost; God’s mercy comes to meet us where we are. The gospel is not a call to climb a ladder to heaven; it is the invitation to come home.

- The inclusive heart of the Father. The feast for the prodigal is not a private party but a public act of communal reconciliation. The church must be a place where repentant sinners are welcomed and where those who have remained at the gate begin to understand the breadth of grace.

- The danger of self-righteousness. The elder brother’s story warns us that fidelity without mercy can become a form of pride that distorts the very posture of belonging to God.

- Repentance as restoration, not merely remorse. The younger son’s confession includes a plan for a new life as a hired servant; but the father’s response—restoration to sonship—speaks of a deeper reality: to be received as a child of the Father is to be reconstituted into the family of grace.

Application: what this means for us today

- Are we the prodigal, or are we the elder brother? Most of us inhabit a mix. We may wander in some area of life—time, resources, relationships, or attention—yet we still want to belong only on our own terms. Others among us may be faithful in outward things but harbor a cold, structural resentment toward those who repent and return.

- If you feel far away, hear the Father’s voice. The text does not say the father waited patiently for the son to come to his senses and then judged him when he did not. It says the father scanned the road, ran to greet him, embraced him, and re-clothed him in grace. That is not a metaphor for emotional sentiment; it is a living picture of divine initiative. When you stumble and return, you are not met with a shrug or a lecture; you are met with mercy that reshapes your identity.

- If you feel at home but suspicious of grace, hear the father’s invitation to the elder child inside you. Are you counting the favors you deserve or enjoying the abundance of being in the Father’s house? The feast is an invitation to abandon the posture of awayness, to participate truly in the life of the community, and to rejoice when mercy is extended to others.

- The church’s mission of hospitality. The parable asks us to consider the church as a place of boundary-crossing grace. Do we practice hospitality to those who come dragging far more than baggage than we want to carry? Do we celebrate when a sinner returns, or do we whisper concerns about the “times” and “most appropriate places” for repentance? The Father’s insistence on celebration challenges us to become a people who throw open doors to welcome the lost and broken.

- Mercy that transforms daily life. The prodigal’s return alters a family’s rhythm in an observable way—celebration, restored identity, forgiven debt. When grace takes root in us, it should transform our behavior: generosity, warmth, and a refusal to reduce people to their worst moments. Grace is not a social program; it is a life-altering relationship with the God who loves us first.

- A personal invitation to daily repentance. The parable invites us into a rhythm of returning home. We often wander—through fear, pride, or distraction—and we must continually return to the Father’s house where mercy is abundant. The practice of confession, repentance, and renewed trust is not merely inward piety; it is a social act of restoration—families, churches, neighborhoods, and the world being drawn into the joy of being truly known and loved.

A clear, compelling conclusion

If you take away one thing from this parable, let it be this: home is not a place you reach by earning it; home is a person you come to meet—your Father who runs to meet you, who welcomes you back, who clothes you in dignity, and who invites you to feast at his table. The father’s welcome in Luke 15 reveals the heart of God: generous, uncalculating, and unending. The prodigal’s return is not a one-time event; it is the daily rhythm of life in the Father’s house, where even the wayward son and the self-righteously faithful are invited to the same meal and to the same life.

Let us hear this as good news that reshapes our days. If you have known shame because you wandered, know this: the Father is not shamed by your return; he celebrates. If you have stood at the door, feeling you have never deserved a place at the feast, hear him call you back in mercy: you are loved, you are seen, you are restored as child, not servant. And for those who struggle with extending grace to others—perhaps to a prodigal in your own family, or a neighbor whose life looks different from what you expected—let the Father’s hospitality melt the ice of judgment. Remember that the feast is not for the already righteous alone but for the dead and found, the lost and the found, the far and the near.

May the Spirit of Christ deepen our sense of hospitality. May we feel, with the Father, the ache of the wandering and the joy of homecoming, so that, in all our days, we live as a people who celebrate mercy and extend mercy in turn. And may we, by grace, become known as a church where every return is a welcome, every confession met with embrace, and every life restored to the Father’s table.

Prayer

Lord our God, you see our hearts better than we see them ourselves. You know the places we have gone to forget your face and the ways we pretend we can stand on our own. Thank you for sending your Son to seek and to save the lost, and for the Father who runs toward the returning child with open arms. Help us to hear your invitation into the feast, to lay down our judgments, and to celebrate every story of mercy. Teach us to forgive as you forgive, to welcome as you welcome, and to live in the joyful abundance of your grace. Through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

zJADJB_hzs1Tx21VPGawx.text:
Some years ago a pastor told the story of a young woman who moved to a new city for her first job. She was bright and capable, but lonely. In the first weeks, she tried to build a life: a gym membership, a few new friends, a rhythm of work and weekends. One Friday night she found herself at a bar with coworkers. It was fun—at first. The laughter was easy, the drinks kept coming, the ache of being unknown eased for a while. The next morning, the ease was gone, replaced by a dull heaviness. She began to repeat the cycle: another night out, another attempt to buy belonging, another morning with regret. Months later, after a particularly painful weekend, she sat on her apartment floor and whispered through tears, “I don’t know how I got here.” Then she said something even more honest: “I want to go home.”

That longing—*to go home*—is one of the most human desires we have. Not merely a zip code, but a place where you are safe, known, and received. Luke 15 is a chapter about lost things and found joy, and the parable we call “The Prodigal Son” is really a story about home: leaving it, forgetting it, resenting it, and being invited back into it. It’s a story Jesus tells not to entertain but to reveal the heart of God and the true condition of ours.

### Setting the Scene: Why Jesus Tells This Story

We need the context. Luke 15 begins with an accusation: “Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke 15:1–2). Jesus is not merely teaching; He is *welcoming*. He is eating with people religious leaders considered unclean, morally compromised, socially beneath them. And the grumbling reveals the deeper issue: the Pharisees and scribes did not just object to the sinners’ behavior; they objected to Jesus’ *posture*. “This man receives sinners.”

So Jesus tells three parables: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and then—climaxing the sequence—a lost son. Each story escalates: one out of a hundred, one out of ten, and then one out of two. And in each story, heaven’s joy is not restrained, polite satisfaction, but celebration. God is not stingy with mercy. He is not reluctant to forgive. He delights to bring the lost home.

### The Younger Son: Rebellion and the Far Country

Jesus begins: “There was a man who had two sons” (v. 11). Immediately, we are meant to see ourselves somewhere in this family. The younger son says something stunning: “Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me” (v. 12). In that culture, asking for the inheritance early was not a neutral financial request. It was a relational rupture. It was, in effect, saying: *I want your stuff, not you. I want your gifts, not your presence. I wish you were dead so I could live the life I want.*

And shockingly, the father divides the property between them. The father allows the son the dignity—and the danger—of choice. God’s love does not control us like puppets. He does not force closeness. He lets the son walk away.

The text says, “Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country” (v. 13). That phrase—*far country*—is more than geography. It is spiritual distance. It is what happens when we treat God as irrelevant, when we decide we can define life on our own terms. The son squanders his property in “reckless living.” The word suggests wasteful, dissolute, scattered existence. He doesn’t simply spend money; he spends himself.

Then, as often happens in Scripture and in life, circumstances tighten: “And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need” (v. 14). Notice: the famine reveals what was always true. The son was building his life on a foundation that could not hold. When the money ran out, the friends likely did too. The far country is attractive until it is not.

He hires himself out, and Jesus chooses an image designed to sting Jewish listeners: the son feeds pigs (v. 15). Pigs were unclean. The son has not only fallen economically; he has fallen socially, spiritually, ceremonially. And it gets worse: “He was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything” (v. 16). The far country makes promises: freedom, pleasure, control. But it often ends with hunger—hunger for love, for meaning, for peace—and the realization that what we’ve chased cannot feed us.

Here is one of the most important lines in the parable: “But when he came to himself…” (v. 17). Repentance often begins with sanity. Sin is not merely breaking rules; it is losing ourselves—forgetting who we are and whose we are. Coming to himself, he remembers his father’s house: “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!” (v. 17). He forms a plan: “I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you’” (v. 18). Notice the order: against heaven—against God—and before you—against the father. Sin is always vertical and horizontal. It is never private. It always reaches Godward and neighborward.

He continues: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants” (v. 19). There is humility here, but also a misunderstanding. He assumes the best he can hope for is a contract. He thinks he can return on the basis of a lesser identity: not son, but servant. He believes he must manage the shame by negotiating.

Many of us approach God this way. We imagine that if we have failed badly enough, the best we can do is come back as spiritual day laborers: “I’ll keep my head down, I’ll work hard, I’ll never ask for much.” We think the Father might tolerate us, but surely not delight in us.

So he “arose and came to his father” (v. 20). Repentance is not just regret; it is return. It is movement toward God.

### The Father: Compassion That Runs

Now comes the heartbeat of the parable: “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (v. 20).

The father *saw* him. That implies watching. Waiting. Hoping. The father is not inside with crossed arms, refusing to look down the road. He is scanning the horizon. And when he sees him, he feels compassion—gut-level mercy. Then he runs. In that culture, dignified patriarchs did not run; it was considered shameful. To run, he would hike up his robe, expose his legs, risk public mockery. But the father is willing to bear shame in order to reach his son.

This is the Gospel in miniature. The Father’s love is not theoretical. It moves. It crosses distance. It absorbs humiliation. And ultimately, in the full story of Scripture, it is not only the father who runs—it is God who comes all the way to us in Jesus Christ, bearing our shame at the cross to bring us home.

The son begins his rehearsed confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son…” (v. 21). But notice: he doesn’t even get to finish the speech. He never gets to say, “Treat me as a hired servant.” The father interrupts with joy-soaked authority: “Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet” (v. 22).

Each item matters. The best robe is honor, restoration, covering. The ring is likely a signet ring—authority, belonging, family identity. Shoes mean he is not a barefoot servant; he is a son. Then the father says, “Bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate” (v. 23). This is not a quiet reinstatement; it is a public feast. The father is not trying to save face; he is throwing a party.

Why? “For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (v. 24). The father does not describe the son as “a disappointment” or “a cautionary tale.” He uses resurrection language. Lostness is a kind of death. Coming home is a kind of life from the dead. And then the simplest line: “And they began to celebrate.”

This is what God is like. He is holy, yes. Sin is serious, yes. But when the sinner repents, God is not calculating what you owe. He is rejoicing that you are home.

### The Older Son: The Far Country at Home

At this point, Jesus could end the story. Many of us would. The moral would be clear: no matter how far you’ve gone, you can come home. But Jesus goes on, because He’s speaking to the grumblers too. There is another kind of lostness—less obvious, more respectable, and just as deadly.

The older son comes in from the field, hears music and dancing, and asks what’s happening. When he learns his brother has returned and the fattened calf has been killed, he becomes angry and refuses to go in (v. 28). The father, again, takes initiative: “His father came out and entreated him” (v. 28). The father goes out to the rebellious younger son *and* the resentful older son. He is a father to both.

The older son’s speech reveals his heart: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command” (v. 29). Listen to the language: *served*, *command*. Not loved, not enjoyed, not shared life with. He relates to the father like an employee. He continues: “Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (v. 29). Do you hear the distance? *My friends*, not *our family*. He does not see the father as his joy; he sees him as a boss who hasn’t paid properly.

Then the contempt: “But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!” (v. 30). He can’t even say, “my brother.” He says, “this son of yours.” Resentment fractures family.

The older brother represents the Pharisees and scribes, and he also represents a temptation for any religious person: the belief that obedience earns us leverage over God. That if we are good, God owes us a life we want. And when grace is given to someone we consider undeserving, we feel cheated.

But the father answers tenderly: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31). The older brother’s tragedy is that he has been near the father without enjoying him. The feast was always available, because the father was always there. Yet his heart was in a far country of self-righteousness.

The father continues: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (v. 32). Notice the father gently corrects him: *this your brother*. Grace re-names people. It restores relationship. And the father insists: celebration is not optional; it is *fitting*. When the lost are found, joy is the only appropriate response.

And then Jesus ends the parable without telling us whether the older brother goes in. That is deliberate. It leaves the Pharisees—and us—with a question: Will you join the Father’s joy, or will you stand outside, clutching your record, missing the feast?

### Applications: Coming Home, and Welcoming Home

1) **If you are in the far country, you can come home.**  
Some of you may feel you’ve wandered too far—morally, relationally, spiritually. Perhaps your far country is obvious: addiction, secrecy, betrayal. Perhaps it is quieter: years of prayerlessness, a slow drift into cynicism, a life built around success while God remains a footnote. Hear the word of the Lord: the Father is not waiting to humiliate you. He is watching for you. The turning point in the story is not the son cleaning himself up—it is the son *getting up and going*. You do not have to fix yourself to come home. You come home to be healed.

Repentance may include confession, restitution, hard conversations, and wise boundaries. But at its heart, repentance is returning to the Father, trusting His character. The Gospel does not say, “Earn your way back.” It says, “You are received because of grace.” In Christ, the Father runs to meet you.

2) **If you are the older brother, you can come inside.**  
It is possible to be externally obedient and internally far. To be dutiful but joyless. To do “church things” while resenting grace given to others. To compare, to keep score, to feel superior—yet strangely empty. The older brother is lost not because he is immoral, but because he is self-centered. He loves his own righteousness more than he loves his father.

If this is you, the invitation is not to try harder. The invitation is to be with the Father—really with Him—to receive His love not as wages but as gift. And to let His joy become your joy when others are restored.

3) **If you are the church, you are called to mirror the Father.**  
Luke 15 began with “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” That’s the accusation. Let it become our reputation. The church is meant to be the kind of community where repentant people are not merely allowed to attend, but *welcomed home*. That does not mean we minimize sin. The father does not call the far country good. But he does call the returning son beloved.

So what does it look like for us to be a “homecoming people”? It looks like patient, prayerful waiting for those who wander. It looks like running—taking initiative in reconciliation when possible. It looks like robes and rings—tangible restoration, not perpetual suspicion. It looks like celebration: honest testimony, visible joy, practical support. And it looks like resisting the older-brother posture that says, “They don’t deserve this.”

### A Clear Invitation and Conclusion

The parable of the Prodigal Son is not finally about two brothers; it’s about one Father. And through Jesus, we are being shown the heart of God: a Father who bears the cost of love, who absorbs the insult of rejection, who runs toward sinners, who restores identity, and who invites the resentful into joy.

Where are you in the story today?

Maybe you are weary, hungry, and far from home. The path back begins with simple honesty: “Father, I have sinned.” You may feel unworthy—and you are, in the sense that none of us can demand grace. But you are not unwelcome. In Christ, the Father has made a way for you to come home.

Maybe you are the older brother, standing outside the celebration, arms crossed, heart tight. Hear the Father’s entreaty: “Son… you are always with me.” Stop living as a servant trying to earn what has already been offered. Come into the feast. Let grace be grace.

And for all of us: will we join the Father’s celebration? When the lost return, will we clap with heaven—or grumble with the Pharisees?

The final image of the parable is an open door, music playing, a father pleading, and a feast prepared. The Gospel places that door before every one of us. Home is not a place you deserve; it’s a place you’re invited to.

So arise. Come to the Father. And when you see others coming down the road—weak, limping, ashamed—be the kind of people who make room at the table. Because this is what is fitting: “We had to celebrate and be glad, for this brother of yours was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.” Amen.

Months later, after a particularly painful weekend, she sat on her apartment floor and whispered through tears, “I don’t know how I got here.” Then she said something even more honest: “I want to go home.”

That longing—to go home—is one of the most human desires we have. Not merely a zip code, but a place where you are safe, known, and received.

Luke 15 is a chapter about lost things and found joy. And the parable we call “The Prodigal Son” is really a story about home: leaving it, resenting it, forgetting it, and being invited back into it. Jesus tells it not to entertain but to reveal the heart of God—and, if we let Him, to tell us the truth about our own.

## Why Jesus Tells This Story

Luke sets the scene with an accusation: “Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke 15:1–2).

Notice what offended them. Not simply that sinners existed. Not even merely that Jesus taught them. But that “this man receives sinners.” He welcomes them. He eats with them. He treats them as guests, not as a problem to manage from a distance.

So Jesus tells three parables—lost sheep, lost coin, and then the longest and most personal: lost son. The stories escalate: one out of a hundred, one out of ten, then one out of two. And in each one, the recovery is followed by celebration. Heaven’s response to repentance is not begrudging tolerance but joy.

This parable is Jesus’ answer to the grumbling. It’s also His invitation to anyone listening—whether you feel far from God, or uncomfortably close to Him but strangely cold inside.

## The Younger Son: The Far Country

Jesus begins simply: “There was a man who had two sons” (v. 11). That means from the first sentence, the story is wide enough for all of us. There are at least two ways to be lost.

The younger son makes a request that would have landed like a slap: “Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me” (v. 12). In that culture, asking for your inheritance early wasn’t a savvy financial move. It was a relational rupture. It was effectively saying, “I want your things, not you. I want your gifts, not your presence.”

And then comes a detail that is easy to miss: “And he divided his property between them” (v. 12). Between them. The older son receives his share too. He watches his brother cash out and walk away. No protest. No pleading. No “Dad, this will break your heart.” The older brother’s coldness doesn’t begin later at the party; it’s there in the opening scene. The family fractures, and the “good son” quietly accepts the benefits of the father while remaining distant from the father’s heart.

“Not many days later,” the younger son gathers everything and goes “into a far country” (v. 13). That phrase is more than mileage; it’s spiritual distance. The far country is any place—external or internal—where we try to build life without the Father.

He squanders his property in reckless living, and then the inevitable tightening comes: “When he had spent everything, a severe famine arose… and he began to be in need” (v. 14). The famine doesn’t create the emptiness; it exposes it. When the money goes, the illusion goes too.

He hires himself out, and Jesus chooses an image that would make His Jewish hearers wince: the son ends up feeding pigs (v. 15). Unclean animals. Unclean work. Unclean life. He is so hungry that he longs for the pods the pigs eat, “and no one gave him anything” (v. 16). Sin always advertises freedom. But it often ends in hunger and isolation.

Then we come to the turning point: “But when he came to himself…” (v. 17). Repentance often begins with sanity—waking up, seeing clearly again. Sin is not merely breaking rules; it is losing ourselves.

But we should also be honest about what the text shows us: his first clear thought is about bread. “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!” (v. 17). Is this pure repentance, or is it partly pragmatic? Mixed motives, maybe. Need, certainly. And here is good news for people whose hearts feel complicated: the Father in this story does not wait for perfect motives before He moves in mercy. The son’s repentance may begin in hunger, but the Father’s grace begins in compassion.

The son rehearses his speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (vv. 18–19). He plans to add, “Treat me as one of your hired servants.” In other words: “Let me come back on a contract. Let me manage my shame by bargaining.”

Many of us have tried to come home that way. We don’t say it out loud, but we think it: “God, I’ll make this up to You. I’ll stay small. I’ll prove myself. I’ll work off the debt.” We imagine the best we can hope for is tolerated servant-status.

So he gets up and goes. Repentance is not just regret; it is return. It is movement toward the Father.

## The Father: Compassion That Runs

Now we reach the heartbeat of the parable: “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (v. 20).

The father saw him—meaning he was looking. Waiting. Hoping. And when he sees him, he feels compassion. Not disgust. Not suspicion. Compassion.

And then: he ran. In that world, dignified patriarchs did not run. Running meant hiking up your robe, exposing your legs, risking public shame. But this father is willing to look foolish in the village in order to get to his son before anyone else can. He runs to cover his child with embrace before the community can cover him with contempt.

This is the Gospel in miniature. God’s love does not coerce us—but it does pursue us. It moves. It crosses distance. It absorbs shame. And in the larger story of Scripture, God does not only run down a road in a parable; He comes all the way to us in Jesus Christ, bearing our shame at the cross to bring us home.

The son begins the confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son…” (v. 21). And then—this is one of the most astonishing mercies in the Bible—he can’t finish. He never gets to say, “Treat me as a hired servant.” The father interrupts him with action:

“Bring quickly the best robe… put it on him… put a ring on his hand… and shoes on his feet” (v. 22).

The best robe is honor, restoration—covering where there was shame. The ring is belonging and authority; it says, “You are family.” Shoes say, “You’re not coming back barefoot like a servant; you’re coming back as a son.”

Then the father commands a feast: “Bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate” (v. 23). Not a private reinstatement. A public party. Grace refuses to whisper.

Why this celebration? “For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (v. 24).

That is resurrection language. When the father says “dead and alive,” he is using the very grammar of the Gospel itself. This is the pattern God loves: death giving way to life. And for Christians, we cannot hear those words without thinking of the deeper miracle—what God does in Christ.

Scripture says we were dead in our trespasses, but God makes us alive with Christ. In baptism, Paul says, we are buried with Him and raised with Him (Romans 6). So when the father says, “dead and alive again,” he is not exaggerating. He is naming what repentance and grace truly are: a kind of resurrection. The lost aren’t merely improved. They are brought back to life.

“And they began to celebrate” (v. 24).

If the parable ended there, it would already be one of the most beautiful stories ever told.

But Jesus isn’t finished—because there is another kind of lostness in the room. And it’s respectable. It’s religious. It’s sitting in the seats of honor.

## The Older Son: Lost While Staying Home

The older son comes in from the field and hears music and dancing. He asks what happened, and when he learns his brother is home and the fattened calf has been killed, he becomes angry and refuses to go in (vv. 25–28).

Once again, the father takes initiative: “His father came out and entreated him” (v. 28). The father goes out to the younger son in the far country, and he goes out to the older son in the yard. He is a father to both.

And then the older brother speaks—and his words reveal what he’s been carrying for years:

“Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command” (v. 29).

Listen to that vocabulary: served, command. Not “I loved you.” Not “I enjoyed being with you.” He relates to his father like an employee relates to a boss.

And then: “Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (v. 29). Not “with you.” Not “with our family.” My friends. The older brother is physically near and relationally far. He has been living at home in a far country of self-righteousness.

And then he says the line that shows how resentment breaks relationships: “But when this son of yours came…” (v. 30). He can’t even say, “my brother.” He distances himself. He keeps his hands clean by keeping his heart hard.

If you want a contemporary picture of the older brother, it often looks like this:

- The longtime church member who quietly resents the attention given to a newly converted person with a dramatic testimony.
- The parent who has tried to “do everything right” and now feels bitter that life has not turned out the way they expected—“God, I served You. Why didn’t You give me what I earned?”
- The believer who can list their sacrifices but can’t remember the last time they actually delighted in the Father.
- The person who obeys, but only because obedience feels like leverage.

And if we’re honest, the older brother can show up not only in individuals but in whole church cultures—where grace is preached but suspicion is practiced; where returning sinners are watched for failures instead of welcomed with joy.

The father answers with tenderness: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31). In other words: “You never had to earn a feast. You never had to bargain for love. You have been living like a servant in your own house.”

Then the father insists: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (v. 32). He gently corrects him: this your brother. Grace renames people. It restores relationship. And the father says celebration isn’t optional; it is fitting. It matches reality. When the dead live again, joy is the only sane response.

And then Jesus ends the story without telling us whether the older brother goes in.

That’s not a missing detail. That is the point. The parable is unfinished by design. Jesus makes the hearer a kind of co-author. Pharisees and scribes—will you enter the Father’s joy, or will you stay outside, clinging to your record?

And church—what about us?

## Bringing It Home: Where Are You in the Story?

Before we turn this into a lesson about “those people,” Jesus places an open door in front of every heart.

Some of you know the far country well. It may be obvious—addiction, secrecy, betrayal, bitterness, choices you never thought you’d make. Or it may be subtle—years of drifting prayerlessness, a life so crowded with comfort and success that God has been gently pushed to the margins. You’re functioning, but you’re hungry.

And maybe, like that young woman on her apartment floor, the truest thing you can say is: “I want to go home.”

Here is the hope of this parable: you do not have to fix yourself to come home. You come home to be healed.

Yes, coming home may involve confession. It may involve restitution. It may involve telling the truth to people you’ve harmed. It may involve wise boundaries and a long road of rebuilding trust. The parable ends at the feast, but real life often continues into slow, steady restoration.

But hear this clearly: restoration is immediate in identity even when it is ongoing in healing. The Father does not put you on probation before He calls you “my son.” The embrace comes before the resume. The robe comes before the track record.

Others of you have stayed near the Father outwardly, but inwardly you are tired. Maybe you’ve been faithful for years, but joy has drained out of your discipleship. You find yourself keeping score—of your service, your sacrifices, your wounds, your unanswered prayers. You may not say it, but something in you feels like God owes you.

The Father’s invitation to you is not “try harder.” It is “come closer.” Not merely to the rules of the house, but to the heart of the Father. “You are always with me.” The tragedy of the older brother is not that he lacked access; it’s that he didn’t enjoy what he already had.

And then there’s the invitation for us together—as a church.

Luke 15 began with a complaint: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” What if that became our reputation? Not that we are casual about sin, but that we are confident in grace. Not that we excuse the far country, but that we know the way home.

What might it look like to be a “homecoming people”?

It can be as concrete as:

- When someone returns after a long absence—after divorce, relapse, jail, humiliation—we don’t make them “earn their way” back into community by performing shame. We greet them. We listen. We make space. We help them take next steps.
- When a new believer comes in with messy history and imperfect language, we don’t treat them like a threat to the church’s image. We treat them like a miracle.
- When someone confesses sin, we don’t turn it into gossip. We turn it into prayer, accountability, and hope.

In other words: we learn to run—not with enabling, not with naivete, but with compassionate initiative. “Robes and rings” might look like tangible support, a place at the table, a ride to a recovery meeting, a meal train, a mature believer walking with them for months, not days. It might look like celebrating progress instead of demanding instant perfection.

And it also means this: we refuse the older brother’s posture. We refuse to stand outside joy because grace offended our sense of fairness.

## One Door, One Feast, One Father

In the end, this parable is not finally about two sons. It’s about one Father.

A Father who endures the insult of rejection.
A Father who keeps watch down the road.
A Father who runs toward returning sinners.
A Father who restores identity before performance.
A Father who goes out to the resentful as well as the reckless.
A Father who says, “It is fitting to celebrate.”

So where are you today?

If you are in the far country, the path home may be as simple—and as hard—as getting up and going: “Father, I have sinned.” Even if your motives feel mixed, even if all you have is hunger and a shred of hope, come. The Father is more ready than you are.

If you are the older brother, hear the Father’s entreaty: “Son… you are always with me.” Stop living like a servant trying to earn what has already been offered. Come into the feast.

And when you see someone else coming down the road—weak, limping, ashamed—don’t become the committee of suspicion. Be the people who make room at the table.

The final image Jesus leaves us is an open door, music playing, a father pleading, and a feast prepared. The story is unfinished because the response is still being written.

The Father is watching the road. He sees you.

Come home. Amen.

Some years ago a pastor told the story of a young woman who moved to a new city for her first job. She was bright and capable, but lonely. In the first weeks, she tried to build a life: a gym membership, a few new friends, a rhythm of work and weekends. One Friday night she found herself at a bar with coworkers. It was fun—at first. The laughter was easy, the drinks kept coming, the ache of being unknown eased for a while. The next morning, the ease was gone, replaced by a dull heaviness. She began to repeat the cycle: another night out, another attempt to buy belonging, another morning with regret.

Months later, after a particularly painful weekend, she sat on her apartment floor and whispered through tears, “I don’t know how I got here.” Then she said something even more honest: “I want to go home.”

That longing—*to go home*—is one of the most human desires we have. Not merely a zip code, but a place where you are safe, known, and received. Luke 15 is a chapter about lost things and found joy, and the parable we call “The Prodigal Son” is really a story about home: leaving it, forgetting it, resenting it, and being invited back into it.

Jesus tells this story not to entertain but to reveal the heart of God—and to expose the true condition of ours.

## Setting the Scene: Why Jesus Tells This Story

We have to begin with the context. Luke 15 opens with a clash:

“Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke 15:1–2).

Jesus is not merely teaching; He is *welcoming*. He is eating with people the religious leaders considered unclean, morally compromised, socially beneath them. And the complaint isn’t only about the sinners. It’s about Jesus’ posture: “This man receives sinners.”

So Jesus answers with three parables: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and then—climaxing the sequence—a lost son. Each story escalates: one out of a hundred, one out of ten, and then one out of two. And in each story, heaven’s joy is not restrained, polite satisfaction. It’s celebration. God is not stingy with mercy. He is not reluctant to forgive. He delights to bring the lost home.

## The Younger Son: Rebellion and the Far Country

Jesus begins, “There was a man who had two sons” (v. 11). Immediately, we should locate ourselves somewhere in this family.

The younger son makes a request that would have been scandalous: “Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me” (v. 12). In that culture, this wasn’t a neutral financial conversation. To ask for the inheritance early was to treat the father as if he were already dead. It was a relational rupture. It was, in effect, saying: *I want your stuff, not you. I want your gifts, not your presence. I want my life—without you in it.*

And shockingly, the father divides the property between them. He does not force the son’s affection. He allows him the dignity—and the danger—of choice. Love does not manipulate. Love does not chain. The father lets him go.

“Not many days later,” the son gathers all he has and “took a journey into a far country” (v. 13). That phrase—*far country*—is more than geography. It’s spiritual distance. It’s the posture of the heart that says, “God, I can build my life without You.” It’s what happens when we treat God as irrelevant, or burdensome, or simply in the way.

There, the son squanders his property in “reckless living.” He doesn’t merely spend money; he spends himself. He scatters his life. And then—like so many stories in Scripture, and like so many stories in real life—circumstances close in:

“When he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need” (v. 14).

Notice: the famine reveals what was always true. The foundation was never strong. The far country feels like freedom until the bill comes due. When the money runs out, the friends often do too. The promises evaporate. And now the son is hungry in every sense of the word.

Jesus chooses an image meant to sting Jewish listeners: the son is feeding pigs (v. 15). Pigs were unclean. This isn’t only economic collapse; it’s a picture of spiritual degradation. And it gets worse: “He was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything” (v. 16). No one. The far country can be crowded and still utterly lonely.

Then comes one of the most important lines in the entire parable: “But when he came to himself…” (v. 17).

Repentance often begins with sanity. Sin is not merely breaking rules; it is losing ourselves—forgetting who we are and whose we are. The son “comes to himself,” and in that moment he remembers his father’s house: “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!” (v. 17)

He forms a plan: “I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you’” (v. 18). Notice the order: against heaven—against God—and before you—against his father. Sin is never only private. It always reaches Godward and neighborward.

And then: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants” (v. 19). There’s humility here, but there’s also misunderstanding. He assumes the best he can hope for is a contract. He believes home can only be re-entered through a payback plan.

Many of us approach God like that. We imagine that if we’ve failed badly enough, the best we can do is come back as spiritual day laborers: “I’ll keep my head down. I’ll work hard. I’ll never ask for much.” We think God might tolerate us, but surely He won’t delight in us.

But then the son does the one thing he must do: “He arose and came to his father” (v. 20). Repentance is not just regret; it is return. It is movement toward God.

## The Father: Compassion That Runs (and the Christ Who Makes It Possible)

Now we reach the heartbeat of the parable:

“But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (v. 20).

The father *saw* him. That implies watching—waiting—hoping. He is not inside with crossed arms refusing to look down the road. He is scanning the horizon. And when he sees him, he feels compassion—gut-level mercy. Then he runs.

In that culture, dignified patriarchs did not run. To run, a man like this would have to hike up his robe, expose his legs, risk public mockery. It would look undignified. It could even look shameful. But the father is willing to bear shame in order to reach his son.

This is the gospel in miniature. God’s love is not theoretical. It moves. It crosses distance. It absorbs humiliation to bring the lost home.

And we should say it plainly: this isn’t only a description of God’s heart; it is a preview of what God will *do*. Jesus—telling this parable while receiving sinners—does not stand at a safe distance from our mess. He comes into it. The Father’s willingness to bear shame is fully realized in Jesus Christ, who took our shame upon Himself at the cross. The welcome home is not sentimental denial of sin; it is costly mercy, purchased by the Son of God so that repentant sinners are not merely tolerated, but truly restored.

Now the younger son begins his rehearsed confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son…” (v. 21). But he doesn’t even get to finish. He never gets to say, “Treat me as a hired servant.” The father interrupts with joy-soaked authority:

“Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet” (v. 22).

Each item matters. The best robe is honor—covering—restoration. The ring is likely a signet ring: identity, belonging, authority in the family. The shoes mean he is not a barefoot servant; he is a son. And then the father says, “Bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate” (v. 23).

This is not a quiet reinstatement. It is a public feast. The father is not saving face; he is throwing a party.

Why? “For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (v. 24). The father does not describe the son as “a disappointment” or “a cautionary tale.” He uses resurrection language. Lostness is a kind of death. Coming home is a kind of life from the dead. “And they began to celebrate.”

That is what God is like. He is holy—yes. Sin is serious—yes. But when the sinner repents, God is not calculating what you owe. He is rejoicing that you are home.

## The Older Son: The Far Country at Home

Jesus could end the story here. The moral would be clear: no matter how far you’ve gone, you can come home.

But Jesus doesn’t stop, because there are grumblers in the crowd. There is another kind of lostness—less obvious, more respectable, more church-shaped, and just as deadly.

The older son comes in from the field, hears music and dancing, and asks what’s happening. When he learns his brother has returned and the fattened calf has been killed, he becomes angry and refuses to go in (v. 28).

And once again, watch the father’s posture: “His father came out and entreated him” (v. 28). The father goes out to the rebellious younger son *and* to the resentful older son. He is a father to both.

The older son’s speech exposes his heart: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command” (v. 29). Listen to the vocabulary: *served… command.* Not “I have loved you.” Not “I have enjoyed you.” Not “I have been with you.” He relates to the father like an employee.

He continues: “Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (v. 29). *My friends.* Not “our family.” He doesn’t see the father as his joy; he sees him as a boss who hasn’t paid properly.

Then the contempt spills out: “But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!” (v. 30). He can’t even say, “my brother.” He says, “this son of yours.” Resentment fractures family.

The older brother represents the Pharisees and scribes, and he represents a temptation for any religious person: the belief that obedience gives us leverage over God. That if we are “good,” God owes us a certain life. And when grace is given to someone we consider undeserving, we feel cheated.

But the father answers with astonishing tenderness: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31). The older brother’s tragedy is that he has been near the father without enjoying him. The feast was always available, because the father was always there. Yet his heart lived in a far country of self-righteousness.

Then the father insists: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (v. 32). And notice the gentle correction: *this your brother.* Grace re-names people. It restores relationship.

And the parable ends without telling us whether the older brother goes in. That is not a loose end; it is the point. Jesus leaves the Pharisees—and us—standing outside a doorway with music and joy spilling out. The question is not whether the father is gracious. The question is whether we will lay down our pride and enter the celebration.

## A Bridge to Our Lives: Standing at the Threshold

Jesus leaves us at the threshold of the feast. The story is finished, but the invitation is still open. And if we’re honest, most of us can find ourselves in more than one place in this parable depending on the season of life.

So where does this ancient story intersect with you today?

It calls us to at least three responses: coming home, coming inside, and becoming a people who welcome others home.

## Applications: Coming Home, Coming Inside, Welcoming Home

### 1) If you are in the far country, you can come home.

Some of you may feel you’ve wandered too far—morally, relationally, spiritually. Perhaps your far country is obvious: addiction, secrecy, betrayal, choices you never thought you’d make. Or perhaps it is quieter: years of prayerlessness, a slow drift into cynicism, a life built around achievement while God remains a footnote.

Hear the word of the Lord in this parable: the Father is not waiting to humiliate you. He is watching for you.

And notice the sequence: the turning point is not the son cleaning himself up. He still smells like the pigpen. The turning point is that he *gets up and goes*. And while he is still a long way off, the father runs.

So if you are waiting until you feel “worthy,” you will never come. If you are waiting until you’ve made yourself respectable again, you are trusting in respectability, not mercy. The gospel does not say, “Earn your way back.” It says, “Arise. Return. You will be received.”

Now, in real life, repentance will bear fruit. It often includes confession, restitution, hard conversations, and wise boundaries. But hear this clearly: those things are not the price of admission. They are the *fruit* of being restored, not the payment that purchases restoration. The Father’s embrace comes first. The healing work follows.

In Christ, you are not coming to a reluctant God. You are coming to a Father who runs.

### 2) If you are the older brother, you can come inside.

It is possible to be externally obedient and internally far away. To do all the right things and still be hollow. To “serve” God while resenting Him. To show up at church and yet quietly keep score—of your own effort, of other people’s failures, of who gets grace and who doesn’t.

The older brother is lost not because he is immoral, but because he is self-centered. He loves his record more than he loves his father. He wants the father’s things, but not the father himself—just like the younger brother, only in a more respectable form.

And the father comes out to him. The father entreats him. This is pastoral kindness, but it is also a summons: *Come in.*

And let’s not soften the edge of Jesus’ ending. The parable does not allow the older brother to stand outside forever and call it faithfulness. There is a choice to make. If you insist on keeping your pride, you will miss the feast. If you cling to your résumé, you will remain joyless—near God perhaps, but not truly with Him.

The invitation is not “try harder.” The invitation is to stop living like a servant trying to earn what has already been offered, and to live like a child who can finally receive love as gift. Come inside. Join the Father’s joy. Call the sinner “my brother,” because grace has made room for you too.

### 3) If you are the church, you are called to mirror the Father.

Luke 15 began with an accusation: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” May that become our reputation too.

To be clear: mirroring the Father does not mean minimizing sin. The father does not call the far country good. He does not pretend rebellion is maturity. Grace is not denial. But the father does call the returning son beloved. He restores him publicly. He covers him. He celebrates him.

So what does “robes and rings” look like now—among us?

It means we don’t gossip about the returning person’s past as if their worst chapter is their only chapter. It means we refuse the subtle cruelty of “We’re glad you’re back… but we’ll never trust you again.” It means we offer practical help, not just spiritual advice: a meal, a ride, childcare, accountability, a job lead, a sincere invitation to lunch, a place in the life of the community. It means we make room at the table for those who have failed, because Christ made room at the table for us.

And yes, it also means we disciple with wisdom. Sometimes restoration includes boundaries and time and support. The father’s party is not permission to return to the pigpen; it is power to return to sonship. But the posture of the church must never be: “Prove yourself, and then we’ll celebrate.” The posture is: “Welcome home—now let’s walk together into new life.”

Because heaven does not respond to repentance with suspicion. Heaven responds with joy.

## Conclusion: The Open Door and the Choice Before Us

The parable of the Prodigal Son is not finally about two brothers; it’s about one Father. Jesus is showing us the heart of God: a Father who bears the cost of love, who absorbs the insult of rejection, who runs toward sinners, who restores identity, and who invites the resentful into joy.

And through Jesus, this is not merely a story about what God is like. It is a revelation of what God has done. The Father’s welcome is not cheap sentiment; it is purchased grace. The Son of God went into the far country of our sin, carried our shame to the cross, and rose again so that “dead” sons and daughters could come home alive.

So where are you today?

Maybe you are weary, hungry, and far from home. The path back begins with simple honesty: “Father, I have sinned.” You may feel unworthy—and in one sense you are. None of us can demand grace. But you are not unwelcome. The Father is not fooled by your rehearsed speech, and He is not waiting for you to negotiate. He is ready to embrace you.

Maybe you are the older brother, standing outside the celebration, arms crossed, heart tight. Hear the Father’s entreaty: “Son… you are always with me.” Lay down the scoreboard. Stop defining yourself by comparison. Do not miss the feast because you cannot stand grace.

And for all of us: when the lost return, will we clap with heaven—or grumble with the Pharisees? Will we be a homecoming people, or a gatekeeping people?

The final image Jesus leaves us with is an open door, music playing, a father pleading, and a feast prepared. And whether you have run far away or stayed near while your heart grew cold, the gospel places that door before you.

So arise. Come to the Father. And when you see others coming down the road—weak, limping, ashamed—be the kind of people who make room at the table.

Because this is what is fitting: “We had to celebrate and be glad, for this brother of yours was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.” Amen.
