Some years ago a pastor told the story of a young woman who moved to a new city for her first job. She was bright and capable, but lonely. In the first weeks, she tried to build a life: a gym membership, a few new friends, a rhythm of work and weekends. One Friday night she found herself at a bar with coworkers. It was fun—at first. The laughter was easy, the drinks kept coming, the ache of being unknown eased for a while.

The next morning, the ease was gone, replaced by a dull heaviness. She began to repeat the cycle: another night out, another attempt to buy belonging, another morning with regret. Months later, after a particularly painful weekend, she sat on her apartment floor and whispered through tears, “I don’t know how I got here.” Then she said something even more honest: “I want to go home.”

That longing—to go home—is one of the most human desires we have. Not merely a zip code, but a place where you are safe, known, and received. Luke 15 is a chapter about lost things and found joy, and the parable we call “The Prodigal Son” is really a story about home: leaving it, forgetting it, resenting it, and being invited back into it. It’s a story Jesus tells not to entertain, but to reveal the heart of God and the true condition of ours.

And if we listen closely, we’ll discover that there are two “far countries.” One is obvious—the far country of rebellion. The other is harder to see—the far country of self-righteousness. One son is lost in a distant land. The other is lost at home.

## Why Jesus Tells This Story

We need the context. Luke 15 begins with an accusation: “Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke 15:1–2).

Jesus is not merely teaching; He is welcoming. He is sharing a table with people religious leaders considered unclean and morally compromised. And the grumbling reveals the deeper issue. The Pharisees and scribes don’t just object to the sinners’ behavior; they object to Jesus’ posture: “This man receives sinners.”

So Jesus tells three parables: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and then—climaxing the sequence—a lost son. Each story escalates: one out of a hundred, one out of ten, and then one out of two. And in each story, heaven’s joy is not restrained, polite satisfaction, but celebration. God is not stingy with mercy. He is not reluctant to forgive. He delights to bring the lost home.

## The Younger Son: Rebellion in the Far Country

Jesus begins: “There was a man who had two sons” (v. 11). Immediately, we are meant to locate ourselves somewhere in this family.

The younger son says something stunning: “Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me” (v. 12). In that culture, asking for the inheritance early was not a neutral financial request. It was a relational rupture. It was, in effect, saying: *I want your stuff, not you. I want your gifts, not your presence. I’d rather have your things than have you as my father.*

And shockingly, the father divides the property between them. He allows the son the dignity—and the danger—of choice. God’s love is not manipulative. He does not force closeness. He lets the son walk away.

The text says, “Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country” (v. 13). That phrase—*far country*—is more than geography. It is spiritual distance. It is what happens when we treat God as irrelevant, when we decide we can define life on our own terms.

The son squanders his property in “reckless living.” He doesn’t simply spend money; he spends himself—his time, his body, his mind, his dignity. And then, as often happens both in Scripture and in life, the bottom drops out: “And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need” (v. 14).

The famine does not *create* the emptiness; it reveals it. The far country always had hunger underneath the music. And in the mysterious mercy of God, hardship can be a kind of alarm clock. The psalmist says, “Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word… It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes” (Psalm 119:67, 71). Sometimes God uses what we would never choose to help us see what we could not otherwise see.

Jesus chooses an image designed to sting His Jewish listeners: the son ends up feeding pigs (v. 15). Pigs were unclean. The son has not only fallen economically; he has fallen socially, spiritually, ceremonially.

And Jesus presses the humiliation further: “He was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything” (v. 16). The far country makes promises: freedom, pleasure, control. But it often ends with hunger—hunger for love, for meaning, for peace—and the realization that what we’ve chased cannot feed us.

Then comes one of the most important lines in the parable: “But when he came to himself…” (v. 17). Repentance often begins with sanity. Sin is not merely breaking rules; it is losing ourselves—forgetting who we are and whose we are.

He remembers his father’s house: “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!” (v. 17). He forms a plan: “I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you’” (v. 18).

Notice the order: against heaven—and before you. Sin is always vertical and horizontal. It reaches Godward and neighborward. It is never as private as we pretend.

He continues: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants” (v. 19). There is humility here, but there is also a misunderstanding. He assumes the best he can hope for is a contract. He thinks he can manage the shame by negotiating his way into a lower-status return.

Many of us approach God like that. We imagine that if we’ve failed badly enough, the best we can do is come back as spiritual day laborers: “I’ll keep my head down, I’ll work hard, I’ll never ask for much.” We think the Father might tolerate us, but surely not delight in us.

So he “arose and came to his father” (v. 20). Repentance is not just regret; it is return. It is movement toward God—often trembling, often unsure, but moving nonetheless.

And for some of you, that’s the hardest step. Not because you don’t know what you’ve done, but because you fear what you’ll find when you come back: the Father’s anger, the church’s judgment, your own repeated failure. Hear this: you may fear His rejection, but the story tells us He is already looking for you.

## The Father: Compassion That Runs

Now we come to the heartbeat of the parable: “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (v. 20).

The father *saw* him. That implies watching. Waiting. Hoping. The father is not inside with crossed arms refusing to look down the road. He is scanning the horizon.

And when he sees him, he feels compassion—gut-level mercy. This is not sentimental weakness; it is the deep, covenant heart of God. It echoes the great self-revelation of the Lord in Exodus: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Jesus is showing us that God’s mercy is not an abstract doctrine; it is a running Father on a dusty road.

And the father runs. In that culture, dignified patriarchs did not run; it was considered shameful. To run, he would hike up his robe, expose his legs, risk public mockery. But the father is willing to bear shame in order to reach his son.

This is the Gospel in miniature. And it does more than *suggest* kindness; it foreshadows Christ. The Father’s running love points forward to the incarnation—God coming to us while we were still sinners. “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). He did not wait for us to get our act together. He came into our far country. He covered our shame by taking it upon Himself.

The son begins his rehearsed confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son…” (v. 21). And then—perhaps the most surprising detail—he doesn’t even get to finish. He never gets to say, “Treat me as a hired servant.” The father interrupts with joy-soaked authority:

“Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet” (v. 22).

Each item matters.

- **The best robe** is honor and restoration. It is covering where there was shame. It calls to mind Isaiah’s promise: “He has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10). The son doesn’t earn that robe; he receives it.
- **The ring** is belonging and identity—likely a signet ring, a mark of family authority. It’s as if the father is saying, “You’re not on probation; you’re mine.” And it reminds us that in Christ, believers are “sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 1:13–14). God doesn’t merely welcome us emotionally; He marks us as His.
- **The shoes** mean he is not a barefoot servant. He is a son. He is home, not hired.

Then the father says, “Bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate” (v. 23). The fattened calf wasn’t Tuesday dinner. It was reserved for the kind of occasion that changes the household—a wedding, an honored guest, a once-in-a-lifetime joy. And the Bible often describes salvation this way: as a feast, a banquet, a table set by God Himself (Isaiah 25:6–9; see also Jesus’ banquet imagery in Luke 14).

And why such extravagant celebration? “For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (v. 24). The father does not describe the son as “an embarrassment” or “a cautionary tale.” He uses resurrection language. Lostness is a kind of death. Coming home is a kind of life from the dead.

And then the simplest line: “And they began to celebrate.”

Underneath that celebration is a cost. In the story, the father absorbs the loss of the inheritance that was squandered. In the gospel, the Father gives not merely property but His Son. The feast is not cheap. It is made possible because Christ—the true Son—pays what the prodigals could never repay. In a sense, the fattened calf points beyond itself: to the sacrifice that makes joy righteous and welcome possible.

## The Older Son: The Far Country of Self-Righteousness

At this point, Jesus could end the story. Many of us would. The moral would be clear: no matter how far you’ve gone, you can come home.

But Jesus knows not all lostness looks like reckless living. Some lostness wears the mask of duty. Some people never leave the house, yet never love the Father. So He introduces the older brother—the man who is *lost at home*.

The older son comes in from the field, hears music and dancing, and asks what’s happening. When he learns his brother has returned and the fattened calf has been killed, he becomes angry and refuses to go in (v. 28). Make no mistake: this is not a small emotional moment. It is rebellion. The younger son insulted the father by leaving; the older son insults the father by publicly refusing his invitation, rejecting his authority, and opposing his joy.

And once again, the father takes initiative: “His father came out and entreated him” (v. 28). The father goes out to the rebellious younger son and the resentful older son. He is a father to both.

Now, before we criticize the older brother too quickly, we should hear the human ache underneath. Many “older brothers” in congregations have been faithful for years—showing up, serving, praying, giving, enduring. That faithfulness matters. Your service is not worthless. Your perseverance is seen by God.

But faithfulness can curdle into entitlement. Obedience can become a way of controlling God. And that’s where the older brother has drifted.

Listen to his speech: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command” (v. 29). Notice the categories: served, command. Not loved, not delighted in, not walked with. He relates to the father like an employee.

He continues: “Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (v. 29). *My friends*, not *our family.* He doesn’t want the father; he wants the father’s resources for his own party.

Then comes the contempt: “But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!” (v. 30). He can’t even say, “my brother.” He says, “this son of yours.” Resentment fractures family.

This is the Pharisees and scribes in Luke 15. They weren’t merely cautious about sin; they were offended that Jesus would welcome sinners. They wanted a God who rewards the deserving. Jesus reveals a Father who raises the dead and throws parties.

And here’s the warning for us: the older brother is every bit as lost as the younger. The younger says, “I don’t want you, Father.” The older says, “I want what you can give me, but I don’t want to join you in your joy.” One rebels through rule-breaking. The other rebels through rule-keeping. Both are self-centered. Both need grace.

The father answers with tenderness: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31). The older brother’s tragedy is that he has been near the father without enjoying him. The feast was always available—because the father was always there. Yet his heart lived in the far country of self-righteousness.

And the father insists: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (v. 32). Notice the re-naming: *this your brother*. Grace restores relationship. And the father says celebration is not optional; it is fitting. When the lost are found, joy is the only appropriate response.

Jesus ends the parable without telling us whether the older brother goes in. That is not an oversight. It’s an altar call to the grumblers—and to us. Will you join the Father’s joy, or will you stand outside clutching your record and missing the feast?

## From Explanation to Invitation: Where Are You in the Story?

Before we talk about “them,” we have to ask the question Jesus’ parable presses on every heart: **Where are you in the story today?**

Are you in the far country, and you know it?

Are you “at home” outwardly, but far away inwardly?

Or are you learning—slowly, imperfectly—to share the Father’s heart, so that when someone limps home, you don’t cross your arms; you set the table?

## Applications: Coming Home, and Welcoming Home

### 1) If you are in the far country, you can come home.

Some of you may feel you’ve wandered too far—morally, relationally, spiritually. Perhaps your far country is obvious: addiction, secrecy, betrayal. Perhaps it is quieter: years of prayerlessness, a slow drift into cynicism, a life built around success while God remains a footnote.

And you may fear what happens if you return: that God will punish you, that Christians will stare, that you’ll fail again. But look at the father. He is already looking for you.

The turning point in the story is not the son cleaning himself up—it is the son *getting up and going*. You do not fix yourself to come home. You come home to be healed.

Repentance may include confession, restitution, hard conversations, and wise boundaries. But at its heart, repentance is returning to the Father and trusting His character. The gospel does not say, “Earn your way back.” It says, “You are received because of grace.” In Christ, the Father has made a way for you to come home—not as a hired servant, but as a beloved child.

### 2) If you are the older brother, you can come inside.

It is possible to be externally obedient and internally far. To be dutiful but joyless. To do “church things” while quietly keeping score. To resent grace given to someone else because, deep down, you feel unseen.

Maybe you’ve served for years and no one thanked you. Maybe you’ve tried to live cleanly and your life still hurts. And then someone else stumbles in with a dramatic testimony and receives celebration—and something in you says, “What about me?”

A brief picture: I once heard a longtime church member say, not with malice but with real pain, “I’ve been here my whole life. But when someone comes in from the messiest background, it feels like everyone notices them. I don’t think anyone would miss me if I disappeared.” That’s older-brother territory. And it’s more common than we admit.

So hear this: **your faithfulness matters.** Your service is not worthless. But the Father wants to give you more than wages; He wants to give you Himself. The older brother talks like a servant: “I have served you.” But the father answers like a father: “Son, you are always with me.”

The practical step may be this: this week, intentionally rejoice with someone who has received a grace you feel you haven’t. Pray blessing over them out loud. Not because you feel it instantly, but because you want the Father’s heart more than you want your record.

### 3) If you are the church, be a homecoming people.

Luke 15 began with the accusation: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” Let it become our reputation.

To be clear: welcoming sinners does not mean minimizing sin. The father does not call the far country good. But he does call the returning son beloved. And he refuses to make shame the price of re-entry.

So what does “tangible restoration” look like?

It might look like this: someone comes back after a divorce, and instead of treating them like a cautionary tale, you sit with them, listen, and invite them to dinner.

It might mean a person in recovery returns to church, and rather than whispering about their past, you help them find a meeting, connect them to wise accountability, maybe even help with practical needs—rides to work, groceries for a week, a steady friend who checks in.

It might be as simple—and as holy—as turning to someone who looks uncomfortable and saying, “I’m glad you’re here. Would you like to sit with us?”

And it also means we resist older-brother culture: the subtle suspicion that says, “Yes, God forgives you, but we’re going to keep you at arm’s length.” The father doesn’t do arm’s length. He embraces. He covers. He restores. He celebrates.

## Conclusion: The Open Door and the Feast

The parable of the Prodigal Son is not finally about two brothers; it’s about one Father. Jesus is showing us the heart of God: merciful and gracious, abounding in steadfast love. A Father who bears the cost of love, who absorbs the insult of rejection, who runs toward sinners, who restores identity, and who entreats the resentful to come into joy.

So where are you today?

Maybe you are weary, hungry, and far from home. The path back begins with simple honesty: “Father, I have sinned.” You may feel unworthy—and you are, in the sense that none of us can demand grace. But you are not unwelcome. In Christ, the Father has already moved toward you.

Maybe you are the older brother, standing outside the celebration, arms crossed, heart tight. Hear the Father’s voice: “Son… you are always with me.” Stop living as a servant trying to earn what has already been offered. Come into the feast.

And for all of us, here is a specific prayer to carry into this week: **“Father, show me one person I’ve thought of as ‘that son of yours’ instead of ‘my brother’—and give me one concrete step toward welcome.”** A text message. A coffee. An apology. An invitation. A decision to celebrate instead of compete.

The final image of the parable is an open door, music playing, a father pleading, and a feast prepared. The gospel places that door before every one of us. Home is not a place you deserve; it’s a place you’re invited to—because Jesus paid what it cost to bring you there.

So arise. Come to the Father. And when you see others coming down the road—weak, limping, ashamed—be the kind of people who make room at the table.

Because this is what is fitting: “We had to celebrate and be glad, for this brother of yours was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.” Amen.

Jesus tells this parable not to entertain us, and not merely to give us a moral lesson. He tells it to reveal the heart of God—and the true condition of ours.

## Why Jesus Tells This Story

We need the context. Luke 15 begins with a scene that feels strangely familiar: “Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke 15:1–2).

Notice what they’re upset about. They aren’t just bothered that sinners are around; they are bothered by Jesus’ posture toward them. *“This man receives sinners.”* He welcomes them. He stays at the table. He doesn’t hold them at arm’s length.

So Jesus tells three parables in response: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and finally—like the last movement in a symphony—a lost son. Each story escalates: one out of a hundred, one out of ten, and then one out of two. And in each story, when what is lost is found, the result isn’t mild relief; it’s celebration. Heaven’s joy is not restrained, polite satisfaction. God is not stingy with mercy. He delights to bring the lost home.

## The Younger Son: The Far Country

Jesus begins simply: “There was a man who had two sons” (v. 11). Immediately, we are meant to locate ourselves somewhere in this family.

The younger son says something stunning: “Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me” (v. 12). In that culture, asking for your inheritance early wasn’t a neutral financial move. It was a relational rupture. It was, in effect, saying: *I want your stuff, not you. I want your gifts, not your presence. I wish you were dead so I could live the life I want.*

And shockingly, “he divided his property between them.” The father allows the son the dignity—and the danger—of choice. Love does not manipulate. Love does not lock the door and call it safety. The father lets him go.

“Not many days later,” the younger son takes everything and journeys “into a far country” (v. 13). That phrase is more than geography. It is spiritual distance. It’s the posture of a heart that says, “I will define good and evil for myself. I will be my own source of life.”

And the son squanders his property in “reckless living.” He doesn’t simply spend money; he spends himself—his attention, his integrity, his relationships, his body, his future. Sin always makes itself look like freedom at first. It always advertises. It always says, “This will finally make you feel alive.” But it’s a thin kind of life.

Then the story tightens, as it often does in Scripture and in our own experience: “And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need” (v. 14). Notice: the famine reveals what was already true. He built his life on a foundation that couldn’t hold.

He hires himself out, and Jesus chooses an image designed to sting Jewish listeners: he feeds pigs (v. 15). Pigs were unclean. This isn’t just economic collapse; it’s humiliation, alienation, uncleanness. And it gets worse: “He was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything” (v. 16).

The far country is always a country of hunger. It may be hunger for pleasure that never lasts, for approval that always moves the goalposts, for control that slips through your fingers, for comfort that can’t soothe your conscience. The far country makes promises. But it does not feed you.

Then comes one of the most important lines in the parable: “But when he came to himself…” (v. 17). Repentance often begins with sanity. Sin is not merely breaking rules; it is losing ourselves—forgetting who we are and whose we are.

When he comes to himself, he remembers his father’s house: “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!” (v. 17). He forms a plan: “I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you’” (v. 18). Notice the order: against heaven—against God—and before you—against the father. Sin is always vertical and horizontal. It is never merely private.

Then he adds: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants” (v. 19). There is humility here, but there is also misunderstanding. He assumes the best he can hope for is a contract. He thinks he can manage the shame through negotiation: “Let me back in, but only on the lowest rung. I’ll work it off.”

Many of us approach God this way. We imagine that if we have failed badly enough, the best we can do is return as spiritual day laborers—kept at a distance, tolerated but not delighted in. We fear that forgiveness might be possible, but warmth? restoration? celebration? Surely not.

So he “arose and came to his father” (v. 20). Repentance is not just regret; it is return. It is movement toward God.

## The Father: Compassion That Runs

Now we come to the heartbeat of the parable—the moment everything turns:

“But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (v. 20).

The father *saw* him. That implies watching. Waiting. Hoping. The father is not inside with crossed arms, refusing to look down the road. He is scanning the horizon.

And then Jesus says the unthinkable: the father *ran*.

Let that land for a moment. Picture it. A wealthy, dignified patriarch—an elder of the village—lifting his robes, exposing his legs, kicking up dust, moving without concern for decorum or reputation. Imagine the murmurs starting: “Is that him? Is that the father? Why is he running?” And now picture the son—dirty, thin, rehearsing his speech, bracing for the cold stare, for the lecture, for the penalty.

But the father is already there. Arms already reaching. Tears already forming. He embraces him—clings to him. He kisses him—again and again. The father does not wait for the son to clean up. He does not demand proof. He does not keep distance to preserve his honor. He chooses love over dignity.

This is the Gospel in miniature. God’s mercy is not theoretical. It moves. It crosses distance. It bears shame. And in the larger story of Scripture, this running Father points beyond Himself: God does not merely wait at the end of the driveway. In Jesus Christ, God comes all the way into our far country.

The son begins his rehearsed confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son…” (v. 21). But he doesn’t get to finish. He never gets to say, “Treat me as a hired servant.” The father interrupts—not with denial, not with minimizing sin, but with restoration: “Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet” (v. 22).

Each item is a sermon by itself.

The robe is honor—covering where there had been shame.

The ring is belonging—family identity, likely authority, the sign that he is not on probation.

The shoes mean he is not a barefoot servant; he is a son.

Then comes the feast: “Bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate” (v. 23). This is not a quiet reinstatement behind closed doors. This is public joy. The father is not trying to save face; he is throwing a party.

Why? “For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (v. 24). The father uses resurrection language. Lostness is a kind of death. Coming home is a kind of life from the dead. And then the simplest line: “And they began to celebrate.”

This is what God is like. He is holy, yes. Sin is serious, yes. But when the sinner repents, God is not calculating what you owe. He is rejoicing that you are home.

## The Older Son: The Far Country at Home

Jesus could end the story there. Many of us would. We’d send everyone out with damp eyes and relieved hearts: “No matter how far you’ve gone, you can come home.” And that is true.

But Jesus keeps going, because He is not only addressing the wanderers; He is addressing the grumblers. There is another kind of lostness—less obvious, more respectable, and just as deadly.

The older son comes in from the field. He hears music and dancing and asks what’s happening. When he learns his brother has returned and the fattened calf has been killed, he becomes angry and refuses to go in (v. 28).

And again, the father takes initiative: “His father came out and entreated him” (v. 28). Don’t miss that. The father goes out to the younger son *and* the older son. He pursues the rebellious and he pursues the resentful. He is a father to both.

The older son’s speech exposes his heart: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command” (v. 29). Listen to his categories: *served*, *command*. Not loved, not enjoyed, not shared life with. He relates to the father like an employee.

And then the ache underneath: “Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (v. 29). *My friends.* Not “our family.” He doesn’t want the father; he wants what the father can provide. Even obedience has become a strategy for getting what he really loves.

If we’re honest, many of us in the church can slip into the older brother’s shoes. The older brother is the church member who gets irritated when the new convert—messy past, complicated life—gets celebrated, while their own decades of quiet tithing and dependable volunteering feel unnoticed. It’s the believer who hears about grace for “those people” and thinks, “And what about me?”

Then comes the contempt: “But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes…” (v. 30). He can’t even say, “my brother.” He says, “this son of yours.” Resentment fractures family. Self-righteousness always isolates.

The older brother represents the Pharisees and scribes, and he represents a temptation for any religious person: the belief that obedience earns leverage over God. That if we are good, God owes us a life we want. And when grace is lavished on someone we consider undeserving, we feel cheated.

But the father answers tenderly: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31). The older brother’s tragedy is that he has been near the father without enjoying him. The feast was always available, because the father was always there. Yet his heart lived in a far country of comparison and scorekeeping.

The father continues: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (v. 32). Notice the correction: *this your brother*. Grace re-names people. It restores relationship. And the father insists that joy is not optional. When the lost are found, celebration is *fitting*—it is the only response that matches reality.

And then Jesus ends the parable without telling us whether the older brother goes in. It’s an open ending on purpose. Jesus leaves the question hanging in the air for the Pharisees…and for us:

Will we join the Father’s joy, or will we stand outside, clutching our record, missing the feast?

## The Gospel Center: Jesus, the True Elder Brother

At this point we should notice something else: in Jesus’ story, the older brother refuses to go out. He will not cross the threshold. He will not take on shame. He will not absorb cost. He won’t go into the far country to bring his brother home, and he won’t go into the house to share the father’s joy.

But the good news of Christianity is that Jesus is not only the storyteller—He is the fulfillment.

Where the older brother in the parable stays angry and distant, Jesus is the True Elder Brother. He did not stay in the comfort of the Father’s house while we ruined ourselves. He came to us. He entered our poverty. He stepped into our uncleanness. He took the shame we deserved. He went all the way into the far country—down into suffering, down into death—so that we could come home.

And He doesn’t come home to a party at our expense; He makes the party possible at His. He shares His inheritance with sinners. He brings us into His sonship by grace. He puts His name on us. He welcomes us not as hired servants, but as beloved children.

That is why the father can run. That is why the door can be open. Because Jesus has paid what our running cost.

## So Where Are We in the Story?

Because Jesus leaves the ending open, the parable presses in on us personally. It forces us to ask: Where are we in this family?

For some of us, the younger son’s story is not hard to recognize. We know the far country. We have felt the hunger. We have whispered, “How did I get here?”

Maybe your far country is obvious: addiction, secrecy, betrayal, a relationship that is pulling you away from God, patterns you cannot seem to break. Or maybe it’s quieter: years of prayerlessness, a slow drift into cynicism, a life built around success and distraction while God remains a footnote.

Hear the word of the Lord: the Father is not waiting to humiliate you. He is watching for you. The turning point in the story is not the son cleaning himself up—it is the son getting up and going. You do not have to fix yourself to come home. You come home to be healed.

Coming home may include confession, restitution, hard conversations, wise boundaries, and patient rebuilding of trust. Grace does not erase consequences. But grace does meet you on the road. And in Christ, forgiveness is not a cold transaction; it is an embrace.

For others of us, the older brother’s story is the one that stings. It is possible to be externally obedient and internally far. To do “church things” while quietly resenting the grace that others receive. To compare. To keep score. To feel superior—and yet strangely empty.

And here the father’s words are for us too: “Son, you are always with me.” In other words: “You have had Me—and you didn’t know that I was the gift.” The invitation is not to try harder so God will finally celebrate you. The invitation is to stop living like an employee and come live like a child. To receive the Father as Father. To let His joy become our joy when others are restored.

And then there is a corporate word for all of us as a church, because this story started with an accusation: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” May that be said of us.

What does it look like to be a homecoming people?

It looks like patient, prayerful waiting for those who wander instead of writing them off.

It looks like running—taking initiative in reconciliation when possible.

It looks like “robes and rings”—tangible restoration and practical support, not perpetual suspicion.

It looks like celebration—visible joy when someone repents, not quiet judgment that they’re “finally getting it together.”

And it looks like resisting the older-brother posture that says, “They don’t deserve this,” because the truth is: none of us do. That’s why it’s grace.

## Conclusion: The Door Is Open

Remember that young woman sitting on her apartment floor, whispering through tears, “I want to go home”? That sentence is more prayer than she knew. It is the cry of the human heart, whether we have wandered in obvious ways or stayed near and grown bitter.

Luke 15 tells us something we would not dare to assume on our own: when we want to go home, the Father is not standing on the porch with a list. He is on the road. He is looking. And in Jesus Christ, He has already come toward us.

The parable ends with an open door. Music playing. A feast prepared. A father pleading. And two sons who both need grace: one who broke the rules, and one who tried to use the rules.

So where are you today?

If you are weary, hungry, and far from home, the path back begins with simple honesty: “Father, I have sinned.” You may feel unworthy—and you are, in the sense that none of us can demand mercy. But you are not unwelcome. In Christ, the Father has made a way for you to come home.

If you are standing outside the celebration with a tight heart and crossed arms, hear the Father’s entreaty: “Son… you are always with me.” Come inside. Put down the scorecard. Let grace be grace.

And when you see others coming down the road—weak, limping, ashamed—be the kind of people who make room at the table. Because this is what is fitting: “We had to celebrate and be glad, for this brother of yours was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.”

Amen.

UfD7iZqSzBq9rFwN7l-S7.text:
Some years ago a pastor told the story of a young woman who moved to a new city for her first job. She was bright and capable, but lonely. In the first weeks, she tried to build a life: a gym membership, a few new friends, a rhythm of work and weekends. One Friday night she found herself at a bar with coworkers. It was fun—at first. The laughter was easy, the drinks kept coming, the ache of being unknown eased for a while. The next morning, the ease was gone, replaced by a dull heaviness. Soon she was repeating the cycle: another night out, another attempt to purchase belonging, another morning with regret.

Months later, after a particularly painful weekend, she sat on her apartment floor and whispered through tears, “I don’t know how I got here.” Then she said something even more honest: “I want to go home.”

That longing—to go home—is one of the most human desires we have. Not merely a zip code, but a place where you are safe, known, and received. And Jesus, in Luke 15, tells a story that is ultimately about *home*.

Here’s the thesis I want to put in your hands from the beginning: **this parable isn’t primarily about a reckless son and an angry brother; it’s about a Father whose mercy runs to welcome the wanderer and whose love invites the dutiful to share the joy of grace.** Luke 15 shows us the heart of God—and then it presses a question into our lives: will we come home, will we come inside, and will we join the celebration?

## Setting the Scene: Why Jesus Tells This Story

Luke 15 begins with a scene, not a theory. “Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke 15:1–2).

That word—*grumbled*—matters. Their complaint isn’t only about what “those people” have done. Their complaint is about what Jesus is doing: *He receives sinners. He eats with them.* He treats the unclean as welcome guests. He puts them at the table.

So Jesus tells three parables, and they’re meant to land like one unified sermon. A sheep is lost and found. A coin is lost and found. Then a son is lost and found. The stories escalate—one out of a hundred, one out of ten, one out of two—and the chorus is the same: when what is lost is found, there is joy, there is celebration, there is a kind of holy “can you believe it?” ringing through heaven.

So if you want to understand the Prodigal Son, don’t start with the son. Start with the accusation: “This man receives sinners.” And then watch Jesus answer it—not with an argument, but with a portrait of the Father.

And as the story unfolds, remember: Jesus is speaking to two groups at once. To obvious “sinners” who know they’re far. And to “religious” people who are near—but who might be just as lost.

With that in mind, Jesus begins: “There was a man who had two sons” (v. 11). And right away, we’re meant to locate ourselves somewhere in this family.

## The Younger Son: Rebellion and the Far Country

The younger son makes a request that would have sounded like a slap in the face: “Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me” (v. 12). In their culture, an inheritance was normally distributed at death. To ask for it early wasn’t merely financial. It was relational. It was a way of saying, *I want what you can give me, not you. I want your stuff, not your presence. I want life on my terms.*

And shockingly, the father does it. “He divided his property between them.” The father allows the son to walk away. Love, in this world, can be rejected. God does not coerce us into communion. He does not keep us as puppets. He lets the son choose—and that choice carries real danger.

“Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country” (v. 13). The far country is more than miles on a map. It is what happens in the human heart when God becomes irrelevant—when we decide we’ll define good and evil, happiness and meaning, on our own.

The son “squandered his property in reckless living.” He doesn’t only waste money. He wastes himself. He spends his days, his integrity, his relationships, his body, his future. And then, as life so often does, the bottom drops out: “When he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need” (v. 14).

This is what sin does. It promises freedom and delivers hunger. It promises control and delivers slavery. It promises life and delivers emptiness.

And then Jesus chooses an image designed to sting: the son ends up feeding pigs (v. 15). For Jewish listeners, pigs were unclean. In other words, Jesus is saying, “He didn’t just fall down economically. He fell all the way down.” And it gets worse: “He was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything” (v. 16). The far country is always stingy. It takes and takes and takes, and when you have nothing left, it offers you no arms, no table, no home.

Then comes one of the great turning points in Scripture: “But when he came to himself…” (v. 17). Repentance often begins with sanity—when you finally tell the truth about where you are and what your choices have been doing to you.

The Bible has words for this. Repentance is *metanoia*—a change of mind, a turning in the inner person. And it is also *epistrephō*—a returning, a turning back. Repentance is not merely feeling bad; it is coming to your senses and then turning your feet toward the Father.

The son remembers: “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!” (v. 17). And he rehearses his confession: “I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you’” (v. 18).

Notice the honesty: “against heaven and before you.” Sin is vertical and horizontal. It is against God, and it wounds people. And then he adds: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants” (v. 19). There’s humility here—but there’s also a misunderstanding. He assumes he can only come back on the basis of a contract. He thinks he must manage his shame with a deal.

Many people try to come back to God that way. “Let me earn my way into the house again.” “Let me prove I’m serious.” “Let me pay something.” But the gospel is not a wage system. It is a welcome.

So “he arose and came to his father” (v. 20). Regret stays in the pigsty. Repentance gets up. Repentance returns.

And that brings us to the center of the parable—the line everything else is orbiting.

## The Father: Compassion That Runs (and the Gospel That Carries Us)

“But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (v. 20).

The father *saw* him. That means he was looking. Watching. Waiting. Hoping. He wasn’t inside rehearsing a lecture. He was scanning the road.

And the father *felt compassion*. Not annoyance. Not suspicion. Not “we’ll see.” Compassion—deep, gut-level mercy.

Then he *ran*. In that culture, a dignified patriarch did not run. To run meant lifting your robe, exposing your legs, risking public shame. But this father is willing to be thought foolish in order to get to his son. He would rather absorb humiliation than keep distance.

If you’ve ever wondered what God is like toward repentant sinners, Jesus is answering: God is not reluctant. He is not dragging his feet. He runs.

The son begins his confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son…” (v. 21). But he can’t even finish. He never gets to say, “Treat me as a hired servant.” The father interrupts him with grace.

That interruption is the gospel.

The father calls out: “Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet” (v. 22). The robe covers his shame and restores honor. The ring marks him as belonging—family identity, not temporary status. The shoes declare he is not a barefoot servant; he is a son.

Then: “Bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate” (v. 23).

Don’t rush past the feast. Imagine the sensory world of it: the rush of servants, the smells of bread and roasted meat, the hum that turns into music, the voices in the courtyard—some stunned, some whispering, some laughing, some wiping tears. This is not a quiet transaction in the back room. This is public joy. The father isn’t trying to protect his reputation. He is restoring his child.

“For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (v. 24). That is resurrection language. Lostness is a kind of death. Coming home is a kind of life from the dead.

And here we need to say something clearly: this welcome is not sentimental denial of sin. The far country was real. The rebellion was real. The wreckage was real. But grace is more real.

And the “why” of that grace is not ultimately found in the father’s personality; it is found in God’s salvation. **What Jesus sketches in a story, he fulfills in his own life, death, and resurrection.** The Father can run to embrace us because the Son of God came all the way into our far country. He bore shame—not only the embarrassment of town gossip, but the weight of our sin at the cross. And he rose again so that “dead and alive” is not only a metaphor, but a new reality for everyone united to Christ.

The feast is costly. Someone pays. In the gospel, Christ pays. And that is why sinners can come home without pretending they were never lost.

But Jesus isn’t finished. Because Luke 15 is not only about the obvious wanderer. It’s also about the grumblers.

So the camera pans.

## The Older Son: The Far Country at Home

“Now his older son was in the field” (v. 25). He hears music and dancing, asks what’s going on, and when he finds out his brother is home and the fattened calf has been killed, he becomes angry and refuses to go in (vv. 28).

Here is the tragedy: one son is lost in the far country. The other is lost at the front door.

And again the father takes initiative: “His father came out and entreated him” (v. 28). The father goes out to the younger son on the road, and he goes out to the older son in his bitterness. He is a Father to both.

Listen to the older son’s heart: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command” (v. 29). *Served. Command.* Not “I loved you.” Not “I delighted in you.” He speaks like an employee, not a son.

Then: “Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (v. 29). Not “with our family.” *With my friends.* In his mind, the father is a manager withholding wages, not a Father sharing life.

Then comes contempt: “But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!” (v. 30). He cannot say “my brother.” He says, “this son of yours.” Resentment erases relationship.

This is Jesus speaking directly to the Pharisees and scribes—the ones who grumbled that Jesus receives sinners. In the Gospels, you see this pattern repeatedly: the “clean” people who believe their obedience gives them leverage, who view grace as unfair, who want boundaries around mercy.

And if we’re honest, it’s not only “them.” It’s a temptation for the church in every generation. We can keep score. We can measure who has “earned” belonging. We can become experts at correctness while our hearts grow cold.

The father answers with astonishing tenderness: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31). In other words: *You’ve been near me, but you haven’t enjoyed me. You’ve lived like an orphan in my house.*

And then the father insists on the moral logic of grace: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (v. 32). Notice the gentle correction: *this your brother.* Grace renames people. It restores family language.

Jesus ends the parable without telling us whether the older brother goes in. That’s not an oversight. It’s an invitation—and a warning. The door is open. The music is playing. The father is pleading. The question is: will the “religious” heart come inside?

Before we apply this, it might be wise—just for a moment—to let the Holy Spirit search us.

Where do you feel the sting of this story? Where do you feel defensive? Where do you feel seen? Where do you feel hope? Ask God quietly: “Father, where am I in this parable today?”

## Application: Three Homecomings

### 1) If you are in the far country, you can come home

Some of you know that “far country” feeling. Maybe it is obvious: an addiction that has tightened around your life; a secret you’ve protected; a relationship you’ve damaged; a pattern of anger or lust or dishonesty. Or maybe it is quieter and more respectable: years of prayerlessness, a slow drift into cynicism, a life packed with good things that has left no room for God.

Hear this clearly: the Father is not waiting to humiliate you. He is watching for you.

Repentance—*metanoia* and *return*—does not mean you clean yourself up and then approach God. It means you get up and go to him because you’ve finally admitted you cannot save yourself.

A very concrete first step might be as simple as this: today, pray the son’s honest sentence—“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you”—and then tell one trusted Christian this week what’s really going on. Not ten people. One wise person. Ask them to pray with you, and ask them to help you take the next right step.

For some, the next right step will also include accountability and boundaries: counseling, recovery meetings, blocking software, financial transparency, ending a relationship that is pulling you away from God, making restitution where it is possible and safe. None of that earns the Father’s embrace. But it is often part of walking in the Father’s house again—learning a new way to live as a loved son or daughter.

You are not saved by a flawless plan. You are saved by a gracious Father through a crucified and risen Savior.

### 2) If you are the older brother, you can come inside

Maybe you’ve never “left” in the obvious way. You’ve been steady. Responsible. Morally careful. Church-involved. But if you’re honest, grace makes you nervous. You have a hard time celebrating someone else’s restoration because you’re thinking about what they did, what they cost, what they “deserve.”

The older brother’s danger is **self-justifying obedience that withholds grace**. It can sound like, “I did everything right—why don’t I feel joyful?” It can show up as criticism, coldness, sarcasm, or a constant reflex to protect the “good people” from the messy people.

The Father’s invitation to you is not, “Try harder.” It is, “Come be with me.” “You are always with me.” In other words: stop living like an employee in your Father’s house.

A concrete practice for the older-brother heart might look like this for the next month:
- Each week, intentionally speak one sentence of gratitude when you hear about someone’s repentance or growth—say it out loud to God and, when appropriate, to them.
- Invite someone you wouldn’t normally invite into your circle—coffee after church, a meal, a conversation. Not as a project, but as a sibling.
- Ask God to expose where you are keeping score, and then practice a quiet act of generosity that costs you something—because grace always costs someone something.

And if you fear that celebrating grace means excusing sin: remember the father doesn’t call the far country good. He calls the son home. Grace is not denial; grace is rescue.

### 3) If we are the church, we are called to mirror the Father

Luke 15 begins with an accusation: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” May God grant that this becomes the church’s reputation—without compromise, without pretending sin is harmless, but with unmistakable welcome for the repentant.

What would it look like for us to be “homecoming people”?

It looks like patient, prayerful waiting for those who wander—keeping a light on, keeping a heart soft. It looks like taking initiative in reconciliation when possible—making the first call, sending the first message, opening the first door. It looks like “robe and ring” restoration—tangible acts that communicate, “You belong,” while also walking with people into wisdom, healing, and new patterns.

Here is one simple “this week” practice: **look for one person who seems on the margins—new, returning, uncertain, embarrassed—and take one small step of welcome.** Invite them to coffee after church. Sit with them. Learn their name. Ask a real question. Offer prayer. Home is often built with small, repeated acts of attention.

And when someone returns after a long absence—after divorce, after relapse, after bitterness, after shame—let’s resist the older brother’s reflex. Let’s not make them crawl. Let’s not make them prove themselves forever. Let’s walk with them wisely, yes. But let’s welcome them truly.

## Conclusion: The Open Door and the Father’s Joy

This parable is not finally about two brothers; it is about one Father. A Father who runs to welcome the wanderer. A Father who goes out to plead with the resentful. A Father who insists that when the lost are found, celebration is not optional—it is fitting.

And that brings us back to home.

If home is where the heart learns to trust the Father, then the question this morning is not merely, “Do you relate to the younger son or the older son?” The deeper question is: **will you trust the Father’s heart as it is revealed in Jesus Christ?** Will you come home? Will you come inside? Will you join the feast?

Some of you need to get up from the far country and take the first step back. You might come with trembling. You might come with a messy story. You might come with consequences still unfolding. But you will not find a clenched fist. You will find open arms—because Christ has opened the way with his cross and sealed it with his resurrection.

Some of you need to put down the ledger. You need to stop living like a servant trying to earn what has already been given. You need to let the Father’s joy become your joy. You need to come inside.

And all of us—every one of us—are being invited to become the kind of people who make room at the table.

The final image Jesus leaves us is unforgettable: an open door, music playing, a father pleading, and a feast prepared. The gospel places that door before us.

So let’s respond with a simple prayer—whether you whisper it for the first time in years, or whether you pray it as someone who wants their heart softened again:

“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I cannot make myself worthy. But I am coming home. Receive me for Jesus’ sake. And teach me to rejoice when others come home too. Amen.”

Some years ago a pastor told the story of a young woman who moved to a new city for her first job. She was bright and capable, but lonely. In the first weeks, she tried to build a life: a gym membership, a few new friends, a rhythm of work and weekends. One Friday night she found herself at a bar with coworkers. It was fun—at first. The laughter was easy, the drinks kept coming, the ache of being unknown eased for a while.

The next morning, the ease was gone, replaced by a dull heaviness. And so she began to repeat the cycle: another night out, another attempt to buy belonging, another morning with regret. Months later, after a particularly painful weekend, she sat on her apartment floor and whispered through tears, “I don’t know how I got here.” Then she said something even more honest: “I want to go home.”

That longing—to go home—is one of the most human desires we have. Not merely a street address or a childhood bedroom, but a place where you are safe, known, and received. A place where you don’t have to audition for love. A place where you can finally stop pretending.

Luke 15 is a chapter about lost things and found joy. And the parable we call “The Prodigal Son” is really a story about home: leaving it, forgetting it, resenting it, and being invited back into it. It’s a story Jesus tells not to entertain, but to reveal the heart of God—and, if we will let it, to expose the true condition of ours.

## Setting the Scene: Why Jesus Tells This Story

We have to begin where Luke begins. Luke 15 opens with an accusation: “Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke 15:1–2).

It’s not that Jesus is merely teaching. He is *welcoming*. He is receiving people the religious professionals have already written off. He is sharing a table—friendship, fellowship, dignity—with the very people the “clean” crowd believed should stay at a distance.

And that little word “grumbled” is important. This is older-brother energy before we ever meet the older brother. The leaders aren’t just bothered by the sinners’ behavior; they are offended by Jesus’ posture. “This man receives sinners.”

So Jesus tells three parables: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and then—climaxing the sequence—a lost son. Each story escalates: one out of a hundred, one out of ten, and then one out of two. And in each story, heaven’s joy is not restrained, polite satisfaction. It’s celebration. God is not stingy with mercy. He is not reluctant to forgive. He delights to bring the lost home.

## The Younger Son: Rebellion and the Far Country

Jesus begins simply: “There was a man who had two sons” (v. 11). Immediately we should feel the invitation: somewhere in this family, we are here.

The younger son says something stunning: “Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me” (v. 12). In our world, that can sound like an impatient financial request. In that world, it was a relational earthquake. It was the kind of request that basically said, *I want your things, not you. I want your gifts, not your presence. I wish you were dead so I can finally live.*

And shockingly, the father does it. He divides the property between them.

That should sober us. Love does not control like a puppet master. The father does not lock the son in the house. He grants the son the dignity—and the danger—of choice. The Father in heaven does not coerce our hearts. He allows us to walk away. And the tragedy is: we often do.

“Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country” (v. 13). That phrase—*far country*—is more than geography. It is spiritual distance. It is the heart’s decision: *I can be fine without the Father.*

And notice this: the far country isn’t only “wild living” in the obvious sense. For some, it is the bar scene. For others, it is the corner office. It can be a relationship you ask to carry what only God can carry. It can be an ideology—political, cultural, even religious—that becomes your identity and your hope. It can be success, or romance, or control, or resentment. The far country is anywhere you go—internally or externally—to build a life without the Father at the center.

The son squanders his property in “reckless living.” The word suggests wasteful, scattered existence. He doesn’t just spend money; he spends himself. He trades inheritance for a moment. He trades home for appetite.

Then, as often happens in Scripture and in life, circumstances tighten: “And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need” (v. 14). The famine doesn’t create the emptiness; it reveals it. The far country always feels spacious at first—freedom, options, excitement. But sooner or later it shows you what it cannot provide. It cannot keep you. It cannot love you. It cannot feed your soul.

So the son hires himself out, and Jesus chooses an image designed to sting Jewish listeners: he feeds pigs (v. 15). Pigs were unclean animals. This is not just “he got a low-paying job.” This is disgrace. This is humiliation. This is a young man who has fallen so far he can’t even pretend he’s okay anymore.

And then Jesus adds: “He was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything” (v. 16). Don’t let that slide by like a children’s story.

He was envious of the pigs. They had purpose; they had food. He had nothing. Imagine the smell of the pigsty—the sour stench of filth, the slop, the mud caked under fingernails. Imagine the hollow ache in his stomach, the dizziness of hunger. The son of a wealthy landowner, now lower than unclean animals. And no one gives him anything. That’s what the far country does: it promises belonging, but when you’re empty it often disappears.

Then comes one of the most important lines in the parable: “But when he came to himself…” (v. 17). Repentance often begins with sanity. Sin is not merely breaking rules; it is losing yourself—forgetting who you are and whose you are. He “comes to himself,” and for the first time in who knows how long, he sees clearly.

He remembers his father’s house: “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!” (v. 17). He forms a plan: “I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you’” (v. 18). Notice the order: against heaven—against God—and before you—against my father. Sin is always vertical and horizontal. It is never private. It always reaches Godward and neighborward.

He continues: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants” (v. 19). There’s humility here, but there’s also a misunderstanding. He assumes the best he can hope for is a contract. He thinks he can manage his shame by negotiating his status.

Many of us approach God this way. We imagine that if we’ve failed badly enough, the best we can do is come back as spiritual day laborers: “I’ll keep my head down. I’ll work hard. I’ll never ask for much.” We assume the Father might tolerate us, but surely not delight in us.

So he “arose and came to his father” (v. 20). Repentance is not just regret; it is return. It is movement toward God. Not a promise to be better in the pigsty, but a decision to go home.

## The Father: Compassion That Runs (and Bears Shame)

Now we reach the heartbeat of the parable: “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (v. 20).

The father *saw* him. That implies waiting. Watching. Hoping. The father is not inside with crossed arms refusing to look down the road. He is scanning the horizon.

And when he sees him, he feels compassion—gut-level mercy. Then he runs.

In that culture, dignified patriarchs did not run. Men of stature did not hike up their robes and sprint down a road. It was undignified. It risked mockery. It exposed legs. It invited the laughter of the village. But the father runs anyway—because his love is not concerned with protecting his reputation. His love is concerned with reclaiming his child.

And here we should say plainly what this means in the light of the whole Bible. This is not mere sentiment. This is the Gospel.

The father exposes his legs to run; Jesus exposes his body on the cross to save. The father bears the shame of the village; Jesus bears the shame of the world. God does not just wait on the porch tapping his foot; he comes into the mud to lift us out.

The son begins his rehearsed confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son…” (v. 21). It’s true. He isn’t worthy. None of us are. Grace is not given because we deserve it; grace is given because the Father is good.

But notice this: the son never gets to finish the speech. He doesn’t get to say, “Treat me as a hired servant.” The father interrupts him—almost as if the father refuses to let him reduce himself to a transaction. The father will not let his son crawl back on a contract.

He calls out: “Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet” (v. 22). Each detail is loaded with mercy.

The robe is honor—covering, restoration, welcome. The ring is identity—belonging, family authority, a sign that he’s not on probation. The shoes matter too: servants went barefoot. Sons wore shoes. The father is saying, “You are not going to live in my house like a worker trying to earn your keep. You are my child.”

Then: “Bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate” (v. 23). This isn’t a quiet reinstatement. It’s a public feast. The father is not doing damage control; he is throwing a party that the whole community will notice.

Why? “For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (v. 24). The father uses resurrection language. Lostness is a kind of death. Coming home is a kind of life from the dead.

And then Luke says, “And they began to celebrate.” God’s mercy is not reluctant. It is rejoicing.

## The Older Son: The Far Country at Home

And here is where Jesus refuses to let the story become only about the younger brother.

Imagine the scene. The music starts. The scent of roasted meat spreads. Laughter spills out of the house. Servants move quickly. The village is gathering. Something is happening—something big.

But one person is missing.

The older son is out in the field. When he comes near the house, he hears music and dancing and asks what it means. When he learns that his brother has returned and the fattened calf has been killed, he becomes angry and refuses to go in (v. 28).

Think about that. Everyone else is inside celebrating the recovery of a lost son. The father is rejoicing. The servants are busy. The household is full of joy. But the older brother stands outside—close enough to hear the music, too proud to join it. He is physically near the house and emotionally in a far country.

And again, the father takes initiative: “His father came out and entreated him” (v. 28). The father goes out to the rebellious younger son *and* the resentful older son. He is a father to both. He humiliates himself, in a different way now, by leaving his host role at the feast to plead with a sulking child.

The older son’s speech reveals his heart: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command” (v. 29). Listen to the words: *served*. *command*. Not “I loved you.” Not “I enjoyed you.” Not “I’m grateful to be your son.” He sounds like an employee talking to a boss.

Then: “Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (v. 29). Do you hear the distance? *My friends*, not *our family*. He doesn’t see the father as his joy; he sees the father as a paycheck he hasn’t received.

And then the contempt: “But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!” (v. 30). He can’t even say, “my brother.” He says, “this son of yours.” Resentment fractures family. Self-righteousness always isolates.

And this is where we need to see the older brother not as a strange villain from a long-ago culture, but as a mirror held up to religious hearts—including church hearts.

The older brother is the person who says, “I followed all the rules. I saved myself for marriage. I tithed. I volunteered. I voted the right way. I showed up. I served in the nursery for twenty years and no one noticed. Why is *that* guy—who made a mess of everything—getting the microphone, getting attention, getting the fatted calf?”

It’s the bitterness of the obedient.

It’s the sigh when someone with a messy past gets baptized and the room erupts in applause—and a part of you thinks, *Where was my applause?*

It’s the grumble when a celebrity claims Christ and Christians rejoice—and a part of you says, *We’ll see if it lasts.*

It is possible to do many right things and still be far from the Father, because your heart is using obedience as leverage instead of receiving it as love.

But the father answers tenderly: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31). This is heartbreaking. The older brother is living like a spiritual orphan in his own home. The feast has always been available—because the father has always been there. The tragedy is not that he lacked resources; it is that he lacked relationship.

Then the father presses the point: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (v. 32). Notice the gentle correction: *this your brother*. Grace re-names people. It restores relationship.

And then Jesus ends the parable without telling us whether the older brother goes in.

That is not an oversight. It is an altar call.

Jesus is looking at the grumbling Pharisees and scribes, and in love he is saying, “Will you come inside?” And he is looking at us and asking the same: Will you join the Father’s joy, or will you stay outside clutching your record and missing the feast?

## Application: Coming Home, Coming Inside, Becoming a Home

1) **If you are in the far country, you can come home.**  
Some of you know the far country well. Maybe yours is obvious: addiction, secrecy, betrayal, choices you regret. Maybe yours is quieter: years of prayerlessness, a slow drift into cynicism, a life built around achievement while God becomes a footnote. Maybe you’re successful—and starving.

Hear the Word of the Lord: the Father is not waiting to humiliate you. He is watching for you. The turning point in the story is not the son getting cleaned up. It is the son getting up. “I will arise and go.”

You do not have to fix yourself to come home. You come home to be healed.

Yes, repentance may include confession, restitution, hard conversations, accountability, and wise boundaries. Grace is not denial. But at its heart repentance is returning to the Father—trusting his character more than you trust your shame.

If your prayer today is as small as, “Father, I want to come home,” that is a prayer heaven understands.

2) **If you are the older brother, you can come inside.**  
It is possible to be externally obedient and internally far. Dutiful but joyless. Busy in the field and cold in the heart. It is possible to do church activity while resenting the grace God pours on others.

If that’s you, the invitation is not “try harder.” The invitation is “come closer.” The father doesn’t shame the older son; he entreats him: “Son, you are always with me.” In other words: *You don’t need to earn what you already have. You don’t need to perform your way into belonging. You belong.*

And then, as grace begins to thaw our resentment, we learn to rejoice when mercy is given away—because we realize mercy is what we live on too.

3) **As a church, we are invited to mirror the Father—and it is a joy.**  
Luke 15 began with the complaint: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” By God’s grace, may that become the kind of thing people can honestly say about us.

Not because we minimize sin. The father never calls the far country good. He doesn’t congratulate the younger son’s choices. Grace is not a denial of holiness.

But because we know what God is like, we want to be the kind of community where repentant people are not merely allowed to attend, but *welcomed home*. Not as a public relations project. Not as a box to check. As a reflection of our Father’s heart.

What does it look like to be a “homecoming people”?

It looks like patient prayer for wanderers, not cynical commentary about them.  
It looks like taking initiative in reconciliation when it is wise and possible.  
It looks like tangible restoration—robing people with dignity, not keeping them barefoot in suspicion forever.  
It looks like celebration: testimonies, meals, presence, practical help.  
And it looks like refusing the older-brother posture that says, “They don’t deserve this,” remembering that the whole point is: none of us do.

## Conclusion: The Open Door, the Watching Father, the Ready Feast

This parable is not finally about two brothers; it is about one Father.

A Father who allows real choice, and suffers real loss.  
A Father who watches the road.  
A Father who runs—bearing shame to restore the shamed.  
A Father who interrupts our bargaining and answers with adoption.  
A Father who pleads with the resentful and invites them into joy.  
A Father who says, “It was fitting to celebrate.”

So where are you today?

Maybe you are weary, hungry, and far from home. The path back begins with simple honesty: “Father, I have sinned.” You may feel unworthy—and you are, in the sense that none of us can demand grace. But you are not unwelcome. In Jesus Christ, the Father has made a way for you to come home, not as a servant on probation, but as a beloved child.

Maybe you are standing outside, arms crossed, keeping score. Hear the father’s gentle entreaty: “Son… you are always with me.” Stop living like an employee trying to earn what has already been offered. Come into the feast.

And for all of us: when the lost return, will we clap with heaven—or grumble with the Pharisees?

The final image Jesus leaves us is an open door, music spilling out, a father pleading, and a feast prepared. The Gospel places that door before every one of us.

The door is open.  
The Father is watching.  
The feast is ready.

Let’s go home.

Let us pray.
