Some years ago a pastor told the story of a young woman who moved to a new city for her first job. She was bright and capable, but lonely. In the first weeks, she tried to build a life: a gym membership, a few new friends, a rhythm of work and weekends. One Friday night she found herself at a bar with coworkers. It was fun—at first. The laughter was easy, the drinks kept coming, the ache of being unknown eased for a while.

The next morning, the ease was gone, replaced by a dull heaviness. She began to repeat the cycle: another night out, another attempt to buy belonging, another morning with regret. Months later, after a particularly painful weekend, she sat on her apartment floor and whispered through tears, “I don’t know how I got here.” Then she said something even more honest: “I want to go home.”

That longing—*to go home*—is one of the most human desires we have. Not merely a zip code, but a place where you are safe, known, and received.

Luke 15 is a chapter about lost things and found joy, and the parable we call “The Prodigal Son” is really a story about home: leaving it, forgetting it, resenting it, and being invited back into it. It’s a story Jesus tells not to entertain but to reveal the heart of God—and the true condition of ours.

## Setting the Scene: Why Jesus Tells This Story

We need the context. Luke 15 begins with an accusation: “Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke 15:1–2).

Jesus is not merely teaching; He is *welcoming*. He is eating with people religious leaders considered unclean, morally compromised, socially beneath them. And the grumbling reveals the deeper issue: the Pharisees and scribes did not just object to the sinners’ behavior; they objected to Jesus’ *posture*. “This man receives sinners.”

So Jesus tells three parables: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and then—climaxing the sequence—a lost son. Each story escalates: one out of a hundred, one out of ten, and then one out of two. And in each story, heaven’s joy is not restrained, polite satisfaction, but celebration.

God is not stingy with mercy. He is not reluctant to forgive. He delights to bring the lost home.

## The Younger Son: Rebellion and the Far Country

Jesus begins: “There was a man who had two sons” (v. 11). Immediately, we are meant to see ourselves somewhere in this family.

The younger son says something stunning: “Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me” (v. 12). In that culture, asking for the inheritance early was not a neutral financial request. It was a relational rupture. It was, in effect, saying: *I want your stuff, not you. I want your gifts, not your presence. I wish you were dead so I could live the life I want.*

And shockingly, the father divides the property between them. The father allows the son the dignity—and the danger—of choice. God’s love does not control us like puppets. He does not force closeness. He lets the son walk away.

The text says, “Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country” (v. 13). That phrase—*far country*—is more than geography. It is spiritual distance. It is what happens when we treat God as irrelevant, when we decide we can define life on our own terms.

The son squanders his property in “reckless living.” The word suggests wasteful, dissolute, scattered existence. He doesn’t simply spend money; he spends himself.

Then, as often happens in Scripture and in life, circumstances tighten: “And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need” (v. 14). Notice: the famine reveals what was always true. The son was building his life on a foundation that could not hold. When the money ran out, the friends likely did too. The far country is attractive until it is not.

He hires himself out, and Jesus chooses an image designed to sting Jewish listeners: the son feeds pigs (v. 15). Pigs were unclean. The son has not only fallen economically; he has fallen socially, spiritually, ceremonially. And it gets worse: “He was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything” (v. 16).

The far country makes promises: freedom, pleasure, control. But it often ends with hunger—hunger for love, for meaning, for peace—and the realization that what we’ve chased cannot feed us.

Here is one of the most important lines in the parable: “But when he came to himself…” (v. 17). Repentance often begins with sanity. Sin is not merely breaking rules; it is losing ourselves—forgetting who we are and whose we are.

And this is where that young woman’s story comes back into view. “I don’t know how I got here,” she whispered. The younger son, standing among the pigs, has that same moment of stark realization. He wakes up to the truth: *This isn’t who I am. This isn’t what I was made for. This isn’t home.*

Coming to himself, he remembers his father’s house: “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!” (v. 17). He forms a plan: “I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you’” (v. 18). Notice the order: against heaven—against God—and before you—against the father. Sin is always vertical and horizontal. It is never private. It always reaches Godward and neighborward.

He continues: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants” (v. 19). There is humility here, but also a misunderstanding. He assumes the best he can hope for is a contract. He thinks he can return on the basis of a lesser identity: not son, but servant. He believes he must manage the shame by negotiating.

Many of us approach God this way. We imagine that if we have failed badly enough, the best we can do is come back as spiritual day laborers: “I’ll keep my head down, I’ll work hard, I’ll never ask for much.” We think the Father might tolerate us, but surely not delight in us.

So he “arose and came to his father” (v. 20). Repentance is not just regret; it is return. It is movement toward God.

## The Father: Compassion That Runs

Now comes the heartbeat of the parable: “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (v. 20).

The father *saw* him. That implies watching. Waiting. Hoping. The father is not inside with crossed arms, refusing to look down the road. He is scanning the horizon. And when he sees him, he feels compassion—gut-level mercy.

Then he runs. In that culture, dignified patriarchs did not run; it was considered shameful. To run, he would hike up his robe, expose his legs, risk public mockery. But the father is willing to bear shame in order to reach his son.

This is the Gospel in miniature. The Father’s love is not theoretical. It moves. It crosses distance. It absorbs humiliation. And ultimately, in the full story of Scripture, it is not only the father who runs—it is God who comes all the way to us in Jesus Christ, bearing our shame at the cross to bring us home.

The son begins his rehearsed confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son…” (v. 21). But notice: he doesn’t even get to finish the speech. He never gets to say, “Treat me as a hired servant.” The father interrupts with joy-soaked authority: “Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet” (v. 22).

Each item matters.

- **The best robe** is honor, restoration, covering. The son’s shame does not get the final word.  
- **The ring** is likely a signet ring—authority, belonging, family identity.  
- **Shoes** mean he is not a barefoot servant; he is a son.

Then the father says, “Bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate” (v. 23). This is not a quiet reinstatement; it is a public feast. The father is not trying to save face; he is throwing a party.

Why? “For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (v. 24). The father does not describe the son as “a disappointment” or “a cautionary tale.” He uses resurrection language. Lostness is a kind of death. Coming home is a kind of life from the dead. And then the simplest line: “And they began to celebrate.”

This is what God is like. He is holy, yes. Sin is serious, yes. But when the sinner repents, God is not calculating what you owe. He is rejoicing that you are home.

## The Older Son: The Far Country at Home

At this point, Jesus could end the story. Many of us would. The moral would be clear: no matter how far you’ve gone, you can come home.

But Jesus goes on, because He’s speaking to the grumblers too. There is another kind of lostness—less obvious, more respectable, and just as deadly.

The older son comes in from the field, hears music and dancing, and asks what’s happening. When he learns his brother has returned and the fattened calf has been killed, he becomes angry and refuses to go in (v. 28).

And again the father takes initiative: “His father came out and entreated him” (v. 28). The father goes out to the rebellious younger son *and* the resentful older son. He is a father to both.

The older son’s speech reveals his heart: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command” (v. 29). Listen to the language: *served*, *command*. Not loved, not enjoyed, not shared life with. He relates to the father like an employee.

He continues: “Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (v. 29). Do you hear the distance? *My friends*, not *our family*. He does not see the father as his joy; he sees him as a boss who hasn’t paid properly.

Then the contempt: “But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!” (v. 30). He can’t even say, “my brother.” He says, “this son of yours.” Resentment fractures family.

The older brother represents the Pharisees and scribes, and he also represents a temptation for any religious person: the belief that obedience earns us leverage over God. That if we are good, God owes us a life we want. And when grace is given to someone we consider undeserving, we feel cheated.

And here’s the key parallel: earlier we said the younger son went to a “far country”—a place of spiritual distance. The older son has his own far country too. It’s not a map location. It’s a heart location: a spiritual distance even while he is physically at home. He is near the father’s land, near the father’s work, near the father’s house—and yet far from the father’s heart.

But the father answers tenderly: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31). The older brother’s tragedy is that he has been near the father without enjoying him. The feast was always available, because the father was always there. Yet his heart was locked in the joyless far country of self-righteousness.

The father continues: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (v. 32). Notice the father gently corrects him: *this your brother*. Grace re-names people. It restores relationship. And the father insists: celebration is not optional; it is *fitting*. When the lost are found, joy is the only appropriate response.

And then Jesus ends the parable without telling us whether the older brother goes in. That is deliberate. It leaves the Pharisees—and us—with a question: Will you join the Father’s joy, or will you stand outside, clutching your record, missing the feast?

## Application: Coming Home, Coming Inside, Becoming Home

### 1) If you are in the far country, you can come home.

Some of you may feel you’ve wandered too far—morally, relationally, spiritually. Perhaps your far country is obvious: addiction, secrecy, betrayal. Perhaps it is quieter: years of prayerlessness, a slow drift into cynicism, a life built around success while God remains a footnote.

Hear the word of the Lord: the Father is not waiting to humiliate you. He is watching for you.

The turning point in the story is not the son cleaning himself up—it is the son *getting up and going*. You do not have to fix yourself to come home. You come home to be healed.

Repentance may include confession, restitution, hard conversations, and wise boundaries. But at its heart, repentance is returning to the Father, trusting His character. The Gospel does not say, “Earn your way back.” It says, “You are received because of grace.” In Christ, the Father runs to meet you.

### 2) If you are the older brother, you can come inside.

It is possible to be externally obedient and internally far. To be dutiful but joyless. To do “church things” while resenting grace given to others. To compare, to keep score, to feel superior—yet strangely empty.

The older brother is lost not because he is immoral, but because he is self-centered. He loves his own righteousness more than he loves his father.

If this is you, the invitation is not to try harder. The invitation is to be with the Father—really with Him—to receive His love not as wages but as gift. And to let His joy become your joy when others are restored.

Maybe you’ve been “doing the right things” for years, but deep down you feel unseen, unrewarded, and resentful. The father’s words are for you too: “Son, you are always with me.” In other words: *You don’t have to earn a place at the table—you’ve been invited to enjoy the Father himself.*

Come into the feast.

### 3) If we are the church, we are called to mirror the Father.

Luke 15 began with: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” That’s the accusation. Let it become our reputation.

The church is meant to be the kind of community where repentant people are not merely allowed to attend, but *welcomed home*. That does not mean we minimize sin. The father does not call the far country good. But he does call the returning son beloved.

So what does it look like for us to be a “homecoming people”?

- It looks like patient, prayerful waiting for those who wander.
- It looks like running—taking initiative in reconciliation when possible.
- It looks like celebration: honest testimony, visible joy, practical support.

And it looks like “robes and rings”—tangible restoration, not perpetual suspicion. In modern terms, that might mean offering practical help to someone rebuilding their life after a fall: meals, childcare, a ride to counseling or recovery meetings, help finding work, or simply steady friendship. It might mean publicly celebrating a testimony of repentance and restoration—without turning someone into a spectacle—rather than holding them at arm’s length forever as “the one who messed up.”

Of course, wisdom and boundaries matter. Trust is rebuilt over time, and consequences can be real. But the posture of the church cannot be: *You may sit in the back, but you will never belong.* The father does not say, “Let him sleep in the barn until we see how serious he is.” He restores sonship and then begins the work of healing inside the safety of home.

And we must resist the older-brother posture that says, “They don’t deserve this.” If grace only goes to those who “deserve it,” it is no longer grace.

## Conclusion: The Open Door and the Father’s Joy

The parable of the Prodigal Son is not finally about two brothers; it’s about one Father. And through Jesus, we are being shown the heart of God: a Father who bears the cost of love, who absorbs the insult of rejection, who runs toward sinners, who restores identity, and who invites the resentful into joy.

Where are you in the story today?

Maybe you are weary, hungry, and far from home. The path back begins with simple honesty: “Father, I have sinned.” You may feel unworthy—and you are, in the sense that none of us can demand grace. But you are not unwelcome. In Christ, the Father has made a way for you to come home.

Maybe you are the older brother, standing outside the celebration, arms crossed, heart tight. Hear the Father’s entreaty: “Son… you are always with me.” Stop living as a servant trying to earn what has already been offered. Come into the feast. Let grace be grace.

And for all of us: will we join the Father’s celebration? When the lost return, will we clap with heaven—or grumble with the Pharisees?

The final image of the parable is an open door, music playing, a father pleading, and a feast prepared. The Gospel places that door before every one of us.

Home is not a place you deserve; it’s a place you’re invited to.

So arise. Come to the Father. And when you see others coming down the road—weak, limping, ashamed—be the kind of people who make room at the table.

Because this is what is fitting: “We had to celebrate and be glad, for this brother of yours was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.” Amen.

Jesus begins simply: “There was a man who had two sons” (v. 11). Right away, we’re meant to locate ourselves somewhere in this family.

The younger son says something stunning: “Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me” (v. 12). In that culture, asking for the inheritance early was not a neutral financial request. It was a relational rupture. It was, in effect, saying: *I want your stuff, not you. I want your gifts, not your presence. I wish you were dead so I could live the life I want.*

And shockingly, the father divides the property between them.

The father allows the son the dignity—and the danger—of choice. God’s love is not controlling love. He does not force closeness. He does not coerce affection. He lets the son walk away.

“Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country” (v. 13). That phrase—*far country*—is more than geography. It’s spiritual distance. It’s what happens when we treat God as irrelevant, when we decide we can define life on our own terms. The son squanders his property in “reckless living.” He doesn’t simply spend money; he spends himself.

Then life tightens: “And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need” (v. 14). Sometimes the famine is literal. Sometimes it’s relational. Sometimes it’s an inner emptiness that shows up when the party ends and the lights come on. But either way, notice this: the famine reveals what was always true. The son was building his life on a foundation that could not hold.

When the money runs out, the friends often do too.

He hires himself out, and Jesus chooses an image designed to sting Jewish listeners: the son feeds pigs (v. 15). Pigs were unclean. The son has not only fallen economically; he has fallen socially, spiritually, ceremonially. And it gets worse: “He was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything” (v. 16). The far country makes promises: freedom, pleasure, control. But it often ends with hunger—hunger for love, for meaning, for peace—and the realization that what we’ve chased cannot feed us.

Then comes one of the most important lines in the parable: “But when he came to himself…” (v. 17). Repentance often begins with sanity. Sin is not merely breaking rules; it is losing ourselves—forgetting who we are and whose we are.

And we should add: we do not usually “come to ourselves” by sheer willpower. Scripture teaches that repentance is a gift. Often it is the Holy Spirit who mercifully turns on the light—who convicts us of our true poverty, who makes the far country taste like ash, who awakens in us the courage to whisper, “I want to go home.”

Coming to himself, the son remembers his father’s house: “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!” (v. 17). He forms a plan:

“I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you’” (v. 18).

Notice the order: against heaven—against God—and before you—against the father. Sin is always vertical and horizontal. It is never truly private. It always reaches Godward and neighborward.

Then he adds: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants” (v. 19).

There is humility here, but also a misunderstanding. He assumes the best he can hope for is a contract. He thinks he can manage shame by negotiating a reduced identity: not son, but servant.

Many of us approach God this way. We imagine that if we have failed badly enough, the best we can do is come back as spiritual day laborers: *I’ll keep my head down, I’ll work hard, I’ll never ask for much. Maybe God will tolerate me—surely He won’t delight in me.*

But repentance is not just regret; it’s return. And so “he arose and came to his father” (v. 20). He starts walking home.

## The Father: Compassion That Runs

Now we come to the heartbeat of the parable:

“But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (v. 20).

The father *saw* him. That implies watching. Waiting. Hoping. The father is not inside with crossed arms, refusing to look down the road. He is scanning the horizon. And when he sees him, he feels compassion—gut-level mercy.

Then he runs.

In that culture, dignified patriarchs did not run; it was considered shameful. To run, he would hike up his robe, expose his legs, risk public mockery. But the father is willing to bear shame in order to reach his son.

This is the Gospel in miniature. The Father’s love is not theoretical; it moves. It crosses distance. It absorbs humiliation. And in the full story of Scripture, it goes even further: in Jesus Christ, God comes all the way to us, bearing our shame at the cross to bring us home.

The son begins his rehearsed confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son…” (v. 21).

But he doesn’t get to finish.

He never gets to say, “Treat me as a hired servant.” The father cuts him off—not because confession doesn’t matter, but because the negotiation doesn’t. The father will not accept a demotion, because he cannot bear to lose the *son*. Grace is not a partial rehire; it is a full restoration of relationship.

The father says, “Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet” (v. 22).

Each item is a sermon all by itself.

- The **robe** is honor—covering, welcome, dignity restored.
- The **ring** is belonging and identity—the family name, the sign of sonship.
- The **shoes** are freedom—the mark that he is not a barefoot slave but a cherished child.

When you come home to God, He doesn’t simply cancel your debt. In Christ, He restores your **honor** (the robe), your **identity** (the ring), and your **freedom** (the shoes). He does not only forgive you; He reclaims you.

Then the father says, “Bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate” (v. 23). This is not a quiet reinstatement. It’s a public feast. The father is not trying to save face; he is declaring love.

Why? “For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (v. 24). He doesn’t describe the son as “a disappointment” or “a project.” He uses resurrection language. Lostness is a kind of death. Coming home is a kind of life from the dead.

“And they began to celebrate.”

This is what God is like. Yes, He is holy. Yes, sin is serious. But when the sinner repents, God is not calculating what you owe. He is rejoicing that you are home.

## The Older Son: The Far Country at Home

At this point, many of us would end the story. The moral seems complete: no matter how far you’ve gone, you can come home.

But Jesus cannot end it here, because He’s not only speaking to the younger sons in the crowd. He is also speaking to the grumblers—the Pharisees and scribes. And Jesus knows something we often forget: the greatest danger to the Kingdom is not only the one who runs far away, but the one who never leaves the field and yet never enters the Father’s joy.

So we must now turn our attention to the older brother—who represents a different kind of far country, the one we can carry inside us.

To make this tangible, think of a workplace where one employee has always been steady. Shows up early. Never causes trouble. Quietly carries the load. Then another employee—who has been unreliable for years—finally hits rock bottom, gets help, turns things around. And the manager throws a celebration: public praise, a bonus, a welcome back.

And the faithful employee thinks, *What about me? Where’s my recognition? Why does the one who wasted everything get the party?*

That is the older brother.

He comes in from the field, hears music and dancing, and asks what’s happening. When he learns his brother has returned and the fattened calf has been killed, he becomes angry and refuses to go in (v. 28).

And here is something tender: the older brother is not just mean; he is weary. He has been dutiful, but duty without delight becomes drudgery. And drudgery, over time, turns into resentment. His heart is far away because he has mistaken service for relationship.

Once again, the father takes initiative: “His father came out and entreated him” (v. 28). The father goes out to the rebellious younger son *and* the resentful older son. He is a father to both.

The older son finally speaks, and his words reveal his theology:

“Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command” (v. 29).

Listen to the language: *served… command.* It’s the vocabulary of an employee, not a son. He continues: “Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (v. 29). Again—*my friends.* Not *our family.* He does not see the father as his joy; he sees him as a boss who hasn’t paid properly.

Then he says, “But when this son of yours came…” (v. 30). He can’t even say, “my brother.”

This is where the parable presses into the Pharisaic objection—and into the religious heart in any age. The older brother’s complaint is essentially: *Your grace violates my sense of justice and merit.*

This is the tension between **law** and **grace**.

The older brother is operating under a “law” system—not merely God’s holy commands, but a mindset of earning: *If I perform, I deserve. If I obey, you owe.* Grace, on the other hand, is the father’s posture: *I give because I love. I restore because you are mine.*

The older brother cannot rejoice because grace feels like an injustice. But the father is not unjust—he is generous. He is not denying righteousness—he is refusing to reduce sonship to wages.

The father answers with gentleness: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31).

That line is both comforting and heartbreaking. The older brother has been near the father without enjoying him. He has lived in the house of abundance as if it were a scarcity economy. He has measured love in goats and calves rather than receiving the greatest gift: “You are always with me.”

The father continues: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (v. 32). Notice: he re-names the relationship—*this your brother.* Grace restores family.

And Jesus ends the parable without telling us whether the older brother goes in. It’s deliberate. It leaves the Pharisees—and it leaves us—with an open question:

Will you join the Father’s joy, or will you stand outside, clutching your record, missing the feast?

## Application: Coming Home, Coming Inside, Becoming a Home

So where are you in the story?

### 1) If you are in the far country, you can come home.

Some of you may feel you’ve wandered too far—morally, relationally, spiritually. Perhaps your far country is obvious: addiction, secrecy, betrayal. Perhaps it is quieter: years of prayerlessness, a slow drift into cynicism, a life built around achievement while God becomes an afterthought.

Hear this clearly: the Father is not waiting to humiliate you. He is watching for you.

The turning point in the story is not the son cleaning himself up. It is the son *getting up and going*. You do not fix yourself in order to come home. You come home in order to be healed.

Yes, repentance may include confession, restitution, hard conversations, and wise boundaries. But at its heart, repentance is returning to the Father and trusting His character.

And when you return, God does not merely say, “Fine, you can stay in the shed.” He restores what sin tried to destroy. In Christ, He gives you the robe (honor), the ring (identity), and the shoes (freedom). He calls you “son,” “daughter,” not “case,” not “project,” not “employee.”

### 2) If you are the older brother, you can come inside.

Some of you have tried so hard to do the right thing. You’ve carried responsibility. You’ve served. You’ve stayed. And somewhere along the way, joy leaked out and bitterness moved in.

You may not say it out loud, but your heart has whispered, *God, I’ve done my part. Now you owe me. A better life. A smoother road. More recognition. Fewer prodigals getting parties.*

If that’s you, you are not being mocked here—you are being invited. The father goes out to you too.

The invitation is not, “Try harder.” The invitation is, “Stop living like a servant when you are a son.” Come inside. Let the Father be your portion, not your payroll department. Lay down the exhausting math of merit. Ask God to turn your “I have to” back into “I get to.” And when grace is given to someone else, let it become proof that grace is real—not evidence that God has forgotten you.

### 3) Church, let’s become a homecoming people.

Luke 15 began with an accusation: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” By God’s grace, may that be said of us—not as a scandal, but as a testimony.

So let’s make this practical.

- Sometimes “running” looks like taking the first step toward someone who has been absent—not with interrogation, but with a simple message: *We miss you. Are you okay?*
- Sometimes “the robe and the ring” look like tangible restoration: not forever treating repentant people as second-class Christians, not keeping them on probation as a permanent identity, but walking with wisdom *and* real trust as fruit of repentance appears.
- Sometimes “killing the fattened calf” looks like celebration that costs us something: making room at the table, giving time, offering rides, mentoring a new believer, hosting a meal for someone who’s trying to rebuild life.
- And sometimes the most spiritual thing we do is refuse the older-brother posture in ourselves—refuse the quiet grumbling that says, *Why are they getting attention? Why do they get grace?*

When someone takes a step toward Christ—whether it’s dramatic or quiet, whether they’ve been gone ten years or ten weeks—we don’t just nod politely. We rejoice, because heaven rejoices.

## Conclusion: The Open Door and the Prepared Feast

Whether you are running toward home, standing resentfully outside, or trying to organize the party, this parable is ultimately about the relentless, extravagant love of the Father.

And the good news is not finally about two brothers. It’s about one Father—whose compassion runs, whose arms are open, whose joy is not fragile, whose grace is not scarce.

Where are you today?

Maybe you are weary, hungry, and far from home. The path back begins with simple honesty: “Father, I have sinned.” You may feel unworthy—and you are, in the sense that none of us can demand grace. But you are not unwelcome. In Christ, the Father has made a way for you to come home.

Maybe you are the older brother, standing outside the celebration, arms crossed, heart tight. Hear the Father’s entreaty: “Son… you are always with me.” Stop living as a servant trying to earn what has already been offered. Come into the feast. Let grace be grace.

And for all of us: will we join the Father’s celebration? When the lost return, will we clap with heaven—or grumble with the Pharisees?

The final image of the parable is an open door, music playing, a father pleading, and a feast prepared. The Gospel places that door before every one of us.

Home is not a place you deserve. It’s a place you’re invited to.

So arise. Come to the Father. And when you see others coming down the road—weak, limping, ashamed—be the kind of people who make room at the table.

Because this is what is fitting: “We had to celebrate and be glad, for this brother of yours was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.” Amen.

Some years ago a pastor told me about a young woman I’ll call Anna. Anna moved to a new city for her first job—bright, capable, and quietly lonely. The first weeks were full of good intentions: a gym membership, a few new friends, a rhythm of work and weekends. But loneliness has a way of looking for company, and one Friday night she ended up at a bar with coworkers.

It was fun—at first. The laughter came easily, the drinks kept coming, and for a few hours the ache of being unknown felt smaller. But the next morning the ease was gone, replaced by a dull heaviness. And then the cycle started to repeat: another night out, another attempt to buy belonging, another morning with regret.

Months later, after a particularly painful weekend, Anna sat on her apartment floor and whispered through tears, “I don’t know how I got here.” Then she said something even more honest: “I want to go home.”

That longing—to go home—is one of the most human desires we have. Not merely a zip code, but a place where you are safe, known, and received.

And yet if we’re honest, home can be complicated. Sometimes the person farthest from home is the one who left loudly. Sometimes the person farthest from home is the one who stayed—physically near, spiritually distant, doing all the right things but never enjoying love.

Jesus tells a story exactly for that kind of room—rooms like this one—where there are people lost in different ways: some obviously, some invisibly. He tells it to reveal not merely a moral lesson, but the heart of God.

### Why Jesus Tells This Story

Luke 15 begins with a scene, not a theory: “Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke 15:1–2).

That word *receives* is the spark. Jesus is not merely teaching at sinners from a safe distance; He is welcoming them, sitting at table with them, treating them as people worth His presence. The religious leaders aren’t only offended by the sinners’ mess—they’re offended by Jesus’ welcome.

So Jesus tells three parables: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and then a lost son. They build in intensity: one out of a hundred, one out of ten, and then one out of two. And each story ends the same way: not with cold relief, but with joy—celebration, community, gladness.

Then Jesus gives us the longest, most personal of the three. We often call it “the Prodigal Son,” but that title can hide what Jesus is doing. He’s painting a portrait—through the father in the story—of what God is like. Not that God is identical to every detail of a human parent, but that in this father’s posture we see something true and blazing about the Father who sent the Son: the God who welcomes sinners, and who confronts self-righteousness, and who invites both kinds of lostness into His joy.

### The Younger Son: Leaving Home for the “Far Country”

Jesus begins simply: “There was a man who had two sons” (v. 11). In other words: this story has room for more than one kind of heart.

The younger son says to his father, “Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me” (v. 12). In that culture, this wasn’t a neutral financial conversation. It was a relational rupture. It was, in effect: *I want your things, not you. I want your gifts, not your presence. I want my life without your life in it.*

And shockingly, “he divided his property between them” (v. 12). The father does not chain the son to the house. Love does not control like that. The father lets him go.

“Not many days later,” the younger son liquidates what he has and travels “into a far country” (v. 13). That phrase—*far country*—is more than geography. It’s spiritual distance. It’s the posture that says, “God may exist, but I will live as though He doesn’t matter. I will define good and evil for myself. I will spend my life where I think life is.”

There he squanders his wealth in reckless living. And then, as so often happens, the props holding up his new freedom kick out from under him: “And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose… and he began to be in need” (v. 14). The far country always promises freedom, pleasure, control. But it cannot promise faithfulness. When circumstances change, it cannot hold you.

So the son hires himself out, and Jesus chooses an image meant to land with force: he ends up feeding pigs (v. 15). He has fallen in every direction—financially, socially, spiritually. And it becomes so desperate that he longs to eat what the pigs eat, “and no one gave him anything” (v. 16). That last phrase is devastating. The far country takes, but it does not give. It flatters, but it does not feed.

Then comes one of the most hopeful lines in the whole parable: “But when he came to himself…” (v. 17). Repentance often begins with sanity. Sin isn’t only breaking rules; it’s losing yourself—forgetting who you are, and whose you are.

He remembers his father’s house: even the hired servants have bread. And he forms a plan: “I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you’” (v. 18). Sin always reaches upward toward God and outward toward others. It’s never as private as we pretend.

Then he adds: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants” (v. 19). There’s real humility there, but also a misunderstanding. He assumes the best possible future is a contract. He thinks he can manage his shame by negotiating his way back.

Many of us try the same thing with God. We don’t say it out loud, but we live as if the best we can hope for is tolerance. “I’ll keep my head down. I’ll work hard. I’ll never ask for much. Maybe God will let me stay in the back of the house.”

But then the son does the one thing he must do: “And he arose and came to his father” (v. 20). Repentance is more than regret. It is return. It is movement toward the One you ran from.

### The Father: Compassion That Moves Toward the Lost

Now we come to the heart of the parable—not the son’s speech, but the father’s response.

“But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (v. 20).

Notice the verbs. The father *saw*. That suggests he was looking—watching the road, scanning the horizon, hoping. He *felt compassion*—not annoyance, not suspicion, not “let him sweat a bit.” Compassion. And then he *ran*.

In that culture, a dignified patriarch didn’t run. Running meant lifting your robes, exposing your legs, risking public shame. But the father is willing to be undignified if it means closing the distance. He chooses the shame of running over the coldness of waiting.

Let that land: the son has rehearsed a speech. The father has already begun moving.

Here’s a picture to make it modern. Imagine a parent who hasn’t slept well in months because a son or daughter is gone—gone into addiction, gone into a relationship that is destroying them, gone into a bitterness that has swallowed them whole. Imagine that parent who keeps glancing at the driveway, not because they’re naïve, but because love does that. And then one afternoon a figure appears at the end of the street—thin, hesitant, not sure they’ll be received. And that parent does not sit on the couch and wait for an apology at the door. They move. They hurry. They go outside. They close the distance.

That is what this father does. And Jesus is not merely describing a good human parent. He is unveiling something true about God: the God the Pharisees think is stingy and reluctant is, in fact, compassionate—moving toward repentant sinners with welcome.

The son begins his confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son…” (v. 21). And then something astonishing happens: the father doesn’t let him finish. The son never gets to say, “Treat me as a hired servant.” The father will not negotiate sonship. He will not accept the terms of shame.

Instead, he turns to the servants and says, “Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet” (v. 22). This isn’t merely clean clothing. It’s restoration.

- The robe is honor and covering—“You belong here.”
- The ring, likely suggesting belonging and even authority in the household, signals, “You’re family.”
- The shoes say, “You’re not coming back as a barefoot laborer. You’re not hired help. You’re my son.”

Then the father says, “Bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate” (v. 23). The father doesn’t stage a quiet re-entry. He throws a feast. He goes public with grace.

Why? “For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (v. 24). This is resurrection language. Lostness is a kind of death. Coming home is a kind of life from the dead.

And “they began to celebrate” (v. 24). That’s what the Father’s house sounds like when sinners come home: music.

### The Older Son: Staying Near, Living Far

Jesus could have ended there. Many of us would. Younger son returns, father forgives—beautiful moral, happy ending.

But Jesus keeps going because He’s not only talking to obvious prodigals. He’s talking to grumblers. He’s talking to the kinds of lost people who don’t look lost.

“Now his older son was in the field” (v. 25). He’s been working. He hears music and dancing and asks what’s happening. When he finds out his brother is back and the fattened calf has been killed, “he was angry and refused to go in” (v. 28).

And again the father moves. “His father came out and entreated him” (v. 28). Don’t miss that: the father goes to the younger son in the far country, and he goes to the older son in the front yard. He pursues both.

The older son answers, “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command” (v. 29). Hear his relationship with the father: *served… command.* He speaks like an employee, not a son. And then: “Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (v. 29). Not “with you.” Not “with our family.” Just “my friends.” He has been in the house, but his heart has been elsewhere.

Then the contempt spills out: “But when this son of yours came…” (v. 30). He can’t say, “my brother.” Resentment de-families people. It rewrites relationships so that we can justify our coldness.

Now, let’s be gentle here, because many people in church know this older-brother life from the inside. What does it feel like to be him?

It feels like always being the responsible one. It feels like doing what’s right and never being noticed. It feels like watching others wreck their lives and then get attention when they crawl back. It feels like carrying quiet anger while still showing up, still working, still doing your duty. It feels like believing that if you do enough, God will finally give you what you deserve.

And that’s exactly the trap: the older brother thinks obedience is a lever. “I have served. I have never disobeyed. Therefore you owe me.” But love cannot be earned like wages. And when we turn the Father into a boss, we lose the joy of being a child.

The father replies tenderly: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31). In other words: “You’ve been near me the whole time, but you’ve lived as though my heart is closed. You’ve mistaken my house for a workplace. You could have asked. You could have enjoyed. You could have come in.”

Then the father says, “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (v. 32). And notice: “this *your brother*.” The father is gently re-naming reality. Grace restores relationship, not just behavior.

Jesus ends the parable without telling us whether the older brother goes in. That’s not an oversight; it’s an invitation. The Pharisees are listening. The door is open. The music is playing. The Father is pleading. The question hangs in the air: Will you join the joy of God—or will you stand outside clutching your record?

And that’s the seam where the story becomes personal. It’s one thing to analyze two brothers. It’s another thing to hear Jesus ask, “Where are you in this?”

So let’s step out of the narrative and into our lives.

### Where Are You in the Story?

**1) If you are in the far country, you can come home.**  
Some of you hear the younger son and think, *That’s me.* You may not be in a dramatic rebellion, but you are hungry. You are tired of pretending. You are weary of the cycle: pleasure that fades, control that collapses, shame that grows.

The turning point in the story is not that the son cleans himself up. It’s that he gets up. “I will arise and go to my father.”

If you can pray nothing else today, pray the first honest line: “Father, I have sinned.” And then take the next step toward home—talk to a trusted believer, confess what needs confessing, ask for help. Repentance may involve hard conversations and real changes, but at its core it is return. You are received not because you can pay your way back, but because God’s heart is to welcome—and because Christ has borne the cost of your homecoming.

**2) If you are the older brother, you can come inside.**  
Some of you are not tempted by the far country out there; you are tempted by the far country at home: resentment, comparison, quiet superiority, joylessness.

Here’s a diagnostic question, simple but revealing: When someone who has failed badly is restored—when the addict gets clean, when a marriage is rescued, when a person who hurt you starts to change—is your first instinct joy, or suspicion? Do you find yourself thinking, *They don’t deserve this*?

If so, you may be standing outside the feast.

And hear this carefully: the father does not shame the older brother. He comes out to him. He entreats him. God is not only willing to forgive your obvious sins; He is willing to heal your hidden ones—the ones that look like faithfulness on the outside but are bitter on the inside.

What would it mean for you to “come in”? It might mean telling God the truth: “Father, I’m angry. I feel overlooked. I feel like I’ve been trying to earn what you wanted to give.” It might mean letting go of the scoreboard. It might mean receiving your identity not as a worker with a performance review, but as a beloved child.

The tragedy of the older brother is not that he lacked information. It’s that he missed the father’s presence. “You are always with me,” the father says. That’s not a rebuke; it’s an invitation: *Come enjoy what has been yours all along.*

**3) If you belong to this church, be a person who makes room.**  
Luke 15 began with an accusation: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” What if that became our reputation?

Not as a slogan, but as a practice—on a Tuesday, not just on a Sunday.

It can look as simple as this: when someone disappears for months and then comes back, you don’t corner them with questions. You sit with them. You say, “We’ve missed you. There’s a seat for you.” When someone confesses sin, you don’t make them pay with perpetual suspicion; you help them take wise steps forward while still treating them as a person God welcomes. When someone returns, you don’t whisper; you rejoice.

And this is not only a question for “the church” as an institution. It’s a question for you and me personally: when someone comes home, will you be the one who makes room at the table—or the one who stands back, arms crossed?

### The Cross: The Cost of the Welcome

One more thing needs to be said, because the parable is honest, but it’s not the whole story.

The parable shows the Father’s heart—His compassion, His pursuit, His joy. But it doesn’t explain the cost of forgiveness. In real life, someone always pays. When the younger son wastes the inheritance, the father absorbs the loss. He doesn’t pretend it didn’t happen. He bears it.

And in the full sweep of Scripture, that is exactly what God does—only infinitely more. The Father’s welcome is not sentimental. It is costly.

How can God run to sinners without making light of sin? How can He embrace the guilty and still be holy?

Because the Son goes to the cross.

In Jesus Christ, God does not merely watch the road for us; He comes down the road for us. He takes on our flesh. He enters our far country. He bears our shame—not just the shame of an undignified run, but the shame of a crucified death. So where are you today?

The Feast That Never Ends  
A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32  

1. A Father on the Porch  

A few summers ago I visited a parishioner named Dorothy, ninety-three years young, who insisted on sitting on her front porch every evening. She told me she was “waiting for the wind to bring Johnny home.” Johnny was her youngest—her “late-in-life miracle,” she called him—who had stormed out at nineteen after a fight about curfews and credit-card debt. Thirty-one years, three rehab stints, two marriages, and one closed adoption later, Johnny phoned from a truck stop in Toledo: “Mom, I don’t know if you want to see me.” Dorothy said, “I’ll leave the porch light on. You can’t miss it.” At 2:37 a.m. she heard gravel crunch, and there he was—forty pounds heavier, hair gone gray, still her boy. She didn’t wait for him to reach the steps; she met him on the sidewalk, held his face in her trembling hands, and whispered, “I knew the wind would blow you home.”  

That porch light is the closest image I know to the heart of the parable we call “The Prodigal Son.” But the story is bigger than one wayward child; it is Jesus’ picture of the God who refuses to dim the lights, the household that will not cancel the feast, the love that outlives every pigpen we insist on building for ourselves.  

2. The Story Jesus Told (Luke 15:11-32)  

Jesus is dining with tax-collectors and sinners, and the Pharisees are muttering. So he tells three stories—lost sheep, lost coin, lost son—each ending in a party. The third is the longest, most emotionally complex. Let’s walk through it slowly.  

A. The Request (v. 11-12)  
“Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me.” In Jewish law the younger son would receive one-third of the estate after the father’s death. To ask early is tantamount to saying, “You are worth more to me dead than alive.” The father could have stonewalled, hired lawyers, or disowned the boy. Instead he “divided his living”—literally, his bios, his life—between them. Grace begins by handing itself over to be trampled.  

B. The Far Country (v. 13-16)  
“Not many days later the younger son gathered all…and took his journey.” The verb is apostasas—from which we get “apostasy.” He goes to a “far country,” outside the covenant, where the Torah’s early-warning systems cannot chase him. There he “scattered” (diaskorpizō) the inheritance; the same verb is used for seed thrown on rocky soil in the parable of the sower. Waste is built into the plot. Famine follows; the pigpen is the last stop for a Jewish boy. He feeds the unclean animals and “no one gave him anything.” Notice the triple negation: no bread, no compassion, no nameless benefactor. Sin is always a sentence that begins with “no one.”  

C. The turning point (v. 17)  
“But when he came to himself…” Not “when he came to his senses”—that’s too cerebral. The Greek is eis heauton de elthōn—he came to his self, his true self hidden in the father’s heart. Repentance is not a calculation but a recognition: “I am still someone’s child.” He rehearses a speech: “Make me as one of your hired servants.” The wages of a day-laborer were enough to survive, but never enough to belong.  

D. The Run (v. 20)  
“While he was still a long way off, his father saw him…” The verb is aorist: the father “saw,” suddenly, as if he had been scanning the horizon daily. Then he “ran.” Aristocratic Palestinian patriarchs do not sprint through dusty streets; they walk with retinue. The father bears the indignity, hikes up his robe, exposes his ankles, and runs because etiquette will not outrank love.  

E. The Embrace (v. 20-24)  
Before the son finishes his carefully rehearsed apology, the father interrupts with four verbs: “felt compassion, ran, embraced, kissed.” Only then does he call for the best robe (the one reserved for honored guests), a ring (signet of authority, not servanthood), and shoes (slaves went barefoot). The feast—“kill the fatted calf”—is covenant language: “Let us cut, eat, and rejoice.” The calf has been grain-fed for a year; this is not a spontaneous barbecue but a planned extravagance, as if the father had been prepping for a celebration he refused to believe would never come.  

F. The Older Son (v. 25-32)  
He hears music and refuses to enter. Customs required the eldest to co-host village festivities; his boycott is a public insult. The father “came out”—again leaving the house, again bearing shame—and pleaded. The older son’s speech is a litany of slave-language: “I have slaved for you…you never gave me a kid.” He has reduced relationship to transaction. But the father reminds him: “All that is mine is yours.” The feast is not a reward for repentance; it is the eternal nature of the household. The parable ends unresolved; Jesus leaves the Pharisees standing outside the music, the porch light still on, the door still open.  

3. What Kind of God Is This?  

A. A God Who Risks  
Augustine noted that by giving the inheritance the father “lost” what was his, yet gained the son. Grace is not safe; it mortgages possessions to buy the beloved.  

B. A God Who Runs  
Athanasius said the Incarnation is the eternal sprint of God toward us. Every Eucharist is the ongoing arrival of the running Father.  

C. A God Who Feasts  
The calf, the ring, the robe are not props but sacraments: here the far country becomes near, the hungry become heirs, time itself bends toward supper.  

4. Two Lost Sons, One Found Father  

Tim Keller reminds us the parable is not called “The Prodigal Son” but “The Lost Sons.” The younger is lost in rebellion; the elder is lost in religion. One insults the father with riotous living; the other insults him with resentful obeying. Both need re-birth, not reform. The younger’s healing begins when he faces his unworthiness; the elder’s healing begins when he faces his un-love. The church is the household where both surprises keep happening: the scandal of forgiveness and the scandal of inclusion.  

5. Porch Lights for Monday Morning  

A. For the Runners  
Some of us are still in the far country, feeding pigs we never meant to own—credit cards, click bait, hidden search histories, bottles in the bottom drawer. Jesus’ word is not “Clean up first” but “Remember who you are.” Start walking. The light is on.  

B. For the Responsible  
Some of us are elder brothers: we tithe, we serve coffee, we know the liturgy by heart, yet rage when grace is given to people who “didn’t earn it.” The invitation is to come inside, trade the ledger for laughter, discover that obedience without joy is just another pigpen.  

C. For the Weary Parents  
Some of us stand on porches: children addicted, spouses silent, dreams deferred. The parable says you cannot chase your beloved into the far country without becoming part of the mess. But you can keep the light on, keep scanning the horizon, keep trusting that the same wind that took them can bring them back.  

D. For the Whole Church  
Every time we share the peace, pass the cup, hand a visitor a bulletin, we rehearse the feast that never ends. The Eucharist is the fatted calf, roasted and ready, announcing that the dead can rise, the lost can be found, the older can still come in.  

6. A Closing Picture  

Dorothy’s porch light is still burning. Johnny relapsed twice after that first homecoming, but he keeps coming back. Last Christmas he helped serve communion, tears sliding into the chalice. After the service he told me, “Preacher, I finally get it: the feast isn’t just for the day I come home; the feast is what keeps me home.”  

Friends, the table is set. The music has started. The robe is shoulder-wide, the ring is sized for you, the calf is fragrant with mercy. Whether you smell of pigpen or Pharisee, the Father is running.  
Come inside.  
The porch light is not going out.

The Feast That Never Ends  
Luke 15:11–32  
Sunday Morning, Ordinary Time  

I want to tell you about a porch light that refuses to die.

Dorothy was ninety-three when I first visited her in the little yellow house on Maple. Every evening she dragged a wicker rocker to the edge of her porch and sat with a sweater across her knees, even in July. “I’m waiting for the wind to bring Johnny home,” she said. Johnny was her youngest, the baby who came after two miscarriages and a decade of quiet bedrooms. At nineteen he had exploded over curfews and credit-card debt, slammed doors, and peeled out of the driveway in a rust-red Chevette. Thirty-one years, three rehabs, two marriages, and one closed adoption later, Dorothy’s phone rang at 1:12 a.m. A voice thick with road weariness: “Mom, I don’t know if you want to see me.” She did not hesitate. “I’ll leave the porch light on. You can’t miss it.” At 2:37 she heard gravel crunch under Michelin tires. Before Johnny could kill the engine, Dorothy was off the porch, barefoot on the cold sidewalk, cupping the face of a fifty-year-old man who still smelled like diesel and regret. “I knew the wind would blow you home,” she whispered.

That porch light is the closest image I know to the parable we usually call “The Prodigal Son.” But the story is bigger than one wayward child. It is Jesus’ picture of the God who refuses to dim the lights, the household that will not cancel the feast, the love that outlives every pigpen we insist on building for ourselves.

Listen to the story again—not as a morality play you memorized in felt-board Sunday school, but as a movie you walk into, knees dusty, mouth tasting of your own far country.

A man has two sons. The younger steps forward, eyes steady, voice polite and lethal: “Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me.” In our ears it sounds like a young adult asking for an advance on his inheritance. In Palestinian ears it is a death sentence: “I wish you were dead.” Jewish law allows the younger son one-third of the estate after the funeral; this boy wants it before. The father could refuse, could hire lawyers, could cut the will in half and disinherit the brat. Instead, Luke tells us, “he divided his living”—his bios, his very life—between them. Grace begins by handing itself over to be trampled.

Within days the boy stuffs a duffel with cash and heads south. The far country is not measured in miles; it is any place where God’s voice is muted by other music. At first the nightlife is dazzling. Lamps flicker in the warm dusk, wine flows the color of rubies, laughter ricochets off stone. He tips servers the equivalent of a month’s rent, buys rounds for strangers who slap his back and call him “brother.” Weeks blur into months. The wallet thins, the crowd thins, the invitations dry up. A famine stalks the land—not just of bread, but of belonging. The only job he can find is slopping pigs, animals that embody everything his upbringing called unclean. He stands knee-deep in their stench, envying their pods because no one gives him anything. Sin is always a sentence that begins with “no one.”

Luke writes, “When he came to himself.” Not “when he came to his senses”—that sounds like a spreadsheet correction. The Greek is eis heauton de elthōn: he descended into his true self, the self that had never stopped being a son. He rehearses a speech: “Make me as one of your hired servants.” A day-laborer earns enough to survive, but never enough to belong. He is still negotiating wages when he turns toward home.

While he is still a long way off—down the bend, a dot on the horizon—the father sees him. The verb is aorist, a snapshot: one glance and the old man’s heart detonates with compassion. Then the patriarch does the unthinkable: he gathers his robes and runs. Aristocratic Palestinian fathers do not sprint; they process, attended by servants. But etiquette will not outrank love. He hikes up fabric, exposes ankles to shame, and sprints through the dust he once watched his boy kick up in anger. Before the son can finish his carefully rehearsed apology, the father interrupts with four verbs: felt compassion, ran, embraced, kissed. Only then does he call for the best robe—the one kept for honored guests—a ring that carries the family seal, and shoes because slaves go barefoot. The feast is already in motion: “Bring the fatted calf, the one we’ve grain-fed for a year, and kill it.” This is not a spontaneous barbecue; this is a celebration the father had been planning in his imagination every night the porch light stayed on.

He hears tambourines, smells roasted meat, sees servants scurrying with garlands. He calls one over, asks what the commotion means. When he learns the prodigal has returned, his shoulders stiffen. Jesus is dining with tax-collectors and sinners, and the Pharisees are muttering. So he tells three stories—lost sheep, lost coin, lost son—each ending in a party. The third is the longest, most emotionally complex. Let’s walk through it slowly.

There he “scattered” (diaskorpizō) the inheritance; the same verb is used for seed thrown on rocky soil in the parable of the sower. Waste is built into the plot. Sin is always a sentence that begins with “no one.”

“But when he came to himself…” Not “when he came to his senses”—that’s too cerebral. The Greek is eis heauton elthōn—he came to his self, his true self hidden in the father’s heart. The father “came out”—again leaving the house, again bearing shame—and pleaded. The older son’s speech is a litany of slave-language: “I have slaved for you…you never gave me a kid.” He has reduced relationship to transaction. But the father reminds him: “All that is mine is yours.” The feast is not a reward for repentance; it is the eternal nature of the household. The parable ends unresolved; Jesus leaves the Pharisees standing outside the music, the porch light still on, the door still open.  

3. What Kind of God Is This?  

A. A God Who Risks  
Augustine noted that by giving the inheritance the father “lost” what was his, yet gained the son. Grace is not safe; it mortgages possessions to buy the beloved.  

B. A God Who Runs  
Athanasius said the Incarnation is the eternal sprint of God toward us. Every Eucharist is the ongoing arrival of the running Father.  

C. A God Who Feasts  
The calf, the ring, the robe are not props but sacraments: here the far country becomes near, the hungry become heirs, time itself bends toward supper.  

D. A God Who Scandalizes  
This is the God the Pharisees could not fit into their ledgers. He shames himself before he will shame a sinner. He throws parties for the undeserving and calls the worthy to lay down their calculators. The older son is not angry at his brother; he is angry at his father’s reckless mercy. And that, Jesus says, is the final lostness—refusing to rejoice because someone else got what they didn’t deserve.  

4. Two Lost Sons, One Found Father  

Tim Keller reminds us the parable is not called “The Prodigal Son” but “The Lost Sons.” The younger is lost in rebellion; the elder is lost in religion. One insults the father with riotous living; the other insults him with resentful obeying. Both need re-birth, not reform. The younger’s healing begins when he faces his unworthiness; the elder’s healing begins when he faces his un-love. The church is the household where both surprises keep happening: the scandal of forgiveness and the scandal of inclusion.  

Which brings us to this Monday morning. If the Spirit has been nudging you, chances are you already know which brother you resemble. Let’s name the places where the porch light is still burning.  

5. Porch Lights for Monday Morning  

A. For the Runners  
Some of us are still in the far country, feeding pigs we never meant to own—credit cards, click bait, hidden search histories, bottles in the bottom drawer. Jesus’ word is not “Clean up first” but “Remember who you are.” Start walking. The light is on.  

B. For the Responsible  
Some of us are elder brothers: we tithe, we serve coffee, we know the liturgy by heart, yet rage when grace is given to people who “didn’t earn it.” Remember, Jesus told this story because the Pharisees—the religious professionals—were furious that he welcomed “sinners.” They stood outside muttering, just like the older brother. The invitation is to come inside, trade the ledger for laughter, discover that obedience without joy is just another pigpen, and that the Father’s joy is not a reward for work but the very air of the household.  

C. For the Weary Parents  
Some of us stand on porches: children addicted, spouses silent, dreams deferred. The father did not chase his son, but he also never stopped believing the boy’s true identity was “beloved.” He scanned the horizon daily, trusting that the same road that took the boy away could bring him home. Your role is to reflect the Father’s unshakeable conviction that the beloved are still beloved, even when they are far away. Keep the light on, yes—but also keep your own heart soft, lest you become an older brother when they finally crunch the gravel.  

D. For the Whole Church  
Every time we share the peace, pass the cup, hand a visitor a bulletin, we rehearse the feast that never ends. The Eucharist is the fatted calf, roasted and ready, announcing that the dead can rise, the lost can be found, the older can still come in. The table is not a reward for good behavior; it is the porch light made of bread and wine.  

6. A Closing Picture  

Dorothy’s porch light is still burning. Johnny relapsed twice after that first homecoming, but he keeps coming back. Last Christmas he helped serve communion, tears sliding into the chalice. After the service he told me, “Preacher, I finally get it: the feast isn’t just for the day I come home; the feast is what keeps me home.”  

Friends, the table is set. The music has started. The robe is shoulder-wide, the ring is sized for you, the calf is fragrant with mercy. Whether you smell of pigpen or Pharisee, the Father is running.  
Come inside.  
The porch light is not going out.

The Light That Keeps Moving  
A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32  

1. A Father on the Porch  

Dorothy was ninety-three and stubborn about her front porch. Every evening, even in Ohio drizzle, she dragged a lawn-chair out and watched the road.  
“Waiting for the wind to bring Johnny home,” she told me.  
Johnny was her youngest—her “late-in-life miracle”—who left at nineteen after a screaming match over curfews and credit-card debt. Thirty-one years, three rehabs, two marriages, and one closed adoption later, he phoned from a Toledo truck stop:  
“Mom, I don’t know if you want to see me.”  
Dorothy said, “I’ll leave the porch light on. You can’t miss it.”  
At 2:37 she heard gravel crunch. She didn’t wait for him to reach the steps; she met him on the sidewalk, held his weathered face, whispered, “I knew the wind would blow you home.”  

That porch light is the closest picture I know of the heart of the story we call “The Prodigal Son.” But the parable is bigger than one wayward child. It is Jesus’ snapshot of a God who refuses to dim the lights, a household that will not cancel the feast, a love that outlives every pigpen we insist on building for ourselves.  

2. Two Boys, One Broken Heart (Luke 15:11-32)  

Jesus is eating with tax-collectors and sinners; Pharisees mutter. So he tells three stories—lost sheep, lost coin, lost sons—each ending in music. Let’s walk through the longest, most emotionally complicated, in two movements.  

A. The Younger Son’s Journey  

(1) The Ask (v. 11-12)  
“Father, give me the share that belongs to me.”  
Jewish law said the younger son would receive one-third—after the father’s death. To ask early is to say, “I wish you were dead.” Shockingly, the father “divided his life between them.” Notice the word *them*. The older boy also cashes out; he just stays put. Both sons receive their inheritance up-front. Grace hands itself over to be wounded.  

(2) The Far Country (v. 13-16)  
“Not many days later the younger son gathered all…and took his journey.”  
The Greek verb is *apostasas*—“he revolted completely.” He scatters the money; famine follows; the pigpen is the last stop for a kosher kid. He feeds unclean animals, and “no one gave him anything.” Three strikes: no food, no compassion, no nameless donor. Sin always ends in a sentence that begins with “nobody.”  

(3) The Turning Point (v. 17)  
“But when he came to himself…”  
Not “when he came to his senses.” The original says he returned *to his self*, the self the father had always imagined. Repentance is remembering whose child you are. He rehearses: “Make me a hired hand”—a wage that keeps you alive but never invites you inside.  

B. The Father’s Extravagant Welcome  

(1) The Run (v. 20)  
“While he was still a long way off, his father saw him…”  
Aorist tense—one glance, daily practiced. Then he *ran*. Middle-eastern patriarchs do not sprint; they delegate dignity. This father hikes up his robe, flashes his ankles, and bears the neighborhood’s laughter, because protocol will not outrank love. Athanasius said the Incarnation is the eternal sprint of God toward us.  

(2) The Embrace (v. 20-24)  
Before the boy finishes his apology, the father interrupts with four verbs: “felt compassion, ran, embraced, kissed.” Only then comes the best robe (honored guest), the ring (authority to transact), shoes (no slave wears shoes). Next, “kill the fatted calf”—an animal grain-fed for a year, waiting for a celebration the father refused to believe would never come. In that culture sharing the meat sealed a covenant: “Let us cut, eat, and rejoice together.” The feast is not a reward for repentance; it is the permanent nature of the household.  

(3) The Older Brother (v. 25-32)  
He hears music and boycotts. Customs required the eldest to co-host; his refusal is a public slap. The father *comes out again*, bearing shame a second time, and pleads. The son’s speech is a ledger:  
“These many years I have *served* you…you never gave me a kid.”  
Notice the verb *served*—literally, “slaved.” He has relationship reduced to transaction. Yet the father answers with tenderness: “All that is mine is yours.” The feast was always his, but joy cannot be forced.  

The parable ends unresolved: will the older son enter? Jesus leaves the Pharisees—and us—standing outside the music, the porch light still on, the door still open.  

3. Two Lost Sons, One Found Father  

Tim Keller reminds us the parable could be called “The Lost Sons.”  
- Younger lost in **rebellion**: “I’ll break the rules.”  
- Older lost in **religion**: “I’ll keep the rules and make you owe me.”  
Both insult the father; both need re-birth, not reform.  
The younger’s healing begins when he faces his unworthiness; the elder’s begins when he faces his un-love. The church is the household where both surprises keep happening: the scandal of forgiveness and the scandal of inclusion.  

4. Porch Lights for Monday Morning  

A. For the Runners—still feeding pigs we never meant to own  
Maybe your far country is a browser history, a bottle in the bottom drawer, a 3 a.m. lie you keep telling yourself. Jesus’ word is not “Clean up first.” It is “Remember whose child you are.” Start walking. The light is moving toward you.  

B. For the Responsible—tired, faithful, secretly angry  
Imagine Sarah: twenty-three years of perfect attendance, treasurer of the Women’s League, and she watches the pastor welcome back the guy who emptied the youth fund. She feels acid in her throat.  
If that’s you, hear the Father: “You have never lacked my love, only my party.” Obedience that has forgotten how to sing is still lostness. Come inside; the music is for you too.  

C. For the Weary Parents—on porches that feel like watch-towers  
Some of you have waited years, and the gravel still hasn’t crunched. The parable promises no timetable; it promises that the Father’s waiting is as faithful as his running. Keep the light on, but let the church be the porch with you.  

D. For the Whole Church—every time we share bread and cup  
The Eucharist is the fatted calf, roasted and ready, announcing that the dead can rise and the lost can be found. Every communion is a rehearsal of the feast that never ends.  

5. A Closing Picture and a Next Step  

Dorothy’s porch light is still burning. Johnny relapsed twice after that first homecoming, but he keeps coming back. Last Christmas he helped serve communion, tears sliding into the chalice. Afterward he said, “Preacher, I finally get it: the feast isn’t just for the day I come home; the feast is what keeps me home.”  

So—  
- If you smell of pigpen, the robe is shoulder-wide.  
- If you smell of ledger-pages, the ring is sized for you.  
- If you smell of tears on a porch, the father is already running your road.  

This week identify your pigpen—what you feed that never feeds you back—or identify your ledger—where you keep score. Bring whichever it is to the table today.  

The music has started. The porch light is not going out.  
Come inside.
