The Feast That Never Ends  
A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32  

1. A Father on the Porch  

A few summers ago I visited Dorothy, ninety-three years young, who insisted on sitting on her front porch every evening. She told me she was “waiting for the wind to bring Johnny home.” Johnny was her youngest—her “late-in-life miracle”—who had stormed out at nineteen after a fight about curfews and credit-card debt. Thirty-one years, three rehab stints, two marriages, and one closed adoption later, Johnny phoned from a truck stop in Toledo: “Mom, I don’t know if you want to see me.” Dorothy said, “I’ll leave the porch light on. You can’t miss it.” At 2:37 a.m. she heard gravel crunch, and there he was—forty pounds heavier, hair gone gray, still her boy. She met him on the sidewalk, held his face in her trembling hands, and whispered, “I knew the wind would blow you home.”  

That porch light is the closest image I know to the heart of the parable we call “The Prodigal Son.” But the story is bigger than one wayward child; it is Jesus’ picture of the God who refuses to dim the lights, the household that will not cancel the feast, the love that outlives every pigpen we insist on building for ourselves.  

2. The Story Jesus Told (Luke 15:11-32)  

Jesus is dining with tax-collectors and sinners; Pharisees mutter. So he tells three stories—lost sheep, lost coin, lost son—each ending in a party. Let’s walk through the longest and most emotionally complex.  

A. The Request (v. 11-12)  
“Father, give me the share…that falls to me.” Jewish law gave the younger son one-third after the father’s death. To ask early is to say, “You are worth more to me dead than alive.” The father could have hired lawyers. Instead he “divided his living”—literally his bios, his life—between them. Grace begins by handing itself over to be trampled.  

B. The Far Country (v. 13-16)  
“Not many days later…he journeyed.” The Greek verb is apostasas—he apostatized, stepped outside the covenant. There he “scattered” the inheritance, seed on rocky ground. Famine follows; the pigpen is the last stop for a Jewish boy. He feeds unclean animals while “no one gave him anything.” Sin always ends in a triple negation: no bread, no compassion, no nameless benefactor.  

C. The Turning (v. 17)  
“But when he came to himself…” Not “came to his senses”—he came to his true self, the one hidden in the father’s heart. Repentance begins with memory: “I am still someone’s child.”  

D. The Run (v. 20)  
“While he was still a long way off, his father saw him…” The tense is sudden; the father has been scanning the horizon daily. Then he “ran.” Respectable elders did not sprint; they hired messengers. The father bears the indignity because etiquette will not outrank love.  

E. The Embrace (v. 20-24)  
Before the boy finishes his apology, the father interrupts with four verbs: felt compassion, ran, embraced, kissed. He orders the best robe (honored guest), a ring (signet of authority), shoes (slaves went barefoot). The fatted calf has been grain-fed for a year; this is planned extravagance, as if the father had been prepping for a celebration he refused to believe would never come.  

F. The Older Son—Also Lost (v. 25-32)  
He hears music and refuses to enter. Customs required the eldest to co-host; his boycott is public shaming. The father “came out”—again leaving the house, again bearing shame—and pleaded. The son’s speech is a ledger: “I have slaved…you never gave me a kid.” He has reduced relationship to transaction. The father answers, “All that is mine is yours.” The feast is not a reward for repentance; it is the permanent nature of the household. Jesus ends the story with the older brother still outside, the porch light still on, the door still open.  

Notice: the parable is not called “The Prodigal Son” but “The Lost Sons.” The younger is lost in rebellion; the elder is lost in religion. One insults the father with riotous living; the other with resentful obeying. Both need re-birth, not reform.  

3. A God Who Risks, Runs, and Feasts  

A. A God Who Risks  
Augustine noted that by giving the inheritance the father “lost” possessions yet gained the son. Grace mortgages itself to buy the beloved.  

B. A God Who Runs  
The church fathers saw the Incarnation as the eternal refusal of God to remain distant—what we might call the divine sprint toward dust. Every Communion is the ongoing arrival of that running Father.  

C. A God Who Feasts  
The calf, the ring, the robe are sacraments: here the far country becomes near, the hungry become heirs, time bends toward supper. This is not a single banquet; it is the hors d’oeuvre of Revelation 19, the marriage supper of the Lamb that will outlast time.  

4. Two Lost Sons, One Found Father—And Us  

Johnny told me that the second time he relapsed he was sure the porch light had finally burned out. He drove past the house twice, headlights off, afraid the bulb would be dark. It wasn’t. Dorothy had screwed in a dusk-to-dawn sensor years earlier. “I never want him to think the house is closed,” she said.  

Some of us are still in the far country, feeding pigs we never meant to own—credit-card balances, doom-scrolling timelines, bottles in the bottom drawer. Jesus’ word is not “Clean up first” but “Remember who you are.” Start walking. The light is on.  

Some of us are elder brothers: we tithe, we serve coffee, we know the liturgy by heart, and we are exhausted. We carry the church budget, the aging parents, the moral weight of the family. When grace is handed to people who “didn’t earn it,” it feels like betrayal. The invitation is to come inside, trade the ledger for laughter, discover that obedience without joy is just another pigpen.  

Some of us stand on porches: children addicted, spouses silent, dreams deferred. Keeping the light on may mean answering the 3 a.m. call—or refusing to enable chaos while refusing to lock the door. It means having the counselor’s number ready, the bedroom made up, the boundaries clear, and the porch bulb replaced every year.  

And some of us are the church. Our budgets are feast-preparation, not maintenance. Our buildings are porches, not fortresses. When we share the peace, pass the cup, hand a visitor a bulletin, we rehearse the feast that never ends. The Lord’s Supper is the fatted calf, roasted and ready, announcing that the dead can rise, the lost can be found, the older can still come in.  

6. Come Inside  

Dorothy’s porch light is still burning. Johnny relapsed again, but he keeps coming back. Last Christmas he helped serve communion, tears sliding into the chalice. After the service he told me, “Preacher, I finally get it: the feast isn’t just for the day I come home; the feast is what keeps me home.”  

Friends, the table is set. The music has started. The robe is shoulder-wide, the ring sized for you, the calf fragrant with mercy. Whether you smell of pigpen or Pharisee, the Father is running.  

So come inside.  
The porch light is not going out.

rxZ1gGVPdyqD8GCXt-NCO.text:
The Other Son in the Mirror  
A sermon on Luke 15:11-32  

1. The hook—when the lights come on  

In the winter of 2019, a young man named Marcus was dropped at the greyhound station in our city with a duffel bag, a dead cell-phone, and the address of our church’s shelter.  He had burned every bridge—taken every cent from his widowed mother’s retirement, sold her car for half its value, and disappeared for three years.  On the night he arrived, we gave him the bottom bunk in a room with four other men.  He wept himself to sleep, not from regret, but from the shock of being received.  

Three weeks later, his mother, Mrs. Alvarez, phoned the office.  She had driven four hours, sat in our parking lot for an hour more, and finally walked in carrying a foil pan of tamales.  She spotted Marcus sweeping the cafeteria.  The room froze.  Marcus dropped the broom.  She took three steps, opened her arms, and the whole shelter heard him sob, “Mom, I’m sorry.  I don’t deserve this.”  She answered only, “You’re my son.  Come home.”  

That scene is the closest I have ever come to watching Scripture happen in real time.  It is also only half the story.  Because when the celebration dinner was held in our fellowship hall, Mrs. Alvarez’s older son—steady, reliable, the one who had stayed home to pay the mortgage—stood outside the double-doors, arms crossed, refusing to enter.  “She never threw me a party,” he muttered.  And in that moment we had not one, but two prodigals: one who left home in the body, and one who left home in the heart.  

2. The text—listening again with first-century ears  

Luke 15 is one long answer to one short accusation: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them” (v. 2).  Jesus tells three stories—lost sheep, lost coin, lost son—each ending in a feast.  The third story is the longest, most detailed parable He ever spoke.  It is not called “the prodigal son,” but “the two lost sons,” or better, “the running father.”  Three characters, three movements, three mirrors.  

A. The younger son—radical disrespect  
“Give me the share of the estate that falls to me” (v. 12).  Jewish law allowed a father to divide property during his lifetime, but the request is tantamount to saying, “I wish you were dead.”  The father complies: he liquidates land, herds, and honor.  The boy converts inheritance into cash, cash into distant pleasure, and pleasure into pig-slop.  Jesus’ hearers would have expected lightning.  Instead they get a father who keeps scanning the horizon.  

B. The father—scandalous compassion  
“While he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran” (v. 20).  Noble Palestinian landowners did not run—ever.  The robe hikes up, the sandals slap dust, the crowd gawks.  Before the son can finish his rehearsed speech, the father interrupts: “Bring the best robe”—the ceremonial robe worn at banquets—“put a ring on his hand”—the family signet, authority restored—“sandals on his feet”—only sons wore shoes; servants went barefoot.  Then the feast: “the fatted calf,” enough meat for an entire village.  This is not private forgiveness; it is public rehabilitation.  

C. The older son—polite rebellion  
He hears music, refuses to enter.  The father—again!—goes out, this time to the elder.  The older son’s speech is precise: “Look, these many years I have served you” (v. 29).  The Greek word is douleuō, “I slaved.”  No intimacy, no joy, no sonship—only contract.  He has never asked for a goat; his obedience has been calculation.  He accuses the brother of consorting with prostitutes—an ugly detail nowhere in the story; he projects sin onto the repentant to justify his own resentment.  The feast is ready, but he stands in the outer darkness of his own choosing.  

3. Exegetical surprises—what we almost miss  

1. Both sons are lost.  One by breaking commands, the other by keeping them.  Sin is not only deviation but also diversion: the younger diverts grace into license; the elder diverts grace into wages.  

2. The father loses twice.  He surrenders property to the younger, then dignity to the younger, then intimacy to the elder.  The cross is already hidden in the story: the father absorbs shame so his children can live.  

3. The story ends unresolved.  We are not told whether the elder enters the feast.  Jesus leaves the ending open because the Pharisees are still standing outside the banquet of grace.  The question is hurled into the crowd: will you come in?  

4. Application—finding ourselves in the painting  

A. To the younger prodigals—those who left  
Some of us carry the smell of the far country: bankruptcy, addiction, divorce, abortion, betrayal.  Shame tells us to negotiate our way back as hired hands—offer restitution, serve on every committee, never ask for too much.  The parable forbids it.  You are welcomed not because you have a plan but because you have a Father.  Repentance is not the price of admission; it is the door through which the Father runs.  Bring your hunger, your stench, your empty pockets; the robe is already tailored, the ring already engraved.  The feast begins before you finish the sentence.  

B. To the elder prodigals—those who stayed  
Some of us have never left home, yet we stand outside the music.  Our obedience has been loveless, our service resentful.  We keep score: I tithe, I teach Sunday school, I memorize verses—where’s my calf?  The horror is that we can be in the field of grace while missing the heart of the Father.  The remedy is not more striving but astonishment: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31).  The elder son already owns the estate; he simply never asked.  Move from the economics of merit to the ecology of gift.  The party is not reward for the younger; it is revelation for the older.  Come in, pick up the tambourine, dance with the ex-prostitutes, discover that joy is the final righteousness.  

C. To the fathers and mothers—those who wait  
Maybe you are the one scanning the road, the porch light burning holes in the dark.  God assigns you the impossible task of letting your children choose famine so they can discover grace.  You will be asked to absorb shame, to run when dignity says walk, to celebrate when justice says scold.  Do it anyway.  Your tears are seeds; the feast will sprout.  

D. To the church—God’s banquet committee  
We are entrusted with two ministries: the robe and the dance.  The robe is the garment of baptismal identity—put it on prodigals before they smell like church.  The dance is the rhythm of celebration—train our hearts to rejoice when the wrong people get saved.  Whenever we grade grace on a curve, we become elder-brother congregations, museums of resentment.  Whenever we fling doors wide, we become Father-houses where the only admission ticket is emptiness.  

5. The invitation—will you come to the party?  

Jesus does not tell this story to illustrate forgiveness; He tells it to invite us into it.  Every Eucharist is the fatted-calf feast.  The table is set, the music tuned, the invitations sent.  Some of us need to come home from the far country of self-indulgence; others from the near country of self-righteousness.  Both journeys require the same first step: admit we are starving.  

I close with the words of a 19th-century Russian priest, John of Kronstadt, who was once asked how he dealt with sinners.  He replied, “I never notice the sins; I only notice the image of God in every person, distorted by sin, calling for restoration.”  That is the Father’s eyesight.  He does not see failure or success; He sees His child, far off or close by, and He runs.  

So this morning, the porch light is on, the band is tuning, the aroma of grace drifts down the street.  The question is not, “Are you worthy?”  The question is, “Will you come?”  Whether your pockets are full of pig-slop or Pharisee-prayers, drop them both.  The Father is already on the road, robe flapping, arms open, shouting your name above the music.  Run to Him.  Run past your shame.  Run past your pride.  Run into the feast that never ends.  And when you arrive, don’t be surprised if you find the elder brother still outside.  Go back out, take his stubborn hand, and say, “Brother, the music is better in here.  Everything the Father has is ours.”  

In the name of the Father who runs, the Son who comes home, and the Spirit who fills the house with music.  Amen.

aCqERAGxQxVhN5w5f0R7f.text:
Come Home—Both of You  
A sermon on Luke 15:11-32  

1. The lights come on  

Picture the fellowship-hall door cracked open just enough for the smell of tamales to leak into the parking lot.  Inside, someone has strung Dollar-Store streamers across the ceiling and plugged in a Bluetooth speaker.  A dozen shelter guests are clapping off-rhythm while a young man—call him Marcus—wipes his eyes with the sleeve of a borrowed shirt.  His mother has driven four hours with a foil pan and a heart pounding louder than the bass.  She doesn’t know the words to the song, but she sings anyway, because her son is alive.  

Outside, leaning against a dusty Civic, is the older brother—let’s call him Luis.  He paid the mortgage while Mom cleaned hotel rooms.  He never asked for a party; he just kept the lights on.  Now the lights are flashing inside and he is counting streamers, calculating injustice.  Same house, same blood, two hearts: one thawing, one freezing.  

That parking-lot scene is the only sermon illustration I know that refuses to stay in the past tense.  Every time we open Luke 15, the door swings open again and the music leaks out.  Jesus tells this story to answer a one-sentence accusation: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.”  He answers with three parties—sheep, coin, son—each ending in music.  The longest song is about two boys who both miss home, and a father who refuses to stop running after them.  

2. One sentence before we start  

Grace always outruns the runners—whether we run away by breaking the rules or run away by keeping them.  The only ticket to the feast is emptiness, and the Father is already on the porch scanning the road.  

3. Scene one: the younger son—language of hunger  

“Father, give me the share that is coming to me.”  
In first-century ears that sentence is a funeral bell: Dad, I wish you were dead.  Jewish law allows a living inheritance, but no honorable son requests it.  The father liquidates the land—soil that bears his grandfather’s footprints—counts out coins, and hands over the future.  

The boy converts inheritance into miles, miles into women, women into hunger, hunger into pig slop.  Finally he wakes up: the trough is cleaner than his conscience.  He rehearses a speech: “Make me a hired hand.”  It’s a negotiation, not a confession; he still thinks in wages.  

He starts home.  While he is a dot on the horizon, the father hikes up his robe, flashes knee to the village, and runs.  Nobles don’t run; they process.  But this father chooses shame so his son can keep dignity.  Before the boy finishes his deal-making, the father interrupts:  
- Best robe—party clothes, not work coveralls.  
- Ring—family credit card, signature restored.  
- Sandals—sonship, not servanthood.  
- Fatted calf—enough meat for the whole neighborhood.  

One hymn writer calls this “the love that will not let me go.”  I call it the first Eucharist: bread broken before repentance is complete, wine poured while shame is still talking.  

4. Scene two: the father—language of abundance  

The father loses twice.  First his property, then his reputation.  He absorbs both so his children can live.  The cross is hidden here not as a proof-text, but as a pattern: God chooses the costly road so we can come home free.  

Notice the feast is public.  Forgiveness is never private in Jesus’ stories; it always spills onto the dance floor.  The village is invited because joy is the final righteousness.  

5. Scene three: the older son—language of accounting  

He hears the bass line from the field, refuses to enter.  The father—again!—goes out, this time to the elder.  Listen to the son’s ledger:  
“These many years I have slaved for you… you never gave me a goat… this son of yours…”  
No intimacy, no joy, no sonship—only contract.  He has never asked for a goat; his obedience has been calculation.  He accuses the brother of prostitutes—an ugly detail nowhere in the text.  We invent sins for others when we need to justify our resentment.  

The father pleads: “Everything I have is yours.”  The elder already owns the estate; he simply never trusted the heart of the giver.  The story ends unresolved because Jesus is still pleading on the porch with every congregation that mistakes church for performance.  

6. Where are we in the painting?  

A. To the younger prodigals—those who left  
Maybe your far country is an emptied bank account, an abortion you never mention, a marriage you nuked on social media.  Shame tells you to negotiate: I’ll serve on three committees, I’ll read the Bible in a year, I’ll fund a well in Africa.  The parable forbids it.  You are welcomed not because you have a payment plan but because you have a Father.  Bring your hunger, your smell, your empty pockets; the robe is already monogrammed.  The feast starts before you finish the sentence.  

Monday step: Write one sentence of raw confession on a card and slip it into the offering plate.  No fixes, no promises—just “I’m starving for home.”  Let the Father run.  

B. To the elder prodigals—those who stayed  
Some of us have never left home, yet we stand outside the music counting worship-services attended, verses memorized, tithes itemized.  The horror is that you can be in the field of grace while missing the heart of the Father.  The remedy is not more striving but astonishment: “All that is mine is yours.”  Move from wages to wonder.  The party is not reward for the younger; it is revelation for you.  Pick up the tambourine, dance with the ex-addict, discover that joy is the final commandment.  

Monday step: Choose one celebration this week that you did not earn—sunset, grandchild’s giggle, free coffee—and give thanks out loud.  Tell your heart that the ledger is closed.  

C. To the moms and dads—those who wait  
God gives you the impossible task of letting your children choose famine so they can discover grace.  You will be asked to absorb shame, to run when dignity says walk, to celebrate when justice says scold.  Do it anyway.  Your porch light is a seed; the feast will sprout.  

Monday step: Text or call the child you’re tempted to lecture and send only this: “I love you.  The door is open.”  No sequel, no sub-clause.  

D. To the church—God’s banquet committee  
We are entrusted with two ministries:  
- Robe ministry: wrap people in identity before they smell like church.  
- Dance ministry: teach our feet to rejoice when the wrong people get saved.  

Whenever we grade grace on a curve, we become elder-brother congregations, museums of resentment.  Whenever we fling doors wide, we become Father-houses where the only admission ticket is emptiness.  

Monday step: Invite one person to lunch who still smells like the far country—recovery group, parolee, recently divorced—and let them talk uninterrupted for an hour.  Pick up the tab.  

7. The table is already set  

Every Sunday we reenact this parable in fifteen minutes flat.  The procession up the aisle is the father running.  The bread broken is the fatted calf.  The cup poured is the ring slipped on our finger.  Whether your pockets are full of pig-slop or Pharisee résumés, drop them both.  The question is not “Are you worthy?”  The question is “Will you come?”  

So this morning the porch light is on, the band is tuning, the aroma of grace drifts down the street.  Run to Him.  Run past your shame.  Run past your pride.  Run into the feast that never ends.  And when you arrive, don’t be surprised if you find the elder brother still outside.  Go back out, take his stubborn hand, and say, “Brother, the music is better in here.  Everything the Father has is ours.”

The Other Son in the Mirror  
Luke 15:11-32  

1. When the lights come on  

In the winter of 2019, a young man named Marcus was dropped at the Greyhound station with a duffel bag, a dead cell-phone, and the address of our church’s shelter.  He had burned every bridge—emptied his widowed mother’s retirement account, sold her car for half its value, and vanished for three years.  That first night we gave him the bottom bunk in a room with four strangers.  He wept himself to sleep, not from regret, but from the shock of being received.  

Three weeks later, Mrs. Alvarez phoned the office.  She had driven four hours, sat in our parking lot for an hour more, and finally walked in carrying a foil pan of tamales.  She spotted Marcus sweeping the cafeteria.  The room froze.  Marcus dropped the broom.  She opened her arms, and the whole shelter heard him sob, “Mom, I’m sorry.  I don’t deserve this.”  She answered only, “You’re my son.  Come home.”  

That scene is the closest I have ever come to watching Scripture happen in real time.  It is also only half the story.  Because when we threw a celebration dinner in the fellowship hall, Mrs. Alvarez’s older son—steady, reliable, the one who had stayed home to pay the mortgage—stood outside the double-doors, arms crossed.  “She never threw me a party,” he muttered.  In that moment we had two prodigals: one who left home in the body, and one who left home in the heart.  

2. Listening again with first-century ears  

Luke 15 is one long answer to one short accusation: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them” (v. 2).  Jesus tells three stories—lost sheep, lost coin, lost son—each ending in a feast.  The third story is the longest parable He ever spoke.  Tradition calls it “the prodigal son,” but the text is bigger: it is “the two lost sons,” or better, “the running Father.”  Three characters, three movements, three mirrors.  

A. The younger son—radical disrespect  
“Give me the share of the estate that falls to me” (v. 12).  Jewish law permitted a living division, but the request is tantamount to saying, “I wish you were dead.”  The father complies: he liquidates land, herds, and honor.  The boy converts inheritance into cash, cash into distant pleasure, pleasure into pig-slop.  First-century listeners would have expected lightning.  Instead they get a father who keeps scanning the horizon.  

B. The father—scandalous compassion  
“While he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran” (v. 20).  Noble landowners did not run—ever.  The robe hikes up, the sandals slap dust, the crowd gawks.  Before the son finishes his rehearsed speech, the father interrupts: “Bring the best robe”—the banquet robe—“put a ring on his hand”—the family signet, authority restored—“sandals on his feet”—only sons wore shoes; servants went barefoot.  Then the feast: “the fatted calf,” enough meat for a village.  This is not private forgiveness; it is public rehabilitation.  Romans 5:8 happens before the boy can draw a breath: while we are still a long way off, God runs.  

C. The older son—polite rebellion  
He hears music, refuses to enter.  The father—again!—goes out, this time to the elder.  His speech is precise: “Look, these many years I have served you” (v. 29).  The Greek word is douleuō, “I slaved.”  No intimacy, no joy, no sonship—only contract.  He has never asked for a goat; his obedience has been calculation.  He accuses the brother of consorting with prostitutes—an ugly detail nowhere in the story; he projects sin onto the repentant to justify his resentment.  The feast is ready, but he stands in the outer darkness of his own choosing.  

3. What we almost miss  

1. Both sons are lost.  One by breaking commands, the other by keeping them.  Sin is not only deviation but also diversion: the younger diverts grace into license; the elder diverts grace into wages.  

2. The father loses twice.  He surrenders property to the younger, dignity to the younger, then intimacy to the elder.  The cross is already hidden in the story: the father absorbs shame so his children can live.  

3. The story ends unresolved.  We are not told whether the elder enters.  Jesus leaves the ending open because the Pharisees are still standing outside the banquet.  The question is hurled into the crowd: will you come in?  

4. Finding ourselves in the painting  

A. To the younger prodigals—those who left  
Some of us carry the smell of the far country: bankruptcy, addiction, divorce, betrayal.  Shame tells us to negotiate our way back as hired hands—serve on every committee, never ask for too much.  The parable forbids it.  You are welcomed not because you have a plan but because you have a Father.  Repentance is not the price of admission; it is the door through which the Father runs.  Bring your hunger, your stench, your empty pockets; the robe is already tailored, the ring already engraved.  

B. To the elder prodigals—those who stayed  
Some of us have never left home, yet we stand outside the music.  Our obedience has been loveless, our service resentful.  We keep score: I tithe, I teach Sunday school, I memorize verses—where’s my calf?  The horror is that we can be in the field of grace while missing the heart of the Father.  The remedy is not more striving but astonishment: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31).  The elder son already owns the estate; he simply never asked.  Move from the economics of merit to the ecology of gift.  The party is not reward for the younger; it is revelation for the older.  Come in, pick up the tambourine, discover that joy is the final righteousness.  

C. To the waiting household—parents, mentors, church  
Maybe you are the one scanning the road, the porch light burning holes in the dark.  God assigns you the impossible task of letting your children choose famine so they can discover grace.  Like Abraham climbing Moriah, you surrender the future you cherish, trusting that the same God who asked for the knife also provides the ram.  Your tears are seeds; the feast will sprout.  And when it does, your job is to fling doors wide, put on music, and train our hearts to rejoice when the wrong people get saved.  We are the robe-and-dance people: we wrap prodigals in baptismal identity before they smell like church, and we teach the elders to twirl before they feel like dancing.  

5. Will you come to the party?  

Jesus does not tell this story to illustrate forgiveness; He tells it to invite us into it.  Every Eucharist is the fatted-calf feast.  The table is set, the music tuned, the invitations sent.  Some of us need to come home from the far country of self-indulgence; others from the near country of self-righteousness.  Both journeys require the same first step: admit we are starving.  

I close with the words of a wise spiritual writer: “I never notice the sins; I only notice the image of God in every person, distorted by sin, calling for restoration.”  That is the Father’s eyesight.  He does not see failure or success; He sees His child, far off or close by, and He runs.  

So this morning, the porch light is on, the band is tuning, the aroma of grace drifts down the street.  The question is not, “Are you worthy?”  The question is, “Will you come?”  Whether your pockets are full of pig-slop or Pharisee-prayers, drop them both.  The Father is already on the road, robe flapping, arms open, shouting your name above the music.  Run to Him.  Run past your shame.  Run past your pride.  Run into the feast that never ends.  And when you arrive, don’t be surprised if you find the elder brother still outside.  Go back out, take his stubborn hand, and say, “Brother, the music is better in here.  Everything the Father has is ours.”  

In the name of the Father who runs, the Son who comes home, and the Spirit who fills the house with music.  Amen.

“Give me the share of the estate that falls to me” (v. 12).  Jewish law allowed a father to divide property during his lifetime, but the request is equivalent to saying, “I wish you were dead.”  The father complies: he liquidates land, herds, and honor.  The boy converts inheritance into cash, cash into distant pleasure, pleasure into pig-slop.  Jesus’ hearers would have expected lightning.  Instead they get a father who keeps scanning the horizon.  

B. The father—scandalous compassion  
“While he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran” (v. 20).  Patriarchs in Palestine did not run—ever.  The robe hikes up, the ankles flash, the crowd gawks.  Before the son can finish his rehearsed speech the father interrupts: “Bring the best robe”—the banquet robe—“put a ring on his hand”—the family signet, authority restored—“sandals on his feet”—only sons wore shoes; servants went barefoot.  Then the feast: “the fatted calf,” enough meat for a village.  This is not private forgiveness; it is public rehabilitation.  

C. The older son—polite rebellion  
He hears music, refuses to enter.  The father—again!—goes out, this time to the elder.  His speech is precise: “Look, these many years I have served you” (v. 29).  The Greek verb is *douleuō*, “I slaved.”  No intimacy, no joy, no sonship—only contract.  He has never asked for a goat; his obedience has been calculation.  He accuses the brother of consorting with prostitutes—an ugly detail nowhere in the story; he projects sin onto the repentant to justify his resentment.  The feast is ready, but he stands in the outer darkness of his own choosing.  

3. What we almost miss  

Having listened with first-century ears, let us now listen for the chords we almost miss.  

First, both sons are lost.  One breaks commands, the other keeps them.  Sin is not only deviation but diversion: the younger diverts grace into license; the elder diverts grace into wages.  Both are estranged; both need the running father.  

Second, the father loses twice.  He surrenders property to the younger, then dignity to the younger, then intimacy to the elder.  In each case he absorbs the shame his sons refuse to carry.  Here the shadow of the cross falls across the story: the Father who will one day watch His true Son carry the ring, the robe, the sandals of a rebel world, and run all the way to Golgotha so that every prodigal can come home.

4. Finding ourselves in the painting  

A. To the younger prodigals—those who left  
Some of us carry the smell of the far country: bankruptcy, addiction, divorce, abortion, betrayal.  Shame tells us to negotiate our way back as hired hands—serve on every committee, never ask for too much.  The parable forbids it. Bring your hunger, your stench, your empty pockets; the robe is already tailored, the ring already engraved.  The feast begins before you finish the sentence.  

B. To the elder prodigals—those who stayed  
Some of us have never left home, yet we stand outside the music.  Our obedience has been loveless, our service resentful.  We keep score: I tithe, I teach, I memorize—where’s my calf?  The horror is that we can be in the field of grace while missing the heart of the Father.  The remedy is not more striving but astonishment: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (v. 31).  The elder already owns the estate; he simply never asked.  Move from the economics of merit to the ecology of gift.  The party is not reward for the younger; it is revelation for the older.  Come in, pick up the tambourine, discover that joy is the final righteousness.  

C. To the mothers and fathers—those who wait  
Perhaps you are the one scanning the road, the porch light burning holes in the dark.  God assigns you the impossible task of letting your children choose famine so they can discover grace.  You will be asked to absorb shame, to run when dignity says walk, to celebrate when justice says scold.  Do it anyway.  Your tears are seeds; the feast will sprout.  And when the feast comes, do not be surprised if the older siblings sulk.  Keep the music playing; keep the table open.  The Father who runs is also the Father who waits.  

D. To the church—God’s banquet committee  
We are entrusted with two ministries: the robe and the dance.  The robe is the garment of baptismal identity—put it on prodigals before they smell like church.  The dance is the rhythm of celebration—train our hearts to rejoice when the wrong people get saved.  Whenever we grade grace on a curve we become elder-brother congregations, museums of resentment.  Whenever we fling doors wide we become Father-houses where the only admission ticket is emptiness. 5. Will you come to the party?  

Jesus does not tell this story to illustrate forgiveness; He tells it to invite us into it.  Every Eucharist is the fatted-calf feast.  The table is set, the music tuned, the invitations sent.  Some of us need to come home from the far country of self-indulgence; others from the near country of self-righteousness.  Both journeys require the same first step: admit we are starving.  

I close with the words of a nineteenth-century Russian priest, John of Kronstadt, who was once asked how he dealt with sinners.  He replied, “I never notice the sins; I only notice the image of God in every person, distorted by sin, calling for restoration.”  That is the Father’s eyesight.  He does not see failure or success; He sees His child, far off or close by, and He runs.  

So this morning the porch light is on, the band is tuning, the aroma of grace drifts down the street. And when you are inside, if you catch a glimpse of an older brother still outside, remember: everything the Father has is already yours.  Go back out, take his stubborn hand, and pull him toward the music.  The table is big enough for every lost son and every lost daughter—and, thank God, it is big enough for every lost older brother too.  

In the name of the Father who runs, the Son who comes home, and the Spirit who fills the house with music.  Amen.

She'd cook his favorite meal—pot roast with carrots and those buttery rolls he loved—and she'd put out the blue ceramic plate, the one he'd made in third grade, the one with his handprint and the crooked "I love you, Mom" painted on the back. Her other children would say, "Mom, he's not coming. He hasn't called in months. Please stop torturing yourself." But Margaret would just smile and say, "I know. But I want everything to be ready. Just in case."

One Tuesday, at 6:47 PM, the doorbell rang. There he stood—thinner than she remembered, with a shadow in his eyes that hadn't been there before. He opened his mouth to speak, but before he could get out "Mom, I'm sorry," she had already pulled him into her arms, pot roast forgotten, and was crying into his shoulder, saying, "You're home. You're home. That's all that matters."

Friends, that is not just a mother's love. That is a glimpse into the very heart of God.

The Parable of the Prodigal Son is perhaps the most beloved story Jesus ever told, yet it remains the most misunderstood. We call it the story of the Prodigal Son, but it's really the story of a father who was prodigal—extravagantly, recklessly generous with his love. And if we're honest, it's also the story of two lost sons who represent two ways we all wander from our Father's house.

Let me invite you back to the context. Jesus is telling this story to a very specific audience—Pharisees and scribes who are grumbling that Jesus "receives sinners and eats with them." They see him sharing meals with tax collectors and prostitutes, and it offends their religious sensibilities. So Jesus tells three stories in a row: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and then this, the lost son. Each story builds to the same crescendo: there is joy in heaven when the lost are found. But this final story carries a twist that goes straight for the self-righteous heart.

Let's walk through it carefully.

**The Younger Son: The One Who Ran**

The story begins with a shocking request. The younger son says, "Father, give me the share of the property that will belong to me." In that culture, this was unspeakable. He was essentially saying, "I wish you were dead. Give me my inheritance now." A father could refuse, and most would. But this father does something extraordinary—he divides his property between his sons. He gives away his life while he's still living.

The son takes his inheritance and runs. He goes to a far country, which isn't just geography—it's a far country of the heart. And there, Luke tells us, he squanders everything in "dissolute living." The word "dissolute" means scattered, fragmented. He scatters himself on fleeting pleasures until the money is gone, the friends are gone, and a famine hits. Suddenly, he's feeding pigs—a job that would have made any good Jewish boy ritually unclean—and he's so hungry he wants to eat the pig feed.

But then, Jesus says something profound: "He came to himself." Some translations say "he came to his senses," but it's deeper than that. It's not just that he got smart; he woke up to who he truly was. He remembered his father's house. He remembered that even his father's hired hands had bread to spare. So he rehearses a little speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired hands."

Notice what he's doing. He's still trying to earn his way back. He's willing to be a servant. He's not asking for restoration; he's asking for employment. He's got a transactional mindset because that's all he knows.

So he heads home, practicing his speech the whole way. And while he's still far off—still rehearsing his lines, still trying to figure out how to earn his way back—his father sees him. That means the father was watching. Waiting. Scanning the horizon day after day.

And then the father does something scandalous. He runs. In that culture, a man of his age and status never ran. It was undignified. It showed his ankles. It was shameful. But this father doesn't care about his dignity. He runs to his son, throws his arms around him, and kisses him before the son can even finish his speech.

The son starts his rehearsed lines: "Father, I have sinned..." But the father isn't listening. He's already calling for the best robe (which would be his own robe, a sign of honor), a ring (a sign of authority, sonship), and sandals (which servants didn't wear, but sons did). He's not taking him back as a servant. He's restoring him completely as a son. Then he orders a feast: "Kill the fatted calf! Let's celebrate!"

This is pure, unmerited, extravagant grace. The son did nothing to earn it. He just came home.

**The Older Son: The One Who Stayed**

But the story doesn't end there. The older son is out in the field, working. He hears music and dancing and asks a servant what's going on. When he learns his brother is back and there's a feast, he refuses to go in.

Now, let's be honest—many of us identify with this guy. He's been faithful. He's done everything right. He's never disobeyed. He's the responsible one. And now his screw-up brother gets a party? It's not fair.

The father comes out to him—just as he went out to the younger son. He pleads with him. But the older son unloads: "Look! All these years I've been working like a slave for you, and you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends!"

Do you hear his words? "I've been working like a slave." This son, who never left home, doesn't realize he's been living in the house as a slave, not a son. He's been obeying, but he's never understood his father's heart. He's been keeping score, calculating what he's earned. His obedience has been a transaction, not a relationship.

And then this devastating line: "But when this son of yours came back..." Not "my brother," but "this son of yours." He's disowned his own flesh and blood. He's standing in the dark, outside the celebration, and he doesn't even realize he's lost.

The father responds with the same tenderness: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours." Everything the father has has always been available to the older son, but he's never received it. He's never let himself rest in his father's love. He's too busy earning what was already his.

**Two Lost Sons, One Prodigal Father**

Here's the theological heart of the story: Both sons are lost, but in opposite directions. The younger son wants freedom so he can do whatever he wants. The older son wants righteousness so he can get whatever he deserves. Both are trying to control their lives through performance—one through rebellion, one through rule-keeping. And both have missed the central truth: they are loved sons, not employees.

The younger son's sin was obvious: wild living, moral failure. The older son's sin was subtle: self-righteousness, resentment, a refusal to celebrate grace. And here's the twist Jesus is dropping on the Pharisees: The older son is them. They're standing outside God's party, angry that sinners are being welcomed in.

But here's the deeper truth that should shake us all: The older son is also us. How often have we resented God's grace toward others? How often have we thought, "I've been faithful, God, and this is how you reward me while that person gets blessed?" How often has our obedience become a bargaining chip?

Tim Keller points out that we should call this the Parable of the Prodigal God, because God's grace is the truly reckless thing in this story. The word "prodigal" means recklessly extravagant, spending everything. The father spends his dignity by running. He spends his wealth on a son who squandered it. He spends his joy on those who don't deserve it. That's our God.

He ran to him while he was still dirty, still smelly, still rehearsing his half-baked speech. Grace meets us in our brokenness, not after we've cleaned ourselves up.

Hear this: Your Father is scanning the horizon for you. He's not waiting for you to get your speech perfect. He's not waiting for you to prove you've changed. He's waiting for you to simply turn toward home. The moment you do, he'll run to meet you. The robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The feast is already cooking. You don't have to earn your way back into the family. You just have to receive his embrace.

But maybe, just maybe, you're the older son. You've been in church your whole life. You've served on committees and taught Sunday school and given your tithe. You've been faithful. But deep down, you're exhausted. You're keeping score. You're resentful that God seems to bless people who haven't worked as hard as you. You've confused the Father's house with a workplace, and his love with a paycheck. You've never really tasted joy because you've been too busy earning it.

If that's you, hear the Father's words to you today: "Everything I have is yours." The celebration isn't for your brother; it's for you too. But you have to come in. You have to lay down your scorecard and pick up the joy of sonship. You have to learn to dance.

And here's the hardest word: We, the church, have a tendency to become the older brother. We can create communities that welcome the repentant sinner but secretly resent them. We can make our churches places where people have to clean up their act before they belong. We can celebrate God's grace in theory but resist it in practice when it gets too messy, too undeserved.

But Jesus is inviting us into a different kind of community—a community that joins the Father's feast, that runs with him toward the broken, that celebrates every lost sheep that comes home. A community that understands we are all, every one of us, prodigals who've been found by a prodigally gracious God.

**The Feast Is Now**

The most overlooked detail in this story is that the feast happens immediately. The father doesn't say, "Let's see if he can stay clean for six months, then we'll celebrate." He doesn't put him on probation. He doesn't say, "We'll start with the servant's quarters and work our way up." No—the celebration starts the moment the son returns.

The Father is waiting. The feast is ready. Come home. And when you get here, don't just sit in the corner making a list of who else doesn't deserve to be here. Grab a plate. Grab a dance partner. Join the joy.

Because the joy of the Father is the only thing that can fill the ache in your wandering heart. The grace of the Father is the only thing that can break the chains of your self-righteousness. And the love of the Father—the reckless, running, robe-giving, feast-throwing love—is the only love that can truly bring you home.

Let's pray.

*Father, we thank you that you are the God who runs. That you see us while we are still far off. That your grace is not a reward for our performance but the gift of your heart. For those of us who have wandered far, give us the courage to turn toward home. Make us a people who celebrate your prodigal grace, who join your feast, who know we are beloved sons and daughters. We pray this in the name of the one who told this story, Jesus our brother. He's not taking him back as a servant. He's restoring him completely as a son. Then he orders a feast: "Kill the fatted calf! Let's celebrate!"

This is pure, unmerited, extravagant grace. The son did nothing to earn it. He just came home.

We want to cheer here. The music is swelling, the calf is roasting, the aroma of celebration fills the air. But Jesus, being the master storyteller, lets the music fade as he pans the camera to the older brother standing in the dark.

**The Feast Is Already Prepared**

I want to tell you about a woman named Margaret. Every Tuesday night for seven years, she set a place at her dining room table for her son who wasn't there. She'd cook his favorite meal—pot roast with carrots and those buttery rolls he loved—and she'd put out the blue ceramic plate, the one he'd made in third grade, the one with his handprint and the crooked "I love you, Mom" painted on the back. Her other children would say, "Mom, he's not coming. He hasn't called in months. Please stop torturing yourself." But Margaret would just smile and say, "I know. But I want everything to be ready. Just in case."

One Tuesday, at 6:47 PM, the doorbell rang. There he stood—thinner than she remembered, with a shadow in his eyes that hadn't been there before. He opened his mouth to speak, but before he could get out "Mom, I'm sorry," she had already pulled him into her arms, pot roast forgotten, and was crying into his shoulder, saying, "You're home. You're home. That's all that matters."

Friends, that is not just a mother's love. That is a glimpse into the very heart of God.

The Parable of the Prodigal Son is perhaps the most beloved story Jesus ever told, yet it remains the most misunderstood. We call it the story of the Prodigal Son, but it's really the story of a father who was prodigal—extravagantly, recklessly generous with his love. And if we're honest, it's also the story of two lost sons who represent two ways we all wander from our Father's house.

Let me invite you back to the context. Jesus is telling this story to a very specific audience—Pharisees and scribes who are grumbling that Jesus "receives sinners and eats with them." They see him sharing meals with tax collectors and prostitutes, and it offends their religious sensibilities. So Jesus tells three stories in a row: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and then this, the lost son. Each story builds to the same crescendo: there is joy in heaven when the lost are found. But this final story carries a twist that goes straight for the self-righteous heart.

Let's walk through it carefully.

**The Younger Son: The One Who Ran**

The story begins with a shocking request. The younger son says, "Father, give me the share of the property that will belong to me." In that culture, this was unspeakable. He was essentially saying, "I wish you were dead. Give me my inheritance now." A father could refuse, and most would. But this father does something extraordinary—he divides his property between his sons. He gives away his life while he's still living.

The son takes his inheritance and runs. He goes to a far country, which isn't just geography—it's a far country of the heart. And there, Luke tells us, he squanders everything in "dissolute living." The Greek word is *asotos*—from which we get our word "prodigal"—meaning wasteful, riotous, scattered. He scatters himself on fleeting pleasures until the money is gone, the friends are gone, and a famine hits.

This famine is more than bad luck. Throughout Scripture, famine functions as what the Puritans called "severe mercy"—the painful discipline that awakens the wandering heart. Think of Joseph, sold by his brothers into slavery, who later tells them, "You meant it for evil, but God meant it for good." Think of Naomi, who loses everything in Moab but says to her daughters-in-law, "The Lord has afflicted me." The famine is not random; it's the merciful constraint that makes the far country unbearable, that makes home imaginable again. Sometimes God's love comes disguised as emptiness, forcing us to remember the bread we once took for granted.

Suddenly, the boy is feeding pigs—a job that makes any good Jewish boy ritually unclean—and he's so hungry he wants to eat the pig feed. But then, Jesus says something profound: "He came to himself." Some translations say "he came to his senses," but it's deeper than that. The phrase *eis heauton elthon* means he returned to his true self, his created identity. Sin doesn't just make us bad; it makes us *not ourselves*. It fragments us, scatters us across our desires, until we forget who we are. Repentance isn't just behavior modification; it's a homecoming to the self God made us to be—a self that can only be fully realized in relationship with the Father.

So he rehearses a speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired hands." Notice what he's doing. He's still trying to earn his way back. He's willing to be a servant. He's not asking for restoration; he's asking for employment. He's got a transactional mindset because that's all he knows.

So he heads home, practicing his speech the whole way. And while he's still far off—still rehearsing his lines, still trying to figure out how to earn his way back—his father sees him. That means the father was watching. Waiting. Scanning the horizon day after day.

And then the father does something scandalous. He runs. In that culture, a man of his age and status never ran. It was undignified. It showed his ankles. It was shameful. But this father doesn't care about his dignity. He runs to his son, throws his arms around him, and kisses him before the son can even finish his speech.

The son starts his rehearsed lines: "Father, I have sinned..." But the father isn't listening. He's already calling for the best robe (which would be his own robe, a sign of honor), a ring (a sign of authority, sonship), and sandals (which servants didn't wear, but sons did). These aren't just nice gifts—they're covenantal tokens. The robe is the *stolē*, the festal garment prophesied in Isaiah 61:10: "He has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness." The ring bears the family seal, echoing how the Spirit seals us as God's own (Ephesians 1:13). The sandals mark him as a free person, shod with "the preparation of the gospel of peace" (Ephesians 6:15). He's not taking him back as a servant. He's restoring him completely as a son, reinstating him in the covenant family. Then he orders a feast: "Kill the fatted calf! Let's celebrate!"

This is pure, unmerited, extravagant grace. The son did nothing to earn it. He just came home.

**The Older Son: The One Who Stayed**

But every story has another side, and Jesus hasn't finished dropping his theological bombs. The older son is out in the field, working. He hears music and dancing and asks a servant what's going on. When he learns his brother is back and there's a feast, he refuses to go in.

Now, let's be honest—many of us identify with this guy. He's been faithful. He's done everything right. He's never disobeyed. He's the responsible one. And now his screw-up brother gets a party? It's not fair.

Let me tell you about Robert. He's been a deacon for thirty years. Never missed a business meeting, never questioned the budget, never complained about the building fund. He's the first to arrive and the last to leave. But when the church welcomed a recovering addict into membership—someone with face tattoos and a past that made the elders nervous—Robert stopped coming to potlucks. "I've been here every Sunday for thirty years," he told the pastor. "She shows up for six months and suddenly she's the hero?" The pastor just listened, then asked, "Robert, when was the last time you enjoyed being here?" Robert couldn't remember.

The father comes out to Robert—just as he went out to the younger son. He pleads with him. But the older son unloads: "Look! All these years I've been working like a slave for you, and you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends!"

Do you hear his words? "I've been working like a slave." This son, who never left home, doesn't realize he's been living in the house as a slave, not a son. He's been obeying, but he's never understood his father's heart. He's been keeping score, calculating what he's earned. His obedience has been a transaction, not a relationship.

And then this devastating line: "But when this son of yours came back..." Not "my brother," but "this son of yours." He's disowned his own flesh and blood. He's standing in the dark, outside the celebration, and he doesn't even realize he's lost.

The father responds with the same tenderness: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours." Everything the father has has always been available to the older son, but he's never received it. He's never let himself rest in his father's love. He's too busy earning what was already his.

Here's the theological heart of the story: Both sons are lost, but in opposite directions. The younger son wants freedom so he can do whatever he wants. The older son wants righteousness so he can get whatever he deserves. Both are trying to control their lives through performance—one through rebellion, one through rule-keeping. And both have missed the central truth: they are loved sons, not employees.

The younger son's sin was obvious: wild living, moral failure. The older son's sin was subtle: self-righteousness, resentment, a refusal to celebrate grace. And here's the twist Jesus is dropping on the Pharisees: The older son is them. They're standing outside God's party, angry that sinners are being welcomed in.

But here's the deeper truth that should shake us all: The older son is also us. How often have we resented God's grace toward others? How often have we thought, "I've been faithful, God, and this is how you reward me while that person gets blessed?" How often has our obedience become a bargaining chip?

**The Prodigal God**

We should call this the Parable of the Prodigal God, because God's grace is the truly reckless thing in this story. The word "prodigal" means recklessly extravagant, spending everything. The father spends his dignity by running. He spends his wealth on a son who squandered it. He spends his joy on those who don't deserve it. That's our God.

This is the God who gives manna that can't be stored, who pours out 153 fish on disciples who'd caught nothing, who saves the best wine for last at a wedding where the hosts are already drunk. This is the God who "wastes" his finest robe on a boy who smells like pig slop, who "wastes" a fatted calf on a son who'd rather eat carob pods. God's grace isn't efficient—it's extravagant. It doesn't calculate return on investment; it simply gives.

This parable shows us that God's grace doesn't come in response to our perfect repentance. The father didn't wait for the son to get his act together. He ran to him while he was still dirty, still smelly, still rehearsing his half-baked speech. Grace meets us in our brokenness, not after we've cleaned ourselves up.

But it also shows us that God's grace can be resisted. The older son stood outside, refusing to come in. The father didn't drag him. He invited, he pleaded, but he allowed him his freedom—even the freedom to stay outside the party.

He's waiting for you to simply turn toward home. The moment you do, he'll run to meet you. The robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The feast is already cooking. You don't have to earn your way back into the family. You just have to receive his embrace.

But maybe, just maybe, you're the older son. You've been in church your whole life. You've served on committees and taught Sunday school and given your tithe. You've been faithful. But deep down, you're exhausted. You're keeping score. You're resentful that God seems to bless people who haven't worked as hard as you. You've confused the Father's house with a workplace, and his love with a paycheck. You've never really tasted joy because you've been too busy earning it.

If that's you, hear the Father's words to you today: "Everything I have is yours." The celebration isn't for your brother; it's for you too. But you have to come in. You have to lay down your scorecard and pick up the joy of sonship. You have to learn to dance.

You grew up in the faith, drifted into rebellion, then came back and became so zealous that you became a new kind of Pharisee. You've experienced grace but now want to police it. You've been forgiven but now demand purity from others. You're exhausted from trying to prove you're not the person you used to be. If that's you, the Father's word is the same: "Stop performing. Start receiving. The feast is for you, not your resume."

It's not just that he got smart; he woke up to who he truly was. He remembered his father's house. He remembered that even his father's hired hands had bread to spare. Notice what he's doing. He's still trying to earn his way back. He's willing to be a servant. He's not asking for restoration; he's asking for employment. He's got a transactional mindset because that's all he knows.

This is pure, unmerited, extravagant grace. The son did nothing to earn it. He just came home. The Father is waiting. The feast is ready. Come home. And when you get here, don't just sit in the corner making a list of who else doesn't deserve to be here. Grab a plate. Grab a dance partner. Join the joy.

Because the joy of the Father is the only thing that can fill the ache in your wandering heart. The grace of the Father is the only thing that can break the chains of your self-righteousness. And the love of the Father—the reckless, running, robe-giving, feast-throwing love—is the only love that can truly bring you home.

**The Father's Extravagant Welcome**

I want to begin with a story that landed in my inbox this past week. A friend wrote to me about her brother who, fifteen years ago, walked out of their parents' lives. No dramatic fight, no single moment of rupture—just a gradual cooling until one day he stopped returning calls. He moved across the country, changed his number, and for all intents and purposes, became a stranger. The parents grieved him like a death. They wondered what they had done wrong, replayed every conversation, every parenting decision. Then, two weeks ago, out of the blue, a text appeared on their mother's phone: "Mom, can I come home?"

My friend described what happened next. Her mother didn't text back. She didn't call. She got in her car and drove to the airport—a four-hour round trip—without even knowing if he was already on a plane. She stood at arrivals for three hours, holding a sign like she was waiting for a visiting dignitary. When he finally emerged, looking thin and weary, she didn't wait for him to apologize. She dropped the sign, ran to him, and held his face in her hands as if he were the most precious thing she had ever seen. "Let's go home," she said. "I've already called the butcher. We're having brisket tonight."

That, dear friends, is the gospel in a single, messy, modern moment. That is what Jesus is trying to tell us in the story we know as the Parable of the Prodigal Son. Except Jesus tells it even more scandalously, even more extravagantly, because in his story, the father doesn't wait for a text. He watches the road. And when he sees that familiar silhouette on the horizon, he doesn't walk—he *runs*.

Let's sit with this passage for a moment. Luke 15:11-32. You know it well. A man has two sons. The younger demands his inheritance early—a request that in first-century Jewish culture was roughly equivalent to saying, "Father, I wish you were dead." Shockingly, the father grants it. The son takes his share, travels to a distant country, and squanders everything in reckless living. A famine hits. Desperate, he hires himself out to feed pigs, an occupation that makes him ritually unclean and spiritually bankrupt. He longs to eat the pods the pigs are eating. No one gives him anything.

Then comes the moment we often call repentance, though it's more like clarity: "When he came to himself, he said, 'How many of my father's hired servants have bread enough and to spare, but here I am dying of hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants."'" This is not a speech of deep contrition. It's a calculated plan. He knows his father's generosity extends even to servants. He'll take whatever crumbs he can get.

But here's where the story turns. While he is still far off, his father sees him. The Greek verb here is in the imperfect tense—it suggests ongoing action. The father has been *watching*, waiting, scanning the horizon day after day. And when he sees him, he is moved with compassion. The Greek word is *splagchnizomai*—it means his guts churned, his deepest insides were stirred. This is not polite parental affection. This is visceral, physical love.

And then, the most undignified moment: the father runs. In that culture, patriarchs did not run. They walked with measured dignity. Running meant hitching up your robes, exposing your legs, looking foolish. But this father doesn't care about dignity. He runs to his son, embraces him, and kisses him. The son starts his rehearsed speech—"Father, I have sinned..."—but the father isn't even listening. He's already issuing orders: "Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found."

Let's pause here. The robe, the ring, the sandals—these aren't just nice gifts. The robe is the father's own, the best one, signifying full restoration to the family. The ring is the family signet, giving the son authority to transact business again. The sandals—only family members wore them, not servants. In one breathtaking moment, the father completely restores the son. No probation period. No penance. No conditions. Just grace, lavish and unmerited.

Now, we could stop here and have a perfectly lovely sermon about God's forgiveness. "Come home, prodigal! God will welcome you!" And that would be true. But Jesus doesn't stop the story there, and neither can we. Because there's another brother.

The older brother is in the field, working. He hears music and dancing. He calls a servant and asks what's going on. When he learns his younger brother has returned and his father has killed the fattened calf, he refuses to go in. He is angry. The father comes out and entreats him. The older son's response is blistering: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"

Notice the language. "This son of yours." He won't even claim him as a brother. And notice his view of his own relationship with the father: "I have served you." Not "I have lived as your son," but "I have served you." He sees his faithfulness as a transaction. He's earned something. He's been keeping score.

The father's response is gentle: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."

The story ends there, abruptly. We don't know if the older brother goes in. We don't know if he reconciles. We're left hanging because Jesus is asking his listeners—those Pharisees who complained that he ate with sinners—a question: Will you join the party? Will you understand the heart of your Father?

Now, let's do the careful work of interpretation. This parable is the third in a series in Luke 15. It follows the lost sheep and the lost coin. In each, something is lost and then found, and each ends with a celebration. But this third story complicates things by adding the older brother. Why? Because Jesus is speaking directly to those who, like the older brother, see themselves as faithful, obedient, and deserving. The Pharisees, who prided themselves on keeping the law, who tithed mint and dill and cumin, who never left the father's house, so to speak—they are the older brother. And they are scandalized that Jesus would welcome "those people": tax collectors, sinners, prostitutes.

The parable reveals that there are two ways to be lost. There is the younger son's way: through rebellion, through leaving, through obvious sin. And there is the older son's way: through obedience, through staying, through religious pride. Both are alienated from the father. Both misunderstand his heart. The younger son thinks he must earn his way back into the father's good graces. The older son thinks he has earned his place in the father's house. Both are wrong. The father's love is not transactional. It is not a wage to be earned. It is a gift, freely given.

This is the scandal of grace. It offends our sense of fairness. Shouldn't the prodigal at least have to grovel a bit more? Shouldn't there be some probation? Some penance? Some consequence? But grace doesn't work that way. Grace is the father running. Grace is the robe before the apology is finished. Grace is the feast before the repentance is perfected.

Friends, I suspect most of us in this room identify more with the older brother than the younger. Most of us haven't run off to far countries with inheritance money. Most of us have been fairly responsible. We've stayed in the church. We've tried to live decent lives. We see ourselves as the faithful ones. And that makes this parable deeply uncomfortable. Because it asks us to examine our hearts. Do we, like the older brother, resent God's generosity toward those we deem unworthy? Do we keep score? Do we think we've earned God's favor through our good behavior?

I remember a woman in a previous congregation who pulled me aside after a service where I had preached on God's grace. She was upset. "Pastor," she said, "I've been faithful my whole life. I've served on every committee, taught Sunday school, given faithfully. And you're telling me that God loves the person who shows up once a year at Christmas exactly as much as he loves me?" I could hear the older brother in her voice. And I understood it. It's not fair.

But I gently asked her, "Do you love God because he owes you something? Or do you love him because he first loved you?" She looked at me for a long moment. "I think," she said quietly, "I've been trying to earn what was already mine."

That's the trap of the older brother. He couldn't see that everything the father had was already his. He was living in abundance but experiencing it as scarcity. He was in the father's house but didn't know the father's heart.

And here's the deeper theological truth: we are all, in some sense, both sons. We have all, at times, demanded our autonomy from God. We've taken his blessings and run. We've tried to find life in far countries of our own making—whether through addiction, or ambition, or approval-seeking, or any number of ways we try to fill the God-shaped void. And we have all, at times, been the older brother—self-righteous, judgmental, resentful of grace that seems too free, too broad, too scandalous.

But the parable isn't ultimately about the sons. It's about the father. It's about a love so extravagant it shatters cultural norms. It's about a grace so profound it runs toward us while we're still far off. It's about a joy so complete it throws parties for the undeserving.

The father in this story is the God revealed in Jesus Christ. This is the God who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one. This is the God who sweeps the house until the lost coin is found. This is the God who runs toward prodigals and pleads with older brothers. This is the God who eats with sinners and welcomes the unwelcome.

So what does this mean for us, here, today?

First, if you are in a far country, if you have taken your blessings and squandered them, if you feel unworthy to be called God's child—come home. The father is watching the road. He sees you while you are still far off. He is already running. You don't need to have your act together. You don't need to craft the perfect apology. You just need to turn toward home. Repentance is not about perfecting your confession; it's about turning your face toward the father. He will do the rest.

But second, if you are the older brother—if you've been faithful, if you've served, if you're angry that God's grace seems too free—check your heart. Are you serving the father because you love him, or because you think you can earn his love? Do you see God's grace as something you deserve, or as an unmerited gift? Can you rejoice when the lost are found, even when they haven't paid their dues? Can you see that everything the father has is already yours, not as a wage, but as a gift?

The church has often been better at welcoming prodigals than at challenging older brothers. We've created beautiful ministries for those returning from far countries. But we've sometimes nurtured a culture where the faithful feel entitled, where we measure spirituality by attendance and service, where we keep score. We must repent of that. We must become a community that not only welcomes sinners but also challenges religious pride. We must be a place where both sons can find their way back to the father's heart.

Finally, this parable calls us to become like the father. To be people who run toward the broken. To be people who throw parties for the undeserving. To be people whose compassion moves from their guts, who are willing to look foolish in the eyes of the world for the sake of love. To be people who plead with the angry and the self-righteous to join the celebration.

The father doesn't say to the older brother, "You're right, I was unfair." He says, "Come in. Your brother was dead. Celebrate." The father won't diminish the joy of the found to appease the resentment of the faithful. He invites the older brother to enlarge his heart, to enter into the joy, to understand that grace is not a limited resource to be hoarded but an infinite fountain to be shared.

My friend's mother didn't wait to hear her son's full confession before she planned the brisket. She saw him, she ran, she embraced. That's the picture Jesus wants us to carry. That's the God he reveals. A God who is more willing to welcome than we are to return. A God whose grace is more scandalous than we imagine. A God who invites us all—prodigals and older brothers alike—to come home, not as servants, but as beloved children.

The party is already started. The father is watching the road. The question is not whether God will welcome you. The question is: will you come? And if you're already in the house, will you join the celebration?

Let's pray.

Gracious Father, we thank you for this parable that reveals your heart. For the younger son in each of us, grant the courage to come home. For the older brother in each of us, grant the grace to rejoice. Help us to live not as those trying to earn your love, but as those who have been loved beyond measure. Make us a people who run toward the lost, who throw parties for the found, who reflect your extravagant welcome. In the name of the one who came to seek and save the lost, Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.
