I want to begin with a story that landed in my inbox this past week. A friend wrote to me about her brother who, fifteen years ago, walked out of their parents' lives. No dramatic fight, no single moment of rupture—just a gradual cooling until one day he stopped returning calls. He moved across the country, changed his number, and for all intents and purposes, became a stranger. The parents grieved him like a death. They wondered what they had done wrong, replayed every conversation, every parenting decision. Then, two weeks ago, out of the blue, a text appeared on their mother's phone: "Mom, can I come home?"

My friend described what happened next. Her mother didn't text back. She didn't call. She got in her car and drove to the airport—a four-hour round trip—without even knowing if he was already on a plane. She stood at arrivals for three hours, holding a sign like she was waiting for a visiting dignitary. When he finally emerged, looking thin and weary, she didn't wait for him to apologize. She dropped the sign, ran to him, and held his face in her hands as if he were the most precious thing she had ever seen. "Let's go home," she said. "I've already called the butcher. We're having brisket tonight."

That, dear friends, is the gospel in a single, messy, modern moment. That is what Jesus is trying to tell us in the story we know as the Parable of the Prodigal Son. Except Jesus tells it even more scandalously, even more extravagantly, because in his story, the father doesn't wait for a text. He watches the road. And when he sees that familiar silhouette on the horizon, he doesn't walk—he *runs*.

Let's sit with this passage for a moment. Luke 15:11-32. You know it well. A man has two sons. The younger demands his inheritance early—a request that in first-century Jewish culture was roughly equivalent to saying, "Father, I wish you were dead." Shockingly, the father grants it. The son takes his share, travels to a distant country, and squanders everything in reckless living. A famine hits. Desperate, he hires himself out to feed pigs, an occupation that makes him ritually unclean and spiritually bankrupt. He longs to eat the pods the pigs are eating. No one gives him anything.

Then comes the moment we often call repentance, though it's more like clarity. The text says, "When he came to himself"—the Greek is *eph' heauton elthe*, literally "he came upon himself." It's a moment of awakening, of finally seeing his own condition clearly. He realizes: "How many of my father's hired servants have bread enough and to spare, but here I am dying of hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'" This is not a speech of deep contrition. It's a calculated plan. He knows his father's generosity extends even to servants. He'll take whatever crumbs he can get.

But notice something crucial: while his *speech* is transactional, his *turning* toward home is not. The moment he resolves to return, to face his father, to risk everything on the hope of mercy—that is the true beginning of repentance. He doesn't need to perfect his confession. He just needs to turn his face toward home.

And here's where the story turns. While he is still far off, his father sees him. The Greek verb here is in the imperfect tense—it suggests ongoing action. The father has been *watching*, waiting, scanning the horizon day after day. And when he sees him, he is moved with compassion. The Greek word is *splagchnizomai*—it means his guts churned, his deepest insides were stirred. This is not polite parental affection. This is visceral, physical love.

And then, the most undignified moment: the father runs. In that culture, patriarchs did not run. They walked with measured dignity. Running meant hitching up your robes, exposing your legs, looking foolish. But this father doesn't care about dignity. He runs to his son, embraces him, and kisses him. The son starts his rehearsed speech—"Father, I have sinned..."—but the father isn't even listening. He's already issuing orders: "Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. Let's pause here. The robe, the ring, the sandals—these aren't just nice gifts. The robe is the father's own, the best one, signifying full restoration to the family. The ring is the family signet, giving the son authority to transact business again. The sandals—only family members wore them, not servants. In one breathtaking moment, the father completely restores the son. No probation period. No penance. No conditions. Just grace, lavish and unmerited.

The older brother is in the field, working. He hears music and dancing. He calls a servant and asks what's going on. When he learns his younger brother has returned and his father has killed the fattened calf, he refuses to go in. He is angry. The father comes out and entreats him. The older son's response is blistering: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. Notice the language. "This son of yours." He won't even claim him as a brother. And notice his view of his own relationship with the father: "I have served you." Not "I have lived as your son," but "I have served you." He sees his faithfulness as a transaction. He's earned something. He's keeping score.

The father's response is gentle and profoundly strategic: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found." He doesn't argue fairness. He *re-frames* the relationship. He calls him "Son"—reminding him of his identity. He affirms "you are always with me"—reminding him of his unbroken presence. He is trying to persuade the older son to accept the *gift* of sonship rather than clinging to the *labor* of servitude. The father won't diminish the joy of the found to appease the resentment of the faithful. He invites the older brother to enlarge his heart.

The story ends there, abruptly. We don't know if the older brother goes in. We don't know if he reconciles. We're left hanging because Jesus is asking his listeners—those Pharisees who complained that he ate with sinners—a question: Will you join the party? Will you understand the heart of your Father?

Now, let's do the careful work of interpretation. This parable is the third in a series in Luke 15. It follows the lost sheep and the lost coin. In each, something is lost and then found, and each ends with a celebration. But this third story complicates things by adding the older brother. Why? Because Jesus is speaking directly to those who, like the older brother, see themselves as faithful, obedient, and deserving.

The Pharisees, who prided themselves on keeping the law, who tithed mint and dill and cumin, who never left the father's house, so to speak—they are the older brother. And they are scandalized that Jesus would welcome "those people": tax collectors, sinners, prostitutes. The Pharisees believed righteousness was *earned* through meticulous adherence to the Law. For them, God's favor was a wage paid to the deserving. The father's indiscriminate generosity—running to a sinner, throwing a party before any penance—wasn't just surprising; it was an affront to their entire system of merit. It threatened the foundation of their religious identity.

The parable reveals that there are two ways to be lost. There is the younger son's way: through rebellion, through leaving, through obvious sin. And there is the older son's way: through obedience, through staying, through religious pride. Both are alienated from the father. Both misunderstand his heart. The younger son thinks he must earn his way back into the father's good graces. The older son thinks he has earned his place in the father's house. Both are wrong. The father's love is not transactional. It is not a wage to be earned. It is a gift, freely given.

This is the scandal of grace. It offends our sense of fairness. Shouldn't the prodigal at least have to grovel a bit more? Shouldn't there be some probation? Some penance? Some consequence? Friends, I suspect most of us in this room identify more with the older brother than the younger. Most of us haven't run off to far countries with inheritance money. Most of us have been fairly responsible. We've stayed in the church. We've tried to live decent lives. We see ourselves as the faithful ones. And that makes this parable deeply uncomfortable. Because it asks us to examine our hearts. Do we, like the older brother, resent God's generosity toward those we deem unworthy? Do we keep score? Do we think we've earned God's favor through our good behavior?

I remember a woman in a previous congregation who pulled me aside after a service where I had preached on God's grace. She was upset. "Pastor," she said, "I've been faithful my whole life. I've served on every committee, taught Sunday school, given faithfully. And you're telling me that God loves the person who shows up once a year at Christmas exactly as much as he loves me?" I could hear the older brother in her voice. And I understood it. It's not fair.

But I gently asked her, "Do you love God because he owes you something? Or do you love him because he first loved you?" She looked at me for a long moment. "I think," she said quietly, "I've been trying to earn what was already mine."

We must repent of that. We must become a community that not only welcomes sinners but also challenges religious pride.

The father doesn't say to the older brother, "You're right, I was unfair." He says, "Come in. Your brother was dead. Celebrate." The father won't diminish the joy of the found to appease the resentment of the faithful. He invites the older brother to enlarge his heart, to enter into the joy, to understand that grace is not a limited resource to be hoarded but an infinite fountain to be shared.

My friend's mother didn't wait to hear her son's full confession before she planned the brisket. She saw him, she ran, she embraced. That's the picture Jesus wants us to carry. That's the God he reveals. A God who is more willing to welcome than we are to return. A God whose grace is more scandalous than we imagine. A God who invites us all—prodigals and older brothers alike—to come home, not as servants, but as beloved children.

The party is already started. The father is watching the road. The question is not whether God will welcome you. The question is: will you come? And if you're already in the house, will you join the celebration?

For the older brother in each of us, grant the grace to rejoice. Help us to live not as those trying to earn your love, but as those who have been loved beyond measure. Make us a people who run toward the lost, who throw parties for the found, who reflect your extravagant welcome. In the name of the one who came to seek and save the lost, Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

This is the God who runs toward prodigals and pleads with older brothers. This is the God who eats with sinners and welcomes the unwelcome.

And when he sees him, he is moved with compassion. The Greek word is *splagchnizomai*—it means his guts churned, his deepest insides were stirred. This is not polite parental affection. This is visceral, physical love.

And then, the most undignified moment: the father runs. In that culture, patriarchs did not run. They walked with measured dignity. Running meant hitching up your robes, exposing your legs, looking foolish. But this father doesn't care about dignity. He runs to his son, embraces him, and kisses him. The son starts his rehearsed speech—"Father, I have sinned..."—but the father isn't even listening. He's already issuing orders: "Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and was found."

Let's pause here. The robe, the ring, the sandals—these aren't just nice gifts. The robe is the father's own, the best one, signifying full restoration to the family. The ring is the family signet, giving the son authority to transact business again. The sandals—only family members wore them, not servants. In one breathtaking moment, the father completely restores the son. No probation period. No penance. No conditions. Just grace, lavish and unmerited.

Now, we could stop here and have a perfectly lovely sermon about God's forgiveness. "Come home, prodigal! God will welcome you!" And that would be true. But Jesus doesn't stop the story there, and neither can we. Because there's another brother.

The older brother is in the field, working. He hears music and dancing. He calls a servant and asks what's going on. When he learns his younger brother has returned and his father has killed the fattened calf, he refuses to go in. He is angry. The father comes out and entreats him. The older son's response is blistering: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"

Notice the language. "This son of yours." He won't even claim him as a brother. And notice his view of his own relationship with the father: "I have served you." Not "I have lived as your son," but "I have served you." He sees his faithfulness as a transaction. He's earned something. He's been keeping score.

Here's the irony: the older brother has already received his inheritance. The estate was divided back in verse 12. Everything the father has is already his. His complaint about "never giving me a young goat" is factually wrong—he has the whole estate at his disposal. He is living in abundance but experiencing it as scarcity. He is in the father's house but doesn't know the father's heart.

The father's response is gentle: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and was found."

The story ends there, abruptly. We don't know if the older brother goes in. We don't know if he reconciles. We're left hanging because Jesus is asking his listeners—those Pharisees who complained that he ate with sinners—a question: Will you join the party? Will you understand the heart of your Father?

Now, let's do the careful work of interpretation. This parable is the third in a series in Luke 15. It follows the lost sheep and the lost coin. In each, something is lost and then found, and each ends with a celebration. But this third story complicates things by adding the older brother. Why? Because Jesus is speaking directly to those who, like the older brother, see themselves as faithful, obedient, and deserving. The Pharisees, who prided themselves on keeping the law, who tithed mint and dill and cumin, who never left the father's house, so to speak—they are the older brother. And they are scandalized that Jesus would welcome "those people": tax collectors, sinners, prostitutes.

The parable reveals that there are two ways to be lost. There is the younger son's way: through rebellion, through leaving, through obvious sin. And there is the older son's way: through obedience, through staying, through the subtle temptation to view God's love as a wage we've earned. Both are alienated from the father. Both misunderstand his heart. The younger son thinks he must earn his way back into the father's good graces. The older son thinks he has earned his place in the father's house. Both are wrong. The father's love is not transactional. It is not a wage to be earned. It is a gift, freely given.

This is the scandal of grace. It offends our sense of fairness. Shouldn't the prodigal at least have to grovel a bit more? Shouldn't there be some probation? Some penance? Some consequence? But grace doesn't work that way. Grace is the father running. Grace is the robe before the apology is finished. Grace is the feast before the repentance is perfected.

It's easy to stand outside the story and judge the older brother. But Jesus told this to people who were standing outside the party judging the guests. He told it to people exactly like him—to people exactly like us.

I suspect most of us in this room identify more with the older brother than the younger. Most of us haven't run off to far countries with inheritance money. Most of us have been fairly responsible. We've stayed in the church. We've tried to live decent lives. We see ourselves as the faithful ones. And that makes this parable deeply uncomfortable. Because it asks us to examine our hearts.

I remember a woman in a previous congregation who pulled me aside after a service where I had preached on God's grace. She was upset. "Pastor," she said, "I've been faithful my whole life. I've served on every committee, taught Sunday school, given faithfully. And you're telling me that God loves the person who shows up once a year at Christmas exactly as much as he loves me?" I could hear the older brother in her voice. And I understood it. It's not fair.

But I gently asked her, "Do you love God because he owes you something? Or do you love him because he first loved you?" She looked at me for a long moment. "I think," she said quietly, "I've been trying to earn what was already mine."

That's the trap of the older brother. He couldn't see that everything the father had was already his. He was living in abundance but experiencing it as scarcity. He was in the father's house but didn't know the father's heart.

Recognizing ourselves in the older brother is painful, but it's not fatal. The father comes out to him, just as he ran to the younger son. He doesn't leave him alone in his resentment. He pleads. He invites. He waits.

And here's the deeper theological truth: we are all, in some sense, both sons. We have all, at times, demanded our autonomy from God. We've taken his blessings and run. We've tried to find life in far countries of our own making—whether through addiction, or ambition, or approval-seeking, or perfectionism, or workaholism, or the relentless respectability of always being right, always being good, always being in control. And we have all, at times, been the older brother—self-righteous, judgmental, resentful of grace that seems too free, too broad, too scandalous.

But the parable isn't ultimately about the sons. It's about the father. It's about a love so extravagant it shatters cultural norms. It's about a grace so profound it runs toward us while we're still far off. It's about a joy so complete it throws parties for the undeserving—a feast that echoes the great banquet of Isaiah 25 and anticipates the wedding supper of the Lamb in Revelation 19.

The father in this story is the God revealed in Jesus Christ. This is the God who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one. This is the God who sweeps the house until the lost coin is found. This is the God who runs toward prodigals and pleads with older brothers. This is the God who eats with sinners and welcomes the unwelcome.

So what does this mean for us, here, today?

First, if you are in a far country, if you have taken your blessings and squandered them, if you feel unworthy to be called God's child—come home. The father is watching the road. He sees you while you are still far off. He is already running. You don't need to have your act together. You don't need to craft the perfect apology. You just need to turn toward home. Repentance is not about perfecting your confession; it's about turning your face toward the father. He will do the rest.

But second, if you are the older brother—if you've been faithful, if you've served, if you're angry that God's grace seems too free—check your heart. Are you serving the father because you love him, or because you think you can earn his love? Do you see God's grace as something you deserve, or as an unmerited gift? Can you rejoice when the lost are found, even when they haven't paid their dues? Can you see that everything the father has is already yours, not as a wage, but as a gift?

The church has often been better at welcoming prodigals than at challenging older brothers. We've created beautiful ministries for those returning from far countries. But we've sometimes nurtured a culture where the faithful feel entitled, where we measure spirituality by attendance and service, where we keep score. We must repent of that. We must become a community that not only welcomes sinners but also challenges the subtle drift toward transactional faith. We must be a place where both sons can find their way back to the father's heart.

The older brother missed the party because he was "in the field" working. Duty blinded him to joy happening right nearby. How often do we miss what God is doing because we're too busy with religious activity? Too consumed with doing things for God to notice what God is already doing?

Finally, this parable calls us to become like the father. To be people who run toward the broken. To be people who throw parties for the undeserving. To be people whose compassion moves from their guts, who are willing to look foolish in the eyes of the world for the sake of love. To be people who plead with the angry and the self-righteous to join the celebration.

The father doesn't say to the older brother, "You're right, I was unfair." He says, "Come in. Your brother was dead. Celebrate." The father won't diminish the joy of the found to appease the resentment of the faithful. He invites the older brother to enlarge his heart, to enter into the joy, to understand that grace is not a limited resource to be hoarded but an infinite fountain to be shared.

My friend's mother didn't wait to hear her son's full confession before she planned the brisket. She saw him, she ran, she embraced. That's the picture Jesus wants us to carry. That's the God he reveals. A God who is more willing to welcome than we are to return. A God whose grace is more scandalous than we imagine. A God who invites us all—prodigals and older brothers alike—to come home, not as servants, but as beloved children.

The music is already playing. The fattened calf is roasting. The father is standing at the door, looking not down the road this time, but into the field, waiting for you. The party has begun. The question is not whether God will welcome you. The question is: will you come in?

Let's pray.

Gracious Father, we thank you for this parable that reveals your heart. For the younger son in each of us, grant the courage to come home. For the older brother in each of us, grant the grace to rejoice. Help us to live not as those trying to earn your love, but as those who have been loved beyond measure. Make us a people who run toward the lost, who throw parties for the found, who reflect your extravagant welcome. In the name of the one who came to seek and save the lost, Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

# Coming Home: The Father's Extravagant Welcome

**Luke 15:11-32**

Pastor Sarah had been staring at her phone for three days. Her twenty-three-year-old son, Michael, had sent his last message on Tuesday: "I need space. Don't contact me." That was it. No explanation, no location, just silence. She'd been up since 4 AM again, her thumb hovering over his name, wanting to call but remembering his words. She'd made his favorite banana bread yesterday, wrapped it in foil, and set it by the door—just in case. She'd checked her phone sixty-three times. And then, at 11:47 AM on that ordinary Saturday, it buzzed. Two words: "Mom, I'm..." The message cut off, but it didn't matter. She was already grabbing her keys.

That, my friends, is a glimpse into the heart of our Father. That desperate, undignified, no-matter-what love that cannot help but run toward the child who is trying to come home.

Today we find ourselves in the most famous story Jesus ever told. It's so familiar we might think we know it by heart, but I want to invite you to hear it fresh—as if for the first time. Because whether you see yourself as the rebel, the rule-keeper, or somewhere in between, this story has something to say to you. It has something to say about who God is, who we are, and what it means to truly come home.

## The Context: A Story for the Offended

Before we dive in, we need to understand the setting. Luke tells us that "all the tax collectors and sinners were coming near to listen to Jesus," and the Pharisees and scribes were grumbling, saying, "This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them." Do you hear that? The religious people were offended by Jesus's guest list. And so Jesus tells three stories: one about a lost sheep, one about a lost coin, and then this—the story of lost sons. Each story escalates. The sheep is 1 in 100. The coin is 1 in 10. But the son? He is 1 of 2—half the family. The stakes are intimate, personal, and devastating.

This is Jesus's final answer to those who think grace is too extravagant, too easy, too offensive. It's His most comprehensive picture of what the Kingdom of God looks like when it collides with human brokenness.

## The Younger Son: The Geography of Lostness

"There was a man who had two sons. The younger of them said to his father, 'Father, give me the share of the property that will belong to me.'" Now stop there. In first-century Jewish culture, this request is unspeakable. It's not just asking for an early inheritance; it's saying, "Father, I wish you were dead." The father would be expected to refuse, to discipline, to protect the family honor. But this father does something shocking: "So he divided his property between them."

He gives his son the freedom to leave. He doesn't control him. He doesn't manipulate him. He releases him. And the son "gathered all he had and traveled to a distant country, and there he squandered his property in dissolute living." The Greek word for "squandered" is *diaskorpizō*—to scatter, to waste, to throw about. It's the same word used for seed scattered on different soils. This is prodigal living—not just spending, but scattering his life to the wind.

But then famine comes. And here's where the story takes its turn. The younger son "came to himself." Now, we often hear this as repentance, but it's more profound than that. In the ancient world, "coming to yourself" meant waking up to reality, remembering who you truly are. He remembers his father's house. He rehearses his speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired hands."

Notice the progression: confession, humility, and a proposed solution. He's willing to be a servant. He'll take the lowest position. He's not demanding anything—he's just hoping for survival.

## The Father: The Geography of Grace

Now comes the moment that has captivated hearts for two thousand years. "But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion; he ran and put his arms around him and kissed him." 

Let's pause. In that culture, a dignified patriarch never ran. It was shameful—exposing his legs, showing a lack of control. But this father doesn't care about his dignity. He runs. He runs to his child before the child can even finish his confession. He doesn't wait for the full apology. He doesn't make him grovel. He doesn't say, "Well, you made your bed..." No. He runs.

And then he interrupts his son's carefully rehearsed speech. The son gets out his confession—"Father, I have sinned"—but before he can say "treat me like a hired hand," the father is already calling for the best robe, a ring for his finger, sandals for his feet. Each detail is significant. The robe is the father's own—the best one, probably his own festal garment. The ring is the signet ring, the symbol of authority to transact business in the father's name. The sandals—slaves went barefoot, but sons wore shoes. And then the feast: "let us eat and celebrate; for this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!"

Do you see? The father doesn't just forgive; he restores. He doesn't just accept; he honors. He gives him back his sonship, not as a reward for repentance but as a gift of grace. The celebration isn't because the son earned it, but because the father's heart is a fountain of joy that cannot be contained when his child comes home.

## The Older Son: The Geography of Resentment

But then the story takes another turn. The older brother is in the field. He's been working. He's been faithful. And when he hears the celebration, he refuses to go in. His father comes out to him—just as he ran to the younger son—and pleads with him. And what does the older son say? "Listen! For all these years I have been working like a slave for you, and I have never disobeyed your command; yet you have never given me even a young goat so that I might celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear the language? "Working like a slave." He's been keeping score. He's been serving not out of love, but out of duty. He's been faithful, but joyless. And he's angry—not just at his brother, but at his father's grace. "But when this son of yours came back, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fatted calf for him!"

Notice he won't even say "my brother." It's "this son of yours." The older son is lost too, but his lostness looks different. It's not the lostness of rebellion; it's the lostness of resentment. He's been in the father's house, but he's never been home. He's been near the father, but he's never known his heart.

And the father's response? "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But we had to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found."

The father doesn't rebuke him. He doesn't say, "How dare you!" He simply invites him in. He reminds him of his place—you're my son, everything I have is yours. But he also reminds him of what's important: the joy of restoration. The feast is not a reward for bad behavior; it's the natural response of a heart that loves without condition.

## The Missing Ending: Which Son Will You Be?

Here's what we often miss: Jesus never tells us what the older son does. Does he go in? Does he stay outside? The story ends with the father's invitation hanging in the air. And that's because Jesus is looking at the Pharisees—and at us—and asking: Which son will you be? Will you come into the celebration?

The parable isn't just about the prodigal's return. It's about the older brother's refusal to celebrate. It's about two ways of being lost, and one way of being found. It's about grace that scandalizes the rule-keepers and saves the rule-breakers.

## Application: Where Are You in the Story?

So where are you this morning? Perhaps you're the younger son. You've wandered far. You've squandered something precious. Maybe you're in the pigpen of your own choices, and you're just now coming to yourself. Maybe you're rehearsing your speech, thinking you need to get your act together before you can come home. Hear this: the Father is already running. You don't have to clean yourself up. You don't have to earn your way back. You just have to turn toward home. The robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The feast is prepared. Come home.

Or perhaps you're the older son. You've been faithful. You've served. You've done everything right. But inside, you're seething. You see others getting grace they don't deserve, and it burns you up. You've been working for God, but you've lost the joy of sonship. You've confused proximity with intimacy. You've mistaken service for relationship. The Father is pleading with you: "All that is mine is yours." But you can't receive it until you let go of your scorecard. You can't celebrate until you see that grace isn't a limited resource. Someone else being welcomed doesn't diminish your place at the table—it proves the table is big enough for everyone.

Maybe you're somewhere in between. Most of us are. We've got a bit of the rebel and a bit of the Pharisee in us. We want grace for ourselves but struggle to extend it to others. We want to be forgiven but find it hard to forgive. We want to be celebrated but resist celebrating those we think don't deserve it.

Here's the truth that might unsettle us: The Father's love is prodigal. Not "prodigal" as in repentant, but "prodigal" as in extravagant, lavish, wasteful. He throws his love around with abandon. He doesn't calculate worthiness. He doesn't measure performance. He just loves. And that love is both our salvation and our challenge.

## The Feast: Where Everyone Belongs

This story tells us something profound about the Kingdom of God: it's a feast, not a performance review. It's a celebration, not a courtroom. The Father's house is not a place where you earn your keep; it's a place where you learn to live in the reality of being loved.

And here's the scandal: both sons are invited. The one who squandered and the one who served. The one who confessed and the one who complained. The one who came crawling back and the one who stood his ground. The Father's love doesn't discriminate between types of lostness. He runs to the far country, and he comes out to the field. He meets us wherever we are.

But you have to come in. You have to accept the robe. You have to put on the ring. You have to join the feast. The younger son almost didn't, because he thought he had to be a servant. The older son almost didn't, because he thought he deserved to be the guest of honor. Both had to learn the same lesson: you're not what you do. You're who the Father says you are. And the Father says you're His beloved child.

## Conclusion: The Invitation Still Stands

So here we are, two thousand years later, still living in the unresolved ending of Jesus's story. The music is playing. The table is set. The fatted calf has been killed. The celebration is ready. And the Father is still pleading: "Come in."

Maybe you've been avoiding this house because you think your mistakes are too big. Come in. The Father's grace is bigger.

Maybe you've been standing outside because you think your faithfulness has been overlooked. Come in. The Father has seen every moment, and He wants you to know the joy you've been missing.

Maybe you've been watching from a distance, unsure if there's a place for you. Come in. There's a robe with your name on it.

The French theologian Henri Nouwen once said that after meditating on this parable for years, he realized that the real call is to become like the Father—to be the one who runs, who welcomes, who celebrates. And that's our call too. Not just to receive grace, but to become agents of it. To be people who throw parties for prodigals. To be people who leave our dignity at the door and run toward the ones who are trying to find their way home.

So this morning, as we prepare to leave this place, I want you to hear the Father's words as if they were spoken directly to you—because they are:

"Child, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But we had to celebrate and rejoice, because you were dead and have come to life; you were lost and have been found."

The table is set. The music is playing. The Father is waiting.

Will you come in?

Let us pray.

# Coming Home: A Sermon on the Prodigal Son

## The Far Country in Our Hearts

Several years ago, I met a woman named Margaret in a hospital waiting room. Her son David had been admitted after a near-fatal overdose. For twenty minutes, she told me their story—not with anger or shame, but with a weariness that comes from years of prayer and disappointment. David had left home at eighteen, angry about rules he thought were unfair, convinced his father and I were holding him back from "living his truth." He took his college fund and disappeared. For three years, they heard nothing. No calls on holidays. No response to messages. Just silence.

Then, at two in the morning last Tuesday, the phone rang. It was a social worker from a hospital in another state. David had listed his mother as an emergency contact. Before she could even process what she was hearing, Margaret was in her car, driving through the night. "I didn't stop for coffee," she told me. "I didn't even pack a bag. I just needed to get to him."

When she arrived, she found her son—thirty pounds lighter, track marks on his arms, weeping in a hospital gown that barely fit him. He could barely look at her. "Mom, I'm so sorry. I don't deserve for you to be here." She didn't lecture him. She didn't ask for explanations. She just climbed into that narrow hospital bed, wrapped her arms around him, and said, "Let's go home."

Friends, that is not just a mother's love. That is a glimpse into the very heart of God.

## The Setting: Why Jesus Told This Story

The parable we know as "The Prodigal Son" doesn't begin with a wayward child. It begins with grumbling religious leaders. Luke tells us that "all the tax collectors and sinners were gathering around to hear Jesus," and the Pharisees and teachers of the law began muttering: "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them."

Notice that word: *welcomes*. Not just tolerates, not just preaches at, but *welcomes*. Shares meals with. Treats as family. This so scandalized the religious establishment that Jesus tells not one, not two, but three parables to answer their objection—the lost sheep, the lost coin, and then this, the lost son.

The third story is different. It's not about searching; it's about waiting. It's not about lostness out in the world; it's about lostness that chooses to walk away. And most importantly, it's not just about one lost son. It's about two.

## The Younger Son: The Journey Into Lostness

We know this part well. The younger son comes to his father and makes a request that in his culture was equivalent to saying, "I wish you were dead." "Father, give me my share of the estate." In Jewish law, the younger son would receive one-third of the inheritance, but only after the father's death. This son isn't just asking for money; he's severing relationship. He's treating his father as if he's already dead.

And here's what astonishes me: the father gives it to him. He doesn't fight. He doesn't manipulate. He doesn't hold a family meeting to shame the boy into staying. He gives him the freedom to leave. God will not love us into submission. He will not coerce our devotion. The greatest gift God gives us is the freedom to walk away—even from Him.

So the son goes to "a distant country." The Greek word is *makran*—not just geographically far, but existentially distant. It's the far country of our hearts when we deliberately choose anything over God. He squanders his wealth in "wild living"—the word is *asotos*, meaning unsavable, dissolute, wasteful. And when the money runs out, so do his so-called friends. A famine hits, and suddenly he's feeding pigs—an unclean animal for a Jewish boy—and not even the pods he's feeding them will satisfy his hunger.

But notice the turning point. Scripture says, "He came to his senses." Not "he got desperate" or "he hit rock bottom," but "he came to his senses." True repentance isn't just crisis management; it's finally seeing reality as it is. It's remembering who you are and whose you are. He rehearses his speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants."

Even his repentance is measured, calculated. He's not hoping for restoration; he's hoping for employment. He'll settle for being a servant. That's how grace works on us before we fully understand it—we think small while God is planning a feast.

## The Father: The God Who Runs

Now we come to the moment that defines everything. "But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him."

Stop there. In that culture, a patriarch never ran. It was considered undignified for an older man to hike up his robes and expose his legs. Respectable fathers didn't run; they waited to be approached. But this father runs. He doesn't wait for the apology. He doesn't make his son crawl. He sprints toward his returning child with abandon that would have shocked Jesus' hearers.

Before the son can even finish his carefully rehearsed speech, the father is already ordering the best robe—the one reserved for honored guests—the ring, symbolizing restored authority, and sandals, a sign of sonship, not servanthood. And then the feast: "Kill the fattened calf. Let's celebrate!" Not a quiet family dinner, but a community-wide party.

This is the scandal of grace. It doesn't wait for us to get cleaned up. It doesn't require us to earn our way back. It meets us in our shame and restores us before we can prove ourselves worthy. The father isn't interested in what his son deserves; he's interested in what his son *is*—his child, his beloved.

## The Older Brother: The Other Lost Son

But the story doesn't end there. The older brother is in the field, working. He hears music and dancing and calls over a servant to ask what's happening. When he learns his brother is back and there's a party, "he became angry and refused to go in."

This is crucial. The Pharisees listening to Jesus would have identified completely with the older brother. He's done everything right. He's stayed home. He's obeyed. He's worked. And now his faithfulness feels like a waste. "All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders," he tells his father. Notice his language: *slaving*, not serving. He doesn't see his sonship as a gift but as a burden. He's been keeping score.

The father goes out to him, just as he ran to the younger son. He pleads with him. "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

The father's love is not diminished by extending grace to the younger son; it's multiplied. The older brother's inheritance hasn't been reduced; his position hasn't changed. But his heart has. He's just as lost as his brother ever was—lost in his self-righteousness, lost in his resentment, lost in his belief that love must be earned.

## Two Ways to Be Lost

Here's what Jesus is telling the Pharisees—and us: There are two ways to be lost. There's the lostness of rebellion, which is obvious. We see it in addiction, in promiscuity, in the ways we chase everything but God. But there's also the lostness of religion, which is subtler and perhaps more dangerous. It's the lostness that stays in the Father's house but never tastes the Father's joy. It's the lostness that serves but doesn't love, that obeys but doesn't trust.

The younger son wanted the father's stuff without the father. The older son wanted the father's farm but resented the father's heart. Both were trying to use the father to get what they really wanted—pleasure for one, reward for the other. Neither understood that the father himself was the treasure.

And here's the stunning truth: the father treats both sons the same way. He gives both freedom. He runs to both. He pleads with both. He doesn't love the younger son more because he's repentant, nor does he love the older son less because he's angry. His love isn't based on performance; it's based on relationship. You are my child. That's it. That's the whole equation.

## The Application: Where Do You See Yourself?

So where do you see yourself in this story?

Perhaps you're the younger son. You've walked away from God, either through dramatic rebellion or quiet drift. You've been living in the far country, and it's cost you more than you wanted to pay. Maybe you're feeding pigs right now—not literal swine, but the addictions, the compromises, the empty pursuits that leave you starving while you serve them. Maybe you're rehearsing your speech, thinking you need to get your act together before you can come home.

Hear me: the Father is already running. You don't have to clean up. You don't have to have the right words. You just have to turn toward home. Repentance is simply that—turning. It's the smallest step in the right direction, and it's enough to make the Father sprint to meet you. The robe is ready. The ring is waiting. The feast is prepared. Come home.

But maybe, just maybe, you're the older brother. You've been in church your whole life. You've served on committees, taught Sunday school, given your tithe. And you're angry. Angry that God seems to welcome people who haven't paid their dues. Angry that the church celebrates those with dramatic conversion stories while your quiet faithfulness feels invisible. Angry that the Father's grace seems reckless, unfair, wasteful.

If that's you, the Father comes to you too. He doesn't rebuke you for your anger; he invites you into the party. He reminds you that everything he has is yours. But he also invites you to lay down your ledger. Your service was never meant to be slavery. Your obedience was meant to be joy. The inheritance was always yours, but you were so busy working for it that you forgot you already had it.

The older brother missed the party because he was standing outside with his righteousness. Don't make the same mistake. The Father's house is a place of celebration, not calculation. Come in.

## The Deeper Truth: We Are Both Sons

But here's the deepest truth: we are all, each of us, both sons. We all have the rebel and the Pharisee warring within us. We all have moments when we demand our way and run, and moments when we stand outside the party with our arms crossed, judging who gets to be inside.

The genius of Jesus' parable is that it doesn't let any of us off the hook. It confronts the libertine and the legalist, the sinner and the saint. It tells us that God's grace is far more scandalous than we want to believe, and far more personal than we dare to hope.

The father in the story doesn't give his sons a lecture on responsibility. He doesn't make the younger son sign a contract promising to shape up. He doesn't tell the older son to stop being so sensitive. He just keeps being a father. He keeps loving, keep pursuing, keeps celebrating.

That's the God revealed in Jesus Christ. A God who runs toward us while we are still far off. A God who throws parties for sinners. A God who is just as concerned with the self-righteous heart of the older brother as He is with the rebellious heart of the younger.

## The Invitation to the Feast

The parable ends without resolution. We don't know if the older brother ever goes into the party. Jesus leaves it open because He's inviting the Pharisees—and us—to write our own ending. Will we come in? Will we lay down our resentment and join the celebration? Will we trust that the Father's love is big enough for all of us?

The table is set. The music is playing. The fattened calf has been prepared. This is not just a story about a wayward child; it's an invitation to the feast of grace.

Maybe you've been running. The Father is watching the road for you.

Maybe you've been standing outside, arms crossed. The Father is coming out to plead with you.

Either way, the feast is ready. The only question is: will you come?

Let's pray.

*Gracious Father, we confess that we have been both sons. We have demanded our way and squandered your gifts. We have served you with resentful hearts, keeping score of our goodness. Forgive us for misunderstanding your love. Forgive us for thinking it must be earned. Today, we accept your scandalous grace. We come home. We come into the party. And we ask that you would give us the Father's heart—to rejoice when the lost are found, to celebrate when sinners repent, to love as we have been loved. In the name of Jesus, who told this story so we might know your heart. Amen.*

Beloved, I want you to imagine a scene that would have made any respectable first-century Jew gasp in horror. A young man walks into his father’s courtyard—not to wish him good morning, not to ask a blessing, but to say, *“Father, give me the share of the estate that will belong to me.”* In that culture, in that time, this was not merely rude; it was violent. It was the equivalent of looking your parent in the eye and saying, *“I wish you were dead. You are worth more to me as an inheritance than as a father. Give me what I would get when you’re in the ground, because as far as I’m concerned, you’re already there.”*

The neighbors would have expected the father to strike him. To drive him out with shame. To sit shiva for him as if he truly were dead. Instead, Jesus tells us something that should stop us in our tracks: *“So he divided his property between them.”* The father grants the request. He liquidates assets—land that had been in the family for generations, perhaps—turns them into cash, and hands it over. He lets the son go. He lets him break his heart.

And so begins the parable we often call “The Prodigal Son,” though if we are careful readers of Luke 15, we might better call it “The Parable of the Two Lost Sons,” or perhaps “The Parable of the Running Father.” Because this story Jesus tells—not in a synagogue, but over a meal with tax collectors and sinners, while the Pharisees grumble outside—is not merely a morality tale about a wayward boy who learns his lesson. It is a revelation of the heart of God, and a mirror held up to our own.

**The Journey Down and the Turning**

The younger son takes his blood-money and runs. He goes to a far country—not just geographically distant, but culturally, spiritually distant. He wants to get as far from his father’s house as possible, as if distance could somehow erase the shame of what he has done. And there, Jesus tells us with painful economy, he “squandered his property in reckless living.” The Greek word for “squandered” is *diaskorpizo*—to scatter to the wind. He threw it away. And when a severe famine hits, he finds himself empty, feeding pigs—an unclean animal for a Jewish boy—and so hungry he longs to eat the pods they are eating.

This is the bottom. This is the place where all his self-sufficiency has brought him: a pig pen, alone, starving, covered in the filth of his choices. And here, in this lowest place, Jesus says something beautiful: “He came to himself.” The Greek is *eis heauton elthon*—he came to himself. He remembered who he was. He remembered that back home, even the hired servants have bread to spare. He remembers his father—not as a taskmaster, but as a provider. And he rehearses a speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.”

Notice something important here. His repentance is real, but it is still tinged with calculation. He is willing to be a slave. He is willing to work his way back into the household, perhaps over years, earning his keep, slowly climbing back up the ladder of acceptance. He has a plan. He has a speech. He is prepared to grovel, to negotiate, to perform his way home.

But grace does not negotiate. Grace runs.

**The Undignified Father**

While the son is still a long way off—while he is still rehearsing his speech, while he is still smelling like pigs and sweat and failure—his father sees him. How long had the father been watching? Days? Months? Years? Jesus doesn’t say, but we know this father has not forgotten his boy. He has been scanning the horizon. And when he sees that familiar silhouette, that stumbling gait, Jesus gives us one of the most shocking verbs in the entire New Testament: *“He ran.”*

In the ancient Near East, elderly patriarchs did not run. It was beneath their dignity. They moved with measured steps, surrounded by the gravity of their status. To run was to gather up your robes, to expose your legs, to look ridiculous, to risk tripping in the dust. But this father runs. He runs because love cannot wait. He runs because compassion overrides honor. He runs because the only thing that matters is that his boy is home.

And here is the miracle: the father reaches his son *before* the son can deliver his speech. While the boy is still trying to say, “Make me a slave,” the father is embracing him. While the boy is confessing his unworthiness, the father is calling for the best robe—the family robe, the one that marks him as a son, not a servant. He puts a ring on his finger—signet ring, authority restored. He puts sandals on his feet—slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes. And he orders the fatted calf killed—the animal reserved for the most joyous occasions, the one that says, “We are not having a quiet supper. We are having a feast.”

The father will not let his son earn his way back. He will not let him live in the servant’s quarters. He restores him completely, immediately, extravagantly. This is not just forgiveness; this is adoption. This is the gospel in narrative form: we come home planning to pay our debt, and we find a party already in progress, prepared for us before we even asked.

**The Elder Brother and the Other Lostness**

But the story does not end there. If it ended with the embrace and the music, it would be lovely, but incomplete. Jesus has one more character to show us, and this character is the reason he is telling the story in the first place. Remember the context: the Pharisees and scribes are grumbling because Jesus receives sinners. They are standing outside the party, angry that grace is being shown to the undeserving. So Jesus brings on the older brother.

He is in the field. He is working. He has never left. He has been faithful, dutiful, obedient. But when he hears the music and dancing, he refuses to go in. He summons a servant—not his father—to ask what is happening. And when his father comes out to plead with him (notice the father goes out to the older son just as he ran to the younger—this father is always pursuing), the older son unleashes his bitterness: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fatted calf for him!”

Do you hear it? He speaks of slavery, not sonship. “I have served you.” He speaks of wages, not inheritance. “You never gave me…” He cannot even bring himself to say “my brother.” He says, “this son of yours.” And he accuses his brother of sins the text never mentions—prostitutes—revealing the lurid imagination of resentment.

The father’s response is gentle, heartbreaking, and firm: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” Everything the father has has always belonged to the older son. He never needed to earn a goat; he owned the whole flock. But he was so busy working for approval that he never realized he already had it. And now, because of his bitterness, he is missing the party. He is standing outside the house, lost in his own field, while the feast goes on without him.

**Where Are You in the Story?**

So where do we find ourselves this morning?

Perhaps you are the younger son. Perhaps you have wandered far. Perhaps you have made choices that have left you in your own kind of pig pen—ashamed, exhausted, wondering if you have burned too many bridges to come back. Listen carefully: the Father is scanning the horizon for you. He is not waiting for you to clean yourself up. He is not waiting for you to prove your sincerity with years of good behavior. He is waiting to run to you. He is waiting to clothe you in the righteousness of Christ, to put the family ring on your finger, to kill the fatted calf and throw a party in your honor. Come home. Come home now, while you are still a long way off. Let him interrupt your prepared speech with his embrace.

Or perhaps you are the older son. Perhaps you have stayed in the church. You have obeyed the rules. You have never scandalized anyone with wild living. But your heart is hard. You look at the grace given to others—the recovering addict welcomed at the altar, the former criminal baptized in the river, the messy broken people finding joy in the gospel—and you feel a surge of resentment. “I worked so hard. Why do they get the party?” Dear friend, everything the Father has is already yours. You do not need to earn love; you have it. But you must come in to the party. You must learn to rejoice when the lost are found, or you will find yourself outside the very kingdom you thought you were building.

Or perhaps you are the church itself. Perhaps we have been the older brother, standing at the door, judging who deserves to be let in. Jesus is inviting us to become like the Father—to run toward the messy, the broken, the rebellious. To embrace before people have their theology straight. To throw parties for prodigals. To get our robes dirty in the dust of welcome.

**The Invitation**

The story ends, remarkably, with an ellipsis. We do not know if the older brother came in. Jesus leaves us hanging, because we are meant to finish the story. The music is still playing. The fatted calf is still roasting. The Father is still standing at the edge of the light, looking out into the darkness, waiting.

To the younger son, he says, “Come home.”

To the older son, he says, “Come in.”

And to all of us, he says, “There is bread enough and to spare. There is a robe waiting. There is a ring ready. The party is still going on.”

Do not let shame keep you away. Do not let bitterness keep you outside. The Father is running toward you, arms open, eyes bright with love. Come home. Come in. The feast is ready, and there is a place at the table with your name on it.

He runs because compassion overrides honor. He runs because the only thing that matters is that his boy is home.

And here is the miracle: the father reaches his son *before* the son can deliver his speech. While the boy is still trying to say, “Make me a slave,” the father is embracing him. He puts a ring on his finger—a signet ring, authority restored. He puts sandals on his feet—slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes. So where do we find ourselves this morning?

Perhaps you are the younger son. Perhaps you have wandered far. Perhaps you have made choices that have left you in your own kind of pig pen—ashamed, exhausted, wondering if you have burned too many bridges to come back. Listen carefully: the Father is scanning the horizon for you. He is not waiting for you to clean yourself up. He is not waiting for you to prove your sincerity with years of good behavior. He is waiting to run to you. He is waiting to clothe you in the righteousness of Christ, to put the family ring on your finger, to kill the fatted calf and throw a party in your honor. Come home. Come home now, while you are still a long way off. Let him interrupt your prepared speech with his embrace.

Or perhaps you are the older son. Perhaps you have stayed in the church. You have obeyed the rules. You have never scandalized anyone with wild living. But your heart is hard. You look at the grace given to others—the recovering addict welcomed at the altar, the former criminal baptized in the river, the messy broken people finding joy in the gospel—and you feel a surge of resentment. “I worked so hard. To the older son, he says, “Come in.”

And to all of us, he says, “There is bread enough and to spare. There is a robe waiting. There is a ring ready. The party is still going on.”

Do not let shame keep you away. Do not let bitterness keep you outside. The Father is running toward you, arms open, eyes bright with love. Come home. Come in. The feast is ready, and there is a place at the table with your name on it.

**The Road Home**

There is a photograph that circulates occasionally on social media—an airport arrival gate, sometime in the early morning hours. A father stands alone, slightly apart from the crowd, his hands clasped behind his back, his eyes fixed on the corridor where deplaning passengers will emerge. He has been standing there for two hours. His posture is still, but his eyes are alive with a mixture of anxiety and hope. When the figure finally appears—a son returning from military deployment, or perhaps from years of estrangement—the father does not wait for the boy to reach him. He breaks into a run. He weaves through the crowd, oblivious to the stares, and seizes his son in an embrace that looks almost violent in its tenderness. The son drops his bag. The father will not let go.

It is a modern echo of an ancient scene. And if that image stirs something in your chest—some longing, some ache, some recognition—then you are beginning to understand why Jesus told this particular story. Not just as a morality tale about repentance, and certainly not as a simple lesson about forgiveness, but as a revelation of the very heart of God.

**The Context of Grace**

We find ourselves in Luke 15, where Jesus has been eating with tax collectors and sinners. The Pharisees and scribes are grumbling, muttering that this rabbi welcomes sinners and eats with them. In response, Jesus tells three stories: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son. The progression is deliberate. The sheep wanders away through foolishness; the coin is lost through no fault of its own; but the son? The son *leaves*. He chooses the far country. He sins with his eyes wide open. And it is this third story that Jesus stretches out into a full drama with three acts, because it is this story that most mirrors the human condition—and most scandalizes our sense of fairness.

**The Descent and the Turning**

The younger son’s request is shocking. “Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.” In the patriarchal culture of first-century Palestine, this is tantamount to saying, “I wish you were dead.” The father, by rights, could have driven him out with blows and curses. Instead, he divides the living. He grants the request. And the son gathers it all—liquidates his future, his security, his name—and journeys to a far country.

What follows is not just a fall, but a collapse. The Greek text emphasizes the rapidity: he squandered, he spent, he was devoured. He hires himself out to a Gentile pig farmer—a detail no Jewish listener could miss without wincing. He is feeding swine, unclean animals, and he is so desperate that he longs to eat the pods they eat. He has hit bottom. He is as far from home as geography and dignity will allow.

But then comes the crucial phrase: “He came to himself.” The Greek implies more than just regret. It is a remembering. He recalls who he is. “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread?” He rehearses a speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.” It is a good speech. It is honest. It acknowledges sin without excuse. He will practice it all the way home.

**The Undignified Father**

But here the story pivots in a way that would have stunned Jesus’ original audience. While the son is still a long way off, the father sees him. This detail is loaded with meaning. It means the father has been watching. Day after day, he has stood on the roof or at the city gate, scanning the horizon for a figure he cannot yet see but refuses to stop hoping for.

And then the father does something extraordinary. He runs. 

In ancient Near Eastern culture, elderly patriarchs did not run. To run was to expose one’s legs, to shame oneself, to abandon dignity. But this father hitches up his robes and sprints. He reaches his son before the son can reach him. He interrupts the rehearsed speech. He falls on the boy’s neck and kisses him—not a chaste peck, but the *kataphileō*, the continuous, overwhelming kisses of complete restoration.

The son manages to get out only part of his speech: “I am not worthy.” But the father is already calling for the best robe—the family robe, perhaps the father’s own—to cover the rags. He demands a ring for the finger, a sign of authority and sonship, and sandals for the feet, indicating he is not a slave but a free man. And then the feast: “Kill the fattened calf.” In a village culture where meat was rare, this is an announcement to the whole community. My son was dead; now he lives. The music begins. The dancing starts.

**The Elder Brother and the Missing Party**

But the story does not end with the embrace. There is a third character: the older son. He has been working in the field—dutiful, obedient, keeping the rules. When he hears the music and learns the cause, he refuses to go in. He stands outside, arms crossed, heart hardening. He shames his father publicly by refusing to act as host, forcing the father to leave the party—*again*—to come out and plead with him.

The older son’s speech is dripping with resentment: “I have served you for so many years; I never disobeyed; yet you never gave me even a young goat.” Notice the pronouns: *I, I, I*. And notice the accusation: “This son of yours” (he cannot bring himself to say “my brother”) “devoured your property with prostitutes.” Whether this is true or slander, we do not know; the younger son’s sins have become, in the older brother’s mind, a currency by which he measures his own worth.

The father’s response is gentle but firm: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” The older son has confused proximity with relationship. He has lived in the house but missed the heart. He has served as a slave when he was meant to rejoice as an heir. And the story ends with the father’s plea hanging in the air: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive.”

We are never told if the older brother enters the feast.

**Where Do You Stand?**

So where do we find ourselves in this story? 

Perhaps some of us are in the far country today. We have taken our inheritance—our gifts, our years, our health—and spent them on things that have devoured us. We have rehearsed our speeches. We have calculated how to earn our way back to respectability, if not to intimacy. Hear this good news: the Father is already running toward you. You do not have to finish the speech. You do not have to scrub away the pigpen smell. You only have to turn toward home, and you will find yourself engulfed in an embrace that restores your name before you can apologize for your shame.

But perhaps more of us are in the field. We have stayed in the church. We have kept the commands. We have not gone to the wild places, and we feel a creeping resentment that grace seems so… *indiscriminate*. We look at those who come stumbling in, smelling of cigarettes and bad decisions, and we think, “They don’t deserve the party.” We have confused the gospel with fairness. We have forgotten that we, too, are prodigals—just prodigals who never left the yard. The Father leaves the party to find us, too. He invites us to drop our ledgers, to set down our calculators, and to come dance.

**The Party Continues**

This parable is not ultimately about sin management or moral improvement. It is about the character of God. It reveals a Father whose love is not passive but active, not dignified but desperate, not conditional but reckless. It reveals a God who runs toward shame, who pays the price of humiliation to restore the humiliated, who keeps the feast open even when the religious refuse to attend.

The music is still playing. The fattened calf has been prepared. Whether you are coming from the pig farms of failure or the fields of resentment, the road leads to the same house. The Father is watching the horizon. He has seen you already, while you are still a long way off.

Come home. Not to a performance review. Not to a probationary period. But to a ring, a robe, a feast, and a kiss. Come home to the party you did not earn but cannot lose. Come home, because in the economy of grace, the only thing required is the willingness to be found.

And when you enter, do not be surprised if you find the Father running to meet you. He has been waiting for this moment all along.

He hires himself out to a Gentile pig farmer—a detail no Jewish listener could miss without wincing. He is feeding swine, unclean animals, and he is so desperate that he longs to eat the pods they eat. He has hit bottom. He is as far from home as geography and dignity will allow.

But then comes the crucial phrase: “He came to himself.” The Greek implies more than just regret. It is a remembering. He recalls who he is. “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread?” He rehearses a speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.” It is a good speech. It is honest. It acknowledges sin without excuse. He will practice it all the way home.

But here the story pivots in a way that would have stunned Jesus’ original audience. While the son is still a long way off, the father sees him. This detail is loaded with meaning. It means the father has been watching. Day after day, he has stood on the roof or at the city gate, scanning the horizon for a figure he cannot yet see but refuses to stop hoping for.

And then the father does something extraordinary. He runs.

He reaches his son before the son can reach him. He interrupts the rehearsed speech. He falls on the boy’s neck and kisses him—not a chaste peck, but the *kataphileō*, the continuous, overwhelming kisses of complete restoration.

We know this calculus, do we not? Perhaps you have served on the church board for twenty years, teaching Sunday school, locking up after the potlucks, while newcomers stumble in with their messy lives and their instant grace. Perhaps you have watched someone with a past like a crime novel receive immediate acceptance, while your own quiet faithfulness seems to go unnoticed. You keep a ledger. You tally the hours. You have confused the gospel with fairness, and like the workers in the vineyard who labored all day, you resent the eleventh-hour recipients of equal grace. You are not in the far country; you are in the field. But you are just as lost.

The father’s response is gentle but firm: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” The older son has confused proximity with relationship. He has lived in the house but missed the heart. He has served as a slave when he was meant to rejoice as an heir. And the story ends with the father’s plea hanging in the air: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive.”

So where do we find ourselves in this story? 

Perhaps some of us are in the far country today. We have taken our inheritance—our gifts, our years, our health—and spent them on things that have devoured us. We have rehearsed our speeches. The robe is ready. The ring is sized for your finger. The calf—purchased at cost, prepared with sacrifice—awaits.

It reveals a Father whose love is not passive but active, not dignified but desperate, not conditional but reckless. It reveals a God who runs toward shame, who pays the price of humiliation to restore the humiliated, who keeps the feast open even when the religious refuse to attend.

The music is still playing. The fattened calf has been prepared. Whether you are coming from the pig farms of failure or the fields of resentment, the road leads to the same house. The Father is watching the horizon. He has seen you already, while you are still a long way off.

Come home. Not to a performance review. Not to a probationary period. But to a ring, a robe, a feast, and a kiss. Come home to the party you did not earn but cannot lose. Come home, because in the economy of grace, the only thing required is the willingness to be found.

For we are all prodigals—some who left, and some who stayed away while remaining inside. And we are all met by a God who runs, who embraces, who feasts, and who sends us back out to scan the horizon for anyone else who might be turning toward home.
