# The Two Lost Sons and the One True Father

## A Sermon on Luke 15:11-32

---

It was the coldest December I can remember, and I found myself in a downtown coffee shop, warming my hands around a mug that was more prop than pleasure. Across from me sat a man in his sixties, silver-haired, with the bearing of someone who had once commanded rooms. He was a retired executive, a deacon in his church for thirty years, a man whose reputation for integrity was unimpeachable. And he was weeping.

"I've done everything right," he said, his voice breaking. "I never left. I never squandered. I served that church through three pastors, two splits, and a building campaign. But when I pray, I hear nothing. When I serve, I feel nothing. And I look at my brother—my brother who drank his way through two marriages, who mocked our faith for decades, who only came back to God when his liver failed—and I watch my parents weep with joy over his return, and I feel something I can barely admit. I feel angry. I feel that it isn't fair. And worst of all, I wonder if my father ever loved me at all."

I sat with him for two hours that night. And I have sat with him, in different forms, a hundred times since. Because the church is full of elder brothers. We have built such excellent systems for welcoming home the prodigals that we have sometimes forgotten that the elder brother never left the porch—and that his soul is in equal danger.

This morning, I want us to walk slowly through what I believe is the most psychologically penetrating and spiritually devastating story Jesus ever told. We call it the Parable of the Prodigal Son, but that title, given to us by later tradition, misleads us. This is not one parable but two. It is not about one lost son but two. And it is not finally about either son, but about the father whose love exposes and heals them both.

---

## The Younger Son: The Journey Into Distance

Jesus tells us that a certain man had two sons. The younger comes to his father and demands his share of the inheritance. In the ancient world, this was not merely impulsive youth. It was a statement of profound contempt. By asking for his inheritance while his father still lived, the younger son was saying, in effect: "I wish you were dead. Your continuing existence is an obstacle to my happiness."

The father, remarkably, complies. He divides his property between them. The Greek word Luke uses—*ousia*, substance, life—suggests that the father is being asked to tear his own life apart. And he does. This is our first glimpse of the father's character: he is a man who permits himself to be wounded in order to preserve relationship. He does not disown his son. He does not protect his dignity. He simply lets him go, carrying the wound of rejected love.

The younger son journeys to a far country. The Greek *chora makros*—literally, "long land"—carries echoes of exile, of the distance Adam put between himself and Eden, of the prodigious wandering of the human heart away from its source. There, Jesus tells us, he squandered his property in reckless living. The word *asotos*, from which we get "prodigal," means "unsaved," "lost beyond recovery." He was living as if there were no tomorrow, no consequences, no father.

Then comes the famine. In the ancient imagination, famine was never merely agricultural; it was theological. The land itself withdraws its blessing. The younger son hires himself out to a Gentile—already a profound degradation for a Jewish man—and finds himself feeding pigs, unclean animals, so hungry that he longs to eat their slop. He has hit bottom. He has become less than human in his own eyes.

And here, Luke tells us, "he came to himself." The Greek is striking: *eis heauton elthon*—"he came into himself." This is not merely decision-making. It is the recovery of identity, the return to sanity, the moment when the fog of self-deception clears and he remembers who he is and whose he is. "How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, and I am dying here with hunger!"

He prepares a speech. "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants." It is a good speech. It is humble. It is accurate. It shows proper shame. And it is entirely inadequate to the love he is about to encounter.

---

## The Father: The Journey Into Grace

While the son is still a long way off, his father sees him. The verb Luke uses—*eiden*—suggests recognition, habitual watching. This father has been looking down the road. Day after day, year after year, he has kept vigil. His love has not been conditional on his son's return; it has created the possibility of return.

And he runs. In the ancient world, dignified men did not run. They processed. To run was to expose the legs, to abandon decorum, to make oneself ridiculous. But this father runs. He runs not because he is undignified, but because his dignity has been entirely redefined by love. He reaches his son, embraces him—*epipipto*, falls upon his neck—and kisses him.

The son tries to deliver his speech. He gets as far as "I am no longer worthy to be called your son." But the father interrupts. He will not hear of servanthood. He calls for the best robe—the family robe, the sign of full restoration. He places a ring on his hand—authority, sonship. He puts sandals on his feet—slaves went barefoot; sons wore shoes. And he orders the fatted calf killed—the animal reserved for the greatest celebrations, perhaps years in the preparing.

"For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found." The father speaks in the language of resurrection. This is not mere forgiveness. This is new creation. The son who wished his father dead discovers that his father's love is stronger than death itself.

---

## The Elder Son: The Journey Into Resentment

But the story is not over. The elder son is in the field. He is working, as he has always worked. He hears music and dancing—*symphonia*, a word suggesting harmony, joy, the restoration of right order—and asks what is happening. A servant tells him: "Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound."

And the elder son becomes angry. The Greek *orgizo* suggests not mere irritation but deep, burning wrath. He refuses to go in. This is his first act of rebellion—not in the field, not in the far country, but at the very threshold of his father's house. And his father, again, goes out to him. The same verb: *exelthon*. The father who ran to the younger son now pleads with the elder. His love is inexhaustible, undiscriminating, unearned.

The elder son delivers his own speech. Unlike his brother's, it is full of accusation. "Look, these many years I have served you"—*douleuo*, the word for slavish labor, not filial devotion—"and I never disobeyed your command." He speaks of commands, not relationship. He speaks of service, not love. "Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends."

Do you hear it? The younger son wanted his father's goods without his father. The elder son wants his father's goods—his recognition, his reward—without his father. Both have treated the father as a means to an end. Both have been living in the far country, one in riotous excess, the other in resentful obedience. The younger son's rebellion was obvious. The elder son's was hidden, respectable, approved by all the right people. But it was rebellion nonetheless.

"But when this son of yours came"—not "my brother," but "this son of yours," disowning the relationship—"who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!" The elder son has been keeping score. He knows exactly what his brother did, or imagines he does. His righteousness has become a weapon, his service a contract he believes has been breached.

---

## The Father's Final Word

The father responds with tenderness that breaks my heart every time I read it. "Son"—*teknon*, my child, the same term of affection he used for the younger son—"you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours." The elder son has not lost his inheritance. He has lost his enjoyment of it. He has been living in abundance as if it were scarcity, in sonship as if it were slavery.

"It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found." The father speaks the same words, offers the same grace. But the story ends with the elder son outside, his fate unresolved. Jesus leaves us there, on the porch, with the music playing and the father pleading. Will he go in? Will we?

---

## The Application: Finding Ourselves in the Story

I have preached this text many times, and I have learned that every congregation contains both sons. Some of you came in this morning carrying the shame of the younger brother. You know what it is to squander, to wander, to wake up in the pigsty of your own making. You have prepared your speeches. You have practiced your humility. And I am here to tell you: the Father is running. He will not let you finish your speech. He will not accept your servanthood. He is falling on your neck, kissing your shame away, calling for the robe and the ring. You are not a hired servant. You are a son. You are a daughter. Come home.

But others of you came in as the elder brother. You have never left the church. You have served on committees and taught Sunday school and given sacrificially. And somewhere along the way, service became slavery, devotion became duty, love became law. You have been keeping score. You have been watching the door, not to welcome the wanderers home, but to monitor who gets what. You have been angry, and you have not known why. You have been outside, and you have not known how to go in.

The Father is coming out to you too. He is not angry. He is not disappointed. He is pleading. "All that is mine is yours." The party is not a subtraction from your inheritance; it is a revelation of its true nature. Joy is not a limited resource. Grace is not a zero-sum game. The Father's love is not a wage to be earned but a gift to be received—and received again, and again, until we learn to receive it like children.

And perhaps there are some here who need to become the father. Perhaps you have been wounded by someone who wished you dead, who squandered what you gave, who only returns when the famine bites. The parable calls you to run. It calls you to absurd, undignified, extravagant grace. It calls you to interrupt the speeches of self-condemnation, to refuse the logic of merit, to kill the fatted calf for those who do not deserve it—for none of us deserve it. This is what it means to be formed in the image of the Father who sends rain on the just and the unjust, who gave his Son while we were still enemies.

---

## Conclusion: The Only Son Who Never Left

But I would be failing you if I stopped there. Because Jesus told this story to Pharisees and scribes who were grumbling that he received sinners and ate with them. And he told it on his way to Jerusalem, where he would be crucified. The Father in this parable is not a sentimental figure. He is a wounded figure. He tears his life apart to give the inheritance. He runs to embrace the undeserving. He goes out to plead with the angry. And he does all this knowing that the younger son will likely leave again, that the elder son may never come in, that his love will be exploited and rejected and resented.

This is the love that took flesh in Jesus Christ. He is the true elder brother who did not resent our return but accomplished it. He is the true prodigal who left the Father's house not in contempt but in obedience, who journeyed to the far country of our sin and death, who fed the pigs of our humanity and was made to feel less than human, who came to himself in Gethsemane and said "Not my will but yours," who was embraced by the Father in the resurrection morning.

And he is the Father's invitation to us all. To the younger brothers: he has already taken your shame. To the elder brothers: he has already fulfilled your obedience. To all of us: he is the feast, he is the music, he is the joy that makes angels sing over one sinner who repents.

The music is playing. The Father is waiting. Will you go in?

---

*In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.*

# The Father Who Runs

There's a photograph that circulated online a few years ago that stopped people cold. It shows an elderly man standing at an airport arrivals gate, pressed against the glass, squinting into the crowd. His son had been estranged from the family for seven years—seven years of silence, seven years of hurt, seven years of wondering if this day would ever come. And there he stood, not waiting passively, but *looking*, *searching*, *hoping*.

When the son walked through the doors, the father didn't hesitate. He didn't stand on dignity. He crossed the distance with whatever was left of his seventy-eight-year-old legs and wrapped his son in his arms and wept.

Someone captured that moment on a phone. The internet called it "the most beautiful thing I've ever seen."

Friends, that image—powerful as it is—gives us only a pale shadow of what Jesus describes in Luke chapter fifteen. Because what happens in this parable makes even the most devoted father look restrained.

---

Let's set the scene. Jesus is at a dinner table. The religious leaders—the scribes and Pharisees—are grumbling. They've been watching Jesus welcome sinners, eat with them, fellowship with them. And it bothers them. "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them," they mutter.

So Jesus tells them three parables: a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one lost, a woman who searches her house high and low for a lost coin, and then this one—the story of a father and his two sons.

Notice the context: Jesus tells these parables *in response to criticism for showing grace*. The religious leaders were scandalized that Jesus would associate with the outcasts. And Jesus says, in effect: "You think *I'm* the scandal? Let me tell you about a father whose love is even more extravagant than my welcome."

And so we enter the story.

---

The younger son speaks first, and his words are brutal. "Father, give me my share of the estate."

In that culture, to ask for your inheritance while your father was still alive was to say something like: "I wish you were dead. I can't wait for you to be gone so I can have what's mine." It was a profound insult—a declaration that the father was already nothing to him.

And the father *gives it to him*.

I want us to sit with that for a moment. This father could have refused. He could have corrected the boy, disciplined him, taught him the meaning of respect. But instead, he lets him go. He honors the boy's choice, even when that choice is a knife in the heart.

This is not weakness. This is something harder. This is love that refuses to control, that allows the beloved to make mistakes, that holds loosely enough to let go.

The son takes his inheritance—a fortune in that day—and he leaves. He travels to a distant country. And there, the text says, he "squandered his wealth in wild living."

The word "squandered" is gentle. What actually happened was worse. He lived recklessly, self-destructively, in every way imaginable. He wasted not just money but himself—his identity, his dignity, his health.

And then the famine came.

It's a detail we might skip over, but it's crucial. The famine wasn't punishment from God; it was simply life. The son had burned every bridge. He had no money, no friends, no family. And now he found himself in the most degrading situation imaginable: hired to feed pigs.

In a Jewish context, pigs were unclean. This was as low as it gets. And even the pigs were fed better than he was. He was so hungry he would have eaten the pods the pigs ate—food that wasn't even meant for humans.

And in that moment, something shifted.

---

"He came to his senses."

That's what the text says. And I love that phrase. It wasn't that he suddenly remembered doctrine or felt guilty about sin in the abstract. He came to *his senses*—he realized the absurdity of his situation. He, a son, was starving while his father's hired workers had plenty. He had hit bottom, and bottom woke him up.

So he made a decision. He would go home. Not as a son—he knew he didn't deserve that anymore. But as a hired worker. At least he would have food.

Notice what he planned to say: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired workers."

It was a humble plan. A realistic plan. A plan that, if we're honest, sounds more like what we might expect from God: "Okay, you've messed up. You can come back, but don't expect the same treatment. Earn your place."

But that's not what happened.

---

The son is still a long way off when the father sees him.

Here's what stops me every time: the father *saw him* while he was still a long way off. He was watching. He was waiting. He was scanning the horizon day after day, looking for a figure that might never come.

And when he saw him, he didn't walk. He didn't jog. The text says he *ran*.

In that culture, running was considered undignified for a man of status. Older men didn't run. But this father ran. He ran because his love couldn't wait, couldn't walk, couldn't do anything but sprint toward his boy.

And then he *embraced* him. The son probably expected a lecture, a reckoning, a "I told you so." Instead, he got a kiss. The father kissed him—again and again—a traditional greeting that in this context was an act of total acceptance, total forgiveness, total restoration.

The son starts his confession: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy—"

But he doesn't get to finish. The father interrupts him. He calls to his servants: "Quick! Bring the best robe, the ring, the sandals." And then he orders a feast. The fatted calf is killed. Music and dancing begin.

This is not a father who is reluctantly letting his son back in. This is a father who is *celebrating*. The word "prodigal" means "recklessly extravagant"—and that's exactly what this father's love is. He doesn't just forgive; he over-forgives. He doesn't just restore; he restores with abundance.

---

Now enter the older brother.

He comes in from the field and hears the music and dancing. He asks what's happening, and when he learns it's his brother's return, he is *angry*. He won't go in.

The father comes out and pleads with him. "Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

And the older brother responds with what sounds almost reasonable. He's been faithful all these years. He's never disobeyed. And he's never been given even a young goat to celebrate with his friends. It's not fair.

But listen to the father's response: "You are always with me, and everything I have is yours."

The older brother already had everything. He had the father's love, the father's presence, the father's inheritance. What he lacked was not more *stuff*—it was the *joy* of receiving what he already had. He was so focused on his brother's failure that he missed his own blessing.

---

So what is this parable about?

It's about a God who runs toward us when we're still a long way off. It's about a love that doesn't wait for us to clean up our act before welcoming us home. It's about grace that is reckless, extravagant, more than we could ever ask or imagine.

But it's also about us—about the older brother who lives inside every human heart.

Because here's the thing: we are *all* in this story.

Some of you know what it's like to be the younger son. You've walked away. You've made mistakes that you can't undo. You've felt the shame of hitting bottom, of being so far from home that you didn't think you could ever come back. And maybe today, you're still out there, still trying to earn your way, still thinking that you need to become worthy before you can approach the father.

Let me speak to you: You don't. The father is already running. The feast is already prepared. The ring is already in his hand. All you need to do is turn toward home.

But maybe you're not the younger son. Maybe you're the older brother. You've stayed. You've been faithful. You've done what was expected. And yet when you look at others—others who have wasted their lives, others who have made a mess of everything—you find yourself judging, resenting, keeping count. You think: *It's not fair. Where's my celebration?*

The father's words are for you too: "Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours."

You don't need to compete for God's love. You already have it. The question is whether you'll let yourself *enjoy* it—or whether you'll let resentment steal your joy.

---

Here's the deepest truth of this parable: the father represents God. And what does this tell us about God?

It tells us that God is not waiting for us to perform. God is not keeping a ledger of our sins and our righteousness. God is not standing at a distance, arms crossed, ready to judge.

God is running. God is embracing. God is celebrating.

The religious leaders in Jesus' day thought they knew what God was like. They thought God loved the righteous and hated sinners. And Jesus tells this parable to say: *You have it backwards*. God loves the lost so much that he runs to meet them. God celebrates the return of the one who was dead.

And here's the part that should change everything: *we are invited to do the same*.

The father says to the older brother, "We had to celebrate." Not "you may celebrate" or "I decided to celebrate." *We had to*. It was necessary. It was essential. The celebration of grace is not optional; it is the very heart of what it means to be God's people.

---

Where are you in this story today?

Maybe you're the younger son, and you need to come home. Maybe you've been running from God, running from the church, running from the people who love you. Maybe you've squandered something precious, and you're ashamed, and you don't think there's any way back.

Here's what I want you to know: the father sees you. He's been watching the road. He's been waiting. And the moment you turn toward him, he'll run to meet you. Not with judgment. Not with conditions. With a robe and a ring and a feast.

Maybe you're the older brother. You've done everything right. You've stayed faithful. And yet you've been bitter, keeping score, resenting the grace shown to others. The father invites you to put down your resentment, to come inside, to join the celebration. Your inheritance is already yours. Your joy is already available. Stop watching the road for the ungrateful and start receiving what you already have.

Or maybe you're the father. Maybe you have a son or a daughter, a friend or a family member, who has walked away. And you've been waiting, watching, hoping. The father in this story invites you to keep watching, to keep loving, to keep running toward them when they finally turn.

---

The father in this parable is not a symbol or an idea. He is God—our God—who loved us enough to send his only Son, who ran to meet us while we were still far away, who embraced us with infinite love, who killed the fatted calf for us, who prepared a feast that will never end.

And the question he asks us today is simple: *Will you come inside?*

The music is playing. The table is set. The celebration is waiting.

Let us go in, and be glad.

# The Father Who Runs

There's a photograph that circulated online a few years ago that stopped people cold. It shows an elderly man standing at an airport arrivals gate, pressed against the glass, squinting into the crowd. His son had been estranged from the family for seven years—seven years of silence, seven years of hurt, seven years of wondering if this day would ever come. And there he stood, not waiting passively, but *looking*, *searching*, *hoping*.

When the son walked through the doors, the father didn't hesitate. He didn't stand on dignity. He crossed the distance with whatever was left of his seventy-eight-year-old legs and wrapped his son in his arms and wept.

Someone captured that moment on a phone. The internet called it "the most beautiful thing I've ever seen."

Friends, that image—powerful as it is—gives us only a pale shadow of what Jesus describes in Luke chapter fifteen. Because what happens in this parable makes even the most devoted father look restrained.

---

Let's set the scene. Jesus is at a dinner table. The religious leaders—the scribes and Pharisees—are grumbling. They've been watching Jesus welcome sinners, eat with them, fellowship with them. And it bothers them. "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them," they mutter.

So Jesus tells them three parables: a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one lost, a woman who searches her house high and low for a lost coin, and then this one—the story of a father and his two sons.

Notice the context: Jesus tells these parables *in response to criticism for showing grace*. The religious leaders were scandalized that Jesus would associate with the outcasts. And Jesus says, in effect: "You think *I'm* the scandal? Let me tell you about a father whose love is even more extravagant than my welcome."

And so we enter the story.

---

The younger son speaks first, and his words are brutal. "Father, give me my share of the estate."

In that culture, to ask for your inheritance while your father was still alive was to say something like: "I wish you were dead. I can't wait for you to be gone so I can have what's mine." It was a profound insult—a declaration that the father was already nothing to him.

And the father *gives it to him*.

I want us to sit with that for a moment. This father could have refused. He could have corrected the boy, disciplined him, taught him the meaning of respect. But instead, he lets him go. He honors the boy's choice, even when that choice is a knife in the heart.

This is not weakness. This is something harder. This is love that refuses to control, that allows the beloved to make mistakes, that holds loosely enough to let go.

The son takes his inheritance—a fortune in that day—and he leaves. He travels to a distant country. And there, the text says, he "squandered his wealth in wild living."

The word "squandered" is gentle. What actually happened was worse. He lived recklessly, self-destructively, in every way imaginable. Maybe it was addiction. Maybe it was greed. Maybe it was the slow erosion of everything that once gave his life meaning—the relationships he abandoned, the opportunities he wasted, the person he was becoming but could no longer recognize. He wasted not just money but himself—his identity, his dignity, his health.

And then the famine came.

It's a detail we might skip over, but it's crucial. The famine wasn't punishment from God; it was simply life. The son had burned every bridge. He had no money, no friends, no family. And now he found himself in the most degrading situation imaginable: hired to feed pigs.

In a Jewish context, pigs were unclean. This was as low as it gets. And even the pigs were fed better than he was. He was so hungry he would have eaten the pods the pigs ate—food that wasn't even meant for humans.

And in that moment, something shifted.

---

"He came to his senses."

That's what the text says. And I love that phrase. It wasn't that he suddenly remembered doctrine or felt guilty about sin in the abstract. He came to *his senses*—he realized the absurdity of his situation. He, a son, was starving while his father's hired workers had plenty. He had hit bottom, and bottom woke him up.

So he made a decision. He would go home. Not as a son—he knew he didn't deserve that anymore. But as a hired worker. At least he would have food.

Notice what he planned to say: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired workers."

It was a humble plan. A realistic plan. A plan that, if we're honest, sounds more like what we might expect from God: "Okay, you've messed up. You can come back, but don't expect the same treatment. Earn your place."

But that's not what happened.

---

The son is still a long way off when the father sees him.

Here's what stops me every time: the father *saw him* while he was still a long way off. He was watching. He was waiting. He was scanning the horizon day after day, looking for a figure that might never come.

And when he saw him, he didn't walk. He didn't jog. The text says he *ran*.

In that culture, running was considered undignified for a man of his status. Older men didn't run. But this father ran. He ran because his love couldn't wait, couldn't walk, couldn't do anything but sprint toward his boy.

And here's where we see the heart of God breaking through even this beautiful human story: this running is more than affection. This is the active, covenantal love of God—the *hesed* of the Old Testament—the steadfast, relentless love that refuses to wait for human merit, that pursues the lost even when there's no guarantee of return. The same God who declared through the prophet Hosea, "How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel?" This father running is a picture of the very heart of God.

And then he *embraced* him. The son probably expected a lecture, a reckoning, a "I told you so." Instead, he got a kiss. The father kissed him—again and again—a traditional greeting that in this context was an act of total acceptance, total forgiveness, total restoration.

The son starts his confession: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy—"

But he doesn't get to finish. The father interrupts him. He calls to his servants: "Quick! Bring the best robe, the ring, the sandals." And then he orders a feast. The fatted calf is killed. Music and dancing begin.

This is not a father who is reluctantly letting his son back in. This is a father who is *celebrating*. The word "prodigal" means "recklessly extravagant"—and that's exactly what this father's love is. He doesn't just forgive; he over-forgives. He doesn't just restore; he restores with abundance.

And notice this: the father's joy isn't just about the son coming home. It's about something happening in heaven. Earlier in this same chapter, Jesus says, "I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need to repent" (Luke 15:7). The celebration in this father's house echoes a celebration in the very courts of God. The running, the embrace, the feast—these are heaven's response to grace.

---

Now enter the older brother.

He comes in from the field and hears the music and dancing. He asks what's happening, and when he learns it's his brother's return, he is *angry*. He won't go in.

The father comes out and pleads with him. "Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

And the older brother responds with what sounds almost reasonable. He's been faithful all these years. He's never disobeyed. And he's never been given even a young goat to celebrate with his friends. It's not fair.

But listen to what his complaint reveals: he saw the father's love as a salary he had earned, not a gift he already possessed. He was demanding a bonus for obedience, failing to see that the entire estate—the Father himself—was already his. He viewed love as a finite resource that had to be guarded, measured, and distributed according to merit. And so when the father poured out abundance on the unworthy son, the older brother felt robbed—not because he had less, but because he couldn't bear to see grace given to someone who hadn't earned it.

The father's response is profound: "You are always with me, and everything I have is yours."

The older brother already had everything. He had the father's love, the father's presence, the father's inheritance. What he lacked was not more *stuff*—it was the *joy* of receiving what he already had. He was so focused on his brother's failure that he missed his own blessing.

---

Here's the deepest truth of this parable: the father represents God. And what does this tell us about God?

It tells us that God is not waiting for us to perform. God is not keeping a ledger of our sins and our righteousness. God is not standing at a distance, arms crossed, ready to judge.

God is running. God is embracing. God is celebrating.

The religious leaders in Jesus' day thought they knew what God was like. They thought God loved the righteous and hated sinners. And Jesus tells this parable to say: *You have it backwards*. God loves the lost so much that he runs to meet them. God celebrates the return of the one who was dead.

And here's the part that should change everything: *we are invited to do the same*.

The father says to the older brother, "We had to celebrate." Not "you may celebrate" or "I decided to celebrate." *We had to*. It was necessary. It was essential. The celebration of grace is not optional; it is the very heart of what it means to be God's people.

---

So what is this parable about?

It's about a God who runs toward us when we're still a long way off. It's about a love that doesn't wait for us to clean up our act before welcoming us home. It's about grace that is reckless, extravagant, more than we could ever ask or imagine.

But it's also about us—about the older brother who lives inside every human heart.

Because here's the thing: we are *all* in this story.

Some of you know what it's like to be the younger son. You've walked away. You've made mistakes that you can't undo. You've felt the shame of hitting bottom, of being so far from home that you didn't think you could ever come back. And maybe today, you're still out there, still trying to earn your way, still thinking that you need to become worthy before you can approach the father.

Let me speak to you: You don't. The father is already running. The feast is already prepared. The ring is already in his hand. All you need to do is turn toward home.

But maybe you're not the younger son. Maybe you're the older brother. You've stayed. You've been faithful. You've done what was expected. And perhaps you aren't angry so much as *tired*—tired of keeping score, tired of feeling like you have to prove your worth every single day, tired of looking at others who have wasted their lives and wondering why they get grace when you've given everything.

The father's words are for you too: "Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours."

You don't need to compete for God's love. You already have it. The question is whether you'll let yourself *enjoy* it—whether you'll come inside and join the celebration, or whether you'll stay in the field resenting the feast you were invited to all along.

Or maybe you're the father. Maybe you have a son or a daughter, a friend or a family member, who has walked away. And you've been waiting, watching, hoping. If you are in this position—a parent, a mentor, a leader—the parable demands that you resist the urge to wait until they are "good enough." Your role is to watch the horizon. And when you see the slightest movement toward home, you must run to meet them, because that is the posture of God. That is what it means to represent a father whose love is extravagant beyond measure.

---

The father in this parable is not a symbol or an idea. He is God—our God—who loved us enough to send his only Son, who ran to meet us while we were still far away, who embraced us with infinite love, who killed the fatted calf for us, who prepared a feast that will never end.

And the question he asks us today is simple: *Will you come inside?*

The music is playing. The table is set. The celebration is waiting—not just for the lost to return, but for the found to stop resenting the feast and start enjoying it. Not for the faithful to keep earning what they already possess, but to rest in the security of what they already are: beloved children, fully known, fully accepted, fully loved.

Let us go in, and be glad.

It's about a God who runs toward us when we're still a long way off. It's about a love that doesn't wait for us to clean up our act before welcoming us home. It's about grace that is reckless, extravagant, more than we could ask or imagine.

But it's also about us—about the older brother who lives inside every human heart.

Because here's the thing: we are *all* in this story.

Some of you know what it's like to be the younger son. You've walked away. You've made mistakes that you can't undo. You've felt the shame of hitting bottom, of being so far from home that you didn't think you could ever come back. And maybe today, you're still out there, still trying to earn your way, still thinking that you need to become worthy before you can approach the father.

Let me speak to you: You don't. The father is already running. The feast is already prepared. The ring is already in his hand. All you need to do is turn toward home.

But maybe you're not the younger son. Maybe you're the older brother. You've stayed. You've been faithful. You've done what was expected. And yet when you look at others—others who have wasted their lives, others who have made a mess of everything—you find yourself judging, resenting, keeping count. You think: *It's not fair. Where's my celebration?*

The father's words are for you too: "Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours."

You don't need to compete for God's love. You already have it. The question is whether you'll let yourself *enjoy* it—or whether you'll let resentment steal your joy.

---

Here's where we must go deeper. The father in this parable is not just a symbol or an idea. He is God—our God—and this story is pointing forward to something even more extraordinary.

One day the Father would actually give up his true Son to death on a cross—so that every prodigal could come home. The feast that celebrates our return was purchased with blood. The robe that covers our shame was torn apart on Calvary. The ring that marks us as children came at the cost of the One who was called accursed.

Here's what I want you to know: the father sees you. He's been watching the road. He's been waiting. And the moment you turn toward him, he'll run to meet you. Not with judgment. Not with conditions. With a robe and a ring and a feast.

Maybe you're the older brother. You've done everything right. You've stayed faithful. And yet you've been bitter, keeping score, resenting the grace shown to others. The father invites you to put down your resentment, to come inside, to join the celebration. Your inheritance is already yours. Your joy is already available. Stop watching the road for the ungrateful and start receiving what you already have.

Or maybe you're the waiting heart. Maybe you're a mother who's been praying for a child who won't answer the phone. Maybe you're a grandparent who hasn't seen your grandkids in years. Maybe you're someone who has been faithful to a community that has forgotten you. The father in this story invites you to keep watching, to keep loving, to keep running toward them when they finally turn.

---

---

The father in this parable is not a symbol or an idea. He is God—our God—who loved us enough to send his only Son, who ran to meet us while we were still far away, who embraced us with infinite love, who paid the ultimate price so that the feast could be ours.

The music is playing. The table is set. The celebration is waiting.

I want to invite you, right now, to respond. If you're the younger son, if you need to come home, I'd ask you to fill out one of the "Come Home" cards in your pew. You don't have to share your story with anyone—just let us know you want prayer, want connection, want to take the first step.

And if you've never trusted in Jesus before—if you've never known this father who runs—I'd ask you to simply pray with me right now. Ask him to find you, wherever you are. Ask him to run toward you. Ask him to put the robe on your shoulders and the ring on your finger and seat you at the feast that will never end.

Let us pray.

---

Let us go in, and be glad.

# The Father Who Runs

There's a photograph that circulated online a few years ago that stopped people cold. It shows an elderly man standing at an airport arrivals gate, pressed against the glass, squinting into the crowd. His son had been estranged from the family for seven years—seven years of silence, seven years of hurt, seven years of wondering if this day would ever come. When the son walked through the doors, the father didn't hesitate. He crossed the distance with whatever was left of his seventy-eight-year-old legs and wrapped his son in his arms and wept.

Someone captured that moment on a phone. The internet called it "the most beautiful thing I've ever seen."

Friends, that image is powerful. But I want to suggest it gives us only a pale shadow of what Jesus describes in Luke chapter fifteen. Here's why: the father in the photo waited at the airport. He didn't know when his son would come. But in the parable, the father is already watching. He's been scanning the horizon day after day, not waiting passively but *looking*, *searching*, *hoping*. And when he sees his son in the distance, he doesn't walk—he runs. That's not just affection; that's desperation. That's a love so fierce it abandons dignity.

And there's more. When the son in the photo was reunited with his father, he got an embrace. That's beautiful. But the father in Jesus' story gives his son more than an embrace. He gives him a robe—the best robe—to cover his rags. He gives him a ring—signifying sonship, authority, belonging. He gives him sandals to replace his broken feet. And then he throws a feast. Not a quiet dinner. Not a "welcome back, let's talk." A celebration. Music. Dancing. The fatted calf killed. The whole village invited to rejoice.

The photograph moves us because we see a father who loves. The parable moves us because we see a father whose love is *reckless*—extravagant beyond measure, lavish beyond reason, more than the son could ever ask or imagine. That's the kind of love God has for us.

---

Let's set the scene. Jesus is at a dinner table. The religious leaders—the scribes and Pharisees—are grumbling. They've been watching Jesus welcome sinners, eat with them, fellowship with them. And it bothers them. "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them," they mutter.

So Jesus tells them three parables. First: a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one lost. Second: a woman who searches her house high and low for a lost coin. Third: this story of the father and his two sons.

Notice: these three parables are not separate. They are one argument, escalating in intensity. The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine—that's remarkable. The woman turns the house upside down—that's even more dramatic. But this father? He runs. He embraces. He celebrates. The accumulation is clear: God's joy over the lost is so great that it justifies leaving the ninety-nine, turning the house upside down, abandoning dignity, throwing open the doors and inviting everyone to feast.

Jesus tells these parables *in response to criticism for showing grace*. The religious leaders were scandalized that Jesus would associate with outcasts. And Jesus says, in effect: "You think *I'm* the scandal? Let me tell you about a father whose love is even more extravagant than my welcome. If you have a problem with grace, you have a problem with God."

---

Now the younger son speaks, and his words are brutal. "Father, give me my share of the estate."

In that culture, to ask for your inheritance while your father was still alive was to say something like: "I wish you were dead. I can't wait for you to be gone so I can have what's mine." It was a profound insult—a declaration that the father was already nothing to him.

And the father *gives it to him*.

I want us to sit with that for a moment. This father could have refused. He could have corrected the boy, disciplined him, taught him the meaning of respect. But instead, he lets him go. He honors the boy's choice, even when that choice is a knife in the heart.

This is not weakness. This is something harder. This is love that refuses to control, that allows the beloved to make mistakes, that holds loosely enough to let go. It is the kind of love that hurts, that waits, that hopes against hope.

The son takes his inheritance and leaves. He travels to a distant country. And there, the text says, he "squandered his wealth in wild living." The word "squandered" is gentle. What actually happened was worse. He wasted not just money but himself—his identity, his dignity, his health.

And then the famine came.

It's a detail we might skip over, but it's crucial. The famine wasn't punishment from God; it was simply life. The son had burned every bridge. He had no money, no friends, no family. And now he found himself in the most degrading situation imaginable: hired to feed pigs.

In a Jewish context, pigs were unclean. This was as low as it gets. And even the pigs were fed better than he was. He was so hungry he would have eaten the pods the pigs ate—food that wasn't even meant for humans.

And in that moment, something shifted.

---

"He came to his senses."

That's what the text says. And I love that phrase. It wasn't that he suddenly remembered doctrine or felt guilty about sin in the abstract. He came to *his senses*—he realized the absurdity of his situation. He, a son, was starving while his father's hired workers had plenty. He had hit bottom, and bottom woke him up.

So he made a decision. He would go home. Not as a son—he knew he didn't deserve that anymore. But as a hired worker. At least he would have food.

Notice what he planned to say: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired workers."

It was a humble plan. A realistic plan. A plan that, if we're honest, sounds more like what we might expect from God: "Okay, you've messed up. You can come back, but don't expect the same treatment. Earn your place."

But that's not what happened.

---

The son is still a long way off when the father sees him.

Here's what stops me every time: the father *saw him* while he was still a long way off. He was watching. He was waiting. He was scanning the horizon day after day, looking for a figure that might never come.

And when he saw him, he didn't walk. He didn't jog. The text says he *ran*.

In that culture, running was considered undignified for a man of status. Older men didn't run. But this father ran. He ran because his love couldn't wait, couldn't walk, couldn't do anything but sprint toward his boy.

But there's something deeper here. In the ancient world, gods were understood to be beyond emotional affect—impassible, unchanging, unmoved by human affairs. And yet here is the God of Israel running. Running! The Creator of the universe, the Holy One of Israel, sprinting down a dusty road toward a runaway child. This is not a God who is distant, unmoved, keeping his distance until we prove ourselves worthy. This is a God whose love makes him *vulnerable*—vulnerable to joy, to grief, to longing. A God who runs toward us not because we have earned it but because that's who he is.

And then he *embraced* him. The son probably expected a lecture, a reckoning, a "I told you so." Instead, he got a kiss. The father kissed him—again and again—a traditional greeting that in this context was an act of total acceptance, total forgiveness, total restoration.

The son starts his confession: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy—"

But he doesn't get to finish. The father interrupts him. He calls to his servants: "Quick! Bring the best robe, the ring, the sandals." And then he orders a feast. The fatted calf is killed. Music and dancing begin.

This is not a father who is reluctantly letting his son back in. This is a father who is *celebrating*. The word "prodigal" means "recklessly extravagant"—and that's exactly what this father's love is. He doesn't just forgive; he over-forgives. He doesn't just restore; he restores with abundance. He doesn't wait for the son to prove himself worthy; he lavishes worth upon him even as he arrives in rags.

---

Now enter the older brother.

He comes in from the field and hears the music and dancing. He asks what's happening, and when he learns it's his brother's return, he is *angry*. He won't go in.

The father comes out and pleads with him. "Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

And the older brother responds with what sounds almost reasonable. He's been faithful all these years. He's never disobeyed. And he's never been given even a young goat to celebrate with his friends. It's not fair.

But listen to what his complaint reveals: he thinks relationship with the father is a *transaction*. He's been keeping score. He's been serving God as if under a contract: "I've done everything right. Where's my reward?" He doesn't understand that he already has everything—the father's love, the father's presence, the father's inheritance. What he lacked was not more *stuff*—it was the *joy* of receiving what he already had. He was so focused on his brother's failure that he missed his own blessing.

The father's response is stunning: "You are always with me, and everything I have is yours."

Everything. Already. Always.

The older brother had been serving a master he already owned. He had been working for a father who had already given him everything. And yet he couldn't enjoy it because he was too busy keeping score.

---

So what is this parable about?

It's about a God who runs toward us when we're still a long way off. It's about a love that doesn't wait for us to clean up our act before welcoming us home. It's about grace that is reckless, extravagant, more than we could ever ask or imagine.

But here's the deeper truth: the grace in this parable is not just generous—it is *gratuitous*. It is given not because of anything in us but because of who God is. The son couldn't earn his way back. He couldn't perform his way into favor. The father ran to him not because the son had cleaned himself up, but because that's what fathers do. The feast was not a reward for repentance; it was an expression of love that existed before the son ever turned around.

And this is where the parable cuts deepest: we are *all* in this story. We have all wandered. We have all resented someone else's welcome. We have all stood outside the feast while the celebration happened without us.

---

Here's the truth: we don't need to become worthy before we approach the father. We *can't* become worthy. That's not how grace works. The father is already running. The feast is already prepared. The ring is already in his hand. All we need to do is turn toward home.

But there's another word here for those of us who have stayed. Who have been faithful. Who have done what was expected. And when we look at others—others who have wasted their lives, others who have made a mess of everything—we find ourselves judging, resenting, keeping count. We think: *It's not fair. Where's my celebration?*

The father's words are for us too: "You are always with me, and everything I have is yours."

You don't need to compete for God's love. You already have it. You never had to earn it. The question is whether you'll let yourself *enjoy* it—whether you'll come inside and join the feast, or whether you'll stand outside in your resentment, missing the joy that's already yours.

---

The father in this parable is not a symbol or an idea. He is God—our God—who loved us enough to send his only Son, who ran to meet us while we were still far away, who embraced us with infinite love, who killed the fatted calf for us, who prepared a feast that will never end.

And here is the deepest scandal of this story: the father invites the older brother into the celebration. Not as an afterthought. Not with resentment. But with the same lavish love. The feast is not complete until everyone is inside.

The question he asks us today is simple: *Will you come inside?*

The music is playing. The table is set. The celebration is waiting.

Let us go in, and be glad.

The son takes his inheritance—a fortune in that day—and he leaves. He travels to a distant country. And there, the text says, he "squandered his wealth in wild living."

The word "wild living" is gentle. What actually happened was worse. He might as well have been posting his exploits on Instagram, burning through relationships and credit cards, trying to fill a God-shaped hole with everything but God. He wasted not just money but himself—his identity, his dignity, his health.

And then the famine came.

It's a detail we might skip over, but it's crucial. The famine wasn't God's punishment; it was the natural consequence of living in a broken world without community. Sometimes grace lets us feel the weight of our choices so we'll remember the weight of our identity.

The son had burned every bridge. He had no money, no friends, no family. And now he found himself in the most degrading situation imaginable: hired to feed pigs.

In a Jewish context, pigs were unclean. This was as low as it gets. And even the pigs were fed better than he was. He was so hungry he would have eaten the pods the pigs ate—food that wasn't even meant for humans.

And in that moment, something shifted.

---

"He came to his senses."

That's what the text says. And I love that phrase. The Greek literally says he "came to himself"—he remembered who he truly was. It wasn't that he suddenly remembered doctrine or felt guilty about sin in the abstract. He realized the absurdity of his situation. He, a son, was starving while his father's hired workers had plenty. He had hit bottom, and bottom woke him up.

So he made a decision. He would go home. Not as a son—he knew he didn't deserve that anymore. But as a hired worker. At least he would have food.

Notice what he planned to say: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired workers."

It was a humble plan. A realistic plan. A plan that, if we're honest, sounds more like what we might expect from God: "Okay, you've messed up. You can come back, but don't expect the same treatment. Earn your place."

But that's not what happened.

---

The son is still a long way off when the father sees him.

Here's what stops me every time: the father *saw him* while he was still a long way off. He was watching. He was waiting. He was scanning the horizon day after day, looking for a figure that might never come.

And when he saw him, he didn't walk. He didn't jog. The text says he *ran*.

In that culture, running was considered undignified for a man of status. Older men didn't run. But this father ran. He ran because his love couldn't wait, couldn't walk, couldn't do anything but sprint toward his boy.

And then he *embraced* him. The son probably expected a lecture, a reckoning, a "I told you so." Instead, he got a kiss. The father kissed him—again and again—a traditional greeting that in this context was an act of total acceptance, total forgiveness, total restoration.

The son starts his confession: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy—"

But he doesn't get to finish. The father interrupts him. He calls to his servants: "Quick! Bring the best robe, the ring, the sandals." And then he orders a feast. The fatted calf is killed. Music and dancing begin.

This is not a father who is reluctantly letting his son back in. This is a father who is *celebrating*. The word "prodigal" means "recklessly extravagant"—and that's exactly what this father's love is. He doesn't just forgive; he over-forgives. He doesn't just restore; he restores with abundance.

We had to celebrate. It wasn't optional. It was necessary.

But the feast, you see, was only half the story.

---

Now enter the older brother.

He comes in from the field and hears the music and dancing. He asks what's happening, and when he learns it's his brother's return, he is *angry*. He won't go in.

The father comes out and pleads with him. "Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

And the older brother responds with what sounds almost reasonable. He's been faithful all these years. He's never disobeyed. And he's never been given even a young goat to celebrate with his friends. It's not fair.

But listen to what his complaint reveals: the older son had never once thrown a party with his friends. He'd never understood that everything was already his. He was living in the father's house like a hired worker, not a son. He had the inheritance but never enjoyed it. He had the father's love but never received it.

And let's be honest—haven't we all felt that sting? The older brother's complaint isn't crazy; it's human. He's not a villain; he's a mirror.

He's like the church member who sees someone baptized after a messy divorce and thinks, "I've been faithful for decades and never got a special service." He's the one who hears about the former addict getting a ministry position and feels a knot in his stomach. He's the parent who watches a rebellious child receive grace and wonders, *What about me? What about my faithfulness?*

The father's response is tender: "You are always with me, and everything I have is yours."

The older brother already had everything. He had the father's love, the father's presence, the father's inheritance. What he lacked was not more *stuff*—it was the *joy* of receiving what he already had. He was so focused on his brother's failure that he missed his own blessing.

---

So what is this parable about?

It's about a God who runs toward us when we're still a long way off. It's about a love that doesn't wait for us to clean up our act before welcoming us home. It's about grace that is reckless, extravagant, more than we could ever ask or imagine.

But it's also about us—about the older brother who lives inside every human heart.

Because here's the thing: we are *all* in this story.

Some of you know what it's like to be the younger son. You've walked away. You've made mistakes that you can't undo. You've felt the shame of hitting bottom, of being so far from home that you didn't think you could ever come back. And maybe today, you're still out there, still trying to earn your way, still thinking that you need to become worthy before you can approach the father.

Let me speak to you: You don't. The father is already running. The feast is already prepared. The ring is already in his hand. All you need to do is turn toward home.

But maybe you're not the younger son. Maybe you're the older brother. You've stayed. You've been faithful. You've done what was expected. And yet when you look at others—others who have wasted their lives, others who have made a mess of everything—you find yourself judging, resenting, keeping count. You think: *It's not fair. Where's my celebration?*

The father's words are for you too: "You are always with me, and everything I have is yours."

You don't need to compete for God's love. You already have it. The question is whether you'll let yourself *enjoy* it—or whether you'll let resentment steal your joy.

And as a church, we are called to be the feast, not the older brother. When someone walks through our doors, still smelling like the pigpen, our job isn't to say "clean up first." Our job is to put on the music and start the celebration.

---

Here's the deepest truth of this parable: the father represents God. And what does this tell us about God?

It tells us that God is not waiting for us to perform. God is not keeping a ledger of our sins and our righteousness. God is not standing at a distance, arms crossed, ready to judge.

God is running. God is embracing. God is celebrating.

I know for some, "father" is a complicated word. If your father was not safe, please hear this: the father in this story is the father you should have had, the one your soul longs for. He is the perfect expression of what divine love looks like—not absent, not controlling, but present, patient, and running toward us with open arms.

The religious leaders in Jesus' day thought they knew what God was like. They thought God loved the righteous and hated sinners. And Jesus tells this parable to say: *You have it backwards*. God loves the lost so much that he runs to meet them. God celebrates the return of the one who was dead.

And here's the part that should change everything: *we are invited to do the same*.

The father says to the older brother, "We had to celebrate." Not "you may celebrate" or "I decided to celebrate." *We had to*. It was necessary. It was essential. The celebration of grace is not optional; it is the very heart of what it means to be God's people.

---

Where are you in this story today?

Maybe you're the younger son, and you need to come home. Maybe you've been running from God, running from the church, running from the people who love you. Maybe you've squandered something precious, and you're ashamed, and you don't think there's any way back.

Here's what I want you to know: the father sees you. He's been watching the road. He's been waiting. And the moment you turn toward him, he'll run to meet you. Not with judgment. Not with conditions. With a robe and a ring and a feast.

Maybe you're the older brother. You've done everything right. You've stayed faithful. And yet you've been bitter, keeping score, resenting the grace shown to others. The father invites you to put down your resentment, to come inside, to join the celebration. Your inheritance is already yours. Your joy is already available. Stop watching the road for the ungrateful and start receiving what you already have.

Or maybe you're watching a road. Maybe you have a son or a daughter, a friend or a family member, who has walked away. And you've been waiting, hoping, leaving the porch light on. The father in this story says to you: keep scanning the horizon. Keep your running shoes on. Love doesn't give up.

---

The father in this parable is not a symbol or an idea. He is God—our God—who loved us enough to send his only Son, who ran to meet us while we were still far away, who embraced us with infinite love, who killed the fatted calf for us, who prepared a feast that will never end.

Like that father at the airport, our God stands pressed against the glass of heaven, waiting. But this father doesn't just cross the terminal—he sprints down the road. The question isn't whether he'll welcome you.

The question is: will you let him?

The music is playing. The table is set. The celebration is waiting.

Let us go in, and be glad.

# The Father Who Runs

There's a photograph that circulated online a few years ago that stopped people cold. It shows an elderly man standing at an airport arrivals gate, pressed against the glass, squinting into the crowd. His son had been estranged from the family for seven years—seven years of silence, seven years of hurt, seven years of wondering if this day would ever come. And there he stood, not waiting passively, but *looking*, *searching*, *hoping*.

When the son walked through the doors, the father didn't hesitate. He didn't stand on dignity. He crossed the distance with whatever was left of his seventy-eight-year-old legs and wrapped his son in his arms and wept.

Someone captured that moment on a phone. The internet called it "the most beautiful thing I've ever seen."

Friends, that image—powerful as it is—gives us only a pale shadow of what Jesus describes in Luke chapter fifteen. Because what happens in this parable makes even the most devoted father look restrained.

Here's something we often miss about this parable's title: we call it the Parable of the Prodigal Son, but the word "prodigal" actually describes the *father*. Prodigal means "recklessly extravagant"—wastefully, lavishly generous. The son was wasteful, yes, but the father is the one whose love is prodigal. And that's the point.

---

Let's set the scene. Jesus is at a dinner table. The religious leaders—the scribes and Pharisees—are grumbling. They've been watching Jesus welcome sinners, eat with them, fellowship with them. And it bothers them. "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them," they mutter.

So Jesus tells them three parables: a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one lost, a woman who searches her house high and low for a lost coin, and then this one—the story of a father and his two sons.

Notice the context: Jesus tells these parables *in response to criticism for showing grace*. The religious leaders were scandalized that Jesus would associate with the outcasts. And Jesus says, in effect: "You think *I'm* the scandal? Let me tell you about a father whose love is even more extravagant than my welcome."

And so we enter the story.

---

The younger son speaks first, and his words are brutal. "Father, give me my share of the estate."

In that culture, to ask for your inheritance while your father was still alive was to say something like: "I wish you were dead. I can't wait for you to be gone so I can have what's mine." It was a profound insult—a declaration that the father was already nothing to him.

And the father *gives it to him*.

I want us to sit with that for a moment. This father could have refused. He could have corrected the boy, disciplined him, taught him the meaning of respect. But instead, he lets him go. He honors the boy's choice, even when that choice is a knife in the heart.

This is not weakness. This is something harder. This is love that refuses to control, that allows the beloved to make mistakes, that holds loosely enough to let go.

The son takes his inheritance—a fortune in that day—and he leaves. He travels to a distant country. And there, the text says, he "squandered his wealth in wild living."

The word "squandered" is gentle. What actually happened was worse. He lived recklessly, self-destructively, in every way imaginable. He wasted not just money but himself—his identity, his dignity, his health.

And then the famine came.

It's a detail we might skip over, but it's crucial. The famine wasn't punishment from God; it was simply life. The son had burned every bridge. He had no money, no friends, no family. And now he found himself in the most degrading situation imaginable: hired to feed pigs.

In a Jewish context, pigs were unclean. This was as low as it gets. And even the pigs were fed better than he was. He was so hungry he would have eaten the pods the pigs ate—food that wasn't even meant for humans.

And in that moment, something shifted.

---

"He came to his senses."

That's what the text says. And I love that phrase. It wasn't that he suddenly remembered doctrine or felt guilty about sin in the abstract. He came to *his senses*—he realized the absurdity of his situation. He, a son, was starving while his father's hired workers had plenty. He had hit bottom, and bottom woke him up.

So he made a decision. He would go home. Not as a son—he knew he didn't deserve that anymore. But as a hired worker. At least he would have food.

Notice what he planned to say: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired workers."

It was a humble plan. A realistic plan. A plan that, if we're honest, sounds more like what we might expect from God: "Okay, you've messed up. You can come back, but don't expect the same treatment. Earn your place."

But that's not what happened.

---

The son is still a long way off when the father sees him.

Here's what stops me every time: the father *saw him* while he was still a long way off. He was watching. He was waiting. He was scanning the horizon day after day, looking for a figure that might never come.

And when he saw him, he didn't walk. He didn't jog. The text says he *ran*.

In that culture, running was considered undignified for a man of status. Older men didn't run. But this father ran. He ran because his love couldn't wait, couldn't walk, couldn't do anything but sprint toward his boy.

But here's what we often miss: in that honor-shame culture, the father's actions were not just undignified—they were *dangerous*. By running to embrace his shame-filled son without requiring public restitution, without making the son earn his way back, the father risked alienating the entire village. He was absorbing his son's shame into his own reputation. He was saying, "My honor is less important than my son's life." That's not just love. That's a kind of holy recklessness that puts everything on the line.

And then he *embraced* him. The son probably expected a lecture, a reckoning, a "I told you so." Instead, he got a kiss. The father kissed him—again and again—a traditional greeting that in this context was an act of total acceptance, total forgiveness, total restoration.

This is not a father who is reluctantly letting his son back in. This is a father who is *celebrating*. Notice what he gives: the *best* robe—that covers the son's rags, his shame, his defilement. The *ring*—that restores his authority, his identity as son, not servant. The *sandals*—that distinguish him from a slave, who would go barefoot. This is total re-creation. Not mere tolerance. Full restoration.

And the feast requires sacrifice. The fatted calf must die. Celebration in God's economy is not free—it is purchased, at great cost, by the lamb that is slain.

---

But the story isn't over. Because while the music plays inside, someone is standing outside in the dark.

---

Now enter the older brother.

He comes in from the field and hears the music and dancing. He asks what's happening, and when he learns it's his brother's return, he is *angry*. He won't go in.

The father comes out and pleads with him. "Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

And the older brother responds with what sounds almost reasonable. He's been faithful all these years. He's never disobeyed. And he's never been given even a young goat to celebrate with his friends. It's not fair.

But listen to the father's response: "You are always with me, and everything I have is yours."

The older brother already had everything. He had the father's love, the father's presence, the father's inheritance. What he lacked was not more *stuff*—it was the *joy* of receiving what he already had. He was so focused on his brother's failure that he missed his own blessing.

Here's the thing about the older brother that we need to see: his pain was real. His exhaustion was real. He had been faithful in a way his brother had not, and no one seemed to notice. He had stayed in the field while his brother partied. He had carried the weight while his brother played. And now, the one who shamed the family gets the feast.

If you identify with the older brother today—if you've been the one who showed up, who stayed, who did what was asked, who never caused trouble—I want you to know: your Father sees you. He knows you've been standing in the field while others played. He knows your service is real, your faithfulness is genuine, and your weariness is not imagined.

But here's the healing word: you already have everything. Your inheritance is not waiting for someone else's failure to earn it. The father's love for you is not a leftover love, a second-tier love, a love measured by comparison to the prodigal. "Everything I have is yours."

The question is not whether you *have* the father's love—you do. The question is whether you'll *receive* it. Whether you'll let yourself be nourished at the feast. Whether you'll put down the ledger and pick up the bread.

---

But there's something deeper here, something that completes the story in a way the parable itself doesn't.

The older brother never comes inside. The parable ends with him standing outside, refusing the party. And that is the tragedy: the father's love reaches the rebel, but the religious leader—the one who thinks he's righteous—refuses it.

But here's where the story continues in Luke's Gospel: *Jesus* is the true Elder Brother. He is the one who has kept the Father's commands perfectly, who has stayed in the field, who has done everything right. And what does he do? He leaves the feast. He goes out to find the grumbling scribes and Pharisees—the older brothers who think they deserve more—and he invites them in.

The father in the parable cannot complete the story; he can only plead from outside. But Jesus can. Jesus is the Elder Brother who comes out to find both lost brothers—yes, both the younger son who wandered and the older son who resented—and he says to both: "Come, everything is yours. The feast is ready. You are welcome."

---

So what is this parable about?

It's about a God who runs toward us when we're still a long way off. It's about a love that doesn't wait for us to clean up our act before welcoming us home. It's about grace that is reckless, extravagant, more than we could ever ask or imagine.

But it's also about us—about the older brother who lives inside every human heart.

Because here's the thing: we are *all* in this story.

Some of you know what it's like to be the younger son. You've walked away. You've made mistakes that you can't undo. You've felt the shame of hitting bottom, of being so far from home that you didn't think you could ever come back. And maybe today, you're still out there, still trying to earn your way, still thinking that you need to become worthy before you can approach the father.

Let me speak to you: You don't. The father is already running. The feast is already prepared. The ring is already in his hand. All you need to do is turn toward home.

And here's something else: the famine is real. The consequences are real. Coming home doesn't mean your mistakes magically disappear. But it does mean something more important than that: it means you are no longer outside. You are no longer a hired worker. You are a son. You are *home*.

But maybe you're the older brother. You've stayed. You've been faithful. You've done what was expected. And yet when you look at others—others who have wasted their lives, others who have made a mess of everything—you find yourself judging, resenting, keeping count. You think: *It's not fair. Where's my celebration?*

The father's words are for you too: "You are always with me, and everything I have is yours."

You don't need to compete for God's love. You already have it. The question is whether you'll let yourself *enjoy* it—whether you'll come inside and feast, or whether you'll stand outside with your arms crossed, watching the road, keeping score.

---

And maybe there's a third group here today: maybe you're the father.

Maybe you have a son or a daughter, a friend or a family member, who has walked away. You've been waiting, watching, hoping. You've felt the sting of their absence, the weight of their choices, the ache of not knowing if they'll ever come home.

The father in this story invites you to keep watching. To keep loving. To keep running toward them when they finally turn. And to remember: the feast is ready. There is always room for one more.

---

But there's one more thing, and it's the deepest thing.

This parable is not just about individual homecoming. It's about *community*. The father doesn't throw a private dinner; he kills the fatted calf for the whole village. The celebration is corporate. The feast is shared.

And here's what that means for us: we are invited to be the community that runs with the Father. When the lost come home, we are the ones who sing. When the dead come back to life, we are the ones who dance. We are the arms that embrace, the voices that celebrate, the hands that set the table.

The question is not just "Where am I in this story?" but "Am I helping tell the story?" Am I part of the celebration, or am I grumbling at the gate? Who is it that I think doesn't deserve a seat at Jesus' table? The former addict? The political opponent? The one whose sin looks different than mine?

The father runs. And we are invited to run with him.

---

Remember that father at the airport? He ran with seventy-eight-year-old legs. But our Father runs with the energy of infinite love, and the embrace he offers doesn't just last for a moment in a viral photo—it lasts for eternity.

The music is playing. The table is set. The fatted calf is killed. The celebration is waiting.

And the question he asks us today is simple: *Will you come inside?*

Let us go in, and be glad.
