# The Father Who Runs

*A Sermon on the Parable of the Prodigal Son*

---

Let me tell you about a father I know. His name is George, and for three years he watched his front door like a man watching the ocean for a ship that might never come in. His son had left under a cloud of anger and broken promises—walked out with a suitcase and a demand for his inheritance, not even looking back. George stayed. He kept the porch light on. He kept a room ready. And every single day, he walked to the end of the driveway and looked down the road, hoping.

One afternoon, the phone rang. It was his son—broken, broke, standing at a bus station three hundred miles from home, asking if he could come home. George didn't hesitate. He said, "Get on the next bus. I'll be there to pick you up." And then he did something his neighbors saw: he ran. Not drove—*ran* down the driveway, tears streaming down his face, as if his son were already visible on the horizon.

That's the image Luke gives us in one of the most famous parables ever told. A father who runs. A father who sees his son while the boy is still "a long way off" and is moved with compassion. A father who embraces, who kisses, who throws a party for someone who doesn't deserve it.

This is the heart of God.

---

Let's look at this passage together. Jesus tells us about two sons and a father. The younger son makes an extraordinary request: "Father, give me my share of the estate." In that culture, this was more than rude—it was a virtual death wish. He was saying, "I wish you were dead. I want my inheritance now." The father, remarkably, gives in. He divides his property between both sons.

The younger son takes everything, travels to a distant country, and squanders it in reckless living. Then comes the famine—not just any famine, but a "severe" one. And suddenly, the money is gone. The friends are gone. The son finds himself in a pig pen, so hungry he's envying the pods the pigs eat. This is rock bottom. This is the far country.

But here's what I want you to notice: *when* does the son come to his senses? Not when he runs out of money. Not when the friends leave. He comes to his senses when he *hungers*. There's something about need that wakes us up. The son realizes that even his father's hired servants have enough to eat. And so he makes a decision: he will go home. Not as a son—*as a hired servant*. He's learned something about grace: he doesn't deserve to be a son anymore. But maybe, just maybe, there's mercy.

And so he begins the long walk home.

But the father sees him first. While the son is still a long way off—before the apology, before the speech, before anything—the father sees him. And what does he do? He *runs*. In that culture, running was undignified. It was something only slaves did. But the father runs, throws his arms around him, and kisses him.

The son begins his prepared speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son."

But he doesn't get to finish. The father interrupts and calls for the best robe, a ring, sandals—signs of sonship, of full restoration. And then he orders the fattened calf to be killed. They're going to celebrate.

This is scandalous grace. The son who wasted everything, who disgraced the family, who should have come home in shame—he's welcomed as if nothing happened. Actually, more than "nothing happened"—he's welcomed with *more* than he had before. The fatted calf. The ring. The robe. This is the extravagant love of God.

---

But the story doesn't end there, because there's another son. The older son comes in from the field, hears the music and dancing, and asks what's happening. When he learns it's a celebration for his brother, he refuses to go in. He's angry. He's been working hard all day, and what does his father do? Throw a party for the one who wasted everything!

The father comes out and pleads with him. "Son, you have always been with me, and everything I have is yours." Notice: the father doesn't rebuke him. He doesn't say, "You should be more grateful." He gently reminds him of the relationship: *you are with me; everything is mine.* And then he says, "But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

This is the hard part of the parable, because many of us see ourselves in the older son. We haven't run away. We've stayed. We've worked. We've done what's right. And we look around at others—people who made messes, people who broke our hearts, people who seem to get off easy—and we feel something that might be harder to name than we want to admit. Envy. Judgment. A sense that it's not *fair*.

But here's what the father says to the older son: *he was lost and is found.* The celebration isn't because sin doesn't matter. It's because *nothing* matters more than a lost person being found. Not your sense of fairness. Not your calculations of who deserves what. Nothing.

---

Now, what does this mean for us?

Maybe you feel like the younger son today. You've been in the far country. Maybe it's not pigs and pods—maybe it's addiction, or bitterness, or a secret sin, or a relationship you destroyed, or a dream that turned to ash. Maybe you're standing at the edge of your own home, thinking you don't deserve to come back. Let me tell you what the Father says: *Run to him.* He's already running to meet you. Your sin is real, but his grace is bigger. He doesn't welcome you as a hired servant—he welcomes you as a *son*. As a *daughter*.

Maybe you feel like the older son. You've stayed. You've been faithful. You've kept the faith when others wandered. And you're looking at someone else's welcome—someone who hurt you, someone who didn't deserve it, someone who seems to get off easy—and you're angry. Let me ask you gently: Is your righteousness becoming a barrier to grace? The father says to you: *Everything I have is yours.* You don't need to compete for his love. You already have it. The celebration of another person's return isn't a threat to your inheritance—it's a preview of the feast to come.

Or maybe you feel like the father. You're watching someone you love spiral away. You've kept the light on. You've kept the room ready. You've prayed and waited and hoped, and you're getting tired. This parable is for you. Keep watching. Keep waiting. Keep the door open. That one who seems lost—God sees them "while they are still a long way off." Keep running toward them with love.

---

I want to close with one more image. In this parable, the father doesn't just wait—he *runs*. In a culture where dignity meant walking slowly, where older men didn't sprint across fields, this father runs. Why? Because love cannot wait. Because when you see someone you love coming home, you *run*.

That's the heart of God. Not a distant deity, keeping score. Not a cosmic judge, weighing your sins against your righteousness. A Father who sees you while you're still a long way off. A Father who runs. A Father who throws his arms around you before you can say you're sorry—because he's been wanting to hold you that whole time.

The party is ready. The calf is fattened. The robe is waiting. The ring is on the table.

All you have to do is come home.

---

*Let us pray.*

Father, thank you for seeing us while we are still far off. Thank you for running toward us when we don't have the strength to run to you. For those who feel like strangers, welcome us as your sons and daughters. For those who feel forgotten, remind us that you have everything for us. # The Father Who Runs

*A Sermon on the Parable of the Prodigal Son*

---

There is a detail in this parable that most of us skim over, but in the first-century Palestinian world where Jesus told this story, it would have made people gasp.

The father runs.

In that culture, an older man of status did not run. Running was undignified—it was what slaves did, what messenger boys did. A respectable father walked. He maintained his honor. He waited for his son to come to him, to bow low, to offer the proper words of apology and submission.

But this father doesn't wait. He doesn't walk. He *runs*.

And not just runs—Luke tells us he was "moved with compassion" (ἐσπλαγχνίσθη), a word that literally means his insides churned with emotion. He sees his son while the boy is still "a long way off" (μακράν), and something in him breaks open. He runs across the field, throws his arms around him, and kisses him—κατεφίλησεν, the Greek says, an intensive form meaning he kissed him again and again, not the polite single kiss of social obligation.

This is the image Jesus gives us of God. Not a distant father waiting for us to clean ourselves up before we approach. A father who sees us while we're still a mess, still far off, still calculating whether we can say the right words—and runs.

This is the heart of God. And it's scandalous.

---

Let's look at this passage together, because the details matter.

Jesus tells us about two sons and a father. The younger son makes an extraordinary request: "Father, give me my share of the estate." In that culture, this was more than rude—it was a virtual death wish. The inheritance wouldn't come until the father died. By demanding his share now, the son was saying, "I wish you were dead. I want what's mine, and I want it now."

This was a profound cultural taboo. The son was not just asking for money—he was rejecting his father's authority, his family's identity, his role in the household. He was, in effect, declaring himself already dead to this family.

And remarkably, the father gives in. He divides his property between both sons. We might expect the father to refuse, to discipline, to hold onto control. But he lets him go. Why? Because love does not coerce. The father allows his son the freedom to choose—even if that choice leads to destruction.

The younger son takes everything, travels to a "distant country" (χώραν ἀπόκεντρον)—the Greek word literally means "a country cut off," a land of exile, separated from everything familiar—and squanders it in reckless living. Then comes the famine, not just any famine, but a "severe" one. And suddenly, the money is gone. The friends are gone. The son finds himself in a pig pen, so hungry he's envying the pods the pigs eat. This is rock bottom. This is the far country.

But here's what I want you to notice: *when* does the son come to his senses? Not when he runs out of money. Not when the friends leave. He comes to his senses when he *hungers*. There's something about need that wakes us up. The son realizes that even his father's hired servants have enough to eat. And so he makes a decision: he will go home. Not as a son—*as a hired servant*. He's learned something about grace: he doesn't deserve to be a son anymore. But maybe, just maybe, there's mercy.

And so he begins the long walk home.

But the father sees him first. While the son is still a long way off—before the apology, before the speech, before anything—the father sees him. And what does he do? He runs. In that culture, running was undignified. It was something only slaves did. But the father runs, throws his arms around him, and kisses him again and again.

The son begins his prepared speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son."

But he doesn't get to finish. The father interrupts and calls for the best robe, a ring, sandals—signs of sonship, of full restoration. And then he orders the fattened calf to be killed. This wasn't just any calf—it was the most expensive animal, reserved for the most important guests, the greatest celebrations.

They're going to celebrate. This is scandalous grace. The son who wasted everything, who disgraced the family, who should have come home in shame—he's welcomed as if nothing happened. Actually, more than "nothing happened"—he's welcomed with *more* than he had before. The fatted calf. The ring. The robe. This is the extravagant love of God.

---

But the story doesn't end there, because there's another son. The older son comes in from the field, hears the music and dancing, and asks what's happening. When he learns it's a celebration for his brother, he refuses to go in. He's angry. He's been working hard all day—παρεγενόμην, the Greek says, he has been present, he has been faithful—and what does his father do? Throw a party for the one who wasted everything!

The father comes out and pleads with him. "Son, you have always been with me, and everything I have is yours." Notice: the father doesn't rebuke him. He doesn't say, "You should be more grateful." He gently reminds him of the relationship: *you are with me; everything is mine.* And then he says, "But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

This is the hard part of the parable, because many of us see ourselves in the older son. We haven't run away. We've stayed. We've worked. We've done what's right. And we look around at others—people who made messes, people who broke our hearts, people who seem to get off easy—and we feel something that might be harder to name than we want to admit. Envy. Judgment. A sense that it's not *fair*.

But here's what the father says to the older son: *he was lost and is found.* The celebration isn't because sin doesn't matter. It's because *nothing* matters more than a lost person being found. Not your sense of fairness. Not your calculations of who deserves what. Nothing.

---

Now, what does this mean for us?

Maybe you feel like the younger son today. You've been in the far country. Maybe it's not pigs and pods—maybe it's addiction, or bitterness, or a secret sin, or a relationship you destroyed, or a dream that turned to ash. Maybe you're standing at the edge of your own home, thinking you don't deserve to come back. Maybe you've rehearsed the speech so many times: "I'm not worthy to be called your child."

Let me tell you what the Father says: *Run to him.* He's already running to meet you. Your sin is real, but his grace is bigger. He doesn't welcome you as a hired servant—he welcomes you as a *son*. As a *daughter*. And here's the thing: he's not just restoring you to where you were before. He's giving you something *more*. The ring. The robe. The fatted calf. This is not a return to the status quo—this is resurrection.

Maybe you feel like the older son. You've stayed. You've been faithful. You've kept the faith when others wandered. You've shown up. And you're looking at someone else's welcome—someone who hurt you, someone who didn't deserve it, someone who seems to get off easy—and you're angry. Maybe you've been waiting for them to "pay their dues" before they'll be accepted.

Let me ask you gently: Is your righteousness becoming a barrier to grace? The father says to you: *Everything I have is yours.* You don't need to compete for his love. You already have it. The celebration of another person's return isn't a threat to your inheritance—it's a preview of the feast to come. The question is not "Do they deserve this?" The question is "Can I celebrate what my Father celebrates?"

Maybe you feel like the father. You're watching someone you love spiral away. You've kept the light on. You've kept the room ready. You've prayed and waited and hoped, and you're getting tired. Maybe you've almost given up.

This parable is for you. Keep watching. Keep waiting. Keep the door open. That one who seems lost—God sees them "while they are still a long way off." Don't stop looking down that road. Keep running toward them with love. Your love might be the thing that breaks them open, that helps them come to their senses, that shows them there's still a home to return to.

---

I want to close with one more thought.

In this parable, the father doesn't just wait—he *runs*. In a culture where dignity meant walking slowly, where older men didn't sprint across fields, this father runs. Why? Because love cannot wait. Because when you see someone you love coming home, you *run*.

That's the heart of God. Not a distant deity, keeping score. Not a cosmic judge, weighing your sins against your righteousness. A Father who sees you while you're still a long way off. A Father who runs. A Father who throws his arms around you before you can say you're sorry—because he's been wanting to hold you that whole time.

And here's the thing that should change everything: this is not a story about a father who finally relents. It's a story about a father who has been waiting, watching, running *the entire time*. The son was coming home because the father was already running to meet him. The grace was not earned on the road—it was waiting at the door.

The party is ready. The calf is fattened. The robe is waiting. The ring is on the table.

All you have to do is come home.

---

*Let us pray.*

Father, thank you for seeing us while we are still far off—for looking down the road with watching eyes and a running heart. Thank you that your love is not earned but given, not deserved but extravagant. For those who feel like strangers today, may they know the embrace that interrupts their apology and says, "You are mine." For those who feel forgotten or overlooked, remind us that everything you have is ours. For those who are waiting for someone to come home, give us the patience and relentless love of the father in this story. Help us to celebrate—not when others deserve it, but when the lost are found and the dead are alive. Let our lives be a running toward, a door held open, a feast that never ends. In Jesus' name, amen.

# The Father Who Runs

*A Sermon on the Parable of the Prodigal Son*
Text: Luke 15:11-32

---

Let me tell you about a father I know. His name is George, and for three years he watched his front door like a man watching the ocean for a ship that might never come in. His son had left under a cloud of anger and broken promises—walked out with a suitcase and a demand for his inheritance, not even looking back. George stayed. He kept the porch light on. He kept a room ready. He kept the son's favorite cereal in the cabinet, just in case. And every single day, sometimes twice a day, he walked to the end of the driveway and looked down the road, hoping against hope.

One afternoon, the phone rang. It was his son—broken, broke, standing at a bus station three hundred miles from home, asking if he could come home. George didn't hesitate. He said, "Get on the next bus. I'll be there to pick you up." And then he did something his neighbors saw: he ran. Not drove—*ran* down the driveway, tears streaming down his face, as if his son were already visible on the horizon.

That's the image Luke gives us in one of the most famous parables ever told. A father who runs. A father who sees his son while the boy is still "a long way off" and is moved with compassion. A father who embraces, who kisses, who throws a party for someone who doesn't deserve it.

This is the heart of God.

---

But before we get to the heart of God, we need to understand why Jesus told this story in the first place. Turn back one page in your Bible—Luke chapter 15, verses 1 and 2. Here's what happened: "Now the tax collectors and sinners were all gathering around to hear Jesus. But the Pharisees and the teachers of the law muttered, 'This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.'"

This is important. Jesus tells this parable as an *answer* to the grumbling of the religious leaders. They're scandalized that Jesus would sit down at a table with people who had messed up—people the religious establishment had written off. The question behind this parable is a question we still ask today: *What do we do with people who have messed up? Do we welcome them, or do we write them off? Do we eat with them, or do we look the other way?*

And Jesus answers with a story about a father and two sons—a story that would have made the Pharisees very uncomfortable. Because in this story, the one who looks most like the religious establishment is not the hero.

Let's look at the passage together.

---

The younger son makes an extraordinary request: "Father, give me my share of the estate." In that culture, this was more than rude—it was a virtual death wish. He was essentially saying, "I wish you were dead. I want my inheritance now, while you're still breathing." This was a profound insult, a declaration that the son could not wait for his father to die to receive what was coming to him. The son was saying, in effect, "I want you out of my life."

The father, remarkably, gives in. He divides his property between both sons. And the younger son takes his portion, sells what he can, and leaves. He travels to a distant country—geographically far from home, but spiritually far as well. And there, in that far country, he squanders everything.

Now, I want us to pause here for a moment, because the text says he "squandered his wealth in reckless living." But that's a polite way of saying it. Let's paint the picture. Imagine the glitter of casino lights. The loud laughter of "friends" who only stick around when there's money to spend. The parties that go on too late, the drinks that blur the edges of everything, the morning-after regret that fades by noon only to start again. He didn't just spend money—he spent himself. He spent his character, his reputation, his dignity. He spent until there was nothing left.

And then came the famine. Not just any famine, but a "severe" one. And suddenly, the money is gone. The friends are gone. The illusion is shattered. The son finds himself in a pig pen—feeding pigs, which for a Jewish man was the height of uncleanness—so hungry that he's envying the pods the pigs eat. He would have eaten that slop himself if anyone had offered it.

This is rock bottom. This is the far country.

But here's what I want you to notice: *when* does the son come to his senses? Not when he runs out of money. Not when the friends leave. He comes to his senses when he *hungers*. There's something about need that wakes us up. The son realizes that even his father's hired servants have enough to eat—more than enough. And in that moment of hunger, something shifts.

And so he makes a decision: he will go home. Not as a son—he knows he doesn't deserve that anymore. He'll go home *as a hired servant*. He's learned something about grace, or at least the edge of it: he doesn't deserve to be a son, but maybe, just maybe, there's mercy. Maybe there's food. Maybe there's a place at the table, even if it's at the back of the house.

And so he begins the long walk home.

---

But here's where the story turns—and this is the part that should stop us in our tracks. The father *sees* him first. While the son is still a long way off—before the apology, before the rehearsed speech, before anything—the father sees him. And what does he do? He *runs*.

Now, we need to understand what this meant in that culture. Running was undignified. It was something only slaves and servants did. A respectable older man in that culture would never run—it would expose his legs beneath his robe, and he would become a laughingstock to anyone who saw him. A father in that culture would wait inside the house, dignified, waiting for his son to come to him, to bow low, to beg for mercy.

But this father doesn't wait. He runs. He humiliates himself—publicly, in full view of the village—to get to his son as fast as possible. He exposes himself to shame because nothing, *nothing*, is more important than getting to his boy.

And he embraces him. He kisses him. Not a formal, polite kiss—an embrace of overwhelming love, the kind of embrace that says, "I've missed you. I've missed you so much."

The son begins his prepared speech—the one he practiced all the way home: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son."

But he doesn't get to finish. The father interrupts him. He doesn't even let him finish the apology. And he calls for the best robe—not just any robe, but the *best* one, the one saved for special occasions. He calls for a ring—likely a signet ring, a ring that signified authority, that gave the son the legal right to act on the father's behalf. He calls for sandals—because slaves went barefoot, but sons wore sandals. This wasn't just a welcome; it was a *total reinstatement*. The son who should have come home as a hired servant was welcomed as if he had never left.

And then he orders the fattened calf to be killed. They're going to celebrate.

This is scandalous grace. The son who wasted everything, who disgraced the family, who should have come home in shame—he's welcomed as if nothing happened. Actually, more than "nothing happened"—he's welcomed with *more* than he had before. The fatted calf. The ring. The robe. The sandals. This is the extravagant love of God. This is a father who cannot wait to hold his child.

---

But the story doesn't end there, because there's another son. The older son.

He comes in from the field—having worked hard all day, having done everything right, having stayed when his brother left. He hears the music and dancing, and he asks what's happening. When he learns it's a celebration for his brother, he refuses to go in. He's angry. He's been working, and what does his father do? Throw a party for the one who wasted everything!

Now, here's where this gets uncomfortable. The older brother isn't just a sibling who's jealous. He's the one Jesus is actually talking to—the grumbling Pharisees who muttered about Jesus eating with sinners. The older brother represents the religious establishment, the people who think they deserve God's favor because of their good behavior, their church attendance, their moral performance.

The father comes out and pleads with him. "Son, you have always been with me, and everything I have is yours." Notice: the father doesn't rebuke him. He doesn't say, "You should be more grateful." He gently reminds him of the relationship: *you are with me; everything is mine.* And then he says, "But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

Here's the hard truth: the older brother has forgotten what it means to be a *son*. He's been working like a *slave*. He says he has "slaved" for his father—there's that word again, *douleuo*, which means "to serve as a bondservant." The older brother has turned the father into a master and the family relationship into a work contract. He's been keeping score. He's been calculating what he deserves.

And when someone else gets something he didn't calculate for, he can't handle it. It feels *unfair*. It feels *wrong*.

But here's what the father says to the older son: *he was lost and is found.* The celebration isn't because sin doesn't matter. It's because *nothing* matters more than a lost person being found. Not your sense of fairness. Not your calculations of who deserves what. Nothing.

We all have a little older brother in us, don't we? We see the news story about the celebrity who hits rock bottom and finds Jesus, and we think, "Really? Him? What about me? I've been paying my taxes and going to church. I've been faithful. I've been working hard." We look at someone else's welcome—someone who hurt us, someone who didn't deserve it, someone who seems to get off easy—and we feel something that might be harder to name than we want to admit. Envy. Judgment. A sense that it's not *fair*.

But the father says to us: *everything I have is yours.* You don't need to compete for my love. You already have it. The celebration of another person's return isn't a threat to your inheritance—it's a preview of the feast to come.

---

So what does this mean for us today?

Maybe you feel like the younger son. You've been in the far country. Maybe it's not pigs and pods—maybe it's the scrolling late at night that leaves you empty. Maybe it's the addiction no one knows about. Maybe it's the bitterness that's calcified in your heart. Maybe it's a relationship you destroyed and can't fix. Maybe it's a dream that turned to ash, and you've been standing in the wreckage wondering how you got here. Maybe you're standing at the edge of your own home, thinking you don't deserve to come back. You rehearsed the apology all the way here.

Let me tell you what the Father says: *Run to him.* He's already running to meet you. He saw you while you were still a long way off. Your sin is real, but his grace is bigger. He doesn't welcome you as a hired servant—he welcomes you as a *son*. As a *daughter*. He puts the ring on your finger and says, "You are mine."

Maybe you feel like the older son. You've stayed. You've been faithful. You've kept the faith when others wandered. You've done the right thing when no one was watching. And you're looking at someone else's welcome—someone who hurt you deeply, someone who broke your trust, someone who seems to get off easy—and you're angry. The music and dancing feel like a slap in the face.

That's the scandal. Jesus is not just telling a nice story about forgiveness. He's doing something far more dangerous: he's *defending* his practice of table fellowship with people the religious establishment has written off. He's saying that God's kingdom looks like a dinner party where the outcasts are honored guests.

And so Jesus tells three stories in a row—the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. Each one answers the same complaint: *Why do you welcome them?* And each answer is the same: because that's what love does. When something precious is lost, you don't calculate whether it deserves to be found. You *search*. You *search*. You *run*.

So when we come to this parable, we're not just hearing a lovely story about a father and his sons. We're hearing Jesus defend the very heart of God against a religious system that had made exclusion a theology.

---

Now, let's look at the passage itself.

Jesus tells us about two sons and a father. The younger son makes an extraordinary request: "Father, give me my share of the estate." In that culture, this was more than rude—it was a legal and public act of disownment. He was saying, "I wish you were dead. I want my inheritance now, and I want nothing more to do with you." In the ancient world, this was called *kezazah*—the "cutting off" ceremony. The son was effectively saying, *I renounce my place in this family.*

The father, remarkably, gives in. He divides his property between both sons. And the younger son takes his portion, liquidates everything, and travels to a distant country where no one knows his name. There he squanders it in reckless living—wine, women, whatever the pagan culture offered to a young man with money to burn.

Then comes the famine—not just any famine, but a "severe" one. And suddenly, the money is gone. The so-called friends are gone. The son finds himself in a pig pen, so hungry he's envying the pods the pigs are eating. He has hit rock bottom. He is in the far country.

But here's what I want you to notice: *when* does the son come to his senses? Not when he runs out of money. Not when the friends leave. He comes to his senses when he *hungers*. There's something about need that wakes us up. The son realizes that even his father's hired servants have enough to eat—better food than this. And so he makes a decision: he will go home. Not as a son—*as a hired servant*. He's learned something about grace: he doesn't deserve to be a son anymore. But maybe, just maybe, there's mercy.

In that culture, running was undignified. It was something only slaves did. A respected elder *walked*. The son begins his prepared speech—the one he practiced all the way home: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son."

Your job is not to fix them, but to keep the light of Christ's love shining. And when they finally turn toward home—even if it's been years, even if you've almost given up—run to meet them. Don't walk. Don't wait. *Run.*

---

I want to close with one more image. In this parable, the father doesn't just wait—he *runs*. In a culture where dignity meant walking slowly, where older men didn't sprint across fields, this father runs. Why? Because love cannot wait. Because when you see someone you love coming home, you *run*.

Just like George running down his driveway, ignoring his neighbors and his dignity, our heavenly Father runs toward us. He is not a distant deity, keeping score. Not a cosmic judge, weighing your sins against your righteousness. A Father who sees you while you're still a long way off. A Father who runs. A Father who throws his arms around you before you can say you're sorry—because he's been wanting to hold you that whole time.

And here's the thing: he's not just waiting in the past, or waiting for some future moment of perfection. He is running toward you, right now, in this moment. Today. This very second, if you turned toward him, he would run.

The party is ready. The calf is fattened. The robe is waiting. The ring is on the table.

All you have to do is come home.

---

*Let us pray.*

Father, thank you for seeing us while we are still far off. Thank you for running toward us when we don't have the strength to run to you. For those who feel like strangers, welcome us as your sons and daughters. For those who feel forgotten, remind us that you have everything for us. For those who are waiting for someone to come home, give us the patience and love of the father in this story. Let us celebrate, always, that the lost are found and the dead are alive. In Jesus' name, amen.

# The Father Who Runs

*A Sermon on the Parable of the Prodigal Son*

---

Let me tell you about a father I know. His name is George, and for three years he watched his front door like a man watching the ocean for a ship that might never come in. His son had left under a cloud of anger and broken promises—walked out with a suitcase and a demand for his inheritance, not even looking back. George stayed. He kept the porch light on. He kept a room ready. He kept the portrait of his boy on the mantel, right where it had always been. And every single day, he walked to the end of the driveway and looked down the road, hoping.

One afternoon, the phone rang. It was his son—broken, broke, standing at a bus station three hundred miles from home, asking if he could come home. George didn't hesitate. He said, "Get on the next bus. I'll be there to pick you up." And then he did something his neighbors saw: he ran. Not drove—*ran* down the driveway, tears streaming down his face, as if his son were already visible on the horizon.

That's the image Luke gives us in one of the most famous parables ever told. Jesus tells this story as the crescendo of three tales about lost things—the lost sheep, the lost coin, and this lost son—each ending in a party, because heaven's math is different than ours. A father who runs. A father who sees his son while the boy is still "a long way off" and is moved with compassion. A father who embraces, who kisses, who throws a party for someone who doesn't deserve it.

This is the heart of God.

---

Let's look at this passage together. Jesus tells us about two sons and a father. The younger son makes an extraordinary request: "Father, give me my share of the estate." In that culture, this was more than rude—it was a virtual death wish. He was saying, "I wish you were dead. I want my inheritance now." The very asking was a kind of violence—a son essentially telling his father he couldn't wait for him to die. The father, remarkably, gives in. He divides his property between both sons.

The younger son takes everything, travels to a distant country, and squanders it in reckless living. The Greek word here is *asōtōs*—literally "without saving," wastefully, extravagantly destructively. He lives like there's no tomorrow, because in his mind, there might as well not be. And then comes the famine—not just any famine, but a "severe" one. And suddenly, the money is gone. The friends are gone. The party is over, and the music has stopped.

The son finds himself in a pig pen, so hungry he's envying the pods the pigs eat. Can you imagine that? A Jewish boy, raised in a clean household, now longing for the slop fed to unclean animals. This is rock bottom. This is the far country.

But here's what I want you to notice: *when* does the son come to his senses? Not when he runs out of money. Not when the friends leave. He comes to his senses when he *hungers*. There's something about need that wakes us up. The pain of empty stomach becomes the ache of an empty soul. And the son realizes something remarkable: even his father's hired servants have enough to eat. Not just enough—*plenty*. The lowest person in his father's household eats better than this.

And so he makes a decision: he will go home. But notice what he plans to say. He rehearses it on the long walk back: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants."

Here's what's crucial: the son still thinks in terms of transaction. He's learned something about sin, but he hasn't learned anything about grace. He thinks he can negotiate his way back into the household. He thinks the path to restoration is through hard work and humble pleading—through earning back what he lost. He hasn't yet learned that in his father's house, relationship isn't earned—it's given.

And so he begins the long walk home.

But the father sees him first. While the son is still a long way off—before the apology, before the speech, before anything—the father sees him. And what does he do? He *runs*. In that culture, running was undignified. It was something only slaves did. A respected elder walked. But this father runs, his robes flying behind him, across the field, toward his boy.

He throws his arms around him and kisses him. Again. And again. The Greek suggests an ongoing action—over and over, as if he can't stop, as if three years of waiting are being expressed in this one embrace.

The son begins his prepared speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son."

But he doesn't get to finish. The father interrupts—and this interruption is everything. He calls for the best robe, not just any robe—the *first* robe, the one saved for the most honored guests. He puts a ring on his finger, the family seal, the sign of authority. He puts sandals on his feet, not the barefoot of a servant, but the footwear of a son. And then he orders the fattened calf to be killed. The best meat. The finest wine. The biggest party.

This is scandalous grace. The son who wasted everything, who disgraced the family, who should have come home in shame—he's welcomed as if nothing happened. Actually, more than "nothing happened"—he's welcomed with *more* than he had before. The fatted calf. The ring. The robe. This is the extravagant love of God. Not a God who grudgingly accepts us back. A God who runs to us, who embraces us before we can say we're sorry, who celebrates as if we were the one who never left.

---

But the story doesn't end there, because there's another son. The older son comes in from the field, hears the music and dancing, and asks what's happening. When he learns it's a celebration for his brother, he refuses to go in. He's angry. He's been working hard all day in the field, and what does his father do? Throw a party for the one who wasted everything!

The father comes out and pleads with him. "Son, you have always been with me, and everything I have is yours."

Now, listen carefully. The father isn't saying the inheritance is intact—the younger son already took his share. What the father is saying is something more profound: *you have me.* The relationship itself is the inheritance. "Everything I have is yours" means "I am your father. That has never changed. That will never change."

And then he says, "But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

This is the hard part of the parable, because many of us see ourselves in the older son. We haven't run away. We've stayed. We've worked. We've done what's right. We've shown up. And we look around at others—people who made messes, people who broke our hearts, people who seem to get off easy—and we feel something that might be harder to name than we want to admit. Envy. Judgment. A sense that it's not *fair*.

But here's what the father says to the older son: *he was lost and is found.* The celebration isn't because sin doesn't matter. It's because *nothing* matters more than a lost person being found. Not your sense of fairness. Not your calculations of who deserves what. Not the ledger you've kept in your heart. Nothing.

This is the calculus of heaven—and it's meant to crash into our earthly bookkeeping.

---

Now, what does this mean for us?

Maybe you feel like the younger son today. You've been in the far country. Maybe it's not pigs and pods—maybe it's the bottle you promised you'd stop reaching for. Maybe it's the affair that ended your marriage. Maybe it's the words you said to your daughter that you can never take back. Maybe it's the resentment you nurse like a treasured wound, the one you won't let go of because at least it feels familiar. Maybe you're standing at the edge of your own home, thinking you don't deserve to come back. That maybe you've used up all your chances.

Let me tell you what the Father says: *Run to him.* He's already running to meet you. Your sin is real, but his grace is bigger. He doesn't welcome you as a hired servant—he welcomes you as a *son*. As a *daughter*. The robe is already being wrapped around your shoulders. The ring is already on your finger.

Maybe you feel like the older son. If so, hear this first: your faithfulness matters. Your father sees it. The years you stayed weren't wasted. The obedience wasn't pointless. But here's the danger: what if your faithfulness has become a ledger you keep? What if you've confused the father's house with a workplace where you earn bonuses? What if your righteousness has become a barrier to grace—not just for others, but for yourself?

The father says to you: *Everything I have is yours.* You don't need to compete for his love. You already have it. The celebration of another person's return isn't a threat to your inheritance—it's a preview of the feast to come. Could it be that you've been standing outside the party, keeping the books, while the music plays on without you?

Or maybe you feel like the father. You're watching someone you love spiral away. You've kept the light on. You've kept the room ready. You've prayed until your voice is hoarse, watched until your eyes ache, hoped until hope itself feels like a wound. You've answered the phone at 2 AM more times than you can count, not knowing if it's crisis or confession. And you're tired.

This parable is for you. Keep watching. Keep waiting. Keep the door open. That one who seems lost—God sees them "while they are still a long way off." Keep running toward them with love. Like George sprinting down his driveway, not caring who saw, because love cannot wait.

---

I want to close with one more image. In this parable, the father doesn't just wait—he *runs*. In a culture where dignity meant walking slowly, where older men didn't sprint across fields, this father runs. Why? Because love cannot wait. Because when you see someone you love coming home, you *run*.

That's the heart of God. Not a distant deity, keeping score. Not a cosmic judge, weighing your sins against your righteousness. A Father who sees you while you're still a long way off. A Father who runs. A Father who throws his arms around you before you can say you're sorry—because he's been wanting to hold you that whole time.

Can you smell the roast? Can you hear the music spilling from the windows? The robe is already warming by the fire. The ring is polished. The calf is fattened. The party is ready.

And just like George—your Father is running toward you right now.

All you have to do is come home.

---

*Let us pray.*

Father, thank you for seeing us while we are still far off. Thank you for running toward us when we don't have the strength to run to you. For those who feel like strangers, welcome us as your sons and daughters. For those who feel forgotten, remind us that you have everything for us. For those who are waiting for someone to come home, give us the patience and love of the father in this story. Let us celebrate, always, that the lost are found and the dead are alive. In Jesus' name, amen.

# The Welcome That Changes Everything

## A Sermon on the Parable of the Prodigal Son

---

There's a story I want to share with you this morning—a story that might sound familiar, but one that never loses its power to surprise us. Not long ago, I read about a man named Richard. Richard was a successful businessman, a man who had built a comfortable life for himself and his family. But somewhere along the way, he had drifted far from the faith of his childhood. He hadn't abandoned it deliberately; it had just slowly faded, like a photograph left too long in the sun.

One winter evening, alone in a hotel room thousands of miles from home, Richard found himself unable to sleep. Something was missing—something he couldn't name. He turned on the television, and by chance, landed on a broadcast of a church service. The pastor was speaking about forgiveness, about a love that welcomes sinners home. Richard, a man who hadn't prayed in decades, found himself on his knees in that hotel room, weeping.

"I don't know if you're real," he said to God, "but if you are, I need you."

That was the beginning of Richard's journey back. And here's what strikes me: he didn't come home to a cold reception. He didn't have to earn his way back. He came home to arms flung wide, to a father who had been watching the road every single day, who had never stopped hoping.

This is the story Jesus tells in Luke chapter 15—the parable we call the Prodigal Son. But I wonder if we've heard it so often that we've forgotten just how radical it is. Let's look at it together.

---

**The Request That Shook the Village**

Jesus begins: "There was a man who had two sons."

Right away, we're in a family story. And this is no ordinary family—this is a household of means. The father is clearly a man of wealth, a landowner with hired hands, with livestock, with enough to divide an inheritance. This is a family with reputation, with expectations, with a place in the community.

Then the younger son does the unthinkable. He says to his father, "Give me my share of the estate."

Can you imagine? In that culture, this was more than rude—it was devastating. What he was really saying was, "I wish you were dead. I can't wait for you to be gone so I can take what's mine and leave." The younger son was essentially telling his father, "Your presence is a burden. Your guidance is a cage. I want my inheritance now, while you're still alive, because I don't want anything from you except your money."

And the father—here's where the story turns astonishing—*he gives it to them*. He divides his property between both sons. He doesn't argue. He doesn't refuse. He doesn't lecture. He lets them go.

I think we sometimes read this and assume the father was harsh, that he simply gave up on his son. But I don't believe that's it at all. I believe he let them go because he understood something profound: love that is forced is not love. You cannot make someone stay. You cannot compel respect. You can only offer it and hope.

So the younger son takes his inheritance—everything he has—and he leaves. He travels to a distant country, and there he squanders it. The text says he "wasted his possessions in prodigal living." The word "prodigal" actually means "spending liberally, extravagantly, even recklessly." And that's exactly what he does. He lives for pleasure, for self-gratification, for the moment. He has forgotten about tomorrow because today is so intoxicating.

And then, as it always does, the bottom falls out.

---

**The Pig Pen and the Awakening**

A severe famine strikes the land. The younger son finds himself with nothing—no money, no friends, no prospects. He's so desperate that he takes a job feeding pigs. Now, for Jewish listeners, this would have beenhorrifying. Pigs were unclean animals. A Jew working with pigs was rock bottom. And even that job falls apart—the pigs' food looks better than what he has to eat.

There he is, in a pig pen, hungry, ashamed, alone. And something breaks open in him.

He comes to his senses.

That phrase is so important. It's not that he decides to be smarter about his sin. It's not a business decision. He *comes to his senses*—like waking from a dream, like seeing clearly for the first time. And what does he see?

He sees that his father's hired hands have more than enough to eat while he starves. He sees that he has been a fool. He sees that he has wounded his father, betrayed his family, wasted his life. And he makes a decision.

"I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired hands."

Do you hear what's happening? The son is not coming home expecting a feast. He's coming home expecting to work. He's coming home with a rehearsed speech, a plan to earn back what he's lost. He wants to restore himself, to prove that he's changed.

But here's what he doesn't know—he can't possibly know—his father has other plans.

---

**The Father Who Runs**

"So he got up and went to his father."

The son begins the long journey home. He's rehearsing his speech. He's preparing for embarrassment, for a cold welcome, for the long road of making things right.

And then he looks up.

His father is coming toward him.

Not walking. Not striding. *Running*. In that culture, running was undignified for a man of standing. It was something servants did, not fathers. But this father runs, and when he reaches his son, he does something almost unthinkable in that culture: he embraces him. He throws his arms around him. He kisses him.

The son begins his prepared speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy—"

But the father isn't listening to the speech. The father cuts him off and calls to his servants: "Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let us eat and celebrate."

A feast. Not a lecture. Not a probation period. A feast.

"For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

---

**The Brother Who Couldn't Celebrate**

Now here's where the story takes another turn—one we often overlook. The older son comes in from the field. He hears music and dancing. He asks what's happening. When he learns that his brother has returned, that his father has killed the fattened calf, he is filled with anger.

He won't go in.

The father comes out and pleads with him. And listen to what the older son says: "Look! All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours comes back—who squandered your property with prostitutes—you kill the fattened calf for him!"

All these years I've been slaving for you.

There's the problem. Not sin, not rebellion—the older son had never committed the younger son's sins. But he had been serving his father out of obligation, not love. He had been keeping the rules, but his heart was far from his father's. He didn't want a celebration; he wanted justice. He wanted his brother punished, not welcomed.

And the father responds with words that must have been hard to hear: "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

---

**What This Story Means for Us**

So what is Jesus teaching us here? Let's be careful not to miss the forest for the trees.

You've started keeping score. You've looked at others and thought, "Why should they get what they don't deserve?" Friend, the father says to you: Everything I have is yours. Celebrate. Maybe faith has become routine, a list of rules, a comfortable life. This story is for you too: remember the welcome. This is who God is.

So come home. Whatever you've done, wherever you've been, however far you feel—come home. The father is waiting. The father is running. The father is ready to embrace you.

And when you get there, you'll find the table is already set.

Amen.

The kind with thin walls, where you can hear the ice machine humming down the hall, where the carpet smells faintly of cleaning solution, where the bedside lamp flickers if you don't hold it just right. A man is sitting on the edge of the bed at 2 a.m., wide awake, though he hasn't slept well in months. Maybe years.

He's far from home—thousands of miles away on business he no longer cares about. He turned off his laptop an hour ago. He's scrolled through every app on his phone twice. It's more like a hollow place, an emptiness he can't name but has learned to ignore—until now, in this particular room, on this particular night, when ignoring it is no longer possible.

He turns on the television. He flips through the channels—news, infomercials, a cooking show in a language he doesn't speak. And then, almost by accident, he lands on a church service. A pastor is speaking about forgiveness, about a love that welcomes sinners home. The man hasn't prayed in decades. He wasn't even sure he believed anymore. He gets down on his knees on that industrial carpet. He doesn't know what to say. He doesn't have the words. So he just speaks from the hollow place:

"I don't know if you're real," he says. "But if you are, I need you."

That was the beginning of Richard's journey back. And here's what strikes me about his story: he didn't come home to a cold reception. He didn't have to prove himself first. He didn't have to clean up his life before coming to God. He came home to arms flung wide, to a father who had been watching the road every single day, who had never stopped hoping, who was already running toward him before he even took the first step.

Can you imagine? In that culture, this was more than rude—it was devastating. What he was really saying was, "I wish you were dead. I want my inheritance now, while you're still alive, because I don't want anything from you except your money."

And the father—here's where the story turns astonishing—*he gives it to them*. He divides his property between both sons. He doesn't argue. He doesn't refuse. He doesn't lecture. He lets them go.

I think we sometimes read this and assume the father was harsh, that he simply gave up on his son. But I don't believe that's it at all. A severe famine strikes the land. The younger son finds himself with nothing—no money, no friends, no prospects. He's so desperate that he takes a job feeding pigs. Now, for Jewish listeners, this would have been horrifying. Pigs were unclean animals. A Jew working with pigs was rock bottom. And the father responds with words that must have been hard to hear:

"My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and found."

---

I want to speak to you this morning—wherever you are, whatever you're carrying.

Perhaps you identify with the younger son. You know what it's like to be far from God. Maybe not in the dramatic way of the story—no pig pen, no famine. Maybe it's quieter than that. Maybe it's the slow drift, the gradual forgetting, the way faith just slipped away like water through your fingers. You look back at good years wasted, time you can't get back, choices you wish you could undo.

Let me speak directly to you: The father is watching the road. Right now. Today. He has never stopped watching. He saw you walk away, and it broke his heart—but he didn't stop loving you. He didn't stop waiting.

Come home. Not with your rehearsed speech, not with your plan to earn back what you've lost. Come home as you are. The feast is already prepared. The robe is already waiting. The ring is already in his hand.

Perhaps you identify with the older son. You've been faithful. You've stayed. You've done what's right. You've shown up. And somewhere along the way, you've lost the joy of it. You've started keeping score. And you're invited to join the celebration—or get left outside complaining.

---

Jesus begins: "There was a man who had two sons."

This is a family with reputation, with expectations, with a place in the community.

Then the younger son does the unthinkable. He says to his father, "Give me my share of the estate."

Can you imagine? In that culture, this was more than rude—it was devastating. What he was really saying was, "I wish you were dead. I can't wait for you to be gone so I can take what's mine and leave." The younger son was essentially telling his father, "Your presence is a burden. Your guidance is a cage. I want my inheritance now, while you're still alive, because I don't want anything from you except your money."

And the father—here's where the story turns astonishing—*he gives it to them*. He divides his property between both sons. He doesn't argue. He doesn't refuse. He doesn't lecture. He lets them go.

Why? I suspect because he understood something profound: love that is forced is not love. You cannot make someone stay. You cannot compel respect. You can only offer it and hope.

So the younger son takes his inheritance—everything he has—and he leaves. He travels to a distant country, and there he squanders it. The text says he "wasted his possessions in prodigal living." The word "prodigal" actually means "spending liberally, extravagantly, even recklessly." And that's exactly what he does. He lives for pleasure, for self-gratification, for the moment. He has forgotten about tomorrow because today is so intoxicating.

And then, as it always does, the bottom falls out.

---

A severe famine strikes the land. The younger son finds himself with nothing—no money, no friends, no prospects. He's so desperate that he takes a job feeding pigs. Now, for Jewish listeners, this would have been horrifying. Pigs were unclean animals. A Jew working with pigs was rock bottom. And even that job falls apart—the pigs' food looks better than what he has to eat.

There he is, in a pig pen, hungry, ashamed, alone. And something breaks open in him.

He comes to his senses.

That phrase is so important. It's not that he decides to be smarter about his sin. It's not a business decision. He *comes to his senses*—like waking from a dream, like seeing clearly for the first time. And what does he see?

He sees that his father's hired hands have more than enough to eat while he starves. He sees that he has been a fool. He sees that he has wounded his father, betrayed his family, wasted his life. And he makes a decision.

He kisses him.

You've started keeping score. You've looked at others and thought, "Why should they get what they don't deserve?" I want to ask you: Whose celebration did you last refuse to join? Friend, the father says to you: Everything I have is yours. Celebrate. Let go of the resentment. The feast is for you too.

And when you get there, you'll find the table is already set.

Then, as you receive communion in a few minutes, remember: you are coming to the Father's feast. The table is already set. The Father is already running toward you.

Amen.

First, this story is about **God's extravagant grace**. The father represents God—the God who watches the road, who runs to meet us, who embraces us before we can even finish our apology. This is not a God who waits for us to clean up our act. This is a God who welcomes us home while we are still far off. The feast is already prepared. The ring is already on the finger. The robe is already waiting.

Second, this story is about **the two kinds of lostness**. We often think the younger son is the only one who gets lost. But the older son is also lost—lost in self-righteousness, lost in resentment, lost in the lie that obedience earns love. The scribes and Pharisees who were grumbling about Jesus? They were the older son. They thought they deserved God's favor because of what they had done. But that's not how grace works. Grace isn't earned; it's received. Both brothers needed the father's grace. Both brothers needed to be found.

Third, this story reveals **our tendency to compare**. The older son couldn't celebrate because he was too busy comparing. He measured himself against his brother and found himself superior. But that's not how grace works. Grace doesn't make us better than others; it makes us grateful for what we've received. The father had enough for both sons. There was always enough.

---

**Where Do You Find Yourself?**

Perhaps this morning, you identify with the younger son. You know what it's like to be far from God, to have squandered good years, to feel like you've wasted so much. Let me tell you what the father says to you: Come home. Don't rehearse your apology. Don't try to earn your way back. The feast is ready. The father is watching the road. He is running toward you now.

Perhaps you identify with the older son. You've been faithful. You've stayed. You've done what's right. But somewhere along the way, you've lost the joy of being a child. You've started keeping score. You've looked at others and thought, "Why should they get what they don't deserve?"

Friend, I need to tell you something. I've been there too. There have been moments when I've watched someone receive grace—someone who seemed to have squandered so much, someone who had been far from God—and I've caught myself thinking, "But I did the work! I stayed faithful!" And in that moment, I became the older son. I became someone who wanted justice instead of celebration.

If that's you this morning, hear the father's heart: "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours." You don't have to earn what is already yours. You are not a servant; you are a child. Celebrate. Let go of the resentment. The feast is for you too.

Maybe faith has become routine, a list of rules, a comfortable life. This story is for you too: remember the welcome. Remember that you were once lost, that someone ran to meet you, that the feast was prepared before you ever arrived.

---

**The Celebration That Never Ends**

There's one more thing I want you to see. The father didn't just throw a party for his son that day. The father *lives* in celebration. Every day, he watches the road. Every day, he hopes. Every day, he runs to meet the lost.

This is who God is.

Not a grudging forgiver. Not a reluctant welcomer. A father whose love is so extravagant, so unreasonable, so full, that it runs to meet us even when we don't deserve it—*especially* when we don't deserve it.

The Father is not just waiting at the finish line; He is standing on the porch, His eyes fixed on the horizon, ready to run. His love is the only map you need to find your way home.

This is the gospel. This is the good news. Not that God tolerates us, but that God celebrates us. Not that God accepts us someday, but that God has already prepared the feast.

So come home. Whatever you've done, wherever you've been, however far you feel—come home. The father is waiting. The father is running. The father is ready to embrace you.

And when you get there, you'll find the table is already set.

# The Welcome That Changes Everything

## A Sermon on the Parable of the Prodigal Son

---

I want to begin with a story. Several months ago, one of our members—I'll call her Marie—came to me after a Sunday service. She was quiet for a moment, and then she said, "Pastor, I need to tell you something I've never told anyone."

Thirty years ago, Marie had walked away from the church, from her faith, from everything she'd grown up believing. She'd made choices she wasn't proud of—choices that had cost her marriages, jobs, relationships. She'd told herself God had given up on her, so she'd given up on God. Faith had faded like the ink on a diploma she never looked at anymore.

Then, last spring, her adult daughter asked her to come to church. "Just once," her daughter said. "Just come and see."

Marie sat in the back row that morning, arms crossed, ready to prove nothing would change. But the sermon wasn't about rules. It was about a father running. By the time the service ended, Marie was weeping—not from guilt, but from shock. She said to me, "I always thought I'd have to earn my way back. I didn't know the feast was already set."

This morning, I want to show you what Marie discovered: that Jesus tells one story to expose two kinds of lostness—and to reveal a father who runs toward both.

---

**The Setting That Changes Everything**

But first, we need to set the scene. This parable isn't told in a vacuum. Luke tells us that Jesus told this story in response to a specific situation: "Now the tax collectors and sinners were all gathering around to hear Jesus. But the Pharisees and the teachers of the law began to mutter, 'This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.'" (Luke 15:1-2)

The religious elites were furious. How dare Jesus sit at table with them? How dare He treat them as if they belonged?

And so Jesus tells three parables about lost things—a sheep, a coin, a son. Each one is aimed directly at the accusers. Each one says: "You think you've found something? You think you're the ones who get to decide who belongs? Let me show you what God is doing."

In one brilliant stroke, Jesus reveals that the self-righteous are just as lost as the obvious sinners—perhaps even more so, because they don't know they need to be found.

So let's look at this story together.

---

**The Insult That Broke a Family**

Jesus begins: "There was a man who had two sons."

Right away, we're in a family story. And this is no ordinary family—the father is a man of wealth, a landowner with hired hands, with livestock, with enough to divide an inheritance. This is a family with reputation, with expectations, with a place in the community.

Then the younger son does the unthinkable. He says to his father, "Give me my share of the estate."

In that culture, this was devastating. What he was really saying was, "I wish you were dead. I can't wait for you to be gone so I can take what's mine and leave." He was telling his father, "Your presence is a burden. Your guidance is a cage. I want my inheritance now, while you're still alive, because I don't want anything from you except your money."

The village would have gasped. A father running? His robe hiked up, his dignity abandoned?

And the father—here's where the story turns astonishing—*gives it to them*. He divides his property between both sons. He doesn't argue. He doesn't refuse. He doesn't lecture. He lets them go.

Why? Not because he doesn't care. Because grace makes room for human freedom. God doesn't coerce love; He waits for it. He lets us go because love that is forced is not love at all.

So the younger son takes his inheritance—everything he has—and he leaves. He travels to a distant country, and there he squanders it. The text says he "wasted his possessions in prodigal living." He lives for pleasure, for self-gratification, for the moment. He has forgotten about tomorrow because today is so intoxicating.

And then, as it always does, the bottom falls out.

---

**The Pig Pen Where He Remembered**

A severe famine strikes the land. The younger son finds himself with nothing—no money, no friends, no prospects. He's so desperate that he takes a job feeding pigs. Now, for Jewish listeners, this would have been horrifying. Pigs were unclean animals. A Jew working with pigs was rock bottom. And even that job falls apart—the pigs' food looks better than what he has to eat.

There he is, in a pig pen, hungry, ashamed, alone. And something breaks open in him.

He comes to his senses.

Not just seeing his failure, but remembering his father's surprising generosity. Even in his rehearsed speech, there's a flicker of hope that his father might be different than he feared. His father's hired servants had more than enough to eat. What if his father was still that generous—even to a son who had squandered everything?

He comes to his senses and decides to go home. But notice what he plans: "I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired hands."

He's not expecting a feast. He's expecting to work. He's preparing for embarrassment, for a cold welcome, for the long road of making things right.

But here's what he doesn't know—he can't possibly know—his father has other plans.

---

**The Run That Restored a Son**

"So he got up and went to his father."

The son begins the long journey home. He's rehearsing his speech. He's preparing for the worst.

And then he looks up.

His father is coming toward him.

Not walking. Not striding. *Running*. In that culture, running was undignified for a man of standing. It was something servants did, not fathers. But this father runs, and when he reaches his son, he does something almost unthinkable: he embraces him. He throws his arms around him. He kisses him.

The son begins his prepared speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy—"

But the father isn't listening to the speech. The father cuts him off and calls to his servants: "Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let us eat and celebrate."

A feast. Not a lecture. Not a probation period. A feast.

"For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."

This feast was possible because another Son—long before this story was told—would bear the cost of our rebellion. The father could celebrate because the debt had been paid.

---

**The Brother Who Couldn't Enter the Joy**

But every party has a neighbor who isn't celebrating. The older son comes in from the field. He hears music and dancing. He asks what's happening. When he learns that his brother has returned, that his father has killed the fattened calf, he is filled with anger.

He won't go in.

The father comes out and pleads with him. And listen to what the older son says: "Look! All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours comes back—who squandered your property with prostitutes—you kill the fattened calf for him!"

Notice what he calls him: "this son of yours." He's already disowned his brother. Notice what he says about himself: "I've been slaving for you." He's never understood sonship. He's served, but he's never celebrated. He kept the rules, but he never trusted the father's heart.

The father responds with words that must have been hard to hear: "My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and found."

The older son was lost in his own way—lost in resentment, lost in self-righteousness, lost in the lie that obedience earns love. Both brothers needed the father's grace. Both brothers needed to be found.

---

I think of Sarah—a woman in our congregation who's been here for twenty years. She teaches Sunday school. She serves on committees. She never complains—or so she thought. Recently, she told me she can't stand watching new people get welcomed with such fanfare because she feels invisible. "I never left," she said. "Why does he throw a party for them and not for me?"

Sarah is the older son. And Jesus told this story for her.

---

**The Celebration That Never Ends**

So what is this story teaching us? It is about one thing: a father's unreasonable love. And that love does three things—it welcomes the rebel, it woos the rule-keeper, and it exposes the lie that there's not enough grace to go around.

Grace doesn't make us better than others; it makes us grateful for what we've received. The father had enough for both sons. There was always enough.

---

**Where Do You Find Yourself?**

Perhaps this morning, you identify with the younger son. You know what it's like to be far from God, to have squandered good years, to feel like you've wasted so much. Maybe your marriage is in trouble. Maybe you've made mistakes at work. Maybe you've been sitting in that casino parking lot at 2 AM, rehearsing how you'll explain yourself.

Let me tell you what the father says to you: Come home. Don't rehearse your apology. Don't try to earn your way back. The feast is ready. The father is watching the road. He is running toward you now.

Come home might mean walking through these doors next Sunday instead of watching online. It might mean texting that small group leader you've been avoiding. It might mean finally admitting you can't fix yourself.

Perhaps you identify with the older son. You've been faithful. You've stayed. You've done what's right. But somewhere along the way, you've lost the joy of being a child. You've started keeping score. You've looked at others and thought, "Why should they get what they don't deserve?"

Sister, Brother—if that's you—the father says to you: Everything I have is yours. Celebrate. Let go of the resentment. The feast is for you too.

It might mean volunteering to mentor that new believer you're tempted to resent. It might mean prayerfully asking God to soften your heart toward someone who doesn't deserve it.

And if the image of a running father is hard for you—if your own father never ran toward you—know that this father is different. He's been waiting for *you* specifically. This is not a grudging forgiveness; it is extravagant, unreasonable, running love.

---

**The Table That's Already Set**

Here's the最后一 thing I want you to see. The father didn't just throw a party that day. He lives in celebration. Every day, he watches the road. Every day, he hopes. Every day, he runs to meet the lost.

And that feast the father prepared? We eat it together at this table—not because we've earned it, but because He's already run to meet us. Every time we gather here, we proclaim that death is dead, that the lost is found, that the feast is ready.

So come home. Whatever you've done, wherever you've been, however far you feel—come home. The father is waiting. The father is running. The father is ready to embrace you.

And when you get there, you'll find the table is already set.

---

There's a story I want to share with you this morning—a story that might sound familiar, but one that never loses its power to surprise us. Not long ago, I read about a man named Richard. Richard was a successful businessman, a man who had built a comfortable life for himself and his family. But somewhere along the way, he had drifted far from the faith of his childhood. He hadn't abandoned it deliberately; it had just slowly faded, like a photograph left too long in the sun.

One winter evening, alone in a hotel room thousands of miles from home, Richard found himself unable to sleep. Something was missing—something he couldn't name. He turned on the television, and by chance, landed on a broadcast of a church service. The pastor was speaking about forgiveness, about a love that welcomes sinners home. Richard, a man who hadn't prayed in decades, found himself on his knees in that hotel room, weeping.

"I don't know if you're real," he said to God, "but if you are, I need you."

That was the beginning of Richard's journey back. And here's what strikes me: he didn't come home to a cold reception. He didn't have to earn his way back. He came home to arms flung wide, to a father who had been watching the road every single day, who had never stopped hoping.

This is the story Jesus tells in Luke chapter 15—the parable we call the Prodigal Son. But I wonder if we've heard it so often that we've forgotten just how radical it is.

Here's something we often miss: Jesus didn't tell this story in a vacuum. He told it to people who thought they had God all figured out. Luke tells us earlier in chapter 15 that "the tax collectors and sinners were all gathering around to hear Jesus. But the Pharisees and the teachers of the law muttered, 'This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.'" (Luke 15:1-2)

This parable is Jesus' response to that muttering. He's telling a story about a father running to embrace sinners—but He's also telling it to people who stood outside the party, arms crossed, certain they deserved better. That's important to remember as we look at the story together.

I think we sometimes read this and assume the father was harsh, that he simply gave up on his son. But I don't believe that's it at all. I believe he let them go because he understood something profound: love that is forced is not love. You cannot make someone stay. You cannot compel respect. You can only offer it and hope.

So the younger son takes his inheritance—everything he has—and he leaves. He travels to a distant country, and there he squanders it. The text says he "wasted his possessions in prodigal living." The word "prodigal" actually means "spending liberally, extravagantly, even recklessly." And that's exactly what he does. He lives for pleasure, for self-gratification, for the moment. He has forgotten about tomorrow because today is so intoxicating.

And then, as it always does, the bottom falls out.

Now, for Jewish listeners, this would have been horrifying. Pigs were unclean animals. A Jew working with pigs was rock bottom. He comes to his senses.

He sees that his father's hired hands have more than enough to eat while he starves. He sees that he has been a fool. He sees that he has wounded his father, betrayed his family, wasted his life. And he makes a decision.

"I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired hands."

Do you hear what's happening? The son is not coming home expecting a feast. He's coming home expecting to work. He's coming home with a rehearsed speech, a plan to earn back what he's lost. He wanted to earn back his place—to work for his father rather than rest as his son.

And here's what he doesn't know—he can't possibly know—his father has other plans.

---

**The Father Who Runs**

"So he got up and went to his father."

The son begins the long journey home. He's rehearsing his speech. He's preparing for embarrassment, for a cold welcome, for the long road of making things right.

And then he looks up.

His father is coming toward him.

Not walking. Not striding. *Running*. In that culture, running was undignified for a man of standing. It was something servants did, not fathers. And here's something we often forget: this feast cost the father. The best robe, the ring, the fattened calf—these weren't small expenditures. The father was spending *more* to celebrate his son's return than the son had wasted in his rebellion. That's the nature of grace: it's extravagant, even wasteful, never economical, always excessive.
