# The Waiting Father: A Sermon on the Parable of the Prodigal Son

**Luke 15:11-32**

---

## The Prodigal Son by Another Name

A few years ago, I came across a letter that a father had written to his estranged son. The father was in his seventies, and his son had not spoken to him in over a decade. The letter began simply: "Dear Michael, I don't know if you'll ever read this, but I wanted you to know that every morning, I wake up and look at your photograph. Every night, I pray that somehow, somewhere, you are okay. The door of this house has never been locked to you. Not once. Not ever."

There was no anger in the letter. No accusation. Only a father's ache—a heart that remained open despite years of silence and hurt.

When I read that letter, I thought of nothing so much as the father in Jesus' parable of the prodigal son. Here is a man whose son demanded his inheritance, squandered it in distant country, and then returned home. And what did the father do? He did not lecture. He did not hold a grudge. He did not even wait by the door—he ran to meet his boy.

Today, I want to preach to you about this extraordinary father, this rebellious son, and perhaps most challengingly, this elder brother. Because the truth is, we have all been one of them. And today, God invites us to stand in the warmth of a love we do not deserve.

---

## The Context of theparable

To understand this parable properly, we need to remember where Jesus told it and why.

In Luke 15, Jesus is being criticized by the religious leaders—the Pharisees and scribes—who are complaining that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them. These religious elites consider themselves righteous. They keep the rules. They have done nothing to deserve God's favor, they think, and yet here is Jesus, extending table fellowship to the very people the religious establishment despises.

So Jesus tells three parables: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. Each one is about something precious that was lost and then found. Each one is about extravagant joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.

The parable of the prodigal son is the longest and most developed of these three. And it contains within it a startling reversal: the ones who should have been most ready to welcome the returning sinner are actually the ones who stand apart, indignant and unwilling to celebrate.

As we walk through this passage together, I want us to see ourselves clearly—and to see the love of God even more clearly.

---

## The Younger Son: Lost and Found

Jesus says, "There was a man who had two sons." Right away, we have a setup that would have caught his original hearers' attention. In Jewish culture, the inheritance was clear: the elder son received a double portion, and the younger son received his share when the father died. For the younger son to demand his inheritance while his father was still alive was not merely rude—it was a kind of implicit wishing of death upon the father. It was a profound insult.

And yet the father *gave* it to him. He divided his property between them. This father, we must note, is no pushover. He is not naive. He knows what his son is doing. But he loves him enough to let him go.

The younger son takes his portion and travels to a distant country. The text says he "squandered his property in reckless living." The word *reckless* suggests something more than mere extravagance—it suggests a kind of willful destruction, as if the son were trying to erase himself, to become someone other than who he was.

And then comes the famine. Money runs out. The young man finds himself feeding pigs—a job so degrading for a Jewish man that the text almost doesn't name it directly. He is so hungry that he would have eaten the carob pods the pigs ate. No one gave him anything.

This is the moment of hitting rock bottom. And in that moment, something shifts. He comes to his senses. He remembers his father's hired workers, who have plenty to eat. He thinks: *I will arise and go to my father, and I will say, "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants."*

Notice what he plans to say. He does not expect forgiveness. He does not expect a feast. He expects to be taken back as a hired hand—someone who works for a living, who earns his keep. He has humbled himself, yes, but he still carries the weight of his own unworthiness.

And so he begins the journey home.

---

## The Father: Running Toward Us

Now here is the heart of the parable, the image that has moved believers for two thousand years.

*"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."*

I want you to sit with that image for a moment. A middle-aged father, in a culture that valued dignity and decorum, runs. He runs across the fields. He embraces his son. He kisses him. The text uses a word for *kiss* that suggests an emotional, tearful greeting—the kind of kiss a mother gives a child she thought she might never see again.

The father does not wait for the son's speech. He doesn't let him finish his rehearsed apology. The father is so overwhelmed with joy that he immediately begins ordering the celebration: the best robe, a ring for his finger, sandals for his feet, the fatted calf. Kill it. Let us eat and celebrate.

For this son was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.

But wait—there's more. The father does something else remarkable. He goes out to his older son and begs him to come to the feast. The older son is standing outside, refusing to go in. He is angry. He has served his father all these years, never disobeyed a command, and yet his father never gave him even a young goat to celebrate with his friends. But now his brother returns—the brother who squandered his fortune with prostitutes—and the father kills the fatted calf for *him*.

This is where the parable gets uncomfortable. Because the father does not defend himself. He does not argue with the older son. He simply says: *"Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."*

---

## The Older Son: Lost Without Knowing It

We must be careful here not to simply dismiss the older son as the villain of the story. He is not simply wicked. He is, in many ways, the tragic figure. He has done everything right. He has worked hard. He has been faithful. And yet he has missed the deepest truth: that his father's love was always already his.

The older son is lost in a different way. He is lost in his sense of entitlement, in his transactional relationship with his father. He serves, but he does not love. He obeys, but he does not trust. When his brother returns, he does not rejoice. He complains. He judges. He stands outside the celebration.

And the father—listen to this—the father does not condemn him. He does not disinherit him. He goes out and pleads with him. Even now, even in this moment of his son's coldness and anger, the father extends grace.

This is the heart of God. This is the scandal of the gospel: that God welcomes the prodigal and pleads with the self-righteous. That there is room at the table for both. That the father runs to meet us—whether we come with our tails between our legs like the younger son, or whether we stand outside, refusing to come in, like the older son.

---

## Application: Which Son Are You?

Now I want to speak directly to you, because this parable is not merely a story about someone else. It is a mirror.

Maybe you are the younger son today. Maybe you have wandered far from God. Maybe you have made choices you are ashamed of. Maybe you have been living in the far country, chasing things that promised fulfillment but left you empty. Maybe you are feeding pigs right now—doing things you never thought you would do, in a place you never thought you would be.

Let me tell you what the father wants you to know: *He sees you.* Even now, while you are still a long way off, he sees you. And he is running toward you. Not to lecture you. Not to make you prove yourself. Just to hold you. Just to bring you home. The fatted calf is already being prepared. The ring is already on the finger. The robe is already waiting.

You do not have to earn your way back. You simply have to come home.

Maybe, though, you are the older son. Maybe you have been faithful. Maybe you have served God for years. Maybe you look at others—those who have fallen into sin, those who have made messes of their lives—and you feel something closer to contempt than compassion. You have kept the rules. You have done what was expected. And secretly, you wonder why God seems to welcome *them* more than he seems to appreciate *you*.

If that is you, I want to speak a hard but loving word: you have missed the point. The father's love is not a wage to be earned; it is a gift to be received. The celebration is not about the younger son's deserving it—it is about the father's joy in having him back. And your brother—yes, even your wayward brother—belongs to the father too.

The father pleads with you: *Come inside. Celebrate. He was dead and is alive again.*

---

## The Invitation to the Feast

And maybe, finally, you are the father. Maybe you are a parent, looking at a child who has wandered. Maybe you are a friend, waiting for someone who has hurt you. Maybe you are a pastor, looking out at a congregation of broken people who keep failing and keep returning.

The call of this parable is to become like the father: to run toward the lost, to welcome the wandering, to celebrate even when we do not understand, to keep the door open even when we have been hurt.

This is the heart of God. This is the love of Christ, who left the ninety-nine to find the one, who eats with sinners, who dies for the ungodly, who runs to meet us on the road.

The question is not whether you deserve this love. You don't. None of us do. The question is whether you will receive it. Whether you will stop trying to earn it and simply accept it. Whether you will let the father embrace you, clothe you, feast with you.

---

## A Prayer for the Journey Home

Let us pray.

*Father, we confess that we have wandered. We have gone to distant countries, chasing things that could never satisfy. We have stood outside your feast, bitter and self-righteous, judging others while thinking ourselves worthy. We have been lost, and we have not known it.*

*But you see us. You run to meet us. You embrace us. You kiss us with tears of joy.*

*Help us to receive your love—not as something we have earned, but as a gift beyond all imagining. Help us to welcome others as you have welcomed us. Help us to celebrate when the lost are found.*

*For we were dead, and now we are alive. We were lost, and now we are found.*

*Amen.*

## Luke 15:11-32

---

There is a story I want to share with you this morning. It's a story about a young man—let's call him Michael. Michael grew up in a good home. His father was loving, his family was stable, and he had every opportunity a young person could want. But somewhere along the way, Michael became convinced that the grass would be greener on the other side of his father's fence. He looked at his father's rules and felt them as chains. He looked at his inheritance—not yet received, but promised—and decided he wanted it now, on his terms, without the responsibility of belonging to the family.

So one day, Michael went to his father and said something that must have felt like a knife through the old man's heart. He said, "Give me my share of the inheritance." In that culture, what he was really saying was this: "I wish you were dead. I want my money now. I want out."

And the father—can you imagine the grief?—did not argue. Did not refuse. Did not lecture. He divided the property between his two sons, and within days, Michael was gone, headed for a distant country, wallet full of cash and heart full of dreams.

We know how that story ends. Or at least, we think we do. Because the Parable of the Prodigal Son is so familiar that we might think there's nothing left to discover. But I want to suggest to you this morning that we've perhaps sanitized this story, made it safe, when it was meant to be scandalous. So let's go back to the text together and let it surprise us again.

---

**The Journey Away**

Look at verse 13: "Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living."

A far country. That's what sin always is—a journey into a far country. It starts with distance, small distances at first, then greater ones. The younger son didn't leave his father because he hated him; he left because he wanted independence, freedom, excitement. He wanted to live life on his own terms.

And for a while, it worked. The text tells us he squandered his property in "reckless living." The original Greek word here is *asōtōs*—it means living without any restraint, wasting resources on pleasures that can never satisfy. We've all met people like this, haven't we? People who chase every new experience, every new thrill, convinced that the next thing will finally fill the emptiness.

And then the famine came. Isn't that always how it works? The good times don't last. The money runs out. The friends disappear. And suddenly, this young man who left home because he wanted freedom finds himself in a pig pen—literally, feeding pigs, which for a Jewish listener would have been the lowest of the low, the most degrading work imaginable—and he's so hungry that he's envious of the pigs' food.

This is rock bottom. This is the far country. This is what happens when we try to live without God.

And here's where the story could end. It could end in despair. It could end in that pig pen, alone, hungry, forgotten. That's where sin always leads.

---

**The Journey Back**

But look at verse 17: "When he came to himself."

That's a remarkable phrase. It suggests a kind of waking up—a moment of clarity. And what did he realize? He said, "How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!"

He'd been gone for months, maybe years. He'd wasted everything. He'd broken his father's heart. And yet, what he remembered was not his father's rules or his father's discipline. He remembered the bread. The abundance. The love.

I wonder how many of us have been in that place—some far country of our own making—where we finally "came to ourselves" and remembered that there is a Father waiting for us. Maybe it's a marriage that fell apart. Maybe it's an addiction that caught up with us. Maybe it's just the slow realization that the things we chased don't satisfy.

And so the young man decides to go back. But notice what he plans to say: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants."

Do you see what he's planning? He's planning to come back, but on his terms. Not as a son—he knows he doesn't deserve that—but as a hired worker. He's going to earn his way back. He's going to prove himself.

Isn't that so like us? We sin, we stray, and then we try to fix things ourselves. We make promises. We rededicate ourselves. We try to earn back what we've lost. We think that if we work hard enough, behave well enough, maybe God will accept us.

But that's not what happens.

---

Look at verse 20: "And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and had compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him."

Stop right there. The father *ran*.

In that culture, running was considered undignified. It was something that only servants and slaves did. A respectable elder did not run. But this father ran. He saw his son while he was still a long way off—which means he was watching. Every day, perhaps, he was watching the road, waiting, hoping.

# The Endless Embrace: A Sermon on the Prodigal Son

*Luke 15:11-32*

---

## The Welcome We Long For

Let me begin with a story that may sound familiar to some of you.

There was a man—we'll call him David—who hadn't spoken to his father in seven years. A disagreement over life choices had escalated into silence, then into bitterness, and finally into something that felt permanent. David moved across the country. He built a new life. He told himself he was better off. But every year, around the holidays, something would twist in his chest. He'd see a father and son together at a restaurant, or receive a friend's photo of a family gathering, and he'd feel the weight of what he'd lost.

One Thanksgiving, something broke open in him. He bought a plane ticket home. He didn't call ahead. He showed up at his father's door, expecting—what? A lecture? Cold silence? The cold shoulder he deserved for all those years of silence?

His father opened the door. For a moment, they just looked at each other. Then his father did something David never expected: he pulled him into his arms and held him tight, and he started to cry. Not a word about the past. Not a single accusation. Just拥抱—just the embrace of a father who had been waiting, hoping, longing for his son to come home.

David would later say it was the first time he understood what grace meant.

Today, we turn to one of the most famous passages in all of Scripture: the parable of the prodigal son. It's a story so familiar that it can feel worn, like a favorite blanket we've had since childhood. But I want to suggest that we've barely scratched the surface of its depth. There's a reason Jesus told this parable. There's a reason it has echoed through two millennia of human longing. And there's a reason it still has the power to crack open our hearts today.

Let's look at it together.

---

## The Context of the Parable

To understand what Jesus is doing here, we need to see where this parable fits in Luke's Gospel. In chapter 15, Jesus is being criticized by the religious leaders—the Pharisees and scribes—for welcoming sinners and eating with them. They were grumbling, Luke tells us, saying, "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them."

In response, Jesus tells three parables: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. Each one makes the same essential point: when something precious is lost, there is joy in finding it. Heaven rejoices. And Jesus, the shepherd leaving the ninety-nine, the woman searching every corner of her home, the father watching the road—Jesus is the one who celebrates.

The parable of the prodigal Son is the climax of this trilogy. It's the most detailed, the most emotionally rich, and the most challenging. It doesn't just teach us about God's love—it shows us God's love in Technicolor.

---

## The Journey Away

Jesus begins: "There was a man who had two sons."

The younger son comes to his father with a request that would have been shocking in that culture. He says, "Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me." In other words: "I want my inheritance. Now. I want you to treat me as though you're already dead."

This was a profound insult. The younger son was essentially saying, "I can't wait for you to die. I want what's mine, and I want it now. I don't want you—I want your stuff."

And here's the remarkable thing: the father gives it to him. He doesn't refuse. He doesn't lecture. He doesn't hold on tightly to what he has. He lets his son go.

I wonder how that felt for the father. Can you imagine the pain of watching your child walk away? The father knew—this is a son who doesn't understand what he has. He's about to learn the hard way. But he lets him go anyway.

So the younger son takes his inheritance, travels to a distant country, and there he squanders it in reckless living. The text says he "wasted" his possessions in "dissolute living." He lives wildly, carelessly, as if tomorrow doesn't matter.

And then the famine comes. The money is gone. The friends disappear. He's left feeding pigs—an especially degrading job for a Jewish man, since pigs were considered unclean. He's so desperate that he longs to eat what the pigs eat. No one will help him.

This is the bottom. This is what happens when we run from God, when we chase after our own desires, when we think we know better than the Father who loves us. We end up in the pit, hungry, alone, with nothing.

---

## The Return

But then something happens. The text says he "came to himself." That's a beautiful phrase. In his desperation, he wakes up. He remembers. He thinks of his father—maybe for the first time, he truly thinks of him.

And he makes a decision. He'll go back. Not as a son—as a hired hand. He doesn't deserve to be called a son anymore. He knows that. He's prepared to ask for forgiveness, to take the lowest place, to work for wages like any other servant.

So he begins the journey home. This is the turning point. This is what the whole parable has been building toward.

Now watch what happens when the father sees him. The text says: "While he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion for him. He ran and embraced him and kissed him."

Let me pause on this image. The father would have been wearing a long robe—the kind that made running difficult, the kind that announced his dignity and status. But he runs. He abandons propriety. He runs to his son, throws his arms around him, and kisses him.

This is not the response of a wounded parent who has been waiting to say, "I told you so." This is not the response of someone keeping score. This is the response of pure, extravagant, overwhelming love.

The son begins his rehearsed confession: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son."

But the father isn't interested in the confession. He's interested in the son. He doesn't let him finish. He calls his servants—everyone in the household—and he says: "Bring quickly the best robe, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate."

A feast. A celebration. The fatted calf—the best they have—is killed for this son who squandered everything.

---

## The Elder Brother

But here's where the parable takes a turn that often catches us off guard. The older brother is in the field. He comes home and hears music and dancing. He asks what's happening and learns that his brother has returned.

And what does he do? He refuses to go in. He won't celebrate. He's angry.

Now, think about this. On the surface, the older brother seems like the good guy, right? He stayed. He worked. He was faithful. He didn't run off and waste the family's money. He has every right to feel... what? Betrayed? Disrespected? Treated unfairly?

But Jesus isn't finished with him. The father comes out and pleads with him: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found."

And the older brother's response? He's indignant. He says, "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"

Do you hear what's happening here? The older brother is keeping score. He's been计算 his obedience like a ledger, waiting for his reward. And now he's furious that the father would show such grace to someone who doesn't deserve it. He's not celebrating. He's holding onto his resentment, his sense of fairness, his right to be angry.

And the father—the same father who ran to embrace the prodigal—responds with the same grace. He says, "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours."

---

## What This Means for Us

So what is Jesus saying to us today?

First, if you have ever felt like the prodigal son—if you have ever walked away from God, from your family, from the place where you belonged—this parable is for you. It tells you that there is a father who is watching the road, waiting, longing for you to come home. Not to lecture you. Not to make you pay. But to embrace you, to put a ring on your finger, to throw a feast.

The journey home may feel impossible. You may think you've gone too far, wasted too much, burned too many bridges. But the father is not interested in your past. He's interested in you. His arms are open. His love is greater than your shame.

Second, maybe you've never felt like the prodigal. Maybe you've been the older brother. You've stayed faithful. You've done what's right. And you look around at others—others who seem to have walked away from everything, who seem to have squandered their gifts, who seem to have no right to be welcomed—and you feel... what? Resentment? Judgment? The sense that it's not fair?

The parable challenges us, doesn't it? Because the father's love is not a pie. It doesn't run out. The celebration of one son does not diminish the inheritance of another. In fact, the father says, "All that is mine is yours." The older brother already has everything. The feast is not a threat—it's a gift he can join in celebrating.

And here's the hard question: Are you willing to celebrate when someone who doesn't deserve it receives grace? Are you willing to run to the embrace instead of standing outside, angry and indignant?

Third, this parable tells us something about the heart of God. The father in this story is not a distant figure, waiting to judge. He's not keeping a record of wrongs. He's not calculating whether you've been good enough. He's running toward you. He's holding you. He's calling for the feast.

This is who God is. This is what Jesus came to show us.

---

## The Road Home

There is one more detail I want to leave you with. The younger son came home planning to say, "Make me as one of your hired servants." He expected to earn back his place. He expected a contract: you do this, and then maybe, over time, you can regain what you lost.

But the father doesn't make him a servant. He makes him a son. He puts the robe on him. The ring on his finger. The shoes on his feet. Full restoration. Complete acceptance. Not because the son earned it—but because that's who the father is.

That's grace. That's the gospel. Not "I'll love you if you change." But "I'll love you, and through my love, you will change."

---

## An Invitation

So I want to invite you today, whoever you are, wherever you've been, whatever you've done, to come home.

Maybe you left years ago. Maybe you left yesterday. Maybe you've been standing in the far country, staring at the ground, too ashamed to look up. Maybe you've been the older brother, refusing to join the feast, nursing your resentment in the field.

The father sees you. The father loves you. The father is running toward you.

Will you let him embrace you?

Will you come home?

---

*The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the Lord lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.*

# The Welcome That Never Ends

## A Sermon on the Parable of the Prodigal Son

---

I want to begin with a story. A few years ago, I read about a man named Richard\—not his real name\—who had been estranged from his family for over twenty years. He had left home in his early twenties, burned every bridge, made choices that wounded everyone who loved him. His parents had died during his absence. His siblings had moved on, building lives that didn't include him. He had become, in every sense, a ghost to his own family.

Then one Christmas Eve, Richard showed up at his brother's door. He had nowhere else to go. He was broke, homeless, carrying two decades of regret like a millstone around his neck. He expected anger. He expected to be turned away. He expected, at best, a cold welcome and a borrowed couch.

What happened instead was this: his brother saw him standing there, and before Richard could say a word, he was wrapped in an embrace so fierce it knocked the breath out of him. His sister-in-law was crying. His niece and nephew were staring wide-eyed. And his brother kept saying, over and over: "I thought you were dead. I thought you were dead."

They brought him inside. They fed him. They gave him a bed. And that night, as Richard lay in the spare room of his brother's house, he wept in a way he hadn't wept in years.

Friends, that story sounds remarkably familiar, doesn't it? It sounds like a story we've heard before. Because it is a story we've heard before\—told two thousand years ago by a rabbi named Jesus, in a field somewhere in Galilee, to a crowd of tax collectors and sinners, and to a group of religious leaders who were thoroughly scandalized by the company he kept.

Turn with me, please, to Luke chapter 15, and let's hear this parable together. I'm going to read from the familiar King James translation, because there's a music to these words that has echoed through the centuries:

> **Luke 15:11-32** — And he said, A certain man had two sons: And the younger of them said to his father, Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth to me. And he divided unto them his living. And not many days after, the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living. And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want. And he went and joined himself to a citizen of that country; and he sent him into his fields to feed swine. And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him. And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants. And the son said unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son. But the father said to his servants, Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet: And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry: For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.
>
> Now his elder son was in the field: and as he came and drew nigh to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants, and asked what these things meant. And he said unto him, Thy brother is come; and thy father hath killed the fatted calf, because he hath received him safe and sound. And he was angry, and would not go in: therefore came his father out, and entreated him. And he answering said to his father, Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment: and yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends: But when this thy son came, who hath devoured thy living with harlots, thou hast killed for him the fatted calf.
>
> And he said unto him, Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine. It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found.

---

This is, without question, one of the most beloved passages in all of Scripture. It is the story we tell children. It is the image we carry in our minds when we think of God's love. It is, for many of us, the very heart of the gospel.

But I want to suggest this morning that we have sometimes domesticated this parable\—softened its edges, made it comfortable, reduced it to a simple story about forgiveness. And in doing so, we have missed some of its most radical, most challenging, most life-giving truths.

So let us look at this text together, not as a familiar story we've heard a hundred times, but as a word from God that has the power to reorder our lives.

---

**First, let us look at the younger son.**

We know this story well. The younger son asks for his inheritance\—which is essentially saying, "Father, I wish you were dead." In Jewish culture, to demand your portion before your father's death was an act of profound disrespect, even shame. But the father, remarkably, does not refuse. He gives his son what he asks for.

And the son goes off. He goes to a far country\—the text emphasizes this: a *far* country, far from home, far from his father, far from everything he knows. And there he wastes his substance. The word used here is *diaskorpisao*\—it means to scatter, to disperse, to squander utterly. He doesn't just spend money; he destroys it. He destroys himself.

And then comes the famine. And the hunger. And the degradation\—feeding pigs, the most unclean animal in Jewish culture. He is so desperate that he longs to eat the food given to swine. His situation is as low as low can be.

And it is here, in the pit, that he "comes to himself." This is a remarkable phrase. It suggests that being away from his father had been a kind of madness, a dissociation from his own identity. And now, in his want, he remembers. He remembers who his father is. He remembers the abundance that awaits him at home. He remembers that even the hired servants there have enough.

And so he makes a plan. He will return. Not as a son\—he knows he can't expect that. But as a hired servant. He will earn his keep. He will repay what he owes. He has, at least, his dignity.

But friends, listen: that is not what happens. That is not what happens at all.

---

**Now let us look at the father.**

Because the father is the heart of this parable. And what the father does is almost incomprehensible.

The son is still *a great way off*. He hasn't even arrived. He hasn't made his speech. He hasn't begged for forgiveness. He hasn't promised to work. He is still walking up the road, rehearsing his humble speech, preparing to throw himself on his father's mercy.

But the father *sees him*.

And what does he do? He *runs*.

Now in first-century Palestine, this was extraordinary. Men of status did not run. It was undignified. It was shameful. The long robes that wealthy men wore would have been a hindrance to running. But the father doesn't care about dignity. He doesn't care about propriety. He runs to his son, and he embraces him, and he kisses him.

And the son begins his speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before thee. I am no more worthy to be called thy son."

But the father doesn't let him finish. He doesn't let him become a hired servant. He interrupts. He calls for the best robe\—the family inheritance. He calls for the ring\—the sign of authority, of sonship. He calls for shoes\—the mark of a free person, not a slave. And he calls for the fatted calf\—the feast of feasts, reserved for the most special occasions.

And then he says the words that have echoed through the centuries: "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found."

Do you hear what the father is saying? He is not grateful that his son came home as a servant. He is not satisfied with partial restoration. He restores his son completely, fully, lavishly. The son's sin is not mentioned again. It is not held over him. It is forgiven and forgotten, buried in the depths of the father's love.

This is the gospel, friends. This is what God does. Not a grudging acceptance. Not a conditional welcome. But a *running* embrace. A feast. A ring. A robe. Complete restoration.

---

**Now let us look at the older son.**

Because here is where this parable becomes uncomfortable. Because the older son is not some villain we are meant to despise. The older son is us. The older son is you. The older son is me.

The older son has done everything right. He has served faithfully. He has obeyed. He has never transgressed. And what does he get? A lecture about generosity. A reminder that everything the father has is already his. And a brother who is welcomed home with more fanfare than he has ever received.

And he is *angry*.

He won't go in. He stands outside, refusing to participate in the feast. And when his father comes out and entreats him, his response is bitter: "These many years I have served thee. I have never transgressed thy commandments. And thou never gavest me a kid to make merry with my friends. But when this thy son came\—"

Notice how he says it: "*this thy son*." Not "my brother." Not "the one who was lost." "This thy son." He has already excluded him. He has already decided he does not belong.

And the father's response is beautiful in its patience: "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine."

You see, the older son had misunderstood everything. He thought obedience was a transaction. He thought his good behavior earned him something. He thought love was something to be earned and measured and balanced against the love shown to others.

But the father is saying: "Everything I have is already yours. You don't need to earn it. You don't need to compete for it. The feast is not a reward for your service; it is the family reality you have always lived in. And your brother\—your brother was lost, and now he is found. Can you not rejoice?"

---

**So what does this mean for us?**

This parable speaks to everyone in this room this morning. It speaks to those of you who feel far away. Those of you who have made mistakes, burnt bridges, wasted years on pursuits that left you empty. Those of you who think you have gone too far, fallen too hard, been gone too long. To you, this parable says: *Your father sees you. Even now, even far off, even before you have made it to the road. He is running toward you. Come home.*

But it also speaks to those of you who have stayed. Who have been faithful. Who have worked hard and done right and wondering why it seems like the ones who messed up their lives get all the attention, all the grace, all the celebration. To you, this parable says: *Your place in the family was never in doubt. Your father's love for you was never conditional. And the question is not whether you will get what you deserve\—the question is whether you can welcome home those who don't deserve it as much as you do.*

Because here is the hard truth: the father in this story loves both sons. He runs to embrace the one who was lost. He goes out to plead with the one who is angry. His heart is big enough for both. But the story ends with a question, not an answer: *Will the older son go in to the feast?*

Will we?

---

**A closing invitation**

I want to end with this: the Prodigal Son is not really about sons. It is about a Father. A Father whose love is so vast, so extravagant, so unconditional, that it defies every instinct we have about fairness and merit and earning.

And the question this parable asks us is not "Are you more like the younger son or the older son?" The question it asks is: *Do you believe that this is what your Father is like?*

Because if you do\—if you truly believe that God runs to embrace you, that he clothes you in righteousness, that he throws a feast over your return\—then something changes. Then you can stop earning. Then you can stop competing. Then you can extend to others the same welcome that has been extended to you.

And that, friends, is the kingdom of God. A place where the lost are found. A place where the feast never ends. A place where the father's love is always, always running toward us.

Thanks be to God.

Amen.

# The Waiting Father: A Sermon on the Prodigal Son

**Luke 15:11-32**

---

## The Invitation to Come Home

I want to begin with a story that a friend of mine told me years ago. He was a airline pilot—retired now—but when he was still flying, he told me about a flight he crewed from New York to Los Angeles. About halfway through the flight, a woman came to the cockpit door. She was visibly distressed. She told him that she hadn't spoken to her son in seven years. He'd left home angry, they'd had a terrible fight, and neither one had reached out. She was flying to California to see her brother, but she'd just learned that her son lived in Los Angeles now. She had the address. She didn't know what to do.

My friend listened. Then he said something that surprised her. He said, "Ma'am, you have a window of opportunity here. Life is short. What do you want to have happen?"

She sat in the cockpit for a long time, talking and crying. When the plane landed, she took a taxi to her son's apartment. She didn't know what she would say. She just went.

I don't know the whole rest of that story. But I know this: she got off that plane with a choice. She could have continued to California to see her brother, letting the estrangement continue. Or she could go to her son. She chose to go.

This morning, I want to talk to you about a father who is always waiting, always running, always ready to throw a party—and about the invitation we all have to come home.

---

## The Text

Turn with me, please, to Luke chapter 15. We're looking at verses 11 through 32—the familiar parable of the prodigal son. If you have a Bible, I'd invite you to follow along as I read:

> And he said, "There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, 'Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.' And he divided his living between them. Not many days later, the younger son gathered everything together and went on a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living. And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.
>
> But when he came to himself, he said, 'How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants."' And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. And the son said to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight, and am no longer worthy to be called your son.' But the father said to his servants, 'Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.' And they began to celebrate.
>
> Now the older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And so he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, 'Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.' But he became angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him, but he answered his father, 'Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!' And he said to him, 'Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.'"

This is the Word of the Lord.

---

## The Journey Away

Let me invite you to notice something about this story that we might otherwise miss. When the younger son asks for his inheritance, he's essentially saying to his father, "I wish you were dead." In first-century Jewish culture, asking for your share of the inheritance while your father was still alive was deeply insulting—it was a rejection of the family, an announcement that you couldn't wait to be done with this household. The father could have refused. The father could have punished him. But instead, the text tells us simply that he divided his living between them.

And off the younger son goes. He travels to a far country—Luke uses a phrase that suggests distance, alienation, spiritual emptiness. And he squanders everything. The Greek word here is *diaskorpidzo*, which means to scatter, to disperse, to waste completely. He lives recklessly. And then the famine comes.

Now I want you to picture this young man. He's hit rock bottom. He's feeding pigs—an abomination for a Jewish listener. And he's so hungry that he longs to eat the pods that the pigs eat. Can you imagine? This is a picture of complete desperation. He has lost everything—his money, his dignity, his identity, his hope.

And it's in this moment—lying in the mud, hungry, ashamed—that he "comes to himself."

---

## Coming to Himself

That phrase is so important. *He came to himself.* What does that mean? It means that there was a moment when he realized where he was and how far he'd fallen. It means that somewhere, somehow, a memory surfaced—the memory of his father's house, of abundance, of being known and loved.

And here's what strikes me: the son's plan, when he comes to himself, is not really a plan of faith. He's going to return, yes, but he's going to return as a hired servant. "Treat me as one of your hired servants." He doesn't expect forgiveness. He doesn't expect a party. He expects to earn back what he lost.

But his father has something else in mind entirely.

---

## The Running Father

Now we come to one of the most beautiful images in all of Scripture: the father sees his son while he is still a long way off, and he runs to him.

Let me just pause here and let this sink in. In first-century Palestinian culture, it was inappropriate for a man of status—a landowner, an elder—to run. Running was considered undignified. But this father runs. He runs because he sees his son. He runs because his heart is broken. He runs because he's been waiting, every day, watching the road.

And when he reaches his son, what does he do? He embraces him and kisses him. The Greek word for "kissed" here is in the imperfect tense—it suggests repeated, fervent kissing. This father is holding his son, kissing him again and again, not letting go.

And before the son can even finish his rehearsed speech—"Father, I have sinned... treat me as a hired servant"—the father is already giving orders. Bring the best robe. Put a ring on his hand. Shoes on his feet. Kill the fattened calf. Celebrate.

This is not forgiveness as mere words. This is forgiveness as lavish, extravagant, excessive love.

---

## The Brother Who Stayed

Now we come to the second half of the parable, and this is where things get uncomfortable. Because the older brother—he's been working in the field all day. He comes home and hears the music and dancing. He asks what's going on. And when he finds out—his brother has come home, his father has killed the fattened calf—he becomes angry. He refuses to go in.

And listen to what he says to his father: "Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!"

This is remarkable. The older brother is angry because he has never been celebrated. He's kept the rules. He's done everything right. And yet his father has never thrown him a party. Meanwhile, his brother—his wasteful, sinful, rebellious brother—gets the fatted calf.

Now, let's be honest: don't we know this feeling? Haven't we all, at some point, looked at someone else's forgiveness or blessing and thought, "What about me? I've been faithful. I've stayed. Why do they get the party?"

This is the danger of the older brother's heart. He has never left. He's been in the father's house all along. But he's been there with a ledger. He's been keeping track. And when grace is given to someone who doesn't deserve it, he can't stomach it.

---

## The Heart of the Father

And what does the father do? He comes out again—leaving the celebration to go to his angry son. He entreats him. He says, "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours."

Notice: the father doesn't say, "You're right, he doesn't deserve this." He doesn't diminish the son's sin. He doesn't apologize for showing grace. He simply says: "Everything I have is yours. And it was fitting to celebrate, because your brother was dead and is alive again."

The father's heart is big enough to hold both sons. He runs to the one who returns, and he goes out to the one who refuses to come in. He is grieved by the one who is lost, and he longs for the one who is angry.

This is the heart of God.

---

## For You Today

So what do we do with this parable? I want to suggest three ways it speaks to us today.

**First, maybe you are the younger son.** Maybe you've gone to a far country. Maybe you've squandered things that mattered—your integrity, your relationships, your faith. Maybe you're lying in the mud right now, wondering if there's any way back. Let me tell you: there is. The father is watching the road. He is waiting for you. Not as a hired servant—as a son. He wants to throw a party. Come home.

**Second, maybe you are the older brother.** Maybe you've never left. Maybe you've been faithful. Maybe you've kept the rules. But maybe there's someone in your life—someone who has made mistakes, someone who has failed, someone you think doesn't deserve grace—and you've been keeping a record. You've been standing outside the party, angry. Let me tell you: God's heart is bigger than yours. His grace is not a pie with limited slices. When the lost are found, there is always reason to celebrate.

**Third, maybe you are the father.** Maybe you have someone in your life who has walked away. Maybe you're waiting, watching, hoping. Maybe it's a child, a parent, a friend. The father in this story models something for us: relentless love. Not passive hope, but active waiting. Running. Embracing. Celebrating. Perhaps God is calling you to be the one who goes first, who extends grace, who keeps the door open.

---

## The Invitation

There is a phrase that the father uses in this story that I want to leave you with. When the older brother complains, the father says simply: "It was fitting to celebrate."

It was fitting. It was right. It was appropriate. It was the thing to do.

You know what that means? It means that whenever a lost person is found, whenever a broken person is restored, whenever someone comes home—it is always, always the right time to celebrate. Not because sin doesn't matter. Not because rebellion is harmless. But because love is stronger. Because grace is greater. Because the father is always waiting.

And so I want to invite you this morning—not to do something complicated, but simply to come home. Whatever far country you have traveled to, whatever you have squandered, whatever has left you hungry and ashamed—the father sees you. He is running toward you. He wants to put a ring on your finger and shoes on your feet and throw a party in your name.

Will you let him?

Let us pray.

---

*Father, we thank you that you are a waiting God—a God who runs toward us when we are still far off. Forgive us for the times we have wandered, and forgive us for the times we have resented your grace extended to others. Teach us to celebrate when the lost are found. Teach us to love with open arms. And thank you, Father, that your love is never finished, never exhausted, never too late. In Jesus' name, amen.*

# Detailed Feedback: "Coming Home: The Father Who Runs"

This is an exceptionally well-crafted sermon. It demonstrates genuine homiletical skill across nearly every dimension — theological depth, rhetorical control, pastoral sensitivity, and structural elegance. What follows is a thorough assessment of both its considerable strengths and the relatively few areas where revision could sharpen it further.

---

## 1. Theological Accuracy and Depth of Scriptural Engagement

### Strengths

The exegesis is careful, culturally informed, and consistently tethered to the text without becoming academic. Several moments stand out as particularly strong.

**The cultural weight of the inheritance request** is handled expertly. The line "You are worth more to me as a corpse than as a father" is theologically precise and rhetorically devastating. It communicates what scholars like Kenneth Bailey have spent chapters explaining, and it does so in a single sentence a twelve-year-old could understand.

**The Greek word study is well-deployed.** You use *asōtōs*, *esplanchnisthē*, and the iterative force of the kissing verb without turning the sermon into a linguistics lecture. Each Greek term earns its place by unlocking emotional and theological meaning the English alone cannot carry. The explanation of *esplanchnisthē* as visceral, gut-level compassion — and the connection to Jesus' own compassion elsewhere in the Gospels — is particularly effective because it quietly makes a Christological point without belaboring it: the Father's compassion and Jesus' compassion are the same compassion.

**The symbolic reading of robe, ring, and sandals** is accurate and well-paced. You correctly identify the robe as the father's own, the ring as a signet of authority, and the sandals as the marker distinguishing son from slave. This is strong exegesis presented as narrative momentum rather than footnoted commentary.

**The framing within Luke 15's larger context** is essential and well-handled. You rightly note that this is the third in a trilogy of parables provoked by the Pharisees' grumbling, which gives the older-son section its proper polemical edge.

**The ambiguity of the younger son's repentance** is one of the sermon's most theologically sophisticated moves. "Is this genuine contrition, or is it a survival strategy? Is he truly sorry, or is he just hungry?" This is honest, pastorally brave, and exegetically defensible. The conclusion you draw — that God does not wait for pure motives — is profoundly grace-centered and avoids the trap of either cheapening repentance or making it a meritorious work.

### Areas for Improvement

**The Christological connection arrives very late and somewhat briefly.** The line "in Jesus Christ, hitched up his robes and ran toward us — all the way to a cross" is beautiful and powerful, but it is doing an enormous amount of theological work in a single sentence near the sermon's end. The parable is, after all, told *by* Jesus *about* the Father, and the incarnation is the ultimate enactment of the Father running toward the far country. Consider developing this connection earlier or more fully. One option: when discussing the father's willingness to absorb shame by running, you could note that this self-humiliation foreshadows the cross, where God absorbs not just social shame but the full weight of human sin. This would give the sermon a stronger Christological spine without turning it into a systematic theology lecture.

**The theology of the father "letting go" could use a brief qualifier.** You write, "Love that coerces is not love. The father's grief must have been immense, but he opens his hand and lets his son go." This is a beautiful and largely sound pastoral statement, but it could be read as endorsing a purely libertarian free-will theology that some in your congregation might find theologically thin. You don't need to resolve the tension between divine sovereignty and human freedom in a sermon, but a single clause acknowledging the mystery — something like "and we could spend a lifetime trying to understand why God permits what God grieves" — would add theological texture without derailing the narrative.

**The open ending of the parable deserves slightly more theological weight.** You note that we never learn whether the older son goes inside, and you correctly observe that Jesus leaves this unresolved. But you could press harder on *why* this is theologically significant. The open ending is not just a narrative technique; it is an *invitation*. Jesus is not merely describing the Pharisees' situation — he is actively calling them in. The parable itself enacts the father coming outside. This would deepen the already strong point you are making.

**One minor exegetical note:** You say the father "divides his property between his two sons." Luke 15:12 does say this, and you are right to note it, but it is worth observing that this means the older son has *already received* his share — which makes his later complaint about never receiving "even a young goat" not just bitter but factually wrong. This small detail would sharpen your portrait of the older son's distorted self-perception.

---

## 2. Rhetorical Effectiveness and Persuasive Structure

### Strengths

The rhetorical architecture of this sermon is remarkably assured. Several structural choices deserve specific praise.

**The title works on multiple levels.** "Coming Home: The Father Who Runs" immediately reframes the parable away from the son and toward the father, which is your central interpretive move. The subtitle creates a productive tension — fathers, in this culture, do not run — that the sermon will later exploit.

**The movement from younger son to father to older son follows the parable's own narrative sequence**, which gives the sermon a natural momentum. But you wisely place the theological and emotional climax not at the end of the younger son's section but at the father's running, which is exactly where it belongs.

**The reframing of "prodigal" in the conclusion is the sermon's most powerful rhetorical move.** "It should be called the Parable of the Prodigal Father — because *prodigal* means recklessly extravagant, and that is exactly what this father is." This is not original to you (Henri Nouwen and Tim Keller have made similar moves), but it is executed here with precision and emotional force. The string of participial phrases that follows — "Running when he should walk. Throwing a party when he should be delivering a lecture. Giving a robe when a rebuke would be justified" — has the cadence of a creed. It is genuinely stirring.

**The direct address in the application section** ("Some of you are the younger son... Some of you are the older son... And some of you are both") is a classic homiletical move, but it works here because you have earned it through careful exegesis. The application feels like it grows organically from the text rather than being bolted on.

**The repeated motif of running** — the airport woman runs, the father runs, God in Christ runs toward the cross — provides strong thematic cohesion without feeling forced.

### Areas for Improvement

**The transition between the opening illustration and the exegesis is slightly abrupt.** "I saw the gospel with skin on" is a strong line, but the shift to "The parable of the Prodigal Son is perhaps the most beloved story Jesus ever told" feels like a gear change. Consider a bridging sentence that connects the emotional register of the illustration to the intellectual work of exegesis. Something as simple as "That airport scene has stayed with me because it keeps showing up in Scripture" would smooth the seam.

**The section headers, while useful for a manuscript, may signal a more essay-like structure than a sermon typically has.** If this is intended for oral delivery, consider whether the headers are serving you or creating artificial compartments. The writing itself flows well enough that the headers may be unnecessary. If they are retained for a printed version, they work fine.

**The sentence "If this story doesn't shock you, you haven't understood it yet" is effective but borders on a cliché in contemporary preaching.** Many preachers use this exact framing when approaching familiar texts. Consider whether you can find a fresher way to defamiliarize the parable — perhaps by noting a specific detail that is routinely overlooked, or by quoting a first-century source that illuminates how scandalous the story would have sounded.

---

## 3. Pastoral Warmth and Accessibility

### Strengths

This is where the sermon truly excels. The pastoral voice is consistent, warm without being saccharine, and honest without being cynical.

**The treatment of mixed motives in repentance** is pastorally extraordinary. "We come back to God because we are broken, because we are desperate, because the pigsty has finally become unbearable. We come with mixed motives and half-formed prayers and hearts that are still tangled up in selfishness." This will land with tremendous force for anyone who has ever felt that their return to God was not pure enough. It is the kind of sentence that could change someone's life on a Sunday morning.

**The application to the older son is handled with remarkable gentleness.** You could easily have turned this into a scolding of religious people, but instead you write with genuine empathy: "You have been faithful. You have showed up. And you are exhausted, and you are bitter." This acknowledges the real cost of faithfulness before diagnosing the distortion. That sequence — empathy before correction — is pastorally wise and rhetorically effective.

**The line "the road home is shorter than you think"** is simple, memorable, and deeply comforting. It is the kind of line people will carry with them.

**The parenthetical examples in the application** — "maybe it's addiction, maybe it's a broken relationship, maybe it's a quiet despair that no one else can see" — are well-chosen because they range from visible to invisible struggles, which widens the net of identification.

### Areas for Improvement

**The sermon could benefit from one more moment of pastoral specificity regarding the older son's application.** You name the younger son's pigsty concretely (addiction, broken relationships, quiet despair), but the older son's condition is described more abstractly ("your faith became a transaction instead of a relationship"). What does older-son syndrome look like on a Tuesday afternoon? Consider adding a concrete example: the longtime church member who quietly seethes when a newcomer with a messy past receives public attention; the volunteer who keeps a mental ledger of unreciprocated service; the parent who did everything "right" and cannot forgive a child who didn't. Specificity is the engine of identification.

**The sermon does not address suffering that is not self-inflicted.** Both sons' predicaments are, to varying degrees, consequences of their own choices. But many people in a general congregation are in a "far country" not because they wandered there but because life dragged them there — through illness, loss, abuse, or systemic injustice. A brief acknowledgment that the far country is not always a destination we choose would broaden the sermon's pastoral reach and prevent it from implicitly blaming those who are suffering.

---

## 4. Overall Structure, Flow, and Coherence

### Strengths

The sermon follows a clear and effective arc:

1. **Hook** (airport illustration) → establishes emotional register and thematic frame
2. **Context** (Luke 15 setting) → grounds the parable in its narrative occasion
3. **Younger Son** → exegesis with cultural depth
4. **Father** → theological climax
5. **Older Son** → complicating turn
6. **Application** → direct address to congregation
7. **Conclusion** → reframing of "prodigal," Christological connection, invitation

This is a textbook homiletical structure, and it works because each section builds on the previous one. The sermon never feels like it is circling or repeating itself. It moves forward with purpose.

**The pacing is excellent.** The younger son section is appropriately detailed but does not overstay its welcome. The father section is given the most emotional and theological weight, which is correct given your interpretive thesis. The older son section is slightly shorter, which works because it functions as a complicating counterpoint rather than a second climax.

**The conclusion is strong and well-proportioned.** It does not introduce new material but rather gathers the sermon's threads into a single compelling image: the Father running. The final lines — "The road home is shorter than you think. The Father is already running. Let us come home." — have the simplicity and force of a benediction.

### Areas for Improvement

**The sermon runs slightly long for oral delivery.** At approximately 2,400 words (by my count), it exceeds the upper bound of the target range. The most natural place to trim is the younger son section, which could lose a few sentences without sacrificing substance. For example, the sentence "He has lost not only his money but his identity, his dignity, his place in the community of God's people" is effective but somewhat redundant after the pigsty detail has already made the point viscerally. Similarly, "He is as far from home as it is possible to be" is a strong line but could be cut if space is needed, since the pigsty image already communicates this.

**The horizontal rule after the opening illustration creates a visual break that may be stronger than necessary.** If the sermon is being read aloud, this break doesn't exist. If it is being published, consider whether a simple paragraph break would maintain better flow.

---

## 5. Effective Use of Illustration and Application

### Strengths

**The opening illustration is nearly perfect.** It is specific, sensory, emotionally resonant, and — crucially — it mirrors the parable without being an exact allegory. The woman is not a precise stand-in for the father in the parable; she is a real person whose real action evokes the same emotional truth. This is how illustration should work: not as a one-to-one code but as a rhyme.

Several details make it work especially well. "She dropped the sign" — this is the moment of abandon, the moment dignity gives way to love, and it directly prefigures the father hitching up his robes. "Thin, cautious, eyes cast down" — this is the younger son in three strokes. "I wept, sitting there in my plastic chair with my lukewarm coffee" — the mundane details (plastic chair, lukewarm coffee) ground the moment in reality and prevent it from becoming sentimental.

**The absence of additional illustrations is actually a strength.** Many sermons overload on stories and anecdotes, which can dilute the power of the biblical text. Here, you let the parable itself do the narrative work after the opening, supplementing it with exegetical insight rather than competing stories. This shows confidence in the text.

**The application section avoids the trap of moralism.** You do not end with "so go and be more like the father." Instead, you end with an invitation to receive the father's love. This is theologically appropriate for a grace-centered reading of the parable.

### Areas for Improvement

**Consider adding one brief, concrete illustration in the older son section.** As noted above, the older son's condition is described somewhat abstractly. A short vignette — even two or three sentences — could make this section land with the same force as the younger son's pigsty. The asymmetry between the two sections (one vivid and concrete, the other more conceptual) is the sermon's most notable structural imbalance.

**The phrase "the gospel with skin on" is evocative but has become somewhat worn in evangelical parlance.** Consider whether a fresher formulation might serve you better. Something like "I saw the fifteenth chapter of Luke playing out in Terminal B" would be more specific and more surprising.

---

## Summary Assessment

This is a sermon that demonstrates mature homiletical craft. Its greatest strengths are:

- A commanding opening illustration that earns the congregation's attention and trust
- Exegesis that is culturally informed, textually precise, and narratively compelling
- A pastoral voice that is honest about the complexity of human motivation without becoming cynical
- A clear interpretive thesis (the parable is about the father, not the sons) that is sustained throughout and brought to a powerful climax in the reframing of "prodigal"
- A conclusion that is emotionally resonant, theologically grounded, and appropriately brief

The primary areas for revision are:

1. **Develop the Christological connection earlier and more fully**, so that the cross is not merely a closing flourish but a structural element of the sermon's theology
2. **Add concrete specificity to the older son's application** to match the vividness of the younger son's
3. **Briefly acknowledge non-self-inflicted suffering** to widen the sermon's pastoral reach
4. **Trim approximately 400 words**, primarily from the younger son section, to hit the target length
5. **Freshen two or three phrases** ("gospel with skin on," "if this story doesn't shock you") that have become commonplace in contemporary preaching

As it stands, this sermon would be effective in almost any congregational setting. With the revisions suggested above, it would be exceptional.

This is an exceptionally strong draft. You have captured the emotional core of the text while maintaining a solid theological backbone. The tone is perfectly calibrated for a general congregation—accessible but not shallow, warm but not sentimental.

Here is a detailed breakdown of the sermon based on your criteria, with specific suggestions to take it from "good" to "unforgettable."

### 1. Theological Accuracy and Scriptural Engagement
**Strengths:**
*   **Cultural Context:** You do an excellent job explaining the cultural weight of the younger son’s request ("I wish you were dead") and the indignity of the father running. This is crucial for modern audiences to grasp the shock value of the parable.
*   **Greek Nuance:** The inclusion of *esplanchnisthē* (compassion) and *asōtōs* (dissolute/reckless) adds depth without bogging down the flow.
*   **Ambiguous Repentance:** Your point about the son’s mixed motives ("Is he truly sorry, or is he just hungry?") is theologically astute and pastorally liberating. It aligns well with a Reformed understanding of grace—that God accepts us before we are fully cleaned up.

**Areas for Improvement:**
*   **The "Prodigal" Definition:** In the conclusion, you state, *"prodigal means recklessly extravagant."* While this is a popular homiletic twist (popularized by Tim Keller), strictly speaking, *prodigal* means "wasteful." The theological point you are making is beautiful and correct—God is extravagant with grace—but be careful not to stretch the dictionary definition too far, or you might annoy the linguists in the room.
    *   *Suggestion:* Phrase it slightly differently: *"We usually use the word 'prodigal' to mean wasteful. But it also means spending without holding back. And in that sense, the Father is the true prodigal..."*
*   **Christological Connection:** The ending pivots to the Cross, which is good. However, you could strengthen the link between the "Older Son" and Jesus. The Older Son *refused* to pay the cost of his brother's return (the fatted calf came from the estate he thought was his). Jesus is the "True Older Brother" who *did* pay the cost and *did* come out to bring us in.

### 2. Rhetorical Effectiveness and Persuasive Structure
**Strengths:**
*   **The Hook:** The airport illustration is fantastic. It is visual, emotional, and parallels the text perfectly (the undignified run). It grabs attention immediately.
*   **The "Hinge":** The transition at "But while he was still far off" is handled masterfully. You slow the tempo down right when it matters.
*   **Rhythm:** You use short, punchy sentences effectively ("He ran." "And he wept."). This creates a great cadence for oral delivery.

**Areas for Improvement:**
*   **The Transition to the Older Son:** The shift from the celebration of the younger son to the anger of the older son is a bit abrupt. The congregation often emotionally "checks out" after the younger son returns because they think the happy ending has occurred.
    *   *Suggestion:* Before introducing the Older Son, add a sentence that disrupts the peace. *"If the story ended here, it would be a beautiful story of forgiveness. But Jesus doesn't stop. Because there is someone else in the house."*

### 3. Pastoral Warmth and Accessibility
**Strengths:**
*   **Empathy for the "Pigsty":** You describe the pigsty not just as sin, but as despair and loss of identity. This allows people suffering from depression or shame to identify with the son, not just those with "wild" pasts.
*   **Direct Address:** The use of "Let me be honest with you" creates a sense of intimacy between preacher and pew.

**Areas for Improvement:**
*   **Application for the "Older Son":** The description of the Older Son is clear, but the application could be more specific to the modern churchgoer. "Working like a slave" is a feeling many church volunteers have.
    *   *Suggestion:* When addressing the Older Sons in the conclusion, add a specific example of what that resentment looks like today. *"Maybe you're the one who unlocks the doors every Sunday, and you're wondering why God seems to bless the person who just showed up last week with a messy life, while you feel dry and empty."*

### 4. Overall Structure, Flow, and Coherence
**Strengths:**
*   The structure is logical and follows the text linearly, which is the best approach for this parable.
*   The callback to the opening illustration isn't explicit, but the theme of "running" ties the beginning and end together beautifully.

**Areas for Improvement:**
*   **The Ending:** The final line ("Let us come home") is good, but a bit abrupt.
    *   *Suggestion:* Return to the image of the Father's face or the airport embrace to close the loop emotionally.

### 5. Effective Use of Illustration and Application
**Strengths:**
*   The airport story is the anchor.
*   The "greeting card" metaphor in the intro effectively challenges the audience's familiarity with the text.

**Areas for Improvement:**
*   **Visualizing the Robe/Ring:** You explain the *meaning* of the robe and ring well. You could add a sensory detail to make it land harder.
    *   *Suggestion:* *"The smell of the pigsty was still on the boy's skin when the father put his own robe over his shoulders. Grace covers us before we are clean."*

---

### Actionable Revisions (Line-by-Line Suggestions)

**1. Tweaking the "Prodigal" Definition (Conclusion):**
*   *Current:* "It should be called the Parable of the Prodigal Father — because prodigal means recklessly extravagant..."
*   *Revision:* "It should be called the Parable of the Prodigal Father. We think of 'prodigal' as meaning 'wasteful,' but it also means to spend until you have nothing left. And that is exactly what this father is. He is reckless with his dignity. He is wasteful with his grace."

**2. Deepening the Older Son Application:**
*   *Current:* "You are keeping score with God, and the math never works out in your favor."
*   *Revision:* "You are keeping score with God. You look at your service record, your tithing, your clean moral sheet, and you wonder why the music isn't playing for you. You are working for a wage, but God wants you to enjoy an inheritance."

**3. Strengthening the Christological Conclusion:**
*   *Current:* "This is the God who, in Jesus Christ, hitched up his robes and ran toward us..."
*   *Revision:* "Jesus told this story to show us the Father, but Jesus is also the true Older Brother we never had. The brother in the story stayed outside and refused to pay the cost. But our True Elder Brother, Jesus, left the Father's house, came into the far country, and paid the debt so we could come in. He was stripped of his robe on the cross so we could be clothed in his righteousness."

### Final Verdict
This is a sermon ready to preach. It is theologically sound and emotionally resonant. With the minor tweaks suggested above regarding the "Older Son" application and the Christological connection at the end, it will be a powerful message. **Grade: A-**
